Salam compiles straight to machine code, with no virtual machine and no garbage collector. On the 39 programs that use the same algorithm in every language, Salam averaged 10.6 ms, C 11.7 ms and Rust 11.3 ms: the same range, with small gaps either way. How to use packages from GitHub with salam init and salam add, write your own package with salam.toml, publish it with a git tag and the registry, pick versions and fix the errors you may meet.                           The package manager           Salam packages live in ordinary git repositories. You add one with a single command, import it by its address, and publish your own by pushing a tag.                                                         On this page                            Using a package               Writing a package               Publishing it               Versions               When something goes wrong                                    This page is about packages written by other people, kept in their own repositories. Everything in the standard library ships with the compiler and needs no salam add. The language side, package, include and pub, is taught in lesson 18.  Using a package A project is a folder with a main.salam and a salam.toml. salam init turns the current folder into one and keeps any file that is already there: $ mkdir app && cd app $ salam init Created project 'app':   main.salam   salam.toml   .gitignore  Next steps:   salam run  $ salam add github.com/demo/slug added github.com/demo/slug v1.1.0 salam add looks up the newest release of the repository, downloads it into ~/.salam/pkg and writes it down in two files. salam.toml says what you asked for, and salam.lock records exactly what you got, the commit and a checksum, so every machine builds the same code. [dependencies] "github.com/demo/slug" = "v1.1.0" A package from a repository is imported with a quoted address. The last part of the address becomes the name you use in the code, so github.com/demo/slug is reached as slug: import "github.com/demo/slug"  func main:     println slug.Make("Hello, World!")     println slug.MakeMax("Packages in Salam are simple", 14) end $ salam run hello-world packages-in-sa If two packages would get the same name, give one of them another: import s "github.com/demo/slug" and then s.Make(...). To reach a package inside a repository's folder, add the folder to the address, as in import "github.com/owner/repo/sub". The commands you will use most: CommandWhat it does salam add github.com/owner/repoAdds the newest release; @v1.2.0 picks a tag salam remove github.com/owner/repoTakes it out of salam.toml and salam.lock; the download stays cached salam updateMoves every package, or only the ones you name, to the newest release with the same major version salam depsDownloads what salam.lock lists and checks every checksum; run it after cloning a project salam search wordsLooks in the standard library and in the registry salam install github.com/owner/toolBuilds a program's main.salam and puts it in ~/.salam/bin salam uninstall toolRemoves it again  Commit salam.toml and salam.lock with your code, and leave the downloaded packages out. A fresh clone then needs only salam deps: $ salam deps github.com/demo/slug v1.1.0 dow

Salam is a fast, statically typed, open source programming language you can write in English or in Persian. It compiles to a native executable for Linux, macOS, Windows and the web, and runs in the same range as C and Rust: 10.6 ms on average over 39 benchmark programs, against 11.7 ms for C and 11.3 ms for Rust.                                        Open source, statically typed, bilingual             The Salam programming language             Salam is a general-purpose systems language with one unusual property: every keyword, type, standard library package and error message has both an English and a Persian name, and the two are the same language. Write a program either way and it compiles to the same fast native executable for Linux, macOS, Windows and the web.                            Start learning               Try it in the browser                                         Salam AI: ask anything about Salam               Salam Agent: desktop app for Windows, macOS and Linux               Package manager: use, write and publish packages                          No install needed to start: write and run code in the online editor. Latest release: 0.6.4                      hero.salamCopyimport encoding.json  func main:     println "In the name of God"     repeat 3:         println "Hello"     end     names := ["Ali", "Reza", "Fatemeh", "Erfan"]     each name in names:         println name     end     println json.Marshal(names) endOutputIn the name of God Hello Hello Hello Ali Reza Fatemeh Erfan ["Ali","Reza","Fatemeh","Erfan"]                                                         Why Salam?             Salam aims at the performance of a systems language with the readability of a teaching one.                                                  ⇄               Two languages, one compiler               Keywords, types, the standard library and every diagnostic exist in English and Persian. This is not a skin over an English language: both spellings go through the same lexer, and salam translate converts a program from one to the other.                                         ⚡               Fast and native               Salam compiles through LLVM or C to a native executable. No virtual machine and no garbage collector; the binary is small and runs straight on the operating system.                                         ✓               Statically checked               Types are checked before the program runs, and the compiler rejects the usual quiet mistakes: an unused variable or function, a declaration used before it is defined, an assignment to something declared constant.                                         ◧               The web is part of the language               Salam has a built-in layout language that emits HTML, CSS and JavaScript, and the compiler also targets the browser and WebAssembly.

Getting started The entry point, running a program, printing output, exit codes, input, comments and the shape of a program In this lesson you write and run your first Salam program, learn the handful of commands you will use every day, and get a feel for what Salam code looks like. Hello, world Every Salam program starts at func main, the first thing that runs. A block opens with a colon (:) and closes with end, and indenting the lines inside it keeps the code readable. Text goes between double quotes, and println takes its value without parentheses. In an English file the function is always main; in a Persian file it is always ریشه, never «اصلی». A function with another name compiles but does not run: you get "entry point is missing". The program needs no package line either. hello.salamCopyfunc main:     println "Hello, world!" endOutputHello, world!  Running a program Save your code in a file with a .salam extension, say hello.salam. salam run hello.salam compiles it and runs it straight away. If you want a standalone executable instead, use salam build hello.salam and a native binary appears next to your source. You can also run every example here in the online editor without installing anything.  CommandWhat it does  salam run hello.salamCompiles the program, runs it, and keeps nothing afterwards salam build hello.salamBuilds a native executable named hello that runs without Salam installed salam exec hello.salamRuns the program in the interpreter, with no C compiler involved salam format hello.salamRewrites the file in the standard layout; --check only reports salam translate fa hello.salamWrites a Persian copy, hello.fa.salam; translate en goes the other way salam new shopCreates a project folder shop with a main.salam and a salam.toml inside; salam run in that folder runs it salam add github.com/owner/repoAdds a package from GitHub to the project; remove, update and deps manage the rest (see packages) salam versionPrints the version of the compiler salam upgradeUpgrades the compiler and its standard library to the newest release; --check only reports whether one is out   Printing output println prints its values and moves to the next line; print stays on the same line. Separate several values with commas and Salam writes them out with one space between them. start-print.salamCopyfunc main:     println "Hello", "world"     print "no "     print "line break"     println ""     println "today it is", 20, "degrees" endOutputHello world no line break today it is 20 degrees Any value can be printed as it is: whole and decimal numbers, true and false, the result of a calculation, even a whole list. Here is a small receipt: start-values.salamCopyfunc main:     println "Receipt"     println "notebook", 3, "x", 45     println "pen", 2, "x", 12     println "total:", 3 * 45 + 2 * 12     println "average per item:", (3 * 45 + 2 * 12) / 5.0     println "paid in full:", true     println "aisles:", [4, 7] endOutputReceipt notebook 3 x 45 pen 2 x 12 total: 159 average per item: 31.8 paid in full: true aisles: [4, 7] Three rules cover nearly every printing mistake:  No parentheses around the values: println "hi", not println("hi"). A comma between every two values: println "a", "b". Leaving it out is an error, not a joined string. println always needs a value. For an empty line write println "".  For error messages use printerrln and printerr. They write to standard error, so they stay out of the program's real output and survive being piped elsewhere: with salam run app.salam > out.txt, the normal lines land in the file and the errors still show on screen. start-stderr.salamCopyfunc main:     println "this line goes to standard output"     printerrln "this line goes to standard error" endOutputthis line goes to standard output this line goes to standard error  Exit codes When a program ends it hands the operating system a number, its exit code. Zero means success and anything else means something went wrong; scripts and build tools read it to decide whether to carry on. Give main the return type int and the value you ret becomes the exit code. A plain func main: that simply reaches its end exits with 0. start-exit.salamCopyfunc main: int:     free_mb := 820     needed_mb := 500     if free_mb < needed_mb:         printerrln "not enough space:", free_mb, "MB free,", needed_mb, "MB needed"         ret 1     end     println "enough space, starting the backup"     ret 0 endOutputenough space, starting the backup With 820 MB free the check passes and the program returns 0. Change free_mb to 300 and it prints the message to standard error and exits with 1, which you can see with echo $? right after running it in a Unix shell.  Reading input input reads one line from the user and

Getting started Declaring with :=, mutable variables, scope, globals, constants and naming rules Variables are names for values. In Salam a variable cannot be changed unless you say so, which heads off a whole class of quiet bugs. Declaring a variable := introduces a new name and gives it a value. The type comes from the value, so you do not have to write it: "Maryam" makes a str and 85 makes an int. From then on the type is fixed, and putting text into a number variable later is an error. Names can be several words, such as book price. variables.salamCopyconst MAX := 100  func main:     name := "Maryam"     mut score := 85     score += 10     println name, "scored", score, "out of", MAX endOutputMaryam scored 95 out of 100 A variable always starts with a value. There is no way to declare a name now and fill it in later, so you never read a variable that holds leftover garbage.  Changeable variables A variable declared with := never changes again. If you want to give it a new value later, write mut before the name and then assign with =. The shorthands +=, -= and ++ are there too. var-mut.salamCopyfunc main:     mut counter := 0     counter++     counter += 5     counter++     println "counter:", counter endOutputcounter: 7 Salam is strict about this: if you declare something mut and never change it, or declare a variable and never use it, the program does not compile. The rule catches dead code and typos.  Where a variable lives A variable exists from the line that declares it to the end of the block it was declared in. A name made inside an if is gone once the if closes, and using it afterwards is an "unknown identifier" error. Keep a variable in the smallest block that needs it. var-scope.salamCopyfunc main:     subtotal := 140     if subtotal >= 100:         points := subtotal / 20         println "points earned:", points     end     label := "order"     if subtotal > 120:         label := "large order"         println "inside the block:", label     end     println "after the block:", label endOutputpoints earned: 7 inside the block: large order after the block: order The second if declares its own label. That is allowed in an inner block, and it hides the outer one until the block ends; the outer label is never touched, as the last line shows. This is called shadowing, and it is easy to misread, so use a new name unless you really mean it. Declaring the same name twice in the same block is an error.  Choosing a value without mut A common reason to reach for mut is a value that depends on a condition: declare it empty, then set it in each branch of an if. Most of the time the ternary operator does the same job in one line and the variable can stay unchangeable: var-choose.salamCopyfunc main:     weight_kg := 3     express := true     shipping := weight_kg > 2 ? 15 : 8     speed := express ? "express" : "standard"     println speed, "shipping costs", shipping endOutputexpress shipping costs 15 With more than two cases, a match expression plays the same role. Fewer mut variables means fewer places where a value can change behind your back.  Choosing the type When you want a type other than the default, convert the value with as. A whole number is int (32 bits) by default and a decimal one is f64. var-typed.salamCopyfunc main:     age := 17 as i64     height := 1.75     name := "Negar"     student := true     println name, age, height, student endOutputNegar 17 1.75 true Older Salam code wrote the type before the value, as in age: int = 17. That form was removed and is now a parse error that tells you to write age := 17, or age := 17 as i64 when the type matters. The name: Type form lives on only for function parameters and struct fields.  Global variables Outside any function you can declare global variables with mut and constants with const; every function in the program can reach them. Here a global counts how many times a function has been called: var-global.salamCopyconst RATE := 10  mut calls := 0  func tax(price: int): int:     calls++     ret price * RATE / 100 end  func main:     println tax(2000)     println tax(500)     println "calls:", calls endOutput200 50 calls: 2 Globals go near the top of the file: after the import lines and the constants, and before any type or function. Use them sparingly: a value passed in as a parameter is easier to follow than one that any function might change.  Constants const declares a value that is fixed when the program is compiled. A constant can be computed from numbers and from other constants, so you can name the parts of a calculation instead of writing a bare 604800. Constants also work inside a function, where they are visible only in that function. var-const.salamCopyconst MINUTE := 60 const HOUR := 60 * MINUTE const DAY := 24 * HOUR const APP := "backup"  func main:     const RETRIES := 3     prin

Getting started Whole and decimal numbers, overflow, booleans, characters, mixing types and conversion Salam is statically typed: the type of every value is known before the program runs, and the compiler will not let incompatible types mix. The basic types types-basic.salamCopyfunc main:     number := 42     fraction := 3.14     text := "hello"     flag := false     letter := u'S'     println number, fraction, text, flag, letter endOutput42 3.14 hello false S  TypePersianWhat it holds  intصحیحA 32-bit whole number i8, i16, i64, i128صحیح۸, صحیح۱۶, صحیح۶۴, صحیح۱۲۸A whole number of a fixed width uint, u8 to u128طبیعی, طبیعی۸ to طبیعی۱۲۸An unsigned whole number f64, f32اعشار۶۴, اعشار۳۲A decimal number boolمنطقیtrue or false strرشتهText, in Unicode charنویسهOne character, such as u'S' usize, sizeاندازه مثبت, اندازهA number the width of a memory address  Text has a lesson of its own, strings and text. This one is about numbers, booleans and characters, and about moving values from one type to another.  Number sizes and bases Numbers can be written in base sixteen (0xFF), base two (0b1010) and base eight (0o17), and you can group the digits with _ to make them readable. types-ints.salamCopyfunc main:     small := 120 as i8     big := 9_000_000_000 as i64     unsigned := 4000000000 as uint     println small, big, unsigned     println 0xFF, 0b1010, 0o17 endOutput120 9000000000 4000000000 255 10 15 A whole number literal is an int, unless it is too big for one: 9000000000 becomes an i64 on its own. sizeof gives the size of a type in bytes: types-sizeof.salamCopystruct Point:     x: int     y: int end  func main:     println "i8:", sizeof(i8)     println "int:", sizeof(int)     println "i64:", sizeof(i64)     println "f64:", sizeof(f64)     println "Point:", sizeof(Point) endOutputi8: 1 int: 4 i64: 8 f64: 8 Point: 8 An int runs from about minus two billion to plus two billion, an i64 to about nine quintillion, an i128 to about 1.7 times ten to the 38th. A u8 holds 0 to 255, which is exactly one byte.  When a number does not fit If a calculation goes past the end of its type, the number wraps around to the other end and the program carries on without a word. When the compiler can see the values, as in views += 1000 right after a large constant, it stops the build instead, so this example passes them through a function. A page counter stored in an int turns negative after about two billion views; the same counter in an i64 keeps going. Unsigned types wrap at zero instead, so taking 5 from 3 gives a huge positive number. types-overflow.salamCopyfunc add_views(views: int, more: int): int:     ret views + more end  func main:     println "views as int:", add_views(2147483000, 1000)     mut total := 2147483000 as i64     total += 1000     println "views as i64:", total     stock := 3 as uint     sold := 5 as uint     println "stock left:", stock - sold endOutputviews as int: -2147483296 views as i64: 2147484000 stock left: 4294967294 So pick the type from the largest value you expect, not the first value you see. Use i64 for counters, sizes of files, money in the smallest unit and time in milliseconds, and keep unsigned types for things that really are never negative, such as bytes.  Decimal numbers A decimal literal such as 2.5 is an f64, and it can be written with an exponent: 1.5e3 is 1500. Printing uses the shortest form that reads back as the same number, so 10.0 prints as 10. Decimal numbers are stored in binary, and most decimal fractions have no exact binary form: types-float.salamCopyfunc main:     println 0.1 + 0.2     println 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3     println 10.0, 2.50, 1.5e3, 2.5e-2     price := 19.99     println price * 3     println 0.1 as f32 endOutput0.30000000000000004 false 10 2.5 1500 0.025 59.97 0.10000000149011612 That tiny error is why you should not compare decimal results with ==; check that the difference is small enough instead. f32 (also called float) saves memory but keeps only about seven digits, as the last line shows. For money, where every cent must add up, use the decimal package, or count in whole cents with an i64.  Booleans and characters A bool is true or false, and every condition in Salam has to be one. There is no "truthy" number: if count: is an error (if condition must be bool, got 'i32'); write if count != 0:. A char holds one character. 'A' works for a single byte, such as an English letter or digit; anything else needs the u prefix, as in u'م', and the compiler says so if you forget. Converting a character to int gives its Unicode code, and converting back goes the other way: types-char.salamCopyfunc main:     letter := 'A'     println letter, letter as int     next := (letter as int + 1) as char     println next     mim := u'م'     println mim, mim as int     ready := true     println ready, not ready

Getting started Arithmetic, division and remainder, powers, comparison, logic, the ternary, compound assignment, bitwise flags and precedence Operators work on values: they do arithmetic, compare things and join conditions together. Most of them look the way you expect; this lesson spends its time on the few places where they do not. Arithmetic + - * / % behave as they do in mathematics, and ** raises to a power. Multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction, and parentheses change the order. ops-arith.salamCopyfunc main:     a := 17     b := 5     println a + b, a - b, a * b, a / b, a % b     println 2 ** 10     println (2 + 3) * 4, 2 + 3 * 4 endOutput22 12 85 3 2 1024 20 14 + also joins strings, and with a string on its left it turns a number into text: "total: " + 5 is "total: 5". The strings lesson has more.  Division and remainder Dividing two whole numbers gives a whole number: 17 / 5 is 3, and % gives what is left over, 2. That pair is exactly what you need to split minutes into hours, to count how many tables a group needs, or to tell even numbers from odd ones. ops-divide.salamCopyfunc main:     minutes := 135     println minutes / 60, "h", minutes % 60, "min"     guests := 17     per_table := 4     tables := (guests + per_table - 1) / per_table     println "tables needed:", tables     println "empty seats:", tables * per_table - guests     n := 7     println n, "is", n % 2 == 0 ? "even" : "odd"     println -7 / 2, -7 % 2 endOutput2 h 15 min tables needed: 5 empty seats: 3 7 is odd -3 -1 Two details are worth remembering:  Division cuts toward zero, so -7 / 2 is -3, and the remainder takes the sign of the left side, so -7 % 2 is -1. A test such as n % 2 == 1 therefore misses negative odd numbers; n % 2 != 0 catches them all. % works only on whole numbers; on decimals it is a compile error. Dividing by a literal 0 is a compile error too, but a zero that turns up at run time is not checked for you and can crash the program, so test the divisor first.   Powers ** raises a number to a power, and its result is always an f64, even for two whole numbers. That lets it handle 2 ** 0.5 and 2 ** -1, but it means you convert with as int when you need a whole number back. ops-power.salamCopyfunc main:     bacteria := 100 * 2 ** 10     println "after ten doublings:", bacteria     println 2 ** 0.5, 2 ** -1     println 2 ** 3 ** 2, -2 ** 2, (-2) ** 2     cells := (2 ** 10) as int     println cells / 3 endOutputafter ten doublings: 102400 1.4142135623730951 0.5 512 -4 4 341 ** groups from the right, so 2 ** 3 ** 2 is 2 ** 9, and it binds tighter than a leading minus, so -2 ** 2 is -4, as in mathematics. For the same reason **= works on an f64 variable but not on an int one, because the result would not fit back in.  Comparison A comparison produces a bool. The operators are ==, !=, <, >, <= and >=, and each has a word form as well: eq, neq, lt, gt, lte and gte. Join conditions with and and or, and invert one with not. ops-compare.salamCopyfunc main:     age := 20     println age > 18, age < 18, age == 20, age != 20     println age eq 20, age neq 30     println age gt 18, age lte 20     println age >= 18 and age <= 60     println age < 10 or age > 15     println not (age > 18)     println "apple" < "banana", "apple" == "apple" endOutputtrue false true false true true true true true true false true true Strings compare with the same operators. == checks that the text is the same, and < orders by character code, so every capital letter comes before every small one: "Zebra" < "apple" is true. Comparisons do not chain. 1 < x < 10 compares the bool from 1 < x with 10, and the compiler rejects it (cannot compare 'bool' and 'i32'); write x > 1 and x < 10.  Combining conditions and and or stop as soon as the answer is known. If the left side of and is false, the right side never runs; if the left side of or is true, the same. That makes it safe to guard a risky check with a simple one, as the first if does here: the division only happens when count is not zero. ops-logic.salamCopyfunc check(name: str): bool:     println "  checked", name     ret true end  func main:     count := 0     total := 50     if count > 0 and total / count > 10:         println "large average"     else:         println "no data yet"     end     println false and check("a")     println true or check("b")     println true and check("c")     logged_in := true     banned := false     println "may post:", logged_in and not banned endOutputno data yet false true   checked c true may post: true Only the third call to check ran. not binds tighter than any comparison, so not count == 3 means (not count) == 3 and is an error; write not (count == 3), or simply count != 3. Salam has no &&

Getting started String literals and escapes, joining text, bytes and characters, the str package, comparing text and reading numbers from text Strings hold text, and Salam is Unicode from the ground up, so text in any script behaves like any other text. The one thing to keep in mind is that a string is stored as UTF-8 bytes, and some operations count bytes while others count characters. Ways to write a string  "..." is an ordinary string. Escapes work inside it: \n (a new line), \t (a tab), \", \\, and \uHHHH for any Unicode character by its code. `...` (backticks) is a raw string: everything inside stays exactly as written, backslashes and quotes included, and it may span several lines. It is the easy way to write file paths, regular expressions and JSON. """...""" is a multi-line string in which escapes still work.  str-literals.salamCopyfunc main:     println "first line\nsecond line"     println "column\tcolumn"     println "She said: \"hello\""     println "price in \u20ac, greeting \u0633\u0644\u0627\u0645"     println `the path C:\temp and "quotes", with nothing escaped`     poem := """The children of Adam are limbs of one body, having been created of one essence."""     println poem endOutputfirst line second line column column She said: "hello" price in €, greeting سلام the path C:\temp and "quotes", with nothing escaped The children of Adam are limbs of one body, having been created of one essence. An ordinary "..." string has to end on the line where it starts; for text over several lines use """ or backticks. Persian files have one more form, «...», which an English file does not accept.  Joining strings Join strings with +. When one side is a number or a bool, it is turned into text for you, so no separate conversion is needed. += adds to the end of a mut string. Salam has no "{name}" style interpolation; + is how text is put together. str-concat.salamCopyfunc main:     name := "Arash"     age := 25     message := "Hello " + name + ", you are " + age + " years old."     println message     println "Total: " + 2 + 3     println "Total: " + (2 + 3)     println "price " + 2.5 + ", paid " + true     mut log := "started"     log += ", connected"     log += ", " + 3 + " files sent"     println log endOutputHello Arash, you are 25 years old. Total: 23 Total: 5 price 2.5, paid true started, connected, 3 files sent Look at the second line of output. + works from left to right, so "Total: " + 2 is already text by the time 3 arrives, and the result is Total: 23. Put the arithmetic in parentheses when you want the sum.  Bytes and characters A string is stored as UTF-8. An English letter takes one byte, but é takes two, and so does a Persian letter. That is why there are two kinds of length and two kinds of position:  len(), substr and find count bytes. They are fast, and exact for ASCII text. char_count(), char_substr, char_at and char_find count characters. Use them whenever the text might not be plain English.  str-chars.salamCopyfunc preview(title: str, limit: int): str:     if title.CharCount() <= limit:         ret title     end     ret title.CharSubstr(0, limit) + "..." end  func main:     word := "café"     println word.Len(), word.CharCount()     greeting := "سلام"     println greeting.Len(), greeting.CharCount()     println greeting.CharAt(0), greeting.CharFind("م"), greeting.Find("م")     println word[0], word[0] as int     println preview("Short title", 24)     println preview("A long headline about the weather in Tabriz", 24) endOutput5 4 8 4 س 3 6 c 99 Short title A long headline about th... "سلام" is 8 bytes but 4 characters, and the letter م is character 3 but byte 6. The preview function cuts a title to a number of characters, which is what a reader expects. Cutting it with substr could split a letter in half and print a broken symbol. Indexing with word[0] also reads a single byte, as a char, so it is only the right tool for ASCII. To visit every character, walk the string with each. each ch in s gives each character as a short str, so ch can be compared with "ی" or printed directly, and each i, ch in s adds the character number. It reads the string once from start to end, which is much faster on long text than calling char_at(i) in a repeat loop. When you really want the raw bytes, write each b in s.bytes(): b is a char, and the number beside it is the byte position. str-each.salamCopyfunc main:     word := "سلام"     each ch in word:         print ch + " "     end     println ""     each i, ch in "café":         println i, ch     end     mut vowels := 0     each ch in "Tabriz تبریز":         if ch == "a&

Control flow if, else if and else, comparison words, and and or, early returns, comparing floats and the rules a condition follows Conditions are how a program decides, from its data, which way to go. Salam keeps them strict: a condition is always a real bool, and the compiler points out branches that could never run. if, else if, else The body of an if runs only when its condition holds. Test further conditions with else if, and cover everything that is left with else. The conditions are tried from the top, and only the first one that holds runs, so put the narrowest test first. conditions.salamCopyfunc grade(score: int): str:     if score >= 90:         ret "excellent"     else if score >= 70:         ret "good"     else:         ret "needs more work"     end end  func main:     println grade(95)     println grade(72)     println grade(40) endOutputexcellent good needs more work A score of 95 is also at least 70, but the program prints only excellent: once a branch has run, the rest are skipped.  Short conditions, and joining them A short condition fits on one line, with end at the end of the line. Join several conditions with and and or. cond-inline.salamCopyfunc main:     number := 7     if number % 2 == 0: println "even" else: println "odd" end     if number > 0 and number < 10:         println "a positive single digit number"     end endOutputodd a positive single digit number  Comparison words Every comparison operator also has a word: eq for ==, neq for !=, lt and gt for < and >, and lte and gte for <= and >=. Use whichever reads better; they mean exactly the same. The example also shows the short form of else if: else followed directly by a condition. cond-words.salamCopyfunc ticket(age: int): int:     if age lt 4:         ret 0     else age lte 12:         ret 40     else age gte 65:         ret 50     else:         ret 90     end end  func main:     println ticket(2), ticket(9), ticket(30), ticket(70)     seats := 12     sold := 12     if sold eq seats: println "sold out" end     if sold neq seats: println "seats left" end endOutput0 40 90 50 sold out  and, or and not and and or stop as soon as the answer is known. If the left side of and is false, the right side is never evaluated, and the same goes for or when the left side is true. That makes the left side a guard for the right: test that a count is not zero before dividing by it, or that an index is in range before reading the array. cond-short.salamCopyfunc average(total: int, count: int): int:     if count != 0 and total / count > 0:         ret total / count     end     ret 0 end  func main:     println average(270, 3), average(0, 0)     scores := [12, 18, 7]     i := 5     if i < len(scores) and scores[i] > 10:         println "a high score"     else:         println "no score at", i     end     logged_in := true     banned := false     if logged_in and not banned:         println "welcome back"     end     stock := 3     if not (stock > 5):         println "time to reorder"     end endOutput90 0 no score at 5 welcome back time to reorder not binds tighter than a comparison. not stock > 5 would mean (not stock) > 5, which is an error because stock is not a bool. Write not (stock > 5), or simply stock <= 5. There is no &&, || or ! in Salam; the compiler names the word to write instead.  Choosing a value A variable declared inside a branch disappears at that branch's end. When each branch decides a value, declare the variable with mut before the if and assign it in the branches. For a choice between just two values, the ternary operator condition ? a : b is shorter, and both sides must have the same type. cond-scope.salamCopyfunc main:     weight := 3     express := true     mut cost := 0     if weight <= 1:         cost = 30     else weight <= 5:         cost = 55     else:         cost = 90     end     if express:         cost += 25     end     println "shipping:", cost     label := weight > 2 ? "heavy" : "light"     println label endOutputshipping: 80 heavy  Returning early Deeply nested ifs are hard to read. Inside a function, check for each problem in turn and ret as soon as one is found. What is left at the bottom is the normal case, with no nesting at all. cond-guard.salamCopyfunc check_order(qty: int, stock: int, paid: bool): str:     if qty <= 0:         ret "the quantity must be at least 1"     end     if qty > stock:         ret "only " + stock + " left in stock"     end     if not paid:         ret "waiting for payment"     end     ret "order accepted" end  func main:     println check_order(0, 10, true)     println check_order(12, 10, true)     println check_order(2, 10, false)     println check_order(2, 10, true) endOutputthe quantity must be at least 1 only 10

Control flow repeat with a count, a range and a step, the until loop and its traps, loops that end with break, each over arrays, vectors, maps and strings, nested loops, break N and continue A loop does something several times: a fixed number of times, over a range, while a condition holds, or once for every item in a list. Salam has three loop words, repeat, until and each, and each one fits a different job. repeat repeat 3: runs the body three times. Add in i to get a counter called i that starts at zero, so repeat 4 in i gives 0, 1, 2 and 3. The count may be any whole number expression, such as a variable or v.len(), and a count of zero runs the body no times at all. repeat 1 to 10 walks a range with both ends included, by 3 sets the step, and if the start is greater than the end the loop counts down. loop-count.salamCopyfunc main:     repeat 3:         println "hello"     end     repeat 4 in i:         print i, ""     end     println ""     repeat 10 to 0 by 5 in i:         println "counting down", i     end endOutputhello hello hello 0 1 2 3  counting down 10 counting down 5 counting down 0 The counter belongs to the loop: assigning to i inside the body is a compile error, so the loop always runs the number of times its header says.  Ranges and steps The step after by is always written as a positive number, even when the loop counts down: the bounds alone decide the direction, so repeat 10 to 1 by 3 gives 10, 7, 4 and 1. The step may be a variable. A step of 0, or a negative number written in the code such as by -2, is a compile error (E063). A step held in a variable is only known at run time and is not checked: if it turns out negative, the loop quietly runs zero times. loops.salamCopyfunc main:     repeat 1 to 10 by 3 in i:         println "round", i     end     repeat 10 to 1 by 3 in i:         print i, ""     end     println ""     step := 15     repeat 0 to 60 by step in minute:         print minute, ""     end     println "" endOutputround 1 round 4 round 7 round 10 10 7 4 1  0 15 30 45 60 The direction is decided when the loop starts, from the values the bounds have at that moment. That leads to a trap when a bound is a variable. repeat from to 1 counts down from 3 as expected, but when from is 0 the start is below the end, so the loop counts up and prints 0 1 instead of nothing: loop-range-trap.salamCopyfunc countdown(from: int):     repeat from to 1 in i:         print i, ""     end     println "go" end  func safe_countdown(from: int):     if from >= 1:         repeat from to 1 in i:             print i, ""         end     end     println "go" end  func main:     countdown(3)     countdown(0)     safe_countdown(0) endOutput3 2 1 go 0 1 go go If the start can fall below the end, guard the loop with an if, as safe_countdown does.  The until loop until condition: repeats for as long as the condition holds, and stops once it becomes false. It is the loop other languages call while; Salam has no while keyword. So write the condition the way you want the loop to carry on: until n != 0 keeps going while n is not zero. Reach for until when you do not know in advance how many turns are needed. loop-until.salamCopyfunc digit_sum(number: int): int:     mut n := number     mut sum := 0     until n != 0:         sum += n % 10         n /= 10     end     ret sum end  func main:     println digit_sum(2026), digit_sum(0)     mut savings := 1000.0     mut years := 0     until savings < 2000.0:         savings *= 1.08         years++     end     println "doubled after", years, "years" endOutput10 0 doubled after 10 years The condition is checked before every turn, including the first. That is why digit_sum(0) gives 0: the body never runs. It is also why an inverted condition is dangerous. Write until n == 0 by mistake and the loop runs zero times, with no error at all. When a loop seems to do nothing, check which way round its condition is before anything else.  Loops that end with break Sometimes the place to decide whether to stop is the middle or the end of the body, not the top. Write until true: and leave with break where the decision falls. This is also how to write a loop that runs at least once, which other languages call do-while. The example pages through 23 search results, 10 to a page, and stops after the page that holds the last result. loop-forever.salamCopyfunc main:     total_items := 23     page_size := 10     mut page := 1     until true:         first := (page - 1) * page_size + 1         mut last := page * page_size         if last > total_items:             last = total_items         end         println "page", page, "shows items", first, "to", last         if last == total_items:             break         end         page++     end endOutputpage 1 shows items 1 to 10 page 2 shows items 11 to 20 page 3 s

Control flow Choosing between cases with match and switch: values, strings, enums, data and guards, struct patterns, fallthrough and switch inside loops When a value has several possible cases, reach for match or switch instead of a chain of ifs. match compares a value against patterns and checks that you have covered every case; switch is a statement in the style of C, with ranges, comparisons and fallthrough. match match is an expression: it compares a value against the cases and gives back the result of the branch that matched. Each branch is a pattern, a colon, the result and end. Several cases can share one branch by separating them with commas, and else catches everything left over. match-values.salamCopyfunc grade(score: int): str:     ret match score / 10:         10, 9: "excellent" end         8: "very good" end         7: "good" end         else: "needs more work" end     end end  func main:     println grade(95), grade(80), grade(45) endOutputexcellent very good needs more work When match gives back a value, every branch has to produce one, all of the same type.  match as a statement match can also stand on its own as a statement. A branch may then hold several lines, closed by its end. The subject does not have to be a number: strings work too, and are compared by their contents. The example plays back a list of commands, the way a small command-line tool or chat bot would. match-command.salamCopyfunc main:     commands := ["start", "status", "stop", "jump", "quit"]     mut running := false     each cmd in commands:         match cmd:             "start", "run":                 running = true                 println "starting"             end             "stop":                 running = false                 println "stopping"             end             "status":                 println running ? "running" : "stopped"             end             "quit": println "bye" end             else: println "unknown command:", cmd end         end     end endOutputstarting running stopping unknown command: jump bye Unlike a switch, a match branch never falls into the next one; exactly one branch runs. The patterns for a number or a string are exact values. Ranges such as 1 to 9 and comparisons such as < 0 are not match patterns: for those use switch, shown below.  Matching an enum Over an enum, the patterns are the names of its cases. The bare name Spring is enough, and the full Season.Spring works too. match checks that no case has been left out: match.salamCopyenum Season:     Spring, Summer, Autumn, Winter end  func weather(s: Season): str:     ret match s:         Spring, Autumn: "mild" end         Summer: "hot" end         Winter: "cold" end     end end  func main:     println "spring weather:", weather(Season.Spring)     println "winter weather:", weather(Season.Winter) endOutputspring weather: mild winter weather: cold Delete the Winter branch and the program no longer compiles, and the error names the missing case. So when you add a case to an enum later, the compiler shows you every match that has to learn about it. An else branch turns that check off, so leave it out when you can list every case.  Pulling out data, and guards When enum cases carry data, a pattern can take that data apart: Cash(a) binds the amount to a, and _ skips a value you do not need. Card c binds the whole case, so its fields are reached as c.amount. A branch can also add a guard: if and a condition after the pattern. The guard can use the names the pattern bound, and if it is false, matching goes on to the next branch. match-data.salamCopyenum Payment:     Cash(amount: int)     Card(amount: int, last4: str)     Voucher(code: str)     Free end  func receipt(p: Payment): str:     ret match p:         Cash(a) if a >= 1000: "cash " + a + ", count it twice" end         Cash(a): "cash " + a end         Card(a, last4): "card ending " + last4 + ", " + a end         Voucher(_): "paid with a voucher" end         Free: "nothing to pay" end     end end  func main:     println receipt(Payment.Cash(1500))     println receipt(Payment.Cash(20))     println receipt(Payment.Card(80, "4421"))     println receipt(Payment.Voucher("SPRING"))     println receipt(Payment.Free)     p := Payment.Card(35, "0042")     label := match p:         Card c: "card payment of " + c.amount end         else: "another kind of payment" end     end     println label endOutputcash 1500, count it twice cash 20 card ending 4421, 80 paid with a voucher nothing to pay card payment of 35 A guarded branch does not count as covering its case, which is why Cash(a) appears a second time without a guard.

Functions Declaring and calling functions, early return, default values, several results with tuples, recursion, overloads, reference parameters and main's exit code Functions are named pieces of a program that take input and give back a result. They are how you break a program into small parts that each do one job, can be read on their own and can be used again. Declaring and calling A function is declared as func name(parameters): result type: and its body ends with end. Every parameter is written as name: type, and ret hands the result back to the caller. A function that gives nothing back simply leaves out the result type. fn-basics.salamCopyfunc line total(price: int, quantity: int): int:     ret price * quantity end  func show line(name: str, amount: int):     println name + ":", amount end  func main:     tea := line total(45, 2)     cake := line total(120, 1)     show line("tea", tea)     show line("cake", cake)     show line("total", tea + cake) endOutputtea: 90 cake: 120 total: 210 The order of functions in a file does not matter: main may call a function that is declared further down. A call always needs its parentheses, even when there are no arguments.  Returning early ret leaves the function at once, wherever it stands. That lets you deal with the bad cases first, each with its own ret, and keep the normal path at the bottom without deep nesting. In a function with no result type, a bare ret just leaves. fn-early-return.salamCopyfunc check username(name: str): str:     if len(name) < 3:         ret "too short"     end     if len(name) > 12:         ret "too long"     end     if name == "admin":         ret "reserved"     end     ret "ok" end  func greet(name: str):     if check username(name) != "ok":         println "cannot greet", name         ret     end     println "welcome,", name end  func main:     println check username("al")     println check username("administrator")     println check username("admin")     greet("mina")     greet("x") endOutputtoo short too long reserved welcome, mina cannot greet x A function with a result type must reach a ret on every path. If it can fall off its end, the compiler stops with E071 and asks for a final ret.  Default values A parameter with a default value is optional at the call. Put such parameters after the ones without a default. fn-params.salamCopyfunc welcome(name: str, greeting: str = "Hello"):     println greeting + ",", name end  func area(width: int, height: int = 1): int:     ret width * height end  func main:     welcome("Mina")     welcome("Mina", "Good day")     println area(4), area(4, 5) endOutputHello, Mina Good day, Mina 4 20 A default value must be a constant or built from globals; it cannot refer to another parameter, so func box(w: int, h: int = w) fails with "unknown identifier". Write an overload instead (see below). Salam has no named arguments: the arguments always go in the order of the parameters.  Inferring the result type Leave the result type out and Salam works it out from the ret statements. This is handy for short helpers; for a function others will call, writing the type out makes it easier to read. fn-infer.salamCopyfunc average(a: f64, b: f64):     ret (a + b) / 2.0 end  func larger(a: int, b: int):     if a > b:         ret a     end     ret b end  func main:     println average(3.0, 4.0), larger(8, 3) endOutput3.5 8  Returning several values A function can return more than one value as a tuple. Write the result type as (int, int), build the tuple with ret a, b, and take it apart at the call with hours, minutes := split minutes(135). Use _ for a part you do not need, and put mut in front of a name you will change later. You must give one name for every part, or the compiler stops with E158. fn-tuples.salamCopyfunc split minutes(total: int): (int, int):     ret total / 60, total % 60 end  func main:     hours, minutes := split minutes(135)     println hours, "h", minutes, "min"     whole, _ := split minutes(200)     println whole     trip := split minutes(45)     println trip.0, trip.1     println trip endOutput2 h 15 min 3 0 45 (0, 45) You can also keep the tuple whole and read its parts as trip.0 and trip.1. A tuple works anywhere a type does: as a parameter, a struct field, or in Vector<(int, str)>. It prints as (0, 45) and two tuples compare with ==. When the parts deserve names that callers will read often, a small struct is still the clearer choice. Structs have a lesson of their own; here all you need is that the fields are marked pub so that code outside the struct can read them. fn-results.salamCopystruct Clock:     pub hours: int     pub minutes: int end  func split minutes(total: int): Clock:     ret Clock { hours = total / 60, minutes = total % 60 } end

Functions Functions as values: anonymous functions, the function type, sorting with a comparator, functions that return functions and what a lambda captures In Salam functions are values too: you can build one without a name, keep it in a variable, hand it to another function or get one back as a result. That is how you tell a sort how to order things or a loop what to do with each item. An anonymous function (parameters): body end builds a function with no name, often called a lambda. The body is an ordinary block, so a single ret fits on one line and a longer body spreads over several lines and closes with end. You call it like any other function. lambda.salamCopyfunc apply(f: func (int) int, value: int): int:     ret f(value) end  func main:     double := (n: int): ret n * 2 end     println double(5)     println apply((n: int): ret n * n end, 7)     grade := (score: int):         passed := score >= 10         ret passed ? "pass" : "fail"     end     println grade(14), grade(8) endOutput10 49 pass fail Never write a result type on a lambda: (x: int): int: ret x end does not parse. Salam works the type out from the ret statements. A lambda that returns nothing simply has no ret with a value.  The function type The type of a function is written func (parameter types) result type. func (int) bool takes one int and gives back a bool; func (int) takes an int and gives back nothing. Use such a type for a parameter, and the function accepts any compatible function. When a type is long or used often, give it a name with type. lambda-type.salamCopytype Rule = func (int) bool  func count where(values: int[], keep: Rule): int:     mut n := 0     each v in values:         if keep(v):             n++         end     end     ret n end  func main:     temps := [12, 18, 25, 31, 9, 27]     hot := (t: int): ret t >= 25 end     println "hot days:", count where(temps, hot)     println "cold days:", count where(temps, (t: int): ret t < 10 end) endOutputhot days: 3 cold days: 1 The rule can be a lambda kept in a variable, like hot, or written straight into the call. Either way count where does not know or care what the rule checks.  Passing a named function The bare name of a named function is its address, typed i64, not a value of a function type, so apply all(prices, with tax) is rejected with E012, "cannot pass 'i64' to 'func(i32) i32'". Wrap the function in a lambda that calls it: lambda-named.salamCopyfunc with tax(price: int): int:     ret price + price * 9 / 100 end  func apply all(prices: int[], change: func (int) int):     each i, p in prices:         println i, p, "->", change(p)     end end  func main:     apply all([100, 250], (p: int): ret with tax(p) end) endOutput0 100 -> 109 1 250 -> 272 The i64 form exists for C-style callback slots, such as the routes of a web server. Inside Salam code, the lambda wrapper is the way to go.  Sorting with a comparator A comparator is a function that takes two items and answers "should the first come before the second?". sort.SortBy sorts a Vector with it, so you decide the order: by name, by score, highest first, or anything else. sort.StableSortBy also keeps items that compare equal in the order they already had. lambda-sort.salamCopyimport sort  struct Player:     pub name: str     pub score: int end  func main:     mut team := Vector {} as Vector<Player>     defer team.Free()     team.Push(Player { name = "Sara", score = 72 })     team.Push(Player { name = "Omid", score = 91 })     team.Push(Player { name = "Lena", score = 85 })     team.Push(Player { name = "Arash", score = 85 })     sort.SortBy(team, (a: Player, b: Player): ret a.name < b.name end)     each p in team:         print p.name, ""     end     println ""     sort.StableSortBy(team, (a: Player, b: Player): ret a.score > b.score end)     each p in team:         println p.name, p.score     end endOutputArash Lena Omid Sara  Omid 91 Arash 85 Lena 85 Sara 72 Lena and Arash both have 85. Because the second sort is stable, they stay in the alphabetical order the first sort left them in. The collections lesson covers Vector, and the sort package has the full list of sorting functions.  Returning a function A function may build a lambda and return it. The lambda keeps a copy of the values it uses, so every call to the outer function produces a different function. This is a neat way to make a family of related functions from one recipe. lambda-make.salamCopyfunc discount(percent: int): func (int) int:     ret (price: int): ret price - price * percent / 100 end end  func main:     member := discount(10)     sale := discount(25)     println member(200), sale(200)     println member(80), sale(80) endOutput180 150 72 60  What a lambda captures A lambda copies the outside variables it uses at the moment it is created. Changing the variable afterwards does not reach the lambda, and a lambda

Functions Running cleanup at the end of a block with defer, in what order and when, plus the pure, inline, noinline, noret and deprecated modifiers defer keeps cleanup next to the code that needs it, so it cannot be forgotten on an early return. The function modifiers tell the compiler how a function behaves, and some of them it checks for you. defer A statement written after defer does not run where it stands. It runs when the surrounding block ends. With several defers, the last one runs first, the way you undo steps in reverse order. The commonest use is releasing something right beside the line that acquired it. defer.salamCopyfunc work():     println "starting work"     defer println "first cleanup"     defer println "second cleanup"     println "doing the work" end  func main:     work()     println "after the work" endOutputstarting work doing the work second cleanup first cleanup after the work  Every way out A deferred statement runs whichever way the block is left: at its end, at a ret in the middle, or at a break out of a loop. That is the whole point. A function with several ret statements needs one defer, not a copy of the cleanup before each ret. defer-return.salamCopyfunc find(items: int[], wanted: int): int:     defer println "search for", wanted, "finished"     each i, item in items:         if item == wanted:             ret i         end     end     ret -1 end  func main:     codes := [404, 200, 500]     println "position:", find(codes, 200)     println "position:", find(codes, 301) endOutputsearch for 200 finished position: 1 search for 301 finished position: -1 The deferred line runs after the result has been worked out but before the caller gets it, so it is printed before position:. The same holds in main: a ret 1 still runs main's defers, which is why os.Exit is not allowed there.  defer belongs to its block A defer runs at the end of the block it is written in, not at the end of the function. Inside a loop that means at the end of every round, and inside an if at the end of that branch. defer-blocks.salamCopyfunc main:     repeat 3 in day:         defer println "  close day", day         println "open day", day     end     late := 2     if late > 0:         defer println "  report sent"         println "late orders:", late     end     println "done" endOutputopen day 0   close day 0 open day 1   close day 1 open day 2   close day 2 late orders: 2   report sent done So something acquired inside a loop body and deferred there is released before the next round starts, which is usually exactly what you want.  When the values are read A deferred statement reads its variables when it runs, not when the defer line is reached. If a variable changes in between, the defer sees the new value. To keep the value from the moment of the defer, copy it into another variable first. defer-late.salamCopyfunc main:     mut stage := "start"     defer println "deferred sees:", stage     saved := stage     defer println "saved copy:", saved     stage = "finish"     println "stage now:", stage endOutputstage now: finish saved copy: start deferred sees: finish  Freeing collections A Vector or a HashMap takes memory that you give back with free(). Write defer x.free() on the line right after creating it, and every path out of the function frees it, including the early ret 0 here. defer-free.salamCopyfunc average reading(raw: int[]): int:     mut valid := Vector {} as Vector<int>     defer valid.Free()     each r in raw:         if r >= 0:             valid.Push(r)         end     end     if valid.Len() == 0:         ret 0     end     mut sum := 0     each v in valid:         sum += v     end     ret sum / valid.Len() end  func main:     println average reading([21, -1, 23, 25, -1])     println average reading([-1, -1]) endOutput23 0 The collections lesson covers Vector and HashMap, and the memory lesson explains what needs freeing and why.  Closing files The same pattern closes files. Check that the open worked, then defer the close straight away; the code that follows may return early without leaving the file open. Here main also defers deleting the temporary file, so it is gone when the program ends. defer-file.salamCopyimport os  func save report(path: str, total: int): bool:     f := os.Open(path, "w")     if f == null:         ret false     end     defer f.Close()     f.Write("total: " + total + "\n")     f.Write("status: paid\n")     ret true end  func main:     path := os.TempDir() + "/salam-report.txt"     if not save report(path, 245):         printerrln "cannot write", path         ret 1     end     defer os.Remove(path)     print os.ReadFile(path) endOutputtotal: 245 status: paid A defer may call a function that returns a value, as os.Remov

Data and types Arrays, indexing, arrays of a given size, searching and totals, two dimensional arrays, copies and slices that write through An array holds a fixed number of values of the same type one after another, and you reach each of them by its position. Arrays are the simplest and fastest way to keep a list whose length you know in advance. Building and reading an array Build an array with square brackets. Positions start at zero, and len() gives the number of elements. To change elements, declare the array mut. println prints a whole array at once, and an array may itself hold arrays, as table does here. arr-basics.salamCopyfunc main:     mut numbers := [5, 3, 8, 1]     println numbers[0], numbers[3], len(numbers)     numbers[1] = 90     println numbers     table := [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]     println table[1][2] endOutput5 1 4 [5, 90, 8, 1] 6 The type of numbers is int[4]: the length is part of the type and never changes. When you need a list that grows, use a Vector from the collections lesson.  An array of a given size When you know the length but not yet the values, declare the array with its type: mut votes: int[4]. Numbers start at zero and bool elements at false. Counting things by number is the classic use: arr-sized.salamCopyfunc main:     mut votes: int[4]     ballots := [2, 0, 2, 3, 2, 0]     each b in ballots:         votes[b]++     end     println votes     each option, count in votes:         println "option", option, "got", count     end endOutput[2, 0, 3, 1] option 0 got 2 option 1 got 0 option 2 got 3 option 3 got 1 Do not read the elements of a str array declared this way before you have set them: they hold no string yet, and reading one crashes the program. Build a str array from a literal instead, such as ["", "", ""].  Walking an array each item in array visits the elements in order. With two names, each i, item in array, you also get the position. arrays.salamCopyfunc main:     fruits := ["apple", "pomegranate", "grape"]     each fruit in fruits:         println "I like", fruit     end     println "count:", fruits.Len() endOutputI like apple I like pomegranate I like grape count: 3  Searching and adding up Most work on an array is one loop that carries a result along: a running total, the position of the largest value so far, or the first position that matches. Keep the position rather than the value when you will need both, as with wettest below. A search function returns -1 when nothing matches, a value that cannot be a real position. arr-stats.salamCopyfunc index of(items: str[], wanted: str): int:     each i, item in items:         if item == wanted:             ret i         end     end     ret -1 end  func main:     months := ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun"]     rain := [78, 64, 51, 33, 12, 4]     mut total := 0     mut wettest := 0     each i, mm in rain:         total += mm         if mm > rain[wettest]:             wettest = i         end     end     println "total:", total, "average:", total / len(rain)     println "wettest:", months[wettest], rain[wettest]     println "Apr is month", index of(months, "Apr") + 1     println "Dec found at", index of(months, "Dec") endOutputtotal: 242 average: 40 wettest: Jan 78 Apr is month 4 Dec found at -1 Two arrays of the same element type and length compare with == and !=: they are equal when every element is equal, so [1, 2, 3] == [1, 2, 3] is true. Arrays of different lengths cannot be compared, and neither can arrays with < or >; both are error E021.  Two dimensional arrays An array of arrays is a table: sales[r][c] is row r, column c. len(sales) is the number of rows and len(sales[0]) the number of columns. An array literal may span several lines, which keeps a table readable. each does not walk a two dimensional array (E065), so use repeat with indexes. A single row, sales[r], is an ordinary array and can be handed to a function. arr-grid.salamCopyfunc total(values: int[]): int:     mut sum := 0     each n in values:         sum += n     end     ret sum end  func main:     sales := [         [12, 7, 3, 9],         [5, 11, 8, 6],         [9, 4, 10, 2]     ]     shops := ["north", "south", "east"]     repeat len(sales) in r:         println shops[r], total(sales[r])     end     mut days := ""     repeat len(sales[0]) in c:         mut sum := 0         repeat len(sales) in r:             sum += sales[r][c]         end         days += " " + sum     end     println "per day:" + days endOutputnorth 31 south 30 east 25 per day: 26 22 21 17 To declare an empty table, give both sizes: mut grid: int[3][4].  Arrays are values Assigning an array to another variable copies all of it. So does passing it to a parameter with a fixed size such as int[3], and so does retu

Data and types Growable lists with Vector, key and value pairs with HashMap, sorting, and Set, Stack and Queue An array has a fixed size. A Vector is a list that grows and shrinks, and a HashMap connects every key to a value. Between the two you can hold most of the data a program works with, and the collections package adds a Set, a Stack and a Queue for the jobs they fit better. Vector Build one with Vector {} as Vector<type>. push adds an element at the end, Get and Set read and replace one by its position, pop takes the last one off and returns it, and Len gives the count. each walks the elements in order. vector.salamCopyfunc main:     mut numbers := Vector {} as Vector<int>     defer numbers.Free()     numbers.Push(10)     numbers.Push(20)     numbers.Push(30)     numbers.Set(1, 25)     println numbers.Len(), numbers.Get(1)     last := numbers.Pop()     println last, numbers.Len()     each n in numbers:         println n     end endOutput3 25 30 2 10 25 A Vector and a HashMap both allocate memory. Write defer name.Free() on the line after creating one, so the memory is released when the function ends, however it ends.  Inserting and removing A Vector is not limited to its end. insert(i, x) puts a value at position i and moves the rest along, and remove_at(i) takes one out and gives it back. first() and last() read the two ends, clear() empties the Vector and is_empty() tells you whether anything is left. Square brackets work as they do on an array: v[i] reads and v[i] = x writes. vector-edit.salamCopyfunc main:     mut playlist := Vector {} as Vector<str>     defer playlist.Free()     playlist.Push("Blue in Green")     playlist.Push("So What")     playlist.Push("Naima")     playlist.Insert(0, "Intro")     println playlist     removed := playlist.RemoveAt(2)     println "removed:", removed     println "first:", playlist.First(), "last:", playlist.Last()     playlist[1] += " (live)"     println playlist[1], playlist.Len()     playlist.Clear()     println playlist.IsEmpty() endOutput["Intro", "Blue in Green", "So What", "Naima"] removed: So What first: Intro last: Naima Blue in Green (live) 3 true Positions start at 0 and end at len() - 1. Reading past the end is not quietly ignored: the program stops with Vector.Get: index out of bounds. Inserting or removing near the front moves every element after it, so on a very long Vector, work at the end when you can.  A Vector of structs The element type can be anything, and most real programs keep a list of records: tasks, orders, players. each i, t in tasks gives you the position and the element together. vector-structs.salamCopystruct Task:     pub title: str = ""     pub minutes: int = 0     pub done: bool = false end  func main:     mut tasks := Vector {} as Vector<Task>     defer tasks.Free()     tasks.Push(Task { title = "standup", minutes = 15 })     tasks.Push(Task { title = "write report", minutes = 90 })     tasks.Push(Task { title = "review code", minutes = 40 })      first := tasks.Ref(0)     first.done = true      mut left := 0     each i, t in tasks:         mark := t.done ? "x" : " "         println i + 1, "[" + mark + "]", t.title         if not t.done:             left += t.minutes         end     end     println "minutes left:", left endOutput1 [x] standup 2 [ ] write report 3 [ ] review code minutes left: 130 The loop variable t is a copy of the element. Changing t.done inside the loop would change only the copy and leave the Vector as it was. To change an element in place, take a pointer to it with ref(i) and write through that, as the example does with the first task. The other way is to read the element, change it and put it back with set(i, x). The next lesson covers structs themselves.  Sorting The sort package sorts a Vector in place. sort.Sort puts numbers and strings in ascending order and sort.SortDesc in descending order. For structs, or for any order of your own, sort.SortBy takes a function that answers one question: should a come before b? vector-sort.salamCopyimport sort  struct Player:     pub name: str = ""     pub score: int = 0 end  func main:     mut times := Vector {} as Vector<int>     defer times.Free()     times.Push(42)     times.Push(7)     times.Push(19)     sort.Sort(times)     println times     sort.SortDesc(times)     println times      mut board := Vector {} as Vector<Player>     defer board.Free()     board.Push(Player { name = "Sara", score = 31 })     board.Push(Player { name = "Omid", score = 48 })     board.Push(Player { name = "Lena", score = 27 })     sort.SortBy(board, (a: Player, b: Player): ret a.score > b.score end)     each i, p in board:         println i + 1, p.name, p.score     end endOutput[7, 19, 42] [42, 19, 7]

Data and types Related data together, methods and this, pub and private, printing, copying, static members and embedding A struct gathers several related pieces of data under one name, along with the functions, called methods, that work on them. It is how a Salam program describes the things it deals with: an account, an order, a point on a map. Declaring a struct Every field has a name, a type and, optionally, a default value. A method is a func written inside the struct, and inside it this refers to the value the method was called on. Fields and methods are private by default; pub makes them reachable from outside the struct. structs.salamCopystruct Rectangle:     pub width: int = 1     pub height: int = 1     pub func area(): int:         ret this.width * this.height     end end  func main:     plot := Rectangle { width = 12, height = 8 }     println "area of the plot:", plot.area() endOutputarea of the plot: 96  Creating and printing A struct literal names the fields it sets: Point { x = 3, y = 4 }. Any field you leave out takes its default value. A field declared without a default has to be given every time, or the compiler stops with E028: struct literal 'P' requires field 'x'. A struct can be printed directly, with all of its fields: struct-print.salamCopystruct Point:     pub x: int = 0     pub y: int = 0 end  func main:     p := Point { x = 3, y = 4 }     println p     println Point {} endOutputPoint {x = 3, y = 4} Point {x = 0, y = 0}  Optional fields with T? A field with a default always has a value, so the code that reads it cannot tell "not given" from "given 0". For that, add ? to the type: timeout: int?. Such a field may be left out of a literal and then holds nothing, unless it has its own default, as in retries: int? = 3. A plain value is wrapped for you, and null empties it again. Read it with is_some(), is_none(), unwrap_or(fallback) or unwrap(), or use the fields present and value. struct-optional.salamCopystruct Client:     pub host: str     pub port: int = 443     pub timeout: int? end  func main:     a := Client { host = "a.test" }     println a.port, a.timeout.is_none()     mut b := Client { host = "b.test", timeout = 30 }     println b.timeout.value, b.timeout.unwrap_or(5)     b.timeout = null     println b.timeout.unwrap_or(5) endOutput443 true 30 30 5 int? is another way to write core.Option<int>, and you need no import to use it. Parameters and return types can be optional too. For a local variable write x := 5 as int?, or mut x: int? and give it a value before reading it. Check is_some() before you use value: on an empty field it means nothing, and in an empty str option it is a null pointer that crashes when used. unwrap_or does the check for you. Fields that depend on each other Sometimes a field is optional until another one is given: a user name is fine alone only if there is a password too. Write that as a rule inside the struct, and the compiler checks every struct literal against it: struct-rules.salamCopystruct Client:     pub host: str     pub user: str = ""     pub pass: str = ""     pub token: str = ""     rule user needs pass     rule oneof(user, token) end  func main:     a := Client { host = "db", user = "ali", pass = "secret" }     println a.host, a.user     b := Client { host = "api", token = "abc" }     println b.host, b.token endOutputdb ali api abc rule a needs b, c means that a literal setting a must also set b and c. The other forms take a group: allornone(a, b), oneof(a, b) for exactly one, anyof(a, b) for at least one, and atmostone(a, b). Breaking a rule stops the build with E159. A needs rule can also test a value: rule use_key == true needs key_pem applies only when use_key is true. The value on the right is a literal or a plain enum member. If the literal's value is not a constant, the compiler assumes it may match and asks for the field. Otherwise a rule looks at what the literal writes, not at the values, so user = "" counts as given. It also checks only the literal: changing a field later is not checked. When a guarantee must always hold, use an enum with data or a constructor.  Your own text with to_str The printed form shows every field, which is handy while you write a program but not always what a user should see. Give the struct a method pub func to_str(): str and println uses it instead. It is also used when the struct sits inside another struct, a Vector or an array. struct-tostr.salamCopystruct Money:     pub cents: int = 0     pub func to_str(): str:         rest := this.cents % 100         pad := rest < 10 ? "0" : ""         ret "$" + (this.cents / 100) + "." + pad + rest     end end  struct Item:     pub name: str = ""     pub price: Money = Money {} end  func main:     pen := Item { name = "pen", price = Money { cents = 250 } }     println pen.price     println

Data and types A closed set of cases, chosen values, enums in structs, enums that carry data, generic enums, and keeping a result as a value An enum is a type with a closed set of cases: a traffic light is red, green or yellow and nothing else. Because the compiler knows every case, it can tell you when your code forgets one. A case can also carry data of its own, which makes enums the natural way to say "one of these kinds, with these details". A plain enum Cases are separated by commas and numbered from zero. You can give a case a value of your own, and the cases after it carry on from there. as int gives you the number behind a case. enum-values.salamCopyenum Status:     Draft, Published = 10, Archived end  func main:     state := Status.Published     println state as int, Status.Archived as int     println state == Status.Published endOutput10 11 true .name() gives the name of a case as a string, and .Count() on the enum itself gives the number of cases: enum-name.salamCopyenum Season: Spring, Summer, Autumn, Winter end  func main:     s := Season.Autumn     println s.name()     println "number of seasons:", Season.Count()     println s == Season.Autumn, s as int endOutputAutumn number of seasons: 4 true 2  Enums and match match on an enum lists the cases by their bare names. It must cover every case or end with else; leave one out and the program does not compile: E080: non-exhaustive match on enum 'Light': missing member Yellow. That check is the main reason to use an enum instead of plain numbers or strings. When you add a case later, the compiler points at every match that has to learn about it. enum-state.salamCopyenum Light: Red, Green, Yellow end  func next(l: Light): Light:     ret match l:         Red: Light.Green end         Green: Light.Yellow end         Yellow: Light.Red end     end end  func seconds(l: Light): int:     ret match l:         Red: 30 end         Green: 25 end         Yellow: 5 end     end end  func main:     mut light := Light.Red     mut cycle := 0     repeat Light.Count():         println light.name(), seconds(light)         cycle += seconds(light)         light = next(light)     end     println "full cycle:", cycle, "seconds, back to", light.name() endOutputRed 30 Green 25 Yellow 5 full cycle: 60 seconds, back to Red Each function describes one fact about every state, and Light.Count() makes the loop go round exactly once, however many cases there are. A small state machine like this, where each state knows the next one, turns up everywhere: order processing, game turns, connection status. Write else only when the remaining cases really share one answer. A catch-all else also swallows the cases you add later, and the compiler can no longer remind you about them.  Enums in structs and stored values An enum is a good type for a struct field with a fixed set of states. Printing the struct shows the field as its number, so use name() when a person will read it. enum-order.salamCopyenum Status: Placed, Packed, Shipped, Delivered end  struct Order:     pub id: int = 0     pub status: Status = Status.Placed end  func status_from(code: int): Status:     if code < 0 or code >= Status.Count():         ret Status.Placed     end     ret code as Status end  func main:     mut order := Order { id = 1042 }     order.status = Status.Packed     println order     println order.id, order.status.name()      saved := order.status as int     println "saved as", saved, "read back as", status_from(saved).name()     println "unchecked:", "[" + (9 as Status).name() + "]", "checked:", status_from(9).name() endOutputOrder {id = 1042, status = 1} 1042 Packed saved as 1 read back as Packed unchecked: [] checked: Placed The number is what you store in a file or a database, and code as Status turns it back into a case. That conversion is not checked: 9 as Status is accepted even though no case has the value 9, and its name() is an empty string. When the number comes from outside the program, check it first, as status_from does with Status.Count(). When the cases have values of their own, such as Published = 10, compare against those instead.  Enums that carry data A case can carry named data, such as a radius for a circle. Build one with Shape.Circle(2.0), and use match to tell the cases apart and pull the data out. A branch may add a condition with if. A guarded branch does not count as covering its case, so keep an unguarded branch for the same case after it. enum-data.salamCopyenum Shape:     Circle(radius: f64)     Rectangle(width: f64, height: f64)     None end  func area(s: Shape): f64:     ret match s:         Circle(r): 3.14 * r * r end         Rectangle(w, h) if w == h: w * w end         Rectangle(w, h): w * h end         None: 0.0 end     end end  func main:     println area(Shape.Circle(2.0))     println area(Shape.Rectangle(3.0, 4.0))     println area(Shape.None)     println Shape.Circle(1.5) endOu

Data and types Type aliases, distinct types with their own methods and operators, operator overloading in structs, and or types An int can be a price, a distance or a user id, and the compiler cannot tell them apart. Salam lets you build new types so that code says what a value means, and so that mixing up two kinds of value becomes a compile error instead of a bug. Aliases and distinct types type Id = int is only another name for int and mixes freely with it. type Meter: int, on the other hand, builds a new type on top of int that cannot be confused with a plain int, and that can carry its own methods and operators in a body closed by end. type-alias.salamCopytype Id = int  type Meter: int     func +(other: Meter): Meter:         ret ((this as int) + (other as int)) as Meter     end     func kilometers(): f64:         ret (this as f64) / 1000.0     end end  func main:     id := 42 as Id     println id + 1     road := 1200 as Meter     println (road + road).kilometers() endOutput43 2.4 An alias is useful for a long type you write often, or to give a name to an enum from another place: after type Paint = Color, Paint.Red is the same case as Color.Red. A type error that involves an alias names it too, as in cannot pass 'str' to 'i32' ('Age' is an alias of 'i32').  Distinct types for meaning A distinct type keeps every operator of its base type, and the result has the new type: adding two Cents gives Cents, and < and > work as before. What it does not do is mix with plain numbers. price + 4 with 4 in an int variable stops with E021: operator cannot be applied to 'Cents' and 'i32'; a conversion with as has to be written out, so it is always visible. When an operation with another type makes sense, declare it, as * by a count does here: type-money.salamCopytype Cents: int     func *(count: int): Cents:         ret ((this as int) * count) as Cents     end     func text(): str:         c := this as int         rest := c % 100         pad := rest < 10 ?
