"0" : ""         ret "$" + (c / 100) + "." + pad + rest     end end  func main:     price := 499 as Cents     shipping := 250 as Cents     total := price * 3 + shipping     println total.text(), total > price     println total     people := 2     share := ((total as int) / people) as Cents     println "each pays", share.text() endOutput$17.47 true 1747 each pays $8.73 println total prints the underlying number, so the example asks for the formatted text with its own text() method. A number literal adopts the type it meets, so price + 100 needs no cast, while price * 3 uses the * declared in the type. The base can also be str, bool, char or a float. An Email is still text, but a function that takes one can no longer be handed any string by mistake (E012: argument 1: cannot pass 'str' to 'Email'): type-email.salamCopytype Email: str     func domain(): str:         s := this as str         at := s.Find("@")         ret s.Substr(at + 1, s.Len() - at - 1)     end end  func notify(recipient: Email, subject: str):     println "to", recipient as str, "at", recipient.domain(), "about", subject end  func main:     user := "sara@example.com" as Email     notify(user, "your order") endOutputto sara@example.com at example.com about your order  Operator overloading A method whose name is the operator itself, such as func +(other: Vec): Vec, defines that operator for the struct. It is called when the struct is the left operand. The operators you can define are + - * / % ** == != < > <= >= not [] []=; inventing a new symbol is an error. operator.salamCopystruct Vec:     pub x: int = 0     pub y: int = 0     pub func +(other: Vec): Vec:         ret Vec { x = this.x + other.x, y = this.y + other.y }     end     pub func ==(other: Vec): bool:         ret this.x == other.x and this.y == other.y     end end  func main:     a := Vec { x = 1, y = 2 }     b := Vec { x = 3, y = 4 }     println a + b     println a == b, (a + b) == Vec { x = 4, y = 6 } endOutputVec {x = 4, y = 6} false true  Indexing, negation and the rest The number of parameters decides the kind of operator. func -: Vec with no parameters is negation (-pos), and func -(other: Vec) would be subtraction; define both if you need both. [] takes the index and []= takes the index and the new value, which lets a struct be used with square brackets like an array: operator-more.salamCopystruct Board:     cells: int[9] = [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]     pub func [](i: int): int:         ret this.cells[i]     end     pub mut func []=(i: int, mark: int):         this.cells[i] = mark     end end  struct Vec:     pub x: int = 0     pub y: int = 0     pub func +(other: Vec): Vec:         ret Vec { x = this.x + other.x, y = this.y + other.y }     end     pub func *(k: int): Vec:         ret Vec { x = this.x * k, y = this.y * k }     end     pub func -: Vec:         ret Vec { x = -this.x, y = -this.y }     end

Data and types Generic functions and containers, interfaces, impl, bounds and dyn collections Generics let you write a function or a container once and use it with any type. Interfaces describe what a type can do, so that different types can be handled by the same code. Generic functions and structs Write <T> after the name and the function or struct works for any type T. For every type you actually use, the compiler builds a separate, fully specialised copy, so generic code runs as fast as code written by hand for that type. generics.salamCopystruct Box<T>:     pub inside: T end  func larger<T>(a: T, b: T): T:     if a > b:         ret a     end     ret b end  func main:     println larger(3, 9), larger("a", "b"), larger(2.5, 1.5)     b := Box { inside = "a gift" } as Box<str>     println b.inside endOutput9 b 2.5 a gift The type of a generic function comes from its arguments: larger(3, 9) uses int and larger("a", "b") uses str. You cannot name the type at the call (larger<int>(3, 9) does not parse), so if a literal should have another type, cast it with as. A generic struct takes its type from the cast, as in Box { ... } as Box<str>. The body has to make sense for every type you call it with. larger compares with >, which works for numbers and strings. Call it with two structs and the compiler stops with E021: cannot compare 'P' and 'P'.  A generic container Most generic code you write will be a container: a struct that holds values of some type and offers a small, clear set of operations on them. This stack keeps its items in a Vector<T> and exposes only what a stack should do. The same code serves as an undo history of strings and as a list of page numbers. generics-stack.salamCopystruct Stack<T>:     items: Vector<T> = Vector {}      pub func push(x: T):         this.items.Push(x)     end      pub func pop(): T:         ret this.items.Pop()     end      pub func peek(): T:         ret this.items.Get(this.items.Len() - 1)     end      pub func size(): int:         ret this.items.Len()     end      pub func is_empty(): bool:         ret this.items.Len() == 0     end      pub func free():         this.items.Free()     end end  func main:     undo := Stack {} as Stack<str>     defer undo.Free()     undo.Push("type 'hello'")     undo.Push("make it bold")     undo.Push("delete a line")     println undo.Size(), "steps, last:", undo.Peek()     until not undo.IsEmpty():         println "undo", undo.Pop()     end      pages := Stack {} as Stack<int>     defer pages.Free()     pages.Push(1)     pages.Push(14)     println "back to page", pages.Pop() endOutput3 steps, last: delete a line undo delete a line undo make it bold undo type 'hello' back to page 14 The struct owns a Vector, so it also gets a free method, and each stack is released with defer right after it is created. That is the same habit as for a plain Vector; the memory lesson explains why.  Several type parameters A generic can take more than one type, separated by commas. Pair<A, B> holds two values of different types, and swap turns a Pair<A, B> into a Pair<B, A>. Printing a generic struct shows the types it was built with. generics-pair.salamCopystruct Pair<A, B>:     pub first: A     pub second: B end  func swap<A, B>(p: Pair<A, B>): Pair<B, A>:     ret Pair { first = p.second, second = p.first } end  func main:     stock := Pair { first = "pencils", second = 120 } as Pair<str, int>     println stock     println swap(stock)     point := Pair { first = 2.5, second = -1.0 } as Pair<f64, f64>     println point.first + point.second endOutputPair<str, i32> {first = "pencils", second = 120} Pair<i32, str> {first = 120, second = "pencils"} 1.5  Interfaces An interface is a list of method signatures. A struct that has all of those methods implements the interface automatically; there is no "implements" line to write. A parameter of type dyn Shape accepts any value whose type implements Shape. interface.salamCopyinterface Shape:     func area(): int     func name(): str end  struct Square:     side: int = 0     pub func area(): int: ret this.side * this.side end     pub func name(): str: ret "square" end end  struct Rectangle:     width: int = 0     height: int = 0     pub func area(): int: ret this.width * this.height end     pub func name(): str: ret "rectangle" end end  func describe(s: dyn Shape):     println s.name(), s.area() end  func main:     describe(Square { side = 5 })     describe(Rectangle { width = 4, height = 6 }) endOutputsquare 25 rectangle 24 An interface method may carry a default body. A struct that does not write that method gets the default, and a struct that does write it keeps its own. The default can call the other methods of the interface through th

Larger programs Packages, include and import, pub and privacy, folder packages and project layout Larger programs are written across several files. Each file belongs to a package, and a package shares with the rest of the program only what it marks pub. Packages A file that begins with package name belongs to that package. Only the functions, constants, types and fields marked pub can be used from outside it; everything else is an internal detail that you are free to change later without breaking anyone. A file without a package line is in the package main. pkg-lib.salamCopypackage tools  pub const VERSION := "1.0"  func double(n: int): int:     ret n * 2 end  pub func quadruple(n: int): int:     ret double(double(n)) end This file has no main of its own, so on its own it does not run; it is meant to be included by a program, as in the next section.  Including your own files include name "file.salam" brings in a file of your own project under a short name, and you reach its public members as name.thing. The path is relative to the file that does the including. pkg-include.salamCopyinclude tools "pkg-lib.salam"  func main:     println tools.quadruple(5)     println "tools version:", tools.VERSION endOutput20 tools version: 1.0  The name is optional: include "lib/money.salam" is reached as money.Format(...), after the file name. Give it a name whenever the file name is long or unclear. A path that starts with @/ starts at the project root instead of at the current file, so include "@/lib/money.salam" means the same file from every folder of the project. Build from the project's folder so the root is where you expect it. Do not start a path with ./. The compiler stops with E008: include path './lib/money.salam' must not start with './' and tells you the two spellings it does accept. A file that cannot be found is an error too (E008: included file not found), never something skipped quietly.   Importing a library Standard library packages are imported by name, without quotes: import str, import os. A package inside another one is written with a dot, as in import encoding.json, and is used through its last part, json.Get(...). In short: import is for libraries and include is for your own files. pkg-import.salamCopyimport str import math  func main:     text := "  hello world  "     println str.Trim(text)     println str.Contains(text, "world")     println math.Sqrt(81.0), math.Pow(2.0, 10.0) endOutputhello world true 9 1024 pkg-dotted.salamCopyimport encoding.json  func main:     order := `{"id": 42, "item": "notebook", "qty": 3}`     if not json.Valid(order):         println "not valid JSON"         ret 1     end     println "order", json.GetInt(order, "id")     println json.GetInt(order, "qty"), "x", json.Get(order, "item")     println json.Has(order, "coupon") endOutputorder 42 3 x notebook false An import nobody uses is an error (E082: unused import), so the imports at the top of a file always tell the truth about what the file depends on.  pub and private Privacy works on struct members too. In this bank package, owner is public but balance is not, so the only way to change a balance is through Deposit and Withdraw, which check every amount. The helper valid_amount is private as well. Account.Open is a static constructor, the usual way to hand out a ready-made value of a type whose fields are private. pkg-bank.salamCopypackage bank  pub const MAX_DEPOSIT := 1000000  struct Account:     pub owner: str = ""     balance: int = 0      pub static func Open(owner: str): Account:         ret Account { owner = owner }     end      pub func Balance(): int:         ret this.balance     end      pub mut func Deposit(amount: int): bool:         if not valid_amount(amount) or amount > MAX_DEPOSIT:             ret false         end         this.balance += amount         ret true     end      pub mut func Withdraw(amount: int): bool:         if not valid_amount(amount) or amount > this.balance:             ret false         end         this.balance -= amount         ret true     end end  func valid_amount(amount: int): bool:     ret amount > 0 end pkg-private.salamCopyinclude bank "pkg-bank.salam"  func main:     mut acc := bank.Account.Open("Sara")     println acc.Deposit(500), acc.Withdraw(800), acc.Withdraw(120)     println acc.owner, acc.Balance()     println acc.Deposit(bank.MAX_DEPOSIT + 1) endOutputtrue false true Sara 380 false From the program, acc.balance would be refused with E017: field 'balance' is private in struct 'Account' (mark it 'pub'), and calling the private helper with E017: 'valid_amount' is not exported by package 'bank' (mark it 'pub'). Make something pub because other code is meant to use it, not to silence an error: everything public is a promise you have to keep.  A package across a folder When a pa

Larger programs The strict rules of Salam, the error code for each, and how to fix them The Salam compiler catches a great many mistakes before the program ever runs. Every message says what is wrong, where, and usually how to fix it. This lesson goes through the rules behind the messages you will meet most. Why so strict? Every error the compiler catches is an error that never reaches a user. That is why Salam treats as errors several things that other languages only warn about: a variable nobody reads, a mut that never changes, a branch that can never run. Warnings tend to pile up and get ignored; an error is fixed on the spot, so a Salam program that compiles has no such leftovers in it.  Reading an error A typical message looks like this: [SEMANTIC][ERROR] E013: cannot reassign immutable variable 'total'; declare it 'mut' to reassign it, or assign to its elements or fields instead (app.salam:3:5)  E013 is the error code. It is the same in English and Persian, so it is the thing to search for. Then comes the problem, and after the semicolon the usual fix. Read the message to the end; the fix is often all you need. The end of the line gives the file, line and column: line 3, column 5 of app.salam.  Mistakes in the shape of the code, such as a missing end or a word that is not Salam, are reported by the parser instead. Those show the line itself with a caret under the spot, and often a help: line, for example error: '&&' is not a Salam operator; write 'and'. A Persian file gets its messages in Persian. Fix the first error first. One mistake can cause others further down: misspell a name, and the compiler reports both the unknown name (E001) and the variable you meant, which is now unused (E059).  Nothing unused A variable, parameter, private function or import that nothing uses is an error: E059, E062, E066 and E082. Usually the right fix is to delete it, or to notice that you forgot to use it. Starting the name with _ silences the error, but keep that for the one real case: a signature you do not control. Here every handler must take a user and a text, and Shout has no use for the user: rules-unused.salamCopyinterface Handler:     func handle(user: str, text: str): str end  struct Echo:     pub func handle(user: str, text: str): str:         ret user + " said " + text     end end  struct Shout:     pub func handle(_user: str, text: str): str:         ret text + "!"     end end  func run(h: dyn Handler):     println h.handle("sara", "hello") end  func main:     run(Echo {})     run(Shout {}) endOutputsara said hello hello! Without the _, the compiler would say E062: unused parameter 'user', and its message itself says to use _ only when the signature is fixed.  mut only where things change A variable made with := cannot be reassigned (E013). Add mut when it must change, and only then: a mut that never changes is also an error (E069). Adding to a Vector or a HashMap changes the data it points to, not the variable, so push works without mut. A value fixed for the whole program is a const. rules-mut.salamCopyconst LIMIT := 3  func main:     names := Vector {} as Vector<str>     defer names.Free()     names.Push("Sara")     names.Push("Reza")     names.Push("Mina")     names.Push("Ali")     mut shown := 0     each n in names:         if shown == LIMIT:             break         end         println n         shown++     end     println shown, "of", names.Len(), "shown" endOutputSara Reza Mina 3 of 4 shown  Types are never guessed Salam does not convert between types behind your back. Putting a str where an int belongs is E002 in an assignment and E012 in a call, and a condition must be a real bool: if items: with a number is E021, so write if items > 0:. The two branches of ?: must have the same type. Convert explicitly with as, but not when the value already has that type: n as int on an int is a useless cast, E093.  Every path is checked The compiler follows every path through a function. A function that returns a value must return it on every path (E071: function 'sign' can fall off its end), a match on an enum must cover every member or have an else (E080 names the missing ones), and code after a ret can never run (E070). The same goes for a condition that is always false (E068), an empty if branch (E060) and a statement whose value is thrown away, like n + 1 on its own line (E110). rules-flow.salamCopyenum Light: Red, Yellow, Green end  func action(l: Light): str:     ret match l:         Red: "stop" end         Yellow: "slow down" end         Green: "go" end     end end  func sign(n: int): str:     if n > 0:         ret "positive"     else n < 0:         ret "negative"     end     ret "zero" end  func main:     println action(Light.Yellow), action(Light.Green)     println sign(-4), sign(0), sign(9) endOutputslow down go negat

Larger programs Copies and sharing, copy and deep_copy, freeing memory, who frees a string, pointers and memcheck Salam runs without a garbage collector. Nothing is freed behind your back, and nothing is shared unless you can see why. This lesson shows when a value is copied, when it is shared, and who is responsible for giving memory back. Structs are copied When you put a struct into another variable, or pass it to a function, a copy is made, and changing the copy leaves the original alone. If a function has to change the caller's value, declare the parameter as a reference with &:. A reference also saves copying a large struct; the functions lesson has more on it. mem-copy.salamCopystruct Account:     pub balance: int = 0 end  func deposit(a &: Account, amount: int):     a.balance += amount end  func main:     mut first := Account { balance = 100 }     mut second := first     second.balance = 500     println first.balance, second.balance     deposit(first, 25)     println first.balance endOutput100 500 125  Arrays are copied, slices are views A fixed array such as int[3] is a value too: assigning it or passing it as int[3] copies every element. A slice parameter, int[], is a view of the caller's array, so writing through it changes the original. Choose the parameter type by what the function is allowed to do. mem-array.salamCopyfunc zero_first(scores: int[3]):     scores[0] = 0 end  func zero_first_in_place(scores: int[]):     scores[0] = 0 end  func main:     week := [7, 5, 9]     mut plan := week     plan[1] = 100     println week, plan     zero_first(week)     println week     mut live := [7, 5, 9]     zero_first_in_place(live)     println live endOutput[7, 5, 9] [7, 100, 9] [7, 5, 9] [0, 5, 9]  A Vector shares its storage A Vector or a HashMap is a small header (where the items are, how many there are, how much room is left) that points at storage on the heap. Assigning one copies only the header. Both names then see the same items, so cart.set(0, "rice") shows through view, but each name keeps its own length, so the "tea" pushed through cart is not counted by view. Do not rely on that half-shared state. When you need an independent value, ask for one with copy(), and free it like any other Vector. mem-share.salamCopyfunc main:     cart := Vector {} as Vector<str>     defer cart.Free()     cart.Push("bread")     cart.Push("milk")     view := cart     cart.Set(0, "rice")     cart.Push("tea")     println cart, view      saved := cart.Copy()     defer saved.Free()     cart.Set(1, "eggs")     saved.Push("salt")     println cart, saved endOutput["rice", "milk", "tea"] ["rice", "milk"] ["rice", "eggs", "tea"] ["rice", "milk", "tea", "salt"] A HashMap behaves the same way, and so does a Vector inside a struct: copying the struct copies the header of its Vector, not the items.  copy and deep_copy copy() gives new storage only for the outer container. When the items are containers themselves, as in a Vector of rows, the copy still shares every row. deep_copy() goes all the way down and copies the rows too. Change one seat in the original below: the shallow copy sees it, the deep copy does not. mem-deep.salamCopyfunc free_grid(g: Vector<Vector<int>>):     each row in g:         row.Free()     end     g.Free() end  func main:     seats := Vector {} as Vector<Vector<int>>     repeat 2 in r:         row := Vector {} as Vector<int>         repeat 3 in c:             row.Push(r * 3 + c + 1)         end         seats.Push(row)     end     shallow := seats.Copy()     deep := seats.DeepCopy()     seats.Get(0).Set(0, 0)     println seats     println shallow     println deep     shallow.Free()     free_grid(deep)     free_grid(seats) endOutput[[0, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]] [[0, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]] [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]] Each copy has to be freed, and so does every container a deep copy made: that is why free_grid frees each row before the outer Vector, while the shallow copy, whose rows belong to the original, only frees its own storage. A struct gets copy() and deep_copy() too, built by the compiler from its fields.  Freeing: free and defer Numbers, booleans, plain structs and fixed arrays need no freeing. Anything that holds heap storage does: a Vector, a HashMap, a dyn box, and the strings described in the next section. The habit worth forming is to write defer x.free() on the line right after x is created, so it is freed when the function ends, whatever path it takes. A function that builds and returns a container hands it over: from then on the caller owns it and frees it. Freeing a container frees its own storage, not what the items own, so a map of Vectors frees each Vector first. mem-free.salamCopystruct Student:     pub name: str = ""     pub class: str = "" end  func by_class(all:

Larger programs Code for each operating system and processor, build flags with -D, and debug-only checks, all decided while compiling Sometimes code has to differ a little between Windows, macOS and Linux, or between a debug build and a release build. Salam makes that choice while compiling, so the branch that does not apply is not in the program at all and costs nothing at run time. if at compile time An if at the top level of a file, with a condition known while compiling, keeps only the branch that applies. Whatever is declared inside it, such as constants, globals, extern blocks or functions, exists only on the platforms where that branch is taken. Here each platform gets its own path separator, and the rest of the program uses SEP without caring where it runs: comptime.salamCopyimport str  if SALAM_OS_WINDOWS:     const SEP := "\\" else:     const SEP := "/" end  func main:     path := "home" + SEP + "sara" + SEP + "notes.txt"     parts := str.Split(path, SEP)     defer parts.Free()     println parts.Len(), "parts"     println parts.Get(2) endOutput3 parts notes.txt A top-level if needs a condition the compiler can work out on its own. Writing if count > 3: at the top level is the error "top-level if condition must be a compile-time constant".  The flags you get The compiler defines a set of bool flags that describe the machine the program is built for. One operating system flag and one processor flag are true, plus the family flags that go with them: Linux and macOS also set SALAM_OS_UNIX, Android sets SALAM_OS_LINUX as well, and macOS and the BSDs set SALAM_OS_BSD.  FlagTrue when building for  SALAM_OS_WINDOWSWindows, together with SALAM_OS_WIN64 or SALAM_OS_WIN32 SALAM_OS_LINUXLinux and Android SALAM_OS_MACmacOS SALAM_OS_ANDROIDAndroid SALAM_OS_FREEBSD, SALAM_OS_OPENBSD, SALAM_OS_NETBSDeach BSD SALAM_OS_BSDmacOS and the BSDs SALAM_OS_UNIXevery Unix-like system, WebAssembly included SALAM_OS_WASMWebAssembly SALAM_ARCH_X64, SALAM_ARCH_X8664-bit and 32-bit Intel and AMD SALAM_ARCH_ARM64, SALAM_ARCH_ARM64-bit and 32-bit ARM SALAM_ARCH_RISCV6464-bit RISC-V SALAM_ARCH_WASMWebAssembly SALAM_SAFEany build made without --release  A few more hold a value instead of true or false. SALAM_OS is text such as "windows", "linux", "mac", "android" or "freebsd", and SALAM_ARCH is "x64", "x86", "arm64", "arm", "riscv64" or "wasm". A program compiled to JavaScript (salam js, and the scripts of a page) gets "js" for both, and every SALAM_OS_* and SALAM_ARCH_* flag is false there, because the same code runs in any browser or under Node. SALAM_VERSION is the compiler version as text, such as "0.5.0", and SALAM_VERSION_CODE the same version as a number, 500. In a Persian program each of these names has a Persian spelling; the glossary lists them all.  Inside a function The same if works inside a function body. When its condition is made of these flags, the compiler keeps the branch that applies and throws the others away, exactly as at the top level. An else with a condition chains the platforms: comptime-inline.salamCopyfunc config_dir(app: str): str:     if SALAM_OS_WINDOWS:         ret "C:\\Users\\Public\\AppData\\" + app     else SALAM_OS_MAC:         ret "/Users/Shared/Library/Application Support/" + app     else:         ret "/etc/" + app     end end  func main:     println config_dir("salam")     if SALAM_OS_UNIX:         println "permissions: chmod 600"     end end Always give the platform branches an else. A function that does if SALAM_OS_WINDOWS: ret ... end and then carries on with the Unix code builds fine on Linux, but on Windows that if becomes "always return", and the code after it is error E070, unreachable code. With an else both builds are clean. The branch that is kept is not a block of its own: what it declares stays visible after the if. You can write user := "USERNAME" in the Windows branch and user := "USER" in the other one, and use user below them.  Flags as ordinary values Outside an if these names are plain constants. You can print one, store it in a variable, use it in a switch, or mix it with a test that runs at run time, as in if SALAM_OS_WINDOWS and retries > 0:, where only the second half is left for the running program: comptime-value.salamCopyfunc family(): str:     switch SALAM_OS:         "linux", "android":             ret "linux"         end         "mac", "freebsd", "openbsd", "netbsd":             ret "bsd"         end         "windows":             ret "windows"         end         else:             ret "other"         end     end end  func main:     println "built for", SALAM_OS, "on", SALAM_ARCH     println "family:", family()     wide := SALAM_ARCH_X64 or SALAM_ARCH_ARM64     println "64-bit:", wide     println "s

Larger programs Calling C functions with extern, printf and other variadic functions, pointers and buffers, linking libraries, and handing Salam functions to C Salam talks to C libraries directly, with no glue code and no wrapper generator. That puts the C standard library and every other library written in C within reach of a Salam program. extern Inside an extern: block, declare C functions with their parameter and result types, then call them like any Salam function. The declarations have no body: the code lives in the C library, and Salam only needs to know how to call it. ffi-extern.salamCopyextern:     func sqrt(x: f64): f64     func abs(x: int): int end  func main:     println sqrt(2.0)     println abs(-42) endOutput1.4142135623730951 42 The compiler trusts these declarations completely. If a declaration does not match the real C function, for example an int where C expects a double, nothing warns you and the program reads garbage, so copy each signature carefully from the library's header or manual page.  Matching C types  CSalam  int, unsigned intint (i32), uint (u32) long long, int64_t, uint8_t, ...i64, i64, u8, ... size_tusize ssize_t, intptr_tsize double, floatf64, f32 const char* holding textstr char* or unsigned char* holding bytesu8*, or void* void*, T*void*, T* a function pointervoid*, or extern func (...) R  A Salam str already ends with a zero byte, so it can be passed straight to any C function that wants a string.  printf and other variadic functions A C function that takes a variable number of arguments, such as printf, is declared with ... after its fixed parameters. The C format rules apply: %d for an int, %f for an f64, %s for a str, and widths such as %-8s and %6.2f for columns: ffi-printf.salamCopyextern:     func printf(format: str, ...): int     func strlen(s: str): usize     func atoi(s: str): int     func toupper(c: int): int end  func main:     println "Receipt"     printf("%-8s %3d x %6.2f\n", "coffee", 2, 3.5)     printf("%-8s %3d x %6.2f\n", "bagel", 1, 2.25)     qty := atoi("12") + atoi("30")     println "items:", qty     word := "salam"     println "letters:", strlen(word)     println "first:", char_from_code(toupper(char_code(word))) endOutputReceipt coffee     2 x   3.50 bagel      1 x   2.25 items: 42 letters: 5 first: S Output from printf and from println comes out in the order the program wrote it, because Salam empties its own output buffer before calling a C function that writes. The %-8s padding counts bytes, not letters, so text in Persian or any other non-Latin script lines up differently; for anything but plain ASCII, println or the fmt package is the better tool.  Pointers, buffers and the zero byte Many C functions write into memory you give them. Allocate it with mem, pass the pointer, and free it when you are done; defer right after the allocation keeps that from being forgotten. Index a pointer like an array: buf[i] reads or writes one element. ffi-buffer.salamCopyimport mem  extern:     func snprintf(buf: void*, size: usize, format: str, ...): int     func getenv(name: str): str end  func main:     buf := mem.AllocateZeroed(32 as u64) as u8*     defer mem.Free(buf as void*)      n := snprintf(buf as void*, 32 as usize, "%s-%05d", "INV", 42)     label := buf as str     println n, label      bytes := [72, 105, 0, 33, 33]     repeat 5 in i:         buf[i] = bytes[i] as u8     end     text := buf as str     println "as str:", len(text), "bytes"     mut sum := 0     repeat 5 in i:         sum += buf[i] as int     end     println "through the pointer:", sum      value := getenv("SALAM_EXAMPLE_UNSET")     if (value as void*) == null:         println "SALAM_EXAMPLE_UNSET is not set"     end endOutput9 INV-00042 as str: 2 bytes through the pointer: 243 SALAM_EXAMPLE_UNSET is not set Watch the middle of that output. A str ends at its first zero byte, so the five bytes H i 0 ! ! turn into the two-byte string Hi, and nothing reports it: the rest is simply gone. Text from C is fine as a str; binary data such as images, compressed files or network packets is not. Keep binary data as a pointer and a length, and read it through the pointer, as the loop that adds up all five bytes does. A C function that may return no string, such as getenv for a variable that is not set, returns a null pointer. Check it with (value as void*) == null before you use the value. A string returned by C belongs to the C library, so never free it yourself.  Linking a library Functions from the C standard library need nothing extra. For any other library, tell the linker which one to use with link, written before the extern block. The kind is always written out:  link dynamic "sqlite3" links the shared library, like -lsqlite3 in a C build link static "z" asks for the static library libz.a, which is copied into the prog

Larger programs Threads with spawn and join, sharing data safely, channels and parallel loops A Salam program can do several things at once, across the cores of the processor. This lesson starts a thread, hands it data, and then shows the tools that keep threads from stepping on each other. spawn and join spawn(function) starts the function on a new thread and gives back its handle, a number. join(handle) waits for that thread to finish. Until you join it, the thread and main run side by side, and main should not read what the thread is still writing. threads.salamCopymut message := ""  func worker():     message = "the work was done on another thread" end  func main:     t := spawn(worker)     join(t)     println message endOutputthe work was done on another thread Every thread you start should be joined exactly once. If main returns while a thread is still running, that thread is stopped in the middle of its work.  Giving a thread its own data A thread function may take no parameters, or exactly one pointer: spawn(function, data). The pointer is how each thread gets its own piece of the work, and it is also where the thread leaves its result. The data has to stay alive while the thread runs, so it lives on the heap: allocate it with mem.Allocate and free it after join. threads-arg.salamCopyimport mem  struct Job:     pub from: int = 0     pub to: int = 0     pub sum: i64 = 0 end  func work(j: Job*):     mut total := 0 as i64     repeat j[0].from to j[0].to in i:         total += i as i64     end     j[0].sum = total end  func new job(first: int, last: int): Job*:     j := mem.Allocate(sizeof(Job)) as Job*     j[0] = Job { from = first, to = last }     ret j end  func main:     a := new job(1, 500)     b := new job(501, 1000)     t1 := spawn(work, a)     t2 := spawn(work, b)     join(t1)     join(t2)     println a[0].sum, b[0].sum     println "total:", a[0].sum + b[0].sum     mem.Free(a as void*)     mem.Free(b as void*) endOutput125250 375250 total: 500500 The two threads each sum half of the numbers from 1 to 1000. They never touch the same memory, so they need no coordination at all. That is the easiest kind of concurrent program to get right.  Shared data and the mutex When two threads change the same variable, their updates can collide. count += 1 is really three steps (read, add, write), and if two threads read the same old value, one of the additions is lost. Take the lock out of the next example and the total comes out below 200000, and different on every run. A mutex from the sync package fixes this: between sync.Lock and sync.Unlock only one thread at a time can be inside. Keep that stretch short, and release the mutex with sync.Destroy when the program no longer needs it. threads-mutex.salamCopyimport sync  mut count := 0 mut lock := sync.NewMutex()  func add():     repeat 100000:         sync.Lock(lock)         count++         sync.Unlock(lock)     end end  func main:     t1 := spawn(add)     t2 := spawn(add)     join(t1)     join(t2)     println count     sync.Destroy(lock) endOutput200000  Atomic counters For a single number that many threads bump, the atomic package is lighter than a mutex. atomic.Add does the read, the add and the write as one step that nothing can interrupt. atomic.Load reads the value, and Store, Swap and CompareAndSwap cover the other usual needs. threads-atomic.salamCopyimport atomic  mut hits := atomic.NewI64(0)  func visit():     repeat 100000:         atomic.Add(hits, 1)     end end  func main:     t1 := spawn(visit)     t2 := spawn(visit)     t3 := spawn(visit)     join(t1)     join(t2)     join(t3)     println atomic.Load(hits)     atomic.DestroyI64(hits) endOutput300000  Waiting for a group With many threads, one variable per handle gets awkward. Put the handles in a Vector<i64> and join them in a loop. A sync.WaitGroup answers a related question, "have all of them finished their part?": sync.Add sets how many to wait for, each worker calls sync.Done when it is finished, and sync.Wait blocks until the count reaches zero. threads-waitgroup.salamCopyimport sync  mut done := 0 mut lock := sync.NewMutex() mut group := sync.NewWaitGroup()  func job():     sync.Lock(lock)     done++     sync.Unlock(lock)     sync.Done(group) end  func main:     mut threads := Vector {} as Vector<i64>     defer threads.Free()     sync.Add(group, 5)     repeat 5:         threads.Push(spawn(job))     end     sync.Wait(group)     println "finished:", done     each t in threads:         join(t)     end     sync.DestroyWaitGroup(group)     sync.Destroy(lock) endOutputfinished: 5  Channels A channel from the chan package carries values from one thread to another, so the threads share nothing but the channel itself. init(n) gives it room for n values; send waits while it is full and recv waits while it is empty. After close() nothing more can be sent, and once the remaining values are taken, recv sets its ok argument to false. That is the sign

t: Layout language: common for web and native
x: Layout language The shared Salam layout DSL for web and native apps: elements, attributes, styles, components, parameterized layouts, and simpler value syntax, plus where web and desktop differ Salam's layout DSL is a declarative language for building interfaces: the same structure can produce web output (HTML/CSS/JS) or run as a native UI app drawn by Salam. This lesson covers what is common; web-specific details are in Layout on the web and native desktop details in Layout in native apps. What is shared In both targets you describe the interface as a tree of elements. A page: block (or صفحه:) is the root, each element opens with its name and a colon and closes with end (پایان), and attributes/styles are written as name = value. Element text is usually its content, elements can nest, and the structure stays readable. Top-level page settings such as title, lang, and dir belong to the page. English files default to left-to-right; Persian files default to right-to-left. You can set them explicitly when needed. layout-page.salamCopypage:     title = "My app"     lang = "english"     dir = "left to right"     header:         background = #2563eb         color = "white"         padding = "24px"         heading: size = 1 content = "Welcome to Salam" end     end     box:         padding = "20px"         paragraph: content = "This page was built from Salam code." end     end end  Simpler value syntax In layout/style values you can now write many values in a shorter form: percentages like 50% and 100% without quotes, hex colors like #0f766e without quotes, units such as 12px/1rem/200ms in value contexts, and value lists/groups where supported. For example: box:     width = 50%     max width = 480     padding = 16, 24     background = #f8fafc     color = #0f766e     border = 1, solid, #0f766e end Bare numbers are typically treated as pixels for length-like properties. Strings (such as text content, URLs, or specific textual values) still use quotes.  Elements, attributes, and styles Element and property names are readable (English and Persian aliases). Common elements include box/div, paragraph, heading, link, image, list/item, form, input, and button. Boolean attributes like required = true are meaningful, while false is usually omitted. CSS properties are written alongside elements as attributes. layout-form.salamCopypage:     title = "Contact us"     nav:         link: url = "/" content = "Home" end         link: url = "/blog" content = "Blog" end         link: url = "https://github.com/SalamLang/Salam" target = "new" content = "Source" end     end     image: url = "/logo.png" alt = "Salam logo" end     form:         id = "contact"         label: for = "email" content = "Your email" end         input: id = "email" type = "email" name = "email" placeholder = "you@example.com" required = true end         label: for = "message" content = "Message" end         input: id = "message" type = "text" name = "message" end         button: type = "submit" content = "Send" end     end     list:         item: content = "We answer within a day" end         item: content = "No account needed" end     end end Use constants, global rules, and components to keep styles consistent and avoid repetition: layout-style.salamCopyconst ACCENT := "#0f766e" const GAP := 16  page:     title = "Pricing"     global: box sizing = "border-box" end     global: selector = "body" margin = "0" font family = "sans-serif" end     section:         display = "flex"         gap = GAP + "px"         padding = GAP * 2 + "px"         box:             border = 1px, solid, #ddd             border radius = "12px"             padding = GAP + "px"             heading: size = 2 content = "Free" end             paragraph: content = "For trying things out" end         end         box:             border = 2px, solid + ACCENT             border radius = "12px"             padding = GAP + "px"             heading: size = 2 content = "Pro" color = ACCENT end             button:                 content = "Upgrade"                 background = ACCENT                 color = "white"                 hover background = #115e59                 cursor = "pointer"             end         end     end end  Components and reuse A component (بخش) is a reusable piece of UI with parameters, used like a custom element. content: end marks the slot where nested children are inserted. To share components across files, include them (e.g. include = "parts.s

Layout language Building web output from the layout DSL: salam page build, HTML/CSS/JS, browser events/DOM, parameterized rendering, and serving pages When targeting the web, Salam's layout DSL compiles to HTML, CSS, and (when needed) JavaScript. This lesson focuses on web-specific output and runtime behavior: building, browser/DOM interactivity, and serving pages. Building web output salam page build page.salam produces page.html and page.css, plus page.js when scripts/events are present. Use --inline for a single self-contained HTML file. With multiple inputs (e.g. salam page build home.salam about.salam) each page gets its own HTML and they can share a common style.css. With no file name, the tool typically builds main.salam if present, otherwise layout pages in the folder. Styles are extracted into generated classes/rules in the stylesheet so HTML stays compact and reusable.  Browser events and DOM Event attributes such as click, submit, input, change, etc. become interactive behavior in the browser. Salam handlers attached to events are compiled into the page script for web builds. In handlers you can work with the DOM (e.g. dom.ById/dom.Query) as covered in the events lessons. See Mouse events through State, the DOM and timers for the full browser event/DOM model.  Parameterized layouts and runtime rendering Parameterized layouts can render HTML at runtime with request-specific data, which is useful for Salam web servers. Inserted parameter text is escaped for safety. For sensitive/structured values (URLs, colors, lengths, etc.) validate/parse them appropriately before use. layout-runtime.salamCopypage Card(name: str, score: int):     title = "Card " + name     heading: size = 2 content = name end     if score >= 50:         paragraph: content = "pass" end     else:         paragraph: content = "fail" end     end end  func main:     println Card("Ali", 70) endOutput<!doctype html><html lang="en" dir="ltr"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"><title>Card Ali</title></head><body><h2>Ali</h2><p>pass</p></body></html> layout-server.salamCopyimport net.http import net.router  page Greeting(name: str):     title = "Hello " + name     heading: size = 1 content = "Hello, " + name end     paragraph: content = "This page was rendered on the server." end end  func home(ctx: i64):     mut name := http.Query(ctx, "name")     if name == "":         name = "guest"     end     http.Html(ctx, Greeting(name)) end  func main:     mut r := router.NewRouter()     router.Get(r, "/", home)     mut s := http.NewServer(8080)     http.Use(s, r)     http.Run(s) end  Serving and web projects Built files can be hosted on any static web server, or served locally/production with salam serve. Salam programs can also return rendered HTML using networking packages such as net.http and net.router. layout-inbox.salamCopycomponent Badge(text: str):     span: content = text background = #fde68a end end  page Inbox(user: str, subjects: Vector<str>):     title = "Inbox of " + user     heading: size = 1 content = "Hello, " + user end     if subjects.IsEmpty():         paragraph: content = "No new messages" end     else:         paragraph: content = "Unread: " + subjects.Len() end         list:             each i, s in subjects:                 item: content = (i + 1) + ". " + s end             end         end     end end  func main:     mut subjects := Vector {} as Vector<str>     defer subjects.Free()     subjects.Push("Meeting at 10")     subjects.Push("<b>FREE</b> prize & more")     println Inbox("Sara", subjects)     println Badge("new") endOutput<!doctype html><html lang="en" dir="ltr"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"><title>Inbox of Sara</title></head><body><h1>Hello, Sara</h1><p>Unread: 2</p><ul><li>1. Meeting at 10</li><li>2. &lt;b&gt;FREE&lt;/b&gt; prize &amp; more</li></ul></body></html> <style>.badge-a{background:#fde68a}</style><span class="badge-a">new</span>  Notes  Browser features (forms behavior, media APIs, scrolling, clipboard, storage, etc.) are web-environment specific. Interactive pages rely on the page script running in the browser. For browserless native windows, see Layout in native apps.

Layout language Running the same layout DSL as a native desktop app with --ui=native and Salam's UI engine, and how it differs from web/WebView The same layout DSL can run in a native window instead of a browser. With --ui=native, Salam renders the UI using its own UI engine (no browser engine). This lesson explains the native path, what stays the same, and what differs from web. Run and build natively To run a layout as a native window: salam run app.salam --ui=native salam build app.salam --ui=native run launches the app; build produces a native executable. This uses the layout DSL but targets Salam's native UI runtime instead of generating browser HTML/CSS/JS files.  What stays the same  Tree structure of pages/elements and nesting Attributes and style properties (including simpler values like 50% and #hex) Components (component/بخش), parameters, conditionals/loops in dynamic layouts, and overall DSL patterns  The goal is to share much of the UI description, while runtime behavior and supported features depend on the target engine.  Differences and limitations vs web The native target is not a browser, so web-specific features may be unavailable or behave differently. Elements/capabilities tied to the browser DOM/runtime (such as raw browser scripts, iframes, some web-only media/embed features, or HTML document APIs) do not map the same way. The compiler can report errors/warnings for features not supported in native UI targets. For native interactivity, use patterns and APIs supported by Salam's UI runtime and keep application logic in Salam code as appropriate for the target.  Desktop paths in Salam  Native DSL (--ui=native): UI rendered by Salam's engine; useful when you want a browserless native UI. WebView (gui.webview): a native window hosting HTML/CSS/JS content (Tauri/Electron-like model); useful when you want web tech inside a desktop shell. Other graphics libraries: such as gui.raylib for games/rendering-specific use cases.   For browser output and web deployment, see Layout on the web. For WebView APIs and packaging, see gui.webview docs.

Web pages The shape of a page, headings, paragraphs, line breaks and every text level element: emphasis, quotes, code, edits, dates, abbreviations and mixed direction text Most of a web page is text, and HTML has an element for every kind of text: a heading, a paragraph, a quotation, a piece of code, a date. In Salam you write them with plain readable names and the compiler turns them into the HTML tags. This lesson shows each one with an example you can run. The shape of a page A page: block holds everything on the page. Before the first element you can set things that belong to the page itself: title is the text on the browser tab, lang and dir say which language and which direction the text has, and background, color and the other style properties at that level paint the whole page. Everything else is an element. An element opens with its name and a colon and closes with end, and what goes between is attributes and child elements, written as name = value with no commas. The text of an element is its content attribute. It is always plain text: a < or an & in it is shown as it is and never becomes markup, so text that comes from a user can never break the page. Put several words in one string, or build a string with + from constants and numbers. web-text-article.salamCopypage:     title = "A short article"     global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" max width = 34rem margin = 2rem , auto line height = 1.6 end     heading group:         h1: content = "Why we write pages in Salam" end         paragraph:             content = "Published "             time: datetime = "2026-10-26" content = "26 October 2026" end         end     end     paragraph: content = "A page is a tree of elements. Each element has a name, some attributes and sometimes children." end     heading: size = 2 content = "One language" end     paragraph: content = "The page and the program that serves it are written in the same language, so a name that is wrong is found while compiling." end     line: end     small: content = "Written for the Salam course." end end The preview above is the real page the compiler built. The global line is a style rule for the whole page, and you will meet it again in the CSS lessons; here it only gives the page a readable font and a comfortable width.  Headings Headings give a page its outline. heading takes a size from 1 to 6, and h1 to h6 are the same thing under their HTML names. Use a single level 1 for the title of the page and then go down one level at a time: a level 3 belongs under a level 2, not directly under a level 1. Browsers draw the levels in decreasing sizes, but choose the level for its meaning and change the size with CSS. When a heading has a subtitle, wrap both in a heading group as the example above does.  Paragraphs, breaks and rules paragraph is a block of text, and browsers leave space above and below it. Inside a paragraph, break starts a new line, which is right for an address or a poem and wrong as a way to add space, because empty space is a job for CSS. line draws a horizontal rule between two topics, and word break marks where a long word may be cut if it does not fit. A paragraph can hold child elements next to its own content. The content text always comes first, and the children follow in the order you write them. So a sentence with a bold word in the middle is written as the first part in content, then the bold element, then a span with the rest. The span is a neutral container: it adds no meaning and no look of its own, which makes it the element for styling a few words.  Emphasis and inline text Inline elements live inside a line of text. Several of them look alike in the browser and differ in meaning, and the meaning is what screen readers and search engines use. strong is important text and bold is only bold type. emphasis is stress, the word you say louder, and italic is a different voice, such as a foreign word. mark highlights what is relevant right now, strikethrough shows what is no longer true, and small is for small print. subscript and superscript raise and lower text for formulas. code, keyboard, sample and variable are the four ways to write about computers. web-text-inline.salamCopypage:     title = "Inline text"     global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = 1.5rem line height = 1.7 end     paragraph:         content = "Water is H"         subscript: content = "2" end         span: content = "O and energy is E = mc" end         superscript: content = "2" end         span: content = ". " end         strong: content = "Do not" end         span: content = " drink the " end         emphasis: content = "second" end         span: content = " glass. Press " end         keyboard: conte

Web pages Landmarks such as header, nav, main and footer, then lists, definition lists, details, dialogs, figures and addresses, and how to build a whole blog page from them A page that only uses boxes looks fine in a browser and is a maze for everyone who cannot see it. This lesson shows the elements that name the parts of a page, the elements for lists, and the ones for things that open and close, and it ends with a complete blog page built from them. Boxes and landmarks box and span are the generic containers. A box is a block, it starts on a new line and takes the full width. A span sits inside a line of text. Neither one says anything about its content, so they are the right tools when the only reason for the container is styling. When a part of the page has a job, there is an element that names it. header holds the introduction, nav a group of navigation links, main the content the page is about, aside something related but separate, and footer the closing part. section is a themed group of content that usually starts with a heading, article is a piece that makes sense alone, such as a post or a comment, and search wraps the controls for searching. Browsers draw all of them like a plain box. The difference is for the people who cannot see the page: a screen reader lists these parts as landmarks and lets its user jump to the main content or to the navigation in one key press. Search engines read the outline in the same way. web-structure-landmarks.salamCopypage:     title = "Landmarks"     global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = 0 line height = 1.5 end     header: background = #0f766e color = "white" padding = 10px, 20px         h1: content = "Garden Notes" margin = 0 font size = "1.3rem" end     end     nav: background = #ccfbf1 padding = 8px, 20px display = flex gap = 16         link: url = "#soil" content = "Soil" end         link: url = "#water" content = "Water" end     end     box: display = flex gap = 20 padding = 20         main: flex = 1             section: id = "soil"                 heading: size = 2 content = "Soil" end                 paragraph: content = "Dig in compost before you plant." end             end             section: id = "water"                 heading: size = 2 content = "Water" end                 paragraph: content = "Water early, when the air is cool." end             end         end         aside: width = 160 background = #f1f5f9 padding = 12 border radius = 8             strong: content = "Tip" end             paragraph: content = "A thick layer of mulch keeps the soil damp." end         end     end     footer: padding = 10px, 20px border top = "1px solid #cbd5e1" color = #475569         small: content = "Garden Notes, written by hand." end     end end The example puts a header and a nav above, then a main with two sections and an aside next to it, then a footer. The id on each section is what the links #soil and #water point to: a link that starts with # scrolls to the element with that id. The display = flex and gap lines are CSS and are explained in the CSS lessons. A page can have only one main, and it cannot sit inside an article. The compiler reports an error for a second one (E120). It also refuses a header or a footer inside another header or footer, and an address inside an address. A header or footer inside an article or a section is fine: it then belongs to that part and not to the whole page. When a page has two nav elements, tell them apart with aria label, for example aria label = "Main", so that a screen reader can announce which one it is on.  Lists list is a bullet list. ordered list is a numbered one, for steps and rankings where the order matters. Only item elements can sit directly inside a list, and an item holds the text of the entry in its content. To nest a list, put it inside an item, after the content, as the example does under Olives. Browsers use a different marker for each level. web-structure-lists.salamCopypage:     title = "Lists"     global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = 1.5rem line height = 1.6 end     heading: size = 2 content = "Shopping" end     list:         item: content = "Bread" end         item:             content = "Olives"             list:                 item: content = "Green" end                 item: content = "Black" end             end         end         item: content = "Tea" end     end     heading: size = 2 content = "Countdown" end     ordered list: reversed = true         item: content = "Mix the dough" end         item: content = "Let it rise" end         item: content = "Bake" end     end     heading: size = 2 content =

Web pages Links and anchors, images with alt text and responsive sources, image maps, audio and video with subtitles, frames, embeds, canvas, SVG and math A page is more than text: it links to other pages, shows pictures, plays sound and video and draws shapes. This lesson covers the elements for all of that, and the attributes that make them fast, accessible and safe. Links A link takes the reader somewhere. Its url is required and its content is the text the reader clicks. The address can point to another site, to a file next to your page, or to a place on the same page: a url that starts with # scrolls to the element whose id is the rest of it. Two more kinds are worth knowing. mailto: opens the mail program with a new message, and tel: offers to call the number on a phone. web-media-links.salamCopypage:     title = "Links"     global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = 1.5rem line height = 1.8 end     paragraph:         content = "Read the "         link: url = "#rules" content = "house rules" end         span: content = " first, then write to " end         link: url = "mailto:club@example.com" content = "the club" end         span: content = " or call " end         link: url = "tel:+15550100" content = "555 0100" end         span: content = "." end     end     paragraph:         link: url = "https://example.com/guide" target = "new" rel = "noopener" content = "The full guide (new tab)" end     end     paragraph:         link:             url = "maps/garden.pdf"             download = "garden-map.pdf"             type = "application/pdf"             hreflang = "en"             content = "Download the garden map"         end     end     heading: id = "rules" size = 2 content = "House rules" end     paragraph: content = "Keep the gate closed. Water the beds in the morning." end end The attributes in the example each do one job. target says where the page opens: new is a new tab (the HTML word is _blank, and both work), same is the current tab, and parent and top matter only inside frames. rel describes the relationship to the target. With noopener the new tab cannot reach back to your page, which matters for a link to a site you do not control, and nofollow asks search engines not to count the link. download makes the browser save the file instead of showing it, and its value is the suggested file name. type is the kind of file you expect and hreflang the language of the target page. Both are hints. ping lists addresses that are told when someone follows the link, and referrer policy controls how much of your address the target site is given. Write link text that makes sense on its own, such as "the house rules", and not "click here": screen readers can read out a list of all the links on a page. A link cannot contain another link or a button, and the compiler reports an error (E116) if you try. It also refuses addresses like javascript: that would run code (E018).  Images image shows a picture. The url is required. The text description is the alt attribute, and content sets the same attribute, so you can write whichever reads better. The description is what a screen reader says and what the browser shows when the file cannot be loaded. Describe what the picture tells, not what it is: "A red kite over green hills", not "image". If the picture is only decoration, give it an empty description, alt = "", and screen readers will skip it. When you give neither, the compiler writes the empty one for you. web-media-image.salamCopypage:     title = "Images"     global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = 1.5rem end     paragraph: content = "A photo with a description:" end     image:         content = "A red kite flying over green hills"         width = 160         height = 100         loading = lazy         decoding = async         url = "data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns=%27http://www.w3.org/2000/svg%27%20viewBox=%270%200%20160%20100%27%20width=%27160%27%20height=%27100%27%3E%3Crect%20width=%27160%27%20height=%27100%27%20fill=%27%23bae6fd%27/%3E%3Cpath%20d=%27M0%20100%20Q50%2055%20100%2085%20T160%2075%20V100Z%27%20fill=%27%2316a34a%27/%3E%3Cpath%20d=%27M110%2012%20L130%2032%20L110%2052%20L90%2032Z%27%20fill=%27%23dc2626%27/%3E%3Cpath%20d=%27M110%2052%20Q100%2070%20112%2082%27%20stroke=%27%23475569%27%20fill=%27none%27/%3E%3Ctext%20x=%276%27%20y=%2714%27%20font-size=%2711%27%20font-family=%27sans-serif%27%20fill=%27%230c4a6e%27%3E%3C/text%3E%3C/svg%3E"     end     paragraph: content = "A decorative picture has an empty description:" end     image: alt = "" width = 80 height = 50 url = "data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns=%27htt

Web pages Tables for data: caption, header, body and footer sections, heading cells with scope, spanning cells, column groups, and how to style and scroll a table A table is the right element when your data has rows and columns: prices, timetables, scores. This lesson shows how to build one that screen readers can follow, how to join cells, how to style whole columns, and how to keep a wide table usable on a small screen. When to use a table Use a table for data that you would also put in a spreadsheet: every cell means something because of its row and its column. A list of prices, a school timetable and a table of results are all tables. A page that has a menu on the left and text on the right is not: that is a job for layout with CSS, which the layout lesson teaches. Screen readers announce a table as a table and read each cell together with its headings, so a table used for layout makes the page harder to understand for the people who depend on them.  The parts of a table A table holds rows, and a row holds cells. A cell is written column in Salam. The name can mislead you: column is one cell (HTML td), and the rows are what make up the columns. Rows can go straight into the table, but real tables are split into three sections: header for the headings, main for the data and footer for totals. Inside a table these three words mean the HTML thead, tbody and tfoot. Outside a table the same words are the page header, the main part and the page footer, and the compiler picks the right one from where you wrote it. The caption is the title of the table. It must be the first thing inside the table: the compiler stops with an error if it is not. A table can have only one header and one footer, but as many main sections as you need to group rows. web-tables-basic.salamCopypage:     title = "Price list"     global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = 1.5rem end     global: selector = "th, td" padding = 8px , 14px border bottom = "1px solid #cbd5e1" text align = left end     global: selector = "table" border collapse = collapse end     table:         caption: content = "Fruit prices this week" end         header:             row:                 column: content = "Fruit" end                 column: content = "Kilos" end                 column: content = "Price" end             end         end         main:             row:                 column: content = "Apples" end                 column: content = "3" end                 column: content = "4.50" end             end             row:                 column: content = "Pears" end                 column: content = "2" end                 column: content = "3.20" end             end         end         footer:             row:                 column: content = "Total" end                 column: content = "5" end                 column: content = "7.70" end             end         end     end end Two global rules do the styling here. th, td selects every cell, and the rule gives them padding and a line under them. table with border collapse = collapse joins the lines of neighbouring cells into one. Without CSS a table has no borders at all, so every table you want to look like a table needs some. The cells of the header row became th without you asking. That is the context rule: a column inside header is a heading cell. Browsers draw heading cells in bold and centred, and, more important, they tell assistive technology that these cells are headings. The footer is different. It only holds data cells unless you say otherwise, so the word Total in the last row is plain here. The next section fixes that.  Heading cells and scope Headings are not only in the top row. When the first cell of every row names that row, it is a heading too. Write heading = true on a column and it becomes a th. The word heading here is an attribute of the cell, not the heading element of the text lesson. Then tell the browser which way the heading points with scope: col for a heading that describes the cells below it and row for one that describes the cells to its right. There are two more values for headings that cover a whole group of rows or columns: rowgroup and colgroup. For a simple table browsers guess the scope correctly, but writing it costs nothing and removes the guess. If a heading is long, give it a short form in abbr. A screen reader may read the short form when it repeats the heading for every cell, which saves the listener time. web-tables-scope.salamCopypage:     title = "Row and column headers"     global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end     global: selector = "th, td" padding = 8px, 16px border = 1px, solid, #cbd5e1 end     global: selector = "table" borde

Web pages Forms and every form control: labels, all the input types, validation, text areas, checkboxes, radio buttons, lists, buttons, output, progress and meters, files, and handling a submit in code A form is how a page listens. This lesson covers every form element and every input type, the attributes that make the browser check what was typed, and how to read the values in your own code. Each idea has a live example, and the examples that react to the visitor really work in the preview. The form and the submit A form holds controls and knows where to send them. action is the address that receives the data and method is how it travels: get puts the data into the address and suits searches, post puts it into the body of the request and is the right choice for everything that changes something or is private. When the form has a file input, add enctype = "multipart/form-data". The other form attributes are in the reference below: autocomplete, novalidate, target, rel, accept charset and name. A real send would leave the page, and the previews in this lesson must stay on it. So most examples here listen to the button and decide for themselves what happens. The click attribute of a submit button is a function that runs when the button is pressed. It receives the event, and dom.PreventDefault stops the default action, which is sending the form. That also skips the browser's checks, so the function asks for them: reportValidity checks every field and shows the browser's message at the first bad one, and as bool turns its answer into true or false. After that you read each field with dom.GetValue(dom.ById("id")) and use the text as you like. The event is the plain i64 parameter of the function. On a page of your own you can give the same function to the submit attribute of the form. The browser then runs its checks first and calls your function only when they pass, so reportValidity is not needed. web-forms-signup.salamCopyimport dom  func Join(e: i64):     dom.PreventDefault(e)     if dom.Call0(dom.ById("sign"), "reportValidity") as bool:         name := dom.GetValue(dom.ById("name"))         mail := dom.GetValue(dom.ById("mail"))         dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "Welcome, " + name + ". We will write to " + mail + ".")     end end  page:     title = "Sign up"     global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" max width = "24rem" end     global: selector = "label" display = block margin = 0.8rem, 0, 0.2rem end     global: selector = "input" padding = 6 width = 100% box sizing = "border-box" end     form: id = "sign"         label: for = "name" content = "Your name" end         input: id = "name" name = "name" required = true placeholder = "Ada Lovelace" end         label: for = "mail" content = "Email" end         input: id = "mail" name = "mail" type = email required = true placeholder = "ada@example.com" end         button: type = submit click = Join content = "Join" margin = 1rem, 0 padding = 6px, 18px end     end     paragraph: id = "out" color = #0f766e end end Leave the fields empty and press Join: the browser shows its message and nothing else happens, because reportValidity answered no. Write something that is not an address in the Email field and it refuses again. Only a complete form gets past the if, which is why you can trust the values inside it, at least as far as the browser checks go. Browser checks are for the visitor's comfort, not for security. Anyone can send a request without your page. Whatever your server receives has to be checked on the server again.  Labels Every control needs a label. Connect them in one of two ways. Give the control an id and write the same id in for of the label, as the sign up example does: Salam checks at compile time that an element with that id exists, so a typo cannot silently break the link. Or put the control inside the label, as the pizza example further down does, and no for is needed. Either way a click on the label text focuses the control or ticks the checkbox, and a screen reader reads the label when the control gets the focus. The placeholder attribute is not a label. It is a hint in the empty box, it vanishes when the visitor types and many people find the grey text hard to read. Use it for an example of the format, and keep the label.  Input types input is one element with many faces. Its type decides the face, the keyboard a phone shows, and what the browser checks. Without a type it is a text box. The table lists every type that Salam names, with its Persian name, which you use in Persian files. TypePersianWhat the visitor getsWhat the browser checks textمتنA one line box.Only minlength, maxlength and pattern. passwordگذ

Web pages The settings of the page, the head with meta and links, styles and scripts, templates and shadow trees, the attributes every element has, ARIA, data attributes and splitting a site into files A web page is more than what you see. It has a title, a language, a direction, descriptions for search engines, scripts, and a set of attributes that any element can carry. This lesson covers all of that: the head of the page, scripts and templates, the global attributes, ARIA for assistive technology, data attributes, and how to split a site into reusable parts. Settings of the page itself The first lines inside page:, before any element, describe the page and not something on it. title is the text on the browser tab, in bookmarks and in a search result. lang says which language the text is in, and the values are en, fa and ar. Screen readers choose their voice from it and browsers choose the right quotation marks and word breaks. dir sets the direction of the text: ltr or rtl, or the words left to right and right to left. favicon is the address of the small icon on the tab. A file written in English starts with lang = "en" and dir = "ltr", and a Persian file with fa and rtl, so you write these two only when the page differs from its file. Any style property written at this level, such as background, color or font family, styles the whole page body. web-head-settings.salamCopypage:     title = "Corner Bakery"     lang = "en"     dir = "ltr"     favicon = "/favicon.svg"     background = #fdf6ec     color = #3b2a1a     font family = "Georgia, serif"     padding = 28     meta: name = "description" content = "Fresh bread every morning." end     heading: size = 1 content = "Corner Bakery" end     paragraph: content = "Fresh bread every morning." end     paragraph: content = "The tab says Corner Bakery, the page language is English and the text runs left to right." end end The page does not show most of what you set here, so it is worth knowing what the compiler builds for you. Every page starts with <!doctype html>, then a head that holds <meta charset="utf-8">, which makes every letter of every language display correctly, and <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">, which tells phones to use the real screen width instead of pretending to be a wide desktop. You never have to write these two. Without a title, the tab says "Salam Page".  Meta tags, links and base Some elements describe the page and are never drawn. You can write them anywhere inside page:, and the compiler moves them into the head: meta, head link, base and style. meta carries a fact as a pair, name and content. A description is the summary under a search result. robots with noindex asks search engines to skip the page. theme-color colours the browser bar on a phone. For link previews in chat apps, the Open Graph protocol uses property instead of name: og:title, og:description, og:image. And http_equiv lets a tag behave like an HTTP header. head link connects the page to another address and names the relation in rel. stylesheet loads CSS, icon sets an icon, canonical says which address is the real one when the same page can be reached in several ways, preload asks the browser to start downloading a font or image early, and alternate with a hreflang points to the translation. Its address is url. The name has two words so that it does not clash with link, the clickable link in the body. base changes the address that all relative addresses start from. It can help a page that lives deep in a site, but it changes every relative link and file after it, so most pages leave it out. The example below puts a description and a canonical link in its head, and a button reads them back with dom.Query, which finds an element by a CSS selector, and dom.GetAttr, which reads one of its attributes. web-head-inspect.salamCopyimport dom  func readHead:     html := dom.Query("html")     dom.SetText(dom.ById("out-title"), "Title: " + dom.GetText(dom.Query("title")))     dom.SetText(dom.ById("out-lang"), "Language: " + dom.GetAttr(html, "lang"))     dom.SetText(dom.ById("out-desc"), "Description: " + dom.GetAttr(dom.Query("meta[name=description]"), "content"))     dom.SetText(dom.ById("out-canon"), "Canonical: " + dom.GetAttr(dom.Query("link[rel=canonical]"), "href")) end  page:     title = "Reading the head"     meta: name = "description" content = "A page that reads its own head." end     head link: rel = "canonical" url = "https://example.com/head" end     global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = 1.5rem end     button: click = readHead content = "Read the head" end

Web pages CSS from zero: style properties as attributes, values, units and colors, the box model, sizes, margins, display, overflow, CSS functions, global rules and reusable components CSS decides how every element looks and how much room it takes. In Salam you write each CSS property as an attribute, with spaces instead of dashes, and the compiler checks it before the page is built. This lesson starts from nothing: how values are written, how the box model measures an element, and the properties that control size, space, display and overflow. Style properties are attributes A style property is written exactly like any other attribute: name = value inside the element. Property names have spaces where CSS has dashes, so max-width is max width and border-radius is border radius. A misspelled name is a compile error, and the message suggests the nearest real one. The styles do not stay on the element. The compiler collects the styles of each element into one rule under a short generated class and puts the rules into the stylesheet. box: padding = 20 background = #eef end turns into <div class="a"> and the rule .a{padding:20px;background:#eef}. Elements whose styles are identical share one class, which keeps the page small. You can also give an element a class of your own, but a class name must mean one set of styles. If two elements use the same class with different styles, the compiler stops with error E136 instead of letting one silently override the other. Give each its own class, drop the class and let the compiler name it, or style the shared class once with a global rule (shown below).  Values Most values are one of four things. A bare number is pixels where a length is expected: padding = 24 is 24px, and 1.5 is 1.5px. Properties that take a plain number, such as line height and aspect ratio, keep it as a number. A string holds anything else: units, colors with #, several words. A keyword can be written without quotes: display = flex, overflow = hidden, color = white. And a function with simple arguments can be unquoted too, as in background = rgb(37, 99, 235). Several lengths in one string form a shorthand. padding = "8 40" is 8px 40px: the first number is for top and bottom, the second for left and right. Up to four values are allowed, and a number without a unit gets px while a number with a unit keeps it, so "1rem 2" is 1rem 2px. web-css-values.salamCopypage:     title = "Style values"     global: box sizing = "border-box" end     global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = 20 end     global: selector = "p" margin = 0, 0, 10px end     paragraph: content = "padding = 24" padding = 24 background = #e0f2fe end     paragraph: content = "padding = \"8 40\"" padding = 8, 40 background = #dcfce7 end     paragraph: content = "border = \"3px dashed #0f766e\"" padding = 12 border = 3px, dashed, #0f766e end     paragraph: content = "width = \"60%\"" padding = 12 width = 60% background = #fef9c3 end     paragraph:         content = "background = \"linear-gradient(90deg, ...)\""         padding = 12         color = white         background = "linear-gradient(90deg, #0f766e, #2563eb)"     end end Values can also be computed while compiling: padding = GAP * 2 + "px" uses a constant (the section on reuse below shows how it is declared), and + joins a number and a unit into text. Quote any value that has a #, a % or a unit inside a function, or a space-separated list. The compiler does not accept them bare, and calc() written without quotes is worse: it is accepted and silently becomes an empty calc(). Always write width = "calc(100% - 20px)".  Units A length is a number and a unit. The ones you will use all the time:  px: a CSS pixel. Good for borders and fine details. rem: the font size of the page, normally 16px. Sizes in rem grow when a reader raises the font size in the browser, so use it for text and spacing. em: the font size of the element itself, which makes a padding follow the text size of its own box. %: a share of the parent.
