AbsI, AbsI64, Gcd, GcdI64 and Lcm never return a negative or wrapped value. When the true answer does not fit, they return the largest value of the type: AbsI of the smallest int is 2147483647, and Lcm(65536, 65537) is 2147483647 too. Gcd and GcdI64 stay exact for the smallest value: GcdI64(-9223372036854775808, 4) is 4. Hypot squares its arguments directly, so values above about 1e154 give infinity.   Distances, angles and circles Most geometry in a program is a distance or a direction between two points. Hypot gives the straight line distance, and Atan2 gives the angle of a direction from all four quarters of the plane, which plain Atan cannot tell apart. Convert between degrees and radians at the edges of your program and keep radians inside it. math-guide-geometry.salamCopyimport math import fmt  func distance(x1: f64, y1: f64, x2: f64, y2: f64): f64:     ret math.Hypot(x2 - x1, y2 - y1) end  func heading(x1: f64, y1: f64, x2: f64, y2: f64): f64:     deg := math.Degrees(math.Atan2(y2 - y1, x2 - x1))     if deg < 0.0: ret deg + 360.0 end     ret deg end  func main:     println "distance:", distance(1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 6.0)     println "heading east:", heading(0.0, 0.0, 5.0, 0.0)     println "heading north:", heading(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 5.0)     println "heading south-west:", heading(0.0, 0.0, -3.0, -3.0)     r := 2.5     println "circle area:", fmt.FloatPrec(math.PI * math.Pow(r, 2.0), 2)     println "circumference:", fmt.FloatPrec(math.TAU * r, 2)     x := 10.0 * math.Cos(math.Radians(60.0))     y := 10.0 * math.Sin(math.Radians(60.0))     println "point at 60 degrees:", fmt.FloatPrec(x, 3), fmt.FloatPrec(y, 3) endOutputdistance: 5 heading east: 0 heading north: 90 heading south-west: 225 circle area: 19.63 circumference: 15.71 point at 60 degrees: 5.000 8.660 fmt.FloatPrec from fmt prints a number with a fixed count of decimals, which keeps results such as 8.660254037844386 readable.  Growth, loans and rounding Pow handles compound growth and Log answers the reverse question of how long it takes. To round to a number of decimal places, multiply by Pow10, round, and divide again. The last two lines show why: f64 cannot store 0.1 exactly, so sums of prices pick up tiny errors. math-guide-money.salamCopyimport math import fmt  func round_to(x: f64, places: int): f64:     scale := math.Pow10(places)     ret math.Round(x * scale) / scale end  func monthly_payment(principal: f64, yearly_rate: f64, months: int): f64:     r := yearly_rate / 12.0     ret principal * r / (1.0 - math.Pow(1.0 + r, -(months as f64))) end  func main:     mut balance := 1000.0     repeat 1 to 5 in year:         balance *= 1.06         println "year", year, fmt.FloatPrec(balance, 2)     end     println "after 5 years:", round_to(1000.0 * math.Pow(1.06, 5.0), 2)     println "doubling time at 6%:", fmt.FloatPrec(math.Log(2.0) / math.Log(1.06), 1), "years"     println "monthly payment:", fmt.FloatPrec(monthly_payment(20000.0, 0.18, 36), 2)     println "0.1 + 0.2 =", 0.1 + 0.2     println "rounded:", round_to(0.1 + 0.2, 2) endOutputyear 1 1060.00 year 2 1123.60 year 3 1191.02 year 4 1262.48 year 5 1338.23 after 5 years: 1338.23 doubling time at 6%: 11.9 years monthly payment: 723.05 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004 rounded: 0.3 For real money, where every cent must add up, use decimal instead of f64; the rounding trick above is fine for display and for estimates.  Whole numbers: Gcd and Lcm The greatest common divisor reduces fractions and finds the largest tile or package size that divides evenly; the least common multiple finds the next time two repeating events line up. Both work on int; GcdI64 takes 64-bit values. math-guide-fractions.salamCopyimport math import str  func show(n: int, d: int): str:     g := math.Gcd(math.AbsI(n), math.AbsI(d))     ret str.FromInt(n / g) + "/" + str.FromInt(d / g) end  func add(an: int, ad: int, bn: int, bd: int): str:     common := math.Lcm(ad, bd)     ret show(an * (common / ad) + bn * (common / bd), common) end  func main:     println "12/18 =", show(12, 18)     println "1/4 + 1/6 =", add(1, 4, 1, 6)     println "3/10 + 7/15 =", add(3, 10, 7, 15)     println "buses every 12 and 18 minutes meet every", math.Lcm(12, 18), "minutes"     tiles := math.Gcd(240, 180)     println "largest square tile for a 240 x 180 floor:", tiles     println "tiles needed:", (240 / tiles) * (180 / tiles) endOutput12/18 = 2/3 1/4 + 1/6 = 5/12 3/10 + 7/15 = 23/30 buses every 12 and 18 minutes meet every 36 minutes largest square tile for a 240 x 180 floor: 60 tiles needed: 12  Mean and spread by hand Min, Max, Pow and Sqrt are enough for a small summary of a list. For anything bigger, such as the median, percentiles or a correlation, the stats package already has the functions. math-guide-stats.salamCopyimport math

rand rand Random numbers, text and choices: dice, one-time codes, unique identifiers and shuffling a list. Numbers and collections The rand package makes everyday random values: a number in a range, a chance, a pick from a list, a shuffled order, a readable code and a UUID. Use it for games, simulations, sample data, load tests and identifiers that only need to be unique. For anything an attacker must not guess, use crypto; to summarise the numbers you drew (mean, spread, median), use stats. All functions share one generator: a 64-bit linear congruential generator (the state step of PCG, without its output permutation). It seeds itself from the clock the first time you use it, so a plain program already gets different numbers on each run. Two things change that:  Seed(n) starts from a fixed number, and the same seed always gives the same sequence. That is what a test or a reproducible simulation wants. SeedAuto reseeds from time.Now(), which counts whole seconds. Two programs started in the same second get the same numbers, so do not rely on it to give parallel workers different streams; seed each one with its own number instead.  What people get wrong most often:  Using it for secrets. The next value follows from the previous ones, and the state is seeded from a clock in seconds. Session tokens, reset links and API keys belong to crypto. Calling it on an empty input or a zero bound. IntN(0) and the Choice functions on an empty vector stop the program with modulo by zero. Treating text as letters. TextFrom and ChoiceChar pick bytes, so a Persian alphabet comes out as broken characters.  The generator is one global value with no lock. Threads that draw at the same time can get the same number; draw in one thread, or give each thread its own seeded run. The examples on this page print properties of the values, such as whether they fall in a range, rather than the values themselves, so the output is the same on every run.  Repeatable runs for tests A random program is hard to test because its output changes. Seed fixes the starting point, so the same seed always produces the same sequence. Seed once at the start of a test and compare the results with what you expect. Leave the seed out of the real program, which then seeds itself from the clock. A fixed seed only repeats on the same version of Salam, so compare properties or a whole run, not numbers copied from an old release. rand-guide-tests.salamCopyimport rand  func roll_dice(seed: i64, count: int): Vector<int>:     rand.Seed(seed)     mut out := Vector {} as Vector<int>     repeat count:         out.Push(rand.Int32Range(1, 6))     end     ret out end  func same(a: Vector<int>, b: Vector<int>): bool:     if a.Len() != b.Len(): ret false end     repeat a.Len() in i:         if a.Get(i) != b.Get(i): ret false end     end     ret true end  func main:     mut first := roll_dice(2026, 20)     mut second := roll_dice(2026, 20)     mut other := roll_dice(7, 20)     defer first.Free()     defer second.Free()     defer other.Free()     println "same seed, same rolls:", same(first, second)     println "other seed, same rolls:", same(first, other) endOutputsame seed, same rolls: true other seed, same rolls: false  Dice and simulations Int32Range gives a whole number with both ends included, which is exactly a die. Float gives a value from zero up to one, the building block of a Monte Carlo estimate: here, the share of random points that land inside a quarter circle gives an approximation of pi. With enough samples each face comes up close to one sixth of the time. rand-guide-simulation.salamCopyimport rand import math  func main:     rand.Seed(1)     mut faces := Vector {} as Vector<int>     defer faces.Free()     repeat 7:         faces.Push(0)     end     repeat 60000:         face := rand.Int32Range(1, 6)         faces.Set(face, faces.Get(face) + 1)     end     repeat 1 to 6 in face:         count := faces.Get(face)         println "face", face, "near 10000:", count > 9500 and count < 10500     end     mut inside := 0     total := 200000     repeat total:         x := rand.Float()         y := rand.Float()         if x * x + y * y < 1.0: inside++ end     end     estimate := 4.0 * (inside as f64) / (total as f64)     println "pi estimate within 0.01:", math.Abs(estimate - math.PI) < 0.01 endOutputface 1 near 10000: true face 2 near 10000: true face 3 near 10000: true face 4 near 10000: true face 5 near 10000: true face 6 near 10000: true pi estimate within 0.01: true  Raffles and weighted picks To pick several different winners, shuffle a copy with ShuffleStr and take the first few; the original vector stays as it was. For a weighted choice, such as loot that is common 80% of the time, draw a number in the range of the total weight and walk through the weights until it runs out. rand-guide-draw.salamCopyimport rand  func pick_weighted(names: Vector<str>, weights: Vector<f64>): str:     mut total := 0.0     each w in weights:         total += w     end     mut x := rand.FloatRange(0.0, total)     repeat names.Len() in i:         x -= weights.Get(i)         if x < 0.0: ret names.Get(i) end     end     ret names.Get(names.Len() - 1) end  func main:     rand.Seed(99)     mut entries := Vector {} as Vector<str>     defer entries.Free()     each name in ["Ali", "Sara", "Reza", "Mina", "Omid", "Neda"]:         entries.Push(name)     end     mut order := rand.ShuffleStr(entries)     defer order.Free()     winners := [order.Get(0), order.Get(1), order.Get(2)]     println "3 winners, all different:", winners[0] != winners[1] and winners[1] != winners[2] and winners[0] != winners[2]     println "entries untouched:", entries.Get(0), entries.Len()     mut loot := Vector {} as Vector<str>     mut weights := Vector {} as Vector<f64>     defer loot.Free()

stats stats Descriptive statistics over a list of numbers: mean, median, variance, standard deviation and percentiles. Numbers and collections The stats package answers the first questions you ask of a list of numbers: how many, the total, the typical value, the spread and the extremes. Use it for reports, monitoring (latency percentiles), grading and checking a simulation. It covers descriptive statistics only; there is no mode, correlation, regression or histogram. For scalar maths use math, for fitting models ml, and to generate the numbers in the first place rand. Every function takes a Vector<f64> and never changes it. Whole numbers have to be converted with as f64 on the way in. Median and Percentile sort a private copy on each call, so asking for p50, p90 and p99 sorts three times; that is fine for thousands of values and worth knowing for millions. Variance and standard deviation come in two forms. Variance and Stdev treat the data as a sample of a larger group and divide by n−1; PopVariance and PopStdev treat it as the whole group and divide by n. The sample form is the usual choice. What people get wrong:  Trusting the result of an empty list. Nothing fails: Mean, Median, Min, Max and Percentile return 0, which looks like real data. Check len() first. Reporting the mean of skewed data. One slow request or one very rich customer moves the mean a long way; the median and percentiles do not move. Averaging growth rates with Mean. Factors that multiply need Geomean.   A summary of a class The usual job is a short report on a list of numbers: how many, the middle, the spread and the extremes. Put the values in a Vector<f64> once and call the functions you need; none of them changes the vector. The standard deviation also lets you flag values that are far from the rest: a value more than one standard deviation from the mean is unusual in a small group. stats-guide-report.salamCopyimport stats import conv  func main:     names := ["Sara", "Reza", "Mina", "Ali", "Neda", "Omid", "Leila"]     mut scores := Vector {} as Vector<f64>     defer scores.Free()     each s in [14.5, 17.0, 19.5, 11.0, 16.0, 8.5, 18.0]:         scores.Push(s)     end     mean := stats.Mean(scores)     sd := stats.Stdev(scores)     println "students:", scores.Len()     println "mean:    ", conv.FormatFloatPrec(mean, 2)     println "median:  ", stats.Median(scores)     println "stdev:   ", conv.FormatFloatPrec(sd, 2)     println "range:   ", stats.Min(scores), "to", stats.Max(scores)     println "top 25%: ", stats.Percentile(scores, 75.0), "and above"     each i, name in names:         z := (scores.Get(i) - mean) / sd         if z > 1.0:             println name, "is well above the class:", conv.FormatFloatPrec(z, 2)         else z < -1.0:             println name, "needs help:", conv.FormatFloatPrec(z, 2)         end     end endOutputstudents: 7 mean:     14.93 median:   16 stdev:    3.93 range:    8.5 to 19.5 top 25%:  17.5 and above Mina is well above the class: 1.16 Omid needs help: -1.64 A class or a survey is usually a sample, so Stdev is the right choice. Use PopStdev only when the list holds every member of the group you are describing, for example all the machines in a cluster.  Response times: median and percentiles One slow request can pull the mean far away from what most users see. In this example nine requests take about 40 ms and one takes 1200 ms; the mean says 157 ms, while the median (the 50th percentile) says 41.5 ms. Monitoring therefore uses percentiles: p90 is the time 90% of requests stay under, and p99 shows the worst cases. stats-guide-latency.salamCopyimport stats import conv  func show(label: str, x: f64):     println label, conv.FormatFloatPrec(x, 1), "ms" end  func main:     mut ms := Vector {} as Vector<f64>     defer ms.Free()     each t in [42.0, 38.0, 45.0, 40.0, 39.0, 41.0, 44.0, 37.0, 43.0, 1200.0]:         ms.Push(t)     end     show("mean:", stats.Mean(ms))     show("p50: ", stats.Percentile(ms, 50.0))     show("p90: ", stats.Percentile(ms, 90.0))     show("p99: ", stats.Percentile(ms, 99.0))     show("max: ", stats.Max(ms))     budget := 100.0     if stats.Percentile(ms, 90.0) > budget:         println "alert: p90 is over the budget of", budget, "ms"     else:         println "p90 is within the budget"     end endOutputmean: 156.9 ms p50:  41.5 ms p90:  160.5 ms p99:  1096.1 ms max:  1200.0 ms alert: p90 is over the budget of 100 ms Percentile interpolates between the two nearest values, so with few samples the high percentiles land between a normal value and the outlier. Collect a few hundred values before you trust p99.  Growth rates and the geometric mean When values are multiplied, as with yearly returns or growth factors, the arithmetic mean overstates the result. A gain of 50% followed by a loss of 40% is not an average gain. Geomean gives the single factor that, repeated, reaches the same end value. stats-guide-growth.salamCopyimport stats import conv  func main:     mut factors := Vector {} as Vector<f64>     defer factors.Free()     each f in [1.50, 0.60, 1.20, 1.10]:         factors.Push(f)     end     mut value := 1000.0     each f in factors:         value *= f     end     println "after four years:", conv.FormatFloatPrec(value, 2)     arith := stats.Mean(factors)     geo := stats.Geomean(factors)     println "arithmetic mean factor:", conv.FormatFloatPrec(arith, 4)     println "geometric mean factor: ", conv.FormatFloatPrec(geo, 4)     mut a := 1000.0     mut g := 1000.0     repeat 4:         a *= arith         g *= geo     end     println "replayed with the arithmetic mean:", conv.FormatFloatPrec(a, 2)     println "replayed w

types types Recognising the type of a value from its text: a whole number, a decimal, a boolean or ordinary text? Numbers and collections When data arrives from a CSV file, a form, an environment variable or the command line, everything is text. The types package says what kind of value a piece of text looks like, so you can decide before you convert it. It does not convert anything: once a check passes, conv does the parsing. For whole documents with their own typing rules use encoding.json or encoding.csv. The checks trim spaces first and turn Persian and Arabic digits into English ones, so  ۳۴  is a whole number. A kind is one of five int constants: null (empty text), bool, int, float and string. KindOf tries them in that order, so true is a bool and 12 is an int, never a float. What people get wrong:  Thinking a check means the value fits. IsInt looks only at the characters, so a 20-digit number passes and then conv.ParseInt throws OutOfRange on it. Expecting yes, 1 or on to be a bool. Only true and false count, in any letter case. Expecting blank text to be null. Only text of length zero is TypeKindNull; three spaces are a string.   Check form input before converting it A form field is text, and conv.ParseInt throws a Syntax error on bad text such as 12abc or abc. The checks here answer the same question without an error to catch: IsInt, IsNumeric and IsBool say whether the conversion makes sense, so you can show the user a clear message first. Persian digits pass the checks, and the parsers in conv read them too; this example still runs str.ToEnglishDigits so the text it keeps is plain ASCII. The Persian decimal separator ٫ is accepted by IsNumeric and is not changed by ToEnglishDigits, so replace it with a dot yourself. types-guide-form.salamCopyimport str import conv import types  func main throws:     age := "۳۴"     price := "۱۲٫۵"     count := "12.0"     subscribe := " Yes "     if types.IsInt(age):         println "age:", try conv.ParseInt(str.ToEnglishDigits(age))     end     if types.IsNumeric(price):         clean := str.Replace(str.ToEnglishDigits(price), "٫", ".")         println "price:", (try conv.ParseFloat(clean)) * 2.0, "for two"     end     if types.IsInt(count) == false:         println "count must be a whole number, got", count, "which is", types.KindName(types.KindOf(count))     end     if types.IsBool(subscribe) == false:         println "subscribe must be true or false, got [" + subscribe + "]"     end endOutputage: 34 price: 25 for two count must be a whole number, got 12.0 which is float subscribe must be true or false, got [ Yes ] The checks are strict about the characters: 12.0 is a decimal, not a whole number, and Yes is not a bool. Spaces around a value are ignored by the checks, and conv.ParseInt ignores them too, but trim the text yourself before you store it.  Branch on the kind of a value KindOf returns one of the five TypeKind constants, which suits a switch. Empty text has its own kind, TypeKindNull, so a missing value can fall back to a default rather than being treated as text. Scientific notation such as 1e3 counts as a decimal. types-guide-config.salamCopyimport str import types  func main:     lines := ["port = 8080", "ratio = 0.75", "debug = false", "name = shop", "retries = -3", "timeout =", "limit = 1e3"]     each line in lines:         parts := str.Split(line, "=")         key := str.Trim(parts.Get(0))         value := str.Trim(parts.Get(1))         k := types.KindOf(value)         switch k:             types.TypeKindInt:                 println key, "is a whole number:", value                 break             end             types.TypeKindFloat:                 println key, "is a decimal:", value                 break             end             types.TypeKindBool:                 println key, "is a switch:", str.Lower(value)                 break             end             types.TypeKindNull:                 println key, "has no value, the default is used"                 break             end             else:                 println key, "is text:", value             end         end     end endOutputport is a whole number: 8080 ratio is a decimal: 0.75 debug is a switch: false name is text: shop retries is a whole number: -3 timeout has no value, the default is used limit is a decimal: 1e3  Guess the type of CSV columns Before you import a CSV file into a database you need a type for each column. Look at every cell and widen the guess as you go: whole numbers and decimals together make a decimal column, any text makes a text column, and empty cells do not change the guess. KindName turns the result into a name for a report or a CREATE TABLE statement. types-guide-columns.salamCopyimport str import types  func widen(old: int, cell: str): int:     k := types.KindOf(str.Trim(cell))     if k == types.TypeKindNull: ret old end     if old == types.TypeKindNull or old == k: ret k end     if (old == types.TypeKindInt and k == types.TypeKindFloat) or (old == types.TypeKindFloat and k == types.TypeKindInt):         ret types.TypeKindFloat     end     ret types.TypeKindStr end  func main:     rows := ["id,name,price,stock,active", "1,Tea,4.5,120,true", "2,Coffee,7,,false", "3,Cocoa,5.25,80,TRUE", "4,Mate,6,n/a,true"]     header := str.Split(rows[0], ",")     mut kinds := Vector {} as Vector<int>     defer kinds.Free()     repeat header.Len():         kinds.Push(types.TypeKindNull)     end     repeat 1 to rows.Len() - 1 in r:         cells := str.Split(rows[r], ",")         each c, cell in cells:             kinds.Set(c, widen(kinds.Get(c), cell))         end     end     each c, name in header:         pri

bigint bigint Whole numbers of unlimited size: large factorials, cryptography, and any arithmetic that will not fit in 64 bits. Numbers and collections An i64 stops at about 9.2 × 1018 and wraps around without warning. bigint.Int is a whole number whose size is limited only by memory: use it for factorials and combinatorics, exact counters that can grow without bound, token amounts in their smallest unit, and number theory such as modular exponentiation. For money with a fixed number of decimal places use decimal, and for real keys and signatures use crypto. A number is a sign and a vector of 32-bit limbs. Multiplication is the schoolbook method and conversion to text divides repeatedly, so numbers of a few thousand digits are quick and numbers of a million digits are slow. Most functions return a new number and leave their arguments alone. The ones whose names end in To, From or By, such as AddTo, store the result in their first argument and free its old value for you. They still allocate the new value, so they are not faster; what they save is the bookkeeping of freeing every intermediate result. Release a number you no longer need with Free. What people get wrong:  Copying with =. b := a copies only the header, so both names share one set of limbs, and the next in-place call on b frees the memory a still points to. Use Clone for a second, independent number. Dividing by zero. Div, Rem, Mod and ModExp do not stop the program; they return 0. When the divisor can be zero, use DivMod, which returns false. Expecting an error for impossible input. A negative exponent in Pow, the square root of a negative number and the factorial of a negative number all return 0, and ToStrBase with a base outside 2 to 36 returns empty text.   Past the end of i64 The 93rd Fibonacci number is the first one that does not fit in an i64; with ordinary integers it would wrap around to a negative value without warning. With bigint.Int the loop just keeps going. ToInt converts back and tells you, through its bool argument, whether the value fitted, so you can move to plain integers when the numbers are small again. bigint-guide-fibonacci.salamCopyimport bigint import str  func main:     mut a := bigint.Zero()     mut b := bigint.One()     repeat 1 to 300 in n:         next := bigint.Add(a, b)         bigint.Free(a)         a = b         b = next         if n == 92 or n == 93:             mut fits := false             v := bigint.ToInt(a, fits)             println "F(" + str.FromInt(n) + ") =", bigint.ToStr(a), "fits in i64:", fits, v         end     end     text := bigint.ToStr(a)     println "F(300) has", text.Len(), "digits"     println text     bigint.Free(a)     bigint.Free(b) endOutputF(92) = 7540113804746346429 fits in i64: true 7540113804746346429 F(93) = 12200160415121876738 fits in i64: false 0 F(300) has 63 digits 222232244629420445529739893461909967206666939096499764990979600 Each Add returns a new number, so the loop frees the value it no longer needs before it moves the names along. Without the Free calls the program would still be correct, but it would keep every intermediate number in memory.  Updating one number in a loop A loop that updates one number with Add has to free the old value on every step, as the Fibonacci loop above does. MulIntBy, AddTo, ShlBy and the other functions named with To, From or By do that for you: they put the result into their first argument and free what was there. Build the result in one variable and free it once at the end. bigint-guide-inplace.salamCopyimport bigint  func main:     mut product := bigint.One()     defer bigint.Free(product)     repeat 1 to 50 in i:         bigint.MulIntBy(product, i as i64)     end     mut check := bigint.Factorial(50)     defer bigint.Free(check)     println "50! =", bigint.ToStr(product)     println "same as Factorial(50):", bigint.Equals(product, check)     mut total := bigint.Zero()     defer bigint.Free(total)     mut power := bigint.One()     defer bigint.Free(power)     repeat 64:         bigint.AddTo(total, power)         bigint.ShlBy(power, 1)     end     println "1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 2^63 =", bigint.ToStr(total)     println "that is 2^64 - 1:", bigint.Equals(total, bigint.SubInt(power, 1)) endOutput50! = 30414093201713378043612608166064768844377641568960512000000000000 same as Factorial(50): true 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 2^63 = 18446744073709551615 that is 2^64 - 1: true  Copies and snapshots To keep an old value while you change the number, take a copy with Clone. A plain opening := balance would not work: both names would share the same limbs, and the first AddIntTo would free them under opening, which then prints garbage. Each clone is its own allocation and needs its own Free. bigint-guide-copy.salamCopyimport bigint  func main:     mut ok := false     mut balance := bigint.Parse("900000000000000000000", ok)     mut opening := bigint.Clone(balance)     defer bigint.Free(balance)     defer bigint.Free(opening)     bigint.AddIntTo(balance, 250 as i64)     bigint.MulIntBy(balance, 2 as i64)     println "opening:", bigint.ToStr(opening)     println "now:    ", bigint.ToStr(balance)     mut gain := bigint.Sub(balance, opening)     defer bigint.Free(gain)     println "gain:   ", bigint.ToStr(gain) endOutputopening: 900000000000000000000 now:     1800000000000000000500 gain:    900000000000000000500  Digits of very large numbers ToStr gives the decimal text, so its length is the number of digits. DivModInt divides by an ordinary integer and puts the remainder into an i64, which is the way to walk through the digits one by one, here to add them up. TrailingZeros counts zero bits, not decimal zeros. bigint-guide-digits.salamCopyimport bigint  func digit_sum(x: bigint.Int): i64:     mut rest := bigint.Clone(x)     defer bigint.Free(rest)     mut sum := 0 as i64     until bigint.IsZero(rest) == false:         mut d

decimal decimal Exact decimal numbers for money and accounting, with none of the rounding error of floating point. Numbers and collections In f64, 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3. For science and graphics that tiny error does not matter; for money it does, because a lost cent in the accounts is not acceptable. The decimal package keeps a number as a bigint and a scale, the count of digits after the point, so 10.05 is 1005 with scale 2 and no error can creep in. Use it for prices, invoices, balances, tax and interest. Use f64 and math for measurements and statistics, and plain i64 cents when every amount has the same two places and never exceeds about 92 quadrillion. Addition, subtraction and multiplication are always exact. The scale of a sum is the larger of the two, and the scale of a product is the two added together. Division may not terminate, as one third does not, so Div takes the number of places you want and a Rounding method. Seven methods are offered; accounting usually wants HalfEven, and customer-facing totals often HalfUp. What people get wrong:  Letting the scale grow. Each Mul adds the scales together, so a balance multiplied by a rate every month carries more digits each time. Round to cents after every step that a statement shows. Expecting school rounding from the formatters. ToStrFixed, FormatGrouped, Round and Percent round half to even, so 2.345 shows as 2.34. Call RoundHalfUp first when you want 2.35. Dividing by zero. Div, DivRound and DivInt return 0 instead of stopping the program, so check the divisor yourself. Copying with =. A Dec holds a bigint.Int, so b := a shares its digits; use Clone for an independent copy, and free each number once.   Why not f64? Adding 0.1 ten times in f64 gives 0.9999999999999999, because 0.1 has no exact binary form. The same loop with Dec gives exactly 1.0. Build amounts from text with Parse or from whole cents with FromScaled; FromFloat works when you already have an f64, as long as you say how many places it should keep. decimal-guide-float.salamCopyimport decimal  func main:     mut f := 0.0     repeat 10:         f += 0.1     end     println "f64 sum of ten 0.1:", f, f == 1.0      mut d := decimal.Zero()     tenth := decimal.FromScaled(1, 1)     repeat 10:         d = decimal.Add(d, tenth)     end     println "decimal sum of ten 0.1:", decimal.ToStr(d), decimal.Equals(d, decimal.FromInt(1))      price := decimal.FromFloat(19.99, 2)     println "19.99 from f64:", decimal.ToStr(price)     println "times 3:", decimal.ToStr(decimal.MulInt(price, 3)) endOutputf64 sum of ten 0.1: 0.9999999999999999 false decimal sum of ten 0.1: 1.0 true 19.99 from f64: 19.99 times 3: 59.97  An invoice with discount and tax Prices usually come from a database or a form as text, so Parse is the natural start. MulInt multiplies by a quantity without any rounding, and Percent takes a percentage and rounds the result to the places you ask for, half to even. Print with ToStrFixed so that 12 shows as 12.00, or with FormatGrouped for thousands separators. decimal-guide-invoice.salamCopyimport decimal  struct Line:     pub name: str = ""     pub price: str = ""     pub qty: int = 0 end  func main:     mut lines := Vector {} as Vector<Line>     defer lines.Free()     lines.Push(Line { name = "Notebook", price = "4.75", qty = 3 })     lines.Push(Line { name = "Pen", price = "1.20", qty = 10 })     lines.Push(Line { name = "Backpack", price = "39.90", qty = 1 })      mut subtotal := decimal.Zero()     each l in lines:         mut ok := false         unit := decimal.Parse(l.price, ok)         amount := decimal.MulInt(unit, l.qty as i64)         println l.name, l.qty, "x", decimal.ToStrFixed(unit, 2), "=", decimal.ToStrFixed(amount, 2)         subtotal = decimal.Add(subtotal, amount)     end      discount := decimal.Percent(subtotal, decimal.FromInt(5), 2)     taxable := decimal.Sub(subtotal, discount)     tax := decimal.Percent(taxable, decimal.FromScaled(95, 1), 2)     total := decimal.Add(taxable, tax)     println "subtotal", decimal.ToStrFixed(subtotal, 2)     println "discount 5%", decimal.ToStrFixed(discount, 2)     println "tax 9.5%", decimal.ToStrFixed(tax, 2)     println "total", decimal.FormatGrouped(total, 2, ",", ".") endOutputNotebook 3 x 4.75 = 14.25 Pen 10 x 1.20 = 12.00 Backpack 1 x 39.90 = 39.90 subtotal 66.15 discount 5% 3.31 tax 9.5% 5.97 total 68.81 Round once per step that a real invoice shows (the discount, the tax), not at the very end only. Customers and tax offices check each printed line, so each line must already be in cents. The example does not free its numbers to stay short; a long-running server should Free each one, as the split example does.  Interest and the cost of rounding A bank pays interest in whole cents every year, and those rounded cents then earn interest themselves. The example runs five years with yearly rounding and compares the result with the exact formula: the difference is one cent. Div and DivInt always ask for the number of places and a Rounding method, because a division such as one twelfth has no end. decimal-guide-interest.salamCopyimport decimal  func main:     mut balance := decimal.FromInt(10000)     rate := decimal.FromScaled(15, 3)     one := decimal.FromInt(1)     repeat 1 to 5 in year:         interest := decimal.Round(decimal.Mul(balance, rate), 2)         balance = decimal.Add(balance, interest)         println "year", year, "interest", decimal.ToStrFixed(interest, 2), "balance", decimal.FormatGrouped(balance, 2, ",", ".")     end      factor := decimal.Pow(decimal.Add(one, rate), 5)     exact := decimal.Mul(decimal.FromInt(10000), factor)     println "without yearly rounding", decimal.ToStr(exact)     println "rounded", decimal.ToS

sort sort Sorting vectors with the default or your own comparison, binary search, and a dozen sorting algorithms to learn from. Numbers and collections The sort package orders a Vector and searches one that is already in order. For most work two functions are enough: Sort for numbers and strings, and SortBy when you decide yourself what "smaller" means, students by their marks for instance. Every function is generic, so it works for any element type that supports <, or for any type at all with a comparison of your own. For containers that stay sorted as you add to them (an ordered map, a priority queue) see collections; for the median and percentiles of numbers see stats. The functions sort the vector in place. Sorted and SortedBy return a sorted copy instead and leave the original alone; free the copy when you are done with it. The functions named after an algorithm (quick, merge, bubble and the rest) all give the same order and are here mostly for teaching and comparing; Sort is an introsort, which stays fast on any input. What people get wrong:  Assuming the order of equal elements is kept. Sort, SortDesc, SortBy and SortIndex are not stable. Use StableSortBy when it matters. Using SortBy on data with few distinct keys. It is a plain quick sort, and when many elements compare equal (sorting 100,000 orders by a status with three values) it slows down to quadratic time. StableSortBy is a merge sort and stays fast there. Searching an unsorted vector. BinarySearch, LowerBound and UpperBound return wrong answers without any error when the vector is not sorted the same way. Calling Min or Max on an empty vector. They read element 0 and stop the program.   Sort records by several fields Real data is a vector of structs, and the order has more than one rule: team first, then the highest salary, then the name. Write those rules in one comparison function that returns true when a should come before b, and pass it to SortBy. Compare the first field, and only when it is equal move on to the next. To sort descending on a field, swap the comparison for that field only. sort-guide-records.salamCopyimport sort  struct Employee:     pub name: str = ""     pub team: str = ""     pub salary: int = 0 end  func show(staff: Vector<Employee>):     each e in staff:         println "  " + e.team, e.name, e.salary     end end  func main:     mut staff := Vector {} as Vector<Employee>     defer staff.Free()     staff.Push(Employee { name = "Sara", team = "web", salary = 5200 })     staff.Push(Employee { name = "Omid", team = "data", salary = 6100 })     staff.Push(Employee { name = "Leila", team = "web", salary = 6100 })     staff.Push(Employee { name = "Babak", team = "data", salary = 4800 })     staff.Push(Employee { name = "Nima", team = "web", salary = 5200 })      by_team := (a: Employee, b: Employee):         if a.team != b.team: ret a.team < b.team end         if a.salary != b.salary: ret a.salary > b.salary end         ret a.name < b.name     end     sort.SortBy(staff, by_team)     println "team, then highest salary, then name:"     show(staff)      cheapest := sort.SortedBy(staff, (a: Employee, b: Employee): ret a.salary < b.salary end)     println "lowest paid:", cheapest.Get(0).name     println "still sorted by team:", sort.IsSortedBy(staff, by_team) endOutputteam, then highest salary, then name:   data Omid 6100   data Babak 4800   web Leila 6100   web Nima 5200   web Sara 5200 lowest paid: Babak still sorted by team: true SortBy does not promise to keep equal elements in their old order, which is why the comparison above goes all the way down to the name: with a full tie-break the result is the same however the sort works. SortedBy returns a sorted copy and leaves the original order alone. IsSortedBy checks an order, which is handy in a test or before a binary search.  Sort by one column after another A table that the user sorts by date and then by status should show each status group still in date order. StableSortBy keeps equal elements in the order they arrived, so sorting by the secondary key first and the primary key second gives exactly that. It is a merge sort: it always takes n log n steps and needs a second buffer the size of the vector. sort-guide-stable.salamCopyimport sort  struct Order:     pub id: int = 0     pub status: str = ""     pub placed: str = "" end  func main:     mut orders := Vector {} as Vector<Order>     defer orders.Free()     orders.Push(Order { id = 1041, status = "shipped", placed = "2026-10-03" })     orders.Push(Order { id = 1042, status = "pending", placed = "2026-10-01" })     orders.Push(Order { id = 1043, status = "shipped", placed = "2026-09-28" })     orders.Push(Order { id = 1044, status = "pending", placed = "2026-10-05" })     orders.Push(Order { id = 1045, status = "cancelled", placed = "2026-10-02" })     orders.Push(Order { id = 1046, status = "pending", placed = "2026-09-30" })      sort.StableSortBy(orders, (a: Order, b: Order): ret a.placed < b.placed end)     sort.StableSortBy(orders, (a: Order, b: Order): ret a.status < b.status end)     each o in orders:         println o.status, o.placed, o.id     end endOutputcancelled 2026-10-02 1045 pending 2026-09-30 1046 pending 2026-10-01 1042 pending 2026-10-05 1044 shipped 2026-09-28 1043 shipped 2026-10-03 1041 Dates written as YYYY-MM-DD sort correctly as plain text, which is why the example compares them with <. The same trick fails for D/M/YYYY.  Rank one list by another When the data lives in parallel vectors, such as names, scores and wins, sorting one of them would break the link with the others. SortIndex and SortIndexDesc sort a vector of positions instead and

collections collections Data structures: vector and map, stack, queue, deque, set, linked list, priority queue and counter. Numbers and collections This package holds Salam's data structures. Vector and HashMap, which turn up in every program, are defined here but built in: you can use them without an import. The rest (Stack, Queue, Deque, Set, Counter, PriorityQueue, OrderedMap, LinkedList, CircularList, Pair) and the vector helpers such as clone and IndexOf need import collections. To sort or search a vector use sort; to share a structure between threads, guard it with sync, because none of these types locks. All of them are generic: you set the element type with <...>, as in collections.Stack<str>, and build an empty one with collections.Stack {} as collections.Stack<str>. All of them allocate, so write defer x.Free() right after creating one. Free releases the structure itself, not heap strings or other objects stored in it. Which should you pick? For an ordinary list, Vector; for "last in, first out", Stack; for "first in, first out", Queue; for adding and removing at both ends, Deque; for fast lookup by a key, HashMap; for removing duplicates, Set; for "always give me the smallest", PriorityQueue; and for string settings that must keep their order, OrderedMap. Most of them are thin layers over Vector: a stack is one vector, a queue and a deque are two. What people get wrong:  Copying with =. b := a copies only the vector's header, so both names see the same elements: b.Set(0, x) changes a too, and a push on one can move the memory under the other. Take a real copy with the built-in v.copy() or with collections.clone(v). The same goes for a HashMap (m.copy()) and for any struct holding one. Changing a struct you got from a map. m.Get(k) returns a copy; change it and Put it back. Reading from an empty structure. pop, peek, dequeue, first, last and an index past the end stop the program with a message such as Vector.pop: empty. Check is_empty() first. A --release build leaves the check out, and the same mistake then reads garbage. Printing a map in its own order. each key, value in m visits the slots in hash order, which changes as the map grows. Collect and sort the keys when the order shows.   Vector: insert, remove, copy push and pop work at the end in constant time. Insert and remove_at shift every later element, so they are fine for short lists and slow inside a loop over a long one. IndexOf and contains scan from the front. The example also shows the copy trap from the list above: alias writes straight into line, while the clone keeps its own elements. collections-guide-vector.salamCopyimport collections  func main:     mut line := Vector {} as Vector<str>     defer line.Free()     each name in ["Ali", "Sara", "Reza"]:         line.Push(name)     end     line.Insert(1, "Mina")     println "after insert:", line     served := line.RemoveAt(0)     println "served", served, "->", line     println "Reza is at", collections.IndexOf(line, "Reza"), "and Omid at", collections.IndexOf(line, "Omid")      backup := collections.Clone(line)     defer backup.Free()     alias := line     alias.Set(0, "Neda")     println "alias wrote into line:", line.Get(0)     println "the clone kept:       ", backup.Get(0)      front := collections.Slice(line, 0, 2)     defer front.Free()     println "first two:", front, "last:", line.Last() endOutputafter insert: ["Ali", "Mina", "Sara", "Reza"] served Ali -> ["Mina", "Sara", "Reza"] Reza is at 2 and Omid at -1 alias wrote into line: Neda the clone kept:        Mina first two: ["Neda", "Sara"] last: Reza slice returns a new vector and clamps a range that runs past the end, so it never fails. Printing a vector with println shows its elements, which is handy while debugging.  HashMap: stock by product code A HashMap finds a value by its key in constant time. Get on a missing key returns the zero value of the type (0, empty text, a struct of zeros) and never fails, so ask Has first when a missing key is an error, or use GetOr when a default is right. Struct values come back as copies: change the copy and Put it again. collections-guide-inventory.salamCopyimport sort  struct Stock:     pub name: str = ""     pub qty: int = 0 end  func main:     mut stock := HashMap {} as HashMap<str, Stock>     defer stock.Free()     stock.Put("TEA-01", Stock { name = "Green tea", qty = 40 })     stock.Put("COF-02", Stock { name = "Coffee beans", qty = 12 })     stock.Put("MUG-07", Stock { name = "Mug", qty = 2 })      each sku in ["COF-02", "MUG-07", "TEA-01", "MUG-07", "BAG-99"]:         if not stock.Has(sku):             println "unknown product", sku             continue         end         mut item := stock.Get(sku)         item.qty--         stock.Put(sku, item)     end     println "a missing key gives a zero value:", stock.Get("BAG-99").qty      mut reorder_at := HashMap {} as HashMap<str, int>     defer reorder_at.Free()     reorder_at.Put("TEA-01", 10)      mut skus := Vector {} as Vector<str>     defer skus.Free()     each sku, item in stock:         if item.qty > 0:             skus.Push(sku)         else:             println item.name, "is sold out"         end     end     sort.Sort(skus)     each sku in skus:         item := stock.Get(sku)         low := item.qty <= reorder_at.GetOr(sku, 5)         println sku, item.name, item.qty, "reorder:", low     end endOutputunknown product BAG-99 a missing key gives a zero value: 0 Mug is sold out COF-02 Coffee beans 11 reorder: false TEA-01 Green tea

matrix matrix Linear algebra: matrices, systems of equations, decompositions, eigenvalues and statistics. Numbers and collections This package is complete linear algebra over 64 bit floats: from making a matrix and multiplying through to solving systems, decompositions, eigenvalues and singular values, and statistical tools such as principal component analysis. To solve one system, call Solve; for several systems with one matrix, Decompose once and LUSolve many times. Use it when the answer must be exact to the last digits a double allows: engineering, statistics, finance, geometry. For neural networks and large batches of f32 data see tensor; for means, medians and tests on plain lists, stats; for ready made machine learning models, ml. Things to know  Results carry a little rounding error. Compare with AllClose and a tolerance, and show results with Chop or ToStringPrec. Nothing stops the program. A shape mismatch or a singular matrix gives an empty 0x0 matrix; check is_empty() before you use a result. Every function returns a new matrix that owns its memory. In long loops call free on results you are done with, or use the ...InPlace forms.   Solve a system of equations Three shopping baskets with known totals give three equations in three unknown prices. Put the quantities in a matrix A, the totals in a column b, and Solve returns the column of prices. When the equations do not pin down one answer, Solve returns an empty matrix, so check is_empty before you use the result. Residual computes A x - b, a quick way to see how good a solution is. matrix-guide-prices.salamCopyimport matrix  func build(rows: int, cols: int, numbers: str): matrix.Matrix:     mut data := Vector {} as Vector<f64>     each number in numbers.Split(" "):         data.Push(number.ToFloat())     end     ret matrix.FromArray(rows, cols, data) end  func main:     mut baskets := build(3, 3, "2 1 1 1 3 2 1 0 4")     mut totals := build(3, 1, "9.5 17 17.5")     mut prices := matrix.Solve(baskets, totals)     if prices.IsEmpty():         println "the baskets do not pin down the prices"         ret 1     end     names := ["apple", "bread", "cheese"]     each i, name in names:         println name, matrix.ToStringPrec(matrix.Row(prices, i), 2)     end     mut check := matrix.Residual(baskets, prices, totals)     println "largest error is tiny:", matrix.MaxAbs(check) < 0.000001     mut order := build(1, 3, "4 2 1")     println "4 apples, 2 bread, 1 cheese:", matrix.ToStringPrec(matrix.MatMul(order, prices), 2)     prices.Free()     check.Free() endOutputapple 1.50 bread 2.50 cheese 4.00 largest error is tiny: true 4 apples, 2 bread, 1 cheese: 15.00 The examples build matrices from a string of numbers with a small build helper that calls FromArray; any other way of filling a Vector<f64> row by row works the same.  One matrix, many right-hand sides In engineering the matrix often stays the same while the input changes: the same structure under different loads. Decompose does the expensive work once, and each LUSolve after that is cheap. The decomposition also tells you whether the matrix is singular, before you try to solve anything. matrix-guide-loads.salamCopyimport matrix  func build(rows: int, cols: int, numbers: str): matrix.Matrix:     mut data := Vector {} as Vector<f64>     each number in numbers.Split(" "):         data.Push(number.ToFloat())     end     ret matrix.FromArray(rows, cols, data) end  func main:     mut springs := build(3, 3, "20 -10 0 -10 20 -10 0 -10 10")     mut lu := matrix.Decompose(springs)     if lu.singular:         println "the system has no unique solution"         ret 1     end     loads := ["0 0 5", "5 0 0", "1 1 1"]     each load in loads:         mut force := build(3, 1, load)         mut shift := matrix.LUSolve(lu, force)         println "load", load, "->", matrix.ToStringPrec(matrix.Transpose(shift), 2)         force.Free()         shift.Free()     end     println "determinant", matrix.ToStringPrec(matrix.Full(1, 1, matrix.Det(springs)), 1)     lu.Free()     springs.Free() endOutputload 0 0 5 -> 0.50 1.00 1.50 load 5 0 0 -> 0.50 0.50 0.50 load 1 1 1 -> 0.30 0.50 0.60 determinant 1000.0  Fit a line or a curve to data LinearRegression fits a straight line and returns the intercept and the slope as a column. For a curve, build the columns 1, x, x² with Vandermonde and pass them to LeastSquares. RSquared says how much of the variation the fit explains; 1 means a perfect fit. Here a parabola through fuel use at six speeds gives the most economical speed. matrix-guide-fit.salamCopyimport matrix  func build(rows: int, cols: int, numbers: str): matrix.Matrix:     mut data := Vector {} as Vector<f64>     each number in numbers.Split(" "):         data.Push(number.ToFloat())     end     ret matrix.FromArray(rows, cols, data) end  func r(value: f64): str:     ret matrix.ToStringPrec(matrix.Full(1, 1, value), 2) end  func main:     mut area := build(5, 1, "50 70 90 110 130")     mut rent := build(5, 1, "520 690 910 1080 1300")     mut line := matrix.LinearRegression(area, rent)     println "rent =", r(line.at(0, 0)), "+", r(line.at(1, 0)), "* area"     mut design := matrix.Vandermonde(area, 2)     mut fitted := matrix.MatMul(design, line)     println "R squared", matrix.ToStringPrec(matrix.Full(1, 1, matrix.RSquared(rent, fitted)), 4)     println "100 square meters:", r(line.at(0, 0) + line.at(1, 0) * 100.0)      mut speed := build(6, 1, "40 60 80 100 120 140")     mut fuel := build(6, 1, "7.1 6.0 5.8 6.4 7.5 9.1")     mut curve := matrix.LeastSquares(matrix.Vandermonde(speed, 3), fuel)     a := curve.at(0, 0)     b := curve.at(1, 0)     c := curve.at(2, 0)     best := 0.0 - b

graph graph Graph theory: traversal, shortest paths, spanning trees, flow, coloring, communities and centrality. Numbers and collections This package has more than two hundred graph algorithms. Make a graph with NewUndirected or NewDirected, add edges with add_edge and add_weighted, or read the whole thing from text in one go with FromEdgeList. Nodes are numbered from zero to n minus one; adding an edge to a higher number grows the graph. Everything from traversal and components to shortest paths, spanning trees, flow and cuts, matching, coloring, communities and centrality is ready to use. You can export the result with ToDot or ToMermaid to draw it. The algorithms that solve hard problems, such as maximum clique and Hamiltonian cycle, are meant for small graphs. Use it whenever the data is "things and the links between them": roads, dependencies, networks, social ties, state machines. For linear algebra on grids of numbers use matrix; this package has its own small Matrix type for AdjacencyMatrix and the spectral functions. Things to know  A distance that cannot be reached is GRAPH_INF (1e300), not an error. Test for it before you print or add distances. Dijkstra returns false and leaves every distance at GRAPH_INF when any weight is negative. ShortestPath and ShortestPathLength switch to Bellman-Ford by themselves. Functions that return edges give edge numbers in the order the edges were added; edge_from, edge_to and edge_weight read them back. The graph prepares its adjacency lists on first use and again after you add edges. build does that work up front, which only matters for timing.   Shortest route on a road map Give each city a node number and a name with set_name, add the roads with their length using add_weighted, and call build to prepare the lookup tables (the first algorithm would do it anyway). ShortestPath returns the list of nodes on the shortest weighted route and ShortestPathLength its length. HopPath ignores the weights and finds the route with the fewest stops, which is not the same thing. DijkstraDist gives the distance from one city to all the others in one call. graph-guide-route.salamCopyimport graph  func route_text(g &: graph.Graph, path: Vector<int>): str:     mut text := ""     each i, node in path:         if i > 0: text += " -> " end         text += g.name(node)     end     ret text end  func main:     mut roads := graph.NewUndirected(6)     defer roads.Free()     each i, city in ["Tehran", "Qom", "Kashan", "Isfahan", "Arak", "Yazd"]:         roads.set_name(i, city)     end     roads.add_weighted(0, 1, 140.0)     roads.add_weighted(1, 2, 105.0)     roads.add_weighted(2, 3, 210.0)     roads.add_weighted(1, 4, 135.0)     roads.add_weighted(4, 3, 280.0)     roads.add_weighted(3, 5, 320.0)     roads.add_weighted(2, 5, 560.0)     roads.build()      trip := graph.ShortestPath(roads, 0, 5)     println route_text(roads, trip), "|", graph.ShortestPathLength(roads, 0, 5), "km"     hops := graph.HopPath(roads, 0, 5)     println "fewest stops:", route_text(roads, hops)     dist := graph.DijkstraDist(roads, 0)     each i, d in dist:         println "  Tehran to", roads.name(i), d, "km"     end endOutputTehran -> Qom -> Kashan -> Isfahan -> Yazd | 775 km fewest stops: Tehran -> Qom -> Kashan -> Yazd   Tehran to Tehran 0 km   Tehran to Qom 140 km   Tehran to Kashan 245 km   Tehran to Isfahan 455 km   Tehran to Arak 275 km   Tehran to Yazd 775 km The weights must not be negative for Dijkstra; it returns false if one is. When some are, for example costs that can be refunds, ShortestPath switches to Bellman-Ford on its own, and BellmanFord called directly also reports a negative cycle.  Task order and the critical path A plan where some tasks must wait for others is a directed graph without cycles. TopologicalSort gives an order that respects every dependency and returns false when there is a cycle, that is, when the plan is impossible. TopologicalLayers groups tasks into stages that can run in parallel. With the duration of each task as the weight of its outgoing edges, CriticalPath gives the chain of tasks that decides how long the whole project takes: a delay on any of them delays the release. graph-guide-tasks.salamCopyimport graph  func main:     tasks := ["design", "database", "backend", "frontend", "tests", "release"]     days := [3.0, 2.0, 5.0, 4.0, 2.0, 1.0]     mut plan := graph.NewDirected(6)     defer plan.Free()     each i, name in tasks:         plan.set_name(i, name)     end     each pair in ["0 1", "0 3", "1 2", "2 4", "3 4", "4 5"]:         parts := pair.Split(" ")         from := parts.Get(0).ToInt()         plan.add_weighted(from, parts.Get(1).ToInt(), days[from])     end     plan.build()      mut order := Vector {} as Vector<int>     defer order.Free()     if graph.TopologicalSort(plan, order) == false:         println "the plan has a cycle"         ret 1     end     mut line := "order:"     each t in order:         line = line + " " + plan.name(t)     end     println line      mut layer := Vector {} as Vector<int>     defer layer.Free()     stages := graph.TopologicalLayers(plan, layer)     println "stages:", stages     each i, name in tasks:         println "  stage", layer.Get(i), name     end      critical := graph.CriticalPath(plan)     mut path := "critical path:"     each t in critical:         path = path + " " + plan.name(t)     end     println path endOutputorder: design database frontend backend tests release stages: 5   stage 0 design   stage 1 database   stage 2 backend   stage 1 frontend   stage 3 tests   stage 4 release critical path: design database backend tests rele

os/error os.error The last error from a file or process operation: its code, its message and the path that failed. System and tools When an operation in the fs, fs.dir, os.process or os.temp packages fails, it records a short report here: a code, a message, the operation and the path. Call Clear, run the operation, then ask HasError and Last. It is a single global record, like C's errno, not a returned value. The plain functions of the os package do not record anything here; they only return -1. This package is a different thing from the general-purpose error package, which builds error values to return from your own functions; prefer that for new code that is not about files or processes. Know what the standard packages actually record before you branch on it:  CodeRecorded by  IOErrorAlmost every failure: fs.dir (Mkdir, MkdirAll, Remove, RemoveAll, Copy, Move), fs (AtomicWrite, Copy, Move) and os.temp FileNotFoundOnly fs.Delete, for any failure to delete, a missing permission included ProcessFailedos.process, when a program cannot be started the othersNothing in the standard library yet; they are there for your own Set calls   Reads and plain writes such as fs.ReadText and WriteText record nothing; check their results instead. The messages are fixed English phrases such as delete failed, not the system's reason, and system_code is filled in only by os.process. Check an operation and explain the failure The usual pattern has three steps: call Clear, run the operation, then ask HasError. Last returns an OSError with the code to branch on, the path that failed and the name of the operation, which is enough to turn the failure into a message a person understands. os-error-guide-explain.salamCopyimport os.error import fs  func explain(e: error.OSError): str:     switch e.code:         error.FileNotFound: ret "there is no such file: " + e.path end         error.IOError: ret e.operation + " failed on " + e.path end         error.ProcessFailed: ret "could not start " + e.path end     end     ret "something else went wrong in " + e.operation end  func remove_draft(name: str):     error.Clear()     fs.Delete(name)     if error.HasError():         println "could not delete:", explain(error.Last())         ret     end     println "deleted", name end  func main:     fs.WriteText("draft.txt", "notes")     remove_draft("draft.txt")     remove_draft("draft.txt") endOutputdeleted draft.txt could not delete: there is no such file: draft.txt Compare code with the constants of this package, never message: the message is meant for people and may change between releases.  Errors stay until you clear them A failed call records an error, but a successful call does not remove it. So HasError after a good call can still be true because of something that failed much earlier. Call Clear just before the operation you want to check. os-error-guide-clear.salamCopyimport os.error import fs  func main:     fs.Delete("missing.txt")     fs.WriteText("ok.txt", "fine")     println "after a good write:", error.HasError(), error.LastMessage()     error.Clear()     fs.WriteText("ok.txt", "still fine")     println "after Clear and a good write:", error.HasError()     fs.Delete("ok.txt")     println "after deleting ok.txt:", error.HasError() endOutputafter a good write: true delete failed after Clear and a good write: false after deleting ok.txt: false The record is a single global value for the whole program, so it is not a safe channel between threads: a failure in one thread can overwrite another thread's error before it is read. Check the error in the same thread, right after the call.  Report errors from your own functions Set records an error the same way the standard packages do. A helper that reads files can use it, and its callers then check it with the same HasError and Last they use everywhere else. Pass the name of your function as the operation and the file as the path, so the message says where things went wrong. os-error-guide-own.salamCopyimport os.error import fs  func load_port(path: str): int:     error.Clear()     if not fs.Exists(path):         error.Set(error.FileNotFound, "config file is missing", "load_port", path, 0)         ret 0     end     text := fs.ReadText(path).Trim()     port := text.ToInt()     if port <= 0 or port > 65535:         error.Set(error.InvalidPath, "not a port number: " + text, "load_port", path, 0)         ret 0     end     ret port end  func show(path: str):     port := load_port(path)     if error.HasError():         e := error.Last()         println e.operation + "(" + e.path + "):", e.message         ret     end     println path, "says port", port end  func main:     fs.WriteText("good.conf", "8080\n")     fs.WriteText("bad.conf", "eighty\n")     show("good.conf")     show("bad.conf")     show("none.conf")     fs.Delete("good.conf")     fs.Delete("bad.conf") endOutputgood.conf says port 8080 load_port(bad.conf): not a port number: eighty load_port(none.conf): config file is missing  A program that will not start The os.process package records ProcessFailed here when it cannot start a program at all, for example when the path is wrong. That is different from a program that starts and then exits with a non-zero code: then there is no error here, and you read the code from Wait. os-error-guide-process.salamCopyimport os.error import os.process  func main:     mut args := Vector {} as Vector<str>     defer args.Free()     args.Push("--version")     error.Clear()     mut p := process.StartCaptured("/no/such/program", args)     if error.HasError():         e := error.Last()         println "could not st

os/platform os.platform Identifying the system the program is running on: the operating system, the processor, the core count and the memory. System and tools The os.platform package says at run time what system the program is on: the operating system, the processor family, the number of cores and the amount of memory. Use it for reports and logs, for automatic settings such as a worker count or a cache size, and for small per-system differences such as a file extension. For code that only compiles on one system, use the constants such as SALAM_OS_WINDOWS and conditional compilation instead. For the user and their home folder see os.user; for environment variables, env. The Is... functions, OS and Arch are fixed when the program is compiled, so they cost nothing to call. The hardware questions are asked of the running system, and how they are answered differs:  FunctionLinuxmacOS and BSDWindows  CpuCountsysconf, instantruns sysctlthe NUMBER_OF_PROCESSORS variable TotalMemory/proc/meminforuns sysctlruns PowerShell, often a second or more AvailableMemory/proc/meminfonot known, -1runs PowerShell   What people get wrong: calling the memory functions in a loop (on Windows each call starts PowerShell, so ask once and keep the number), forgetting that every hardware function returns -1 when it cannot find out, and treating CpuCount as physical cores. It counts the logical processors online, hyper-threads included, and inside a container it counts the whole machine. The programs below print whether a rule held rather than the raw numbers, so their output is the same on any machine.  Choose how many workers to run Work that splits into independent pieces, such as resizing images, goes faster with one thread or process per core. CpuCount gives the number of cores; keep the result between one and a limit of your own, because a machine with 128 cores does not mean your job wants 128 threads. os-platform-guide-workers.salamCopyimport os.platform  func worker_count(limit: int): int:     cores := platform.CpuCount()     if cores < 1:         ret 1     end     if cores > limit:         ret limit     end     ret cores end  func main:     workers := worker_count(8)     println "workers between 1 and 8:", workers >= 1 and workers <= 8     println "never more than the cores:", workers <= platform.CpuCount()     one := worker_count(1)     println "with a limit of one:", one endOutputworkers between 1 and 8: true never more than the cores: true with a limit of one: 1 Inside a container the count is the whole machine's, not the share the container may use. If the program runs under Docker or Kubernetes, let a flag or an environment variable override it.  Size a cache from the system memory TotalMemory and AvailableMemory return bytes as an i64. A cache can take a fraction of the total memory, kept between a floor and a ceiling, and never more than half of what is free right now. AvailableMemory returns minus one on systems where it is not known, so check for that before using it. os-platform-guide-memory.salamCopyimport os.platform  const MB := 1048576 as i64  func cache_bytes(): i64:     mut size := platform.TotalMemory() / 16     if size < 64 * MB:         size = 64 * MB     end     if size > 1024 * MB:         size = 1024 * MB     end     free := platform.AvailableMemory()     if free > 0 and size > free / 2:         size = free / 2     end     ret size end  func main:     size := cache_bytes()     println "cache is at most 1 GB:", size <= 1024 * MB     println "cache is positive:", size > 0     free := platform.AvailableMemory()     println "cache fits in free memory:", free < 0 or size <= free endOutputcache is at most 1 GB: true cache is positive: true cache fits in free memory: true  Small differences between systems Most differences between systems are small: Windows programs end in .exe, and each desktop opens a file with a different command. A function that asks IsWindows or IsMac and returns the right piece keeps the rest of the program free of such checks. os-platform-guide-dispatch.salamCopyimport os.platform  func executable(name: str): str:     if platform.IsWindows():         ret name + ".exe"     end     ret name end  func open_command(): str:     if platform.IsWindows(): ret "start" end     if platform.IsMac(): ret "open" end     ret "xdg-open" end  func main:     mut matched := 0     if platform.IsLinux(): matched++ end     if platform.IsWindows(): matched++ end     if platform.IsMac(): matched++ end     if platform.IsFreeBSD(): matched++ end     if platform.IsWasm(): matched++ end     println "at most one system matched:", matched <= 1     println "binary name built:", executable("salam").StartsWith("salam")     println "open command chosen:", open_command().Len() > 0 endOutputat most one system matched: true binary name built: true open command chosen: true  Run time or compile time The functions of this package are answered when the program runs, so both branches of an if are compiled on every system. That fails when one branch calls a function that only exists on one system, such as a Windows API. Then use the constant itself: a plain if SALAM_OS_WINDOWS: is decided while compiling and the other branch is left out. See compile-time code for the full list of constants. os-platform-guide-compile.salamCopyimport os.platform  func linux_when_compiled(): bool:     if SALAM_OS_LINUX:         ret true     else:         ret false     end end  func main:     println "compile time and run time agree:", linux_when_compiled() == platform.IsLinux()     if SALAM_OS_WINDOWS:         println "this line is only compiled on Windows"     else:         println "this line is compiled everywhere else"     end endOutputcompile time and run time agree: true this line is compiled everywhere

os/dl os.dl Loading shared libraries at run time, looking up their functions and calling a function pointer with up to eight integer or pointer arguments. System and tools Most programs link their libraries when they are built. This package is for the other case: the library is chosen while the program runs. Open loads a shared library (dlopen), Sym finds a function or a variable in it by name (dlsym), and Call calls the function pointer you get, with up to eight integer or pointer arguments, and returns the integer or pointer it returns. OpenSelf opens the running program itself, which gives you the C library and everything else already loaded. It is the basis for plug-ins, for probing optional libraries and for tools that load a function they have just written into executable memory. Arguments and the result are size, an integer as wide as a pointer (64 bits on a 64 bit system). Pass a pointer by converting it, (p as void*) as size, and turn a returned pointer back with r as void*. A small integer is passed as it is. The package works on Linux, macOS and the BSDs; on Windows Supported is false and the functions return empty results. What people get wrong:  Calling something that is not a function, or a function with the wrong number of arguments. Call cannot check that; a wrong pointer or a wrong count crashes the program or returns garbage. Give exactly the arguments the C function takes. Calling a function that takes a struct by value or a variable argument list such as printf through Call or CallMixed. Those use a different calling convention. Floating point arguments need CallMixed, and a floating point result needs CallMixedF64. Not checking for null. Open and Sym return null when the library or the symbol is missing, and Call on null returns 0; ask Error why. Using a symbol after Close. Once the last user of a library closes it, its code is gone and a stale pointer crashes. More than 8 arguments: Call refuses and returns 0.  Choosing a function by name at run time The name of the function does not have to be known when the program is written. The example opens the running program itself with OpenSelf, looks each name up with Sym and calls what it finds. A name that does not exist gives null, which the example reports instead of calling it. Pass a library path to Open to do the same with a plug-in file. os-dl-guide-plugin.salamCopyimport os.dl import str  func call_by_name(lib: void*, name: str, arg: size): str:     fn := dl.Sym(lib, name)     if fn == null:         ret name + ": not found"     end     ret name + ": " + str.FromInt(dl.Call(fn, [arg]) as i64) end  func main:     if not dl.Supported():         println "dynamic loading is not available here"         ret     end     lib := dl.OpenSelf()     if lib == null:         println "cannot open the program:", dl.Error()         ret     end     defer _closed := dl.Close(lib)     text := "salam"     println call_by_name(lib, "strlen", (text as void*) as size)     println call_by_name(lib, "labs", (0 - 42) as size)     println call_by_name(lib, "no_such_function", 1 as size) endOutputstrlen: 5 labs: 42 no_such_function: not found Opening a library by path Library file names differ between systems, so a portable program tries a few and uses the first that opens. Open returns null for one that does not exist and Error says why. Always pair a successful Open with Close, and do not use a symbol after its library is closed. os-dl-guide-open.salamCopyimport os.dl import str  func open_first(paths: str[]): void*:     each path in paths:         lib := dl.Open(path)         if lib != null:             ret lib         end     end     ret null end  func main:     if not dl.Supported():         println "dynamic loading is not available here"         ret     end     lib := open_first(["libno-such-library.so", "libc.so.6", "libc.dylib", "/usr/lib/libSystem.B.dylib", "libc.so.7"])     if lib == null:         println "no C library found:", dl.Error()         ret     end     defer _closed := dl.Close(lib)     println "opened a C library"     text := "shared library"     length := dl.Call(dl.Sym(lib, "strlen"), [(text as void*) as size])     println "strlen says", str.FromInt(length as i64) endOutputopened a C library strlen says 14 Functions Supportedfunc Supported(): boolTrue where dynamic loading works (every system except Windows).os-dl-Call.salamCopyimport os.dl  func main:     if not dl.Supported():         println "not supported here"         ret     end     lib := dl.OpenSelf()     defer dl.Close(lib)     text := "hello, world"     length := dl.Call(dl.Sym(lib, "strlen"), [(text as void*) as size])     println "strlen:", length     println "labs:", dl.Call(dl.Sym(lib, "labs"), [(0 - 42) as size])     println "missing symbol:", dl.Sym(lib, "no_such_function") == null     missing := dl.Open("libno-such-library.so.9")     println "missing library:", missing == null, dl.Error().Len() > 0 endOutputstrlen: 12 labs: 42 missing symbol: true missing library: true true Openfunc Open(path: str): void*Loads the shared library at path (a name such as libm.so.6 is searched for by the system) and returns its handle, or null.The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-dl-Call.salam OpenSelffunc OpenSelf(): void*Opens the running program, so Sym can find the C library and anything else already loaded. null where it is not supported.The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-dl-Call.salam Symfunc Sym(lib: void*, name: str): void*The address of the function or variable called name in the library, or null. Use null checks, not exceptions.The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-dl-Call.salam Closefunc Close(lib: void*): boo

os/mmap os.mmap Memory pages with read, write and execute permissions: map, change the permissions of and release them. System and tools Ordinary allocation (mem.Allocate) gives memory you can read and write. This package gives you whole pages straight from the operating system and lets you choose what the program may do with them: PROT_READ, PROT_WRITE and PROT_EXEC, combined with |. Alloc maps zero-filled pages, Protect changes the permissions (mprotect) and Free unmaps them. Use it for guard pages, for read-only data that must not change by accident, and for loading machine code: write the bytes while the page is writable, switch it to read and execute, then call it with os.dl. Sizes are rounded up to whole pages by the system; PageSize tells the page size (usually 4096, 16384 on Apple silicon). The package works on Linux, macOS and the BSDs. On Windows Supported is false and Alloc returns null. What people get wrong:  Asking for write and execute together. Several systems refuse it (SELinux, hardened kernels, macOS on Apple silicon, which also needs a special MAP_JIT flag this package does not set). Do it in two steps: map as PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE, fill, then Protect to PROT_READ | PROT_EXEC. Passing a different size to Free or Protect than to Alloc. Use the same size; the permissions of whole pages change. Using the memory after Free, or writing to a page that is now read-only. Both crash the program at once. Machine code is only valid for one processor family. Code written for x86-64 will not run on an ARM computer, and some ARM systems need the instruction cache flushed after the code is written.  Running a few machine instructions The example below maps a page, writes seven bytes of x86-64 code that add up its first two arguments, makes the page executable and calls it. It only runs on a 64 bit x86 system, which the example checks with SALAM_ARCH_X64. os-mmap-guide-jit.salamCopyimport os.dl import os.mmap  func main:     if not SALAM_ARCH_X64 or not mmap.Supported():         println "this example needs 64 bit x86 and mmap"         ret     end     page := mmap.PageSize()     code := mmap.Alloc(page, mmap.PROT_READ | mmap.PROT_WRITE)     bytes := code as u8*     program := [0x48, 0x89, 0xf8, 0x48, 0x01, 0xf0, 0xc3]     repeat 7 in i:         bytes[i] = program[i] as u8     end     mmap.Protect(code, page, mmap.PROT_READ | mmap.PROT_EXEC)     println "40 + 2 =", dl.Call(code, [40 as size, 2])     mmap.Free(code, page) endOutput40 + 2 = 42 A table that cannot be changed by accident Fill a page while it is writable, then make it read-only with Protect. From then on a stray write stops the program at once instead of silently corrupting the table, and reads keep working. Make it writable again when the data has to change. The example does that with a table of squares. os-mmap-guide-readonly.salamCopyimport os.mmap  func main:     if not mmap.Supported():         println "memory mapping is not available here"         ret     end     page := mmap.PageSize()     table := mmap.Alloc(page, mmap.PROT_READ | mmap.PROT_WRITE)     defer _freed := mmap.Free(table, page)     cells := table as i32*     repeat 16 in i:         cells[i] = i * i     end     println "filled:", cells[3], cells[15]     println "read-only:", mmap.Protect(table, page, mmap.PROT_READ)     println "still readable:", cells[4]     println "writable again:", mmap.Protect(table, page, mmap.PROT_READ | mmap.PROT_WRITE)     cells[4] = 99     println "after the change:", cells[4] endOutputfilled: 9 225 read-only: true still readable: 16 writable again: true after the change: 99 Constants and variables PROT_NONEconst PROT_NONE: i32 = 0Permission value: the pages may not be touched.os-mmap-Alloc.salamCopyimport os.mmap  func main:     page := mmap.PageSize()     block := mmap.Alloc(page, mmap.PROT_READ | mmap.PROT_WRITE)     if block == null:         println "mapping failed"         ret     end     bytes := block as u8*     bytes[0] = 7 as u8     bytes[page - 1] = 9 as u8     println bytes[0], bytes[1], bytes[page - 1]     println mmap.Protect(block, page, mmap.PROT_READ)     println bytes[0]     println mmap.Free(block, page) endOutput7 0 9 true 7 true PROT_READconst PROT_READ: i32 = 1Permission value: the pages may be read.The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-mmap-Alloc.salam PROT_WRITEconst PROT_WRITE: i32 = 2Permission value: the pages may be written.The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-mmap-Alloc.salam PROT_EXECconst PROT_EXEC: i32 = 4Permission value: the pages may be run as machine code.The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-mmap-Alloc.salam Functions Supportedfunc Supported(): boolTrue where memory mapping works (every system except Windows).The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-mmap-Alloc.salam PageSizefunc PageSize(): intThe size of one memory page in bytes.The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-mmap-Alloc.salam Allocfunc Alloc(size: int, prot: int): void*Maps size bytes (rounded up to whole pages) of zero-filled private memory with the given permissions and returns its address, or null when it fails, when size is not positive and on Windows.The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-mmap-Alloc.salam Protectfunc Protect(p: void*, size: int, prot: int): boolChanges the permissions of the pages that hold size bytes from p; true on success. p must be the address of a page, as returned by Alloc.The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-mmap-Alloc.salam Freefunc Free(p: void*, size: int): boolUnmaps the pages; true on success. The memory must not be used afterwards.The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-mmap-Alloc.salam

os/process os.process Running other programs, talking to them through pipes, reading with a time limit, telling an exit code from a signal, and stopping them. System and tools The os.process package runs another program directly, with no shell in between. The program's path and its arguments are given separately, so nothing has to be quoted and spaces or special characters in an argument cause no trouble. Use it to call tools such as git, ffmpeg or a compiler with file names that came from a user. For a quick one-line shell command use os (Run, RunCapture) or os.shell; when a program cannot start at all, the reason is recorded in os.error. A run has up to four steps: Start or StartCaptured launches the program and returns at once, Wait blocks until it exits and returns the exit code, ReadStdout and ReadStderr read what a captured run printed, and Cleanup deletes the two temporary files that held it. A captured program gets an empty standard input. For a program you talk to while it runs, with pipes, time limits and exit codes or signals, use Command, Launch and Child, described in the sections below.
