For a program that must see a terminal, use os.pty. What people get wrong:  Treating IsRunning as a live check. It reports a flag that Start sets and only Wait, Kill or Terminate clear; it stays true after the program has exited on its own. Killing without waiting. Kill and Terminate only send the signal. Call Wait afterwards, or the finished process stays in the process table as a zombie. Expecting a timeout from Wait. Wait on a Process waits as long as the program runs. To give up after a while use a Child (see below), whose Wait takes a time limit. Forgetting Cleanup. Each captured run leaves two files in the temporary folder until you call it.  On Windows the arguments are joined into one command line with quotes around those that contain spaces, and the ANSI CreateProcessA starts the program. An argument that itself contains a ", or text outside the system code page such as Persian, does not arrive intact there; Fork and WaitPid return -1. Pass arguments exactly as they are Each element of the argument vector reaches the program as one argument, byte for byte. Spaces, quotes, a $ or a ; mean nothing special, because no shell reads them. That makes this package the safe way to pass file names and other text that came from a user. os-process-guide-args.salamCopyimport os.process  func main:     mut args := Vector {} as Vector<str>     defer args.Free()     args.Push("[%s]\n")     args.Push("two words")     args.Push("it's quoted")     args.Push("$HOME")     args.Push("*.txt; rm -rf x")     mut p := process.StartCaptured("printf", args)     process.Wait(p)     print process.ReadStdout(p)     process.Cleanup(p) endOutput[two words] [it's quoted] [$HOME] [*.txt; rm -rf x] The program name is looked up on the PATH like in a terminal, so printf works without a full path. The vector does not include the program name itself; the package adds it. This exactness holds on Linux and macOS; see the note above for Windows.  Exit code, output and error output A program reports success with exit code zero and anything else on failure, and it writes its complaints to the error output. After Wait, read both: ReadStdout for the results and ReadStderr for the reason it failed. Call Cleanup after reading, because the captured output is kept in temporary files until then. os-process-guide-exitcode.salamCopyimport os.process  func main:     mut args := Vector {} as Vector<str>     defer args.Free()     args.Push("-c")     args.Push("echo copying files; echo disk is full >&2; exit 3")     mut p := process.StartCaptured("sh", args)     code := process.Wait(p)     out := process.ReadStdout(p).Trim()     err := process.ReadStderr(p).Trim()     process.Cleanup(p)     println "output:", out     if code != 0:         println "failed with code", code, "and said:", err         ret 0     end     println "all good" endOutputoutput: copying files failed with code 3 and said: disk is full  Run several programs at once StartCaptured returns as soon as the program has started, so you can start several and wait for them afterwards. The total time is about that of the slowest one rather than the sum of all. Waiting in the order you started them keeps the output in a fixed order, even when a later job finished first. os-process-guide-parallel.salamCopyimport os.process  func job(name: str, seconds: str): process.Process:     mut args := Vector {} as Vector<str>     defer args.Free()     args.Push("-c")     args.Push("sleep " + seconds + "; echo " + name + " done")     ret process.StartCaptured("sh", args) end  func main:     mut jobs := Vector {} as Vector<process.Process>     defer jobs.Free()     jobs.Push(job("thumbnails", "0.3"))     jobs.Push(job("search index", "0.1"))     jobs.Push(job("sitemap", "0.2"))     println "started", jobs.Len(), "jobs"     repeat jobs.Len() in i:         mut p := jobs.Get(i)         code := process.Wait(p)         println code, process.ReadStdout(p).Trim()         process.Cleanup(p)     end endOutputstarted 3 jobs 0 thumbnails done 0 search index done 0 sitemap done Keep the number of programs you run at once reasonable; os.platform's CpuCount is a good limit for work that keeps the processor busy.  A helper that runs a program and returns its output Most programs need the same few lines every time: start, check that it started, wait, read, clean up. Put them in one function. A defer right after the start makes sure Cleanup runs on every way out of the function, and an out-parameter tells the caller whether the program succeeded. os-process-guide-helper.salamCopyimport os.error import os.process  func cap

os/shell os.shell Running a command and getting its exit code, its output and its errors together. System and tools The os.shell package runs a command, waits for it and gives back the whole result at once in a CmdResult: the exit code, the standard output and the error output. It is a thin layer over os.process (StartCaptured, Wait, read, Cleanup) for the common case where you want all three and do not need to run anything in parallel. Compared with os.RunCapture in os, it also captures the error output and, through Run, passes arguments without a shell. The three functions differ in who reads the command:  FunctionShellArgumentsResult  Run(program, args)nonea vector, passed exactlyCmdResult; code -1 when the program cannot start Exec(command)nonethe string split on single spacesCmdResult System(command)/bin/sh -c, or cmd on Windowsthe shell parses themexit code only; output goes to the screen   Exec splits the command on spaces alone and no shell is involved: pipes (|), redirection (>), quoting and tabs do not work. For those, call sh -c through Run, as the first example does. Every call waits for the command to finish, with no timeout, and keeps the whole output in memory. The command gets an empty standard input, so a tool that asks a question reads end of file. Pipes and redirection through sh For a pipeline, hand the whole script to sh -c. Wrapping that in a small function keeps the call sites short, and the result still has all three parts: the code of the last command, the output and the error output. os-shell-guide-pipe.salamCopyimport os.shell  func sh(script: str): shell.CmdResult:     mut args := Vector {} as Vector<str>     defer args.Free()     args.Push("-c")     args.Push(script)     ret shell.Run("sh", args) end  func main:     r := sh("printf 'red\nblue\nred\ngreen\nred\n' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 1")     if r.code != 0:         println "the pipeline failed:", r.err         ret 0     end     println "most common:", r.out.Trim()     r2 := sh("echo saved > notes.txt && cat notes.txt && rm notes.txt")     println r2.code, r2.out.Trim() endOutputmost common: 3 red 0 saved Only put text you wrote yourself into such a script. Values from users belong in separate arguments of Run, where no shell can read them.  Work with the output line by line Most tools print one item per line. Trim the output, split it on newlines and handle each line. The program below lists the current directory with ls and picks out the CSV files. os-shell-guide-lines.salamCopyimport os import os.shell  func main:     os.WriteFile("a.csv", "1,2
")     os.WriteFile("b.csv", "3,4
")     os.WriteFile("notes.txt", "hi
")     r := shell.Exec("ls")     mut csv := 0     each name in r.out.Trim().Split("
"):         if name.EndsWith(".csv"):             println "found", name             csv++         end     end     println csv, "csv files"     os.Remove("a.csv")     os.Remove("b.csv")     os.Remove("notes.txt") endOutputfound a.csv found b.csv 2 csv files To list files in a real program, prefer fs.dir or os: they need no external program and they work the same on Windows. Running a tool is the right choice when the tool does the real work, such as git or ffmpeg.  Check whether a command worked A command that fails returns a non-zero code and usually says why in the error output. Check code first; err is for the message you show or log. A program that cannot be found at all comes back with code -1 instead of stopping your program, and the reason is in os.error. os-shell-guide-check.salamCopyimport os.shell  func attempt(command: str):     r := shell.Exec(command)     if r.code == 0:         println "ok:", command         ret     end     println "failed:", command, "with code", r.code     println "  has an error message:", r.err.Len() > 0 end  func main:     attempt("ls .")     attempt("ls no-such-folder")     println "exit code of false:", shell.System("false") endOutputok: ls . failed: ls no-such-folder with code 2   has an error message: true exit code of false: 1 The exact codes and messages belong to each tool and differ between systems: ls returns 2 for a missing folder on Linux and 1 on macOS. Test for zero or non-zero unless the tool documents its codes.  Exec does not understand quotes Exec only splits on spaces, so quotes stay in the text and a quoted phrase still becomes two arguments. When an argument contains a space, use Run with the arguments in a vector, or let sh -c read the quotes. os-shell-guide-quote.salamCopyimport os.shell  func main:     r := shell.Exec("echo 'two words'")     println "Exec:", r.out.Trim()     mut args := Vector {} as Vector<str>     defer args.Free()     args.Push("two words")     r2 := shell.Run("echo", args)     println "Run: ", r2.out.Trim()     mut script := Vector {} as Vector<str>     defer script.Free()     script.Push("-c")     script.Push("echo 'two words'")     r3 := shell.Run("sh", script)     println "sh -c:", r3.out.Trim() endOutputExec: 'two words' Run:  two words sh -c: two words  NeedUse  A simple command with no quotes or special charactersExec Arguments with spaces or text from usersRun with a vector Pipes, redirection, &&Run("sh", ...) with -c Only the exit code, output straight to the screenSystem Start without waiting, or stop a programos.process   Types CmdResultstruct CmdResultThe result of a command.NameTypeDescriptioncodeint = 0The exit code; zero means success, 128 plus the signal number when a signal ended it, and -1 when the program could not start.outstr = ""The standard output, newlines included; it s

os/temp os.temp Making a temporary file or directory under a unique name. System and tools For data that is only needed while the program runs, make a temporary file or directory: an unpacked archive, a file being built before it is published, the output of a tool. File and Directory create an empty one in the system temporary folder under a random name (salam- and 16 hex digits from crypto), so several copies of the program running at once do not collide, and return its path. Removing it is up to you: nothing is cleaned up when the program exits. Read and write the files with fs, and build paths inside a temporary directory with fs.path. For replacing a real file safely, fs.AtomicWrite is often the better tool. What people get wrong:  Not checking Directory. It returns empty text when it fails, and a later path.Join("", name) then writes into the current folder. Trusting File blindly. It always returns a path, even when the file could not be created, and it creates the file first and narrows its permissions right after, so for a moment it has the default permissions. For secrets, make a Directory (only you can enter it) and create the files inside it. Moving a finished file out with a rename. The temporary folder is often on another disk, where a rename fails; copy it instead.  A scratch directory for one job The usual pattern is three lines: make a directory with Directory, put defer temp.RemoveDir(work) right under it, and build every path inside it with path.Join. The deferred call runs on every way out of the function, an early ret included, so the directory is gone however the job ends. Directory returns an empty string when it cannot make the directory, so check for that before you use it. os-temp-scratch.salamCopyimport fs.dir import fs import fs.path import os.temp  func main:     work := temp.Directory()     if work == "":         println "could not make a work directory"         ret 1     end     defer temp.RemoveDir(work)     fs.WriteText(path.Join(work, "part-1.txt"), "Salam ")     fs.WriteText(path.Join(work, "part-2.txt"), "world
")     mut joined := ""     each name in ["part-1.txt", "part-2.txt"]:         joined += fs.ReadText(path.Join(work, name))     end     print joined     println dir.ListFiles(work).Len(), "parts,", dir.Size(work), "bytes"     ret 0 endOutputSalam world 2 parts, 12 bytes  Build a file in steps, then publish it When a file is written in several steps, write it to a temporary file first and copy it to its real name only when it is complete. Whoever reads people.csv then never sees half of it. Use fs.Copy here, not fs.Move: the temporary directory is often on another disk (a tmpfs in memory on many Linux systems), and a rename cannot cross disks. os-temp-staging.salamCopyimport fs import os.temp  func main:     staging := temp.File()     fs.Append(staging, "id,name
")     fs.Append(staging, "1,Sara
")     fs.Append(staging, "2,Reza
")     rows := fs.ReadLines(staging)     println "staged", rows.Len(), "lines"     if fs.Copy(staging, "people.csv") == 0:         println "published people.csv,", fs.Size("people.csv"), "bytes"     end     temp.Remove(staging)     println "staging left behind:", fs.Exists(staging)     print fs.ReadText("people.csv")     fs.Delete("people.csv") endOutputstaged 3 lines published people.csv, 22 bytes staging left behind: false id,name 1,Sara 2,Reza When the whole content is ready in one string, fs.AtomicWrite is simpler: it writes the temporary copy next to the target, on the same disk, and renames it in one step.  Who can read a temporary file The system temporary directory is shared by every account on the machine. That is why File makes its file readable and writable by you alone (600) and Directory makes its directory open to you alone (700). A token or a downloaded document you put there stays out of reach of other users. Leave it like that, and widen the permissions with fs.Chmod only when another account really has to read the file. os-temp-permissions.salamCopyimport fs import os.temp  func main:     secret := temp.File()     work := temp.Directory()     println "file:", fs.Permissions(secret)     println "directory:", fs.Permissions(work)     temp.Remove(secret)     temp.RemoveDir(work) endOutputfile: 600 directory: 700  Errors, and where the files go Remove and RemoveDir return 0 on success and -1 on failure, and they record an IOError in os.error. The usual failure is removing the same file twice. RemoveDir on a directory that is already gone counts as success. os-temp-errors.salamCopyimport os.error import os.temp  func main:     p := temp.File()     println "first remove:", temp.Remove(p)     error.Clear()     println "second remove:", temp.Remove(p)     if error.HasError():         println "message:", error.LastMessage()         println "is an I/O error:", error.LastCode() == error.IOError     end endOutputfirst remove: 0 second remove: -1 message: failed to remove temp file is an I/O error: true The files go into the directory that os.TempDir names: the TEMP, TMP or TMPDIR environment variable, checked in that order, and /tmp when none is set. Nothing removes them when the program exits, and a program that crashes leaves them behind, so a long running service should give each job its own directory and remove it when the job is done. The names are random (salam- and hex digits), so never compare them or show them in output that someone reads later. os/user os.user Who is running the program, and the standard directories that belong to them. System and tools The os.user package answers two questions: who is running the program (Username, Uid, Gid), and where that user's files belong (HomeDir, ConfigDir, CacheDir). Programs usually keep their settings in the user config directory and throwaway data in the user cache directory; this package gives the conventional path on each system, for instance ~/.config on Linux and %APPDATA% on Windows. Note that macOS also gets ~/.config and ~/.cache, the convention of command line tools, rather than ~/Library. For the machine rather than the user, see os.platform; for reading other environment variables, env; for joining paths onto these folders, fs.path. How the directories are found These functions do not ask the operating system for a list of folders. They read environment variables, the same way most command line tools do, which also means that whoever starts the program can point them somewhere else:  FunctionLinux, macOS and BSDWindows  HomeDir$HOME%USERPROFILE% ConfigDir$XDG_CONFIG_HOME, else ~/.config%APPDATA% CacheDir$XDG_CACHE_HOME, else ~/.cache%LOCALAPPDATA% Username$USER, else $LOGNAME, else the user database%USERNAME%   The example sets the variables itself with env.Set, so it prints the same on every Unix machine: os-user-resolve.salamCopyimport env import os.user  func main:     env.Set("HOME", "/home/sara")     env.Unset("XDG_CONFIG_HOME")     env.Unset("XDG_CACHE_HOME")     println "home:  ", user.HomeDir()     println "config:", user.ConfigDir()     println "cache: ", user.CacheDir()     env.Set("XDG_CONFIG_HOME", "/data/sara/config")     env.Set("XDG_CACHE_HOME", "/fast-disk/cache")     println "config:", user.ConfigDir()     println "cache: ", user.CacheDir() endOutputhome:   /home/sara config: /home/sara/.config cache:  /home/sara/.cache config: /data/sara/config cache:  /fast-disk/cache  Settings and cache for your own program Give your program its own folder inside each of these directories, named after the program, and create it with dir.MkdirAll before the first write: on a fresh account even ~/.config may not exist yet. Settings belong in the config folder. Anything you can rebuild, such as downloads or a search index, belongs in the cache folder, which the user or a cleanup tool may empty at any time. The first line of this example points HOME at a folder in the current directory so that running it does not touch your real settings. A real program leaves that line out. os-user-app-dirs.salamCopyimport env import fs.dir import fs import fs.path import os import os.user  func main:     env.Set("HOME", path.Join(os.Cwd(), "demo-home"))     env.Unset("XDG_CONFIG_HOME")     env.Unset("XDG_CACHE_HOME")     config := path.Join(user.ConfigDir(), "notes")     cache := path.Join(user.CacheDir(), "notes")     dir.MkdirAll(config)     dir.MkdirAll(cache)     settings := path.Join(config, "settings.ini")     repeat 2 in run:         if fs.Exists(settings):             println "run", run + 1, "found", fs.ReadText(settings).Trim()         else:             fs.WriteText(settings, "theme=dark\n")             println "run", run + 1, "wrote the default settings"         end     end     fs.WriteText(path.Join(cache, "index.bin"), "0123456789")     println "settings at ~/" + path.Rel(user.HomeDir(), settings)     println "cache holds", dir.Size(cache), "bytes"     dir.RemoveAll(user.HomeDir()) endOutputrun 1 wrote the default settings run 2 found theme=dark settings at ~/.config/notes/settings.ini cache holds 10 bytes  Expanding ~ in paths from users The shell turns ~/notes into a full path before your program sees it, but a path read from a settings file or typed at a prompt still starts with ~. Neither fs nor fs.path expands it, so replace it yourself with HomeDir: os-user-expand-home.salamCopyimport env import fs.path import os.user import str  func expand(p: str): str:     if p == "~": ret user.HomeDir() end     if str.StartsWith(p, "~/"):         ret path.Join(user.HomeDir(), p.Substr(2, p.Len() - 2))     end     ret p end  func main:     env.Set("HOME", "/home/sara")     each p in ["~", "~/notes/today.md", "/etc/hosts", "reports/may.csv"]:         println p, "->", expand(p)     end endOutput~ -> /home/sara ~/notes/today.md -> /home/sara/notes/today.md /etc/hosts -> /etc/hosts reports/may.csv -> reports/may.csv  Things to watch for  Username is fine for a greeting or a log line, but it comes from environment variables that anyone starting the program can change. Never use it to decide what someone is allowed to do. Uid and Gid are -1 on Windows. On Unix a Uid of 0 means the program runs as root, which is worth a warning in a tool that should not. When its variable is not set, for example in a service started with an empty environment, HomeDir returns an empty string, and ConfigDir and CacheDir on Unix then return the relative paths .config and .cache. Check HomeDir first; otherwise your files silently land in the current directory.  Functions Usernamefunc Username(): strThe name of the current user: $USER, else $LOGNAME, else the system user database; %USERNAME% on Windows. It can be changed by whoever starts the program.os-user-Username.salamCopyimport os.user  func main:     println user.Username().Len() > 0     println user.Uid() >= 0, user.Gid() >= 0     println user.HomeDir().Len() > 0     println user.ConfigDir().Len() > 0, user.CacheDir().Len() > 0 endOutputtrue true true true true true Uidfunc Uid(): intThe numeric user id from the system, 0 for root; minus one

fs fs Reading, writing, copying and moving files, file information, times and permissions, and MD5 and SHA digests. System and tools The fs package is everything you need to work with one file: read it whole or as lines, write, append, replace it safely, copy, move and delete it, look up its size, times and permissions, change the permissions, hash it and guess its MIME type. One import is enough: import fs, then fs.ReadText(path). For folders use fs.dir, for paths fs.path, and for streaming a large file the handle functions of io. The simpler os package covers whole-file reads, folder listings and existence checks. The old fs.file package still works but is deprecated: it forwards every call to fs. In new code write import fs and fs.ReadText instead of import fs.file and file.ReadText. Writes return the number of bytes written, or -1. Reads return empty text when the file cannot be opened, the same as for an empty file; ask Exists when the difference matters. What people get wrong:  Treating it as binary-safe. Every read and write goes through a str, which ends at the first zero byte, so ReadAll, ReadBytes, WriteBytes and the digest functions cut a binary file short. For images, archives and other binary data use ReadBinaryFile and WriteBinaryFile from archive, which carry a pointer and a length, and the pointer forms in crypto such as Sha256Bytes. Expecting Move to cross disks. It is a rename and fails between file systems; fs.dir.Move falls back to copying, or copy and delete yourself. Assuming AtomicWrite keeps the old file's permissions. It writes a new file, which gets the default permissions; a file you had narrowed to 0o600 becomes readable again unless you Chmod it after each save. Using Exists to mean "is a file". It is true for directories too; combine it with fs.dir.IsDir.  Times are whole seconds since the start of 1970 (Unix time), as an i64. Every function returns -1 when the path does not exist or the system cannot answer. Write permissions in octal, such as 0o644, meaning the owner reads and writes and everyone else reads. Permissions returns the same digits as an ordinary number, such as 644, so that it reads easily. The two are not the same number (0o644 is 420), so never pass the result of Permissions back to Chmod unchanged. Read a settings file line by line ReadLines splits a file at its line breaks and drops a trailing , so a file saved on Windows reads the same as one saved on Linux. That makes simple key = value files easy: trim each line, skip blank lines and comments, and split at the first =. fs-guide-config.salamCopyimport fs import str  func main:     fs.WriteText("app.conf", "# shop settings
name = Corner Shop

port = 8080
currency = IRR
")     settings := HashMap {} as HashMap<str, str>     each line in fs.ReadLines("app.conf"):         t := line.Trim()         if t.Len() == 0 or str.StartsWith(t, "#"): continue end         eq_at := str.IndexOf(t, "=")         if eq_at < 0: continue end         settings.Put(t.Substr(0, eq_at).Trim(), t.Substr(eq_at + 1, t.Len() - eq_at - 1).Trim())     end     println settings.Size(), "settings"     println "name:", settings.Get("name")     println "port:", settings.Get("port")     fs.Delete("app.conf") endOutput3 settings name: Corner Shop port: 8080 For a format with sections, quoting or nesting, use a real parser such as encoding.toml, encoding.json or encoding.envfile.  Append to a log Append opens the file, adds the text at the end and closes it again, and creates the file on the first call. Each call is a separate open and close, which is fine for a line now and then. For a busy log, open the file once with Open(p, "ab"), write through io.Write and Close it at the end. fs-guide-log.salamCopyimport fs  func log(line: str):     fs.Append("app.log", line.Concat("
")) end  func main:     log("started")     log("loaded 3 orders")     log("sent invoice 1042")     log("stopped")     lines := fs.ReadLines("app.log")     println "log has", lines.Len(), "lines,", fs.Size("app.log"), "bytes"     println "last two:"     mut i := lines.Len() - 2     until i < lines.Len():         println " ", lines.Get(i)         i++     end     fs.Delete("app.log") endOutputlog has 4 lines, 50 bytes last two:   sent invoice 1042   stopped  Check that a file arrived intact Download pages often publish a SHA-256 digest next to each file. Compute the digest of your copy with Sha256Hex and compare the two: a change of even one byte gives a completely different digest. Md5Hex and Sha1Hex are fine for noticing accidental changes, such as a cache key, but anyone can build two different files with the same MD5 or SHA-1 on purpose, so do not trust them against an attacker. fs-guide-checksum.salamCopyimport fs  func verify(p: str): bool:     want := fs.ReadText(p.Concat(".sha256")).Trim()     ret fs.Sha256Hex(p) == want end  func main:     fs.WriteBytes("release.tar", "pretend this is a release archive")     fs.WriteText("release.tar.sha256", fs.Sha256Hex("release.tar").Concat("
"))     println "intact:", verify("release.tar")     fs.Append("release.tar", "!")     println "after a change:", verify("release.tar")     fs.Delete("release.tar")     fs.Delete("release.tar.sha256") endOutputintact: true after a change: false The digest functions read the file into a string first, and a Salam string ends at the first zero byte. For text files that does not matter. A binary file that contains a zero byte, which most archives and images do, is hashed only up to that byte, so check such files with the system sha256sum or with the buffer functions in crypto, such

fs/dir fs.dir Creating, listing, copying, moving and removing directories. System and tools The fs.dir package covers everything you do with directories: create them, list them, walk a tree, measure it, copy, move and delete it. It is built on the folder functions of os and adds two things: when a function fails it records the detail (an IOError with the operation and the path) in os.error, and Move works across disks. For files use fs, and to build the paths fs.path. Listing functions return bare names; Walk returns full paths. Functions that change the disk return 0 or -1. What people get wrong:  Using Exists for files. Here it is true only for a directory; for files use fs.Exists. Expecting Copy and Move to refuse an existing target. Both merge into it: files with the same name are replaced and other files stay. Pointing RemoveAll, Walk, Size or Copy at a tree with symbolic links. They follow a link to a folder as if it were part of the tree, so RemoveAll deletes the contents of the link's target and a link loop never ends.  Create a project layout MkdirAll creates every missing parent and succeeds when the folder is already there, so it is the safe choice for setting up a layout that may partly exist. List, ListDirs and ListFiles return bare names, not full paths, in whatever order the file system keeps them, and that order differs between systems. Sort them with sort.Sort before you show or compare them. fs-dir-guide-skeleton.salamCopyimport fs.dir import fs import sort  func main:     each d in ["shop/src/models", "shop/src/views", "shop/tests", "shop/docs"]:         dir.MkdirAll(d)     end     fs.WriteText("shop/main.salam", "func main:
end
")     fs.WriteText("shop/README.md", "# Shop
")     fs.WriteText("shop/src/models/order.salam", "")     top := dir.ListDirs("shop")     sort.Sort(top)     println "folders:", top     files := dir.ListFiles("shop")     sort.Sort(files)     println "files:  ", files     println "src has", dir.ListDirs("shop/src").Len(), "folders"     dir.RemoveAll("shop") endOutputfolders: ["docs", "src", "tests"] files:   ["README.md", "main.salam"] src has 2 folders  Walk a whole tree Walk returns the path of every file below a directory, already joined to the directory you passed in, so each one can go straight to an fs function. Directories themselves are not in the list, and like the listing functions it has no fixed order. This example counts files by extension and adds up their sizes, which is what Size does in one call. fs-dir-guide-walk.salamCopyimport fs.dir import fs import fs.path  func main:     dir.MkdirAll("site/pages/blog")     dir.MkdirAll("site/assets/img")     fs.WriteText("site/pages/index.html", "<h1>Home</h1>")     fs.WriteText("site/pages/blog/first.html", "<p>First post</p>")     fs.WriteText("site/assets/style.css", "body { margin: 0 }")     fs.WriteText("site/assets/img/logo.svg", "<svg/>")     counts := HashMap {} as HashMap<str, int>     mut bytes := 0 as i64     each p in dir.Walk("site"):         ext := path.Ext(p)         if counts.Has(ext): counts.Put(ext, counts.Get(ext) + 1) else: counts.Put(ext, 1) end         bytes += fs.Size(p)     end     each ext in [".html", ".css", ".svg"]:         println ext, counts.Get(ext)     end     println "total:", bytes, "bytes, same as dir.Size:", bytes == dir.Size("site")     dir.RemoveAll("site") endOutput.html 2 .css 1 .svg 1 total: 54 bytes, same as dir.Size: true  Keep rotating backups Copy copies a tree with everything in it (file contents only; permissions are not kept), and Move renames one, falling back to copy and delete when the rename fails, for example because the target is on another disk.
