fs/path fs.path Working with file paths: joining them, separating the name and the extension, absolute and relative paths, and a safety check. System and tools The fs.path package takes paths apart and puts them together: join, split, clean, make absolute or relative, and check that a path from a user stays inside a folder. Every function is a thin name over the same function in filepath (with Filename for Base, Dirname and Parent for Dir), so pick one of the two packages and use it throughout a program. One name differs in meaning: filepath.Base keeps the extension, while path.Basename drops it; fs.path reads naturally next to fs and fs.dir. Do not build paths by concatenating strings; Join puts the separator in for you. The separator is always /, on Windows too: every function first turns \ into /, and Windows accepts / in paths. When a path comes from a user, check it with IsSafe before opening it, so that nobody climbs out of the permitted directory with ../... Every function here works on the text of the path alone. None of them looks at the disk, except Abs, Rel and IsSafe with a relative path, which read the current directory. To create, read or list files, combine this package with fs.dir, fs or io, as the guide below does. What people get wrong:  Expecting Join to clean up. It only adds or merges the separator, so Join("a/b", "../c") is a/b/../c; pass the result through Clean. An absolute second part does not replace the first either, unlike Python's os.path.join. Reading Ext as the whole extension. It is only the last one: .gz for backup.tar.gz, and empty for a dot file such as .bashrc. Comparing paths as text without Clean. docs/./cv.pdf and docs/cv.pdf are the same file. Comparisons are also case sensitive, which is wrong on Windows and on default macOS disks.  Serving a file a user asked for A download handler gets a name such as 2026/report.pdf from the request and has to turn it into a file inside one folder. IsSafe simplifies the joined path first and then checks that it still starts with the folder, so a/../b.txt is fine while ../secret.txt and a/../../etc/passwd are refused. An empty name is refused too. fs-path-guide-safe.salamCopyimport fs.path  func resolve(root: str, requested: str): str:     if not path.IsSafe(root, requested): ret "" end     ret path.Clean(path.Join(root, requested)) end  func main:     root := "/srv/uploads"     each name in ["avatar.png", "2026/report.pdf", "a/../b.txt", "../secret.txt", "a/../../etc/passwd", "/etc/passwd", ""]:         full := resolve(root, name)         if full.Len() == 0:             println "refused", "[" + name + "]"         else:             println "serve  ", full         end     end endOutputserve   /srv/uploads/avatar.png serve   /srv/uploads/2026/report.pdf serve   /srv/uploads/b.txt refused [../secret.txt] refused [a/../../etc/passwd] serve   /srv/uploads/etc/passwd refused [] Look at the /etc/passwd line: Join does not let an absolute second part replace the first, so the result lands inside the folder and is safe. The check works on text only; it does not follow symbolic links, so do not put links that point outside the folder in a directory you serve.  Mapping one folder tree onto another A static site generator reads content/blog/hello.md and writes public/blog/hello.html. Rel gives the part below the source folder, Dirname and Stem take it apart, and Join and Clean build the new path. Stem removes only the last extension, so salam.v2.md keeps its .v2. fs-path-guide-output.salamCopyimport fs.path  func output_for(src_root: str, out_root: str, file: str): str:     rel := path.Rel(src_root, file)     folder := path.Join(out_root, path.Dirname(rel))     page := path.Stem(rel).Concat(".html")     ret path.Clean(path.Join(folder, page)) end  func main:     src := "/site/content"     out := "/site/public"     each file in ["/site/content/index.md", "/site/content/blog/hello.md", "/site/content/blog/2026/salam.v2.md"]:         println path.Rel(src, file), "->", output_for(src, out, file)     end endOutputindex.md -> /site/public/index.html blog/hello.md -> /site/public/blog/hello.html blog/2026/salam.v2.md -> /site/public/blog/2026/salam.v2.html For a file directly in the source folder Dirname returns .; the final Clean removes the /. that Join leaves behind. The example uses absolute paths because Rel makes relative ones absolute against the current directory first.  Making a new name next to a file To put a backup, a thumbnail or a converted copy next to the original, keep the folder and change only the name. Here Stem and Ext turn plan.md into plan.bak.md, and fs.dir and io do the actual work on disk. fs-path-guide-backup.salamCopyimport fs.path import fs.dir import io  func backup_name(p: str): str:     name := path.Stem(p).Concat(".bak").Concat(path.Ext(p))     ret path.Join(path.Dirname(p), name) end  func main:     dir.MkdirAll("notes/2026")     each p in ["notes/todo.txt", "notes/2026/plan.md"]:         io.WriteFile(p, "draft of ".Concat(path.Filename(p)))         copy := backup_name(p)         io.WriteFile(copy, io.ReadFile(p))         println p, "saved as", copy     end     println io.ReadFile("notes/2026/plan.bak.md") endOutputnotes/todo.txt saved as notes/todo.bak.txt notes/2026/plan.md saved as notes/2026/plan.bak.md draft of plan.md  Which function for which job Several functions here have close names. Filename keeps the extension; Basename and Stem both drop it. Normalize only changes \ to /; Clean is the one that resolves . and ...  You wantCallFor /home/sara/docs/cv.pdf  The folderDirname or Parent/home/sara/docs The name with its extensionFilenamecv.pdf The name without its extensionStem or Basenamecv The extensionExt.pdf Fold

filepath filepath Path functions that never touch the file system; the same work as the fs.path package. System and tools The filepath package takes path strings apart and builds them: Join, Dir, Base, Ext, Stem, Clean, Abs, Rel and the IsSafe check for paths that come from users. It works on strings alone and never touches the file system, apart from Abs, Rel and IsSafe, which read the current directory for a relative path. Use it in build tools, static site generators, upload handlers and anywhere a path is computed rather than typed. To act on the files themselves, pair it with fs, fs.dir or os. The fs.path package is a set of other names for the same functions; use whichever reads better to you, but one per program. The names differ a little: Base here is Filename there, and Dir is Dirname. Watch out for path.Basename, which is Stem and drops the extension, unlike Base. Paths always come out with / as the separator, on Windows too, and Windows accepts that. What people get wrong:  Expecting Join to clean the result. It only places one / between the parts: Join("a/b", "../c") is a/b/../c, and an absolute second part is appended, not substituted. Call Clean afterwards. Comparing paths as plain text. Clean both first, and remember that the comparison is case sensitive. Trusting a user's path without IsSafe. Even after Join, ../../etc/passwd climbs out of your folder.  Windows paths A path pasted by a Windows user, or read from a Windows config file, uses \. Every function here calls Normalize first, so Dir, Base and Join accept both kinds. IsAbs also treats a drive letter such as C:/ as absolute. filepath-guide-windows.salamCopyimport filepath  func main:     raw := "C:\\Users\\Sara\\Documents\\cv.pdf"     p := filepath.Normalize(raw)     println p     println filepath.IsAbs(p), filepath.IsAbs("Documents\\cv.pdf")     println filepath.Dir(p)     println filepath.Base(p), filepath.Stem(p), filepath.Ext(p)     println filepath.Join("C:\\Users\\Sara", "Pictures\\cat.jpg")     println filepath.Clean("D:/games/../music/./song.mp3") endOutputC:/Users/Sara/Documents/cv.pdf true false C:/Users/Sara/Documents cv.pdf cv .pdf C:/Users/Sara/Pictures/cat.jpg D:/music/song.mp3 In a Salam string a single backslash is written \\. Clean treats the drive as an ordinary first part, so C:/../x becomes x; do not climb above the drive with ...  Edge cases worth knowing The table below runs Dir, Base, Ext and Clean over inputs that often cause bugs: the root, an empty string, a trailing slash, a dot file and a double extension. filepath-guide-edges.salamCopyimport filepath import fmt  func show(p: str):     print fmt.PadRight("[" + p + "]", 20)     print fmt.PadRight(filepath.Dir(p), 10)     print fmt.PadRight(filepath.Base(p), 16)     print fmt.PadRight("[" + filepath.Ext(p) + "]", 8)     println filepath.Clean(p) end  func main:     println "path                dir       base            ext     clean"     each p in ["/", "", "docs/", "/var/log/app.log", ".bashrc", "backup.tar.gz", "../up/x.txt", "a/./b/../c.txt"]:         show(p)     end endOutputpath                dir       base            ext     clean [/]                 /         /               []      / []                  .         .               []      . [docs/]             .         docs            []      docs [/var/log/app.log]  /var/log  app.log         [.log]  /var/log/app.log [.bashrc]           .         .bashrc         []      .bashrc [backup.tar.gz]     .         backup.tar.gz   [.gz]   backup.tar.gz [../up/x.txt]       ../up     x.txt           [.txt]  ../up/x.txt [a/./b/../c.txt]    a/./b/..  c.txt           [.txt]  a/c.txt The rules it shows: a trailing slash is ignored; an empty path counts as .; a name that starts with a dot, like .bashrc, has no extension; Ext returns only the last extension, so test for .tar.gz with str.EndsWith when you need it. Dir does not simplify, so call Clean first when the path may contain . or ...  Grouping files by extension Ext with a HashMap counts files by type, for a report or to pick a handler for each file. A second vector remembers the order in which the extensions first appeared, so the output does not depend on the map's internal order. filepath-guide-group.salamCopyimport filepath  func main:     files := ["src/main.salam", "src/util.salam", "README.md", "docs/guide.md", "logo.svg", "Makefile", "docs/intro.md"]     order := Vector {} as Vector<str>     defer order.Free()     counts := HashMap {} as HashMap<str, int>     each f in files:         mut ext := filepath.Ext(f)         if ext.Len() == 0: ext = "(none)" end         if counts.Has(ext):             counts.Put(ext, counts.Get(ext) + 1)         else:             counts.Put(ext, 1)             order.Push(ext)         end     end     each ext in order:         println ext, counts.Get(ext)     end endOutput.salam 2 .md 3 .svg 1 (none) 1 Ext keeps the case of the name, so photo.JPG gives .JPG. Pass it through str.Lower before comparing when the files come from a camera or from Windows. Constants and variables Separatorconst Separator: str = "/"The separator between the parts of a path: always /, on Windows too.filepath-Join.salamCopyimport filepath  func main:     p := filepath.Join("projects", "salam/main.salam")     println p, filepath.Separator     println filepath.Dir(p), filepath.Base(p), filepath.Ext(p), filepath.Stem(p)     println filepath.Normalize("a//b/./c/"), filepath.Clean("a/b/../c")     println filepath.IsAbs("/usr/bin"), filepath.IsAbs(p), filepath.IsAbs(filepath.Abs(p))     println filepath.Rel("/a/b", "/a/b/c/d")     println filepath.IsSafe("/srv", "x/y"), file

env env Environment variables: reading them with the right type, .env files, the run profile, and masking sensitive values. System and tools Settings such as a server port, a database address and API keys belong in environment variables rather than in the code, the "twelve-factor" way of configuring a service. The env package reads them with the right type and a default, masks secrets for logs, loads .env files, picks files per environment and fills ${NAME} templates. For the bare value of one variable, os.Env is enough; to parse or write .env files as data without touching the environment, use encoding.envfile; for command line options, flag. The "profile" says whether the program is running in development, test or production. It is read from SALAM_ENV; when that is unset or empty, APP_ENV and then ENV are tried, and the default is development. Profile returns the value lower-cased but otherwise as written. IsProduction, IsDevelopment and IsTest also accept prod, dev and testing, but LoadProfile uses the name as written, so SALAM_ENV=prod loads .env.prod, not .env.production. What people get wrong:  Trusting the typed getters to validate. GetInt gives the default for abc and 12px just as for a missing variable, and GetBool knows only lower case true, 1, yes, on and false, 0, no, off, so DEBUG=True gives the default. Expecting a .env file to win. Load and LoadProfile never replace a variable that is already set, which is right in production; Overload and LoadDotEnv do replace. Logging secrets. Pass them through Mask, and keep .env.local files out of version control.   Reading the whole configuration at start-up Read every setting once, in one function, into a struct. The rest of the program then takes the struct and never calls env itself, which keeps the list of variables in one place and makes the code easy to test. Print the configuration at start-up, but pass secrets through Mask first. env-guide-config.salamCopyimport env import str  struct Config:     pub host: str = ""     pub port: i64 = 0     pub workers: i64 = 0     pub debug: bool = false     pub db_url: str = ""     pub api_key: str = "" end  func load_config(): Config:     ret Config {         host = env.GetOr("APP_HOST", "127.0.0.1"),         port = env.GetInt("APP_PORT", 8080),         workers = env.GetInt("APP_WORKERS", 4),         debug = env.GetBool("APP_DEBUG", false),         db_url = env.GetOr("APP_DB_URL", "sqlite://app.db"),         api_key = env.Get("APP_API_KEY")     } end  func main:     env.Set("APP_PORT", "9000")     env.Set("APP_DEBUG", "yes")     env.Set("APP_API_KEY", "sk-test-1234567890")     env.Unset("APP_HOST")     env.Unset("APP_WORKERS")     env.Unset("APP_DB_URL")     c := load_config()     println "listening on", c.host + ":" + str.FromInt(c.port as int)     println "workers:", c.workers, "debug:", c.debug     println "database:", c.db_url     println "api key:", env.Mask(c.api_key)     if c.api_key.Len() == 0: println "warning: APP_API_KEY is not set" end endOutputlistening on 127.0.0.1:9000 workers: 4 debug: true database: sqlite://app.db api key: sk****90  What a .env file can contain A .env file has one NAME=value per line. Lines starting with # are comments, a leading export is allowed so the same file works with a shell, and values may be in double or single quotes. Inside double quotes and unquoted values, ${NAME} is replaced; single quotes keep the text exactly as written. env-guide-dotenv.salamCopyimport env import io  func main:     io.WriteFile(".env", "# local settings
export APP_NAME=\"Salam Shop\"
APP_PORT=8080
APP_URL=http://localhost:${APP_PORT}
APP_GREETING='hello ${APP_NAME}'
EMPTY=
")     env.Set("APP_PORT", "3000")     println "read:", env.Load(".env")     println env.Get("APP_NAME")     println env.Get("APP_PORT")     println env.Get("APP_URL")     println env.Get("APP_GREETING")     println env.Has("EMPTY"), "[" + env.Get("EMPTY") + "]", env.GetOr("EMPTY", "fallback") endOutputread: 4 Salam Shop 3000 http://localhost:8080 hello ${APP_NAME} true [] fallback Three things to notice. Load never replaces a variable that is already set, so APP_PORT stays 3000, and the number it returns counts only the variables it actually set. A ${APP_PORT} inside the file uses the file's own value. And an empty value is set but empty: Has says true while GetOr gives the default.  One set of files per environment LoadProfile reads up to four files from a folder, later ones winning over earlier ones: .env, .env.local, .env.<profile> and .env.<profile>.local. Commit the first and third, and keep the .local files, which hold each developer's own values and secrets, out of version control. A variable that is already set in the real environment still wins over every file. env-guide-profiles.salamCopyimport env import io  func main:     io.WriteFile(".env", "DB_HOST=localhost
LOG_LEVEL=debug
CACHE=off
")     io.WriteFile(".env.local", "DB_HOST=127.0.0.1
")     io.WriteFile(".env.production", "DB_HOST=db.internal
LOG_LEVEL=warn
")     io.WriteFile(".env.production.local", "LOG_LEVEL=error
")     env.Set("SALAM_ENV", "production")     env.Set("CACHE", "on")     println "profile:", env.Profile(), env.IsProduction()     println "loaded:", env.LoadProfile(".")     println "DB_HOST =", env.Get("DB_HOST")     println "LOG_LEVEL =", env.Get("LOG_LEVEL")     println &quot

flag flag Reading command line options such as --port 8080 and -v with the right type, and generating the help text. System and tools The flag package reads command line options. Each flag has a long name (--port), an optional short name (-p), a kind (bool, string, int or float), a default value and a line of help. The value can be given either way: --port=8080 or --port 8080. Any argument that is not a flag is "positional", and after -- everything counts as positional. For a program with subcommands such as tool build and tool test, see cli; for settings from the environment, env. The steps are always the same: New, one Add... per flag, Parse with the arguments (without the program's own name), then check Parse's result and HelpWanted before reading values with GetStr, GetInt, GetFloat and GetBool. --help and -h are always recognised and reserved, and the Usage text is generated for you. What people get wrong:  Forgetting that a value flag takes the next argument whatever it is. --name --verbose sets the name to --verbose. Passing negative numbers as positional arguments. -5 looks like a flag and gives "unknown flag"; put -- before it, or use --offset=-5 for a flag value. Expecting a bad boolean to be an error. --verbose=maybe is accepted and reads as false; only true, 1, yes and on are true.  Reading the real command line os.Args returns every argument, with the program's own name first. cli.RemainingArgs drops that first item, which gives exactly what Parse wants. A program then checks three things in order: did parsing fail, was help asked for, and only then does it read the values. Exit with code 2 on a usage error, as most command line tools do. flag-guide-args.salamCopyimport cli import flag import os  func main:     mut argv := cli.RemainingArgs(os.Args())     defer argv.Free()     if argv.Len() == 0:         each a in ["--name", "Sara", "-n", "2", "--excited"]: argv.Push(a) end     end     mut f := flag.New("greet", "prints a greeting")     defer flag.Free(f)     flag.AddStr(f, "name", "", "world", "who to greet")     flag.AddInt(f, "times", "n", 1, "how many times")     flag.AddBool(f, "excited", "e", false, "end with three exclamation marks")     if not flag.Parse(f, argv):         println "greet:", flag.Error(f)         ret 2     end     if flag.HelpWanted(f):         print flag.Usage(f)         ret 0     end     line := "Hello, " + flag.GetStr(f, "name") + (flag.GetBool(f, "excited") ? "!!!" : ".")     repeat flag.GetInt(f, "times") as int:         println line     end     ret 0 endOutputHello, Sara!!! Hello, Sara!!! Run it as salam run greet.salam --name Ali -n 3 to pass your own arguments. When it gets none, as here, it uses a built-in sample so that the output above stays the same.  Reporting bad input Parse stops at the first problem and returns false, and Error says what went wrong in one line, ready to print. There are four kinds: a value that is not a whole number, a value that is not a decimal, a flag that was never declared, and a flag at the end of the line with no value after it. flag-guide-errors.salamCopyimport flag import str  func try_line(line: str): int:     argv := str.Split(line, " ")     defer argv.Free()     mut f := flag.New("resize", "resizes images")     defer flag.Free(f)     flag.AddInt(f, "width", "w", 800, "the new width in pixels")     flag.AddFloat(f, "quality", "q", 0.9, "the JPEG quality")     flag.AddStr(f, "out", "o", "out", "the output directory")     if not flag.Parse(f, argv):         println "error:", flag.Error(f)         ret 2     end     println "ok: width", flag.GetInt(f, "width"), "quality", flag.GetFloat(f, "quality"), "files", flag.Positional(f)     ret 0 end  func main:     each line in ["-w 640 a.jpg", "--width=wide a.jpg", "--quality=0,5 a.jpg", "--height 100", "a.jpg -o"]:         println "$ resize", line         println "exit code", try_line(line)     end endOutput$ resize -w 640 a.jpg ok: width 640 quality 0.9 files ["a.jpg"] exit code 0 $ resize --width=wide a.jpg error: invalid int value for --width: wide exit code 2 $ resize --quality=0,5 a.jpg error: invalid float value for --quality: 0,5 exit code 2 $ resize --height 100 error: unknown flag: --height exit code 2 $ resize a.jpg -o error: missing value for flag: -o exit code 2 The messages are in English. Unknown flags and missing values stop the parse where they occur; numbers are checked after the whole line has been read, in the order the flags were declared. Decimal values need a dot (or the Persian ٫), so 0,5 is rejected. Number flags accept Persian digits as well. When a flag is given twice, the last value wins.  Flag, then environment, then default Many programs read a setting from a flag, fall back to an environment variable, and use a built-in default last. WasSet makes that possible: it tells "the user typed --port 8080" apart from "8080 is just the default", which GetInt alone cannot. flag-guide-precedence.salamCopyimport env import flag import str  func port_from(line: str): i64:     argv := str.Split(line, " ")     defer argv.Free()     mut f := flag.New("server", "")     defer flag.Free(f)     flag.AddInt(f, "port", "p", 8080, "the port to listen on")     flag.Parse(f, argv)     if flag.WasSet(f, "port"): ret flag.GetInt(f, "port") end     ret env.GetInt("PORT", flag.GetInt(f, "port")) end  func main:     env.Unset("PORT")     println "nothing

cli cli Command line programs with several commands, like git commit, and asking the user questions. System and tools Many tools have several commands: git commit, salam build, salam run. The cli package holds the list of commands, works out from the first argument which one was asked for, and builds the overall help text. It also asks the user questions in the terminal with Prompt, PromptOr and Confirm. It is deliberately small and does not parse options. Pick the package by the shape of your program:  One command with options, such as resize --width 800 photo.png: flag alone is enough. Several commands, each with its own options: cli picks the command and a flag set per command reads its options. Full-screen or coloured terminal output: term.  The things people get wrong:  Dispatch wants the arguments without the program's name. os.Args includes it, so pass RemainingArgs(os.Args()). help, -h, --help, version, -v and --version are taken by Dispatch, and inside each command flag treats -h and --help as a help request. Never register h as a short flag of your own. Command names match exactly: no prefixes, aliases or case folding, and Register does not reject a duplicate (the first one wins). RemainingArgs returns a new vector; free it with defer rest.free().   A tool with several commands The usual shape: Dispatch picks the command from the first argument, RemainingArgs hands everything after it to that command, and each command declares its own flag set, so todo add and todo list can have different options. Each command returns an exit code. cli-guide-subcommands.salamCopyimport cli import flag import str  func cmd_add(argv: Vector<str>): int:     mut f := flag.New("todo add", "adds a task")     defer flag.Free(f)     flag.AddInt(f, "priority", "p", 3, "1 is the most urgent")     if not flag.Parse(f, argv):         println "todo add:", flag.Error(f)         ret 2     end     if flag.HelpWanted(f):         print flag.Usage(f)         ret 0     end     words := flag.Positional(f)     defer words.Free()     println "added [" + str.Join(words, " ") + "] with priority", flag.GetInt(f, "priority")     ret 0 end  func cmd_list(argv: Vector<str>): int:     mut f := flag.New("todo list", "lists the tasks")     defer flag.Free(f)     flag.AddBool(f, "all", "a", false, "include finished tasks")     if not flag.Parse(f, argv):         println "todo list:", flag.Error(f)         ret 2     end     println "listing", flag.GetBool(f, "all") ? "all tasks" : "open tasks"     ret 0 end  func run(app &: cli.App, line: str): int:     argv := str.Split(line, " ")     defer argv.Free()     command := cli.Dispatch(app, argv)     rest := cli.RemainingArgs(argv)     defer rest.Free()     if command == "add": ret cmd_add(rest) end     if command == "list": ret cmd_list(rest) end     if command == cli.CmdVersion:         println app.name, app.version         ret 0     end     if command == cli.CmdUnknown: println "todo: unknown command:", argv.Get(0) end     print cli.Usage(app)     ret command == cli.CmdHelp ? 0 : 2 end  func main:     mut app := cli.New("todo", "a small task list", "0.3.0")     cli.Register(app, "add", "add a task")     cli.Register(app, "list", "show the tasks")     each line in ["add -p 1 buy milk", "list --all", "add --priority=high call mom", "add --help", "--version", "remove 3"]:         println "$ todo", line         println "exit", run(app, line)     end endOutput$ todo add -p 1 buy milk added [buy milk] with priority 1 exit 0 $ todo list --all listing all tasks exit 0 $ todo add --priority=high call mom todo add: invalid int value for --priority: high exit 2 $ todo add --help Usage: todo add [options] [args]   adds a task Options:   -p, --priority <int>  1 is the most urgent (default: 3)   -h, --help  show this help exit 0 $ todo --version todo 0.3.0 exit 0 $ todo remove 3 todo: unknown command: remove todo 0.3.0 a small task list  Usage: todo <command> [options]  Commands:   add           add a task   list          show the tasks  Run 'todo <command> --help' for help on a specific command. exit 2 cli.Usage ends with a hint to run todo <command> --help, but answering it is each command's job: check flag.HelpWanted after parsing and print flag.Usage, as add does here. Both help texts are generated in English; only your descriptions appear as you wrote them.  Wiring it to the real arguments In a real program the arguments come from os.Args. Drop the program's own name with RemainingArgs and pass the rest to Dispatch. With no arguments at all Dispatch returns CmdHelp, so running the tool bare prints its help, which is what users expect. cli-guide-main.salamCopyimport cli import os  func main:     mut app := cli.New("notes", "keeps short notes", "1.2.0")     cli.Register(app, "new", "write a new note")     cli.Register(app, "show", "print every note")     argv := cli.RemainingArgs(os.Args())     defer argv.Free()     command := cli.Dispatch(app, argv)     if command == cli.CmdHelp:         print cli.Usage(app)         ret 0     else command == cli.CmdVersion:         println app.version         ret 0     else command == cli.CmdUnknown:         println "notes: no such command:", argv.Get(0)         ret 2     end     println "running", command, "with", cli.RemainingArgs(argv)     ret 0 endOutputnotes 1.2.0 keeps short notes  Usage: notes <command> [options]  Commands:   new           write a new note   show          print every note  Run 'notes <command

config config Reading and writing INI, env and YAML settings files with dotted keys. System and tools The config package reads a program's settings from INI, YAML or env files and keeps them as one ordered list of keys and text values. Keys in sections are dotted: the key host in the [db] section of an INI file, or under db: in YAML, becomes db.host. Whatever the file format, the rest of the program reads settings the same way. Use it for flat settings files that people edit by hand. For neighbouring jobs:  A single environment variable of the running process: env or os. A .env file with full control over quoting, export lines and errors: encoding.envfile, which this package uses underneath. YAML with lists or nested data you want to walk: encoding.yaml. JSON or TOML: encoding.json, encoding.toml. Command line options: flag.  The usual pattern is to read the default settings, Merge the current environment's settings on top, and then read the values with the right type. Every value is stored as text; GetInt, GetFloat and GetBool convert it when you read it, and their last argument is the value to use when the key is not there at all. The things people get wrong:  Nothing here reports an error. A missing or unreadable file gives an empty config, a line without = is skipped, and the typed getters fall back to your default for a value that is not a number. Check the file and the important keys yourself, as the guides below show. GetBool is true only for true, 1, yes and on, written in lower case. TRUE and Yes are false. In INI and env files a # after a space starts a comment (in INI a ; does too). Put quotes around values that contain them, such as passwords. A Config owns its memory: free each one you make, including the new ones that Merge and Section return, and free the vector Keys returns.   Layered settings: defaults, then overrides Most programs read settings from more than one place: defaults shipped with the program, a file for the server it runs on, and a few values given on the command line. Merge takes two configs and returns a third in which the second one wins. Chain it to stack as many layers as you need. Keys keep the order of the base, and keys that only the override has are added at the end. config-layers.salamCopyimport config  func main:     defaults := "name = shop
workers = 4
debug = false

[db]
host = localhost
port = 5432
"     production := "workers = 16

[db]
host = db.internal
pool = 20
"     mut base := config.ParseINI(defaults)     defer config.Free(base)     mut prod := config.ParseINI(production)     defer config.Free(prod)     mut flags := config.New()     defer config.Free(flags)     config.Set(flags, "debug", "yes")     mut step := config.Merge(base, prod)     defer config.Free(step)     mut final := config.Merge(step, flags)     defer config.Free(final)     print config.FormatINI(final)     println "workers:", config.GetInt(final, "workers", 1)     println "debug:", config.GetBool(final, "debug", false)     println "db:", config.Get(final, "db.host"), config.GetInt(final, "db.port", 5432), config.GetInt(final, "db.pool", 5) endOutputname = shop workers = 16 debug = yes [db] host = db.internal port = 5432 pool = 20 workers: 16 debug: true db: db.internal 5432 20 The production file only names what differs (workers, db.host and a new db.pool), so the defaults stay the single place that lists every setting. db.port was never overridden and keeps its default.  Sections and your own settings struct Passing one big config around means every part of the program sees every key. Section cuts out the keys under one name and drops the prefix, so a function that sets up the database only gets host, port and pool. Reading those into a struct once, at startup, keeps the rest of the code free of key names and string conversions. config-sections.salamCopyimport config  struct Database:     pub host: str = ""     pub port: i64 = 0     pub pool: i64 = 0 end  func read_database(c &: config.Config): Database:     ret Database {         host = config.GetOr(c, "host", "localhost"),         port = config.GetInt(c, "port", 5432),         pool = config.GetInt(c, "pool", 10)     } end  func main:     text := "server:
  port: 8080
  host: 0.0.0.0
database:
  host: db.local
  port: 6432
log: warn
"     mut c := config.ParseYAML(text)     defer config.Free(c)     mut server := config.Section(c, "server")     defer config.Free(server)     keys := config.Keys(server)     defer keys.Free()     each k in keys:         println "server", k, "=", config.Get(server, k)     end     mut dbc := config.Section(c, "database")     defer config.Free(dbc)     d := read_database(dbc)     println d.host, d.port, d.pool     println config.Len(c), config.Has(c, "log"), config.Has(c, "server") endOutputserver port = 8080 server host = 0.0.0.0 db.local 6432 10 5 true false A YAML map such as server: is flattened into dotted keys, so the config holds only the leaf values: Has(c, "server") is false, while Has(c, "server.port") is true. Keys lists the keys in file order.  Reading files: comments, quotes and missing files LoadINI, LoadYAML and LoadEnv read the whole file and parse it. If the file is not there they return an empty config without a word, so a typo in the path quietly leaves every setting at its default. Check the path first with fs and decide what a missing file means for your program. config-files.salamCopyimport config import fs import io  func load_settings(path: str): config.Config:     if not fs.Exists(path):         println "no", path, "found, using built-in defaults"         mut c := config.New()         config.Set(c, "server.port", "8080")         ret c     end     ret config.LoadINI(path) e

log log Recording what a program does, with levels, a prefix, structured fields, JSON output and writing to a file. System and tools For a program running on a server, println is not enough: you need to know how important each message is and when it was written, and to be able to silence the unimportant ones. The log package has four levels, debug, info, warn and error, and records only the messages at or above the level you set; the default level is info. Each line goes out in plain text or as one JSON object, to standard error, standard output or a file that can rotate. A text line looks like 2026-10-17 13:09:22 [INFO] shop order 1042 accepted: the local time, the level, the prefix and the message. The examples below turn the time off with ShowTime(false) so their output is stable. All settings are global to the program: call SetLevel, SetFormat, SetPrefix and one of ToStderr, ToStdout or ToFile once near the start of main, and every package that imports log writes the same way. For a quick look at a value while you work on the code, debug is the better tool; for timing and memory figures, runtime. The things people get wrong:  A file log is buffered. Lines reach the disk when the buffer fills or at CloseFile, so tail -f lags behind and a crash loses the last lines. Call CloseFile on every way out of the program. The text format writes the message as it is. A value from a user that holds a line break starts a fake log line; use JSON, which escapes it (see below). The settings are plain globals with no lock. Change them at startup only, not while other threads are logging. The time is local time with no zone offset, also in JSON. Run servers with TZ=UTC when logs from several machines are compared.   Choose the level from the settings The level should not be fixed in the code. During development you want debug messages; on a busy server you want warnings and errors only. Read the level as text from a settings file or the environment and turn it into a number with ParseLevel. It accepts debug, info, warn, warning and error in any case, and falls back to info for anything else, so a typo never silences the log completely. log-level-config.salamCopyimport log import config  func setup(text: str):     mut c := config.ParseEnv(text)     defer config.Free(c)     level := log.ParseLevel(config.GetOr(c, "LOG_LEVEL", "info"))     log.SetLevel(level)     log.SetPrefix(config.GetOr(c, "APP_NAME", "app"))     println "-- level", log.LevelName(log.GetLevel()) end  func work():     log.Debug("cache lookup for key user:7")     log.Info("order 1042 accepted")     log.Warn("payment provider answered slowly")     log.Error("could not send the receipt email") end  func main:     log.ToStdout()     log.ShowTime(false)     setup("LOG_LEVEL=debug
APP_NAME=shop
")     work()     setup("LOG_LEVEL=warning
APP_NAME=shop
")     work()     setup("LOG_LEVEL=loud
")     work() endOutput-- level DEBUG [DEBUG] shop cache lookup for key user:7 [INFO] shop order 1042 accepted [WARN] shop payment provider answered slowly [ERROR] shop could not send the receipt email -- level WARN [WARN] shop payment provider answered slowly [ERROR] shop could not send the receipt email -- level INFO [INFO] app order 1042 accepted [WARN] app payment provider answered slowly [ERROR] app could not send the receipt email The config package used here is described on its own page, config. The prefix is a good place for the program's name, so that lines from several programs in one log stay apart.  JSON logs for a log collector Text lines are easy to read; JSON lines are easy for tools such as Loki, Elasticsearch or a cloud log service to search. SetFormat(FormatJSON) turns every line into one JSON object with level, the optional prefix, msg, and one member for each key given to the ...KV functions. With the time switched on, a time member in ISO 8601 comes first. log-json-requests.salamCopyimport log import str  struct Request:     pub method: str = ""     pub path: str = ""     pub status: int = 0     pub ms: int = 0 end  func record(r: Request):     mut keys := Vector {} as Vector<str>     mut vals := Vector {} as Vector<str>     defer keys.Free()     defer vals.Free()     keys.Push("method")     vals.Push(r.method)     keys.Push("path")     vals.Push(r.path)     keys.Push("status")     vals.Push(str.FromInt(r.status as i64))     keys.Push("ms")     vals.Push(str.FromInt(r.ms as i64))     if r.status >= 500:         log.ErrorKV("request failed", keys, vals)     else r.status >= 400:         log.WarnKV("request rejected", keys, vals)     else:         log.InfoKV("request served", keys, vals)     end end  func main:     log.ToStdout()     log.ShowTime(false)     log.SetFormat(log.FormatJSON)     log.SetPrefix("api")     record(Request { method = "GET", path = "/products", status = 200, ms = 12 })     record(Request { method = "POST", path = "/login", status = 401, ms = 3 })     record(Request { method = "GET", path = "/report \"q3\"", status = 503, ms = 950 }) endOutput{"level": "INFO", "prefix": "api", "msg": "request served", "method": "GET", "path": "/products", "status": "200", "ms": "12"} {"level": "WARN", "prefix": "api", "msg": "request rejected", "method": "POST", "path": "/login", "status": "401", "ms": "3"} {"level": "ERROR", "prefix": "api", "msg": "request failed", "method": "

debug debug Tools for finding a bug: assertions, a hand-kept call stack, tracing and timing. System and tools The debug package holds a few small tools for when the program is not doing the right thing. Assert checks a condition that should always hold. Enter and Exit keep a call stack by hand, so an error message can say where in the program it happened. Trace prints what the program is doing, the timers show which part is slow, and MemStats counts allocations to find a leak. It is meant for development. For messages a running service keeps, use log; for exact timing and allocation counters in your own code, runtime and mem; for benchmarks inside tests, testing. The things people get wrong:  Assert is an ordinary function: it runs in release builds too, and its message is built even when the condition holds. Keep expensive work out of the message. The stack, the trace switch and the timers are globals with no lock, shared by every thread. In a program with threads the stack mixes frames from all of them. The stack is only as good as its Enter and Exit calls. Always pair them with defer debug.Exit(). MemStats only has numbers in a build with memory counting on; a normal run gets a line saying so.  Trace lines and failed assertions go to standard error, so they do not mix with the program's normal output.  Say where an error happened An error message like empty price is hard to act on in a big program: which item, and who asked for it? Call Enter at the start of the functions you care about and defer debug.Exit() right after it, so the frame is removed on every return path. Stack then gives the path from the outermost frame to the current one, joined with >. The frame is just text, so it can carry the item being worked on. debug-stack-errors.salamCopyimport debug  func fail(msg: str): bool:     println "error in", debug.Stack() + ":", msg     ret false end  func parse_price(text: str): bool:     debug.Enter("parse_price")     defer debug.Exit()     if text.Len() == 0:         ret fail("empty price")     end     ret true end  func load_item(name: str, price: str): bool:     debug.Enter("load_item " + name)     defer debug.Exit()     ret parse_price(price) end  func load_catalogue(): int:     debug.Enter("load_catalogue")     defer debug.Exit()     mut loaded := 0     if load_item("tea", "4.50"): loaded++ end     if load_item("cake", ""): loaded++ end     if load_item("milk", "1.20"): loaded++ end     ret loaded end  func main:     println load_catalogue(), "items loaded, depth now", debug.Depth() endOutputerror in load_catalogue > load_item cake > parse_price: empty price 2 items loaded, depth now 0 After the outer function returns, Depth is back at 0. If it is not, some function called Enter without a matching Exit, which is exactly the bug that defer prevents.  Trace the calls of a recursive function EnableTrace(true) switches tracing on: from then on Enter and Exit print an enter and an exit line, and Trace prints its message after the current stack. With tracing off, Trace prints nothing, so trace calls can stay in the code and be switched on with a flag, for instance from a setting or a command line option. debug-trace-calls.salamCopyimport debug import str  func fib(n: int): int:     debug.Enter("fib " + str.FromInt(n as i64))     defer debug.Exit()     if n < 2:         debug.Trace("base case")         ret n     end     ret fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2) end  func main:     debug.Trace("not printed, tracing is off")     debug.EnableTrace(true)     result := fib(3)     debug.EnableTrace(false)     debug.Trace("not printed either")     printerrln "fib(3) =", result endOutput[TRACE] fib 3: enter [TRACE] fib 3 > fib 2: enter [TRACE] fib 3 > fib 2 > fib 1: enter [TRACE] fib 3 > fib 2 > fib 1: base case [TRACE] fib 3 > fib 2 > fib 1: exit [TRACE] fib 3 > fib 2 > fib 0: enter [TRACE] fib 3 > fib 2 > fib 0: base case [TRACE] fib 3 > fib 2 > fib 0: exit [TRACE] fib 3 > fib 2: exit [TRACE] fib 3 > fib 1: enter [TRACE] fib 3 > fib 1: base case [TRACE] fib 3 > fib 1: exit [TRACE] fib 3: exit fib(3) = 2 Reading the lines from top to bottom shows the order of the calls; the indentation you would draw by hand is the length of each stack. All of it goes to standard error, like the last line, which this example prints with printerrln.  Time parts of a program StartTimer starts a named timer and StopTimer returns the milliseconds since it started, measured with the monotonic clock, so a change of the system time does not disturb it. Starting a timer that already exists restarts it. StopTimer does not remove the timer: calling it again later gives a larger number, which is handy for lap times. A name that was never started gives 0. debug-timers.salamCopyimport debug  func busy(n: int): int:     mut total := 0     repeat n in i:         total = (total + i * i) % 1000003     end     ret total end  func main:     debug.StartTimer("all")     debug.StartTimer("step")     a := busy(200000)     first := debug.StopTimer("step")     debug.StartTimer("step")     b := busy(200000)     second := debug.StopTimer("step")     total := debug.StopTimer("all")     later := debug.StopTimer("all")     println a == b     println "both steps fit in the total:", first + second <= total     println "a timer keeps running after StopTimer:", later >= total     println "unknown timer:", debug.StopTimer("never started") endOutputtrue both steps fit in the total: true a timer keeps running after StopTimer: true unknown timer: 0 Times differ from run to run and from machine to machine, so the example only prints comparisons. In your own program print the numbers themselves, for instanc

runtime runtime Facts about the running program: the system, the memory, the uptime and the build options. System and tools The runtime package answers questions about the running program and the machine under it: which system and processor, how many cores, how much memory, how long the program has been up and how it was compiled. It is what a /health route, a startup log line or a benchmark guard needs. It gathers facts from os.platform and adds the uptime and the build flags. For details such as the host name or the kernel version, use os.platform directly; for the program's own allocation counts, mem; for timing a piece of code, time or the timers in debug. Where the numbers come from:  SystemCpuCountTotalMemoryAvailableMemory, UsedMemory  Linuxa system callreads /proc/meminforeads /proc/meminfo Windowsthe NUMBER_OF_PROCESSORS variableruns PowerShellruns PowerShell macOS, BSDruns sysctlruns sysctlminus one   The things people get wrong:  The memory functions are not free everywhere. On Linux they read a small file, but on Windows each call starts PowerShell and takes a good part of a second. Cache the numbers, or refresh them on a timer, instead of reading them on every request. Every number can be minus one when the system does not report it. Check before you do arithmetic. The memory figures are for the whole machine, not this program. In a container you see the host's memory, not the container's limit. The uptime counts from MarkStart. Without it the clock starts at the first UptimeMs call, so the first health check reports 0. It uses the wall clock, so changing the system time moves it.   A /health route A load balancer, Docker's HEALTHCHECK or a monitoring service calls a health route every few seconds to see whether the program is alive. Call MarkStart first thing in main, so the uptime counts from the start of the program and not from the first request, and answer with a small JSON object built from the runtime facts. runtime-health.salamCopyimport runtime import net.http import net.router import conv import str  func health(ctx: i64):     mut body := `{"status": "ok", "os": "` + runtime.OS() + `", "arch": "` + runtime.Arch() + `"`     body = body + `, "cpus": ` + conv.FormatInt(runtime.CpuCount() as i64)     body = body + `, "uptime_ms": ` + conv.FormatInt(runtime.UptimeMs())     body = body + `, "used_memory": ` + conv.FormatInt(runtime.UsedMemory())     body = body + `, "build": "` + runtime.BuildFlags() + `"}`     http.Json(ctx, body) end  func main:     runtime.MarkStart()     mut r := router.NewRouter()     router.Get(r, "/health", health)     mut s := http.NewServer(19734)     http.Use(s, r)     println http.RunBackground(s)     res := http.Get("http://127.0.0.1:19734/health")     body := http.Body(res)     println http.Status(res), http.GetHeader(res, "content-type")     println str.StartsWith(body, `{"status": "ok"`), str.Contains(body, `"uptime_ms": `) endOutputtrue 200 application/json true true The example starts the server in the background with net.http and calls its own route, so it runs without anything else. The numbers in the body change on every run, so it prints only the status, the content type and two checks. A real body looks like {"status": "ok", "os": "linux", "arch": "x64", "cpus": 8, "uptime_ms": 5412, "used_memory": 6442450944, "build": "release"}.  Report memory in a readable way TotalMemory and AvailableMemory return bytes, and minus one where the system does not report them. UsedMemory is the difference, or minus one when either is missing. Turn the bytes into MiB for people, and handle the minus one before doing any arithmetic, or a percentage of a negative number ends up on a dashboard. runtime-memory.salamCopyimport runtime import conv  func mib(bytes: i64): str:     if bytes < 0: ret "unknown" end     ret conv.FormatInt(bytes / (1024 * 1024)) + " MiB" end  func memory_line(total: i64, available: i64): str:     if total < 0 or available < 0:         ret "memory: not reported on this system"     end     percent := (total - available) * 100 / total     ret "memory: " + mib(total - available) + " of " + mib(total) + " in use (" + conv.FormatInt(percent) + "%)" end  func main:     println memory_line(8589934592, 2147483648)     println memory_line(17179869184, 15032385536)     println memory_line(0 - 1, 0 - 1)     line := memory_line(runtime.TotalMemory(), runtime.AvailableMemory())     println line.Len() > 0     used := runtime.UsedMemory()     println used <= runtime.TotalMemory() endOutputmemory: 6144 MiB of 8192 MiB in use (75%) memory: 2048 MiB of 16384 MiB in use (12%) memory: not reported on this system true true The first three lines use fixed numbers so the output is the same everywhere; the last two call the real functions.  Size a worker pool from the core count A server or a batch job often starts one worker per core. CpuCount gives the cores that are online, but a sensible rule also lets the operator override it, puts a ceiling on very large machines and falls back to a small number when the count is unknown. Summary puts the main facts in one line, which is handy to log once at startup. runtime-workers.salamCopyimport runtime import str  func pick_workers(cpus: int, configured: int): int:     if configured > 0: ret configured end     if cpus < 1: ret 2 end     if cpus > 16: ret 16 end     ret cpus end  func main:     println "8 cores, nothing configured:", pick_workers(8, 0)     println "64 cores, nothing configured:", pick_workers(64, 0)     println "core count unknown:", pick_workers(0 - 1, 0)     println "configured by hand:", pick_workers(8, 3)     workers := pick_workers(runtime.CpuCount(), 0)     println "here:", workers

testing testing Writing tests for your code: equality assertions, a pass and fail count, and a summary at the end. System and tools A test is a small program that checks your code does what it should. The testing package has assertions that print a clear message when they fail but do not stop the program, so every check runs and Summary says at the end how many passed and how many failed. Put tests in a file whose name ends in _test.salam, write each one as a function whose name starts with test_, and run them all with salam test, locally or in CI (see below). A test file can also be an ordinary program with its own main, started with salam run. Summary returns the number of failures, and returning it from main makes the program end with a non-zero code when something failed, which is what turns a CI job red. For checks inside the program itself, conditions that must never be false in production code, use Assert from debug instead, which stops the program. To time code, see debug and time. The things people get wrong:  A failure line says what differed, not where. In a loop over cases, use AssertMsg and put the case name in the message (see below). Strings are printed without quotes, so a stray space is invisible in got hello  want hello. Put brackets around values in your own messages. An exit code only has 8 bits, so 256 failures read as exit code 0. A suite that can have that many should return failures > 0 ? 1 : 0. The counters are plain globals with no lock: call the assertions from the main thread only.   Running tests with salam test salam test finds every *_test.salam file under the current directory (or the files and directories you name), and in each one calls every function whose name starts with test_ (آزمون in a Persian file) and that takes no arguments. You do not write main: the runner writes its own, in memory, and reports each test by name: salam test                      # every test file under this directory salam test calc_test.salam      # one file salam test --run=parse          # only tests whose name contains "parse" salam test '--run=^test_add$'   # exactly test_add (^ and $ anchor the name) salam test --interp             # on the interpreter, no C compiler needed Each file runs in its own process, so a crash fails that file and the others still run. The command ends with exit code 1 when any test failed, when a test file does not compile, and when --run matches no test at all. --format=teamcity prints TeamCity service messages instead of plain lines, which is what the JetBrains plugin reads to show the test tree; a file that has its own main and no test_ functions is run as one test that passes when it exits with 0.  Table driven tests When one function has to give the right answer for many inputs, put the inputs and the expected answers in an array of small structs and loop over it. Adding a case is then one line, and every case runs even when an earlier one fails. testing-guide-table.salamCopyimport testing import str  struct Case:     pub n: int = 0     pub want: str = "" end  func fizzbuzz(n: int): str:     if n % 15 == 0:         ret "FizzBuzz"     else n % 3 == 0:         ret "Fizz"     else n % 5 == 0:         ret "Buzz"     end     ret str.FromInt(n) end  func main:     cases := [         Case { n = 1, want = "1" },         Case { n = 3, want = "Fizz" },         Case { n = 5, want = "Buzz" },         Case { n = 9, want = "Fizz" },         Case { n = 10, want = "Buzz" },         Case { n = 15, want = "FizzBuzz" },         Case { n = 98, want = "98" }     ]     each c in cases:         testing.AssertEqStr(fizzbuzz(c.n), c.want)     end     ret testing.Summary() endOutput-- tests: 7 passed, 0 failed The program returns what Summary returns, so it ends with exit code 0 when everything passed. Run it like any other program: salam run fizzbuzz_test.salam echo $?  Failure messages that point at the case AssertEqStr inside a loop prints strings differ: got ... want ..., which leaves you to work out which row of the table it was. Give each case a name and build the message yourself with AssertMsg. Brackets around the values show spaces at the edges, which is exactly the bug in this example. testing-guide-labels.salamCopyimport testing import str  struct Case:     pub name: str = ""     pub input: str = ""     pub want: str = "" end  func slug(title: str): str:     ret str.Replace(str.Lower(title), " ", "-") end  func check(c: Case):     got := slug(c.input)     testing.AssertMsg(got == c.want, c.name + ": got [" + got + "] want [" + c.want + "]") end  func main:     cases := [         Case { name = "plain words", input = "Hello World", want = "hello-world" },         Case { name = "trailing space", input = "Release notes ", want = "release-notes" },         Case { name = "one word", input = "Salam", want = "salam" }     ]     each c in cases:         check(c)     end     failures := testing.Summary()     println "exit code:", failures > 0 ? 1 : 0 endOutputFAIL: trailing space: got [release-notes-] want [release-notes] -- tests: 2 passed, 1 failed exit code: 1  Group the tests of each function A long test file is easier to read when each function under test gets its own test function. Failed counts every failure so far; remember it at the start of a group and compare at the end to report the group as a whole. testing-guide-groups.salamCopyimport testing  func clamp(v: int, low: int, high: int): int:     if v < low:         ret low     end     if v > high:         ret high     end     ret v end  func average(values: Vector<int>): f64:     if values.Len() == 0:         ret 0.0     end     mut total := 0     each v in values:         total += v     end     re

error error The one Error type behind throw, try and catch: a kind, a message, where it happened, and a retry policy. System and tools A function that can fail says so in its signature with throws, and reports the failure with throw. The caller either passes the error on with try, or handles it in a try: ... catch e: ... end block. What travels is always an Error from this package, so an error from a JSON decoder, a file read and your own code all look the same to the caller. Error and ErrorKind need no import; import error only for the helper functions below. An Error has a kind, such as ErrorKind.NotFound, for the code to decide on, and a message for a person to read. Parsers also fill in where the problem is: an offset, a line and column, and a path such as $.users[3].age. A package can put a precise code of its own, such as json.trailing_data, next to the general kind. When an error passes through a layer that knows more, wrap adds that layer's explanation in front, and the kind stays the same. Under the hood a throws function returns a Throws value, and try checks it right after the call. Nothing is unwound and nothing is hidden: defer runs as with any other early return, and a call that can throw always carries try or sits inside a try: block. A bug, such as an index out of bounds, is not an error value: it still stops the program, and catch does not see it. Related: Option in the core package keeps a value or its absence in one place, for when a value may simply be missing rather than having gone wrong; declare your own Ok/Err enum when you want to store a result instead of handling it right away, as the enums lesson shows. The things people get wrong:  A call to a throws function needs try in front of it, or a try: block around it. The compiler refuses it otherwise (E155). try on its own passes the error to the caller, so it only works in a function that is itself throws (E156). In main, either declare func main throws: or use a try: block. try x catch fallback evaluates the fallback first, every time. Keep it a plain value. wrap, with_code, with_path and with_position return a new error and leave the old one as it was. Decide by kind or is, not by reading the message: messages are for people and may change.   Errors through the layers of a program A typical program has layers: one reads data, the next builds something from it, and the top one answers a user. Each layer that can fail is throws. A middle layer that has something to add catches the error, wraps it, and throws it again; the top layer decides what to do by kind. error-guide-layers.salamCopyfunc load user(id: int): str throws:     if id <= 0:         throw Error.New(ErrorKind.InvalidArgument, "the id must be positive")     end     if id != 7:         throw Error.New(ErrorKind.NotFound, "no such user").with_code("user." + id)     end     ret "Leila" end  func greeting(id: int): str throws:     try:         ret "Welcome back, " + load user(id)     catch e:         throw e.wrap("could not build the greeting")     end end  func status for(e: Error): int:     if e.is(ErrorKind.NotFound):         ret 404     else e.is(ErrorKind.InvalidArgument):         ret 400     end     ret 500 end  func main:     each id in [7, 3, -1]:         try:             println 200, greeting(id)         catch e:             println status for(e), e.ToStr()             if e.code != "":                 println "    code:", e.code             end         end     end endOutput200 Welcome back, Leila 404 could not build the greeting: no such user     code: user.3 400 could not build the greeting: the id must be positive Wrapping keeps the kind of the original error, so the top layer can still see that the root cause was "not found" and answer 404. The code carries a detail, here the missing id, that the code can read without parsing text.  A retry loop ShouldRetry answers the whole question in one call: is the error the kind that may go away by itself (Unavailable, Timeout or Io), and are there attempts left? DelayForAttempt gives the wait before the next try, doubling each time up to the maximum. When the attempts run out, the last error is wrapped and thrown to the caller. error-guide-retry.salamCopyimport error import sync  mut calls := 0  func fetch price(): int throws:     calls++     if calls < 3:         throw Error.New(ErrorKind.Unavailable, "the price service is busy")     end     ret 4200 end  func steady price(): int throws:     mut policy := error.NewRetryPolicy(5, 10, 80)     mut attempt := 1     until true:         try:             ret fetch price()         catch e:             if not error.ShouldRetry(policy, e, attempt):                 throw e.wrap("gave up after " + attempt + " attempts")             end             wait := error.DelayForAttempt(policy, attempt)             println "attempt", attempt, "failed:", e.message, "| waiting", wait, "ms"             sync.SleepMs(wait)         end         attempt++     end end  func main:     try:         println "price:", steady price()     catch e:         println e.ToStr()     end     bad := Error.New(ErrorKind.InvalidArgument, "unknown product")     mut policy := error.NewRetryPolicy(5, 10, 80)     println "retry a bad request?", error.ShouldRetry(policy, bad, 1) endOutputattempt 1 failed: the price service is busy | waiting 10 ms attempt 2 failed: the price service is busy | waiting 20 ms price: 4200 retry a bad request? false An invalid argument is never retried: sending the same bad request again gives the same answer. In a server, keep the total wait well below the time the caller is willing to wait for you.  Collect every problem at once For a form or a config file, stopping at the first mistake makes the user fix them one by one. An Error is an ordinary value, so collect them in a vector instead and

mem mem Working with memory directly: allocating and freeing, copying, arenas and pools, and leak checking. System and tools Most programs never need this package: vectors, maps and strings look after their own memory. The mem package is for low-level work, such as talking to a C library, filling a byte buffer by hand or building a data structure of your own. Its functions are thin wrappers over the C allocator (malloc, realloc, free, memcpy), plus two allocators of its own and leak counters.  Allocate, Reallocate and Free: one block at a time, freed by you. An arena is one large block you take pieces off the front of and then release all at once; it is very fast for many small objects that share a lifetime. A pool hands out and takes back blocks of one fixed size, in any order.  For a growing list of values, Vector is the safer choice; for bytes and binary formats, see encoding.binary. To watch memory from outside a function, debug has MemStats and runtime reports the machine's memory. The things people get wrong:  Nothing is checked. Writing past the end of a block, freeing it twice or using it after Free, ArenaReset or PoolFree corrupts memory without an error message. salam memcheck finds these for blocks from Allocate, but not inside an arena or a pool, which are one block to it. Give memory back the way it was taken: mem.Free for Allocate, the C library's own function for what a C library returns. In a -DSALAM_MEM_DEBUG build every block from Allocate has a hidden 8 byte header, so mixing the two crashes there even when a normal build seems fine. Check for null. Allocate, ArenaAlloc and PoolAlloc all return it when there is no memory or no room. The arena and the pool hand out memory aligned to 8 bytes, which suits every Salam type but not data that needs 16 byte alignment.   A buffer that grows The classic use of Reallocate is a buffer that does not know its final size. Keep the length and the capacity next to the pointer, and when the buffer is full ask for twice as much. Reallocate keeps the old contents, may move them to a new address, and works on a null pointer as well, so the first growth needs no special case. mem-guide-buffer.salamCopyimport mem  struct Buffer:     pub data: u8* = null     pub len: u64 = 0     pub cap: u64 = 0 end  func append(b &: Buffer, byte: u8):     if b.len == b.cap:         mut next := b.cap * (2 as u64)         if next == (0 as u64):             next = 4 as u64         end         b.data = mem.Reallocate(b.data as void*, next) as u8*         b.cap = next         println "grew to", b.cap, "bytes"     end     b.data[b.len] = byte     b.len++ end  func main:     mut b := Buffer {}     text := "Hello, arena and pool!"     repeat text.Len() in i:         append(b, text[i] as u8)     end     println "length:", b.len, "capacity:", b.cap     mut sum := 0     repeat b.len as int in i:         sum += b.data[i] as int     end     println "byte sum:", sum     mem.Free(b.data as void*) endOutputgrew to 4 bytes grew to 8 bytes grew to 16 bytes grew to 32 bytes length: 22 capacity: 32 byte sum: 1941 Doubling means 22 bytes cost only four reallocations, and a million bytes about twenty. Always store the pointer that Reallocate returns: the old one may no longer be valid. For most programs a Vector<u8> does exactly this for you.  An arena per request An arena shines when many small objects live and die together, such as everything made while handling one request or parsing one line. Allocate from the arena while you work, then call ArenaReset once at the end instead of freeing each object. The memory is reused for the next round, so the program never asks the system for more. mem-guide-arena.salamCopyimport mem  struct Token:     pub start: int = 0     pub size: int = 0 end  func tokenize(a &: mem.Arena, line: str): int:     mut count := 0     mut i := 0     until i < line.Len():         if line[i] == ' ':             i++         else:             t := mem.ArenaAlloc(a, sizeof(Token)) as Token*             t[0] = Token { start = i }             until i < line.Len() and line[i] != ' ':                 i++             end             t[0].size = i - t[0].start             count++         end     end     ret count end  func main:     mut arena := mem.NewArena(4096 as u64)     lines := ["GET /index.html HTTP/1.1", "POST /api/orders HTTP/1.1", "DELETE /api/orders/7"]     each line in lines:         n := tokenize(arena, line)         println n, "tokens,", mem.ArenaUsed(arena), "bytes used"         mem.ArenaReset(arena)     end     println "after the last reset:", mem.ArenaUsed(arena), "bytes used of", mem.ArenaCapacity(arena)     mem.ArenaFree(arena) endOutput3 tokens, 24 bytes used 3 tokens, 24 bytes used 2 tokens, 16 bytes used after the last reset: 0 bytes used of 4096 Each allocation is rounded up to a multiple of 8 bytes, which is why one Token of two ints takes 8. ArenaAlloc returns null when the arena is full, so check the result or make the arena big enough for the largest round. After ArenaReset every pointer from the arena is stale; do not keep them across rounds.  A pool of fixed size blocks A pool suits objects of one size that come and go in any order, such as the nodes of a list or a tree. PoolFree puts a block back on the pool's free list and the next PoolAlloc hands it out again, with no call to the system allocator either way. A pool has a fixed number of blocks; PoolAlloc returns null when they are all in use. PoolFree does not check its argument: a block freed twice goes on the free list twice and is later handed out to two owners. mem-guide-pool.salamCopyimport mem import str  struct Node:     pub value: int = 0     pub next: Node* = null end  func push(p &: mem.Pool, head: Node*, value: int): Node*:     n := mem.PoolAlloc(p) as Node*     if n == null:         println "pool is full, dropping&quo

term term Text colour and style, cursor movement, progress bars, reading keys and the mouse, and the terminal size. System and tools The term package has what a command line program needs to look good in a terminal: text colour and style, columns that line up, progress bars and spinners, and for full screen programs, cursor movement, the alternate screen and reading keys one at a time. The colour functions, such as Red, return a new string and print nothing. In the default ColorAuto mode they add nothing when the output goes to a file or another program, when NO_COLOR is set or when TERM=dumb, so the text stays plain; SetColorMode changes that, for a --color option for instance. The functions whose names start with Seq only return an escape sequence, and the one with the same name without the prefix sends it right away. To read keys, put the terminal into raw mode with MakeRaw or MakeCbreak, and always put it back with Restore. For one line questions such as a name or a yes or no, cli is simpler; for log lines, log; for padding plain text, fmt. The things people get wrong:  Padding coloured text with len. A colour code adds bytes but no columns; use PadRight and the other functions here, which measure with Width. Trusting Width with every script. It counts one column per character: Chinese and Japanese characters, which take two columns, count as one, and invisible ones such as the zero width non-joiner in Persian می‌شود count as one too. Tables of such text need padding of your own. Leaving the terminal in raw mode. Call Restore with defer right after MakeRaw, and leave the alternate screen and show the cursor on every way out. Expecting a progress bar in a log. BarDraw draws nothing when the output is not a terminal, and BarFinish prints the final bar once, so a CI log gets one clean line.   A coloured table that lines up A colour code adds bytes to a string but no columns on the screen, so padding with len would push every coloured cell out of line. PadRight, PadLeft and Truncate measure with Width, which skips escape codes, so a table lines up whether its cells are coloured or not. term-guide-table.salamCopyimport term  struct Service:     pub name: str = ""     pub status: str = ""     pub memory: i64 = 0     pub uptime ms: i64 = 0 end  func colored status(s: str): str:     if s == "running":         ret term.Green(s)     else s == "degraded":         ret term.Yellow(s)     end     ret term.Red(s) end  func main:     services := [         Service { name = "api", status = "running", memory = 157286400, uptime ms = 93784000 },         Service { name = "search-indexer", status = "degraded", memory = 1073741824, uptime ms = 4500000 },         Service { name = "mail", status = "stopped", memory = 0, uptime ms = 0 }     ]     println term.Bold(term.PadRight("SERVICE", 14) + " " + term.PadRight("STATUS", 9) + " " + term.PadLeft("MEMORY", 9) + "  UPTIME")     each s in services:         name := term.PadRight(term.Truncate(s.name, 14), 14)         status := term.PadRight(colored status(s.status), 9)         mut up := "-"         if s.uptime ms > 0:             up = term.FormatDuration(s.uptime ms)         end         println name, status, term.PadLeft(term.FormatBytes(s.memory), 9), "", up     end endOutputSERVICE        STATUS       MEMORY  UPTIME api            running    150.0 MB  26h 03m search-indexer degraded     1.0 GB  1h 15m mail           stopped         0 B  - The output above is plain because the program's output went to a file, not a terminal. Run it in a terminal and the status column turns green, yellow and red, with no change to the code. FormatBytes and FormatDuration turn raw numbers into the short forms people expect in a status table.  Colour on screen, plain text in the log The same line often goes to two places: the terminal, where colour helps, and a log file, where escape codes are noise. Build the line once and pass it through Strip for the file. The colour functions already return plain text when colour is off, but Strip also cleans text that was coloured earlier or came from another program. term-guide-log.salamCopyimport term  func status line(tag: str, message: str): str:     mut label := "[" + tag + "]"     if tag == "ok":         label = term.Green(label)     else tag == "warn":         label = term.Yellow(label)     else tag == "fail":         label = term.Bold(term.Red(label))     end     ret term.PadRight(label, 7) + message end  func main:     term.SetColorMode(term.ColorAlways)     line := status line("warn", "cache is 91% full")     println "bytes:", line.Len(), "| columns on screen:", term.Width(line)     mut log file := Vector {} as Vector<str>     defer log file.Free()     log file.Push(term.Strip(status line("ok", "config loaded")))     log file.Push(term.Strip(line))     log file.Push(term.Strip(status line("fail", "could not reach the mail server")))     println "--- the log file ---"     each entry in log file:         println entry     end endOutputbytes: 33 | columns on screen: 24 --- the log file --- [ok]   config loaded [warn] cache is 91% full [fail] could not reach the mail server The example forces colour on with SetColorMode(ColorAlways) so the difference between bytes and columns is visible. Leave the mode at ColorAuto in real programs: it turns colour off for pipes, files and NO_COLOR, which is what users expect.  A progress bar that also works in CI NewBar takes the total and a label; BarAdd moves it on and redraws it in place, and BarFinish fills it and ends the line. The fields change the look: a fixed width instead of one worked out from the terminal, the fill and empty characters, and show_count or show_

cpu cpu Use the processor's AES and carry-less multiply instructions, and ask what the processor offers. System and tools Modern processors can run one round of AES, or multiply two 64-bit values without carries, in a single instruction. This package makes those instructions available on u128 values, and tells you at run time whether the machine in front of you has them. tls uses it for AES-GCM, so the VPN and proxy protocols and the TLS record layer run on the fast path by themselves; most programs never need to call this package. The instructions are real only when the program is built with the LLVM backend, which every release build uses. On the C backend, the native backend, the interpreter and in the browser every function still works, but as a slow software model of the instruction, and HasHardwareCrypto is false so that callers choose their own faster code. The software model gives the same bytes, which is what lets a test run the same data both ways. Things to know:  Test first, then call. The Hw functions work everywhere, but only where HasHardwareCrypto is true are they one instruction each. The switch is read when a cipher is made. SetHardware(false) affects the next AeadNew or one shot call, not a context that already exists. The environment variable SALAM_NO_HWCRYPTO does the same for a whole run. HwClmul wants a literal. Its third argument becomes part of the instruction, so write 0, 1, 16 or 17 there, not a variable. Constant time. The instructions take the same time for any data, which the table based software AES cannot promise.   Check the fast path against the slow one SetHardware turns the fast path off, so one program can seal the same message both ways and compare. This is how the tests of the package check that the two paths give the same bytes. On a machine without the instructions both runs take the software path and the answer is still the same. cpu-guide-switch.salamCopyimport cpu import mem import tls  func hex(p: void*, n: int): str:     b := p as u8*     digits := "0123456789abcdef"     mut s := ""     repeat n in i:         v := b[i] as int         s += digits.Substr(v >> 4, 1)         s += digits.Substr(v & 15, 1)     end     ret s end  func seal(): str:     key := mem.AllocateZeroed(16 as u64)     nonce := mem.AllocateZeroed(12 as u64)     msg := mem.AllocateZeroed(32 as u64)     out := mem.AllocateZeroed(48 as u64)     tls.AesGcmSealRaw(key, 16, nonce, null, 0, msg, 32, out)     r := hex(out, 48)     mem.Free(key)     mem.Free(nonce)     mem.Free(msg)     mem.Free(out)     ret r end  func main:     cpu.SetHardware(true)     fast := seal()     cpu.SetHardware(false)     slow := seal()     println "same bytes:", fast == slow     println "tag:", fast.Substr(64, 32) endOutputsame bytes: true tag: 40490af4805606b2a3a2e793e3500066 The tag line is the tag of 32 zero bytes under an all zero key and nonce; the algorithm fixes it, so it is the same on every machine. software pathSetHardware(false) or SALAM_NO_HWCRYPTO=1 One round of AES on a blockHwAesEnc and HwAesEncLast A carry-less product, as in GHASHHwClmul Move a block in and out of memoryHwLoad and HwStore Reverse the bytes of a block, or swap its halvesHwBswap and HwSwap64   Constants and variables FEATURE_HW_CRYPTOconst FEATURE_HW_CRYPTO: i32 = 1The bit of Features that says the AES and carry-less
