os/pty os.pty Running a program on a pseudo terminal: waiting for its prompt, typing keys, and changing the window size. System and tools Some programs behave differently when they are not on a terminal: a shell shows no prompt, a REPL does not echo or edit the line, stty has no size to report. The os.pty package starts a program attached to a pseudo terminal, a pair of devices that look like a real terminal to the program, and gives you the other end. What you write is typed keys; what you read is what a person would see on the screen, including the characters the terminal echoes back. Open takes the same Command as os.process (program, arguments, folder and environment; the stream modes do not apply, because all three streams are the terminal) and returns the same Child. So Write, ReadUntil, ReadFor, ReadAvailable, Wait, Kill and Close work as described there. Two things differ: output and error output arrive mixed in one stream, and CloseStdin sends Ctrl-D, the end-of-input key, because closing the terminal would hang the program up. What people get wrong:  Sending 
 for Enter. A terminal sends  when Enter is pressed and the line discipline turns it into a newline for programs that read lines, so type . A program in raw mode sees the  itself. Expecting 
 in the output. The terminal turns each newline into 
, so look for 
 when waiting for a line end. Reading without a time limit. Use ReadUntil with a prompt and a number of milliseconds, and check timed_out, so a program that never prints the prompt cannot hang yours. Forgetting that your own typing is echoed. After Write the first thing to come back is the echo of what you typed. Setting TERM. Programs that draw on the screen read it; put it in the command with Env("TERM", "xterm").  This package works on Linux, macOS and the BSDs. On Windows Supported returns false and Open returns a child whose ok is false. Open a terminal and type into it Start the program with Open and the window size in rows and columns (0 means 24 by 80). Writing the text of a key press, with  for Enter, reaches the program as input; reading returns the terminal echo first and then the program's answer. Calling CloseStdin ends the input of a program such as cat. os-pty-guide-open.salamCopyimport os.process import os.pty  func main:     mut cmd := process.NewCommand("cat")     mut term := pty.Open(cmd, 24, 80)     term.Write("typed on a terminal")     echoed := term.ReadUntil("terminal
", 2000)     println "the terminal echoed it:", not echoed.timed_out     echoed.Free()     answer := term.ReadUntil("terminal
", 2000)     println "cat answered:", not answer.timed_out     answer.Free()     term.CloseStdin()     println "exit:", term.Wait(2000).code     term.Close()     cmd.Free() endOutputthe terminal echoed it: true cat answered: true exit: 0  Wait for a prompt An interactive program prints a prompt and then waits. ReadUntil returns as soon as the prompt text has arrived, or reports timed_out after the time you gave. That is the loop of every terminal test: wait for the prompt, type a line, wait for the answer. os-pty-guide-prompt.salamCopyimport os.process import os.pty  func main:     mut cmd := process.NewCommand("sh")     cmd.Arg("-c")     cmd.Arg("printf 'name? '; read name; echo \"hi $name\"")     mut term := pty.Open(cmd, 24, 80)     ask := term.ReadUntil("name? ", 2000)     println "prompt seen:", not ask.timed_out     ask.Free()     term.Write("Sara")     reply := term.ReadUntil("hi Sara", 2000)     println "reply seen:", not reply.timed_out     reply.Free()     println "exit:", term.Wait(2000).code     term.Close()     cmd.Free() endOutputprompt seen: true reply seen: true exit: 0  Change the window size Resize sets the size of the terminal and the system tells the program, which is how a full-screen program learns to redraw. GetSize reads the size back. The program sees the new size the next time it asks, for example through stty size. os-pty-guide-resize.salamCopyimport os.process import os.pty  func main:     mut cmd := process.NewCommand("sh")     cmd.Arg("-c")     cmd.Arg("stty size; read x; stty size")     mut term := pty.Open(cmd, 24, 80)     first := term.ReadUntil("24 80", 2000)     println "first size seen:", not first.timed_out     first.Free()     println "resize:", pty.Resize(term, 50, 132)     term.Write("")     second := term.ReadUntil("50 132", 2000)     println "second size seen:", not second.timed_out     second.Free()     println "exit:", term.Wait(2000).code     term.Close()     cmd.Free() endOutputfirst size seen: true resize: true second size seen: true exit: 0  NeedUse  Start a program on a terminalOpen Type keysChild.Write, with  for Enter Wait for a promptChild.ReadUntil with a time limit See everything printed in a periodChild.ReadFor Send the end-of-input keyChild.CloseStdin Change or read the window sizeResize, GetSize Know whether terminals are availableSupported Pipes instead of a terminalos.process   Types Sizestruct SizeThe size of a terminal window in character cells.NameTypeDescriptionrowsint = 0The number of rows.colsint = 0The number of columns.os-pty-Resize.salamCopyimport os.process import os.pty  func main:     mut cmd := process.NewCommand("sh")     cmd.Arg("-c")     cmd.Arg("read line; stty size")     mut term := pty.Open(cmd, 24, 80)     println "start:", pty.GetSize(term).rows, pty.GetSize(term).cols     println "resized:", pty.Resize(term, 40, 120)     println "now:", pty.GetSize(term).rows, pty.GetSize(term).cols     term.Write("go")     out := term.ReadUntil("40 120", 2000)     println "child sees the new size:", not out.ti

os/signal os.signal Waiting for operating system signals: stopping cleanly on Ctrl+C or SIGTERM, noticing terminal resizes, and controlling which thread receives a signal. System and tools A signal is a short message the operating system sends to a process: Ctrl+C sends SIGINT, kill and container runtimes send SIGTERM, and a terminal sends SIGWINCH when its window changes size. By default most signals end the program on the spot, in the middle of whatever it was writing. The os.signal package lets a program take the signals it cares about as ordinary events and react to them at a safe point in its own code. The model is the same for every use: block the signals, then wait for them. A blocked signal is not delivered; it waits in a queue until a thread asks for it with WaitSignal, Wait or WaitTimeout. Blocking is per thread, and a new thread copies the mask of the thread that started it, so block in main before you start any thread. Then no worker is interrupted, and the one thread that waits receives the signal. Sets, masks and snapshots are memory blocks the package allocates for you; free each one with mem.Free when you are done. The package grew out of the terminal library tui, which uses it to redraw when the window is resized. Signals exist on Linux, Android, macOS and the BSDs. On Windows every function is a safe stub: WinchSupported is false, sets are null and waits return WaitInvalid, so the same program compiles everywhere and can fall back to polling. Stop cleanly on Ctrl+C or SIGTERM Put SIGINT and SIGTERM in a set, block it, do the work, then wait. WaitSignal returns the number of the signal that arrived, so the program can save its state and exit on its own terms. The example sends itself SIGTERM with Raise so it finishes by itself; in a real program the signal comes from the keyboard or from kill. os-signal-guide-shutdown.salamCopyimport mem import os.signal  func main:     stop := signal.NewSet()     defer mem.Free(stop)     _ := signal.AddSignal(stop, signal.SigInt)     _ := signal.AddSignal(stop, signal.SigTerm)     if not signal.Block(stop):         println "could not block the stop signals"         ret 1     end     println "working; press Ctrl+C or run kill to stop"     _ := signal.Raise(signal.SigTerm)     sig := signal.WaitSignal(stop)     if sig == signal.SigInt:         println "Ctrl+C: saving and leaving"     else sig == signal.SigTerm:         println "SIGTERM: saving and leaving"     else:         println "wait failed with status", sig         ret 1     end     ret 0 endOutputworking; press Ctrl+C or run kill to stop SIGTERM: saving and leaving  Workers keep running, one thread waits Block first, then start the threads: they inherit the mask, so a signal never lands in the middle of a worker. main waits for the signal and then tells the workers to stop through an atomic flag (see atomic), and joins them. os-signal-guide-threads.salamCopyimport mem import sync import atomic import os.signal  mut stopping := atomic.NewFlag(false)  func worker(_arg: void*):     until not atomic.Get(stopping):         sync.SleepMs(10)     end     println "worker saw the stop request" end  func main:     stop := signal.NewSet()     defer mem.Free(stop)     _ := signal.AddSignal(stop, signal.SigTerm)     _ := signal.Block(stop)     t := spawn(worker, null)     _ := signal.Raise(signal.SigTerm)     println "main got signal", signal.WaitSignal(stop)     atomic.Set(stopping, true)     join(t)     atomic.DestroyFlag(stopping)     println "clean exit" endOutputmain got signal 15 worker saw the stop request clean exit  Notice a terminal resize SIGWINCH is ignored by default, and on macOS an ignored signal is thrown away even when it is blocked. InstallWinchHandler therefore installs a handler that does nothing, and blocks the signal, so resizes queue up. WaitTimeout waits with a limit, which lets a loop check other things between resizes. Hand the value it returned back to Restore at the end. A signal only says that the size may have changed, and several resizes can arrive as one, so read the new size with term.Size() after every wake-up. os-signal-guide-resize.salamCopyimport mem import os.signal  func main:     if not signal.WinchSupported():         println "no SIGWINCH here: poll term.Size() instead"         ret 0     end     prev := signal.InstallWinchHandler()     if prev == null:         println "could not install the handler"         ret 1     end     set := signal.NewWinchSet()     out := mem.AllocateZeroed(8 as u64)     println "nothing yet:", signal.WaitTimeout(set, out, 100) == signal.WaitTimedOut     _ := signal.WakeWinch()     println "after a resize:", signal.WaitTimeout(set, out, 1000) == signal.WaitArrived     println "signal number:", (out as i32*)[0]     mem.Free(out)     mem.Free(set)     println "restored:", signal.Restore(signal.WinchSignal, prev)     mem.Free(prev)     ret 0 endOutputnothing yet: true after a resize: true signal number: 28 restored: true  NeedUse  Wait for Ctrl+C or SIGTERMNewSet, AddSignal, Block, WaitSignal Wait with a time limitInstall, then WaitTimeout React to terminal resizesInstallWinchHandler, NewWinchSet, WaitWinch or WaitTimeout Wake a waiting threadRaise, or WakeWinch for SIGWINCH Save and put back a thread's maskCurrentMask, SetMask Send a signal to another programChild.Signal in os.process A full-screen terminal programtui, which does all of this for you   What to keep in mind:  SIGKILL and SIGSTOP can never be blocked, waited for or handled. Only one thread in the process may wait at a time; a second waiter gets WaitBusy instead of half the signals. Signals of one kind do not stack up: two SIGWINCH sent while one is already pending arrive as one. tui tui Full-screen terminal programs: widgets, layout, focus, keys, mouse and resizing, drawn into a buffer and repainted only where something changed. System and tools tui builds full-screen terminal programs: file managers, dashboards, installers, editors, anything that takes over the window instead of printing lines. It is retained mode: you build a tree of long-lived widgets once, change their state when something happens, and the Screen turns key presses, clicks and resizes into events, and widget drawings into frames. It repaints only the cells that changed, so a large screen stays fast over a slow connection. It sits on top of term and uses os.signal to learn about window resizes. The library started as basalam by Parsa and is now part of the standard library. The pieces:  Screen owns the terminal, the widget tree, the focus and the event loop. NewTerminalScreen sizes it to the terminal; NewScreen gives a fixed size and never touches the terminal, which is how you test. Widgets are structs that embed BaseWidget and override what they need: render to draw, handle_event to react, focusable to take keys. Ready-made ones: Text, Input, Button, Checkbox, List, Progress, Separator, Table, TableView, Panel and Modal. Layout containers (Row, Column, Grid, Stack) give their children positions, so you never compute coordinates by hand. Events go first to the focused widget and bubble up to its parents until one consumes them; whatever nobody consumes reaches the optional Keymap and then your loop.  A complete program A widget, a screen, and the event loop. start switches the terminal to raw mode and the alternate screen; the defer screen.close() right after it puts the terminal back on every exit path, so a crash never leaves the user's shell broken. next_event waits for the next key, click, tick or resize; dispatch hands it to the widgets; present draws what changed. A key the widgets did not consume is yours: here q quits. This program needs a real terminal, so the page only compiles it. tui-guide-hello.salamCopyimport term import tui  struct Hello:     pub use tui.BaseWidget     pub presses: int = 0      pub func render(buf: tui.Buffer, bounds: tui.Rect):         buf.put_str(bounds.x + 2, bounds.y + 1, "Hello from tui!", tui.Style { bold = true, fg = tui.Cyan })         buf.put_str(bounds.x + 2, bounds.y + 3, "Enter pressed " + this.presses + " times", tui.StyleDefault)         buf.put_str(bounds.x + 2, bounds.bottom() - 1, "q quits", tui.Style { dim = true })     end      pub func handle_event(event: tui.Event): bool:         if event.is_key(term.KeyEnter):             this.presses++             ret true         end         ret false     end end  func main:     if not term.IsTerminal():         printerrln "run me in a terminal"         ret 1     end     mut screen := tui.NewTerminalScreen(Hello {})     screen.start()     defer screen.Close()     screen.present()     mut ev := tui.Event {}     until screen.next_event(ev):         consumed := screen.dispatch(ev)         if not consumed and (ev.is_char("q") or ev.is_ctrl("c")):             screen.stop()         end         screen.present()     end     ret 0 end  See a frame without a terminal A screen made with NewScreen never touches the terminal. You can still send it events with dispatch (or post and next_event), draw with draw, and read every row back with buffer.row_text. That is how the examples on this page produce their output, and how you write tests for your own screens. tui-guide-preview.salamCopyimport term import tui  struct Hello:     pub use tui.BaseWidget     pub presses: int = 0      pub func render(buf: tui.Buffer, bounds: tui.Rect):         tui.DrawBorder(buf, bounds, tui.BorderStyle.Rounded, tui.StyleDefault, "hello")         buf.put_str(bounds.x + 2, bounds.y + 1, "Hello from tui!", tui.Style { bold = true })         buf.put_str(bounds.x + 2, bounds.y + 2, "Enter pressed " + this.presses + " times", tui.StyleDefault)     end      pub func handle_event(event: tui.Event): bool:         if event.is_key(term.KeyEnter):             this.presses++             ret true         end         ret false     end end  func show(s: tui.Screen):     s.draw()     repeat s.buffer.height in y:         println s.buffer.row_text(y)     end end  func main:     mut s := tui.NewScreen(Hello {}, 30, 4)     defer s.Close()     show(s)     enter := tui.Event { kind = tui.KeyEvent, key = term.Key { code = term.KeyEnter } }     _ := s.dispatch(enter)     _ := s.dispatch(enter)     show(s) endOutput╭─ hello ────────────────────╮ │ Hello from tui!            │ │ Enter pressed 0 times      │ ╰────────────────────────────╯ ╭─ hello ────────────────────╮ │ Hello from tui!            │ │ Enter pressed 2 times      │ ╰────────────────────────────╯  Lay out a screen Hand widgets to a container and the container places them. A Column stacks its children; set_height with a LayoutSize chooses each share: Fixed cells, a Fill weight of what is left, or Pref for the widget's own preferred size. Make the container the root of the screen, and add each child to the screen too: the container decides where, the screen decides what is drawn and focused. On a resize the screen gives the root the new size and the layout runs again. tui-guide-layout.salamCopyimport tui  func fixed(n: int): tui.LayoutSize:     ret tui.LayoutSize { kind = tui.SizeKind.Fixed, cells = n } end  func main:     title := tui.NewText("Downloads") as dyn tui.Widget     rule := tui.NewSeparator() as dyn tui.Widget     mut bar := tui.NewProgress()     bar.set_progress(40)     progress := bar as dyn tui.Widget     mut body := tui.NewText("salam-0.6.3.ta

time time The current time, durations, formatting and parsing dates, the monotonic clock, timers and tickers. Time and concurrency The time package reads the clock, turns dates into text and back, does date arithmetic, measures how long code takes and waits. It works with two kinds of value:  An instant is an i64 count of seconds since the start of 1970 in UTC, the Unix epoch. Now returns one, and dates are stored, compared and sent as instants. A duration is a Duration, a span with nanosecond precision such as 1h30m, which you can add up, compare and print.  There are also two clocks. The wall clock (Now, NowMillis) tells the date and can jump when the system time is set. The monotonic clock (MonoNanos) only moves forward and is the one to measure spans and deadlines with; timers and tickers use it. For the Persian and Hijri calendars and for named time zones such as Asia/Tehran, see calendar. For timing parts of a program while you debug it, debug has named timers. The things people get wrong:  Year, FormatDate, Format, FormatISO and Weekday use the machine's local time zone, so the same instant prints differently on a server set to UTC and a laptop in Tehran. Use the ...UTC functions and FormatISOUTC for anything stored or compared. FormatISO has no offset, so the text cannot be read back to the same instant on another machine. Send FormatISOUTC or FormatRFC3339. Days(30) is 30 times 24 hours, not a month. There is no month arithmetic; build the date with FromUTCParts and a month one higher (it rolls 13 over into January). FromUTCParts and FromLocalParts accept any numbers and roll over: 30 February becomes 1 March. The parse functions, by contrast, throw for a day that the month does not have. Timing code with Now. It has whole seconds and follows clock changes; use MonoNanos.   Dates from text, and date arithmetic Dates usually arrive as text: from JSON, a database or a form. ParseISO reads the ISO 8601 form and returns the instant. Bad input is common, so it is declared throws: catch the error with try: ... catch e: and report or skip the value. Once you have an instant, arithmetic is plain integer arithmetic: AddDuration moves it, and DiffSeconds gives the distance between two instants. time-guide-expiry.salamCopyimport time import str  func days left(expires: i64, today: i64): i64:     ret time.DiffSeconds(expires, today) / time.SecondsPerDay end  func main:     today := time.FromUTCParts(2026, 3, 10, 9, 0, 0)     signups := ["2026-01-15T08:30:00Z", "2026-02-20T18:45:00Z", "2026-03-09T23:10:00Z", "not a date"]     each s in signups:         mut p := 0 as i64         try:             p = time.ParseISO(s)         catch e:             println "skipping \"" + s + "\":", e.message             continue         end         expires := time.AddDuration(p, time.Days(30))         left := days left(expires, today)         if left < 0:             println time.FormatISOUTC(p), "expired", -left, "days ago"         else:             println time.FormatISOUTC(p), "ends on", time.FormatISOUTC(expires), "(" + str.FromInt(left) + " days left)"         end     end endOutput2026-01-15T08:30:00Z expired 24 days ago 2026-02-20T18:45:00Z ends on 2026-03-22T18:45:00Z (12 days left) 2026-03-09T23:10:00Z ends on 2026-04-08T23:10:00Z (29 days left) skipping "not a date": expected a digit in the year, found 'n' The example fixes "today" with FromUTCParts so its output never changes; a real program would use Now(). Adding Days(30) adds exactly 30 times 24 hours. In UTC that is always 30 calendar days, but in a zone with daylight saving the local clock time can move by an hour, so keep stored instants in UTC and convert only for display.  Timeouts from settings A setting such as timeout = 1m30s is easier to read than a number of milliseconds. ParseDuration understands h, m, s, ms, us and ns, in any combination and with fractions. It throws on text it cannot read, and the error's message says why. Check the value against sensible limits too: a parse that worked is not yet a value that makes sense. time-guide-timeouts.salamCopyimport time  func read timeout(name: str, text: str, fallback: time.Duration): time.Duration:     mut d := fallback     try:         d = time.ParseDuration(text)     catch e:         println name + ": cannot read", "\"" + text + "\" (" + e.message + "), using", fallback.ToStr()         ret fallback     end     if d.less(time.Milliseconds(100)) or time.Minutes(10).less(d):         println name + ":", d.ToStr(), "is out of range, using", fallback.ToStr()         ret fallback     end     println name + ":", d.ToStr()     ret d end  func main:     connect := read timeout("connect", "2.5s", time.Seconds(5))     request := read timeout("request", "1m30s", time.Seconds(30))     retry := read timeout("retry", "soon", time.Seconds(1))     idle := read timeout("idle", "2h", time.Minutes(5))     worst := connect.Add(request.mul(3)).Add(retry.mul(2))     println "worst case for three tries:", worst.ToStr()     println "idle in milliseconds:", idle.millis() endOutputconnect: 2.5s request: 1m30s retry: cannot read "soon" (expected a number, found 's'), using 1s idle: 2h0m0s is out of range, using 5m0s worst case for three tries: 4m34.5s idle in milliseconds: 300000 Durations add, subtract, multiply and compare without any unit conversions, and to_str prints them in the same short form that ParseDuration reads. When a quick default is enough, ParseDurationOr does the parse and the fallback in one call.  When the text is not a date ParseISO, ParseISONanos, ParseISOIn, ParseHTTPDate, ParseFormat and ParseDuration either return a value or throw an Error; nothing half-read co

calendar calendar The Jalali, Hijri and Gregorian calendars: conversion, day arithmetic, month names and time zones. Time and concurrency This package works with three calendars: Jalali (Solar Hijri, the official calendar of Iran and Afghanistan), Hijri (lunar) and Gregorian. A date is a plain struct of year, month and day, and each calendar has its own conversion, validation, day arithmetic and month name functions. The Hijri calendar here is arithmetic: months alternate between 30 and 29 days and are not adjusted by sighting the moon, so a date can be one day off from the official calendar of a given country. There are three ways to turn an instant into a date: EpochToJalali and its siblings use the machine local time, WallClockJalali takes a fixed time zone such as Tehran, and LoadZone covers zones that observe daylight saving.  Use it to show dates the way people in Iran, Afghanistan or the Arab world read them, to take a Jalali date from a form, and to turn a meeting time in one city into the time in another. Instants, durations and the clock itself are in time; store instants there and convert to a calendar only for display. For Persian digits in the output, see i18n. The things people get wrong:  Taking today's date on a server with TodayJalali or EpochToJalali. Those use the machine's zone, and a server set to UTC is still on yesterday until 03:30 in Tehran. Use WallClockJalali(time.Now(), TZTehran()). Mixing the two weekday numberings. JalaliWeekday takes a Julian day number and counts from Saturday as 0; Weekday, WeekdayJalali and the other Weekday... functions count from Sunday as 0. Converting unchecked input. The conversions do not validate, so 31 Esfand or month 13 gives a wrong date instead of an error. Check with IsValidJalaliDate and its siblings first. Expecting the Hijri dates to match an official calendar to the day, or the fixed TZLondon and TZNewYork zones to follow daylight saving. They do not; use LoadZone for that.  The Jalali conversion is the standard arithmetic one (as in the jalaali libraries), which works for the years -61 to 3177 and agrees with the official Iranian calendar for the years in use today.  Birthdays and anniversaries in Jalali Dates are plain structs, so date logic is ordinary code: build the date in the current year, compare it with today using CompareJalali, and move to the next year if it has passed. DaysBetweenJalali counts the days in between, and JalaliToGregorian gives the same day in the other calendar. calendar-guide-birthday.salamCopyimport calendar  func next birthday(born: calendar.JalaliDate, today: calendar.JalaliDate): calendar.JalaliDate:     mut target year := today.year     mut target day := born.day     if born.month == 12 and target day == 30 and not calendar.IsLeapJalali(target year):         target day = 29     end     mut next := calendar.JalaliDate { year = target year, month = born.month, day = target day }     if calendar.CompareJalali(next, today) < 0:         target year++         target day = born.day         if born.month == 12 and target day == 30 and not calendar.IsLeapJalali(target year):             target day = 29         end         next = calendar.JalaliDate { year = target year, month = born.month, day = target day }     end     ret next end  func main:     today := calendar.JalaliDate { year = 1405, month = 7, day = 25 }     born := calendar.JalaliDate { year = 1370, month = 9, day = 3 }     mut age := today.year - born.year     birthday now := calendar.JalaliDate { year = today.year, month = born.month, day = born.day }     if calendar.CompareJalali(birthday now, today) > 0:         age--     end     next := next birthday(born, today)     println "age:", age     println "next birthday:", calendar.FormatJalali(next), "(" + calendar.JalaliMonthNameEn(next.month) + ")"     println "days to go:", calendar.DaysBetweenJalali(today, next)     println "in the Gregorian calendar:", calendar.FormatGregorian(calendar.JalaliToGregorian(next))     leap := calendar.JalaliDate { year = 1403, month = 12, day = 30 }     println "born on 30 Esfand 1403, celebrates in 1405 on:", calendar.FormatJalali(next birthday(leap, today)) endOutputage: 34 next birthday: 1405-09-03 (Azar) days to go: 38 in the Gregorian calendar: 2026-11-24 born on 30 Esfand 1403, celebrates in 1405 on: 1405-12-29 One case needs care: 30 Esfand exists only in leap years. Before building a date in another year, check it with IsLeapJalali or IsValidJalaliDate; the example moves such a birthday to 29 Esfand. AddYearsJalali and AddMonthsJalali do the same clamping for you when you only need to move a date.  Drawing a month A month view needs two numbers: the weekday of the first day and the length of the month. JalaliWeekday numbers the days from Saturday as 0, which is how Persian calendars are laid out, and DaysInJalaliMonth gives the length. calendar-guide-month.salamCopyimport calendar import str  func main:     shown year := 1405     shown month := 7     first := calendar.JalaliDate { year = shown year, month = shown month, day = 1 }     println calendar.JalaliMonthNameEn(shown month), shown year     println "Sa Su Mo Tu We Th Fr"     offset := calendar.JalaliWeekday(calendar.JalaliToJDN(first))     mut line := ""     repeat offset:         line += "   "     end     days := calendar.DaysInJalaliMonth(shown year, shown month)     repeat 1 to days in d:         if d < 10:             line += " "         end         line += str.FromInt(d)         if (offset + d) % 7 == 0:             println line             line = ""         else:             line += " "         end     end     if line != "":         println line.Trim()     end     println "starts on", calendar.FormatGregorianLongEn(calendar.JalaliToGregorian(first)) endOutputMehr 1405 Sa Su Mo Tu We Th Fr              1  2  3  4  5  6  7  8  9 1

thread thread Holding and waiting for the threads that spawn creates. Time and concurrency In Salam you start a function that should run alongside the rest of the program with spawn. It takes a function with no parameters and no result and gives back a number, the thread's handle. join, or thread.Join, waits for that thread to finish. The thread package wraps that handle in a Thread so you can keep several of them in a vector and wait for all of them at once, and SpawnStack starts a thread with a stack of the size you choose. Threads share the program's globals and heap; for shared data use sync or atomic, to pass values between threads chan, and to spread a loop over every core pool. A thread cannot be stopped from outside; to ask one to finish early, use ctx or an atomic flag it checks.  Split one job across threads The most common use of threads is to cut a big job into parts and give each part its own thread. Give each thread its own piece of memory to write its answer into, start them all, then wait for all of them with JoinAll. Because no two threads write to the same place, there is nothing to lock. spawn also takes a second argument, a pointer the function receives as its parameter; that is how each thread learns which part is its own. thread-guide-split.salamCopyimport thread import mem  struct Part:     pub first: i64 = 0     pub last: i64 = 0     pub sum: i64 = 0 end  func add range(p: Part*):     mut total := 0 as i64     mut i := p[0].first     until i <= p[0].last:         total += i         i++     end     p[0].sum = total end  func new part(first: i64, last: i64): Part*:     p := mem.Allocate(sizeof(Part)) as Part*     p[0] = Part { first = first, last = last }     ret p end  func main:     size := 250 as i64     mut parts := Vector {} as Vector<Part*>     defer parts.Free()     mut group := Vector {} as Vector<thread.Thread>     defer group.Free()     repeat 4 in w:         p := new part((w as i64) * size + 1, (w as i64 + 1) * size)         parts.Push(p)         group = thread.Collect(group, spawn(add range, p))     end     thread.JoinAll(group)     mut total := 0 as i64     each p in parts:         println p[0].first, "to", p[0].last, "=", p[0].sum         total += p[0].sum         mem.Free(p as void*)     end     println "total:", total endOutput1 to 250 = 31375 251 to 500 = 93875 501 to 750 = 156375 751 to 1000 = 218875 total: 500500 The parts may finish in any order, but the program reads the answers only after JoinAll and in the order it stored them, so the output is always the same.  Do something else while a thread works A thread does not have to be part of a group. Start one slow task in the background, carry on with other work on the main thread, and call Join at the point where you need the result. Until Join returns, do not read what the thread is writing. thread-guide-background.salamCopyimport thread  mut words := 0 mut lines := 0  func count text():     text := "the quick brown fox
jumps over
the lazy dog"     mut reading := false     lines = 1     repeat text.Len() in i:         c := text[i]         if c == '
':             lines++         end         if c == ' ' or c == '
':             reading = false         else not reading:             reading = true             words++         end     end end  func main:     worker := thread.New(spawn(count text))     println "main thread: loading settings"     println "main thread: opening the report"     thread.Join(worker)     println "lines:", lines, "words:", words endOutputmain thread: loading settings main thread: opening the report lines: 3 words: 9 Here only the main thread prints. If both threads printed, the lines could come out in a different order on every run.  Deep recursion on a bigger stack A thread from spawn gets the system's default stack, which deep recursion can overflow. SpawnStack starts the function on a stack of the size you ask for. The system may refuse a very large stack, so check the thread with Valid and have a plan for the case where it is not. thread-guide-fallback.salamCopyimport thread  mut depth := 0 as i64  func walk(n: i64): i64:     if n == 0:         ret 0     end     ret 1 + walk(n - 1) end  func deep work(_arg: void*):     depth = walk(300000) end  func main:     t := thread.SpawnStack(deep work, null, (128 * 1024 * 1024) as u64)     if thread.Valid(t):         thread.Join(t)     else:         println "no big stack, running on this thread"         deep work(null)     end     println "depth reached:", depth endOutputdepth reached: 300000 The function given to SpawnStack takes a void*, so the same function can also be called directly with null when no thread could be started.  Pitfalls, and which tool to use  Join every thread you start. A program that returns from main while threads are still running cuts them off midway. Globals are shared by every thread. Two threads that change the same variable without a lock give a different answer from run to run. Output from several threads interleaves in no fixed order. Collect results and print them from one thread. A handle of zero means the thread did not start. Join on it does nothing, so check Valid when it matters. Join each thread exactly once. On Linux and macOS Join also frees the handle, so a second Join of the same thread uses freed memory and can crash. Collect returns the vector it was given, grown by one; always assign the result back, as in group = thread.Collect(group, spawn(work)). sync sync Mutexes, condition variables, wait groups, read-write locks, semaphores and once, for coordinating threads. Time and concurrency When several threads change the same variable they have to take turns, or the result depends on the order the threads happen to run in. The sync package has the classic tools for taking turns, built on the operating system's threads library:  A mutex: each thread takes the lock before touching the data and releases it afterwards. An RWMutex lets many readers in at once. A condition variable: a thread sleeps until another one says that something has changed. A wait group: call Add before starting a piece of work, Done at its end, and Wait until the count is back to zero. A semaphore caps how many threads are inside a part at once, and a once runs setup a single time.  Threads themselves come from spawn and the thread package. For a single shared number, atomic is cheaper than a lock; to hand values from one thread to another, chan does the locking and waiting for you; to cancel work, ctx. The things people get wrong:  Using a value that was never created. Every tool here is made with a New... function; a zero sync.Mutex {} has no lock inside and crashes on Lock. Globals are declared with {} and created at the top of main. Locking twice. A mutex is not reentrant: a thread that calls Lock on a mutex it already holds waits forever. Do holds a lock while its function runs, so calling Do on the same Once from inside it hangs too. Waiting on a condition without a loop. WaitCond can return before the condition is true; always wait inside until not condition:. Forgetting Destroy.... Each tool holds operating system memory; destroy it after the last thread that uses it has been joined.   Keep data consistent with a mutex A lock is not only for counters. Anything that has to stay true across several variables, such as "the money in all accounts adds up to the same total", needs every change to happen while the lock is held. Take the lock at the top of the function and put Unlock in a defer, so it is released on every return path, including the early ret. sync-guide-transfer.salamCopyimport sync  mut accounts := Vector {} as Vector<int> mut lock := sync.Mutex {} mut group := sync.WaitGroup {}  func transfer(from: int, dest: int, amount: int): bool:     sync.Lock(lock)     defer sync.Unlock(lock)     if accounts.Get(from) < amount:         ret false     end     accounts.Set(from, accounts.Get(from) - amount)     accounts.Set(dest, accounts.Get(dest) + amount)     ret true end  func clerk():     repeat 1000 in i:         transfer(i % 3, (i + 1) % 3, 7)     end     sync.Done(group) end  func main:     lock = sync.NewMutex()     group = sync.NewWaitGroup()     accounts.Push(500)     accounts.Push(300)     accounts.Push(200)     sync.Add(group, 4)     mut workers := Vector {} as Vector<i64>     defer workers.Free()     repeat 4:         workers.Push(spawn(clerk))     end     sync.Wait(group)     each t in workers:         join(t)     end     total := accounts.Get(0) + accounts.Get(1) + accounts.Get(2)     println "money in the bank:", total     println "a transfer that is too big:", transfer(0, 1, 100000)     accounts.Free()     sync.DestroyWaitGroup(group)     sync.Destroy(lock) endOutputmoney in the bank: 1000 a transfer that is too big: false Four threads move money around 4000 times and the total is still 1000. Without the lock two threads could read the same balance at once and one of the changes would be lost.  Many readers, few writers When data is read far more often than it is changed, such as settings or a cache, a plain mutex makes readers wait for each other for no reason. An RWMutex lets any number of readers in together with RLock, and gives a writer the data to itself with WLock. sync-guide-settings.salamCopyimport sync  mut settings := HashMap {} as HashMap<str, int> mut guard := sync.RWMutex {} mut reads := 0 mut count lock := sync.Mutex {}  func reader():     repeat 200:         sync.RLock(guard)         limit := settings.Get("limit")         sync.RUnlock(guard)         if limit > 0:             sync.Lock(count lock)             reads++             sync.Unlock(count lock)         end     end end  func writer():     repeat 1 to 5 in v:         sync.WLock(guard)         settings.Put("limit", v * 10)         sync.WUnlock(guard)     end end  func main:     guard = sync.NewRWMutex()     count lock = sync.NewMutex()     settings.Put("limit", 5)     a := spawn(reader)     b := spawn(reader)     w := spawn(writer)     join(a)     join(b)     join(w)     println "reads:", reads     println "final limit:", settings.Get("limit")     settings.Free()     sync.Destroy(count lock)     sync.DestroyRWMutex(guard) endOutputreads: 400 final limit: 50 A reader must never write while holding only the read lock. If a reader may need to change the data, take the write lock instead.  Limit how many run at once A Semaphore holds a number of permits. Acquire takes one and waits when none are left, Release gives it back. With two permits, at most two threads are inside the guarded part at any moment, which is how you cap parallel downloads or database connections. sync-guide-limit.salamCopyimport sync  mut slots := sync.Semaphore {} mut lock := sync.Mutex {} mut running := 0 mut busiest := 0 mut finished := 0  func download():     sync.Acquire(slots)     sync.Lock(lock)     running++     if running > busiest:         busiest = running     end     sync.Unlock(lock)     sync.SleepMs(20)     sync.Lock(lock)     running--     finished++     sync.Unlock(lock)     sync.Release(slots) end  func main:     slots = sync.NewSemaphore(2)     lock = sync.NewMutex()     mut jobs := Vector {} as Vector<i64>     defer jobs.Free()     repeat 6:         jobs.Push(spawn(download))     end     each t in jobs:         join(t)     end     println "downloads finished:", finished

atomic atomic A counter and a flag that several threads can change safely without taking a lock by hand. Time and concurrency For a simple counter that several threads increment, you do not have to build a lock yourself: I64 in this package does each operation in one indivisible step. CompareAndSwap is the base of most lock-free algorithms: it changes the value only if it is still the one you expected. With gcc, clang and the LLVM backend each operation is one of the processor's atomic instructions. Under tcc, which lacks them, each cell is protected by a small lock instead; the results are the same, only slower.  There are two types: I64, a shared 64-bit whole number, and Flag, a shared true or false. Both are small handles to a cell on the heap, so passing one to a function or a thread by value shares the same cell. For anything bigger than one value, use sync; to pass values between threads, chan. The things people get wrong:  Using a cell that was never created. atomic.I64 {} has no cell and crashes on the first Add; make it with NewI64 or NewFlag, for a global at the top of main. Combining two operations. if Load(a) < 10: Add(a, 1) end is two steps, and another thread can act in between; that is what CompareAndSwap in a loop is for. Destroying too early. DestroyI64 frees the cell for every copy of the handle; call it once, after every thread that uses it has been joined.  There is no subtract: Add(a, -1) counts down.  Hand out unique numbers Add returns the value after the addition, and no two callers can get the same one. That makes it a ready made source of unique ids, ticket numbers or slot indexes, shared by any number of threads with no lock in sight. atomic-guide-ids.salamCopyimport atomic  mut next id := atomic.I64 {} mut taken := Vector {} as Vector<i64>  func hand out():     repeat 100:         id := atomic.Add(next id, 1)         taken.Set(id as int - 1, taken.Get(id as int - 1) + 1)     end end  func main:     next id = atomic.NewI64(0)     repeat 400:         taken.Push(0)     end     a := spawn(hand out)     b := spawn(hand out)     c := spawn(hand out)     d := spawn(hand out)     join(a)     join(b)     join(c)     join(d)     mut twice := 0     each n in taken:         if n != 1:             twice++         end     end     println "last id:", atomic.Load(next id)     println "ids given out more than once:", twice     taken.Free()     atomic.DestroyI64(next id) endOutputlast id: 400 ids given out more than once: 0 Four threads took 100 ids each, and every id from 1 to 400 was given out exactly once. Each thread then writes only to the slot its own id names, which is why the vector needs no lock either.  Update with CompareAndSwap Some updates are not a plain addition: "keep the largest value seen so far" has to read the value, decide, and write. Doing that in two steps would let another thread slip in between. The answer is a loop: read the value, compute the new one, and ask CompareAndSwap to store it only if the value has not changed meanwhile. If it has, read again and retry. atomic-guide-max.salamCopyimport atomic  mut highest := atomic.I64 {}  func record(value: i64):     mut seen := atomic.Load(highest)     until value > seen:         if atomic.CompareAndSwap(highest, seen, value):             ret         end         seen = atomic.Load(highest)     end end  func low readings():     repeat 500 in i:         record((i * 7 % 900) as i64)     end end  func high readings():     repeat 500 in i:         record((i * 13 % 1000) as i64)     end end  func main:     highest = atomic.NewI64(0)     a := spawn(low readings)     b := spawn(high readings)     join(a)     join(b)     println "highest reading:", atomic.Load(highest)     atomic.DestroyI64(highest) endOutputhighest reading: 993 The loop also stops as soon as the stored value is already at least as large, so most calls do not write at all.  A stop signal for a worker A Flag is the simplest way to tell a long running thread to finish: the worker checks it each round, and the main thread sets it when it is time. A plain bool global is not enough, because nothing guarantees the worker ever sees the change. atomic-guide-stop.salamCopyimport atomic import sync  mut stop := atomic.Flag {} mut rounds := atomic.I64 {}  func worker():     until not atomic.Get(stop):         atomic.Add(rounds, 1)         sync.SleepMs(1)     end end  func main:     stop = atomic.NewFlag(false)     rounds = atomic.NewI64(0)     t := spawn(worker)     until atomic.Load(rounds) < 20:         sync.SleepMs(1)     end     atomic.Set(stop, true)     join(t)     println "worker ran at least 20 rounds:", atomic.Load(rounds) >= 20     println "stop flag:", atomic.Get(stop)     atomic.DestroyFlag(stop)     atomic.DestroyI64(rounds) endOutputworker ran at least 20 rounds: true stop flag: true  Only the first one wins TestAndSet turns the flag on and tells you whether you were the one who did it. When several threads race for one job, such as sending a single alert or doing a one time cleanup, exactly one of them gets true. atomic-guide-first.salamCopyimport atomic  mut claimed := atomic.Flag {} mut winners := atomic.I64 {} mut losers := atomic.I64 {}  func attempt claim():     if atomic.TestAndSet(claimed):         atomic.Add(winners, 1)     else:         atomic.Add(losers, 1)     end end  func main:     claimed = atomic.NewFlag(false)     winners = atomic.NewI64(0)     losers = atomic.NewI64(0)     mut threads := Vector {} as Vector<i64>     defer threads.Free()     repeat 8:         threads.Push(spawn(attempt claim))     end     each t in threads:         join(t)     end     println "winners:", atomic.Load(winners), "losers:", atomic.Load(losers)     atomic.DestroyFlag(claimed)     atomic.DestroyI64(winners)     atomic.DestroyI64(losers) endOutputwinners: 1 losers: 7  Atomic or a lock? An atomic value is right when the shared state is one number or one flag. As

chan chan A channel for passing values from one thread to another, with a buffer, timeouts and closing. Time and concurrency A channel is a queue that several threads send values into at one end and receive from at the other; it handles the locks and the waiting for you. You give the value type when you create it, as in chan.Chan<i64>, and call init with a capacity before using it. When the buffer is full, send waits; when it is empty, recv does. A channel of capacity zero is "unbuffered": the sender waits until a receiver takes the value. After close, sending returns false but receivers still get the values that are left; once the channel is empty, ok turns false and a receiving loop can end. Use a channel when one thread produces values and another consumes them. For shared data that several threads change in place, sync is the better fit; for a counter, atomic; for running the turns of a loop on every core, pool; and for telling workers to stop, ctx. The things people get wrong:  Forgetting init. A channel declared with chan.Chan {} has no buffer or lock yet and crashes on the first send. Using the value from a failed receive. When ok is false the result is a zero value that means nothing. Telling a timeout from the end. recv_timeout sets ok to false both when the time ran out and when the channel is closed and empty; ask is_closed to know which. Sending a Vector or a pointer and then changing it. The channel copies the value, which for those types is only the handle, so both threads see the same memory.   The receive loop Almost every consumer looks the same: receive in an endless until true: loop and break when ok turns false. That happens only after the channel is closed and empty, so no value is lost. The rule that goes with it: the side that sends is the side that closes, once it has nothing more to send. chan-guide-loop.salamCopyimport chan  mut orders := chan.Chan {} as chan.Chan<str>  func checkout():     each id in ["A-1001", "A-1002", "A-1003"]:         orders.send(id)     end     orders.Close()     println "after close, send works:", orders.send("A-1004") end  func main:     orders.init(8)     t := spawn(checkout)     join(t)     println "waiting in the buffer:", orders.Len()     mut ok := true     until true:         id := orders.recv(ok)         if not ok: break end         println "packing", id     end     println "closed and empty:", orders.is_closed(), orders.Len()     orders.Free() endOutputafter close, send works: false waiting in the buffer: 3 packing A-1001 packing A-1002 packing A-1003 closed and empty: true 0 The sender filled the buffer and closed the channel before the receiver even started, and still every order came out. A send after close returns false instead of waiting.  A pipeline of stages Channels connect stages that each do one thing. Here one thread generates numbers, a second squares them, and the main thread adds them up. Each stage closes its output channel when its input runs dry, so the end of the data flows down the pipeline by itself and every loop stops on its own. chan-guide-pipeline.salamCopyimport chan  mut numbers := chan.Chan {} as chan.Chan<i64> mut squares := chan.Chan {} as chan.Chan<i64>  func generate():     repeat 1 to 10 in n:         numbers.send(n as i64)     end     numbers.Close() end  func square():     mut ok := true     until true:         n := numbers.recv(ok)         if not ok:             break         end         squares.send(n * n)     end     squares.Close() end  func main:     numbers.init(2)     squares.init(2)     a := spawn(generate)     b := spawn(square)     mut total := 0 as i64     mut count := 0     mut ok := true     until true:         v := squares.recv(ok)         if not ok:             break         end         total += v         count++     end     join(a)     join(b)     println "values through the pipeline:", count     println "sum of squares:", total     numbers.Free()     squares.Free() endOutputvalues through the pipeline: 10 sum of squares: 385 The channels hold only two values each. When the last stage is slow, the earlier ones wait in send instead of piling up memory, which is called back pressure.  Ask and wait for an answer Two channels make a request and reply pair: one carries questions to a worker, the other brings the answers back. With capacity zero, each send waits until the other side has taken the value, so the two threads move in step and the answers come back in the order the questions went out. chan-guide-reply.salamCopyimport chan  mut requests := chan.Chan {} as chan.Chan<str> mut replies := chan.Chan {} as chan.Chan<str>  func server():     mut ok := true     until true:         name := requests.recv(ok)         if not ok:             break         end         replies.send("hello, " + name)     end end  func main:     requests.init(0)     replies.init(0)     t := spawn(server)     mut ok := true     each name in ["Sara", "Reza", "Mina"]:         requests.send(name)         println replies.recv(ok)     end     requests.Close()     join(t)     requests.Free()     replies.Free() endOutputhello, Sara hello, Reza hello, Mina  Many senders, one receiver When several threads send into one channel, none of them can close it, because each one only knows that it is done. Count the senders with a sync.WaitGroup and let one more small thread wait for the group and then close the channel. chan-guide-fanin.salamCopyimport chan import sync  mut events := chan.Chan {} as chan.Chan<i64> mut senders := sync.WaitGroup {}  func sensor(base: i64):     repeat 5 in i:         events.send(base + i as i64)     end     sync.Done(senders) end  func sensor a(): sensor(100) end func sensor b(): sensor(200) end func sensor c(): sensor(300) end  func closer():     sync.Wait(senders)     events.Close() end  func main:     events.init(

pool pool Parallel loops, a bounded worker pool, goroutine-style tasks, error groups and futures. Time and concurrency If each turn of a loop is independent of the others, such as processing each slot of an array on its own, ParallelFor spreads the turns across several worker threads and waits for all of them. The loop body is a function taking an i64, the turn's number. The package also has a long-lived, bounded worker pool, the Salam answer to goroutines. spawn starts one operating-system thread per call with no limit; a Pool starts its threads once and never more, keeps at most queue tasks waiting, and makes Submit wait when the queue is full, so a fast producer cannot pile up unbounded work. Go runs a task on a shared pool sized to the cores, Group limits how many tasks run at once and keeps the first error, and Async hands back a Future you can Await. To receive from several channels, see Select in chan. Tasks are threads, not green threads: a task that blocks keeps its worker busy, so a task must not wait for a task queued behind it. Use SubmitOrRun when tasks submit tasks. For shared state, use sync and atomic. The things people get wrong:  Relying on the order of the turns, or changing shared data from them without a lock. Each turn writing to its own slot is safe; anything else needs atomic or a mutex. Making the turns too small. Taking the next turn number costs a lock, and every call starts and joins threads, so a turn should do a fair amount of work (see chunks). Calling ParallelFor in a hot loop. Each call pays for creating threads; parallelize the outer loop instead of the inner one.   One turn per row The natural fit for ParallelFor is data laid out in rows, such as the pixels of an image or the lines of a table. Make each turn handle one row: the turns touch different memory, so they need no lock, and the result is the same whatever order they ran in. pool-guide-pixels.salamCopyimport pool import mem import str  mut pixels := null as int* width := 8 height := 6  func brighten row(y: i64):     repeat width in x:         i := (y as int) * width + x         mut v := pixels[i] + 60         if v > 255:             v = 255         end         pixels[i] = v     end end  func main:     pixels = mem.AllocateZeroed(sizeof(int) * ((width * height) as u64)) as int*     repeat width * height in i:         pixels[i] = (i * 37) % 256     end     pool.ParallelFor(height, 3, (y: i64): brighten row(y) end)     repeat height in y:         mut line := ""         repeat width in x:             line = line + str.FromInt(pixels[y * width + x]) + " "         end         println line.Trim()     end     mem.Free(pixels as void*) endOutput60 97 134 171 208 245 255 63 100 137 174 211 248 255 66 103 140 177 214 251 255 69 106 143 180 217 254 255 72 109 146 183 220 255 255 75 112 149 186 223 255 255 78 115 152 189 226 255 The loop body here is a short lambda that calls a named function. Keeping the real work in a named function makes it easy to test on its own, without any threads.  Chunks, not single items Each turn has a small cost of its own, so a million turns that each add one number spend more time on bookkeeping than on adding. Cut the work into a few large chunks instead, let each turn handle one chunk and write its partial result to its own slot, and combine the slots on the main thread at the end. pool-guide-chunks.salamCopyimport pool import mem  mut partial := null as i64* total numbers := 1000000 as i64 chunks := 8  func add chunk(c: i64):     size := total numbers / (chunks as i64)     first := c * size + 1     mut last := first + size - 1     if c == chunks as i64 - 1:         last = total numbers     end     mut s := 0 as i64     mut n := first     until n <= last:         s += n         n++     end     partial[c] = s end  func main:     partial = mem.AllocateZeroed(sizeof(i64) * (chunks as u64)) as i64*     pool.ParallelForAuto(chunks, (c: i64): add chunk(c) end)     mut sum := 0 as i64     repeat chunks in c:         sum += partial[c]     end     println "chunks:", chunks     println "sum of 1 to", total numbers, "=", sum     println "check:", sum == total numbers * (total numbers + 1) / 2     mem.Free(partial as void*) endOutputchunks: 8 sum of 1 to 1000000 = 500000500000 check: true ParallelForAuto picks the number of workers from the processor count. A few chunks per worker is a good size: enough for the work to even out when some chunks are slower, few enough that the overhead stays small.  Combine results with an atomic counter When the turns produce something that has to be added into one place, such as a count of matches, the simplest safe choice is an atomic.I64. Here every number below 100000 is one turn, and each turn that finds a prime adds one to the shared counter. pool-guide-primes.salamCopyimport pool import atomic  mut found := atomic.I64 {}  func is prime(n: i64): bool:     if n < 2:         ret false     end     mut d := 2 as i64     until d * d <= n:         if n % d == 0:             ret false         end         d++     end     ret true end  func main:     found = atomic.NewI64(0)     pool.ParallelFor(100000, pool.CPUCount(), (n: i64):         if is prime(n):             atomic.Add(found, 1)         end     end)     println "primes below 100000:", atomic.Load(found)     atomic.DestroyI64(found) endOutputprimes below 100000: 9592 An atomic add per match is fine when matches are rare compared with the work of each turn. If every turn would update the counter, use partial results per chunk as in the previous section instead.  Rules for the loop body  Never rely on the order of the turns. Turn 5 can finish before turn 0. A turn may write to its own slot freely. Anything shared needs a sync.Mutex or an atomic. Do not print from the loop body; the lines come out mixed up. Store the results and print after ParallelFor returns. ParallelFor waits for every turn, so as soon as it returns all

ctx ctx A context for cancellation and deadlines, passed from the main piece of work down to the smaller ones. Time and concurrency A context tells long-running work when to stop: either someone called Cancel, or its deadline passed. Contexts form a tree: you start from Background and make a child each time with WithCancel, WithTimeout or WithDeadline. Cancelling a context ends all its children, but not its parent. The work should check IsDone from time to time, or wait on it with Wait. Free each context with Free when you are done with it, children before parents.  Use a context when work that may take long has to stop early: a request whose client went away, a batch job with a time budget, a background thread at shutdown. It is built on sync and works across threads. For one stop flag and nothing else, an atomic.Flag is enough; to pass results back, use a chan. The things people get wrong:  Expecting a context to interrupt a call. No standard library function takes one: a network request, a file read or a sync.SleepMs runs to its end. Check IsDone between steps, sleep with Wait, and give network calls their own timeout options. Freeing in the wrong order. A child keeps a copy of its parent that points at the parent's memory, and freeing the root destroys the lock the whole tree shares. Free children first, the root last, each exactly once. Assuming the deadlines follow a steady clock. They are measured with sync.NowMs, which on Linux and macOS is the wall clock, so setting the system time moves them.   Guide: one context per request The usual shape is one context for a whole piece of work, such as an HTTP request or a batch job, and a child for every smaller task it starts. When the request is cancelled, every task under it sees IsDone turn true, while work hanging from another branch keeps going. The program below builds that tree and cancels the request in the middle. ctx-guide-tree.salamCopyimport ctx  func show(name: str, c: ctx.Context):     if ctx.IsDone(c):         println name, "stopped:", ctx.Err(c)     else:         println name, "running"     end end  func main:     root := ctx.Background()     request := ctx.WithCancel(root)     db_query := ctx.WithCancel(request)     cache := ctx.WithCancel(request)     audit := ctx.WithCancel(root)      ctx.Cancel(request)      show("request", request)     show("db query", db_query)     show("cache", cache)     show("audit", audit)     show("root", root)      ctx.Free(audit)     ctx.Free(cache)     ctx.Free(db_query)     ctx.Free(request)     ctx.Free(root) endOutputrequest stopped: cancelled db query stopped: cancelled cache stopped: cancelled audit running root running Cancelling goes down the tree, never up: root and audit are untouched. That is why each task should get its own child instead of sharing the parent: you can stop one task alone by cancelling its child, or all of them by cancelling the parent.  Guide: check between steps A context does not stop anything by force. The work has to look at it, and the right place is between steps, before each item of a loop or before each slow call. Pass the context as the first argument of every function that may take long, and return early when it is done. ctx-guide-steps.salamCopyimport ctx  func copy_files(c: ctx.Context, files: Vector<str>): int:     mut copied := 0     each name in files:         if ctx.IsDone(c):             println "  stopped before", name, "(" + ctx.Err(c) + ")"             ret copied         end         println "  copied", name         copied++     end     ret copied end  func main:     mut files := Vector {} as Vector<str>     files.Push("a.txt")     files.Push("b.txt")     files.Push("c.txt")     root := ctx.Background()      println "normal run:"     live := ctx.WithCancel(root)     println "  total", copy_files(live, files)      println "cancelled by the user:"     stopped := ctx.WithCancel(root)     ctx.Cancel(stopped)     println "  total", copy_files(stopped, files)      println "deadline already passed:"     late := ctx.WithDeadline(root, 1)     println "  total", copy_files(late, files)      ctx.Free(late)     ctx.Free(stopped)     ctx.Free(live)     ctx.Free(root)     files.Free() endOutputnormal run:   copied a.txt   copied b.txt   copied c.txt   total 3 cancelled by the user:   stopped before a.txt (cancelled)   total 0 deadline already passed:   stopped before a.txt (deadline exceeded)   total 0 The same function serves all three cases, and the caller decides which one applies. Err tells the two reasons apart: cancelled when someone called Cancel, deadline exceeded when the time ran out. WithDeadline(root, 1) uses an instant long past, so its context is done from the start.  Guide: time budgets A child can never outlive its parent. A child with a longer timeout than its parent still ends at the parent's deadline, and Deadline reports the nearest deadline of the context and all its parents. A child with a shorter timeout ends earlier on its own, and its parent goes on. ctx-guide-budget.salamCopyimport ctx  func main:     root := ctx.Background()     request := ctx.WithTimeout(root, 2000)     lookup := ctx.WithTimeout(request, 60000)     quick := ctx.WithTimeout(request, 50)      println "root has a deadline:", ctx.Deadline(root) != 0     println "lookup keeps the request budget:", ctx.Deadline(lookup) == ctx.Deadline(request)     println "quick is tighter:", ctx.Deadline(quick) < ctx.Deadline(request)      println "quick finished within 1 s:", ctx.Wait(quick, 1000), ctx.Err(quick)     println "request still running:", not ctx.IsDone(request)      ctx.Free(quick)     ctx.Free(lookup)     ctx.Free(request)     ctx.Free(root) endOutputroot has a deadline: false lookup keeps the request budget: tru

cron cron Cron expressions with optional seconds, interval, daily, weekly, monthly and one-time jobs, tags, limits and hooks, each job on its own thread. Time and concurrency cron parses the usual five-field cron expression (or six, with a leading seconds field), matches it against a time, computes the next matching moment, and runs registered jobs on a one-second tick. It is a library, not a service: it runs inside your program, uses your program's threads and stops when your program stops. The five fields are minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week, in that order. Each field accepts *, a number, a range a-b, a list a,b,c, and a step */n or a-b/n. Months and weekdays also accept three-letter English names such as jan and mon. As in Vixie cron, when both day fields are restricted a time matches either of them; when one is *, both must match. */15 * * * *        every quarter hour 0 9-17 * * mon-fri  every hour from 9 to 17 on weekdays 30 2 1 * *          at 02:30 on the first day of every month 0 0 29 feb *        on February 29 The macros @yearly, @annually, @monthly, @weekly, @daily, @midnight and @hourly expand to the usual five fields.  Parsing and the next run Parse returns an Expr with ok false when the text is not a valid expression. Check ok before you use it. Next returns the first minute strictly after the given time that matches, in the given time zone, or 0 when it finds none within the scan limit. cron-quickstart.salamCopyimport cron  const ZONE := "Invalid/Nowhere" const OFF := 210 const AFTER := 1792800300 as i64  func show(spec: str):     e := cron.Parse(spec)     println spec, e.ok, cron.Next(e, AFTER, ZONE, OFF) end  func main:     show("*/20 * * * *")     show("@daily")     show("0 0 29 feb *")     show("nope")      e := cron.Parse("*/5 * * * *")     println cron.MatchFields(e, 15, 10, 1, 1, 0)     println cron.MatchFields(e, 16, 10, 1, 1, 0)     println cron.OffsetSeconds(ZONE, OFF, AFTER) endOutput*/20 * * * * true 1792800600 @daily true 1792873800 0 0 29 feb * true 1835382600 nope false 0 true false 12600 Times are UTC seconds since the epoch. Next asks the zone database for the offset at each candidate minute, so daylight saving changes are handled. When the zone does not exist, every call takes fallback_minutes instead, which is also what the tests use to stay independent of the machine.  Matching a time you already have MatchFields takes the local minute, hour, day, month and weekday directly, so you can use it on values from your own clock or from a database. MatchesLocal takes a wall-clock instant in seconds, already shifted by the zone offset, and is what the scheduler uses internally. cron-match.salamCopyimport cron  func main:     e := cron.Parse("0 9-17 * * mon-fri")     println cron.MatchFields(e, 0, 9, 1, 1, 1)     println cron.MatchFields(e, 30, 9, 1, 1, 1)     println cron.MatchesLocal(e, 1793005200 as i64) endOutputtrue false true Weekdays are 0 for Sunday through 6 for Saturday; 7 is accepted and treated as Sunday. MatchFields returns false for an expression whose ok is false.  Zones and offsets The scheduler keeps one zone for all jobs. SetZone sets its name and the fallback offset in minutes, used when the name cannot be loaded. OffsetSeconds returns the offset of any zone at an instant, which is useful outside the scheduler too. cron.SetZone("Asia/Tehran", 210) off := cron.OffsetSeconds("Asia/Tehran", 210, 1700000000 as i64) println off / (60 as i64) The default zone is UTC with a fallback of 0. Call SetZone before Run or RunBackground; changing it later affects the next minute, not a job that is already running.  Jobs and the scheduler Add registers a function under a name and an expression and returns the job id, or -1 when the expression does not parse. A job handler takes the job id as an i64. Register every job before you start the scheduler. cron-schedule.salamCopyimport mem import time import cron  mut hits := null as i64*  func tick(id: i64):     atomic_add(hits, 1 as i64)     println "job", id, cron.Name(id as int) end  func main:     hits = mem.AllocateZeroed(8 as u64) as i64*     cron.SetZone("Invalid/Nowhere", 210)      every := cron.Add("every minute", "* * * * *", tick)     nightly := cron.Add("nightly", "0 3 * * *", tick)     broken := cron.Add("broken", "nope", tick)     println cron.Count(), cron.Name(every), cron.Name(nightly), broken     println cron.IsBusy(every)      started := cron.RunDue(1792800300 as i64)     mut waited := 0     until atomic_load(hits) == (0 as i64) or waited >= 200:         time.Sleep(10)         waited++     end     println "started", started, "hits", atomic_load(hits)     println cron.IsBusy(every)      cron.RunBackground()     cron.Stop() end Run blocks and fires the jobs that are due once a minute; RunBackground runs the same loop on its own thread and returns at once. RunDue fires what is due at the given time without waiting for the next minute, which is what a test or a manual tick uses. In every form a job that is still running from an earlier firing is skipped, not queued, so a slow job cannot pile up. Count, Name and IsBusy inspect the table. Stop asks the loop to end after the current job; it does not wait for a running job, and it can be called from a signal handler or another thread. cron.SetZone("UTC", 0) cron.Add("cleanup", "0 3 * * *", cleanup) cron.RunBackground() time.Sleep(60000) cron.Stop()  Seconds A sixth field in front of the minute gives second resolution: */10 * * * * * fires every ten seconds and 0 30 9 * * mon at 09:30:00 on Mondays. With five fields nothing changes: the job fires once in the matching minute.  Setting a time without cron syntax Most schedules are a clock time, so they have helpers that take "HH:MM" or "HH:MM:SS". cron.DailyAt("report", "10:30", report) cron.WeeklyAt("backup", "mon-fri

events events An in-process event emitter: dotted topics with wildcards, one-shot handlers, and an optional worker thread. Time and concurrency events is a small publish and subscribe hub for the inside of one program. You register handlers on a topic, and Emit calls every handler whose topic matches. The payload type is a parameter, so one emitter carries one kind of data: Emitter<int>, Emitter<str>, or an emitter of your own struct. Topics are dot-separated words such as user.login. In a handler's topic, * stands for exactly one word and # for the rest of the topic, including nothing at all, so user.* matches user.login but not user.a.b, and order.# matches order, order.new and order.new.eu. Things to know:  A handler is a lambda, and a lambda captures the variables around it by value. Share state with a pointer, a heap collection or a mut global, as the examples do. Handlers run outside the lock, so a handler may call On, Off or Emit on the same emitter. Handlers added during an Emit first see the next event. On returns an id; Off takes that id. Functions are not compared. An async emitter handles events on the thread you give it. NewAsync makes the queue and starts no thread; run Drain on one thread of your own, and its handlers run one at a time, in the order the events were queued. Flush waits until the queue is empty and the last handler has returned; never call it from inside a handler. Release an emitter with Free. For an async one, call Close and join the thread running Drain first, since Free does not wait for it.   Register, emit, remove On and Once take a topic and a handler. OnAny receives every event. Emit returns how many handlers were called. events-basic.salamCopyimport events  mut e := events.New() as events.Emitter<int> mut log := Vector {} as Vector<str>  func note(s: str):     log.Push(s) end  func main:     e = events.New() as events.Emitter<int>     a := events.On(e, "user.login", (ev: events.Event<int>): note("a " + ev.topic + " " + ev.data) end)     b := events.On(e, "user.*", (ev: events.Event<int>): note("b " + ev.topic + " " + ev.data) end)     _c := events.Once(e, "user.login", (ev: events.Event<int>): note("once " + ev.data) end)     _d := events.OnAny(e, (ev: events.Event<int>): note("any " + ev.topic) end)     _f := events.On(e, "order.#", (ev: events.Event<int>): note("order " + ev.topic) end)      println "count login", events.Count(e, "user.login")     println "count user.a.b", events.Count(e, "user.a.b")     println "count order", events.Count(e, "order")     println "count order.x.y", events.Count(e, "order.x.y")     println "calls", events.Emit(e, "user.login", 1)     println "calls", events.Emit(e, "user.login", 2)     println "calls", events.Emit(e, "user.logout", 3)     println "calls", events.Emit(e, "order.new.eu", 4)     println "calls", events.Emit(e, "other", 5)      println "off a", events.Off(e, a)     println "off a again", events.Off(e, a)     println "off topic", events.OffTopic(e, "user.*")     println "off b", events.Off(e, b)     println "len", events.Len(e)     println "calls", events.Emit(e, "user.login", 6)      selfoff := events.On(e, "x", (ev: events.Event<int>): note("x " + ev.data) end)     _adder := events.On(e, "x", (_ev: events.Event<int>):         _id := events.On(e, "y", (_v: events.Event<int>): note("y") end)         _ok := events.Off(e, selfoff)     end)     println "len before", events.Len(e)     events.Emit(e, "x", 7)     println "len after", events.Len(e)     events.Emit(e, "x", 8)      repeat log.Len() in i:         println log.Get(i)     end     log.Free()     events.Free(e)     ret 0 endOutputcount login 4 count user.a.b 1 count order 2 count order.x.y 2 calls 4 calls 3 calls 2 calls 2 calls 1 off a true off a again false off topic 1 off b false len 2 calls 1 len before 4 len after 4 a user.login 1 b user.login 1 once 1 any user.login a user.login 2 b user.login 2 any user.login b user.logout 3 any user.logout any order.new.eu order order.new.eu any other any user.login any x x 7 any x  Handle events on a worker thread NewAsync makes a queue of the given size, and Drain run on a thread of your own is its worker. EmitAsync puts an event on the queue and returns at once, and waits only when the queue is full. Close stops accepting events; Drain finishes what is queued and returns, so join the thread after it. events-async.salamCopyimport events import mem  mut total := 0 mut last := 0 mut ordered := true mut seen := 0  func add(ev: events.Event<int>):     total += ev.data     if ev.data != last + 1:         ordered = false     end     last = ev.data     seen++ end  func worker(p: events.Emitter<int>*):     events.Drain(p[0]) end  func main:     e := events.NewAsync(4) as events.Emitter<int>     box := mem.AllocateZeroed(sizeof(events.Emitter<int>) as u64) as events.Emitter<int>*     box[0] = e     th := spawn(worker, box)     _id := events.On(e, "tick", (ev: events.Event<int>): add(ev) end)      println "first queued", events.EmitAsync(e, "tick", 1)     repeat 2 to 200 in i:         _ok := events.EmitAsync(e, "tick", i)     end     events.Flush(e)     println "seen", seen     println "total", total     println "ordered", ordered     println "pending", events.Pending(e)      _ok := events.EmitAsync(e, "tick", 201)     _ok2 := events.EmitAsync(e, "other", 9

encoding encoding Turning text and data into Base64, hexadecimal and URL encoding. Encoding and data This package holds the common ways of writing bytes as plain text: Base64 for fitting binary data into JSON or email, hexadecimal for showing bytes, and URL encoding for putting text or special characters into a web address. The larger formats, such as JSON, YAML and XML, have sub-packages of their own, listed in this same group.  Every function takes and returns str, except the two ...Bytes forms, which work on a pointer and a length for binary data. The encoders cannot fail. The decoders Base64Decode, Base64DecodeBytes, HexDecode and URLDecode are declared throws: on bad input they throw an Error whose kind is Syntax (a character that does not belong), UnexpectedEnd (the text stops in the middle of a group, a pair or an escape) or OutOfRange (the buffer is too small), with the byte offset and the line and column of the problem. Neighbouring packages: encoding.binary for numbers packed into bytes, crypto for hashes that you then show in hex, and jwt for tokens. The things people get wrong:  Decoding binary into a str. A str ends at the first zero byte, so Base64Decode and HexDecode cut binary data short; use Base64DecodeBytes into a buffer. Forgetting that decoding can fail. Every decoder call needs try: inside a try: block to handle the error, or in front of the call in a function that is itself throws to pass it on. Expecting HexDecode to skip spaces or a 0x prefix. It reads exactly two hex digits per byte and nothing else; strip separators first. URLEncode writes a space as %20, while URLDecode reads both %20 and + as a space. A % that is not followed by two hex digits, such as the one in 50%, is an error; send it as %25.   Guide: an HTTP Basic login header HTTP Basic authentication sends user:password in Base64 after the word Basic. Base64 is not encryption, anyone can decode it, so this only belongs on HTTPS. Building the header is one call; reading it on the server side means decoding with Base64Decode and splitting at the first colon, since the password itself may contain more colons. encoding-guide-basic-auth.salamCopyimport encoding  func basic_header(user: str, password: str): str:     ret "Basic " + encoding.Base64Encode(user + ":" + password) end  func read_header(header: str, user &: str, password &: str): bool:     if header.Find("Basic ") != 0:         ret false     end     mut pair := ""     try:         pair = encoding.Base64Decode(header.Substr(6, header.Len() - 6))     catch e:         println "refused:", e.ToStr()         ret false     end     colon := pair.Find(":")     if colon < 0:         ret false     end     user = pair.Substr(0, colon)     password = pair.Substr(colon + 1, pair.Len() - colon - 1)     ret true end  func main:     h := basic_header("sara", "p@ss:2026")     println "Authorization:", h      mut user := ""     mut password := ""     if read_header(h, user, password):         println "user:", user         println "password:", password     end     println "bad header accepted:", read_header("Basic !!not-base64!!", user, password) endOutputAuthorization: Basic c2FyYTpwQHNzOjIwMjY= user: sara password: p@ss:2026 refused: base64: invalid character '!' (line 1, column 1) bad header accepted: false Base64Decode throws when the text is not valid Base64, so a garbled header is refused instead of being turned into a random user name.  Guide: what the Base64 decoder accepts Base64Decode accepts the forms Base64 really comes in: padded or unpadded, the standard alphabet (+ and /) or the URL-safe one (- and _), and spaces, tabs and line breaks anywhere, because MIME and PEM files wrap Base64 at 76 or 64 characters. Anything else is an error, so a typo is never turned into damaged bytes. encoding-guide-strict.salamCopyimport encoding  func check(label: str, s: str):     try:         println label, "ok:", encoding.Base64Decode(s)     catch e:         println label, "rejected:", e.kind_name(), "at column", e.column     end end  func main:     check("padded   ", "U2FsYW0=")     check("unpadded ", "U2FsYW0")     check("wrapped  ", "U2Fs\nYW0=")     check("url-safe ", "Pz8_")     check("persian  ", encoding.Base64Encode("سلام"))     check("typo     ", "U2Fs*W0=")     check("cut short", "U2FsY")     check("too much =", "U2E===") endOutputpadded    ok: Salam unpadded  ok: Salam wrapped   ok: Salam url-safe  ok: ??? persian   ok: سلام typo      rejected: syntax error at column 5 cut short rejected: unexpected end of input at column 6 too much = rejected: syntax error at column 5 A character outside both alphabets is a Syntax error at its position; so is anything after the = padding, or more = than the last group needs. Text that stops one character into a group of four, or that starts padding but leaves out an =, is UnexpectedEnd. For binary data use Base64EncodeBytes and Base64DecodeBytes, which work on a pointer and a length, because a str stops at the first zero byte.  Guide: seeing the bytes with hex Hexadecimal writes each byte as two digits, which makes it the easiest way to see what a string really holds. Persian letters take two bytes each in UTF-8, so len of a Persian word counts bytes, not letters. Hex is also the usual form for hashes, keys and colours. encoding-guide-hex.salamCopyimport encoding  func main:     words := ["A", "é", "س", "سلام"]     each w in words:         println w, "is", w.Len(), "bytes:", encoding.HexEncode(w)     end      stored := "d8b3d984d8a7d985"     try:         println "decoded:", encoding
