encoding/json encoding.json Building and reading JSON: from a plain string through automatic struct conversion to streaming. Encoding and data There are three ways to work with JSON here. For simple jobs, functions such as Member, Object and Get work directly on JSON text. For real programs, Marshal and Unmarshal convert a Salam struct to JSON and back. For data whose shape you do not know in advance, Decode returns a dynamic Value. Set the key name of a field with @json "name" above it; @json "-" leaves the field out. Without it, the field's own name becomes the key.  Use this package for APIs, config files and anything another program will read. Its neighbours: encoding.yaml and encoding.toml for files people edit, encoding.msgpack when the data should be small and binary, and encoding.serde to read or write the same struct in several formats. The things people get wrong:  GetInt returns an int, 32 bits, and clamps anything larger: 3000000000 comes back as 2147483647. For ids and timestamps, read the field with Unmarshal into an i64, or parse the text from Get. Get, GetInt and Has look only at the top level of an object. For nested values use GetPath, such as GetPath(text, "user.address.city"). Strict or lenient. Unmarshal throws on a missing field, an unknown key or a type that does not match; UnmarshalLenient keeps the struct's defaults for missing fields and skips unknown keys, but a wrong type still fails. Key order. Marshal writes fields in struct order. A decoded Value object keeps the order of the text and Encode writes its keys in that order; pass sort_keys to Encode when output must be alphabetical.   Guide: load a config file into a struct A config file is the most common JSON a program reads. Describe it as structs, give every field the default you want, and let UnmarshalLenient fill in what the file has. Nested objects map to nested structs and arrays map to Vector fields. encoding-json-guide-config.salamCopyimport encoding.json  struct Database:     pub host: str = "localhost"     pub port: int = 5432     pub pool: int = 4 end  struct Config:     pub name: str = "app"     pub debug: bool = false     pub db: Database = Database {}     pub admins: Vector<str> = Vector {} end  func main:     text := `{   "name": "shop",   "db": {"host": "db.internal", "port": 6432},   "admins": ["sara", "reza"] }`     mut cfg := Config {}     try:         json.UnmarshalLenient(text, cfg)     catch e:         println "bad config:", e.ToStr()         ret 1     end     println "name:", cfg.name     println "debug:", cfg.debug     println "database:", cfg.db.host, cfg.db.port, "pool", cfg.db.pool     println "admins:", cfg.admins.Len(), cfg.admins.Get(0), cfg.admins.Get(1) endOutputname: shop debug: false database: db.internal 6432 pool 4 admins: 2 sara reza The file left out debug and db.pool, so they keep their defaults. That is the reason for the lenient form here: plain Unmarshal is strict and fails with missing key 'pool' when a field is absent, and with unknown key when the file has a key the struct does not. Strict is right for messages between programs, where a missing field is a bug; lenient is right for files people edit by hand. To read a file from disk, pass the text of fs.ReadAll from fs.  Guide: build an API response Going the other way, Marshal turns a struct into compact JSON for the wire and MarshalIndent into readable JSON for logs and files. A Vector of structs becomes an array of objects, quotes inside strings are escaped, and the field order is the order of the struct. encoding-json-guide-response.salamCopyimport encoding.json  struct Item:     pub sku: str = ""     pub title: str = ""     @json "price_cents"     pub price: int = 0     pub in_stock: bool = true end  struct Page:     pub page: int = 1     pub total: int = 0     pub items: Vector<Item> = Vector {}     @json "-"     pub cache_key: str = "" end  func main:     mut p := Page { page = 2, total = 14, cache_key = "products:2" }     p.items.Push(Item { sku = "BK-01", title = "Notebook", price = 1250 })     p.items.Push(Item { sku = "PN-07", title = "Pen \"fine\"", price = 300, in_stock = false })      println json.Marshal(p)     println json.MarshalIndent(p, "  ") endOutput{"page":2,"total":14,"items":[{"sku":"BK-01","title":"Notebook","price_cents":1250,"in_stock":true},{"sku":"PN-07","title":"Pen \"fine\"","price_cents":300,"in_stock":false}]} {   "page": 2,   "total": 14,   "items": [     {       "sku": "BK-01",       "title": "Notebook",       "price_cents": 1250,       "in_stock": true     },     {       "sku": "PN-07",       "title": "Pen \"fine\"",       "price_cents": 300,       "in_stock": false     }   ] } @json "price_cents" renames a field in the JSON without renaming it in the code, and @json "-" keeps internal fields such as cache_key out of the output. Use it for passwords and tokens too, so they can never leak into a response by accident.  Guide: explore JSON of unknown shape When you do not know the shape ahead of time, for example a webhook from another service, Decode gives a tree of Value nodes. Ask each node what it is with IsString, IsInt, IsObject and the rest, then read it with the matching As function. Where a value must be there and of one kind, the checked methods are shorter: doc.field("size").field("w").int() throws MissingKey or TypeMismatch instead of quietly giving 0. encoding

encoding/yaml encoding.yaml Reading YAML by path, building and writing it, and converting it to JSON. Encoding and data YAML is the usual format for configuration files. This package converts YAML to JSON internally, which is what makes its reading functions simple and what lets it work alongside the json package. The reading functions take a path: keys separated by dots, with a list index in square brackets, as in app.hosts[1]. A path that is not there gives an empty string or zero; to tell that apart from a real value, use Has.  It reads the YAML that configuration files use: nested maps, lists in dashed and [flow] form, quoted strings, | and > block text, comments and several documents. For flat key = value settings with sections and overrides, config is simpler, and it reads YAML too. The things people get wrong:  Anchors and aliases (&base, *base, <<: *base) are not supported. A value like &a 1 is read as the string &a 1, and an anchor on a map, as in base: &base followed by indented keys, loses the rest of the document without an error. Write such files out in full, or expand them with another tool first. yes, no, on and off are strings, as in YAML 1.2, so GetBool is false for them. Only true and false are booleans. GetInt returns a 32-bit int and gives 0 for larger numbers. Read sizes, ids and timestamps through ToJSON into an i64 field (see below). Every path function parses the whole text again. For many reads from a large file, call ToJSON or Decode once and work on the result.   Guide: read a config file with defaults The path functions are the quickest way to read a config file. Check first that the sections you depend on exist with HasKeys, then read each setting with the typed getter. For optional settings, wrap Get in a small helper that falls back to a default when Has says the key is not there. encoding-yaml-guide-config.salamCopyimport encoding.yaml  func setting(text: str, path: str, def: str): str:     if yaml.Has(text, path):         ret yaml.Get(text, path)     end     ret def end  func main:     text := `# settings for the shop server:   host: 0.0.0.0   port: 8080   workers: 4 log:   level: debug features:   search: true   beta: false `     mut required := Vector {} as Vector<str>     required.Push("server")     required.Push("log")     if not yaml.HasKeys(text, required):         println "config is missing a section"         ret 1     end      println "listen on", yaml.Get(text, "server.host") + ":" + yaml.Get(text, "server.port")     println "workers:", yaml.GetInt(text, "server.workers")     println "log level:", setting(text, "log.level", "info")     println "log file:", setting(text, "log.file", "stdout")     println "search on:", yaml.GetBool(text, "features.search"), "beta on:", yaml.GetBool(text, "features.beta")     println "feature flags:", yaml.Keys(text, "features") endOutputlisten on 0.0.0.0:8080 workers: 4 log level: debug log file: stdout search on: true beta on: false feature flags: ["search", "beta"] Comments starting with # are ignored. GetInt and GetBool return 0 and false for a missing key, which is also a real value, so a default other than zero needs the Has check.  Guide: YAML into a struct For a config with many fields, a struct is easier to pass around than a text and a list of paths. There is no YAML Unmarshal of its own, but there does not need to be: ToJSON turns the YAML into JSON, and encoding.json fills the struct, with the same @json names and defaults. encoding-yaml-guide-struct.salamCopyimport encoding.yaml import encoding.json  struct Service:     pub name: str = ""     pub image: str = ""     pub replicas: int = 1     pub ports: Vector<int> = Vector {} end  func main:     text := `name: api image: shop/api:2.3 ports:   - 80   - 443 `     mut s := Service {}     try:         json.UnmarshalLenient(yaml.ToJSON(text), s)     catch e:         println "bad service:", e.ToStr()         ret 1     end     println s.name, "runs", s.image     println "replicas:", s.replicas     println "ports:", s.ports.Len(), s.ports.Get(0), s.ports.Get(1) endOutputapi runs shop/api:2.3 replicas: 1 ports: 2 80 443 replicas is not in the file, so it keeps its default of 1 because the lenient form was used. With json.Unmarshal the missing key would be an error.  Guide: walk a list of records A list of objects, such as the jobs of a CI file, is read with Len and an index in the path. Build the path for item i once and add the field names to it. [lint] is the short flow form of a list, and reads the same way as the dashed form. encoding-yaml-guide-list.salamCopyimport encoding.yaml import str  func main:     text := `jobs:   - name: lint     run: salam format --check   - name: test     run: sh tests/run.sh     needs: [lint]   - name: deploy     run: sh deploy.sh     needs: [test]     branch: main `     n := yaml.Len(text, "jobs")     println n, "jobs"     repeat n in i:         at := "jobs[" + str.FromInt(i) + "]"         line := yaml.Get(text, at + ".name") + ": " + yaml.Get(text, at + ".run")         if yaml.Has(text, at + ".needs"):             println line, "(after", yaml.Get(text, at + ".needs[0]") + ")"         else:             println line         end         if yaml.Has(text, at + ".branch"):             println "  only on", yaml.Get(text, at + ".branch")         end     end endOutput3 jobs lint: salam format --check test: sh tests/run.sh (after lint) deploy: sh deploy.sh (after test)   only on main  Guide: several documents in one file Kubernetes manifests and some log formats put several YAM

encoding/csv encoding.csv Reading and writing CSV files, with correct quoting and conversion to a dynamic value. Encoding and data CSV is the simplest table format: one row per line, fields separated by commas. A field containing a comma, a quote or a line break is wrapped in quotes, and a quote inside it is doubled (RFC 4180). This package reads and writes that format, one row at a time with ReadLine and WriteLine or a whole text with ReadAll and WriteAll, and converts it to and from a Value for encoding.json. The ...With variants take a CSVOptions for another separator, such as ; or a tab. The readers are throws: broken input stops with a core Error of kind Syntax that carries the line and column, never with a quietly shortened row. Call them with try, or inside a try: block. The writers cannot fail. Every field is a string; CSV has no numbers or booleans. For spreadsheets with several sheets, formulas or types, see excel; for CSV that feeds a machine learning model, data. The things people get wrong:  The default separator is a comma. A file from a European Excel with ; between fields, or a tab-separated file, reads as one field per line until you pass CSVOptions { separator = ";" } (or "	") to ReadAllWith. A quoted field must be followed directly by the separator or the end of the line. "Pen" ,blue is an error with the code csv.text_after_quote, pointing at the space; a quote inside an unquoted field (5'11") is csv.bare_quote, and a quote that is never closed is csv.unterminated_quote. A quoted field may hold line breaks, and ReadAll keeps them, so the error line is the line in the file, not the row number. ReadLine reads exactly one row and refuses a second one (csv.multiple_rows). ToValue refuses a header with the same column name twice (csv.duplicate_header), because the second column would overwrite the first. FromValue takes the columns from the keys of the first object, in the order they were added, so a table read with ToValue is written back with its columns in the original order.   Guide: totals from a CSV export The typical job is a spreadsheet export: read every row, skip the header, convert the number columns and add them up. ReadAll gives a CSVTable whose rows each hold a fields vector, one string per column. A HashMap keeps the totals and a Vector keeps the cities in the order they first appeared. encoding-csv-guide-report.salamCopyimport encoding.csv  func main throws:     text := `date,city,product,amount 2026-10-01,Tehran,tea,120 2026-10-01,Shiraz,coffee,90 2026-10-02,Tehran,coffee,75 2026-10-02,Tabriz,tea,40 2026-10-03,Shiraz,tea,60 `     mut table := try csv.ReadAll(text)     mut cities := Vector {} as Vector<str>     mut totals := HashMap {} as HashMap<str, int>     mut grand := 0     each i, row in table.rows:         if i == 0 or row.fields.Len() < 4:             continue         end         city := row.fields.Get(1)         amount := row.fields.Get(3).ToInt()         if not totals.Has(city):             cities.Push(city)         end         totals.Put(city, totals.GetOr(city, 0) + amount)         grand += amount     end     each c in cities:         println c, totals.Get(c)     end     println "total", grand     csv.FreeTable(table) endOutputTehran 195 Shiraz 150 Tabriz 40 total 385 Guard against short rows, as the row.fields.len() < 4 check does: a blank line or a hand-edited file can have fewer columns than the header. Free the table with FreeTable when you are done.  Guide: write a CSV file WriteLine joins one row and adds quotes only where they are needed: around a field with a comma, a quote or a line break, with inner quotes doubled. That is what Excel, LibreOffice and most import tools expect, and writing the rows yourself keeps the columns in the order you choose. encoding-csv-guide-export.salamCopyimport encoding.csv  struct Contact:     pub name: str = ""     pub company: str = ""     pub note: str = "" end  func main throws:     mut people := Vector {} as Vector<Contact>     people.Push(Contact { name = "Sara Ahmadi", company = "Nik, Ltd.", note = "prefers email" })     people.Push(Contact { name = "Reza", company = "Pars", note = `said "call me Monday"` })      mut out := ""     mut header := Vector {} as Vector<str>     header.Push("name")     header.Push("company")     header.Push("note")     out = out + csv.WriteLine(header) + "
"     each p in people:         mut f := Vector {} as Vector<str>         f.Push(p.name)         f.Push(p.company)         f.Push(p.note)         out = out + csv.WriteLine(f) + "
"     end     print out      row := try csv.ReadLine(`Reza,Pars,"said ""call me Monday"""`)     println "read back:", row.Get(2) endOutputname,company,note Sara Ahmadi,"Nik, Ltd.",prefers email Reza,Pars,"said ""call me Monday""" read back: said "call me Monday" Write the header row the same way as the data rows. WriteLine does not add the line break, so add "
" yourself, or "
" for tools that insist on it. To save the result, write out with fs.  Guide: CSV to JSON ToValue uses the header row as keys and turns every other row into an object, which encoding.json can then print. That is a small CSV to JSON converter in a few lines. FromValue goes back from an array of objects to CSV text. encoding-csv-guide-json.salamCopyimport encoding.csv import encoding.json import encoding.value  func main throws:     text := "sku,title,stock
BK-01,Notebook,12
PN-07,\"Pen, blue\",0
"     rows := try csv.ToValue(text)     println value.ArrayLen(rows), "rows"     opts := json.JSONOptions { indent = "  ", sort_keys = true }     println json.Encode(rows, opts)      first := value.ArrayGet(rows, 0)     println "stock is a string:&q

encoding/toml encoding.toml Reading and writing TOML configuration files. Encoding and data TOML is the configuration format of [section] tables and key = value lines used by Cargo.toml, pyproject.toml and many server configs. This package reads TOML text into a dynamic Value and writes a Value back as TOML. It has three functions: Decode and Valid for reading, Encode for writing. Decode and Encode are declared throws: on bad input they throw an Error and give back nothing half-read. Pick TOML for files people edit by hand. For data that programs exchange use encoding.json; for YAML files such as CI or Kubernetes configs use encoding.yaml; for KEY=value secrets files use encoding.envfile. If you only want settings loaded from a file with defaults and environment overrides, config may already do the job. How TOML maps to a Value  TOMLValue  [table], [a.b], inline { k = v }, dotted keys a.b = 1object (nested) [[name]]array of objects "basic" with escapes, 'literal'string 42, -7, 1_000, 0x1F, 0o17, 0b101int (64-bit) 3.5, 1e6, inf, nanfloat true, falsebool dates and times such as 1979-05-27T07:32:00Zstring, unchanged   What trips people up  Errors stop the whole read. Decode throws at the first mistake, with e.line and e.column pointing at it, so a typo never silently drops the rest of the file. A key or [table] defined twice, an unquoted word such as mode = fast, a bad escape and an integer that does not fit in 64 bits are all errors. Multi-line strings work. Both """ and ''' are read, including the first-newline trim, line-ending backslash and embedded quotes. Dates stay strings; parse them with time if you need them. Writing is not formatting. Encode writes keys in no fixed order, drops keys whose value is null, and writes an array of objects as an inline array [{...}, {...}] rather than [[table]] blocks. The result is valid TOML that reads back to the same data, but comments and layout of an original file are lost.   Guide: read a project manifest Project files such as Cargo.toml or pyproject.toml mix plain tables, inline tables and arrays of tables. Decode reads the whole file into a Value, or throws if it is not valid TOML; since main is declared throws, a broken file ends the program with the error. From there the value functions walk it. encoding-toml-guide-manifest.salamCopyimport encoding.toml import encoding.value import sort  func main throws:     text := `[package] name = "shop" version = "1.4.0" authors = ["Sara", "Reza"]  [dependencies] http = "2.1" json = { version = "1.0", optional = true } log = "0.9"  [[bin]] name = "shop" path = "src/main.salam"  [[bin]] name = "shop-admin" path = "src/admin.salam" `     doc := try toml.Decode(text)     pkg := value.ObjectGet(doc, "package")     println value.AsString(value.ObjectGet(pkg, "name")), value.AsString(value.ObjectGet(pkg, "version"))     println "authors:", value.ArrayLen(value.ObjectGet(pkg, "authors"))      deps := value.ObjectGet(doc, "dependencies")     names := value.ObjectKeys(deps)     sort.QuickSort(names)     each n in names:         d := value.ObjectGet(deps, n)         if value.IsString(d):             println "dep", n, value.AsString(d)         else:             println "dep", n, value.AsString(value.ObjectGet(d, "version")), "(optional)"         end     end      bins := value.ObjectGet(doc, "bin")     repeat value.ArrayLen(bins) in i:         b := value.ArrayGet(bins, i)         println "binary", value.AsString(value.ObjectGet(b, "name")), "from", value.AsString(value.ObjectGet(b, "path"))     end endOutputshop 1.4.0 authors: 2 dep http 2.1 dep json 1.0 (optional) dep log 0.9 binary shop from src/main.salam binary shop-admin from src/admin.salam A dependency can be a plain version string or an inline table with more detail, so the program asks IsString before reading it. Objects do not keep the order of their keys; sorting ObjectKeys with sort.QuickSort gives a stable listing.  Guide: TOML into a struct For settings you use all over a program, load them into a struct once. Encode the decoded value as JSON with json.EncodeDefault and let json.UnmarshalLenient fill the struct: keys the file leaves out keep the struct's defaults, and a [server] table fills a nested struct. encoding-toml-guide-struct.salamCopyimport encoding.toml import encoding.json  struct Server:     pub host: str = "127.0.0.1"     pub port: int = 8000 end  struct Settings:     pub title: str = ""     pub debug: bool = false     pub server: Server = Server {}     pub allowed: Vector<str> = Vector {} end  func main:     text := `title = "Shop admin" allowed = ["10.0.0.0/8", "192.168.1.0/24"]  [server] port = 9090 `     mut s := Settings {}     try:         doc := toml.Decode(text)         json.UnmarshalLenient(json.EncodeDefault(doc), s)     catch e:         println "bad settings:", e.ToStr()         ret 1     end     println s.title, "debug:", s.debug     println "listen on", s.server.host, s.server.port     println "allowed networks:", s.allowed.Len(), s.allowed.Get(0) endOutputShop admin debug: false listen on 127.0.0.1 9090 allowed networks: 2 10.0.0.0/8  Guide: write a TOML file To write TOML, build a Value object and pass it to Encode. A nested object becomes a [table]. The top level must be an object, since a TOML document is always a table; Encode throws Unsupported for anything else, and for a null inside an array, with e.path naming where it is. encoding-toml-guide-write.salamCopyimport encoding.toml import encoding.value  func replica(host: str, weight: int): value.Value:     mut r := value.NewValueObject()     value.ObjectSet(r, "host", value.ValueString(host))     value.ObjectS

encoding/html encoding.html Turning HTML entities, named and numeric, into text, and text into safe HTML. Encoding and data HTML cannot hold a bare < or & in its text, so they travel as entities: &lt;, &amp;, &eacute; or a number such as &#233; and &#xE9;. Unescape turns every entity in a string back into the character it names; Escape and EscapeText go the other way. Use them when you read text out of a page or a feed, and when you put text of unknown origin into a page. Unescape follows the HTML5 rules the way Python's html.unescape does, and gives the same answer on every input tried against it: all the named entities of the HTML standard (including the ones that stand for two characters), decimal and hexadecimal numbers, the older names that browsers accept without the closing ; (&copy, &amp), numbers 128 to 159 read as Windows-1252 characters, and the replacement character for &#0;, surrogates and numbers beyond Unicode. Anything that is not an entity stays as it is. What people get wrong:  Unescaping text before using it as HTML. After Unescape the text is plain text again; if it goes back into a page, escape it again. Using EscapeText inside an attribute. It leaves quotes alone, so a value with " in it breaks out of href="...". Use Escape for attributes. Expecting Escape to make a URL or a script safe. It only protects the places where HTML text or a quoted attribute goes. A javascript: link or text inside <script> needs more than escaping. Unescaping twice. &amp;lt; is the text &lt;; one pass gives that, a second pass would give <.  The template package has its own EscapeHTML; for XML text and attributes see encoding.xml. Escaping and getting the text back Escaping and unescaping are inverses: whatever Escape produces, Unescape turns back into the original. The example escapes three comments and checks the round trip. encoding-html-guide-roundtrip.salamCopyimport encoding.html  func main:     comments := ["5 < 6 && 7 > 3", `say "hi" & wave`, "it's <b>bold</b>"]     each comment in comments:         escaped := html.Escape(comment)         println escaped         println html.Unescape(escaped) == comment     end endOutput5 &lt; 6 &amp;&amp; 7 &gt; 3 true say &quot;hi&quot; &amp; wave true it&#x27;s &lt;b&gt;bold&lt;/b&gt; true Building markup from untrusted text A name that comes from a user can hold &, < or a quote. Put it in a tag's text with EscapeText and in an attribute value with Escape, which also covers both kinds of quote. In the other direction, text scraped from a page has to go through Unescape before it is compared or shown. encoding-html-guide-page.salamCopyimport encoding.html  func card(name: str, note: str): str:     ret `<div class="card" title="` + html.Escape(name) + `"><h2>` + html.EscapeText(name) + `</h2><p>` + html.EscapeText(note) + `</p></div>` end  func main:     println card("Tom & Jerry", "<b>not bold</b>")     println card(`He said "hi"`, "it's fine")     scraped := "Jos&eacute; &lt;open&gt; &amp; 5 &lt; 6 &#8211; &euro;3"     println html.Unescape(scraped) endOutput<div class="card" title="Tom &amp; Jerry"><h2>Tom &amp; Jerry</h2><p>&lt;b&gt;not bold&lt;/b&gt;</p></div> <div class="card" title="He said &quot;hi&quot;"><h2>He said "hi"</h2><p>it's fine</p></div> José <open> & 5 < 6 – €3 Functions Unescapefunc Unescape(s: str): strReplaces every HTML entity in the text by the characters it stands for: named (&eacute;), decimal (&#233;) and hexadecimal (&#xE9;), with the same rules as Python's html.unescape. Text that is not a valid entity is left unchanged. The result is a new string.encoding-html-Unescape.salamCopyimport encoding.html  func main:     page := "&lt;p&gt;Fianc&eacute; &amp; cr&egrave;me &#8212; &#x20AC;5&lt;/p&gt;"     println html.Unescape(page)     println html.Unescape("Tom &amp; Jerry &copy 2026, a &lt b")     safe := html.Escape(`<a href="x">it's</a>`)     println safe     println html.EscapeText(`<a href="x">it's</a>`)     println html.Unescape(safe) endOutput<p>Fiancé & crème — €5</p> Tom & Jerry © 2026, a < b &lt;a href=&quot;x&quot;&gt;it&#x27;s&lt;/a&gt; &lt;a href="x"&gt;it's&lt;/a&gt; <a href="x">it's</a> Escapefunc Escape(s: str): strReplaces &, <, >, " and ' by &amp;, &lt;, &gt;, &quot; and &#x27;, so the text is safe in HTML text and in a quoted attribute.The example for this item is shown with the ones above: encoding-html-Unescape.salam EscapeTextfunc EscapeText(s: str): strReplaces only &, < and >. Safe in HTML text, not in an attribute.The example for this item is shown with the ones above: encoding-html-Unescape.salam

encoding/url encoding.url Taking a web address apart, building and editing its parameters, and resolving relative addresses. Encoding and data This package works with whole web addresses. Parse splits a URL such as https://user@shop.example.co.uk:8443/path?page=2#top into a URL struct with the fields scheme, userinfo, host, port, path, raw_query and fragment, and String puts it back together. Around that come helpers to edit query parameters, resolve relative links with Join, and find the registrable domain of a host. Use it whenever you have a full address. For the a=1&b=2 part on its own, such as a form body, use encoding.query; for percent-encoding a single string, encoding.URLEncode in encoding; to fetch the address, net.http. Raw and decoded parts The fields hold the text exactly as it appeared, percent escapes included, so String(Parse(x)) normally gives back x. Read the human form with DecodedPath, DecodedUserinfo or Query. When you set a field yourself, put encoded text in it: escape path segments with EncodePathSegment and build queries with SetQuery. What trips people up  Parse throws on text that is not a URL. It is declared throws, so call it with try. It refuses an empty string, a space or control character, a scheme that is not a letter followed by letters, digits, +, - or ., a missing host after :// (only file:/// may have none), a host with characters such as <, a port that is not a number or is above 65535, an IPv6 address without its ], and a % not followed by two hex digits anywhere; the Error has the kind (Syntax, UnexpectedEnd, OutOfRange, InvalidArgument) and the column. A relative reference such as ../a.html or ?page=2 is fine, and text without :// (including mailto:sara@example.com) still has no scheme or host and lands whole in path, so check scheme and host before trusting an address from a user. Nothing is lowercased. HTTPS://Shop.Example.COM keeps its case in scheme and host, and Domain returns Example.COM. Lowercase with str.Lower before you compare hosts or domains. Editing one parameter rewrites the whole query. RemoveParam, SetParam and KeepParams decode the query and encode it again: %20 becomes +, characters such as * get escaped, a bare flag becomes flag=, and repeated keys are grouped together. The meaning stays the same; the text may not. Everything that decodes throws too. Join parses its reference, and DecodedPath, DecodedUserinfo, Query, ParamNames, SetParam, RemoveParam and KeepParams decode a field. An address from Parse always decodes, but a field you set by hand may not.   Guide: strip tracking parameters Links copied from email and social media carry utm_ and click id parameters that only serve analytics. Before you store or compare links, parse them, drop those parameters with RemoveParam, clear the fragment and print the result with String. The parameters that stay keep their order. encoding-url-guide-clean.salamCopyimport encoding.url  func clean(raw: str): str throws:     mut u := try url.Parse(raw)     names := try url.ParamNames(u)     each n in names:         if n.StartsWith("utm_") or n == "fbclid" or n == "gclid":             _ := try url.RemoveParam(u, n)         end     end     u.fragment = ""     ret url.String(u) end  func main:     links := ["https://shop.example/item/42?color=red&utm_source=news&utm_medium=email#reviews", "https://blog.example/post?fbclid=IwAR0abc", "https://example.com/search?q=salam%20lang&utm_campaign=fall&page=2&debug", "https://example.com/sale?off=50%"]     each link in links:         try:             println clean(link)         catch e:             println "skipped:", e.ToStr()         end     end endOutputhttps://shop.example/item/42?color=red https://blog.example/post https://example.com/search?q=salam+lang&page=2&debug= skipped: url: incomplete percent escape (line 1, column 32) ParamNames returns a copy of the names, so removing parameters inside the loop is safe. The last link has a bare %, which is not a valid URL, so Parse throws and the loop skips it with the reason. The fields of URL are plain strings you can set directly, as u.fragment = "" does. The third line shows the rewrite described above: salam%20lang comes out as salam+lang and the bare debug as debug=. Both mean the same to a server, but if you use the cleaned link as a cache or database key, clean every link the same way so equal links give equal text.  Guide: resolve the links of a page A crawler or a link checker finds relative links like ../api/json.html in a page and needs the full address. Join resolves a reference against the page's own URL the way a browser does: ./ and ../ move through the folders, a leading / starts at the site root, //host keeps the scheme, a full URL replaces everything, and a reference of only ?query or #fragment keeps the page itself. encoding-url-guide-links.salamCopyimport encoding.url  func main throws:     page := try url.Parse("https://docs.example.com/guide/start/index.html?lang=en")     hrefs := ["install.html", "./setup/linux.html", "../api/json.html", "/blog/", "https://other.example/x", "//cdn.example.com/app.js", "?lang=fa", "#install"]     each h in hrefs:         println h, "->", url.String(try url.Join(page, h))     end endOutputinstall.html -> https://docs.example.com/guide/start/install.html ./setup/linux.html -> https://docs.example.com/guide/start/setup/linux.html ../api/json.html -> https://docs.example.com/guide/api/json.html /blog/ -> https://docs.example.com/blog/ https://other.example/x -> https://other.example/x //cdn.example.com/app.js -> https://cdn.example.com/app.js ?lang=fa -> https://docs.example.com/guide/start/index.html?lang=fa #install -> https://docs.example.com/guide/start/index.html?lang=en#install These are the rules of R

encoding/query encoding.query Reading and building the query string of a web address, such as q=hello&page=2. Encoding and data A query string is the key=value&key=value text after the ? in a web address, and the same format is the body of an HTML form posted as application/x-www-form-urlencoded. This package reads and writes that text: it undoes the percent escapes and + for spaces, and builds correctly escaped strings from your values. Use it when you hold the query text alone: a form body, the raw_query of a request, a signed API call. When you have a whole address and want to change its parameters, encoding.url has SetParam, RemoveParam and KeepParams on top of this package. Inside a net.http handler, http.Query and http.Form read single values for you; take http.RawQuery and this package when you need repeated keys or want to rewrite the query. Two ways to work  On the text. Get, GetAll and Has take the query string itself. Each call decodes the whole string again, which is fine for reading a handful of values. They never fail: a % that is not followed by two hex digits is kept as written, the way browsers read such a query, so Get("off=50%", "off") is 50%. On a QueryMap. Decode turns the text into a map you can change with Set, Add, Remove and Retain, then write back with Encode. One key may have several values (tag=a&tag=b), so each key holds a list, and the map remembers the order in which keys first appeared. Decode and DecodeWith are strict and declared throws: a broken escape throws an Error of kind Syntax, or UnexpectedEnd when the text stops inside an escape, with its column.  What trips people up  There is no getter on a QueryMap. Read the text with Get, or read the map directly: m.data.has("tag") and m.data.get("tag").items. Missing and empty look the same to Get. Both page= and no page at all return ""; ask Has when it matters. A bare flag counts as present with an empty value, and Encode writes it back as flag=. Numbers are not checked. "12abc".to_int() is 12 and "abc".to_int() is 0, so bound every number you read before using it. Repeated keys are grouped. a=1&b=2&a=3 encodes back as a=1&a=3&b=2. That is the same data, but if a signature or cache key covers the exact text, sign what you send, not what you received. Keys are case sensitive, and a leading ? is skipped by Decode.   Guide: read the parameters of a search page A search page reads a few parameters, gives the missing ones a default, and converts the numbers. Get already decodes the value, so green+tea arrives as green tea. GetAll returns every value of a repeated key, which is how checkbox filters arrive. encoding-query-guide-search.salamCopyimport encoding.query  func main:     qs := "q=green+tea&brand=nik&brand=pars&min=20&page=3&limit=500&ref=100%"      words := query.Get(qs, "q")     mut page := 1     if query.Has(qs, "page"):         page = query.Get(qs, "page").ToInt()     end     mut limit := 20     if query.Has(qs, "limit"):         limit = query.Get(qs, "limit").ToInt()     end     if page < 1: page = 1 end     if limit < 1 or limit > 100: limit = 100 end     brands := query.GetAll(qs, "brand")      println "search for:", words     println "brands:", brands.Len(), brands     println "min price:", query.Get(qs, "min").ToInt()     println "rows", (page - 1) * limit + 1, "to", page * limit     println "ref kept as sent:", query.Get(qs, "ref") endOutputsearch for: green tea brands: 2 ["nik", "pars"] min price: 20 rows 201 to 300 ref kept as sent: 100% Get returns an empty string both for a missing key and for key=, so use Has when the difference matters, as the defaults for page and limit do here. The ref value has a bare %; Get keeps it as sent instead of failing the whole page. Never trust the numbers: the visitor asked for 500 rows, and the handler caps limit at 100 and keeps page at 1 or more, so a bad value cannot make it read the whole table or a negative offset.  Guide: next and previous page links Pagination links must keep every filter the visitor chose and change only the page number. Decode the current query into a QueryMap, Set the page (it replaces all values of that key, or adds the key when it is new) and Encode it again. encoding-query-guide-pages.salamCopyimport encoding.query import str  func page_link(current: str, page: int): str throws:     mut m := try query.Decode(current)     query.Set(m, "page", str.FromInt(page))     ret "/products?" + query.Encode(m) end  func main throws:     current := "category=books&sort=price&tag=new&tag=sale&page=2"     println "prev:", try page_link(current, 1)     println "next:", try page_link(current, 3)     println "first visit:", try page_link("category=books", 2) endOutputprev: /products?category=books&sort=price&tag=new&tag=sale&page=1 next: /products?category=books&sort=price&tag=new&tag=sale&page=3 first visit: /products?category=books&page=2 Set keeps an existing key in its place, so the links differ from the address the visitor came from only in the page number, and a cache sees one address per page instead of one per parameter order.  Guide: HTML form bodies A form sent with method="post" has the body type application/x-www-form-urlencoded, which is the same format as a query string. Decode it with the same functions. Spaces arrive as + and everything else outside plain ASCII as %XX bytes, Persian text included. encoding-query-guide-form.salamCopyimport encoding.query  func main throws:     body := "name=Sara+Ahmadi&city=%D8%B4%DB%8C%D8%B1%D8%A7%D8%B2&note=50%25+off%3F&agree=on"     form := try query.Decode(body)     println "fields:", query.Keys(form)     println &quot

encoding/envfile encoding.envfile Reading and writing .env files, with variable substitution. Encoding and data A .env file holds a program's settings and secrets as one KEY=value per line, the format used by Docker Compose, most twelve-factor apps and tools such as dotenv. This package reads such a file into a Doc, an ordered list of keys and string values, substitutes ${NAME} references, and writes a Doc back as text. It works on text and never touches the process environment. If you only want a .env file's variables available to the program, env.Load(path) in env puts them into the environment in one call (and env.Overload lets the file win over variables already set). config.LoadEnv in config reads one into a Config with typed getters such as GetInt and GetBool. Use this package when you need the file itself: its order, its references, a strict check, or to write it back. For nested settings with numbers and lists, encoding.toml or encoding.yaml fit better. What a line may contain  Blank lines and lines starting with # are skipped, and a UTF-8 byte order mark at the start is ignored. export  before a key is allowed, so a file a shell can source also parses. Keys are letters, digits, _, . and -. Spaces around the = are allowed. An unquoted value runs to the end of the line, minus trailing spaces. A # starts a comment only after a space, so https://x/#top keeps its #. A double-quoted value understands 
, 	, " and \, may span several lines, and takes ${NAME} substitution. A single-quoted value is taken literally, with no escapes and no substitution. A key that appears twice keeps its first position and its last value.  What trips people up  Every value is a string. PORT=8080 gives "8080"; convert it yourself, and remember that "abc".to_int() is 0, not an error. References only look upward. ${NAME} is resolved from lines above it (then from the base document, if you pass one). A name defined further down, or not at all, silently becomes an empty string. Use RefNames on a ParseRaw result to see what a file expects. Parse skips bad lines without a word. A line like SECRET KEY 8f2c just disappears. Load files with ParseStrict at startup. Format drops comments and blank lines; it writes only keys and values.   Guide: shared defaults and local overrides Most projects commit a .env with safe defaults and let each developer keep a .env.local with their own ports and passwords. Parse both and MergeInto the local one: its keys replace the shared ones, and keys that only exist in the shared file stay. GetOr covers settings neither file has. encoding-envfile-guide-layers.salamCopyimport encoding.envfile  func main:     shared := `# committed to the repository APP_NAME=shop PORT=8080 LOG_LEVEL=info DB_URL=postgres://localhost/shop `     local := `# .env.local, kept out of git PORT=9000 DB_URL=postgres://sara:secret@localhost/shop_dev `     mut cfg := envfile.Parse(shared)     mut over := envfile.Parse(local)     envfile.MergeInto(cfg, over)      port := envfile.Get(cfg, "PORT").ToInt()     println envfile.Get(cfg, "APP_NAME"), "on port", port     println "log level:", envfile.GetOr(cfg, "LOG_LEVEL", "warn")     println "workers:", envfile.GetOr(cfg, "WORKERS", "2").ToInt()     println "keys in order:", envfile.Keys(cfg)      envfile.Free(over)     envfile.Free(cfg) endOutputshop on port 9000 log level: info workers: 2 keys in order: ["APP_NAME", "PORT", "LOG_LEVEL", "DB_URL"] Every value is a string; convert numbers with to_int(). A merged key keeps its original place, so Keys still lists them in the order of the shared file. In a real program the two texts come from fs.ReadAll in fs.  Guide: comments, quotes and multi-line values Real .env files mix comments, URLs with # in them, PEM keys pasted over several lines and prices with a $ in them. The program below reads one of each, so you can see where each rule from the list above applies. encoding-envfile-guide-syntax.salamCopyimport encoding.envfile  func main:     text := `export APP_NAME=shop   # trailing comment HOME_URL=https://shop.example/#top MOTD="Welcome!
Orders ship daily." TLS_KEY="-----BEGIN KEY----- MIIEvQIBADANBg -----END KEY-----" PRICE_NOTE='$5 off, literally' EARLY=${LATER} LATER=set below PORT=8080 PORT=9090 `     mut d := envfile.Parse(text)     println "APP_NAME:", envfile.Get(d, "APP_NAME")     println "HOME_URL:", envfile.Get(d, "HOME_URL")     println "MOTD:", envfile.Get(d, "MOTD")     key := envfile.Get(d, "TLS_KEY")     println "TLS_KEY lines:", key.Split("
").Len()     println "PRICE_NOTE:", envfile.Get(d, "PRICE_NOTE")     println "EARLY: [" + envfile.Get(d, "EARLY") + "]"     println "PORT:", envfile.Get(d, "PORT"), "keys:", envfile.Len(d)     envfile.Free(d) endOutputAPP_NAME: shop HOME_URL: https://shop.example/#top MOTD: Welcome! Orders ship daily. TLS_KEY lines: 3 PRICE_NOTE: $5 off, literally EARLY: [] PORT: 9090 keys: 8 The trailing comment after shop is dropped because a space comes before the #; the one in HOME_URL stays. The double-quoted MOTD turns 
 into a real line break, and TLS_KEY keeps its three lines. EARLY is empty because LATER is defined after it, and PORT holds the second value but is counted once.  Guide: references between variables Values can refer to other keys with ${NAME} or $NAME, and ${NAME:-default} falls back when the key is not set. Parse resolves references within the file. To fill some of them from elsewhere, for example secrets that only the server knows, read the file with ParseRaw and resolve it with ExpandDoc and a second Doc of base values. encoding-envfile-guide-expand.salamCopyimport encoding.envfile  func main:     text := `DB_HOST=localhost DB_POR

encoding/value encoding.value A dynamic value for data whose shape you do not know in advance; the shared language of every format in this group. Encoding and data Value is the dynamic data type shared by the encoding packages. One Value is a null, a bool, a 64-bit int, a float, a string, an array of values or an object mapping strings to values, and its kind field says which. encoding.json, encoding.yaml, encoding.toml, encoding.msgpack and others decode into it and encode from it, and encoding.serde converts between formats through it. Reach for a Value when the shape of the data is not known when you write the program: a webhook payload, a config with optional sections, a document you only pass along. When the shape is fixed, decoding straight into a struct (for example with json.Unmarshal) is shorter and checks the types for you. The functions in five groups  JobFunctions  Make a valueValueNull, ValueBool, ValueInt, ValueFloat, ValueString, NewValueArray, NewValueObject Ask the kindIsNull, IsBool, IsInt, IsFloat, IsNumber, IsString, IsArray, IsObject ReadAsBool, AsInt, AsFloat, AsString, ArrayLen, ArrayGet, ObjectGet, ObjectGetOk, ObjectHas, ObjectKeys Read and check, throwing on a wrong kind or a missing keythe methods field, at, int, float, str, bool ChangeArrayPush, ArraySet, ObjectSet, ObjectDelete, ValueClone, ValueFree   What trips people up  The As functions never check the kind. AsString of a number is "" and AsInt of a string is 0. When the data comes from outside, use the checked methods instead: v.field("port").int() throws MissingKey or TypeMismatch with a message that names the key and both kinds, and try v.field("port").int() catch 8080 gives a default. Missing is null, all the way down. ObjectGet on a missing key, or on something that is not an object, returns null, so a chain like ObjectGet(ObjectGet(doc, "a"), "b") is safe. ArrayGet is not: an index past ArrayLen stops the program. Copies share parts. A copy of an object shares its map, so ObjectSet through the copy changes the original. A copy of an array shares its elements but not its length, so ArrayPush on an array you got from ObjectGet is lost until you ObjectSet it back. Use ValueClone for a real copy. Key order depends on how the object was built. ObjectKeys returns keys in the order they were added with ObjectSet, and a decoded JSON document in the order of its text. An object made from a map by ValueObject follows that map's own order. Sort the keys, or encode with sort_keys, when output must be alphabetical.   Guide: walk a whole document A recursive function over Value handles any shape: for an object, visit each key; for an array, each index; anything else is a leaf. This one prints the path of every leaf, which is handy for logging a webhook payload or comparing two documents line by line. encoding-value-guide-walk.salamCopyimport encoding.value import encoding.json import sort import str  func walk(v: value.Value, path: str):     if value.IsObject(v):         keys := value.ObjectKeys(v)         sort.QuickSort(keys)         each k in keys:             walk(value.ObjectGet(v, k), path + "." + k)         end     else value.IsArray(v):         repeat value.ArrayLen(v) in i:             walk(value.ArrayGet(v, i), path + "[" + str.FromInt(i) + "]")         end     else:         println path, "=", value.ToDebugString(v)     end end  func main throws:     doc := try json.Decode(`{"order": 1042, "customer": {"name": "Sara", "vip": true}, "lines": [{"sku": "BK-01", "qty": 2}, {"sku": "PN-07", "qty": 1}], "note": null}`)     walk(doc, "$") endOutput$.customer.name = string(Sara) $.customer.vip = bool(true) $.lines[0].qty = int(2) $.lines[0].sku = string(BK-01) $.lines[1].qty = int(1) $.lines[1].sku = string(PN-07) $.note = null $.order = int(1042) ObjectKeys gives the keys in the order they were added, so a decoded document keeps the order of its text. This program sorts them with sort.QuickSort to print them alphabetically whatever order the input had. ToDebugString shows each leaf together with its kind.  Guide: build a payload with optional fields A struct always writes all its fields. When some fields should only appear when they have a value, as many HTTP APIs expect, build a Value object instead and set only what you have. json.Encode with sort_keys prints it in a stable order. encoding-value-guide-build.salamCopyimport encoding.value import encoding.json  func payload(name: str, email: str, age: int, tags: Vector<str>): value.Value:     mut v := value.NewValueObject()     value.ObjectSet(v, "name", value.ValueString(name))     if email != "":         value.ObjectSet(v, "email", value.ValueString(email))     end     if age > 0:         value.ObjectSet(v, "age", value.ValueInt(age))     end     if tags.Len() > 0:         mut arr := value.NewValueArray()         each t in tags:             value.ArrayPush(arr, value.ValueString(t))         end         value.ObjectSet(v, "tags", arr)     end     ret v end  func main:     opts := json.JSONOptions { sort_keys = true }     mut tags := Vector {} as Vector<str>     println json.Encode(payload("Sara", "", 0, tags), opts)     tags.Push("beta")     tags.Push("vip")     println json.Encode(payload("Reza", "reza@example.com", 41, tags), opts) endOutput{"name": "Sara"} {"age": 41, "email": "reza@example.com", "name": "Reza", "tags": ["beta", "vip"]}  Guide: change a nested field To change something deep in a decoded document, take the inner part with ObjectGet, change it, and store it back with ObjectSet. For objects the store is not strictly needed, because the map is

encoding/serde encoding.serde Detecting the format of a piece of text and converting JSON, YAML, TOML, XML and CSV into one another. Encoding and data This package converts text from one data format to another in one call. Transcode reads the input with the matching decoder, holds it as a Value, and writes it with the target encoder. Detect guesses which format a text is in. The format names are the lowercase strings json, yaml, toml, xml and csv; "JSON" is not recognised. It suits tools that take whatever format a user hands them, and one-off migrations. When your program needs the data itself, call the format's own package (encoding.json, encoding.yaml, encoding.toml, encoding.xml, encoding.csv): they return a Value or fill a struct and give real error messages, while this package only answers yes or no. MessagePack is binary and is not one of the names here; use encoding.msgpack. What survives a conversion Everything passes through a Value, so comments and formatting are always lost, while keys keep the order they were read in. Beyond that, each format can hold less than JSON:  FormatReading givesWriting loses  JSON, YAMLevery kindYAML writes the float 2.0 as 2, which reads back as an int TOMLevery kind except null; dates as stringsnull keys are dropped; the top level must be an object XMLonly strings, objects and arrays (for repeated elements); attributes as @name, text as #text; the outer element's name is droppednumbers and booleans become text; the output is wrapped in <root> CSVan array of objects, one per row, every cell a stringneeds an array of objects; only string fields are written, numbers and booleans come out as empty cells   What trips people up  Detection is a guess. The order is XML (text starts with <), JSON, TOML, CSV, then YAML, and nearly any plain text such as hello world is valid YAML. Pass the format yourself whenever a file extension or Content-Type tells you. Transcode hides failures as an empty string. Use TranscodeStrict, which throws an Error that says what went wrong. CSV in never fails, so any text read as CSV converts without an error.   Guide: accept any format A tool that takes settings or data from users does not have to insist on one format. Detect looks at the text and names the format: XML when it starts with <, JSON when it parses as JSON, then TOML, CSV and finally YAML. Pass that name to TranscodeStrict to turn whatever came in into the one format your code reads. encoding-serde-guide-anything.salamCopyimport encoding.serde  func to_json(text: str): str:     kind := serde.Detect(text)     if kind == "":         ret "(unknown format)"     end     try:         ret kind + " -> " + serde.TranscodeStrict(text, kind, "json")     catch e:         ret "(could not read " + kind + ": " + e.message + ")"     end end  func main:     println to_json("name: shop
port: 8080
")     println to_json("name = \"shop\"
port = 8080
")     println to_json("name,port
shop,8080
")     println to_json(`{"name": "shop", "port": 8080}`)     println to_json("") endOutputyaml -> {"name": "shop", "port": 8080} toml -> {"name": "shop", "port": 8080} csv -> [{"name": "shop", "port": "8080"}] json -> {"name": "shop", "port": 8080} (unknown format) Detection is a guess from the shape of the text. Very short inputs can fit more than one format, and almost any plain text is valid YAML, so when you know the format, from a file extension or a Content-Type header, pass it yourself.  Guide: move a config to another format Changing a project from YAML to TOML, or the other way, is one call. Convert, then check the result: read both the old and the new text back as JSON, decode them, and compare the two values with value.Equal. Comparing the JSON text instead would fail on key order alone. encoding-serde-guide-migrate.salamCopyimport encoding.serde import encoding.json import encoding.value  func main throws:     old := `server:   host: 0.0.0.0   port: 8080 log:   level: info `     as_toml := try serde.TranscodeStrict(old, "yaml", "toml")     print as_toml      before := try json.Decode(try serde.TranscodeStrict(old, "yaml", "json"))     after := try json.Decode(try serde.TranscodeStrict(as_toml, "toml", "json"))     println "same data:", value.Equal(before, after) endOutput[server] host = "0.0.0.0" port = 8080 [log] level = "info" same data: true Comments do not survive, because a Value holds data only, so tell people who edit the file by hand before you convert it.  Guide: XML in and out XML has no arrays or numbers, so the mapping follows a few rules: an @name key becomes an attribute, an array becomes the same element repeated, #text becomes the element's text, and a converted document is wrapped in a <root> element. Reading XML gives every value as a string and attributes as @ keys. encoding-serde-guide-xml.salamCopyimport encoding.serde  func main:     order := `{"@id": 1042, "customer": "Sara", "item": ["tea", "cups"], "total": 39.5, "paid": true}`     x := serde.Transcode(order, "json", "xml")     println x     println "detected:", serde.Detect(x)     println "back:", serde.Transcode(x, "xml", "json")     println serde.Transcode("<book lang=\"fa\"><title>Salam</title><pages>153</pages></book>", "xml", "json") endOutput<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?> <root id="1042"><customer>Sara</customer><item>tea&l

encoding/msgpack encoding.msgpack The compact binary MessagePack format for dynamic values. Encoding and data MessagePack holds the same data as JSON in a shorter binary form that is quicker to read, which suits messages between services, cache entries and RPC. This package turns a Value into a compress.ByteBuf with Marshal and reads one back with Unmarshal (or UnmarshalBytes for raw memory). Both are declared throws: bad data throws an Error, so call them with try. Pick it over encoding.json when both ends are programs and size or speed matters; keep JSON when people read the data or a browser consumes it. For a fixed binary layout of your own, such as a file header, write the fields directly with encoding.binary; for schemas shared across languages, encoding.protobuf. How values are written  ValueMessagePack  null, boolnil, true/false intthe smallest int format that fits, from one byte up to 8 floatalways float64 (9 bytes); float32 is read but never written stringfixstr, str8, str16 or str32 by length array, objectfixarray/array16/array32, fixmap/map16/map32 with string keys   What trips people up  bin and ext are supported. A bin value arrives as KindBytes and an ext value as KindExt, with BytesToBuf and ExtDataToBuf giving the raw bytes. A string still stops at the first zero byte, so keep binary data in the value, not in a str. Map keys must be strings. A map with integer keys, as some other libraries write, is read with every key turned into "", so the entries overwrite each other. Trailing bytes are ignored. Unmarshal reads one value and does not report what follows it or how many bytes it used, so you cannot read several messages from one buffer. Frame each message yourself, for example with a 4-byte length in front. Integers above i64 (a uint64 over 9223372036854775807) wrap around to negative numbers.   Guide: how much smaller is it? MessagePack drops the quotes, colons and commas of JSON, and stores numbers and lengths in as few bytes as it can. For records with short keys and small numbers it usually comes to a half or two thirds of compact JSON. Decode JSON into a Value once, and Marshal writes it as MessagePack. encoding-msgpack-guide-size.salamCopyimport encoding.msgpack import encoding.json import encoding.value import compress  func main throws:     text := `[{"id": 1, "name": "tea", "price": 120, "stock": true},  {"id": 2, "name": "coffee", "price": 90, "stock": true},  {"id": 3, "name": "cocoa", "price": 75, "stock": false}]`     rows := try json.Decode(text)      compact := json.EncodeDefault(rows)     packed := msgpack.Marshal(rows)     println "JSON bytes:       ", compact.Len()     println "MessagePack bytes:", compress.BufLen(packed)      back := try msgpack.Unmarshal(packed)     println "same data:", value.Equal(rows, back) endOutputJSON bytes:        169 MessagePack bytes: 90 same data: true The keys are still written in full in every record, so long key names cost as much as in JSON. If size matters more than that, compress the buffer as well with compress.  Guide: what the bytes look like Each value starts with a type byte. Small integers from 0 to 127 are a single byte, larger ones get a marker such as cc (one byte follows) or ce (four bytes follow). Short strings, arrays and maps carry their length in the first byte: a2 is a string of 2 bytes, 92 an array of 2 items, 81 a map with one pair. encoding-msgpack-guide-bytes.salamCopyimport encoding.msgpack import encoding.value import compress  func hex(v: value.Value): str:     digits := "0123456789abcdef"     mut b := msgpack.Marshal(v)     mut out := ""     repeat compress.BufLen(b) in i:         x := compress.BufGet(b, i)         if i > 0:             out += " "         end         out = out + digits.Substr(x / 16, 1) + digits.Substr(x % 16, 1)     end     compress.BufFree(b)     ret out end  func main:     println "5       ", hex(value.ValueInt(5))     println "-1      ", hex(value.ValueInt(-1))     println "200     ", hex(value.ValueInt(200))     println "70000   ", hex(value.ValueInt(70000))     println "true    ", hex(value.ValueBool(true))     println "null    ", hex(value.ValueNull())     println "1.5     ", hex(value.ValueFloat(1.5))     println "\"hi\"    ", hex(value.ValueString("hi"))      mut arr := value.NewValueArray()     value.ArrayPush(arr, value.ValueInt(1))     value.ArrayPush(arr, value.ValueInt(2))     println "[1, 2]  ", hex(arr)      mut obj := value.NewValueObject()     value.ObjectSet(obj, "a", value.ValueInt(1))     println "{\"a\": 1}", hex(obj) endOutput5        05 -1       ff 200      cc c8 70000    ce 00 01 11 70 true     c3 null     c0 1.5      cb 3f f8 00 00 00 00 00 00 "hi"     a2 68 69 [1, 2]   92 01 02 {"a": 1} 81 a1 61 01 The program reads the buffer byte by byte with compress.BufGet. Turning the buffer into a str first would not work: 70000 contains a zero byte, and a str ends at the first zero. Keep MessagePack data in its ByteBuf, or use BufToBase64 when you need text.  Guide: structs in a cache A cache such as Redis stores bytes, and MessagePack bytes are quicker to read back than JSON. For a struct, go through JSON on the way in and out: json.Marshal and json.Decode give a Value to pack, and json.Unmarshal fills the struct from the unpacked Value. Here a HashMap stands in for the cache. encoding-msgpack-guide-cache.salamCopyimport encoding.msgpack import encoding.json import compress  struct Session:     pub user: str = ""     pub role: str = ""     pub visits: int = 0 end  func save(cache &: HashMap<str, compress.ByteBuf>, key: str, s: Session) throws:     v := try json.Dec

encoding/binary encoding.binary Writing and reading numbers as bytes, big-endian or little-endian. Encoding and data Binary file formats and network protocols store each number as a fixed number of bytes in a fixed order. This package writes and reads such fields: 8, 16, 32 and 64 bit integers, signed or unsigned, and 32 or 64 bit IEEE 754 floats. Big-endian (BE) puts the most significant byte first and is the usual order on the network and in PNG; little-endian (LE) is the other way round and is what x86 and ARM processors use, and formats such as ZIP and WAV. Writers append to a ByteBuf and readers advance a ByteReader, both from compress; that package also has BufPushBytes and RdBytes for raw byte runs such as magic numbers. Use this package when the layout is fixed by a specification or by you. For self-describing data use encoding.msgpack or encoding.protobuf; for hex or Base64 text, encoding. For random access into bytes you already have, such as a file read whole or a memory-mapped binary, use a View: GetU32LE(view, offset) and its relatives read a number at any offset, PutU32LE and its relatives write one, and CStringAt and FixedStringAt read the names that executable formats store. A view checks every access against its length: a getter returns 0 outside it and a setter returns false, so a damaged header cannot read beyond the buffer; call Has first when 0 is a legal value. What trips people up  Every Read... function is throws. When fewer bytes are left than the value needs, it throws a core Error of kind UnexpectedEnd with the code binary.unexpected_end and the reader's position in offset, and the reader does not move. Call it with try inside a decoder that is itself throws, so a truncated file stops with an error instead of decoding zeros. The check costs one comparison per value; a loop of 10 million ReadU32LE calls took about 3 ms with the LLVM backend and about 100 ms with the C backend (gcc or tcc) on a busy 6 core x86-64 machine. 32-bit unsigned values come back in an int, which is signed, so values from 2,147,483,648 up look negative. ReadU32BE and ReadI32BE return the same bits. Widen with (v as i64) & 4294967295. 64-bit unsigned is an i64 too, so values above 9,223,372,036,854,775,807 are negative. Writers do not range check. WriteU8(b, 300) writes 44, the low 8 bits. BinaryOptions is not used by any function yet; the float functions take a big_endian bool instead, and the integer functions carry the order in their names.   Guide: your own file format A binary format usually starts with a few magic bytes that identify it, then a version number and a count, then the records. Write each field with the function for its size and byte order, and read them back in exactly the same order. compress.BufPushBytes writes a fixed text such as the magic, and compress.RdBytes reads it back. encoding-binary-guide-header.salamCopyimport encoding.binary import compress import str  func write_file(scores: Vector<int>): compress.ByteBuf:     mut b := compress.NewByteBuf()     compress.BufPushBytes(b, "SLM1" as void*, 4)     binary.WriteU16LE(b, 2)     binary.WriteU32LE(b, scores.Len())     each s in scores:         binary.WriteI32LE(b, s)     end     ret b end  func read_file(data: compress.ByteBuf, size: int): str throws:     mut r := compress.NewByteReader(data.data, size)     mut head := compress.RdBytes(r, 4)     defer compress.BufFree(head)     if compress.BufToStrUnsafe(head) != "SLM1":         throw Error.At(ErrorKind.Syntax, "not our file", 0)     end     version := try binary.ReadU16LE(r)     if version != 2:         throw Error.At(ErrorKind.Unsupported, "unknown version " + str.FromInt(version), 4)     end     count := try binary.ReadU32LE(r)     if count < 0 or count > 100000:         throw Error.At(ErrorKind.OutOfRange, "implausible count", 6)     end     mut total := 0 as i64     repeat count:         total += (try binary.ReadI32LE(r)) as i64     end     ret str.FromInt(count) + " scores, total " + str.FromInt(total) end  func show(label: str, data: compress.ByteBuf, size: int):     try:         println label, read_file(data, size)     catch e:         println label, e.ToStr()     end end  func main:     mut scores := Vector {} as Vector<int>     scores.Push(120)     scores.Push(-15)     scores.Push(98000)     mut data := write_file(scores)     println "file is", compress.BufLen(data), "bytes"      show("whole file:", data, compress.BufLen(data))     show("first 18:  ", data, 18)     compress.BufSet(data, 4, 9)     show("edited:    ", data, compress.BufLen(data))     compress.BufFree(data) endOutputfile is 22 bytes whole file: 3 scores, total 98105 first 18:   unexpected end of data: needed 4 bytes, 0 left (offset 18) edited:     unknown version 9 (offset 4) read_file checks the magic and the version before trusting the rest, and refuses a count that is too large to be real, so a damaged file cannot make it loop for a long time. It then reads every record with try, so the 18-byte copy, which has room for only two of the three scores, stops at the third with the offset where the data ran out. The checks of its own throw an Error too, so the caller handles every failure in one catch. Changing byte 4 turns the version into 9, which is refused. Keep one byte order for the whole format and write it down in its description.  Guide: read a header of a real format PNG is a good example of a big-endian format. A file starts with an 8 byte signature, then chunks, each with a 4 byte length, a 4 letter type and the data. The first chunk, IHDR, holds the width and height as big-endian 32 bit numbers. The program builds those first bytes itself so it runs without a file; with a real image, read the file into a buffer first and the parsing is the same. encoding-binary-guide-png.salamCopyimport encoding.binary import compress  func fake_png(): compress.ByteBuf

encoding/xml encoding.xml Reading, building and writing XML, with XPath, DTD validation, namespaces and a light simple interface. Encoding and data This package reads, queries, edits and writes XML: feeds, sitemaps, SVG, SOAP replies, office files and old configuration formats. It has three interfaces for three sizes of job.  The document interface is the complete one. Parse reads the text into a Document, and every node has a numeric id you pass to functions such as Name, AttributeValue, Elements and Text. XPath 1.0 queries, namespaces, entities, DTD validation, editing and canonical output all work on it. The simple node interface (Decode, Child, Attr, Encode) keeps the tree in plain XMLNode structs. It suits a small config or API reply you read once, and it is what encoding.serde uses to convert XML to and from a Value. The tokenizer (NewXMLTokenizer, NextToken) hands out start tags, end tags and text one at a time without building a tree.  If you control both ends and only need to move data, encoding.json is simpler. Reach for this package when the other side speaks XML. Untrusted input Parse is safe to run on documents from outside. External entities (<!ENTITY x SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">) are never fetched, so a reference to one fails as undeclared, and entity expansion is capped by max_entity_expansion (256 KB by default) and max_entity_depth (32), which stops the "billion laughs" attack. Element nesting is capped at 1024 levels. Errors Parse, ParseWith, the simple Decode, Evaluate and the Select functions are declared throws: on a broken document or a bad XPath expression they throw an Error and give back nothing half-built. Catch it with try: ... catch e:, or write try before the call in a function that is itself throws. e.message says what is wrong, e.line and e.column point at it (in the expression, for XPath), and e.kind sorts it: Syntax, UnexpectedEnd, NotFound for an undeclared entity, prefix or XPath function, AlreadyExists for an attribute given twice, OutOfRange for the entity and depth limits, InvalidUtf8, TypeMismatch and InvalidArgument. e.code names the common cases exactly, such as xml.unclosed_tag, xml.mismatched_tag or xpath.unknown_function. WellFormed and Valid answer the same question as a plain bool. What trips people up  XPath matches names as written. A name test compares the element's full name, prefix included, with the query. //entry finds Atom entries in a default namespace, and //m:thumbnail works only if the document uses the prefix m. When the prefix may vary, test local-name() and namespace-uri(); the namespaces guide shows how. Every value is text. Text and SelectString return strings; use SelectNumber or convert yourself. Whitespace-only text is dropped by default. Set preserve_whitespace in ParseOptions when indentation matters, for example in mixed content. Free what you take. A Document and each NodeList from Select hold memory until Free and FreeList. The tokenizer does not check the document. It does not match end tags to start tags, it returns the whitespace between elements as text tokens, and it needs the whole text in memory. Run WellFormed first if the input may be broken.   Guide: read a feed with XPath RSS and Atom feeds, sitemaps, SVG and office files are all XML, and XPath is the quickest way to pull values out of them. SelectString and SelectNumber answer a whole query in one call; Select returns the matching nodes, and a query run from one of those nodes is relative to it, so title means the title of that item. encoding-xml-guide-rss.salamCopyimport encoding.xml  func main throws:     feed := `<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?> <rss version="2.0">   <channel>     <title>Salam blog</title>     <item>       <title>Salam 0.5.5 is out</title>       <link>https://example.com/posts/055</link>       <category>release</category>     </item>     <item>       <title>Writing a JSON API</title>       <link>https://example.com/posts/json-api</link>       <category>tutorial</category>     </item>     <item>       <title>The Persian keywords</title>       <link>https://example.com/posts/persian</link>       <category>tutorial</category>     </item>   </channel> </rss>`     mut d := try xml.Parse(feed)     top := xml.DocumentNode(d)     println "feed:", try xml.SelectString(d, top, "/rss/channel/title")     println "posts:", try xml.SelectNumber(d, top, "count(//item)")      mut items := try xml.Select(d, top, "//item[category = 'tutorial']")     each it in items.items:         println "-", try xml.SelectString(d, it, "title"), "<" + try xml.SelectString(d, it, "link") + ">"     end     xml.FreeList(items)     xml.Free(d) endOutputfeed: Salam blog posts: 3 - Writing a JSON API <https://example.com/posts/json-api> - The Persian keywords <https://example.com/posts/persian> The filter [category = 'tutorial'] keeps only the items whose child element has that text. Free the node list with FreeList and the document with Free when you are done.  Guide: namespaces in an Atom feed Atom feeds, SVG, SOAP and office files put their elements in namespaces, often several at once. This feed uses Atom as the default namespace and Media RSS under the prefix m. The program shows how XPath in this package treats names, and the query that works whatever prefix the publisher chose. encoding-xml-guide-namespaces.salamCopyimport encoding.xml  func main throws:     feed := `<feed xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:m="http://search.yahoo.com/mrss/">   <title>Salam videos</title>   <entry>     <title>Install Salam</title>     <m:thumbnail url="https://cdn.example/i

encoding/protobuf encoding.protobuf Reading .proto files, the Protocol Buffers wire encoding, and generating Salam code from them. Encoding and data Protocol Buffers is Google's binary format for structured messages. The shape of the messages is defined in a .proto file, and this package reads it, generates Salam code for the messages and services, and also carries the low level tools for writing and reading fields. In the bytes, every field comes as a tag, the field number and the wire type, followed by its value. Numbers are usually written as a varint: each byte holds 7 bits of the number and its top bit says whether another byte follows.  Use Protocol Buffers when you talk to a service that already speaks it, usually over grpc, or when several languages share one schema. Between Salam programs, or when no .proto file exists, encoding.msgpack needs no schema and encoding.json stays readable. What trips people up  Generated readers do not accept packed repeated numbers. Proto3 writers such as protoc, Go and Java send a repeated int32 as one length-prefixed block by default. The generated Unmarshal reads one tag per element and checks the wire type, so a packed field throws a TypeMismatch error. The generated Marshal writes the unpacked form, which every reader accepts. Decode packed fields by hand as in the packed guide, or mark the field [packed = false] on the other side. The generator skips message, enum and map fields. Members of a oneof become ordinary fields, so nothing stops two of them being set. Write those parts by hand. Varints are u64. ReadVarint returns a u64; cast to i64 or int yourself, and run sint fields through ZigZagDecode64. Every reader throws. A reader that runs out of bytes throws an Error of kind UnexpectedEnd, a varint that does not fit in 64 bits throws OutOfRange, and a tag with field number 0 or wire type 6 or 7 throws Syntax. The error carries the byte offset and a code such as protobuf.truncated. Mark your decoding function throws and call the readers with try, or catch the error in a try: block. ParseFile and the generators throw Syntax with the line and column of the bad token.   The guide below works through the jobs you meet in practice: writing a message by hand, reading one back while skipping fields you do not know, nesting messages, packed repeated numbers, choosing between int64 and sint64, and generating the code from a .proto file instead of writing it. Every byte buffer here is a compress.ByteBuf from compress, so programs import both packages.  Writing a message by hand A message is nothing more than its fields one after another. For each field call WriteTag with the field number from the .proto file and the wire type, then the writer for the value: WriteVarint for integers, enums and booleans, WriteLenPrefixedStr for strings and WriteLenPrefixedBytes for bytes and nested messages. The program below writes User { id: 42, name: "Sara", admin: true } and prints the bytes in hex. encoding-protobuf-encode-user.salamCopyimport encoding.protobuf import compress  func hex(b: compress.ByteBuf): str:     digits := "0123456789abcdef"     mut out := ""     repeat compress.BufLen(b) in i:         v := compress.BufGet(b, i)         if i > 0: out += " " end         out = out + digits.Substr(v / 16, 1) + digits.Substr(v % 16, 1)     end     ret out end  func main:     mut b := compress.NewByteBuf()     protobuf.WriteTag(b, 1, protobuf.WT_VARINT)     protobuf.WriteVarint(b, 42 as u64)     protobuf.WriteTag(b, 2, protobuf.WT_LEN)     protobuf.WriteLenPrefixedStr(b, "Sara")     protobuf.WriteTag(b, 3, protobuf.WT_VARINT)     protobuf.WriteVarint(b, 1 as u64)     println "bytes:", compress.BufLen(b)     println hex(b)     compress.BufFree(b) endOutputbytes: 10 08 2a 12 04 53 61 72 61 18 01 Read the output in pairs: 08 is field 1 with wire type 0, 2a is 42; 12 is field 2 with wire type 2, 04 the length and then the four letters; 18 01 is field 3 set to true. Proto3 leaves out fields that hold their default value (0, an empty string, false), so a sender usually checks the value before it writes the tag.  Reading a message and skipping unknown fields Decoding is a loop: read a tag, look at the field number, read the value with the reader that matches, and repeat until the reader is empty. A field number you do not know must still be stepped over, which is what SkipField does with the wire type. That is how an old program keeps reading messages from a newer one that added fields. Every reader throws when the bytes run out, so the decoding function is marked throws and passes the error on with try: a message that was cut short reaches the caller as one error, never as a half-filled struct. encoding-protobuf-decode-loop.salamCopyimport encoding.protobuf import compress  struct User:     pub id: int = 0     pub name: str = ""     pub admin: bool = false end  func decodeUser(data: void*, n: int): User throws:     mut u := User {}     mut r := compress.NewByteReader(data, n)     until compress.RdLeft(r) > 0:         mut number := 0         mut wire := 0         try protobuf.ReadTag(r, number, wire)         if number == 1:             u.id = try protobuf.ReadVarint(r) as int         else number == 2:             u.name = try protobuf.ReadLenPrefixedStr(r)         else number == 3:             u.admin = try protobuf.ReadVarint(r) != (0 as u64)         else:             println "skipping unknown field", number             try protobuf.SkipField(r, wire)         end     end     ret u end  func main throws:     mut b := compress.NewByteBuf()     protobuf.WriteTag(b, 1, protobuf.WT_VARINT)     protobuf.WriteVarint(b, 42 as u64)     protobuf.WriteTag(b, 9, protobuf.WT_LEN)     protobuf.WriteLenPrefixedStr(b, "added in v2")     protobuf.WriteTag(b, 2, protobuf.WT_LEN)     protobuf.WriteLenPrefixedStr(b, "Sara")     u := try decodeUser(b.data, b.len)     println u.id, u.name, u.admin

compress compress Byte buffers, compression methods from RLE through DEFLATE, gzip, bzip2, zstd and checksums. Encoding and data This package is the base of all binary data work in Salam. ByteBuf, a growable byte buffer, and ByteReader, a cursor over bytes, are what packages such as encoding.binary, archive and encoding.msgpack pass around. On top of them it has gzip, bzip2, raw DEFLATE, a few teaching compressors (RLE, LZ77, LZW, Huffman, BWT), bit-level reading and writing, and the CRC-32 and Adler-32 checksums. To pack several files into one .zip or .tar, use archive, which calls this package for the compression. To write numbers in a fixed byte order, use encoding.binary on the same buffers. For compression, reach for gzip when the data has to be read by other programs. Use bzip2 when the result should be smaller than gzip and a slower pack is fine; it reads and writes standard .bz2 data. The other methods are mostly there to learn from and experiment with, and their output format belongs to this package alone. The examples show that for small data the overhead of Huffman and DEFLATE comes to more than the data itself.  What trips people up  Gzip verifies its checksum. GzipDecompress checks the header, inflates the data, then compares both the CRC-32 and the uncompressed length in the trailer; a mismatch sets ok false and returns an empty buffer. Xz and LZMA writing is a fast match finder, not a tuned one. The packed size is within a few percent of xz at the same level, never smaller. The whole input and the whole result are held in memory, and level 9 asks for a 64 MiB window. The result of a decoder is kept whole in memory too, so use the ...Max functions on data you did not make yourself. Zstandard output is valid, not the smallest. The writer is simple, so ZstdCompressLevel makes frames usually a quarter to a half larger than the zstd tool at the same level; every reader still accepts them. Reading is complete, but only ZstdDecompressDict and ZstdDecompressEx take a dictionary, and the decoder holds the whole result in memory, so use ZstdDecompressMax on data from outside. Bzip2 checks every checksum and can be capped.
