Bzip2Decompress verifies each block CRC and the whole stream CRC and rejects broken tables and indexes, and it accepts several streams one after another and nothing else after them. A tiny file can expand to a huge one, so use Bzip2DecompressMax on data from outside. The method is not stored. Compress output does not say which method made it; keep the method number next to the data. A str stops at the first zero byte. Keep binary data in a ByteBuf; BufToStrUnsafe is for bytes that are really text. Buffers are not freed for you. Call BufFree on buffers you are done with, especially in loops and servers.   The guide below covers the jobs this package is used for day to day: gzipping and bzip2-ing text, laying out your own binary records in a ByteBuf, checking data with CRC-32, and choosing a compression method. Each section has a complete program with its output.  Gzip text for storage or transport GzipCompressStr turns a string into a gzip stream that gzip -d, browsers and every other gzip reader understand, and GzipDecompressBuf turns it back. Gzip output is binary, so when it has to travel inside JSON, a URL or an environment variable, wrap it in Base64 with BufToBase64. On the receiving side encoding.Base64DecodeBytes writes the bytes into a buffer you have made big enough; set the buffer's len to the count it returns. It throws when the text is not Base64 or does not fit, so call it inside try:. compress-guide-gzip.salamCopyimport compress import encoding  func main:     mut log := ""     repeat 20:         log += "GET /api/users 200 12ms\n"     end     packed := compress.GzipCompressStr(log)     println "original:", log.Len(), "bytes"     println "gzipped: ", packed.len, "bytes"     println "ratio:   ", compress.Ratio(packed.len, log.Len())     text := compress.BufToBase64(packed)     println "base64:  ", text.Len(), "characters"     mut ok := false     mut wire := compress.NewByteBufCap(text.Len())     try:         wire.len = encoding.Base64DecodeBytes(text, wire.data, text.Len())         ok = true     catch e:         println "base64:", e.ToStr()     end     println "decoded: ", ok, compress.BufEquals(wire, packed)     back := compress.GzipDecompressBuf(wire, ok)     println "restored:", ok, compress.BufToStrUnsafe(back) == log endOutputoriginal: 480 bytes gzipped:  48 bytes ratio:    0.1 base64:   64 characters decoded:  true true restored: true true A log with the same line twenty times shrinks to a tenth of its size. Base64 costs a third back (64 characters for 48 bytes), which is still far smaller than the original. BufToStrUnsafe copies the bytes into a string, so use it only for data that is really text: a str ends at the first zero byte. Bzip2DecompressBuf reads one or more streams, including old ones with randomised blocks, and checks all CRCs. Encoding and data An archive gathers several files into one. Zip compresses each file on its own; tar only puts the files one after another and is usually gzipped afterwards (.tar.gz). npy npy Reading and writing NumPy .npy and .npz files. Encoding and data .npy files are the standard way NumPy arrays are stored in Python, and .npz keeps several named arrays in one zip archive. With this package you can move data and model weights between Python and Salam. An NpyArray is three things: shape, the size of each dimension; data, every element as an f64 in row-major (C) order; and dtype, the element type the file declared. The guide below goes from the usual case, moving a weight matrix between NumPy and Salam, to checkpoints with several arrays, arrays with more than two dimensions, the file layout itself and what happens with bad files.  Use it at the border with Python: training data prepared with NumPy or pandas, weights from a model trained in PyTorch and exported with NumPy, or results you want to plot in Python. Inside Salam, arrays live in a matrix or a tensor; for model files in other formats see onnx and gguf. For tables that people open in a spreadsheet, CSV with encoding.csv is friendlier. What is supported  ReadWrite  Element typesf8, f4, i1 to i8, u1 to u4, b1, little- or big-endian<f8 only Not readu8 (uint64), f2 (float16), complex, strings and object arrays: an Unsupported error (npy.dtype) Memory orderC order; Fortran order for one or two dimensionsC order .npzboth numpy.savez and numpy.savez_compresseduncompressed, like savez   Every element becomes an f64, so int64 values above 253 (9,007,199,254,740,992) lose their last digits.  Save a matrix for NumPy, and load it back FromMatrix turns a matrix into an NpyArray and WriteNpyFile writes it. In Python, numpy.load("weights.npy") opens the file as a 2 by 3 float64 array. The way back is ReadNpyFile followed by ToMatrix. Both report failure: WriteNpyFile returns false and ReadNpyFile throws, so the program runs it with try. npy-weights.salamCopyimport npy import matrix  func main(): int throws:     mut w := matrix.Zeros(2, 3)     repeat 2 in i:         repeat 3 in j:             w.Set(i, j, (i * 10 + j) as f64 / 4.0)         end     end     mut arr := npy.FromMatrix(w)     if npy.WriteNpyFile(arr, "weights.npy") == false:         println "could not write weights.npy"         ret 1     end     mut back := try npy.ReadNpyFile("weights.npy")     println "shape:", back.shape, "elements:", back.count()     mut m := try npy.ToMatrix(back)     repeat m.rows in i:         println m.at(i, 0), m.at(i, 1), m.at(i, 2)     end     println "same values:", matrix.Sum(m) == matrix.Sum(w)     matrix.Free(m)     matrix.Free(w)     back.Free()     arr.Free()     ret 0 endOutputshape: [2, 3] elements: 6 0 0.25 0.5 2.5 2.75 3 same values: true  Several arrays in one .npz checkpoint A trained model has more than one array: weights, biases, perhaps the mean and spread used to scale the inputs. NpzWrite stores them in one .npz file under the names you give in keys, the same file numpy.savez writes and numpy.load returns as a dictionary. NpzList shows what a file holds and NpzRead takes one array out by name. Below, a tiny linear layer is saved, loaded again and used for a prediction. npy-checkpoint.salamCopyimport npy import matrix  func row(a: f64, b: f64): matrix.Matrix:     mut m := matrix.Zeros(1, 2)     m.Set(0, 0, a)     m.Set(0, 1, b)     ret m end  func load(path: str, key: str): matrix.Matrix throws:     mut arr := try npy.NpzRead(path, key)     defer arr.Free()     ret try npy.ToMatrix(arr) end  func main(): int throws:     mut w := matrix.Zeros(2, 2)     w.Set(0, 0, 0.5)     w.Set(0, 1, -1.0)     w.Set(1, 0, 2.0)     w.Set(1, 1, 0.25)     mut b := row(1.0, 0.0)     mut keys := Vector {} as Vector<str>     keys.Push("W")     keys.Push("b")     mut arrays := Vector {} as Vector<npy.NpyArray>     arrays.Push(npy.FromMatrix(w))     arrays.Push(npy.FromMatrix(b))     println "saved:", npy.NpzWrite("model.npz", keys, arrays)     println "arrays in file:", try npy.NpzList("model.npz")     mut lw := try load("model.npz", "W")     mut lb := try load("model.npz", "b")     mut x := row(3.0, 4.0)     mut xw := matrix.MatMul(x, lw)     mut y := matrix.AddRowVector(xw, lb)     println "prediction:", y.at(0, 0), y.at(0, 1)     try:         load("model.npz", "gamma")     catch e:         println "gamma:", e.ToStr()     end     repeat arrays.Len() in i:         mut a := arrays.Get(i)         a.Free()     end     matrix.Free(w)     matrix.Free(b)     matrix.Free(lw)     matrix.Free(lb)     matrix.Free(x)     matrix.Free(xw)     matrix.Free(y)     ret 0 endOutputsaved: true arrays in file: ["W", "b"] prediction: 10.5 -2 gamma: npy: no array named 'gamma' at model.npz Asking for a name that is not in the file (gamma here) throws a NotFound error with the code npy.missing_key, so a loader can catch it and fall back to a default instead of crashing on an older checkpoint.  Arrays with more than two dimensions A .npy file can hold any number of dimensions, such as a batch of images as (count, height, width). The package reads and writes them all, but ToMatrix only accepts one or two dimensions (a 1-D array becomes a single row) and throws an InvalidArgument error otherwise. For higher dimensions index data yourself: the element at [i][j][k] of shape (A, B, C) is at (i * B + j) * C + k. npy-shapes.salamCopyimport npy import matrix  func at3(a: npy.NpyArray, i: int, j: int, k: int): f64:     rows := a.shape.Get(1)     cols := a.shape.Get(2)     ret a.data.Get((i * rows + j) * cols + k) end  func main(): int throws:     mut cube := npy.NpyArray {}     cube.shape.Push(2)     cube.shape.Push(3)     cube.shape.Push(4)     repeat 24 in n: cube.data.Push(n as f64) end     println "ndim:", cube.ndim(), "count:", cube.count()     println "cube[1][2][3] =", at3(cube, 1, 2, 3)     try:

excel excel Reading and writing Excel (xlsx), OpenDocument (ods) and CSV spreadsheets: sheets, cells, styles, formulas and dates. Encoding and data A workbook holds several sheets, and each sheet holds cells by row and column, from zero. Turn Excel references such as C5 into a row and column with CellRef and ParseCellRef. Open and Save work the format out from the file extension. Formulas are stored and read with their last calculated result, but Salam does not evaluate a formula itself. Use it when people hand you spreadsheets or expect one back: an upload form for price lists, a monthly report for the finance team, an export button. When the data is only ever read by programs, a CSV file with encoding.csv is simpler; for analysis on columns of numbers, load the rows into a table with data. What trips people up  Old .xls files are read. BIFF8 workbooks (Excel 97 to 2003), including OLE2 streams stored in the mini stream, are decoded into sheets, strings, numbers, booleans, dates, errors, merged cells and cached formula values. Save still writes xlsx, ods or csv only. The extension decides the format. DetectFormat, Open and Save look only at the file name, so an xlsx saved as report.dat will not open. Rename uploads, or check the first bytes (PK for xlsx and ods) yourself. Formulas are not evaluated. A formula cell carries the result stored with it; when you write one, compute and pass the result yourself. Rows and columns count from zero, while Excel shows 1 and A. ParseCellRef and CellRef convert. SheetToJSON gives strings only: an array of rows, each an array of the cells' text. Read Cell.kind when you need the numbers.   The guide below covers the jobs that come up in real programs: reading a sheet someone else filled in, building a formatted report, working with dates, turning a workbook into CSV files, and finding values by reference or by content.  Reading rows from a sheet someone else filled in A spreadsheet that people edit by hand is never quite regular: columns move, rows are left empty, a number cell holds a word. Find each column by its header text instead of trusting its position, skip rows with no key, and look at Cell.kind before you treat a value as a number. get_string always gives text, whatever the cell holds, so it is safe for messages. Open reports a file it cannot read through ok and err. excel-read-rows.salamCopyimport excel  func header_col(sheet: excel.Sheet*, name: str): int:     repeat sheet.col_count() in c:         if sheet.get_string(0, c) == name: ret c end     end     ret -1 end  func make_file():     mut book := excel.NewWorkbook()     s := book.add_sheet("grades")     each c, title in ["Name", "City", "Score"]: s.set_string(0, c, title) end     s.set_string(1, 0, "Ali")     s.set_string(1, 1, "Tehran")     s.set_number(1, 2, 17.5)     s.set_string(2, 0, "Sara")     s.set_string(2, 1, "Shiraz")     s.set_number(2, 2, 19)     s.set_string(4, 0, "Reza")     s.set_string(4, 2, "absent")     book.save("grades.xlsx")     book.Free() end  func main:     make_file()     mut ok := false     mut err := ""     mut book := excel.Open("grades.xlsx", ok, err)     if ok == false:         println "cannot open:", err         ret 1     end     sheet := book.sheet_at(0)     name_col := header_col(sheet, "Name")     score_col := header_col(sheet, "Score")     mut total := 0.0     mut counted := 0     repeat sheet.row_count() - 1 in i:         r := i + 1         if sheet.has_cell(r, name_col) == false: continue end         cell := sheet.get_cell(r, score_col)         if cell.kind != excel.CellNumber:             println sheet.get_string(r, name_col), "skipped:", sheet.get_string(r, score_col)             continue         end         println sheet.get_string(r, name_col), cell.num         total += cell.num         counted++     end     println "average of", counted, "=", total / (counted as f64)     book.Free()     ret 0 endOutputAli 17.5 Sara 19 Reza skipped: absent average of 2 = 18.25 Rows count from zero, so the header is row 0 and data starts at row 1. row_count is one past the last row that has a cell, which is why the empty row 3 still appears in the loop and is skipped by has_cell.  Building a formatted report A Style describes bold text, font size, background colour, alignment and number format. Register each style once with book.styles.get_or_add, which returns an id, and give that id to set_style for as many cells as you like. merge_cells joins a range for a title, and set_formula stores a formula together with the value you computed, because Salam writes formulas but does not evaluate them. excel-report.salamCopyimport excel  func main:     mut book := excel.NewWorkbook()     mut sheet := book.add_sheet("March")     title := book.styles.GetOrAdd(excel.Style { bold = true, font_size = 14, align_h = excel.AlignCenter })     head := book.styles.GetOrAdd(excel.Style { bold = true, bg_color = "DDEBF7" })     money := book.styles.GetOrAdd(excel.Style { num_format = "#,##0.00" })     sheet.set_string(0, 0, "Sales, March 2026")     sheet.merge_cells(0, 0, 0, 3)     sheet.set_style(0, 0, title)     each col, name in ["Item", "Qty", "Price", "Total"]:         sheet.set_string(1, col, name)         sheet.set_style(1, col, head)     end     items := ["Tea", "Sugar", "Rice"]     qty := [12, 30, 5]     price := [4.5, 1.25, 9.8]     mut sum := 0.0     repeat 3 in i:         r := i + 2         line := (qty[i] as f64) * price[i]         sheet.set_string(r, 0, items[i])         sheet.set_int(r, 1, qty[i] as i64)         sheet.set_number(r, 2, price[i])         sheet.set_formula(r, 3, excel.CellRef(r, 1) + "*" + excel.CellRef(r, 2), line)         sheet.set_style(r, 3, money)

data data Reading data for machine learning: CSV tables, batching samples, MNIST and images, and synthetic data. Encoding and data This package readies data for training a model. LoadCsv reads a CSV file into a Table, decides for each column whether it holds integers, floats, categories or free text, and turns categories into numbers by itself; split_xy then divides the table into a feature matrix and a label. MatrixDataset hands the rows out in shuffled mini-batches, LoadMnist, LoadIdx and LoadImageFolder read image sets, and the Make... functions build synthetic data from a fixed seed, for trying algorithms out without a file. Everything comes out as a matrix or a tensor, ready for ml and nn. To read a CSV file cell by cell as text, use encoding.csv; for spreadsheets, excel; for arrays saved by NumPy, npy. What trips people up  Category codes depend on the file. Codes are given in order of first appearance, so red may be 0 in the training file and 2 in the test file, and a column with 25 distinct values may be a category in one file and text in another. Load all rows from one file and split them, as the test-set guide does, or map new files through the training table's cat_levels. One bad cell changes a column's kind. A single 12,5 or n/a in a number column turns the whole column into categories or text. Check kinds after loading. Empty cells are NaN in number columns but their own category, the empty string, in category columns. Only commas. The separator is always ,; convert semicolon or tab files first, for example with encoding.csv.  The guide below follows the order of a small machine learning project: load a CSV file and see how its columns were read, split it into features and a label and fit a first model, train in mini-batches, hold back a test set, and read the MNIST file format.  How LoadCsv reads each column LoadCsv looks at every value of a column and picks its kind on its own. All whole numbers give COL_INT, all numbers COL_FLOAT. Text with a limited number of different values (at most 20, or a tenth of the rows when that is more, and fewer than the rows) becomes COL_CAT: each value gets a code from 0 in order of first appearance and cat_levels gives the names back. Text where every row is different, such as a free comment, stays COL_STR. An empty cell in a number column is stored as NaN, which math.IsNaN detects; in a category column it becomes a level of its own. data-columns.salamCopyimport data import matrix import math  func kind_name(k: int): str:     if k == data.COL_INT: ret "int" end     if k == data.COL_FLOAT: ret "float" end     if k == data.COL_CAT: ret "category" end     ret "text" end  func main(): int throws:     text := "id,city,age,income,comment
1,Tehran,34,2.5,fast delivery
2,Shiraz,,3.1,ok
3,Tehran,51,4.0,late
4,Tabriz,28,1.9,good price
"     mut t := try data.LoadCsv(text, true)     each j, name in t.names:         println name, "->", kind_name(t.kinds.Get(j))     end     levels := t.CatLevels("city")     println "city levels:", levels     city := t.ColIndex("city")     age := t.ColIndex("age")     repeat t.rows() in i:         code := t.cells.at(i, city) as int         mut shown := "missing"         if math.IsNaN(t.cells.at(i, age)) == false: shown = "known" end         println "row", i, "city code", code, "=", levels.Get(code), "age", shown     end     mut m := t.ToMatrix()     println "to_matrix keeps", m.cols, "of", t.cols(), "columns"     mut onehot := matrix.Zeros(t.rows(), levels.Len())     repeat t.rows() in i: onehot.Set(i, t.cells.at(i, city) as int, 1.0) end     println "one-hot row 3:", onehot.at(3, 0), onehot.at(3, 1), onehot.at(3, 2)     matrix.Free(onehot)     matrix.Free(m)     t.Free()     ret 0 endOutputid -> int city -> category age -> int income -> float comment -> text city levels: ["Tehran", "Shiraz", "Tabriz"] row 0 city code 0 = Tehran age known row 1 city code 1 = Shiraz age missing row 2 city code 0 = Tehran age known row 3 city code 2 = Tabriz age known to_matrix keeps 4 of 5 columns one-hot row 3: 0 0 1 to_matrix and split_xy leave COL_STR columns out, which is why five columns become four. A category is stored as its code, which suits decision trees; for a linear model or a neural network build one-hot columns from the code, as the last lines do.  From a CSV file to a first model split_xy takes the name of the label column and fills two matrices: every other usable column as features, and the label as a one column matrix. It returns false when the label is missing or is plain text. That is exactly the shape matrix functions expect, so a least squares fit with matrix.LinearRegression is one more line. net/tcp net.tcp TCP servers and clients: listening, connecting, reading and writing, TLS and a connection pool. Network TCP is the base of most internet protocols: a reliable, ordered stream of bytes between two programs. A server listens on a port with Bind and takes each new client with Accept; a client connects with Dial. Accept and Read wait until something arrives, so a server that talks to several clients hands each connection to a thread, as the worker guide shows. Every example runs on 127.0.0.1 and needs no network. Use this package for your own protocols and for talking to servers that have no client in the standard library. For HTTP use net.http; for messages that must not be split or ordered, net.udp; for live two-way traffic with browsers, net.websocket. tls adds encryption on top of a connection from here. What trips people up  An empty Read means three things. The peer closed the connection, the read deadline passed, or an error happened; all return "". A message that starts with a zero byte also comes back empty, and text after a zero byte is lost, so use ReadBytes for binary data. Write may send only part of the text. It makes one system call and returns how many bytes went out. For large data, compare the result with the length, or use WriteBytes, which loops until everything is sent. Messages are not kept apart. TCP is a byte stream; frame your messages with a delimiter or a length, as the framing guide does. Bind listens on every IPv4 interface, not only on 127.0.0.1, so a test server is reachable from the network unless a firewall stops it. IPv6 clients reach it only through BindDual or BindOn("::", port), which accept IPv4 and IPv6 on one socket. Dial accepts IPv6 literals ("::1" or "[::1]") and tries every address a name resolves to. Nothing stops the program on failure. Bind, Accept and Dial return a value with fd -1; check Ok or ConnOk.  A request and reply protocol Most small protocols take turns: the client sends one request, the server sends one reply, and so on until the client hangs up. The server below reads in a loop and stops when Read returns an empty string, which is how TCP tells you the other side closed the connection. The client waits for each reply before it sends the next request, so every Read sees exactly one message. net-tcp-guide-commands.salamCopyimport net.tcp import str  mut server := tcp.Server {}  func reply(line: str): str:     words := line.Split(" ")     command := words.Get(0)     if command == "ADD" and words.Len() == 3:         ret str.FromInt(words.Get(1).ToInt() + words.Get(2).ToInt())     end     if command == "LEN" and words.Len() == 2:         ret str.FromInt(words.Get(1).CharCount())     end     ret "ERR unknown command: " + command end  func serve():     conn := tcp.Accept(server)     tcp.SetReadDeadline(conn, 2000)     mut served := 0     until true:         request := tcp.Read(conn, 1024)         if request == "":             break         end         _ := tcp.Write(conn, reply(request))         served++     end     tcp.Close(conn)     println "server: answered", served, "requests" end  func main:     server = tcp.Bind(0)     t := spawn(serve)     conn := tcp.Dial("127.0.0.1", tcp.Port(server))     tcp.SetReadDeadline(conn, 2000)     each request in ["ADD 2 40", "LEN salam", "PING"]:         _ := tcp.Write(conn, request)         println request, "->", tcp.Read(conn, 1024)     end     tcp.Close(conn)     join(t)     tcp.CloseServer(server) endOutputADD 2 40 -> 42 LEN salam -> 5 PING -> ERR unknown command: PING server: answered 3 requests The server runs in its own thread with spawn and the main program waits for it with join. A real server would call Accept in a loop and hand each connection to a worker; while one client is served, the others wait in the queue of the listening socket.  Serving several clients with worker threads A server that reads from one client at a time stalls everyone behind a slow client. The usual shape is one thread that only accepts, a chan that carries the new connections, and a few worker threads that serve them. A thread receives the connection as its socket number, conn.fd, and turns it back into a Conn with ConnFromFd. net-tcp-guide-workers.salamCopyimport net.tcp import chan import str  mut server := tcp.Server {} mut jobs := chan.Chan {} as chan.Chan<i64>  func acceptor():     repeat 3:         conn := tcp.Accept(server)         if tcp.ConnOk(conn): _ := jobs.send(conn.fd) end     end     jobs.Close() end  func worker():     mut ok := true     until true:         fd := jobs.recv(ok)         if not ok: break end         conn := tcp.ConnFromFd(fd)         tcp.SetReadDeadline(conn, 2000)         request := tcp.Read(conn, 1024)         _ := tcp.Write(conn, "HELLO " + str.Upper(request))         tcp.Close(conn)     end end  func main:     server = tcp.Bind(0)     jobs.init(8 as i64)     a := spawn(acceptor)     w1 := spawn(worker)     w2 := spawn(worker)      names := ["sara", "reza", "mina"]     mut conns := Vector {} as Vector<tcp.Conn>     repeat names.Len():         c := tcp.Dial("127.0.0.1", tcp.Port(server))         tcp.SetReadDeadline(c, 2000)         conns.Push(c)     end     each i, c in conns:         _ := tcp.Write(c, names[i])     end     each i, c in conns:         println names[i], "->", tcp.Read(c, 1024)         tcp.Close(c)     end     join(a)     join(w1)     join(w2)     tcp.CloseServer(server) endOutputsara -> HELLO SARA reza -> HELLO REZA mina -> HELLO MINA The three clients connect before any of them sends a word, and only two workers exist, so the third connection waits in the channel until a worker is free; it is still answered. Closing the channel after the last Accept makes recv report ok false, which ends the worker loops so join returns. In a long-running se

net/udp net.udp Sending and receiving UDP packets, with broadcast and multicast. Network UDP sends separate packets, with no connection and no guarantee that they arrive or arrive in order; in exchange it is fast and simple. It is what DNS, games, live streaming and discovering devices on a local network use. Up to about 1500 bytes per packet is safe. A UDP socket is not tied to one peer. The same socket can send to many addresses and receive from anyone, and every Packet carries from_host and from_port so you know where to answer. Each Send is one packet and each Receive returns one whole packet, so unlike TCP there is no need to find where a message ends. Choose UDP when a late answer is worth nothing (game state, sensor readings, voice) or when one small question gets one small answer. When every byte must arrive, in order, use net.tcp. To look up names, net.dns already speaks the DNS protocol over UDP for you. What trips people up  A timeout looks like an empty packet. Receive returns empty data both when the timeout passed and when a peer really sent zero bytes, so never use empty packets as messages. Too small a buffer cuts the packet. The rest of a packet larger than max is thrown away, not kept for the next call. Pass the largest size your protocol allows (0 means 65536 for Receive). Text stops at a zero byte. Receive gives a str; binary packets need ReceiveBytes. Pick the family that fits. Open and Bind are IPv4. For IPv6 use BindOn("::1", port), BindDual (both families on one socket) and OpenAny (a client socket that can send to both). Senders are reported as text, IPv4-mapped addresses as plain IPv4. Multicast groups are IPv4. Nothing is guaranteed. Packets can be lost, repeated or reordered; the retry guide shows the usual answer.   Answering a request A UDP server binds a port and answers each packet to the address it came from. The client uses Open, which picks a free port for it, sends a packet and waits for the reply on the same socket. Set a timeout on both sides, because a lost packet would otherwise leave Receive waiting forever. net-udp-guide-ping.salamCopyimport net.udp import str  mut server := udp.Socket {}  func pong():     udp.SetTimeout(server, 2000)     mut answered := 0     until answered < 3:         p := udp.Receive(server, 1500)         if p.data == "":             break         end         answered++         _ := udp.Send(server, p.from_host, p.from_port, "pong " + str.FromInt(answered) + " for " + p.data)     end end  func main:     server = udp.BindOn("127.0.0.1", 0)     t := spawn(pong)     client := udp.Open()     udp.SetTimeout(client, 2000)     each name in ["alpha", "beta", "gamma"]:         _ := udp.Send(client, "127.0.0.1", udp.Port(server), name)         reply := udp.Receive(client, 1500)         println reply.data     end     join(t)     udp.Close(client)     udp.Close(server) endOutputpong 1 for alpha pong 2 for beta pong 3 for gamma Binding to 127.0.0.1 with BindOn keeps the server private to this machine. Bind listens on every address, which is what a service on the network needs.  Timeouts and retries UDP never tells you that a packet was lost, so a client that expects an answer has to wait a short time and send again. With SetTimeout, Receive returns a packet with empty data when nothing arrived in time. The server in this example ignores the first two requests, the way a busy network might drop them, and the client tries until it gets an answer or runs out of attempts. net-udp-guide-retry.salamCopyimport net.udp  mut server := udp.Socket {}  func flaky():     udp.SetTimeout(server, 3000)     mut seen := 0     until seen < 3:         p := udp.Receive(server, 1500)         if p.data == "":             break         end         seen++         if seen == 3:             _ := udp.Send(server, p.from_host, p.from_port, "got " + p.data)         end     end end  func ask(sock: udp.Socket, port: int, question: str, tries: int): str:     repeat tries in i:         _ := udp.Send(sock, "127.0.0.1", port, question)         reply := udp.Receive(sock, 1500)         if reply.data != "":             ret reply.data         end         println "attempt", i + 1, "timed out"     end     ret "" end  func main:     server = udp.BindOn("127.0.0.1", 0)     t := spawn(flaky)     client := udp.Open()     udp.SetTimeout(client, 200)     answer := ask(client, udp.Port(server), "status?", 5)     if answer == "":         println "server unreachable"     else:         println "answer:", answer     end     join(t)     udp.Close(client)     udp.Close(server) endOutputattempt 1 timed out attempt 2 timed out answer: got status? Because a request can arrive twice (the first copy was only slow, not lost), a request that changes something should carry an id, so the server can recognise a repeat and answer it without doing the work again. DNS works exactly like this.  Binary packets Compact protocols put numbers in bytes instead of text. SendBytes sends a block of memory as one packet and ReceiveBytes fills a buffer and reports the sender through its last two arguments. The packet here has one byte for the kind of message, one for a sensor number and two for a value, high byte first, which is the usual network order. net-udp-guide-binary.salamCopyimport net.udp import mem  func main:     receiver := udp.BindOn("127.0.0.1", 0)     sender := udp.Open()     udp.SetTimeout(receiver, 2000)      out := mem.AllocateZeroed(8 as u64)     o := out as u8*     o[0] = 1 as u8     o[1] = 42 as u8     o[2] = 1 as u8     o[3] = 44 as u8     sent := udp.SendBytes(sender, "127.0.0.1", udp.Port(receiver), out, 4)     println "sent", sent, "bytes"      buf := mem.AllocateZeroed(1500 as u64)     mut host := ""     mut port := 0     n := udp.ReceiveB

net/dns net.dns Finding the address of a name and asking for any kind of DNS record. Network DNS turns names such as salamlang.ir into IP addresses. Lookup is the simplest way and does what a browser does. The Lookup... functions ask the DNS server for one particular kind of record and are what you want for building network tools or checking the configuration of a domain. A lookup can fail for ordinary reasons: the name does not exist, the network is down or the server is slow. None of the functions stop the program. Lookup and LookupCNAME return an empty string, and the others return an empty list, so check the result before using it. Two different resolvers  Lookup asks the operating system, exactly as connecting by name does: the hosts file, localhost, search domains and the system cache all apply. It returns one IPv4 address. The Lookup... record functions send their own queries over UDP to the servers from DefaultServers: the nameserver lines of /etc/resolv.conf on Linux, macOS and BSD. The hosts file is not used. When there is no such file, which is always the case on Windows, they fall back to the public resolvers 8.8.8.8 and 1.1.1.1, so the names you look up leave your network. Each server gets 3 seconds before the next one is tried.  What trips people up  Large answers can be incomplete. An answer that does not fit in one UDP packet comes back with tc set and is not retried over TCP, so very long TXT records or long lists of addresses may be cut short. QueryServer does not check the answer's id against the question's. On an untrusted network compare Message.id yourself, or prefer a resolver you trust. Everything is plain text on port 53. There is no DNSSEC validation and no DNS over TLS or HTTPS. LookupPTR takes IPv4 addresses only.   Resolve a name, then connect net.tcp and net.udp take a host name or an address, but resolving the name yourself first lets you report a clear error before you try to connect. Lookup uses the operating system resolver, so localhost and the names in the hosts file work too, offline. net-dns-guide-connect.salamCopyimport net.dns import net.tcp  mut server := tcp.Server {}  func greet():     conn := tcp.Accept(server)     _ := tcp.Write(conn, "hello, you found me")     tcp.Close(conn) end  func connect(host: str, port: int): tcp.Conn:     address := dns.Lookup(host)     if address == "":         println "cannot resolve", host         ret tcp.Conn {}     end     println host, "is", address     ret tcp.Dial(address, port) end  func main:     server = tcp.Bind(0)     t := spawn(greet)     conn := connect("localhost", tcp.Port(server))     if tcp.ConnOk(conn):         tcp.SetReadDeadline(conn, 2000)         println tcp.Read(conn, 1024)         tcp.Close(conn)     end     join(t)     tcp.CloseServer(server)     bad := connect("no-such-host.invalid", 80)     println "connected:", tcp.ConnOk(bad) endOutputlocalhost is 127.0.0.1 hello, you found me cannot resolve no-such-host.invalid connected: false The .invalid top level domain is reserved and never exists, which makes it handy for testing the failure path.  Checking the mail setup of a domain Mail for a domain goes to the servers in its MX records, lowest priority number first; the others are fallbacks. The domain's TXT records hold the SPF policy, which says which servers may send mail for it, and the DMARC policy lives in the TXT record of _dmarc. plus the domain. This program needs the internet, so it is only compiled here. Against the real DNS it printed: net-dns-guide-mail.salamCopyimport net.dns  func main:     domain := "gmail.com"     mx := dns.LookupMX(domain)     if mx.items.Len() == 0:         println domain, "has no MX records, mail goes to its A record"     end     mut best := dns.Record {}     each r in mx.items:         println "MX", r.priority, r.data         if best.data == "" or r.priority < best.priority:             best = r         end     end     println "deliver to:", best.data, "first"     each text in dns.LookupTXT(domain):         if text.StartsWith("v=spf1"):             println "SPF:", text         end     end     each text in dns.LookupTXT("_dmarc." + domain):         if text.StartsWith("v=DMARC1"):             println "DMARC:", text         end     end end MX 10 alt1.gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com MX 20 alt2.gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com MX 40 alt4.gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com MX 30 alt3.gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com MX 5 gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com deliver to: gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com first SPF: v=spf1 redirect=_spf.google.com DMARC: v=DMARC1; p=none; sp=quarantine; rua=mailto:mailauth-reports@google.com The records come back in whatever order the server chose, so sort or pick by priority yourself, as the loop does.  Asking one server directly QueryServer skips the system resolver and asks the server you name, which is how you compare what different resolvers say or test your own DNS server. It returns the whole Message: rcode 3 means the name does not exist, and an empty message (no qr flag, id 0) means no answer came back within the timeout. Each record has a ttl, the number of seconds a cache may keep it. A name that is an alias answers with a CNAME record before the address, which is why the loop looks at rtype. This one needs the internet too. net-dns-guide-servers.salamCopyimport net.dns  func show(server: str, name: str):     m := dns.QueryServer(server, name, dns.TypeA, 2000)     if m.id == 0 and not m.qr:         println server, "did not answer"         ret     end     if m.rcode == 3:         println server, "says", name, "does not exist"         ret     end     each r in m.answers.items:         if r.rtype == dns.TypeA:             println server, name, "->", r.data, "for", r.ttl, "s"         else:             println server, name, &q

net/mime net.mime The media type of a file, the Content-Type header, and multipart form bodies. Network A media type (MIME) tells the browser and other programs what the content is, such as image/png. This package finds the type from a file extension and reads the Content-Type header. Forms that upload a file send a multipart/form-data body: several parts with a boundary between them. ParseMultipart reads one and MultipartWriter builds one. The package also has StatusText, the standard reason phrase of an HTTP status code. It is used by net.http, which is where you will usually meet these functions. What trips people up  The type table is short. MimeExt knows about 25 extensions: html htm css js mjs json map png jpg jpeg gif svg ico webp txt md pdf xml wasm zip mp4 webm mp3 wav woff woff2. Everything else, csv, avif, ttf and docx included, becomes application/octet-stream, so handle the extra types your site serves before calling it. Lookups and comparisons are case sensitive. MimeType does not lower the extension, ParseContentType keeps the case of the media type and the parameter names, and ParamGet matches the name exactly, so Charset=UTF-8 is not found by "charset". Lower both sides before comparing. Only three types get a charset: text/html, text/plain and text/markdown come with charset=utf-8; CSS and JavaScript do not. Binary uploads need the bytes. ParseMultipart works on raw memory and keeps each body in a ByteBuf, but if the request body has passed through a str on the way, it is already cut at the first zero byte.   The guide below shows the places a web program meets media types: serving files with the right Content-Type, deciding how to read a request body, and handling file uploads on both sides.  The right Content-Type for a file A browser decides what to do with a response from its Content-Type, not from the file name, so a stylesheet served as application/octet-stream is ignored. MimeType maps a file name to its type by extension, with charset=utf-8 added to HTML, plain text and Markdown, and falls back to application/octet-stream for names it does not know. MimeExt does the same for a bare extension without the dot, such as png, when you have no file name. net-mime-guide-static.salamCopyimport net.mime  func header_for(path: str): str:     ret "Content-Type: " + mime.MimeType(path.Lower()) end  func main:     files := ["index.html", "app.js", "style.css", "logo.svg", "photo.JPG", "fonts/vazir.woff2", "report.pdf", "data.bin", "README"]     each f in files:         println f, "->", header_for(f)     end     println mime.MimeType("photo.JPG"), "(without lower)" endOutputindex.html -> Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8 app.js -> Content-Type: application/javascript style.css -> Content-Type: text/css logo.svg -> Content-Type: image/svg+xml photo.JPG -> Content-Type: image/jpeg fonts/vazir.woff2 -> Content-Type: font/woff2 report.pdf -> Content-Type: application/pdf data.bin -> Content-Type: application/octet-stream README -> Content-Type: application/octet-stream application/octet-stream (without lower) The lookup is case sensitive: photo.JPG is only recognised after lower(). Files from cameras and Windows often have upper case extensions, so lower the name before the lookup, as header_for does.  Reading the Content-Type of a request A server has to look at the Content-Type header before it reads the body: JSON, a URL encoded form and a multipart upload are all read differently. ParseContentType splits the header into media_type and its parameters, and ParamGet returns one parameter, such as charset or boundary, with any quotes removed, or an empty string when it is absent. net-mime-guide-content-type.salamCopyimport net.mime  func describe(header: str): str:     ct := mime.ParseContentType(header)     media := ct.media_type.Lower()     mut charset := mime.ParamGet(ct, "charset")     if charset.Len() == 0: charset = "none" end     if media == "application/json":         ret "JSON body, charset " + charset     else media == "application/x-www-form-urlencoded":         ret "URL encoded form"     else media == "multipart/form-data":         ret "upload, boundary " + mime.ParamGet(ct, "boundary")     else media.Find("text/") == 0:         ret "plain text, charset " + charset     end     ret "unknown: [" + media + "]" end  func main:     println describe("application/json")     println describe("application/json; charset=utf-8")     println describe("application/x-www-form-urlencoded")     println describe("multipart/form-data; boundary=\"abc123\"")     println describe("text/csv;charset=windows-1256")     println describe("Application/JSON")     println describe("") endOutputJSON body, charset none JSON body, charset utf-8 URL encoded form upload, boundary abc123 plain text, charset windows-1256 JSON body, charset none unknown: [] Media types are case insensitive by the standard, but media_type keeps the case it was sent in. Compare ct.media_type.lower(), otherwise a client that sends Application/JSON falls through to the unknown branch.  Building and reading a file upload An HTML form with a file field sends multipart/form-data: each field becomes a part with its own headers, separated by a boundary string. NewMultipartWriter starts one, WriteField adds a text field, WriteFileStr and WriteFileBytes add a file, and CloseWriter returns the finished body. ContentTypeHeader gives the matching header with the boundary in it. On the receiving side, ParseMultipart takes the body and the boundary and returns the parts; a part with a non-empty filename is a file. net-mime-guide-upload.salamCopyimport net.mime import c

net/router net.router Routing HTTP requests, with parameters, groups and static files. Network The router maps a method and a path to a handler function. It is the routing layer of the net.http server: you register routes on a Router, hand it to the server with http.Use, and for every request the server calls Dispatch, copies the path parameters into the request context and calls the handler with that context id. Handlers read parameters with http.Param. Shared work such as access logs, CORS and security headers comes from net.http.middleware, which a handler calls first. A pattern is matched segment by segment:  a literal segment such as /notes must match exactly, byte for byte (so method names and paths are case sensitive); a segment that starts with : is a parameter: /books/:id matches /books/42 with id set to 42; a * matches everything after it, slashes included, without making a parameter.  Most examples below call Dispatch directly instead of starting a server. It is the same lookup the server does, and it makes the rules easy to see and to test. Dispatch returns a Match with matched, the handler fn and the parameters; free it with FreeMatch. Things that catch people out:  Register every route before http.Use. The server keeps its own copy of the router, so a route added afterwards is never seen and answers 404. Trailing slashes only match parameter and wildcard routes. /users/:name also accepts /users/sara/, but the literal route /notes does not accept /notes/. Parameters are not URL-decoded. /tags/open%20source gives open%20source; pass it through http.UrlDecode. The query string is already split off and is read with http.Query. There is no automatic 405 and only one static folder per router; both are covered below.   Routes for a REST resource A resource such as notes usually gets five routes: list and create on the collection, read, replace and delete on one item. Register each method with its own function (Get, Post, Put, Delete, and Patch for partial updates) and read the item id with ParamGet. A path that matches no pattern, or a method with no route, gives matched false, which the server answers with 404. net-router-guide-rest.salamCopyimport net.http import net.router  func list_notes(ctx: i64): http.Text(ctx, "all notes") end func create_note(ctx: i64): http.Text(ctx, "created") end func show_note(ctx: i64): http.Text(ctx, "one note") end func update_note(ctx: i64): http.Text(ctx, "updated") end func delete_note(ctx: i64): http.Text(ctx, "deleted") end  func handler_name(fn: i64): str:     if fn == list_notes: ret "list_notes" end     if fn == create_note: ret "create_note" end     if fn == show_note: ret "show_note" end     if fn == update_note: ret "update_note" end     if fn == delete_note: ret "delete_note" end     ret "?" end  func try_request(r: router.Router, method: str, path: str):     mut m := router.Dispatch(r, method, path)     if m.matched:         id := router.ParamGet(m, "id")         if id.Len() > 0:             println method, path, "->", handler_name(m.fn), "with id", id         else:             println method, path, "->", handler_name(m.fn)         end     else:         println method, path, "-> 404"     end     router.FreeMatch(m) end  func main:     mut r := router.NewRouter()     router.Get(r, "/notes", list_notes)     router.Post(r, "/notes", create_note)     router.Get(r, "/notes/:id", show_note)     router.Put(r, "/notes/:id", update_note)     router.Delete(r, "/notes/:id", delete_note)      try_request(r, "GET", "/notes")     try_request(r, "POST", "/notes")     try_request(r, "GET", "/notes/17")     try_request(r, "PUT", "/notes/17")     try_request(r, "DELETE", "/notes/17")     try_request(r, "DELETE", "/notes")     try_request(r, "GET", "/notes/17/comments") endOutputGET /notes -> list_notes POST /notes -> create_note GET /notes/17 -> show_note with id 17 PUT /notes/17 -> update_note with id 17 DELETE /notes/17 -> delete_note with id 17 DELETE /notes -> 404 GET /notes/17/comments -> 404 A parameter matches exactly one path segment: /notes/17/comments does not reach /notes/:id. Give nested resources their own pattern, such as /notes/:id/comments.  Which route wins When several patterns fit one path, a literal segment beats a parameter and a parameter beats *, so /users/me reaches its own handler even though /users/:name was registered first. Between two wildcard routes the one registered first wins, so register a catch-all /* last, after more specific ones like /assets/*. The output shows three more rules: /users/sara/ with a trailing slash still reaches the parameter route, /users/me/ misses the literal route and lands on /users/:name with name set to me, and a HEAD request falls back to the GET route. net-router-guide-order.salamCopyimport net.http import net.router  func me(ctx: i64): http.Text(ctx, "me") end func user(ctx: i64): http.Text(ctx, "user") end func assets(ctx: i64): http.Text(ctx, "assets") end func page(ctx: i64): http.Text(ctx, "page") end  func handler_name(fn: i64): str:     if fn == me: ret "me" end     if fn == user: ret "user" end     if fn == assets: ret "assets" end     if fn == page: ret "page" end     ret "?" end  func show(r: router.Router, method: str, path: str):     mut m := router.Dispatch(r, method, path)     if m.matched:         println method, path, "->", handler_name(m.fn), m.params.items.Len(), "params"     else:         println method, path, "-> no route"     end     router.FreeMatch(m) end  func main:

net/email net.email Sending email over SMTP and reading it over IMAP and POP3. Network This package speaks the three mail protocols directly over net.tcp and tls: SMTP to send, POP3 and IMAP to read. Use it for password reset mails, alerts and reports from a server, or a script that reads a support inbox. It is a protocol client, not a mail library: it builds simple text and HTML messages, but it has no attachments and no MIME parser, so a fetched message comes back as raw lines. The pieces:  BuildMessage writes the message text: the headers plus a text body, an HTML body, or both as multipart/alternative. Send does a whole SMTP delivery to one recipient in one call. For several recipients, Bcc or a useful error message, drive an SMTPClient step by step; every step returns true or false and leaves the server's answer in last_reply. POP3 (POP3Client) downloads messages and can delete them; IMAP (IMAPClient) leaves them on the server and lets you search, so it is the one to use for a shared mailbox.  Things people get wrong:  Send always encrypts. With use_tls true it uses TLS from the first byte (port 465); with false it upgrades with STARTTLS (port 587) and fails if the server cannot. It logs in with AUTH PLAIN when a user name is given. BuildMessage writes only From, To, Subject and the content headers. It adds no Date or Message-ID and does not encode a non-ASCII subject; see the first guide. Write line breaks in bodies as 
: bare 
 is passed through, and some servers reject it. IMAP Login puts the user name and password in double quotes without escaping. A password that contains " or \ fails; use Command with an IMAP literal or LoginXOAuth2 for those. Fetch returns the reply lines only, not whether the command worked; call Command when you need the status.  The protocol examples talk to a tiny fake server in a thread of the same program, so you can run them offline and see every command that goes over the wire.  What BuildMessage writes BuildMessage(from, to, subject, text, html) returns the full message text that SMTP sends. With only a text body it is a plain text/plain message, with only HTML it is text/html, and with both it becomes multipart/alternative so that each mail program shows the version it prefers. Bodies are UTF-8, so any language works in the body. net-email-plain-message.salamCopyimport net.email import str import encoding  func show(message: str):     each line in str.Split(message, "
"):         println line     end     println "-----" end  func main:     text := email.BuildMessage("shop@example.com", "sara@example.com", "Your code", "Your login code is 4821.", "")     show(text)     html := email.BuildMessage("shop@example.com", "sara@example.com", "Welcome", "", "<h1>Welcome, Sara</h1>")     show(html)     both := email.BuildMessage("shop@example.com", "sara@example.com", "News", "Plain version", "<p>HTML version</p>")     parts := str.Split(both, "Content-Type: ")     each i, part in parts:         if i > 0: println "Content-Type", i, "is", str.Split(part, ";")[0] end     end     subject := "=?UTF-8?B?" + encoding.Base64Encode("Café menu") + "?="     println "encoded subject:", subject endOutputFrom: shop@example.com To: sara@example.com Subject: Your code MIME-Version: 1.0 Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8  Your login code is 4821. ----- From: shop@example.com To: sara@example.com Subject: Welcome MIME-Version: 1.0 Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8  <h1>Welcome, Sara</h1> ----- Content-Type 1 is multipart/alternative Content-Type 2 is text/plain Content-Type 3 is text/html encoded subject: =?UTF-8?B?Q2Fmw6kgbWVudQ==?= The subject is written as it is. Plain ASCII subjects are always safe; for a subject in another script, encode it the way mail headers expect, =?UTF-8?B? plus the Base64 of the text plus ?=, as the last lines do, and pass that string as the subject. To add a Date or Message-ID header, put the line in front of what BuildMessage returns, for example "Date: " + time.FormatHTTPDate(time.Now()) + "
" + message; mail without a date is more likely to be marked as spam.  An SMTP session step by step Send does everything in one call, but driving the client yourself lets you add several recipients, use another login method, or see where a server says no. The steps are always the same: DialSMTP (or DialSMTPTLS), Hello, an Auth... call on a real server, MailFrom, one RcptTo per recipient, Data with the message, and Quit. Each step returns true or false and leaves the server's answer in last_reply. net-email-smtp-session.salamCopyimport net.email import net.tcp  mut server := tcp.Server {} mut seen := Vector {} as Vector<str>  func next_line(conn: tcp.Conn, buf &: str): str:     until buf.Find("
") < 0:         buf += tcp.Read(conn, 4096)     end     at := buf.Find("
")     line := buf.Substr(0, at)     buf = buf.Substr(at + 2, buf.Len() - at - 2)     ret line end  func mail_server():     conn := tcp.Accept(server)     mut buf := ""     _ := tcp.Write(conn, "220 mail.test ready
")     mut open := true     until open:         line := next_line(conn, buf)         seen.Push(line)         if line == "DATA":             _ := tcp.Write(conn, "354 end with a dot
")             mut body := next_line(conn, buf)             until body != ".":                 body = next_line(conn, buf)             end             _ := tcp.Write(conn, "250 queued as 1001
")         else line == "QUIT":             _ := tcp.Write(conn, "221 bye
")             open = false         else:             _ := tcp.Write(conn, "250 ok
