net/websocket net.websocket A two way connection that stays open between browser and server, with rooms for broadcasting. Network A WebSocket is a connection that starts as one HTTP request and then stays open, and either side sends a message whenever it likes: live chat, notifications, dashboards, games. This package has both ends. The server takes connections with Listen and Accept on its own port, and a client connects with Dial; AcceptWSS and DialWSS do the same over TLS. It runs its own listener and does not plug into the net.http server. For the Socket.IO protocol that many JavaScript apps use (events, acknowledgements, reconnection) use net.socketio instead; a plain browser WebSocket talks to this package directly. Core ideas:  Receive blocks until a whole message has arrived and returns a Message; check its kind with IsText, IsBinary and IsClose. Pings are answered for you. Poll waits at most a given time. A Hub groups connections into rooms so one call sends to every member. One connection is read by one thread. To serve many clients, give each connection its own thread.  Things that catch people out:  A Hub has no lock. When several connection threads share it, wrap Register, Unregister and Broadcast in a sync mutex. Keep a copy of the connection for Unregister. When the other side closes, Receive clears conn.fd, and Unregister matches on that socket number, so unregistering with the closed connection removes nothing. Register a copy taken right after Accept and unregister with the same copy. Text stops at a zero byte and is not checked as UTF-8. Send binary data as binary and read it from m.data and m.len; that buffer belongs to the connection and is reused by the next binary message, so copy what you keep. The server takes any origin and offers no subprotocols or compression; check conn.hdr yourself if you need an Origin rule. A frame larger than 100 MB closes the connection.  Each example below runs a server and its clients in the same program, the server in a thread started with spawn, on a free port chosen by Listen(0). That keeps them runnable offline; in a real program the clients are browsers using the JavaScript WebSocket API, which speaks the same protocol.  Typed JSON messages A WebSocket carries text or bytes; the structure is up to you. The common choice is one JSON object per message with a type field, and a server loop that reads a message, looks at the type and answers. Receive waits for the next message, IsText tells text from close or binary frames, and json.Str quotes user text safely when you build a reply by hand. net-websocket-json.salamCopyimport net.websocket import encoding.json  mut server := websocket.Server {}  func chat():     mut conn := websocket.Accept(server)     mut name := ""     until websocket.IsOpen(conn):         msg := websocket.Receive(conn)         if not websocket.IsText(msg): break end         kind := json.Get(msg.text, "type")         if kind == "join":             name = json.Get(msg.text, "name")             _ := websocket.SendText(conn, `{"type": "joined", "users": 1}`)         else kind == "say":             reply := `{"type": "said", "from": ` + json.Str(name) + `, "text": ` + json.Str(json.Get(msg.text, "text")) + `}`             _ := websocket.SendText(conn, reply)         else:             _ := websocket.SendText(conn, `{"type": "error", "reason": "unknown type"}`)         end     end     websocket.Close(conn) end  func ask(c &: websocket.Conn, request: str): str:     _ := websocket.SendText(c, request)     ret websocket.ReceiveText(c) end  func main:     server = websocket.Listen(0)     t := spawn(chat)     mut c := websocket.Dial("127.0.0.1", websocket.Port(server), "/chat")     joined := ask(c, `{"type": "join", "name": "Sara"}`)     println json.Get(joined, "type"), "users:", json.GetInt(joined, "users")     said := ask(c, `{"type": "say", "text": "salam \"everyone\""}`)     println json.Get(said, "from"), "said:", json.Get(said, "text")     println ask(c, `{"type": "dance"}`)     websocket.Close(c)     join(t)     websocket.CloseServer(server) endOutputjoined users: 1 Sara said: salam "everyone" {"type": "error", "reason": "unknown type"} Always answer an unknown type with an error message instead of closing; clients built later may send types an older server does not know.  Rooms with a Hub A chat or a live score page sends one message to many connections. A Hub keeps connections by room name: Register adds a connection to a room, Broadcast sends text to every member and returns how many got it, and RoomSize counts the members. A natural room name is the path the client connected to, which the server sees in conn.path. net-websocket-rooms.salamCopyimport net.websocket import str  mut server := websocket.Server {} mut hub := websocket.NewHub()  func acceptor():     repeat 3:         conn := websocket.Accept(server)         room := str.Replace(conn.path, "/rooms/", "")         websocket.Register(hub, room, conn)     end end  func main:     server = websocket.Listen(0)     port := websocket.Port(server)     t := spawn(acceptor)     mut ali := websocket.Dial("127.0.0.1", port, "/rooms/news")     mut sara := websocket.Dial("127.0.0.1", port, "/rooms/news")     mut reza := websocket.Dial("127.0.0.1", port, "/rooms/sport")     join(t)     println "news:", websocket.RoomSize(hub, "news"), "sport:", websocket.RoomSize(hub, "sport")     println "sent to", websocket.Broadcast(hub, "news"

net/http net.http HTTP servers and clients: handlers, text and JSON responses, cookies and sending requests. Network This package has both halves of HTTP/1.1: a server for web pages and JSON APIs, and a client for calling other services. The server hands each request to a net.router router, which picks the handler by method and path. Every handler takes one i64, the context id of the request; you read the request and write the response with the context functions below, or turn the id into a Context struct with Ctx and call the same names on it. The packages around it:  net.http.middleware for access logs, CORS and cache headers, net.http.session for logins with a cookie, net.http.validate for checking input, and net.http.swagger for API documentation; net.http2 for HTTP/2, and net.websocket for connections that stay open.  Things people get wrong:  Register every route before Use. The server keeps a copy of the router. Post, Put and Patch label a body as a form (application/x-www-form-urlencoded) unless you pass a Content-Type; send JSON with PostWith and that header. The client does not follow redirects unless you ask. A 302 comes back as a 302 with its Location header; set max_redirects in RequestOptions (or call SetMaxRedirects on a client) to follow them. It never hangs or reads without limit: a read or write that is idle for 30 seconds fails, a response over 256 MB fails, and timeout_ms caps the whole request. Ok means a 2xx status. When the server could not be reached at all, Status is 0 and Error says why. A value read from a request is freed when the handler returns; see the end of the page.  The examples run the server with RunBackground on 127.0.0.1 and send requests to it from the same program. A JSON API in one file The most common job is a small JSON API: list some records, show one by its id, and create new ones. Register each route on the router with its handler, hand the router to the server with Use, and start it. Here the records are Salam structs: json.Marshal turns them into the response body, and json.UnmarshalLenient reads the posted body back into a struct, ignoring fields it does not know and leaving the missing ones at their defaults. net-http-guide-api.salamCopyimport net.http import net.router import encoding.json import conv  mut books := Vector {} as Vector<Book>  struct Book:     @json "id"     pub id: int = 0     @json "title"     pub title: str = "" end  func list(ctx: i64):     http.Json(ctx, json.Marshal(books)) end  func show(ctx: i64):     id := conv.AtoiOr(http.Param(ctx, "id"), 0 - 1)     each b in books:         if b.id == id:             http.Json(ctx, json.Marshal(b))             ret         end     end     http.SetStatus(ctx, 404)     http.Json(ctx, `{"error":"no such book"}`) end  func create(ctx: i64):     mut b := Book {}     try:         json.UnmarshalLenient(http.Body(ctx), b)     catch e:         http.SetStatus(ctx, 400)         http.Json(ctx, "{" + json.Member("error", e.ToStr()) + "}")         ret     end     b.id = books.Len() + 1     books.Push(b)     http.SetStatus(ctx, 201)     http.SetHeader(ctx, "Location", "/books/" + b.id)     http.Json(ctx, json.Marshal(b)) end  func main:     mut r := router.NewRouter()     router.Get(r, "/books", list)     router.Get(r, "/books/:id", show)     router.Post(r, "/books", create)     mut s := http.NewServer(19761)     http.Use(s, r)     _ := http.RunBackground(s)     base := "http://127.0.0.1:19761"     a := http.Post(base + "/books", `{"title": "The Little Prince"}`)     println http.Status(a), http.GetHeader(a, "location"), http.Body(a)     _ := http.Post(base + "/books", `{"title": "Rumi"}`)     println http.Body(http.Get(base + "/books"))     println http.Body(http.Get(base + "/books/2"))     c := http.Get(base + "/books/9")     println http.Status(c), http.Body(c)     d := http.Post(base + "/books", `{"title": 7}`)     println http.Status(d), http.Body(d) endOutput201 /books/1 {"id":1,"title":"The Little Prince"} [{"id":1,"title":"The Little Prince"},{"id":2,"title":"Rumi"}] {"id":2,"title":"Rumi"} 404 {"error":"no such book"} 400 {"error": "json: value does not match the expected type (line 1, column 11)"} Nothing is sent until the handler returns: the status, the headers and the body are collected and go out together, and a second body call replaces the first. That is why a handler returns right after it writes an error. A 201 with a Location header is the usual answer to a create, and a 404 with a short JSON error is easier for a client to handle than an empty page. Path parameters such as :id always arrive as text, so convert them with conv.Atoi (or conv.AtoiOr, which gives a fallback for text that is not a number) before comparing.  HTML forms, query strings and redirects A browser form arrives as application/x-www-form-urlencoded. Form reads one field and decodes it, so %40 becomes @ and + becomes a space. Query does the same for the query string. After a successful POST, answer with Redirect so that pressing reload in the browser does not send the form again. net-http-guide-forms.salamCopyimport net.http import net.router import template  mut messages := Vector {} as Vector<str>  func board(ctx: i64):     mut html := "<ul>"     each m in messages:         html = html + "<li>" + template.EscapeHTML(m) + "</li>"     end     http.Html(ctx, html + "</ul>") end  func post(ctx: i64):     name := http.Form(ctx, "name")     text := http.Form(ctx, "text")     if name == "&qu

net/http/middleware net.http.middleware The usual security, cache and CORS headers, and request logging, in one call. Network Five small helpers for net.http handlers: AllowAll for CORS, Secure for basic security headers, NoCache and Cache for caching, and Log for a line per request. Each takes the context id, as the handler does, and only sets response headers (or prints), so you call them on the first lines of a handler. There is no middleware chain in Salam and no way to wrap a handler from outside. A middleware is an ordinary function you call with the context id, and the headers it sets go out with whatever the handler writes after it. That keeps the order visible in the handler itself. For logins use net.http.session, and for checking input net.http.validate. What to know before you rely on them:  AllowAll does not list PATCH. It allows GET, POST, PUT, DELETE and OPTIONS with the Content-Type and Authorization headers, for every origin. A browser refuses a PATCH from another origin, and * cannot be used with cookies; write your own rule for those (last section). Secure is a minimum. It sets nosniff, X-Frame-Options: DENY and X-XSS-Protection, a header current browsers ignore. It sets no Content-Security-Policy and no Strict-Transport-Security. The last call wins. A header set twice with the same name keeps the last value, so NoCache followed by Cache leaves only max-age. Log prints with println before the handler runs, so it shows no status; http.EnableAccessLog on the server logs the status too.   CORS for an API used from a browser A page on another origin can only call your API when the response allows it. For anything other than a simple GET the browser first sends an OPTIONS request, the preflight, and checks the Access-Control-Allow-* headers on the answer. Register an OPTIONS route that calls AllowAll and answers 204 with no body, and call AllowAll in the real handler too. net-http-middleware-cors.salamCopyimport net.http import net.http.middleware import net.router  func preflight(ctx: i64):     middleware.AllowAll(ctx)     http.SetStatus(ctx, 204)     http.Text(ctx, "") end  func notes(ctx: i64):     middleware.AllowAll(ctx)     middleware.NoCache(ctx)     http.Json(ctx, `[{"id":1,"text":"buy bread"}]`) end  func main:     mut r := router.NewRouter()     router.Options(r, "/api/notes", preflight)     router.Get(r, "/api/notes", notes)     mut s := http.NewServer(19765)     http.Use(s, r)     _ := http.RunBackground(s)     url := "http://127.0.0.1:19765/api/notes"     mut asked := http.NewHeaders()     asked.Insert("Origin", "https://app.example.com")     asked.Insert("Access-Control-Request-Method", "GET")     p := http.OptionsWith(url, asked)     println "preflight:", http.Status(p)     each name in ["access-control-allow-origin", "access-control-allow-methods", "access-control-allow-headers"]:         println "  " + name + ": " + http.GetHeader(p, name)     end     g := http.GetWith(url, asked)     println "get:", http.Status(g), http.Body(g)     println "  cache-control: " + http.GetHeader(g, "cache-control")     println "  pragma: " + http.GetHeader(g, "pragma") endOutputpreflight: 204   access-control-allow-origin: *   access-control-allow-methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS   access-control-allow-headers: Content-Type, Authorization get: 200 [{"id":1,"text":"buy bread"}]   cache-control: no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate   pragma: no-cache AllowAll allows every origin, the methods GET, POST, PUT, DELETE and OPTIONS (not PATCH) and the Content-Type and Authorization headers. That suits a public, read only API. An API that uses cookies or other headers needs its own rule, as the last section shows.  One helper per kind of response Instead of repeating the same calls at the top of every handler, group them in a function for each kind of response: private pages that must not be cached and must not appear in a frame, and public files that browsers may keep. Secure adds nosniff, X-Frame-Options: DENY and the XSS header; NoCache forbids caching; Cache allows it for the given number of seconds. net-http-middleware-chain.salamCopyimport net.http import net.http.middleware import net.router  func page(ctx: i64):     middleware.Secure(ctx)     middleware.NoCache(ctx) end  func asset(ctx: i64, seconds: int):     middleware.Cache(ctx, seconds) end  func account(ctx: i64):     page(ctx)     http.Html(ctx, "<h1>Your account</h1>") end  func logo(ctx: i64):     asset(ctx, 86400)     http.Text(ctx, "logo bytes") end  func news(ctx: i64):     asset(ctx, 60)     http.Json(ctx, `["release 0.5.5"]`) end  func main:     mut r := router.NewRouter()     router.Get(r, "/account", account)     router.Get(r, "/logo.svg", logo)     router.Get(r, "/news.json", news)     mut s := http.NewServer(19766)     http.Use(s, r)     _ := http.RunBackground(s)     base := "http://127.0.0.1:19766"     each path in ["/account", "/logo.svg", "/news.json"]:         res := http.Get(base + path)         println path + " cache-control=" + http.GetHeader(res, "cache-control") + " frame=" + http.GetHeader(res, "x-frame-options")     end endOutput/account cache-control=no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate frame=DENY /logo.svg cache-control=max-age=86400 frame= /news.json cache-control=max-age=60 frame= Log prints one line per request with the method and path, which helps while developing. In production, http.EnableAccessLog on the server logs every request with its status, without a call in each handler.  Stricter headers for pages with private data For an invoice or an account page, build on Secure with the headers

net/http/validate net.http.validate Checking form input and answering with a 400. Network Five small checks for input that arrives at a net.http handler: Required, Length, IsEmail, Matches and Assert. The first four take a string and return true or false, so they work anywhere, not only in handlers; Matches also throws when its pattern is not valid. Assert is the one that answers: when its condition is false it sends a 400 with a JSON message. For patterns beyond Matches, such as finding or replacing, use regex directly; for typed JSON bodies, decode with encoding.json and check the fields after. What the checks really test:  Required only rejects the empty string. A value of spaces passes; trim it with str.Trim first. IsEmail only looks for an @ and a dot anywhere, so @. passes. It catches typing slips, nothing more. Matches searches, it does not match the whole value: anchor the pattern with ^ and $. A pattern that does not compile throws the regex error (kind Syntax, code regex.invalid) instead of rejecting every value, so mark the call with try or catch it; in a handler, catch it and answer 500. Assert does not stop the handler, and it pastes the message into the JSON without escaping. Return right after a failed Assert, and keep user input out of its message.  Common rules Each function answers one question about one string. Matches takes a regular expression; anchor it with ^ and $, or it accepts any text that merely contains a match. Length counts characters, not bytes, so a Persian name of four letters has length 4 although it takes eight bytes. net-http-validate-rules.salamCopyimport net.http.validate import str  func check(label: str, ok: bool):     println label + ": " + (ok ? "ok" : "rejected") end  func main throws:     check("empty name", validate.Required(""))     check("name of spaces", validate.Required("   "))     check("trimmed spaces", validate.Required(str.Trim("   ")))     check("username 'ali_75'", try validate.Matches("ali_75", "^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{2,15}$"))     check("username '7up'", try validate.Matches("7up", "^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{2,15}$"))     check("postal code 1234567890", try validate.Matches("1234567890", "^[0-9]{10}$"))     check("color #1e90ff", try validate.Matches("#1e90ff", "^#[0-9a-fA-F]{6}$"))     check("password of 6", validate.Length("abc123", 8, 64))     check("Persian name of 4 letters", validate.Length("مریم", 2, 4))     println "bytes in the name:", "مریم".Len()     check("email a@b.ir", validate.IsEmail("a@b.ir"))     check("email @.", validate.IsEmail("@.")) endOutputempty name: rejected name of spaces: ok trimmed spaces: rejected username 'ali_75': ok username '7up': rejected postal code 1234567890: ok color #1e90ff: ok password of 6: rejected Persian name of 4 letters: ok bytes in the name: 8 email a@b.ir: ok email @.: ok Two of the results are worth a second look. Required only checks that the text is not empty, so a value of spaces passes; trim it first with str.Trim. IsEmail only checks for an @ and a dot, so it catches typing mistakes, not fake addresses. The only real proof that an address works is a confirmation email.  Report every problem at once A form with several fields should tell the user about all the mistakes in one answer, not one per try. Run every check, collect the messages, and send them together with a 422. Building the JSON with json.Str and json.Array escapes the messages correctly. net-http-validate-signup.salamCopyimport net.http import net.http.validate import net.router import encoding.json import str  func signup(ctx: i64):     name := str.Trim(http.Form(ctx, "name"))     email := str.Trim(http.Form(ctx, "email"))     password := http.Form(ctx, "password")     mut problems := Vector {} as Vector<str>     if not validate.Required(name): problems.Push(json.Str("name is required")) end     if not validate.IsEmail(email): problems.Push(json.Str("email is not valid")) end     if not validate.Length(password, 8, 64): problems.Push(json.Str("password needs 8 to 64 characters")) end     if problems.Len() > 0:         http.SetStatus(ctx, 422)         http.Json(ctx, "{" + json.MemberRaw("errors", json.Array(problems)) + "}")         ret     end     http.SetStatus(ctx, 201)     http.Json(ctx, "{" + json.Member("welcome", name) + "}") end  func send(form: str):     mut headers := http.NewHeaders()     headers.Insert("Content-Type", "application/x-www-form-urlencoded")     res := http.PostWith("http://127.0.0.1:19768/signup", form, headers)     println http.Status(res), http.Body(res) end  func main:     mut r := router.NewRouter()     router.Post(r, "/signup", signup)     mut s := http.NewServer(19768)     http.Use(s, r)     _ := http.RunBackground(s)     send("name=+&email=ali&password=123")     send("name=Ali&email=ali%40example.com&password=123")     send("name=Ali&email=ali%40example.com&password=long+enough") endOutput422 {"errors": ["name is required", "email is not valid", "password needs 8 to 64 characters"]} 422 {"errors": ["password needs 8 to 64 characters"]} 201 {"welcome": "Ali"}  Stop at the first problem with Assert For a simple API, Assert is shorter: when the condition is false it answers 400 with {"error": message}. It does not stop the handler, so keep the result in a variable and return when it is false. Otherwise the code after it runs and its response replaces the error. net-http-valid

net/http/session net.http.session User sessions over a cookie: keeping data between requests, and a CSRF token. Network A session keeps each visitor's data on the server and gives the browser nothing but a random id in an HttpOnly cookie. Use it for logins, carts and form tokens on a site built with net.http. When the client is not a browser, or several servers must accept the same login without sharing memory, a signed token from jwt is usually the better fit. The flow in a handler: Start finds the visitor's session from the cookie or makes a new one (and sets the cookie), you read and change values with Value and SetValue, and Save writes the session back. Values are strings. A session expires after max_age seconds without a request; every request that finds it starts the clock again. Things people get wrong:  Forgetting Save. Start returns a copy; changes reach the store only when you save it. Keeping request strings. Param, Form and the like are freed when the handler returns, so copy them with str.Clone before you store them (see the cart). Not calling Regenerate after login, which leaves an id an attacker may have planted in the browser valid. Expecting the sessions to survive. They live in this process's memory: a restart logs everyone out and two server processes do not share them. Two requests from one visitor at the same moment each save their own copy, and the later Save wins.  Log in and log out The usual shape: the login handler checks the password, calls Regenerate so the user gets a fresh id, stores who they are with SetValue and redirects. Every protected page calls Start and checks HasValue. Logging out calls End, which deletes the session on the server and clears the cookie. net-http-session-login.salamCopyimport net.http import net.http.session import net.router  func login(ctx: i64):     if http.Form(ctx, "user") != "sara" or http.Form(ctx, "password") != "open sesame":         http.SetStatus(ctx, 401)         http.Text(ctx, "wrong user or password")         ret     end     mut s := session.Start(ctx)     session.Regenerate(ctx, s)     session.SetValue(s, "user", "sara")     session.Save(s)     http.Redirect(ctx, "/me") end  func me(ctx: i64):     s := session.Start(ctx)     if not session.HasValue(s, "user"):         http.SetStatus(ctx, 401)         http.Text(ctx, "please log in")         ret     end     http.Text(ctx, "hello " + session.Value(s, "user")) end  func logout(ctx: i64):     session.End(ctx)     http.Text(ctx, "logged out") end  func main:     mut r := router.NewRouter()     router.Post(r, "/login", login)     router.Get(r, "/me", me)     router.Post(r, "/logout", logout)     mut srv := http.NewServer(19770)     http.Use(srv, r)     _ := http.RunBackground(srv)     base := "http://127.0.0.1:19770"     mut browser := http.NewClient()     browser.SetHeader("Content-Type", "application/x-www-form-urlencoded")     println http.Body(browser.Get(base + "/me"))     bad := browser.Post(base + "/login", "user=sara&password=guess")     println http.Status(bad), http.Body(bad)     ok := browser.Post(base + "/login", "user=sara&password=open+sesame")     println http.Status(ok), http.GetHeader(ok, "location")     println http.Body(browser.Get(base + "/me"))     println http.Body(browser.Post(base + "/logout", ""))     println http.Body(browser.Get(base + "/me")) endOutputplease log in 401 wrong user or password 302 /me hello sara logged out please log in http.NewClient keeps cookies between requests the way a browser does, which is why the second /me sees the login. A plain http.Get sends no cookies and always looks like a new visitor.  Protect forms with a CSRF token The browser sends the session cookie with every request to your site, even one started by a form on another site. A CSRF token stops that: CSRFToken stores a random token in the session, you put it in a hidden field, and the handler that receives the form checks it with CSRFVerify. A forged form does not know the token and is refused. net-http-session-csrf.salamCopyimport net.http import net.http.session import net.router  func form(ctx: i64):     mut s := session.Start(ctx)     token := session.CSRFToken(s)     session.Save(s)     http.Html(ctx, `<form method="post" action="/email"><input type="hidden" name="csrf" value="` + token + `"><input name="email"></form>`) end  func change_email(ctx: i64):     s := session.Start(ctx)     if not session.CSRFVerify(s, http.Form(ctx, "csrf")):         http.SetStatus(ctx, 403)         http.Text(ctx, "the form has expired, reload the page")         ret     end     http.Text(ctx, "email changed to " + http.Form(ctx, "email")) end  func token_in(html: str): str:     start := html.Find(`value="`) + 7     rest := html.Substr(start, html.Len() - start)     ret rest.Substr(0, rest.Find(`"`)) end  func main:     mut r := router.NewRouter()     router.Get(r, "/email", form)     router.Post(r, "/email", change_email)     mut srv := http.NewServer(19771)     http.Use(srv, r)     _ := http.RunBackground(srv)     url := "http://127.0.0.1:19771/email"     mut browser := http.NewClient()     browser.SetHeader("Content-Type", "application/x-www-form-urlencoded")     token := token_in(http.Body(browser.Get(url)))     println "token length:", token.Len()     forged := browser.Post(url, "email=evil%40example.com")     println http.Status(forged), http.Body(forged)     real := browser.Post(url, "csrf=" + token + "&email=sara%40example.com")     println http.Status(rea

net/http/swagger net.http.swagger Writing OpenAPI documentation for an API and serving the documentation page. Network This package writes the documentation of an HTTP API as an OpenAPI 3.1 document and serves it with a viewer page where people can read each operation and try it. Use it with an API built on net.http and net.router: client generators, API gateways and your own front-end team read the same openapi.json. The viewer is built into the package, so it works offline and loads nothing from a CDN. How it fits together:  A Doc holds the whole document. Route adds an operation (or At picks one that exists), and the calls after it, such as Summary, Query and Returns, describe that operation. Body and response schemas come from a sample value: pass an empty struct and its fields, under their @json names, become a schema under components. Mount adds the viewer and the spec to your router; Problems, Missing and Undocumented check the document in a test.  Things that catch people out:  Mount copies the spec when you call it, and adds routes to the router. Describe every route first, then Mount, then http.Use; a description added after Mount never reaches the page. After an At that finds nothing, the following calls do nothing. Check what At returns, or use Route, which creates the operation. The docs are public. Anyone who can reach the server can read /docs, and the spec is served with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *. Leave Mount out of a production build if the API is private.  Document an API next to its routes The simplest habit is to describe each route right after you register it, so the two never drift apart. Route starts an operation, and the calls after it fill it in. Returns takes a sample value: pass a struct, or an array of one struct for a list, and the schema appears under components. Mount then serves the spec at /docs/openapi.json and the viewer at /docs. net-http-swagger-api.salamCopyimport net.http import net.http.swagger import net.router import encoding.json  struct Task:     @json "id"     pub id: int = 0     @json "title"     pub title: str = ""     @json "done"     pub done: bool = false end  func list(ctx: i64):     http.Json(ctx, `[{"id":1,"title":"write docs","done":false}]`) end  func create(ctx: i64):     http.SetStatus(ctx, 201)     http.Json(ctx, http.Body(ctx)) end  func main:     mut r := router.NewRouter()     mut doc := swagger.New("tasks", "1.0.0")     router.Get(r, "/tasks", list)     _ := swagger.Route(doc, "GET", "/tasks")     swagger.Summary(doc, "all tasks")     swagger.Tag(doc, "tasks")     swagger.Returns(doc, 200, "the tasks", [Task {}])     router.Post(r, "/tasks", create)     _ := swagger.Route(doc, "POST", "/tasks")     swagger.Summary(doc, "add a task")     swagger.Tag(doc, "tasks")     swagger.Accepts(doc, "the new task", Task {})     swagger.Returns(doc, 201, "the task as stored", Task {})     println "missing:", swagger.Missing(doc, r)     swagger.Mount(doc, r, "/docs")     mut s := http.NewServer(19774)     http.Use(s, r)     _ := http.RunBackground(s)     spec := http.Body(http.Get("http://127.0.0.1:19774/docs/openapi.json"))     println json.Keys(json.Get(spec, "paths"))     println json.GetPath(spec, "paths./tasks.post.summary")     println json.GetPath(spec, "paths./tasks.get.responses.200.description")     println json.GetPath(spec, "paths./tasks.get.responses.200.content")     println json.Keys(json.GetPath(spec, "components.schemas.Task.properties"))     println http.Status(http.Get("http://127.0.0.1:19774/docs"))     swagger.Free(doc) endOutputmissing: [] ["/tasks"] add a task the tasks {"application/json":{"schema":{"type":"array","items":{"$ref":"#/components/schemas/Task"}}}} ["id", "title", "done"] 200 Mount takes a copy of the spec when you call it, so document every route first and mount last. Path patterns are written the router's way, /books/:id, and appear in OpenAPI's form, /books/{id}.  Security schemes and saving the spec Declare each way to sign in once, with BearerAuth for tokens in the Authorization header or ApiKeyAuth for a key in a header, query value or cookie. Then mark each operation that needs it with Secure and the scheme's name. WriteSpec saves the spec to a file, for a client generator or for publishing with the site, and SpecFromFile reads one back. net-http-swagger-auth.salamCopyimport net.http.swagger import encoding.json  struct Invoice:     @json "number"     pub number: str = ""     @json "total"     pub total: f64 = 0.0 end  func main:     mut doc := swagger.New("billing", "1.4.0")     swagger.Server(doc, "https://billing.example.com", "production")     swagger.BearerAuth(doc, "user", "JWT")     swagger.ApiKeyAuth(doc, "partner", "header", "X-Partner-Key")     _ := swagger.Route(doc, "GET", "/invoices/:number")     swagger.Summary(doc, "one invoice")     swagger.Secure(doc, "user")     swagger.Returns(doc, 200, "the invoice", Invoice {})     swagger.ReturnsNothing(doc, 401, "no valid token")     _ := swagger.Route(doc, "POST", "/partner/invoices")     swagger.Summary(doc, "a partner sends an invoice")     swagger.Secure(doc, "partner")     swagger.Accepts(doc, "the invoice", Invoice {})     swagger.ReturnsNothing(doc, 202, "accepted")     println "problems:", swagger.Problems(doc).Len()     println swagger.WriteSpec(doc, "opena

net/http2 net.http2 The HTTP/2 protocol from the ground up: frames, HPACK header compression and streams. Network This package implements HTTP/2 at the protocol level: it builds and reads frames, compresses the headers with HPACK and carries several requests at once over one connection as "streams". It is not a web server or a ready client. For an ordinary web server or one-off requests use net.http, which speaks HTTP/1.1; reach for this package when you need the protocol itself, for example to talk to a service that only offers HTTP/2, to test a server, or to send many requests over one connection. How it goes: build a Transport over a TCP or TLS socket, take a connection with NewConn and do the handshake. Then the client sends a request with SendHeaders and reads the answer in StreamAt after AwaitStreamEnd. Over TLS, the client and the server must have agreed on h2 through ALPN. What the package does for you, and what it leaves to you:  It answers pings, sends window updates for flow control, waits for window space in SendData, and refuses server push. You write the pseudo-headers yourself: :method, :scheme, :authority and :path on a request, :status on an answer, before any normal header. A stream's body is collected in memory in s.data until the stream ends, and finished streams stay in the connection, so open a new connection now and then rather than keeping one for millions of requests. A Conn belongs to one thread; nothing in it is locked.   Many requests on one connection The point of HTTP/2 is that one connection carries many requests at the same time. Each request is a stream with an odd id chosen by the client (1, 3, 5 and so on), and the frames of different streams can be interleaved in both directions. The client below sends three requests before reading anything; the server, in the same program, answers them in reverse order, and each answer still lands on the right stream. net-http2-multiplex.salamCopyimport net.http2 import net.tcp import compress  mut server := tcp.Server {}  func serve():     conn := tcp.Accept(server)     mut c := http2.NewConn(http2.PlainTransport(conn.fd), true)     if not http2.ServerHandshake(c):         ret     end     mut ids := Vector {} as Vector<int>     until ids.Len() < 3:         ids.Push(http2.AwaitAnyHeaders(c, 20))     end     mut i := ids.Len() - 1     until i >= 0:         id := ids.Get(i)         path := http2.HeadersGet(http2.StreamAt(c, id).headers, ":path")         mut h := http2.HeaderList {}         http2.HeadersAdd(h, ":status", "200")         _ := http2.SendHeaders(c, id, h, false)         _ := http2.SendData(c, id, compress.BufFromStr("page " + path), true)         i--     end     _ := http2.AwaitStreamEnd(c, 0, 5)     http2.CloseConn(c) end  func request(c &: http2.Conn, path: str): int:     id := http2.NextStreamId(c)     mut h := http2.HeaderList {}     http2.HeadersAdd(h, ":method", "GET")     http2.HeadersAdd(h, ":scheme", "http")     http2.HeadersAdd(h, ":path", path)     http2.HeadersAdd(h, ":authority", "127.0.0.1")     _ := http2.SendHeaders(c, id, h, true)     ret id end  func main:     server = tcp.Bind(0)     t := spawn(serve)     conn := tcp.Dial("127.0.0.1", tcp.Port(server))     mut c := http2.NewConn(http2.PlainTransport(conn.fd), false)     if not http2.ClientHandshake(c):         println "handshake failed"         ret 1     end     mut ids := Vector {} as Vector<int>     each p in ["/a", "/b", "/c"]:         ids.Push(request(c, p))     end     println "three requests sent on streams", ids.Get(0), ids.Get(1), ids.Get(2)     each id in ids:         _ := http2.AwaitStreamEnd(c, id, 50)         s := http2.StreamAt(c, id)         println "stream", id, http2.HeadersGet(s.headers, ":status"), compress.BufToStrUnsafe(s.data)     end     println "connections used: 1, streams:", http2.StreamCount(c)     _ := http2.SendGoAway(c, http2.H2_NO_ERROR, "")     http2.CloseConn(c)     join(t)     tcp.CloseServer(server)     ret 0 endOutputthree requests sent on streams 1 3 5 stream 1 200 page /a stream 3 200 page /b stream 5 200 page /c connections used: 1, streams: 3 AwaitAnyHeaders on the server reads frames until one arrives for a stream whose headers are complete and returns that stream's id, or H2_POLL_ERROR when the connection fails. A request that also has a body sends more frames on the same stream, so a server that accepts bodies should remember which ids it has already seen. AwaitStreamEnd on the client reads frames, for any stream, until the one you asked about has ended; the frames of the others are kept in their streams for later. Its last argument is a limit on how many frames to read, so a broken peer cannot keep you waiting forever.  How much HPACK saves Requests to one site repeat nearly the same headers every time. HPACK sends a header once, stores it in a table that both sides keep in step, and afterwards sends only its index. The first request below is already smaller than its HTTP/1.1 text because of the static table and the Huffman code; the second and third are about a quarter of the size, because almost everything is now in the dynamic table. net-http2-hpack-savings.salamCopyimport net.http2  func request_headers(path: str): http2.HeaderList:     mut h := http2.HeaderList {}     http2.HeadersAdd(h, ":method", "GET")     http2.HeadersAdd(h, ":scheme", "https")     http2.HeadersAdd(h, ":authority", "shop.example.com")     http2.HeadersAdd(h, ":path", path)     http2.HeadersAdd(h, "user-agent", "salam-client/1.0")     http2.HeadersAdd(h, "accept", "application/json")     http2.HeadersAddSensitive(h, "authorization", "Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.e30.x"

net/socketio net.socketio A Socket.IO client: events, acknowledgements, namespaces and automatic reconnection. Network Socket.IO is the usual live messaging library in the Node.js world. This package is a client for Socket.IO 3 and 4 servers (Engine.IO protocol 4), over WebSocket or HTTP long polling; it has no server of its own. Use it when the other side already speaks Socket.IO, for example a Node.js chat or dashboard backend. When you control both ends and the client is a browser, a plain net.websocket server is simpler, because Socket.IO adds its own packet format on top of the WebSocket. The model: Dial connects, On sets a listener for an event and the Emit... functions send events. Nothing is read in the background: listeners run only while the program processes messages with Run, RunFor, Pump, Next or EmitAck. The arguments of every event are a JSON array, read with ArgStr, ArgInt and the like. If the sender wants an answer, the event's ack_id is not negative and you answer it with Reply. For several namespaces on one connection, create a Manager. Things that catch people out:  A program that never pumps never hears anything. Pings from the server are answered while you pump, so a client that sleeps for longer than the server's ping timeout is disconnected. Next returns connection events too, such as EV_CONNECT; loop until the kind you stop on, not until the first event that is not EV_EVENT. Its queue starts with the first Next call and keeps the newest event_queue events (256 by default), dropping the oldest. Free what you build. ArgsFree for argument lists and AckFree for answers, or a long running client keeps growing. Socket.IO 2 servers (from before 2020) speak an older protocol and are not supported.   Handling events in your own loop Listeners with On are the usual style, but sometimes a plain loop reads better: a worker that handles one event at a time, or a program that must also do other work between messages. Next waits up to the given milliseconds and returns one Event. Its kind says what it is: a message from the server (EV_EVENT, with the name and the arguments), a change of the connection such as EV_DISCONNECT (the reason is in message), or EV_TIMEOUT when nothing came. net-socketio-next-loop.salamCopyimport net.socketio import net.websocket  mut server := websocket.Server {}  func fake_server():     mut conn := websocket.Accept(server)     _ := websocket.SendText(conn, `0{"sid":"s1","upgrades":[],"pingInterval":20000,"pingTimeout":5000}`)     m := websocket.Poll(conn, 3000)     if m.kind == websocket.TEXT and m.text == "40":         _ := websocket.SendText(conn, `40{"sid":"a1"}`)         _ := websocket.SendText(conn, `42["price","BTC",61250]`)         _ := websocket.SendText(conn, `42["price","ETH",2410]`)         _ := websocket.SendText(conn, `42["halt","maintenance"]`)         _ := websocket.SendText(conn, "41")     end     _ := websocket.Poll(conn, 1000)     websocket.Close(conn) end  func main:     server = websocket.Listen(0)     t := spawn(fake_server)     mut o := socketio.NewOptions()     o.transports = socketio.TRANSPORT_WEBSOCKET     o.reconnection = false     c := socketio.DialWith("http://127.0.0.1:" + websocket.Port(server), o)      mut going := true     until going:         e := socketio.Next(c, 3000)         if e.kind == socketio.EV_EVENT and e.name == "price":             println "price", socketio.ArgStr(e, 0), socketio.ArgInt(e, 1)         else e.kind == socketio.EV_EVENT:             println "event", e.name, socketio.ArgStr(e, 0)         else e.kind == socketio.EV_DISCONNECT:             println "disconnected:", e.message, e.message == socketio.REASON_SERVER_DISCONNECT             going = false         else e.kind == socketio.EV_TIMEOUT:             println "nothing arrived in time"             going = false         end     end     socketio.Close(c)     join(t)     websocket.CloseServer(server) endOutputprice BTC 61250 price ETH 2410 event halt maintenance disconnected: io server disconnect true The program brings its own tiny server, which speaks the Socket.IO wire format over a WebSocket, so it runs without Node.js. A real server sends the same packets: 42["price","BTC",61250] is an event named price with two arguments, and 41 is the server closing the namespace, which arrives as REASON_SERVER_DISCONNECT. After that reason the client does not reconnect by itself, because the server meant it.  Logging in with a token Socket.IO servers usually check the user in a middleware that reads the auth object of the connection. Put that JSON in Options.auth before dialling. When the middleware says no, the server answers with a connect error instead of a session; Refused is then true and RefusalReason holds the message the server gave. net-socketio-auth.salamCopyimport net.socketio  func main:     mut o := socketio.NewOptions()     o.auth = `{"token":"eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.e30.x"}`     o.reconnection = false     c := socketio.DialWith("https://chat.example.com", o)     if socketio.Refused(c):         println "the server refused us:", socketio.RefusalReason(c)         ret 1     end     if not socketio.IsConnected(c):         println "could not connect:", socketio.LastError(c)         ret 1     end     println "connected as", socketio.Id(c), "over", socketio.TransportName(c)     socketio.Close(c)     ret 0 end This needs a running server, so it is only checked here. With a Node.js server, the matching check is an io.use((socket, next) => ...) that reads socket.handshake.auth.token and calls next(new Error("...")) to refuse.  Acknowledgements in both directions An acknowledgement is Socket.IO's request and reply: the sender numbers an event and the other side answers that number. E

ssh ssh SSH connections, running a command on a server, and working with files over SFTP. Network This package is an SSH client written in Salam and needs neither OpenSSH nor any other library. Make a Config with the host and the user, pick the login method, and connect with Connect; then run a command with Exec, or move files with SftpOpen. It suits automating deployments, backups and checks across a fleet of servers. It is a client only; for plain file transfer with an FTP server see ftp. The host key is checked against the known_hosts file, the way ssh itself does. The buffer and reader functions build and read the data format of the SSH protocol; an ordinary program does not need them. What it supports, and what it does not:  Keys must be RSA, in the OpenSSH format, without a passphrase. Ed25519 and ECDSA keys, the default of recent ssh-keygen, are not read. Make a key for automation with ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -N "" -f deploy_key; a password login with WithPassword also works. The server needs an RSA host key; a server that offers only Ed25519 or ECDSA host keys cannot be checked and the connection fails. Key exchange is curve25519 or Diffie-Hellman group 14, and the ciphers are aes128-ctr and aes256-ctr, which every OpenSSH server accepts. There is no agent support and no port forwarding; an interactive shell with a terminal is available through NewSession, RequestPty and Shell. Each Exec is a fresh shell: a cd or an exported variable does not carry over to the next call.   Run a deployment, step by step Exec runs one command and waits for it, returning its standard output, its standard error and the exit code in an ExecResult. Each call opens a new channel, so a cd in one command does not carry over to the next; join commands with && when they belong together. A deployment is then a list of steps that stops at the first one whose exit code is not zero. ssh-deploy.salamCopyimport ssh import str  func run_steps(client &: ssh.Client, steps: Vector<str>): bool:     each step in steps:         r := ssh.Exec(client, step)         if not r.ok or r.exit_code != 0:             println "FAILED:", step             println str.Trim(r.stderr)             ret false         end         println "ok:", step     end     ret true end  func main:     mut cfg := ssh.NewConfig("app1.example.com", ssh.DefaultPort, "deploy")     if not ssh.WithKeyFile(cfg, "/home/deploy/.ssh/id_rsa"):         println "cannot read the key file"         ret 1     end     ssh.WithHostKeyMode(cfg, ssh.HOSTKEY_MODE_STRICT)     mut client := ssh.Connect(cfg)     if not ssh.Ok(client):         println "connect failed:", ssh.Error(client)         ret 1     end      mut steps := Vector {} as Vector<str>     steps.Push("cd /srv/app && git fetch --quiet && git checkout --quiet v2.4.0")     steps.Push("cd /srv/app && ./salam build --release")     steps.Push("sudo systemctl restart app")     steps.Push("systemctl is-active app")     done := run_steps(client, steps)     ssh.Close(client)     if not done:         ret 1     end     ret 0 end This needs a real server, so it is only checked here. WithKeyFile only reads the file, so it returns false when the path is wrong; a key the package cannot use makes Connect fail instead. For a command that runs for a long time and whose output you want as it comes, such as tail -f, use NewSession, Start and ReadStep with DrainOutput instead, as the example in the reference shows.  Pull a backup over SFTP SSH and SFTP share one connection: run the command that writes the file with Exec, then open SFTP on the same client and fetch it. Stat gives the size, Download copies the file, and Remove cleans up on the server once the copy has arrived. For whole directories there are UploadDir, DownloadDir and MkdirAll. ssh-backup.salamCopyimport ssh  func main:     mut cfg := ssh.NewConfig("db.example.com", 22, "backup")     _ := ssh.WithKeyFile(cfg, "/home/backup/.ssh/id_rsa")     mut client := ssh.Connect(cfg)     if not ssh.Ok(client):         println "connect failed:", ssh.Error(client)         ret 1     end      remote := "/tmp/shop-backup.sql.gz"     dump := ssh.Exec(client, "pg_dump shop | gzip > " + remote)     if dump.exit_code != 0:         println "pg_dump failed:", dump.stderr         ssh.Close(client)         ret 1     end      mut sftp := ssh.SftpOpen(client)     info := ssh.Stat(client, sftp, remote)     println "dump size on the server:", info.size, "bytes"     if ssh.Download(client, sftp, remote, "shop-backup.sql.gz"):         println "downloaded"         _ := ssh.Remove(client, sftp, remote)     else:         println "download failed:", ssh.Error(client)     end     ssh.SftpClose(client, sftp)     ssh.Close(client)     ret 0 end  Host keys and known_hosts The host key is how the client knows it is talking to the right machine and not to someone in between. The mode decides what happens with a key that is not in known_hosts yet. HOSTKEY_MODE_STRICT refuses it, which is right for automation: add the key once by hand, then every later change is an error you want to hear about. HOSTKEY_MODE_ACCEPT_NEW is the default; it records a new key the first time and refuses a changed one later, like StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new in OpenSSH. HOSTKEY_MODE_INSECURE checks nothing and belongs only in tests. ssh-host-keys.salamCopyimport ssh  func attempt(mode: int, label: str):     mut cfg := ssh.NewConfig("new-server.example.com", 22, "admin")     ssh.WithPassword(cfg, "first-login-password")     ssh.WithKnownHostsPath(cfg, "known_hosts")     ssh.WithHostKeyMode(cfg, mode)     mut client := ssh.Connect(cfg)     if ssh.Ok(client):         println label, "connected, host key", ss

ftp ftp An FTP and FTPS client: listing a directory, uploading and downloading files. Network This package connects to FTP servers, for uploading a site to shared hosting or pulling files off old equipment and suppliers' servers. Plain FTP sends the password and the data unencrypted; wherever the server supports it, use DialTLS, which encrypts both the commands and the data with AUTH TLS. When the server also speaks SSH, SFTP through ssh is the better choice: one encrypted connection, no separate data channel. Transfers go in passive mode (EPSV, or PASV when the server lacks it), which works from behind a firewall; active mode (PORT) is not offered. The parsing functions, such as ParseListLine, are available for writing tools of your own too. Things to know:  Call Binary before transfers, or a server in ASCII mode may change line endings inside images and archives. Upload and Download hold the whole file in memory, and an interrupted transfer starts again from the beginning; there is no resume. Fine for site files and reports, not for multi-gigabyte backups. Read, Write and Append carry a str, so they are for text: binary content stops at the first zero byte. Use Upload and Download for anything else. Servers that require TLS session reuse on the data connection refuse every transfer; see the last section.   Publish a site to shared hosting The usual job: connect with DialTLS, refuse to go on unless both the commands and the data are encrypted, log in, and upload a build directory with UploadDir. Switch to binary mode with Binary before any transfer, or some servers will change the line endings inside images and archives. Keeping the old index.html under another name with Rename gives you something to go back to. ftp-publish-site.salamCopyimport ftp  func main:     mut c := ftp.DialTLS("ftp.example-host.com", 21)     if not ftp.Ok(c):         println "cannot connect:", ftp.LastReply(c)         ret 1     end     if not ftp.Secure(c) or not ftp.SecureData(c):         println "the server would not encrypt the session, stopping"         ftp.Close(c)         ret 1     end     if not ftp.Login(c, "site-user", "app-password"):         println "login failed:", ftp.LastCode(c), ftp.LastReply(c)         ftp.Close(c)         ret 1     end     _ := ftp.Binary(c)     _ := ftp.MkdirAll(c, "/public_html")     if ftp.Exists(c, "/public_html/index.html"):         _ := ftp.Rename(c, "/public_html/index.html", "/public_html/index.old.html")     end     if not ftp.UploadDir(c, "dist", "/public_html"):         println "upload failed:", ftp.LastReply(c)         ret 1     end     println "uploaded, index.html is", ftp.Size(c, "/public_html/index.html"), "bytes"     ftp.Quit(c)     ftp.Close(c)     ret 0 end This needs a real server, so it is only checked here. Every function that talks to the server leaves the reply in LastCode and LastReply, so after a false you can always print what the server said.  Fetch only the new files List returns one FileInfo per entry with the name, the size and whether it is a directory or a link. Comparing that with what is already on disk turns a full download into a cheap sync, which suits a nightly job that collects reports from a supplier. ftp-sync-down.salamCopyimport ftp import os  func main:     mut c := ftp.DialTLS("files.example.com", 21)     if not ftp.Ok(c) or not ftp.Login(c, "reports", "app-password"):         println "cannot log in:", ftp.LastReply(c)         ret 1     end     _ := ftp.Binary(c)     _ := os.MkdirAll("reports")     mut fetched := 0     mut skipped := 0     each f in ftp.List(c, "/daily"):         if f.is_dir or f.is_link:             continue         end         local := "reports/" + f.name         if os.Exists(local):             skipped++             continue         end         if ftp.Download(c, "/daily/" + f.name, local):             fetched++         else:             println "failed:", f.name, ftp.LastReply(c)         end     end     println "fetched", fetched, "new files, skipped", skipped     ftp.Quit(c)     ftp.Close(c)     ret 0 end For a stricter check than "the file exists", compare f.size with the local size, or ModTime with the time you stored after the last run.  Read a directory listing yourself FTP has no fixed format for listings; most servers send the same columns as ls -l. ParseListLine reads such a line into a FileInfo, which is useful when you get listings from somewhere else, such as a log or a ListRaw call, and want to work with them without a connection. ftp-listing-report.salamCopyimport ftp import str  func main:     raw := "drwxr-xr-x    2 ftp ftp     4096 Jan 01  2026 old
-rw-r--r--    1 ftp ftp   120034 Oct 02 08:10 sales-2026-10-01.csv

rpc rpc JSON-RPC 2.0 and MessagePack-RPC: a server, a client and registering methods. Network With a remote procedure call one program calls another program's methods as if they were its own routines. On the server side you tie each method to a routine with Register; that routine takes the call's number, reads the parameters with CallParamInt and the like, and answers with Reply... or Fail. The messages are exchanged with the JSON codec (JSON-RPC 2.0) or MessagePack, and over TCP they are separated by one of three framings, line, header (like LSP) or length prefixed; the client and the server must have the same framing. HandleText does the same thing without a network, so you can put RPC behind an net.http route. A small service without a network The quickest way to design an RPC API is to build it with HandleText: it takes one JSON-RPC request (or a batch) as text and returns the answer as text, without any network. Every method is an ordinary function that receives a call slot c; it reads parameters with CallParamStr, CallParamInt and their siblings, and must answer exactly once, with a Reply... function or with Fail. rpc-guide-todo.salamCopyimport rpc import encoding.value  mut todos := Vector {} as Vector<str>  func add_todo(c: i64):     title := rpc.CallParamStr(c, "title", 0)     if title == "":         rpc.FailInvalidParams(c, "title is required")         ret     end     todos.Push(title)     rpc.ReplyInt(c, todos.Len()) end  func list_todos(c: i64):     mut items := value.NewValueArray()     each t in todos:         value.ArrayPush(items, value.ValueString(t))     end     rpc.Reply(c, items) end  func count_todos(c: i64):     rpc.ReplyInt(c, todos.Len()) end  func main:     rpc.RegisterDoc("todo.add", add_todo, "adds a todo and returns how many there are")     rpc.RegisterDoc("todo.list", list_todos, "returns every todo")     rpc.Register("todo.count", count_todos)     println rpc.HandleText(`{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"todo.add","params":{"title":"buy bread"},"id":1}`)     println rpc.HandleText(`{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"todo.add","params":["call Sara"],"id":2}`)     println rpc.HandleText(`{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"todo.add","params":{},"id":3}`)     println rpc.HandleText(`{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"todo.list","id":4}`)     println rpc.HandleText(`[{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"todo.count","id":5},{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"todo.delete","id":6}]`)     println rpc.MethodDoc("todo.add")     todos.Free() endOutput{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "result": 1, "id": 1} {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "result": 2, "id": 2} {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "error": {"code": -32602, "message": "title is required"}, "id": 3} {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "result": ["buy bread", "call Sara"], "id": 4} [{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "result": 2, "id": 5}, {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "error": {"code": -32601, "message": "Method not found"}, "id": 6}] adds a todo and returns how many there are Each parameter is looked up by name and by position at the same time: CallParamStr(c, "title", 0) finds {"title": ...} as well as the first element of [...], so clients can use either style. FailInvalidParams answers with the standard code -32602, and a method that was never registered gets -32601 without any code of yours. Inside a batch, each request gets its own answer, failures included. The registry is global for the whole program, so method state, such as the todo list here, lives in a global variable or behind one. If several connections are served in parallel threads, protect that state with a lock from sync.  A server and a client over TCP For two programs, NewServer with port 0 lets the system pick a free port and Port reports it after Listen. ServeCount serves a fixed number of connections and returns, which suits tests; Serve runs until StopServer. Both answer one connection at a time: while a client stays connected, the next one waits in the queue. When several clients must be served at once, accept the connections yourself with net.tcp (tcp.Bind, then tcp.Accept in a loop) and pass each connection's fd to ServeConn in its own thread from thread. On the other side, DialClient connects, Call sends one request and waits for its answer. rpc-guide-tcp.salamCopyimport rpc import encoding.value import sync  mut server := rpc.NewServer(0, rpc.RPC_CODEC_JSON) mut ready := sync.NewWaitGroup()  func convert(c: i64):     amount := rpc.CallParamFloat(c, "amount", 0)     currency := rpc.CallParamStr(c, "to", 1)     if currency == "EUR":         rpc.ReplyFloat(c, amount * 0.5)         ret     end     rpc.Fail(c, -32010, "unknown currency " + currency) end  func run_server():     _ := rpc.Listen(server)     sync.Done(ready)     _ := rpc.ServeCount(server, 1) end  func main:     rpc.Register("convert", convert)     sync.Add(ready, 1)     t := spawn(run_server)     sync.Wait(ready)      mut client := rpc.DialClient("127.0.0.1", rpc.Port(server), rpc.RPC_CODEC_JSON)     if not rpc.ClientOk(client):         println "cannot connect:", rpc.ClientError(client)         ret 1     end     mut params := value.NewValueObject()     value.ObjectSet(params, "amount", value.ValueFloat(40.0))     value.ObjectSet(params, "to", value.ValueStri

grpc grpc A gRPC server and client over HTTP/2: unary and streaming calls, metadata and status codes. Network gRPC is a way of calling a remote procedure that runs over HTTP/2, and it is common in microservices. On the server side you register each method under its path, like /demo.Greeter/SayHello; the method routine reads the client's message with Recv, answers with Send and ends it with SetStatus or Fail. On the client side, UnaryCall is a plain request, and for streams you use StartCall, SendMessage, RecvMessage and FinishCall. Messages are bytes; you usually build them with protobuf. Choose gRPC when the other side already speaks it, or when you want typed messages and streams between services. For a simpler protocol that also works over plain TCP, standard input and output or an HTTP route, see rpc (JSON-RPC and MessagePack-RPC). Limits of the server side to know before you build on it:  The server handles one connection at a time, and on that connection one call at a time: each method runs to the end before the next stream is read. A long streaming call holds up every other caller. That suits internal tools, tests and light services. The server speaks plaintext HTTP/2 (h2c) only. To accept TLS, put a proxy such as nginx or Envoy in front. The client can use TLS with DialTLS. The connection state lives in one global, so ServeConn must not run in several threads at once.  A unary call with protobuf messages Real gRPC services exchange protobuf messages, not plain strings. A message is a list of fields, each written as a tag (field number and wire type) followed by the value; encoding.protobuf writes and reads them. The example defines a Users.Get method that takes a message with the user id in field 1 and answers with a user message: the id in field 1 and the name in field 2. Server and client run in one program, with the server on a port the system picks. grpc-guide-protobuf.salamCopyimport grpc import encoding.protobuf import compress import sync  mut server := grpc.NewServer(0) mut ready := sync.NewWaitGroup()  func encode_user(id: int, name: str): compress.ByteBuf:     mut b := compress.NewByteBuf()     protobuf.WriteTag(b, 1, protobuf.WT_VARINT)     protobuf.WriteVarint(b, id as u64)     protobuf.WriteTag(b, 2, protobuf.WT_LEN)     protobuf.WriteLenPrefixedStr(b, name)     ret b end  func get_user(c: i64):     mut ok := false     req := grpc.Recv(c, ok)     mut r := compress.ReaderFromBuf(req)     mut field := 0     mut wire := 0     mut id := 0     try:         protobuf.ReadTag(r, field, wire)         id = protobuf.ReadVarint(r) as int     catch e:         grpc.Fail(c, grpc.GRPC_INVALID_ARGUMENT, e.ToStr())         ret     end     if field != 1:         grpc.Fail(c, grpc.GRPC_INVALID_ARGUMENT, "expected field 1 with the user id")         ret     end     if id != 7:         grpc.Fail(c, grpc.GRPC_NOT_FOUND, "no user " + id)         ret     end     mut reply := encode_user(7, "Maryam")     _ := grpc.Send(c, reply)     compress.BufFree(reply)     grpc.SetStatus(c, grpc.GRPC_OK, "") end  func run_server():     _ := grpc.Listen(server)     sync.Done(ready)     _ := grpc.ServeCount(server, 1) end  func ask(ch &: grpc.Channel, id: int) throws:     mut req := compress.NewByteBuf()     protobuf.WriteTag(req, 1, protobuf.WT_VARINT)     protobuf.WriteVarint(req, id as u64)     mut st := grpc.Status {}     answer := grpc.UnaryCall(ch, "/users.Users/Get", req, grpc.NewMetadata(), st)     compress.BufFree(req)     if not grpc.StatusOk(st):         println "user", id, "->", grpc.StatusString(st)         ret     end     mut r := compress.ReaderFromBuf(answer)     mut field := 0     mut wire := 0     try protobuf.ReadTag(r, field, wire)     uid := try protobuf.ReadVarint(r)     try protobuf.ReadTag(r, field, wire)     println "user", uid, "is", try protobuf.ReadLenPrefixedStr(r) end  func main throws:     grpc.RegisterMethod(grpc.MethodPath("users.Users", "Get"), get_user)     sync.Add(ready, 1)     t := spawn(run_server)     sync.Wait(ready)     mut ch := grpc.Dial("127.0.0.1", grpc.Port(server))     grpc.SetTimeout(ch, 5000)     try ask(ch, 7)     try ask(ch, 8)     grpc.CloseChannel(ch)     join(t)     grpc.StopServer(server) endOutputuser 7 is Maryam user 8 -> NOT_FOUND: no user 8 MethodPath builds the path /users.Users/Get from the service and method names, which must match what the other side's .proto file says. When the request is wrong or the record does not exist, the method calls Fail with a status code instead of sending a message. The client checks StatusOk before it reads the answer, and StatusString gives a one line description such as NOT_FOUND: no user 8. Writing the fields by hand is fine for small messages. For a larger API, protobuf.GenerateWithServices turns a .proto file into Salam structs with Marshal and Unmarshal functions plus the service code, so the field numbers live in one place.  Tokens in metadata and error status codes gRPC sends credentials and other per call values as metadata, the gRPC name for HTTP/2 headers. The client adds an entry with MDAdd, and the method reads it with MDGet(CallMetadata(c), ...). Choose the status code by what went wrong: GRPC_UNAUTHENTICATED when no valid credential came, GRPC_PERMISSION_DENIED when the caller is known but not allowed. grpc-guide-auth.salamCopyimport grpc import sync import compress  mut server := grpc.NewServer(0) mut ready := sync.NewWaitGroup()  func balance(c: i64):     mut ok := false     account := grpc.RecvStr(c, ok)     token := grpc.MDGet(grpc.CallMetadata(c), "authorization")     if token == "":         grpc.Fail(c, grpc.GRPC_UNAUTHENTICATED, "missing token")         ret     end     if token != "Bearer good-token":         grpc.Fail(c, grpc.GRPC_PERMISSION_DENIED, "this token cannot read " + account)         ret     end     _ := gr

net/httpd net.httpd A web server driven by a config file: several sites on one port, locations, redirects, caching, static files and FastCGI backends such as PHP. Network This package runs several websites from one process and one set of ports, the job people give to nginx in front of their programs. You describe the sites in a config file, load it, and call Run. The command salam serve --config=web.salam does exactly that, and --test checks the file without starting anything. The config is written in the same block style as the rest of Salam: a setting is name = value, a block opens with name: and closes with end, comments start with //, and a setting and its value stay on one line. Strings are in double quotes, or in backticks when they hold backslashes, like a regular expression. server:     log: access = "/var/log/salam/access.log" end     site:         listen = 80         names = "example.com www.example.com"         root = "/srv/example/public"         index = "index.html"         error page = 404 "404.html"         location "/assets/": cache = 30d end         location "= /health": return = 200 "ok" end         location "/old/": redirect = "https://example.com$uri" code = 301 end     end     site:         names = "blog.example.com *.blog.example.com"         root = "/srv/blog"     end end Two sites on the same port are told apart by the Host header. An exact name wins over a *.example.com wildcard, and a request for a name nobody listed goes to the site marked default = true, or else to the first site on that port. A site that does not say listen listens on port 80; listen = "127.0.0.1:8080" picks the address too. Inside a site, the request path is matched against its location blocks the way nginx does it:  location "= /health": this exact path, and nothing else is tried. location "/assets/": any path starting with it; the longest prefix is remembered. location "^~ /static/": a prefix that also stops the regular expressions from being tried. location "~ \.php$" and "~* \.png$": a regular expression (the second ignores case), tried in file order after the prefixes; the first hit wins, and otherwise the longest prefix is used.  The settings of a site, and of a location unless noted:  SettingMeaning  listen = 80 (site)The port, optionally with an address: listen = "0.0.0.0:8080". It can be repeated. names = "a.com b.com" (site)The host names of the site; *.a.com matches any subdomain. default = true (site)This site answers names no site claims. root = "/srv/site"The folder the request path is appended to. A location with its own root replaces the site's. alias = "/srv/files" (prefix location)The folder that replaces the matched prefix: with location "/dl/": alias = "/srv/files" end, /dl/a.zip is /srv/files/a.zip. index = "index.html index.htm"The files tried for a folder, in order. The default is index.html. return = 200 "ok"Answers at once with a status and an optional text. redirect = "https://$host$request_uri", code = 301Redirects. The code defaults to 301. The variables are $host, $uri, $args, $request_uri and $scheme. At the site level it applies to every request, before any location. cache = 30dSends Cache-Control: public, max-age=... with the files. Units: s, m, h, d, w, y. header = "Name" "value"Adds a response header. Site headers go on every answer, location headers only on that location's. error page = 404 "404.html"The file, relative to the root, sent with that error status. fastcgi_pass = "127.0.0.1:9000"Hands the matched requests to a FastCGI backend, such as php-fpm. fastcgi_index = "index.php"The script used when the path ends in /. The default is index.php. fastcgi_timeout = 30sHow long one backend request may take. The default is 30 seconds. fastcgi_param = "NAME" "value"One more CGI variable, with $uri style variables. It can be repeated.  A location can hand the request to a FastCGI backend instead of reading a file, which is how PHP runs behind Salam: server:     site:         listen = 8080         names = "localhost"         root = "/srv/app/public"         location "~ \.php$":             fastcgi_pass = "127.0.0.1:9000"             fastcgi_index = "index.php"             fastcgi_param = "APP_ENV" "production"         end         location "/":             fastcgi_pass = "127.0.0.1:9000"         end     end end fastcgi_pass is the TCP address of php-fpm, or of php-cgi -b 127.0.0.1:9000. The script is root plus the request path; a path ending in / gets fastcgi_index, and a path with segments after an existing script is split into SCRIPT_NAME and PATH_INFO, so /index.php/a/b runs index.php with PATH_INFO=/a/b. A path that names no file answers 404. Salam fills the usual CGI variables: GATEWAY_INTERFACE, SERVER_SOFTWARE, SERVER_PROTOCOL, REQUEST_METHOD, REQUEST_URI, SCRIPT_NAME, SCRIPT_FILENAME, PATH_INFO, DOCUMENT_ROOT, DOCUMENT_URI, QUERY_STRING, CONTENT_TYPE, CONTENT_LENGTH, SERVER_NAME, SERVER_PORT, REMOTE_ADDR, REDIRECT_STATUS, and HTTP_* for Host, User-Agent, Accept, Accept-Language, Accept-Encoding, Cookie, Referer, Authorization, Origin, Cache-Control, If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since, Range, X-Requested-With, X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Real-IP. fastcgi_param adds or overrides one more and understands $host, $uri, $document_uri, $request_uri, $args, $query_string, $document_root, $root, $script_name, $server_port, $remote_addr and $scheme. A value of $header:Name copies that request header into the variable, which is how a header Salam does not forward by default reaches PHP. The answer is whatever the backend sends: the Status: line sets the status, every other header goes out as it is (several Set-Cookie headers included), and the body is passed through byte for byte. A backend that cannot be reached, or that dies halfway, answers 502. The log: block takes access = "path", where the path can also be "stdout" or "stderr". Each line has the time, the host, the method, the path and the status. The things people get wrong:  Files are only read fr

net/httpd/conf net.httpd.conf The reader of the web server config: blocks, settings and values in Salam block syntax, with positions for errors. Network This package reads text written in the block style that net.httpd uses for its config, and gives back a tree. It knows nothing about web servers: it only recognises the shapes, and net.httpd decides which names are valid. You can use it for settings files of your own that look like Salam. There are two shapes. A setting is a name, an equals sign and one or more values on the same line: max connections = 100. A block is a name, optional strings, a colon, its contents and end: location "/api/": cache = 1h end. A name may be several words (error page), values are strings in double quotes (with 
, 	, " and \), strings in backticks (taken as written, so a regular expression needs no doubling of backslashes), numbers with an optional unit such as 64mb or 30d, and plain words such as tls. Comments are // to the end of the line, or /* ... */. Everything lives in a Doc, a list of nodes that point at each other by number: node 0 is the root, Find and ChildAt move down, and the fields of a node hold its words, labels, values and children. Free the document with Free when you are done with it. The things people get wrong:  A value list ends at the end of the line, at end, or where the next setting starts on the same line, so a = 1 b = 2 is two settings. A bare word at the end of a list is read as a value, which is why listen = 443 tls works. A parse stops at the first error, and ok is then false. The error has the line and the column, and ErrorText puts them in front of the message the way compilers do. Addresses and anything with a colon in it need quotes: listen = "127.0.0.1:8080". Without them the colon would read as the start of a block. A node's words hold its name, so Name joins them with single spaces. Block labels, such as the path of a location, are in labels, not in the name.  Parse a config and read a value Parse returns a Doc. Check ok first, then walk down from the root: Find returns the number of the first child with a given name, and ValueText reads one value of a setting by position. A node number of -1 means the child was not found. net-httpd-conf-guide-parse.salamCopyimport net.httpd.conf  func main:     text := ` server:     max connections = 100     site:         listen = 8080         names = "a.test"     end end `     mut d := conf.Parse(text)     defer conf.Free(d)     if not d.ok:         println conf.ErrorText(d, "app.salam")         ret 1     end     server := conf.Find(d, conf.Root(), "server")     println conf.Name(d, server), conf.Count(d, server)     limit := conf.Find(d, server, "max connections")     println conf.ValueText(d, limit, 0)     site := conf.Find(d, server, "site")     println conf.ValueText(d, conf.Find(d, site, "names"), 0) endOutputserver 2 100 a.test The setting name max connections has two words and is found by that full name with a single space. Always free the document, here with defer, because the nodes are heap memory.  Walk the children and tell the kinds apart To go through everything in a block, use Count and ChildAt, then look at the node itself in d.nodes. A block has block set and its strings in labels; a setting has its values, and each value has a kind that is VAL_WORD, VAL_STR or VAL_NUM, plus the line and column where it was written. net-httpd-conf-guide-walk.salamCopyimport net.httpd.conf  func main:     text := ` server:     site:         listen = 80 tls         names = "a.test"         location "/api/": cache = 1h end     end end `     mut d := conf.Parse(text)     defer conf.Free(d)     site := conf.Find(d, conf.Find(d, conf.Root(), "server"), "site")     repeat conf.Count(d, site) in i:         n := d.nodes.Get(conf.ChildAt(d, site, i))         if n.block:             println "block", conf.Name(d, conf.ChildAt(d, site, i)), n.labels.Get(0), n.line         else:             v := n.values.Get(0)             println "setting", conf.Name(d, conf.ChildAt(d, site, i)), v.text, v.kind == conf.VAL_NUM         end     end endOutputsetting listen 80 true setting names a.test false block location /api/ 6 80 is a number, and tls, which follows it on the same line, is a second value of the same setting. The numbers keep their unit as text, so 30d is one VAL_NUM value whose text is 30d; turning it into seconds is up to the program that owns the config.  Report errors with their position The parser stops at the first error and sets ok to false. ErrorText turns it into file:line:column: message, with the file name you pass in, so a user can jump straight to the spot. net-httpd-conf-guide-errors.salamCopyimport net.httpd.conf  func check(text: str):     mut d := conf.Parse(text)     defer conf.Free(d)     if d.ok:         println "ok"     else:         println conf.ErrorText(d, "app.salam")     end end  func main:     check("listen = 80
