net/fastcgi net.fastcgi A FastCGI client: run PHP or any FastCGI program behind a Salam server. Network FastCGI is the protocol php-fpm and php-cgi -b speak, and this package is a client for it. The web server in net.httpd uses it for the fastcgi_pass setting; you can also use it directly when a program has to hand one request to a PHP script. A request is a list of CGI variables and a body. NewParams makes the list, Add fills it, Connect opens a TCP connection to the backend, and Execute sends everything and waits for the answer. The answer holds the status, every header in the order the backend sent them, and the body as a pointer with a length, so an image or a zip comes back intact. // lang: en package main  import net.fastcgi import net.tcp  func main:     p := fastcgi.NewParams()     defer fastcgi.Free(p)     fastcgi.Add(p, "GATEWAY_INTERFACE", "CGI/1.1")     fastcgi.Add(p, "REQUEST_METHOD", "GET")     fastcgi.Add(p, "SCRIPT_NAME", "/index.php")     fastcgi.Add(p, "SCRIPT_FILENAME", "/srv/app/index.php")     fastcgi.Add(p, "QUERY_STRING", "a=1")      c := fastcgi.Connect("127.0.0.1", 9000, 5000)     if not tcp.ConnOk(c):         println "cannot reach the FastCGI backend"         ret 1     end     defer tcp.Close(c)      r := fastcgi.Execute(c, p, null, 0, 5000)     if not r.ok:         println "the request failed: ", r.error         ret 1     end     println r.status, " ", r.len, " bytes"     fastcgi.FreeResponse(r)     ret 0 end One connection carries one request, which is what php-fpm expects from a simple front end. The timeout is in milliseconds and covers the whole exchange, dialling included; zero means 30 seconds. A backend that closes the connection early, a response without a header block, or a protocol error comes back as ok = false with a message in error, never as a crash. The things people get wrong:  Execute takes the body as a pointer and a length. With no body, pass null and 0; an empty string is not a pointer. Add copies the name and the value, so a temporary string can be freed as soon as Add returns, and Free releases every copy. The body of the answer belongs to the response: call FreeResponse when done with it, or the buffer stays allocated. The address is TCP. php-fpm has to listen on a port such as 127.0.0.1:9000, not on a unix socket, and the CGI variables are yours to fill: a backend needs at least SCRIPT_FILENAME and REQUEST_METHOD to answer. The backend's stderr is not an error. A PHP warning on stderr does not fail the request; only a broken or missing response does.  Describe the request with CGI variables PHP learns about a request only through the variables you send. Make a list with NewParams, add each name and value with Add, and free the list at the end. The items keep the order in which they were added, and Add copies both strings. net-fastcgi-guide-params.salamCopyimport net.fastcgi  func main:     mut p := fastcgi.NewParams()     defer fastcgi.Free(p)     fastcgi.Add(p, "GATEWAY_INTERFACE", "CGI/1.1")     fastcgi.Add(p, "REQUEST_METHOD", "POST")     fastcgi.Add(p, "SCRIPT_FILENAME", "/srv/app/index.php")     fastcgi.Add(p, "SCRIPT_NAME", "/index.php")     fastcgi.Add(p, "QUERY_STRING", "page=2")     fastcgi.Add(p, "CONTENT_TYPE", "application/json")     fastcgi.Add(p, "CONTENT_LENGTH", "13")     each item in p.items:         println item.name + "=" + item.value     end endOutputGATEWAY_INTERFACE=CGI/1.1 REQUEST_METHOD=POST SCRIPT_FILENAME=/srv/app/index.php SCRIPT_NAME=/index.php QUERY_STRING=page=2 CONTENT_TYPE=application/json CONTENT_LENGTH=13 A backend needs at least REQUEST_METHOD and SCRIPT_FILENAME; the other names here are what PHP code usually reads from $_SERVER. For a request with a body, CONTENT_LENGTH must be the exact number of bytes you will send.  Send the request to php-fpm and read the answer Open a connection with Connect and test it with tcp.ConnOk, then call Execute with the connection, the variables, the body and a timeout in milliseconds. A GET has no body, so the body is null and the length 0. net/nats net.nats A NATS client: publish and subscribe, request and reply, queue groups, automatic reconnection, JetStream and a key value helper. Network NATS is a small, fast message bus. Programs publish messages to subjects such as orders.eu.new, other programs subscribe to subjects or patterns, and the server delivers. This package is a client for the core protocol, request and reply, queue groups, headers, JetStream streams and consumers, and a simple key value helper. It speaks the text protocol over TCP or TLS and needs nothing but the standard library. The model: Connect opens a connection and you pass it by reference to every call. Nothing runs in the background. Messages are read, handlers are called and PINGs are answered only while you call Pump, NextMsg, Flush, Request or Fetch, so a program that stops calling them stops answering the server. Failures are values: a call returns false, or a message whose ok is false with the reason in err.  Subjects are tokens joined by dots. * matches one token and a final > matches the rest, in subscriptions only. Queue groups split a subject among workers: each message goes to one member. Payloads are text. A str stops at its first NUL byte, so send binary data encoded, for example with Base64.   Connecting Connect takes a URL such as nats://127.0.0.1:4222; tls:// turns TLS on, and nats://user:password@host or nats://token@host carries credentials. ConnectWith takes an Options value for the rest. A failed connection is a connection with ok false, so check IsConnected and read LastError. mut nc := nats.Connect("nats://127.0.0.1:4222") if not nats.IsConnected(nc):     println nats.LastError(nc) end  Publishing and subscribing Subscribe returns a handle; NextMsg waits for its next message. Or give SubscribeHandler a function and let Pump call it. Flush sends a PING and waits for the PONG, which proves the server has received everything you published before it. sub := nats.Subscribe(nc, "greet.*") nats.Publish(nc, "greet.bob", "hello") m := nats.NextMsg(nc, sub, 1000) println m.subject, m.data  Headers A Header carries key and value pairs next to the payload. NewHeader makes one, HeaderAdd appends a value, HeaderSet replaces the values of a key, HeaderGet and HeaderValues read them, and HeaderEncode and HeaderParse turn a header to and from its wire form. net-nats-headers.salamCopyimport net.nats  func main:     mut h := nats.NewHeader()     nats.HeaderAdd(h, "Trace", "a1")     nats.HeaderAdd(h, "Trace", "b2")     nats.HeaderSet(h, "Tenant", "acme")     println nats.HeaderGet(h, "Tenant"), nats.HeaderCount(h), nats.HeaderHas(h, "Trace")     println nats.ValidSubject("orders.created"), nats.ValidSubject("bad subject") endOutputacme 3 true true false  Subjects and wildcards A subscription may use two wildcards: * stands for exactly one word and > for one or more words at the end. So orders.* matches orders.created but not orders.created.eu, and orders.> matches both but not orders alone. SubjectMatches applies the same rule locally, which makes it handy in tests. ValidSubject rejects an empty name, spaces and control characters, a leading or trailing dot and an empty word between two dots. It returns a Msg, so check ok before reading data. When nothing is subscribed to the subject the server says so and err is no responders; when somebody is subscribed but does not answer in time it is timeout. SubscribeReplier takes a function from a message to the reply text. Nothing runs in the background: handlers run while the connection is being pumped, which Request, NextMsg, Flush and Pump all do. net/tunnel net.tunnel The shared core for proxy and VPN style tools: streams, addresses, dialers and proxy chains, a mixed inbound, routing rules with an Iran preset, share links and v2ray style configs. Network This package is the common core of Salam's proxy tools. It does not speak one proxy protocol itself. It gives the packages of this family one shared shape, so any inbound (the side that accepts clients) can be joined to any outbound (the side that reaches the world): net.socks, net.httpproxy and net.trojan all plug into it, and so will the protocol packages that follow. To see how the pieces fit together in an app, read Building a v2ray style or VPN app. It is a toolkit for a proxy, not for a system wide VPN: there is no virtual network interface, so an application has to be pointed at the local port (SOCKS or HTTP) or be proxy aware. Its purpose is privacy and access to information. Use it on networks and with servers you are allowed to use, and keep the people who rely on it safe. application  ->  inbound  ->  router  ->  outbound  ->  remote server  ->  target              mixed       rules      direct, proxy chain, block              SOCKS/HTTP  .ir direct  Core ideas:  A Stream is a two way byte connection. TCP, TLS, WebSocket and in memory pipes all look the same, so a protocol or a relay never cares what is underneath. An Addr is a target: a host name or IP and a port. Every dialer and every inbound speaks in Addr values. A Dialer opens an outgoing connection. DirectDialer, BlockDialer, Chain (several proxy hops in a row), Fallback and RouterDialer are all dialers, and they nest. A Connector is one proxy hop that a chain can use. An InboundProtocol reads a client's request and answers it; ListenTcp accepts connections and a Handler (usually ForwardHandler) serves them. MixedProtocol puts SOCKS4, SOCKS5 and HTTP proxy on one port. A Router turns a target into a tag (direct, proxy, block) using ordered rules, with IranRouter as a ready preset. ParseLink and ParseSubscription read vmess://, vless://, trojan:// and ss:// share links, and ParseConfig reads v2ray style JSON.  Things that catch people out:  Failure is a closed stream, not an exception. A dial that fails returns a stream whose Ok is false. Check it before you write. A config does not build protocols by itself. BuildDialer knows freedom (direct) and blackhole (block). Any other outbound protocol needs a maker registered with RegisterOutbound; until one is, that outbound refuses traffic instead of leaking it. The packages in this family give you dialers and connectors you can build in code, as the guide below does. It is TCP. Streams carry TCP. UDP relays are the business of the individual protocol packages. Examples use IPv4 loopback; tests cover IPv6 too. Listeners accept ::1 and :: (both families), DirectDialer reaches IPv6 targets and races IPv6 and IPv4 addresses of a name, and the per-source limit treats IPv4-mapped clients as IPv4 and groups IPv6 clients by their /64 prefix. Share links are untrusted input. ParseLink rejects what it cannot read, but a subscription comes from someone else's server. Look at allow_insecure before you trust a node. A Stats value and a IdleTimer own native counters. Free them with FreeStats and Free when you are done.   Building a v2ray style or VPN app A v2ray style app is a small pipeline: something accepts the application's connection (inbound), something decides where it should go (router), and something carries it there (outbound). In Salam each piece is a value, and this package joins them.               +--------------------------- your process ----------------------------+ application   |  inbound          router              outbound                   |   remote server (browser,     |  MixedProtocol  Router            Dialer                   |   (trojan, ...)  curl, app) -> |  SOCKS4/5 + HTTP  rules decide a tag  direct                    | ->      | 127.0.0.1:1080|  -> Session      .ir, private: direct  Via(hop), Chain         |           -> target               |     target Addr everything else: proxy BlockDialer           |               +----------------------------------------------------------------------+                          ForwardHandler relays bytes both ways (Relay) The example runs this whole pipeline on loopback. net/socks net.socks SOCKS4, SOCKS4a and SOCKS5: a client with login, BIND and UDP associate, a server with users, access rules and a pluggable way to reach targets, and a connector for proxy chains. Network SOCKS is the plain, widely supported proxy protocol: a program asks a proxy to connect somewhere on its behalf and then talks through the connection as if it were direct. This package has both sides. Connect is the client; Start runs a server. It also plugs into net.tunnel, as a Socks5Inbound or Socks4Inbound that can share one port with an HTTP proxy, and as a SocksConnector that is one hop of a proxy chain. To see how the pieces fit together in an app, read Building a v2ray style or VPN app. Core ideas:  A client is a value: NewClient or NewClientAuth fills a Client, and Connect returns a ConnectResult with a stream. Failure is a value too: ok is false and code and err say why. SOCKS5 is the default. Set version to Socks4 or Socks4a for older servers. SOCKS4 sends an IPv4 address; SOCKS4a lets the server resolve a name. A name sent to a SOCKS5 or SOCKS4a proxy is resolved by the proxy, so the lookup does not happen on your machine. A server is a ServerConfig given to Start. How it reaches targets is a callback (SetConnector) or a tunnel.Dialer (SetDialer), which is how it is joined to routing rules and proxy chains. Associate opens a UDP relay and Bind waits for an incoming connection. Both are SOCKS5 features the server can switch off.  Things that catch people out:  A server listens on bind_host, which is 127.0.0.1 by default. Set it to 0.0.0.0 (or an address) only on purpose. A SOCKS server without a login that is reachable from outside is an open proxy anyone can abuse. Require a user (AddUser), restrict it with a firewall, or put it behind a tunnel. The login is not encrypted. SOCKS5 user name and password travel in clear text. Use it on a local port or through an encrypted tunnel, or set tls when the proxy is reachable over TLS. The server side of this package speaks plain TCP only. SOCKS4 has no passwords. A server that requires logins refuses SOCKS4 clients, and allow_v4 can switch SOCKS4 off. allow_bind is off by default because BIND makes the proxy open a listening port for the client, and a UDP relay does the same with a UDP port. Those sockets are bound to bind_host too, and that is the address reported to the client. UDP has no fragments. Only fragment 0 is supported, and there is no UDP over SOCKS4. IPv6 works end to end. TCP CONNECT, BIND and the UDP relay carry IPv6 targets (address type 4), and the server can listen on ::1 or on :: for both families. A UDP relay bound to an IPv4 address still reaches IPv6 targets through a second outbound socket. SOCKS4 stays IPv4. Close streams. A stream is an open connection. Close it when you are done.   Using a SOCKS proxy from a program Make a client for the proxy, connect to a target, and use the stream. The proxy here is a local server so the example runs anywhere; in real use it is the address of the proxy you trust. net-socks-guide-client.salamCopyimport net.socks import net.tcp  func echo_conn(arg: i64):     c := tcp.ConnFromFd(arg)     until true:         data := tcp.Read(c, 4096)         if data.Len() == 0:             break         end         tcp.Write(c, data)     end     tcp.Close(c) end  func echo_accept(arg: i64):     srv := tcp.Server { fd = arg }     until true:         c := tcp.Accept(srv)         if not tcp.ConnOk(c):             break         end         socks.Go(echo_conn, c.fd as void*)     end end  func start_echo(): int:     listener := tcp.Bind(0)     socks.Go(echo_accept, listener.fd as void*)     ret tcp.Port(listener) end  func main:     target := start_echo()     mut proxy_cfg := socks.NewServerConfig(0)     socks.AllowPrivate(proxy_cfg, true)     proxy := socks.Start(proxy_cfg)      client := socks.NewClient("127.0.0.1", proxy.port)     result := socks.Connect(client, "127.0.0.1", target)     if not result.ok:         println "the proxy said no:", result.code, result.err         ret     end     result.stream.Write("hello from behind the proxy")     println result.stream.Read(100)     result.stream.Close()     socks.Stop(proxy) endOutputhello from behind the proxy DialConn does the same but returns a plain TCP connection for code that already uses net.tcp. Through a proxy that needs a login use NewClientAuth. To go through two proxies in a row, see tunnel.Chain and the chain example below.  Running a SOCKS server NewServerConfig gives a config for a port; AddUser turns the login on; Start binds and returns at once, and Stop ends it. How the server reaches a target is the part you usually change: leave DirectConnect for a plain proxy, set a callback with SetConnector to route by name, or give it a tunnel.Dialer with SetDialer to use rules, chains and block lists from net.tunnel. allow can refuse commands, hosts or ports before any connection is made. To put SOCKS on the same port as an HTTP proxy, give a Socks5Inbound to a tunnel.MixedProtocol instead of calling Start. Handle serves a single stream you accepted yourself. mut config := socks.NewServerConfig(1080) socks.AddUser(config, "alice", "a long random password") server := socks.Start(config) if not server.ok:     println "port 1080 is busy" end  What to know  The server listens on bind_host (loopback by default). Use a login or a firewall, never an open proxy. The login is plain text. SOCKS4 has no login at all. Names are resolved by the proxy for SOCKS5 and SOCKS4a, and by the client for SOCKS4. Start runs the accept loop on its own thread; connections run on further threads. Stop stops new clients only. The decoders (DecodeRequest, DecodeReply, Decode4Request, DecodeAddress) return the bytes used, 0 for "need more data" and -1 for invalid, so they work on a growing buffer. No logging happens by itself.  Types Addressstruct AddressA host and port as SOCKS sees them: the address type, the text of the host a

net/trojan net.trojan The Trojan protocol: a TLS client and server that look like an ordinary HTTPS site, a fallback website for everyone who is not a client, WebSocket mode, UDP and a connector for proxy chains. Network Trojan is a proxy protocol built to look like nothing. A client opens a normal TLS connection to a server and sends one line that holds a password hash and the target it wants; if the hash is right the server connects there and relays bytes. If the first bytes are not a valid Trojan request, the server does not complain. It hands the connection, bytes and all, to an ordinary website, so a visitor or a probe gets a real page from a real site. This package has both sides: Dial is the client and Serve runs the server. It also plugs into net.tunnel as an Inbound and a Connector for routing and proxy chains. To see how the pieces fit together in an app, read Building a v2ray style or VPN app. Core ideas:  A password is never sent. What goes on the wire is its SHA-224 hash (PasswordHash), as 56 hex characters. The server keeps hashes (AddPassword, AddPasswordHash). TLS does the hiding. The Trojan request is inside the TLS stream, and a server with a valid certificate and a real fallback_port website looks like any HTTPS site. Failure is silent. A wrong password, a browser, a scanner: all get the fallback site. fallbacks counts them. A Link is a connection over TCP, TLS or WebSocket. Dial returns one; read and write it with LinkRead and LinkWriteStr, and close it with LinkClose. use_ws carries Trojan inside a WebSocket so that a CDN or reverse proxy can sit in front. DialUDP opens a UDP session where every packet names its own target (SendUDP, ReadUDPPacket).  Things that catch people out:  Use TLS, with a real certificate. Serve is the real server. ServePlain and ServeWS have no TLS: the password hash and all traffic are readable by anyone on the path, and the hash can be replayed. Use them on loopback, in tests, or behind a reverse proxy that ends TLS. insecure switches certificate checking off; never use it outside a test. The fallback site must be real. A fallback that is missing, empty or obviously fake makes the server easy to recognise. Without fallback_port, a failed client is just disconnected, which is itself a sign. Serve real content, on the same machine, with the same certificate name. WebSocket mode has no fallback. A failed client of ServeWS is simply closed. Let the reverse proxy in front decide what the outside world sees. No replay protection. The request holds no nonce, so anyone who can read it (a plain connection, a broken certificate check) can replay it. net.censor has a censor.ReplayCache and a censor.ProbeGuard, but this package does not use them for you. Where a server listens. Serve (ModeTLS) listens on every IPv4 interface because it is the public face of the server, so use long random passwords. ServePlain and ServeWS listen on 127.0.0.1 unless bind_host says otherwise; give 0.0.0.0 only when something you control reaches them from outside. The password and its hash are equivalent. Whoever has the hash can authenticate. Protect the config like a password file. A Link is not a tunnel.Stream. Link is the package's own connection type. For tunnel.Chain and routing use the Connector and Inbound adapters, which work on streams.   A server, a client and a fallback This runs the whole idea on loopback with no certificate: a Trojan server in front of an echo server, with a web server as the fallback. The real client gets the echo; anyone else sends ordinary web traffic to the same port and gets the web page. In production Serve adds TLS in front of exactly this behaviour. net-trojan-guide-loopback.salamCopyimport mem import net.tcp import net.trojan import sync  mut echo_port := 0 mut web_port := 0 mut web_seen := "" mut ready := sync.NewWaitGroup()  func echo_server():     srv := tcp.Bind(0)     echo_port = tcp.Port(srv)     sync.Done(ready)     until true:         c := tcp.Accept(srv)         until true:             data := tcp.Read(c, 4096)             if data.Len() == 0:                 break             end             tcp.Write(c, "echo:" + data)         end         tcp.Close(c)     end end  func web_server():     srv := tcp.Bind(0)     web_port = tcp.Port(srv)     sync.Done(ready)     until true:         c := tcp.Accept(srv)         web_seen = tcp.Read(c, 4096)         tcp.Write(c, "HTTP/1.1 200 OK

net/doh net.doh Encrypted DNS: a resolver over DNS over HTTPS and DNS over TLS with server failover and a TTL cache, plain UDP DNS as a fallback, presets, and a local stub server for other programs. Network Ordinary DNS asks "what is the address of this name?" in plain text over UDP, so the network between you and the resolver can read every name you look up, and can change or block the answer. DNS over HTTPS (DoH) and DNS over TLS (DoT) send the same question inside an encrypted connection. This package speaks both, and plain UDP DNS too, and adds what a program needs on top: a Resolver that tries a list of servers in order, remembers answers for their TTL and answers LookupHost with a list of addresses. A Stub turns the resolver into a small local DNS server, so other programs can use it by pointing their DNS at it. To see how the pieces fit together in an app, read Building a v2ray style or VPN app. Core ideas:  A Server says how to reach one DNS server: KindDoH (HTTPS POST), KindDoHGet (HTTPS GET), KindDoT (TLS on port 853) or KindUDP (plain). Cloudflare, Google, Quad9 and their DoT forms are ready made, and NewServer, NewDoT and NewPlain make your own. Give a server its IP addresses in addrs. Then the program does not need to resolve the server's own name first, which matters when DNS is exactly what is blocked. Query asks one server once. NewResolver and Resolve ask a list: a server that fails, times out or answers SERVFAIL or REFUSED is skipped for the next, and answers are cached (an answer for its TTL, kept between the limits of SetTTLLimits; a "no such name" answer for a short fixed time). Certificates are checked. insecure turns that off for tests only.  Things that catch people out:  Encrypted DNS hides the question from the network, not from the resolver. The resolver you pick sees every name you look up. Choose one you trust, and remember that connecting to a well known resolver address is itself visible. Blocked resolvers. A network can block the addresses of public DoH servers. Use several servers, keep a plain or private one as the last in the list, and see IranPlainServers for the plain servers used in Iran. Plain DNS is readable and can be changed on the way. No DNSSEC. Answers are trusted as the server gave them; nothing here checks DNSSEC signatures. The stub answers on UDP and TCP (the same port, TCP with the two byte length prefix) and has no access control. It listens on 127.0.0.1 when the host is empty; give 0.0.0.0 only on purpose, because an open DNS server on a public address is abused. Free what you hold. FreeResponse, FreeAnswer and FreeServers release memory; a Resolver and a Stub live until the program ends. The cache and counters are shared across threads and the resolver takes its own lock, so one resolver can serve many threads. IPv6 resolvers work. A server address may be an IPv6 literal, over UDP, TLS or HTTPS. The built-in servers list IPv4 first; WithIPv6, Cloudflare6, Google6 and Quad96 add or use the IPv6 addresses (2606:4700:4700::1111, 2001:4860:4860::8888, 2620:fe::fe). The local stub can listen on ::1 or ::. Connections are reused. DoH over HTTPS keeps its connections alive and reuses them for later queries (up to 8 idle ones, for 30 seconds); a stale one is replaced by a new connection and the query is repeated once. ReusedConnections counts the reuses and CloseIdleConnections closes the idle ones. Iran presets are unverified. The addresses of Shecan, Server403, Electro, Radar and Begzar come from community lists and could not be confirmed against the official sites of those services. Check them before relying on them.   Using a resolver Make a Resolver from a list of servers and ask it. The second lookup of the same name comes from the cache and does not touch the network. The example uses a tiny DNS server on loopback so that it runs anywhere; with real servers use DefaultServers or your own list. net-doh-guide-resolver.salamCopyimport compress import mem import net/censor net.censor Helpers for networks that interfere with traffic: protocol sniffing and TLS server name reading, ClientHello fragmentation, padding, domain rule sets with Iran lists, a probe guard and a replay cache. Network Some networks do not just carry traffic. They look at it: the first bytes of a connection tell a filter which protocol it is, and the server name in the first TLS message tells it which site you are going to. This package is a set of small helpers, each independent of the others, for working with that. Sniff and ParseClientHello read what a filter would read. FragmentClientHello and SNISplitSizes cut that first message into pieces, so that a filter that only looks at one packet never sees the whole name. DomainSet and Classifier decide, from rules, which hosts go direct, through a proxy or nowhere. ProbeGuard, ReplayCache and DecoyResponse are the pieces of a server that does not give itself away to someone who is trying it. To see how the pieces fit together in an app, read Building a v2ray style or VPN app. It does not open any connection and has no state of its own. It works on bytes and text you give it, so it fits in front of any of the proxy packages: net.tunnel, net.socks, net.httpproxy, net.trojan. None of them calls it for you; you wire it in where you need it. Core ideas:  Sniff needs only the first few bytes and says KindTLS, KindHTTP, KindSSH, KindSOCKS5 or KindSOCKS4, or KindTooShort when it cannot tell yet. ParseClientHello reads a TLS ClientHello without a TLS library: server name, offered protocols, whether Encrypted Client Hello is present. Fragmenting is a plan plus a cut. SplitSizes or SNISplitSizes make the plan (sizes that add up to the total), Slice cuts bytes into plain pieces and FragmentRecords cuts one TLS record into several records. FragmentClientHello does the whole job for a ClientHello. Padding hides sizes: WrapRecord and WrapStream add random padding inside records that look like TLS application data, and UnwrapRecord takes it off. A DomainSet holds domain rules (example.com, full:name, keyword:word); a Classifier has three of them and a default and answers DecisionProxy, DecisionDirect or DecisionBlock.  Things that catch people out:  Fragmentation is not encryption and not magic. It helps against filters that look at the first packet or the first record only. Filters change, and many networks reassemble. Test it on the network you actually use, and do not rely on it alone. Padding is not encryption either. WrapStream hides how large the pieces are, not what is in them. Use it inside TLS or another encrypted channel, never in place of one. The padded records use TLS looking headers of this package's own making: they will not pass for real TLS to a careful observer. Fragment before TLS goes out, at the start only. The cut goes on the first record of a handshake. A connection already running is not affected. The Iran lists are starting points. IranDirectList and FilteredList are short, human edited lists that age. Treat them as examples to edit, and keep your own list in a file for AddRules. ProbeGuard and ReplayCache have no lock. They are plain data. When several threads use one, wrap the calls in your own lock. They do not stop a probe by themselves: you call them from your server's accept path. ShouldFallback is a single comparison. A server that has a real website to show is what does the hiding; see the Trojan package. Randomness is secure. RandomInt and RandomBytes draw from the system's secure source. SplitRandom is the one exception: with a seed it is repeatable on purpose, which makes it fine for tests and a poor choice for hiding a pattern.   Fragmenting a TLS hello A client sends its first TLS message as one record. SNISplitSizes finds the server name in it and plans a cut in the middle of the name; Slice cuts the bytes, and the pieces are sent one after another, each in its own packet. A server reads them as one stream and sees the same message. The example sends a ClientHello in two pieces over loopback and shows what the receiving side reads. net-censor-guide-fragment.salamCopyimport net.censor import net.tcp import sync  const HELLO := "160301008c010000880303000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f101112131415161718191a1b1c1d1e1f206465666768696a6b6c6d6e6f707172737475767778797a7b7c7d7e7f80818283000613011302c02b0100003900000014001200000f7777772e6578616d706c652e636f6d000a00040002001d0010000e000c02683208687474702f312e31002b0003020304"  mut port := 0 mut seen := "" mut ready := sync.NewWaitGroup()  func server():     srv := tcp.Bind(0)     port = tcp.Port(srv)     sync.Done(ready)     c := tcp.Accept(srv)     tcp.SetReadDeadline(c, 1500)     until true:         data := tcp.Read(c, 4096)         if data.Len() == 0:             break         end         seen += data.Len() + " "     end     tcp.Close(c) end  func main:     sync.Add(ready, 1 as i64)     t := spawn(server)     sync.Wait(ready)      hello := censor.FromHex(HELLO)     sizes := censor.SNISplitSizes(hello.data, hello.len, false)     mut pieces := censor.Slice(hello.data, hello.len, sizes)     println "server name starts at byte", censor.ParseClientHello(hello.data, hello.len).sni_offset, "and is cut after", sizes.Get(0), "bytes"      conn := tcp.Dial("127.0.0.1", port)     tcp.SetNoDelay(conn, true)     repeat pieces.Len() in i:         piece := pieces.Get(i)         tcp.WriteBytes(conn, piece.data, piece.len)         sync.SleepMs(60)     end     tcp.Close(conn)     join(t)     println "the server read:", seen     println "pieces sent:", pieces.Len()     censor.FreePieces(pieces) endOutputserver name starts at byte 97 and is cut after 104 bytes the server read: 3 8  pieces sent: 2 That cuts the bytes of the stream, which any TCP server reassembles. net/shadowsocks net.shadowsocks A Shadowsocks client and server: AEAD and Shadowsocks 2022 ciphers, ss:// links, simple-obfs, a UDP relay, and a stream that runs over any tunnel.Stream. Network Shadowsocks is a small encrypted proxy protocol. A client connects to a Shadowsocks server and says which host and port it wants to reach; the server connects there and carries bytes both ways. Everything after the first byte looks like random data, so there is no handshake to recognise. net.shadowsocks is a client and a server for it written in Salam, with no native library. It is one of the proxy packages built on net.tunnel and can be plugged into the same routers and chains as the others. The main calls are few. Dial opens a Conn through a server to a target such as example.com:443; Read, Write and Close then work like on any socket. Listen starts a server and Serve or ServeRelay answers clients. Config holds the server address, the cipher method, the password and the optional obfs disguise. Everything else (Buf, Encoder, Decoder, the BLAKE3 and key functions) is the lower level the protocol is built from, public so you can test it or build your own framing.  Quick start This program starts a server on a free port, connects a client through it to example.com:443 and sends one message. The handler never connects to example.com; it only reads the target the client asked for with TargetOf and echoes the bytes back, so the whole run stays on the loopback interface. Stop wakes the accept loop so that Serve returns, and Destroy frees the server. net-shadowsocks-guide-loopback.salamCopyimport mem import net.shadowsocks  const PASSWORD := "correct horse"  mut srv := shadowsocks.Server {} mut seen := ""  func answer(c: shadowsocks.Conn):     t := shadowsocks.TargetOf(c)     seen = t.host + ":" + t.port     buf := mem.Allocate(4096 as u64)     n := shadowsocks.Read(c, buf, 4096)     shadowsocks.Write(c, buf, n)     mem.Free(buf)     shadowsocks.Close(c) end  func serve():     shadowsocks.Serve(srv, (c: shadowsocks.Conn): answer(c) end) end  func main:     srv = shadowsocks.Listen(0, "chacha20-ietf-poly1305", PASSWORD)     println shadowsocks.ServerOk(srv)     t := spawn(serve)      cfg := shadowsocks.Config { host = "127.0.0.1", port = shadowsocks.ServerPort(srv), method = "chacha20-ietf-poly1305", password = PASSWORD }     c := shadowsocks.Dial(cfg, "example.com", 443)     println shadowsocks.Ok(c)     shadowsocks.WriteStr(c, "hello through shadowsocks")     println shadowsocks.ReadStr(c, 4096)     shadowsocks.Close(c)      shadowsocks.Stop(srv)     join(t)     shadowsocks.Destroy(srv)     println "server saw", seen endOutputtrue true hello through shadowsocks server saw example.com:443 A real server uses ServeRelay, which does the forwarding for you: for each client it connects to the requested target and copies bytes in both directions until either side closes. The next example runs a relay in front of a small TCP echo server and sends a message through it. net-shadowsocks-guide-relay.salamCopyimport mem import net.tcp import net.shadowsocks  mut target := tcp.Server {} mut srv := shadowsocks.Server {}  func echo():     c := tcp.Accept(target)     buf := mem.Allocate(4096 as u64)     n := tcp.ReadBytes(c, buf, 4096)     tcp.WriteBytes(c, buf, n)     mem.Free(buf)     tcp.Close(c) end  func serve():     shadowsocks.ServeRelay(srv) end  func main:     target = tcp.Bind(0)     te := spawn(echo)      srv = shadowsocks.Listen(0, "aes-256-gcm", "relay password")     ts := spawn(serve)      cfg := shadowsocks.Config { host = "127.0.0.1", port = shadowsocks.ServerPort(srv), method = "aes-256-gcm", password = "relay password" }     c := shadowsocks.Dial(cfg, "127.0.0.1", tcp.Port(target))     shadowsocks.WriteStr(c, "through the relay")     println shadowsocks.ReadStr(c, 4096)     shadowsocks.Close(c)      join(te)     shadowsocks.Stop(srv)     join(ts)     shadowsocks.Destroy(srv)     tcp.CloseServer(target) endOutputthrough the relay The client side is just Dial with a Config. Dial returns at once without waiting for the server: the target address travels in the first encrypted packet together with your first Write. So a wrong password is not reported by Dial; the server drops the connection and your first Read returns 0 or a negative number. Check Ok for a connection that could not even start (an unknown method, or the server not reachable).  Ciphers The method is a name from this table. LookupMethod turns a name into a Method and returns one with ok false for a name it does not know. The name chacha20-poly1305 is accepted too, as an alias of chacha20-ietf-poly1305. Old stream ciphers such as rc4-md5 and aes-256-cfb are not supported and never will be: they are broken.  MethodKeySaltPassword formNotes  aes-128-gcm16 bytes16 bytesany textClassic AEAD. Slow here, see below. aes-256-gcm32 bytes32 bytesany textClassic AEAD. The default of Config. Slow here, see below. chacha20-ietf-poly130532 bytes32 bytesany textClassic AEAD. The one to prefer. 2022-blake3-aes-128-gcm16 bytes16 bytesbase64 of exactly 16 bytesShadowsocks 2022, TCP and UDP. 2022-blake3-aes-256-gcm32 bytes32 bytesbase64 of exactly 32 bytesShadowsocks 2022, TCP and UDP. 2022-blake3-chacha20-poly130532 bytes32 bytesbase64 of exactly 32 bytesShadowsocks 2022, TCP and UDP.  net-shadowsocks-guide-methods.salamCopyimport net.shadowsocks  func show(name: str):     m := shadowsocks.LookupMethod(name)     println m.name, m.ok, m.key_len, m.salt_len, m.v2022 end  func main:     show("aes-128-gcm")     show("aes-256-gcm")     show("chacha20-ietf-poly1305")     show("2022-blake3-aes-128-gcm")     show("2022-blake3-aes-256-gcm")     show("2022-blake3-chacha20-poly1305")     show("rc4-md5") endOutputaes-128-gcm true 16 16 false aes-2

net/transport net.transport The byte stream under the VPN protocols: TCP, TLS, WebSocket and HTTP upgrade connections with SNI, ALPN and ClientHello fragmentation, plus byte buffers and addresses. Network A proxy protocol such as VLESS or VMess says what the first bytes of a connection mean. It does not say how the connection itself is made, and that is the part a censor looks at: is it plain TCP, TLS to which name, a WebSocket on which path, under which Host header. net.transport is that layer. It turns "connect to this host and port with these settings" into a Conn that is read and written the same way whatever is underneath. The package has four jobs:  Carriers. Dial and Listen work over plain TCP, TLS, WebSocket (alone or inside TLS) and a bare HTTP upgrade. FromStream and AsStream let any net.tunnel stream carry a protocol too, so a protocol can run inside another one. Looking like something else. The TLS server name (sni) and the HTTP Host header are separate settings, so a client can connect to a CDN front name while asking for another site. The WebSocket path works as a shared secret: a request for any other path gets a fake nginx 404 page. ClientHello fragmentation. fragment sends the first bytes of the TLS handshake in small pieces with a pause between them, which defeats some filters that read the server name from the first packet. Shared plumbing. Bytes is the growable buffer the protocol packages build headers in, and Addr is a target address that knows its wire form.   Which carrier a Settings value selects Every dial and listen call takes a Settings value. Its zero value is plain TCP.  SettingsCarrier  network = "tcp" (default)The raw stream, with TLS on top when tls = true. network = "ws"An HTTP/1.1 request that upgrades to a WebSocket, then binary frames. Client frames are masked, as the standard requires. With tls = true this is wss. network = "httpupgrade"The same upgrade request without WebSocket framing: after the 101 answer the bytes flow raw. It is cheaper than ws and looks the same to a proxy that only reads the first request. tls = trueThe client checks the server certificate against the system roots or ca_file, using sni (or the dialed host when it is empty) as the name. The server needs cert_file and key_file.  Any other network text is not rejected here: the connection is simply plain. The link parsers of the protocol packages refuse unsupported types before they get this far.  What trips people up  Accept hands each new connection to a worker. TLS and the WebSocket upgrade run in a worker with a time limit (handshake_timeout_ms, 10 seconds) and at most max_handshakes (128) run at once; a client that stalls is dropped and a connection over the limit is closed at once. Accept then returns the next finished connection, or a closed one whose err says why a handshake failed. AcceptRaw and Upgrade still exist for a loop of your own. sni is not host. sni is the name in the TLS handshake and the name the certificate is checked against; host is the Host header inside the upgrade request. Behind a CDN they usually differ. The ALPN setting is one string. Offer "h2" or "http/1.1", not a list. Over WebSocket use "http/1.1", because the upgrade is an HTTP/1.1 feature. fingerprint changes nothing. The field is kept so links that carry fp=chrome round-trip, but the TLS handshake is this library's own, not a copy of a browser's. A filter that recognizes the handshake shape is not fooled. timeout_ms covers the connect only. For an established connection set read_timeout_ms and write_timeout_ms: a read or write that waits that long ends with 0 or less. They are idle limits, so leave them 0 for a tunnel that may sit quiet. Buffers are manual. NewBytes allocates and FreeBytes frees; nothing collects them. No XHTTP, QUIC or plain HTTP/2 transport. gRPC (network = "grpc"), Reality (security = "reality") and Mux.Cool are here; see the sections below.   Buffers and addresses A Bytes value is a pointer, a length and a capacity. The Put functions append (and grow it), At and Peek16 read back, and ToHex shows the content. A target address is a Addr: NewAddr looks at the text and decides between an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address and a domain name, and PutAddr writes it in the order the VLESS and VMess headers use (port, type, address). ParseUUID turns the usual 36 character text into the 16 bytes a user id is on the wire and sets bad when the text is not a UUID. net-transport-guide-bytes.salamCopyimport net.transport  func main:     mut b := transport.NewBytes(16)     transport.Put8(b, 0x7f)     transport.Put16(b, 443)     transport.PutStr(b, "hi")     println transport.ToHex(b), b.len     println transport.Peek16(b, 1), transport.At(b, 3) as int     transport.FreeBytes(b)      a := transport.NewAddr("example.com", 443)     println a.host, a.port, a.kind == transport.AddrDomain     println transport.NewAddr("192.168.1.9", 80).kind == transport.AddrIPv4     println transport.NewAddr("2001:db8::1", 8080).kind == transport.AddrIPv6      mut wire := transport.NewBytes(32)     transport.PutAddr(wire, a)     println transport.ToHex(wire)     mut back := transport.Addr {}     used := transport.ReadAddr(wire, 0, back)     println used, back.host, back.port     transport.FreeBytes(wire)      id := transport.ParseUUID("b831381d-6324-4d53-ad4f-8cda48b30811")     println id.bad, id.len, transport.FormatUUID(id)     println transport.ParseUUID("not a uuid").bad endOutput7f01bb6869 5 443 104 example.com 443 true true true 01bb020b6578616d706c652e636f6d 15 example.com 443 false 16 b831381d-6324-4d53-ad4f-8cda48b30811 true  Quick start: a client and a server Listen binds a port (0 picks a free one, and ListenerPort says which), Accept waits for a client, and Read and Write move bytes. Read returns 0 or less when the other side has closed. Check Ok after a dial, and read err when it is false. This program runs the server in a thread and talks to

net/vless net.vless The VLESS proxy protocol: client and server, TCP and UDP, vless:// share links, over TCP, TLS, WebSocket or any tunnel stream. Network VLESS is a very small proxy protocol from the Xray and V2Ray family. A client opens a connection to the server and sends one header that says who it is (a UUID), what it wants (a TCP connection, or UDP datagrams) and where to (a host and a port). The server checks the UUID, answers with two bytes and from then on the connection carries the payload unchanged. That is all: VLESS does no encryption of its own. The protection has to come from what carries it, which is why it is used over TLS (transport.Settings.tls), usually inside a WebSocket behind a CDN. This package is both halves. Dial connects a client through net.transport and sends the header; Accept reads the header on a server and checks it against a list of users. Read and Write then move the payload, ReadPacket and WritePacket move UDP datagrams, and ParseLink reads the vless:// share links that apps exchange. AsStream, DialOver and AcceptOver connect it to the net.tunnel streams, so it can be one hop of a chain or run inside another protocol. Importing this package pulls in net.transport, and you need that import yourself to build a Settings value and a target Addr.  What goes on the wire  DirectionBytes  Client to server, onceversion 0, the 16 byte user id, the length of the addon block (0, or the flow name wrapped in a small protobuf message), the command (1 TCP, 2 UDP, 3 mux), the port, the address kind, the address. The mux command has no address. Server to client, onceversion 0 and the addon length (this package skips any addon). Afterwards, TCPthe payload in both directions. Afterwards, UDPeach datagram prefixed by its length in two bytes.  The client does not wait for the server's reply before it sends data. The two byte reply is read by the first Read, and a server that refuses the user simply closes the connection, so the client learns about it there and not from Dial.  What trips people up  Without TLS the user id is visible and nothing is encrypted. A plain TCP VLESS connection is a plain text tunnel with a password in front. Use TLS, or put VLESS inside something that encrypts. A rejected client sees success. Dial only sends the header. A wrong UUID shows up as the first Read failing, on the server as unknown user. The flow must match. A server user created with NewUser(id, "") accepts requests without a flow. A request that names a flow different from the user's is refused. UDP is length prefixed datagrams on the one connection. It is the simple form; Xray's XUDP packet format is not implemented. Close frees the request. Call Close once when you are done, on both sides; it also closes the transport underneath.   The request header EncodeRequest and DecodeRequest are the header on its own, with no connection. They are what the tests compare with known bytes, and they are handy to see exactly what a server will receive. DecodeRequest returns how many bytes it consumed, or -1 when the bytes are cut short, have a wrong version or carry an unknown command. net-vless-guide-header.salamCopyimport net.transport import net.vless  const ID := "b831381d-6324-4d53-ad4f-8cda48b30811"  func main:     mut r := vless.Request {}     r.uuid = transport.ParseUUID(ID)     r.command = vless.CmdTCP     r.addr = transport.NewAddr("example.com", 443)     wire := vless.EncodeRequest(r)     println transport.ToHex(wire)     println wire.len, "bytes: version, 16 id bytes, 0 addon bytes, command, port, address type, length, name"      mut back := vless.Request {}     used := vless.DecodeRequest(wire, back)     println used == wire.len, back.addr.host, back.addr.port, back.command, transport.FormatUUID(back.uuid) == ID      cut := transport.FromHex("00b831381d63244d53ad4f8cda48b3081100" + "0101bb020b6578616d")     println "a truncated header decodes to", vless.DecodeRequest(cut, back)     odd := transport.FromHex("01b831381d63244d53ad4f8cda48b3081100" + "0101bb020b6578616d706c652e636f6d")     println "a wrong version decodes to", vless.DecodeRequest(odd, back) endOutput00b831381d63244d53ad4f8cda48b30811000101bb020b6578616d706c652e636f6d 34 bytes: version, 16 id bytes, 0 addon bytes, command, port, address type, length, name true example.com 443 1 true a truncated header decodes to -1 a wrong version decodes to -1  Share links Apps share a server as one vless://uuid@host:port?query#name text. ParseLink reads it into a Link: check ok first, and read err when it is false. LinkSettings turns the link into the Settings for net.transport (the path's ?ed=2048 suffix becomes early_data), FormatLink goes back to text and DialLink does the whole connect. The parser refuses what the package cannot do, with a message that says why: security=reality, type=grpc, type=h2, type=xhttp, an encryption other than none, and a bad UUID. net-vless-guide-link.salamCopyimport net.vless  func main:     text := "vless://b831381d-6324-4d53-ad4f-8cda48b30811@cdn.example.com:443?encryption=none&security=tls&sni=front.example.net&alpn=http%2F1.1&fp=chrome&type=ws&host=vpn.example.org&path=%2Fws-8f3a%3Fed%3D2048#My%20Server"     l := vless.ParseLink(text)     println l.ok, l.host, l.port, l.remark     println l.security, l.network, l.sni, l.host_header, l.path      s := vless.LinkSettings(l)     println s.network, s.tls, s.sni, s.host, s.path, s.early_data      again := vless.ParseLink(vless.FormatLink(l))     println "round trip keeps the path:", again.path == l.path      println vless.ParseLink("vless://b831381d-6324-4d53-ad4f-8cda48b30811@h:443?security=quic").err     println vless.ParseLink("vless://b831381d-6324-4d53-ad4f-8cda48b30811@h:443?type=kcp").err     println vless.ParseLink("vless://b831381d-6324-4d53-ad4f-8cda48b30811@h:443?encryption=aes").err

net/vmess net.vmess The VMess proxy protocol, AEAD form only: encrypted client and server, TCP and UDP, over TCP, TLS, WebSocket or any tunnel stream, with the cryptographic building blocks exposed. Network VMess is the older protocol of the V2Ray family, and unlike VLESS it encrypts for itself. The client proves it holds a user's UUID with an authentication id that contains the current time, sends the request (the target address and the session keys) encrypted under keys derived from the UUID, and then sends the payload in encrypted chunks. The server answers with its own encrypted header and its own chunks. Anyone watching sees random bytes, whatever carries them. This package implements only the AEAD form, the one used since V2Ray 4.28 and the only one current clients still produce: the user is identified by the encrypted authentication id and the header is sealed with AES-128-GCM. The older MD5 based form, the one that needs alterId to be above 0, is not implemented. Set alterId to 0 on both sides (it is the default in current clients). The package is both halves. Dial connects a client through net.transport and sends the header, Accept reads it on a server, Read and Write move the payload and ReadPacket reads one chunk as a UDP datagram. AsStream, DialOver and AcceptOver connect it to net.tunnel streams. The lower level functions (key derivation, the sealed header, the chunk encoder) are public, because the protocol is easiest to understand, and to test, one piece at a time.  The body encryptions  ConstantWhat it does  SecAES128GCMEach chunk is sealed with AES-128-GCM. The default choice. SecChaCha20Poly1305Each chunk is sealed with ChaCha20-Poly1305. A good choice on a processor without AES instructions. SecNoneThe chunks are framed but not encrypted. The header is still sealed. SecZeroNo chunks and no encryption: the payload follows the header as it is. Only for use inside TLS.  The header is always sealed with AES-128-GCM under keys derived from the UUID, whichever body type is chosen. The options in Request.option are bits: OptChunkStream frames the body in chunks, OptChunkMask hides the chunk lengths with a SHAKE-128 stream, OptPadding adds random padding to each chunk, OptAuthLength authenticates the lengths with the body cipher. Dial uses DefaultOption for the security type; to choose the bits yourself, call Client on a connection you opened.  What trips people up  The two clocks must agree. The authentication id contains the time and a server accepts only ids within TimeWindow seconds, 120, of its own clock. A phone or a server with a wrong clock gets unknown user or stale timestamp and nothing else. This is the first thing to check when a correct UUID is refused. Share one replay filter. Accept remembers the authentication ids it has seen and refuses a repeat. Make one with NewReplayFilter and pass the same one to every Accept call of a server; it is safe to use from several threads. Once it holds more than 4096 ids it drops the ones older than four minutes. A refused client is not told. Dial only sends the header. A wrong UUID, a stale clock or a replayed id makes the server close the connection, and the client sees that as a failed read. The server must support the security type. An Accept that reads a type other than the four above fails with unsupported security type. There are no vmess:// links. The base64 JSON share format of V2RayN and others is not parsed here. Take the fields from it yourself. Close frees the keys. Call Close once on each side when you are done.   The building blocks This program derives a user's command key from a UUID, makes an authentication id for a given time, opens it again (which also gives back the time), shows that another user's key cannot open it, and seals a small header. The numbers that come out are fixed, so they can be compared with another implementation. net-vmess-guide-primitives.salamCopyimport net.transport import net.vmess  const ID := "b831381d-6324-4d53-ad4f-8cda48b30811"  func main:     key := vmess.CmdKey(transport.ParseUUID(ID))     println "command key", transport.ToHex(key)      stamp := 1700000000 as i64     salt := transport.FromHex("a1b2c3d4")     authid := vmess.CreateAuthID(key, stamp, salt)     println "auth id", transport.ToHex(authid)      mut when := 0 as i64     println "opens with the right key:", vmess.OpenAuthID(key, authid, when), when == stamp     other := vmess.CmdKey(transport.ParseUUID("5783a3e7-e373-51cd-8642-c83782b807c5"))     println "refused for another user:", not vmess.OpenAuthID(other, authid, when)      nonce := transport.FromHex("1112131415161718")     sealed := vmess.SealHeader(key, transport.FromStr("a small header"), stamp, salt, nonce)     println "sealed header is", sealed.len, "bytes"     println "time window in seconds:", vmess.TimeWindow     println "default option for aes-gcm:", vmess.DefaultOption(vmess.SecAES128GCM)     println "default option for none:", vmess.DefaultOption(vmess.SecNone)     println "default option for zero:", vmess.DefaultOption(vmess.SecZero) endOutputcommand key b50d916ac0cec067981af8e5f38a758f auth id afabbebf298c2611f08228d760111288 opens with the right key: true true refused for another user: true sealed header is 72 bytes time window in seconds: 120 default option for aes-gcm: 5 default option for none: 1 default option for zero: 0  Quick start: a client and a server over TCP The server listens with transport.Listen, accepts with transport.Accept and hands each connection to vmess.Accept with its list of users and the shared replay filter. The client dials with vmess.Dial and picks the body encryption. The target in the header is what a real server would connect onward to; this echo server just reports it. net-vmess-guide-loopback.salamCopyimport mem import str import sync import net.transport import net.vmes

net/reality net.reality The REALITY security layer of Xray: a client that proves itself inside a TLS 1.3 handshake, a server that shows everyone else the real website, key and short id helpers, and link parameters. Network REALITY is a way to hide a proxy server behind a website that already exists. The client sends an ordinary TLS 1.3 handshake whose server name is that website. Inside the handshake, in a field that is random bytes to everybody else, it puts a small sealed message that only the owner of the server's key can open. If the message opens and the short id is known, the server answers as itself and the connection carries your traffic. If not (a censor probing the address, a browser, a scanner) the server does nothing clever: it forwards the bytes to the real website and forwards the answers back, so the probe sees the real site's real certificate. There is no certificate of your own to find. This package is both halves. DialOver runs the client half on a connected socket and returns a tls.Conn. Accept runs the server half on an accepted socket: it reads the first record, decides, and either returns an authenticated tls.Conn or relays the connection to the destination. GenerateKey and NewShortId make the secrets, and ParseParams and FormatParams read and write the security=reality part of a vless:// link. The ClientHello is built by net.utls so it looks like a browser, and the handshake itself is the TLS 1.3 code of tls.  What happens on the wire  StepWhat  Client helloA browser-like ClientHello with an x25519 key share and the real website as server name. The 32 byte session id is the sealed message. Sealed message16 bytes: three version bytes, one zero byte, the time as 4 bytes and the 8 byte short id. It is sealed with AES-256-GCM. The key is HKDF-SHA256 over the x25519 secret between the client's ephemeral key and the server's static key, with the first 20 bytes of the hello random as salt and REALITY as info. The nonce is the last 12 bytes of the random, and the whole ClientHello (with the session id set to zeros) is the associated data. Server, not authenticatedConnects to the destination, sends it the bytes it has read and copies in both directions until both sides close. Server, authenticatedCompletes a TLS 1.3 handshake with a one-off ed25519 certificate. The certificate's signature field is not a signature: it is HMAC-SHA512 of the certificate's public key under the key derived above. Client checkInstead of checking a certificate chain, the client recomputes that HMAC, and verifies the ed25519 CertificateVerify signature with the certificate's key. Only the real server can produce the HMAC.   What trips people up  The server name must be one of server_names. Otherwise the server forwards you to the website like any stranger, and the client reports server did not sign with ed25519, because the website's certificate is not an ed25519 HMAC certificate. That message means "authentication failed" in every case: wrong public key, unknown short id, wrong name. A current Xray server only accepts a hello with a hybrid key share. Since the ML-KEM change Xray rejects a ClientHello that has no X25519MLKEM768 share before the plain x25519 one. This package always sends one (see the limits), so use the chrome or edge fingerprint with such a server. The firefox and safari profiles send no hybrid share and are not authenticated by it. The destination has to look like your server. Xray makes its handshake records exactly as long as the destination's. The destination should be a TLS 1.3 site that negotiates the same ALPN you offer (usually h2) and does not select X25519MLKEM768, because this package cannot finish a hybrid key exchange (see the limits). Close sockets of failed clients. A rejected client is relayed until it closes; a program that leaves its socket open keeps the relay open too. A short id has to be an even number of hex digits, at most 16. It is zero padded to 8 bytes. An empty short id is the all-zero id and must be in the server's list to work. Clocks. max_time_diff is in milliseconds. It defaults to 60000, so a client whose clock is more than a minute off is sent to the real site; 0 turns the check off (Xray's own default).   Keys and short ids GenerateKey returns an x25519 pair as the 43 character base64url text that Xray prints for xray x25519. The private key stays on the server; the public key goes into every client. PublicKeyOf recomputes the public key from the private one. A short id tells clients apart without any extra key. net-reality-guide-keys.salamCopyimport net.reality  func main:     keys := reality.GenerateKey()     println "private key length:", keys.private_key.Len()     println "public key length:", keys.public_key.Len()     println "public matches private:", reality.PublicKeyOf(keys.private_key) == keys.public_key      sid := reality.NewShortId(4)     println "short id digits:", sid.Len()     println "valid short ids:", reality.ValidShortId(sid), reality.ValidShortId("abcd1234"), reality.ValidShortId("zz")     println "valid public keys:", reality.ValidPublicKey(keys.public_key), reality.ValidPublicKey("short") endOutputprivate key length: 43 public key length: 43 public matches private: true short id digits: 8 valid short ids: true true false valid public keys: true false  Link parameters A REALITY share link is a vless:// link with security=reality and the keys pbk (public key), sid (short id), spx (spider path), sni, fp (fingerprint) and flow. The package that reads vless:// links is net.vless; the part that is about REALITY is here. Give ParseParams the query text (the part after ?) and it fills a Settings; FormatParams goes back. Values are kept as written and are not percent decoded. net-reality-guide-link.salamCopyimport net.reality  func main:     query := "security=reality&pbk=IH8tyHx_SyHSCyaQgNTOvHYefAehmhpbMgkwFeAPnXY&sid=abcd1234&

Network This package joins net.tunnel to every protocol package: socks, http, trojan, vless, vmess and shadowsocks, with the v2ray stream settings of net.transport (tcp, tls, ws, httpupgrade, and TLS hello fragmenting). One call to Register and a v2ray style JSON config runs, both the inbounds and the outbounds.  Register or RegisterWith installs the makers. After that tunnel.CreateInbound, tunnel.CreateOutbound and tunnel.BuildDialer understand every protocol above. StartAll starts every inbound of a config and RunConfig is a whole program: load, check, start, wait for Ctrl-C. Local by default. net/utls net.utls TLS ClientHello fingerprints: build the first message of a TLS 1.3 handshake in the byte layout of Chrome, Firefox or Safari, compute JA3 strings, and run a handshake from it. Network A firewall that cannot read your traffic can still read your first message. The ClientHello of a TLS connection lists the cipher suites, the extensions and their order, the curves and the signature algorithms the client supports, and every TLS library lists them in its own way. That list is a fingerprint (JA3 is the best known way to write it down), and a proxy client that uses the default list of its TLS library has a fingerprint no browser has. This package builds the ClientHello itself, from a description that you can read and change, so that it has the layout of a browser. Profile returns a Spec for a client family. Build turns a spec and some Options (the server name, the ALPN list, whether to shuffle the extensions) into a Hello: the message bytes, with a fresh random, a fresh x25519 key pair and a random session id. WrapClient then runs a TLS 1.3 handshake on a connected socket with that hello and returns an ordinary tls.Conn. JA3 writes down the fingerprint of any hello, and Record wraps it into a TLS record, for example to hand it to the fragmenting helpers of net.censor. net.reality uses this package for the hello it seals its proof into.  The profiles  NameMeant to look like  chrome, edgeA recent Chromium: GREASE values, the hybrid post-quantum key share, ECH GREASE, the ALPS extension, certificate compression, padding to 512 bytes when needed. chrome_120A legacy profile: a Chromium from before the hybrid key share, with no post-quantum group. Xray-core 26.9.9 and later (REALITY since 2026-09-08) drop a hello without X25519MLKEM768, so use it only against older servers (it authenticates against Xray 26.7.28). It is not in ProfileNames; LegacyProfileNames lists it. firefoxFirefox: no GREASE, the suites in its own order, a secp256r1 key share next to x25519, delegated credentials, record size limit. safari, iosSafari and iOS: GREASE, the longer list of older suites, no ECH. randomizedThe Chrome layout with the extensions and the suites shuffled, so that no two hellos have the same JA3.  These are approximations written from memory of what these clients send, not captures. A comparison with a capture of the real browser was not possible here. The structure was checked in two ways: the hellos parse with net.censor.ParseClientHello, and they complete a real TLS 1.3 handshake with the tls server. Browsers change their hello with each release, so treat a profile as a starting point and edit the Spec (it is plain text lists) to match the browser you want to look like.  How a spec is written The lists in a Spec are text of hexadecimal numbers separated by spaces. g0 to g4 are GREASE slots that become a random reserved value (0a0a, 1a1a and so on); pad marks where the padding extension goes. extensions is the order on the wire; 0000 is the server name, 0010 ALPN, 0033 the key share, fe0d ECH GREASE and so on. key_shares says which shares to send: 001d is x25519 with the key pair of the hello, 0017 is a secp256r1 share with random bytes, 11ec is X25519MLKEM768.  What trips people up  The key shares other than x25519 have no key behind them. The secp256r1 share is random bytes, and the ML-KEM part of the hybrid share is a well formed random encapsulation key. A server that picks one of those groups cannot finish the handshake with you; it can for x25519. Pass pq = false to leave the hybrid group out of the hello completely. The hello offers ALPN h2 by default. If the server picks it you are talking to something that expects HTTP/2. For a proxy transport set alpn = "http/1.1", or "none" to leave the extension out. Some bytes are random on purpose. GREASE values, the ECH length, the random, the session id and the key shares change with every Build. JA3 ignores GREASE and key bytes, so the JA3 of a profile is stable. Only TLS 1.3, and no HelloRetryRequest. The handshake from a custom hello fails with a clear message if the server wants a different group or only speaks TLS 1.2. Free the hello. A Hello owns its buffers: call FreeHello when you are done.   Building a hello and reading its JA3 The example builds one hello for each of three profiles with the hybrid share left out, and prints the JA3 strings. A JA3 string is the version, the cipher suites, the extension ids, the curves and the point formats, each as decimal numbers, with GREASE removed. The order of the extension ids is the clearest difference between the profiles. net-utls-guide-profiles.salamCopyimport net.utls  func main:     println "profiles:", utls.ProfileNames()     mut o := utls.Options {}     o.server_name = "www.example.com"     o.pq = false     each name in ["chrome", "firefox", "safari"]:         mut h := utls.Build(utls.Profile(name), o)         println name, "hello is larger than 400 bytes:", h.raw.len > 400         println utls.JA3(h.raw)         utls.FreeHello(h)     end     println "unknown profile is ok:", utls.Profile("netscape").ok endOutputprofiles: chrome,edge,firefox,safari,ios,randomized chrome hello is larger than 400 bytes: true 771,4865-4866-4867-49195-49199-49196-49200-52393-52392-49171-49172-156-157-47-53,0-23-65281-10-11-35-16-5-13-18-51-45-43-27-17513-65037,29-23-24,0 firefox hello is larger than 400 bytes: true 771,4865-4867-4866-49195-49199-52393-52392-49196-49200-49162-49161-49171-49172-156-157-47-53,0-23-65281-10-11-35-16-5-34-51-43-13-45-28-65037,29-23-24-25-256-257,0 safari hello is larger than 400 bytes: true 771,4865-4866-4867-49196-49195-52393-49200-49199-52392-49162-49161-49172-49171-157-156-61-60-53-47-49160-49170-10,0-23-65281-10-11-16-5-13-18-51-45-43-27-21,29-23-24-25,0 unknown profile is ok: false  A handshake from a profile WrapClient takes a connected socket, a spec, the options and a tls.Config. dom dom Working with a web page in the browser: elements, events, timers and JavaScript objects. Web and services This package lets a Salam program drive a web page: find and create elements, change their text, classes and styles, react to clicks and keys, run timers and keep small values in localStorage. A program that uses it runs in the browser. Translate it to JavaScript with salam js app.salam --output=app.js and load it with a <script src="app.js"> tag; main runs once the page is ready, and println writes to the browser console. That is why the examples on this page are only checked, not run. For drawing use web.canvas, for games that read the keyboard every frame web.keys, and for a desktop window around a page webview. Elements and other JavaScript objects are held in an i64 variable, and events and timers take an anonymous function such as (): ... end. Each function maps to one browser call (SetText is textContent, SetStyle is style.setProperty and so on), so the MDN documentation for that call applies. Things that catch people out:  A missing element is JavaScript null, not 0. el == 0 is never true for it, and using it throws. Check with Exists(id) before ById, or with CountOf(QueryAll(sel)) == 0 for a selector. SetHtml runs whatever HTML it gets. Put text from users in with SetText, never with SetHtml. SetStyle takes CSS names such as background-color, not the JavaScript form backgroundColor. OnReady does nothing when called from main, because main already runs after the page is ready and the browser does not repeat the ready event. Put start-up code straight in main. OffEvent needs the very function value you registered, so keep it in a variable; a second lambda with the same body is a different function.   Running the examples Each program below is a whole page's script. Save it as app.salam, translate it, and open an HTML file that loads the result: salam js app.salam --output=app.js echo '<!doctype html><meta charset="utf-8"><body><script src="app.js"></script>' > index.html salam serve . Then visit http://127.0.0.1:8000. Output from println appears in the browser console. With --output=app.html instead, salam js writes one self contained page.  A to-do list Most pages follow the same shape: build the elements once in main, keep the ones you need later in global variables, and react to events. A click handler that is created inside a function, like the one on each new list item, remembers the element it was made for. StoreSetInt and StoreGetInt keep a number in the browser's localStorage, so it survives a reload. dom-todo.salamCopyimport dom  mut list := 0 as i64 mut entry := 0 as i64 mut added := 0  func add_item(text: str):     item := dom.Create("li")     dom.SetText(item, text)     dom.OnEvent(item, "click", ():         dom.ToggleClass(item, "done")     end)     dom.Append(list, item)     added++     dom.StoreSetInt("todo-added", added as i64) end  func main:     dom.SetTitle("To do")     entry = dom.Create("input")     dom.SetAttr(entry, "placeholder", "What needs doing?")     button := dom.Create("button")     dom.SetText(button, "Add")     list = dom.Create("ul")     dom.Append(dom.Body(), entry)     dom.Append(dom.Body(), button)     dom.Append(dom.Body(), list)      dom.OnEvent(button, "click", ():         text := dom.GetValue(entry)         if text.Len() > 0:             add_item(text)             dom.SetValue(entry, "")         end     end)     dom.OnEventE(entry, "keydown", (e: i64):         if dom.EventKey(e) == "Enter":             dom.PreventDefault(e)             text := dom.GetValue(entry)             if text.Len() > 0:                 add_item(text)                 dom.SetValue(entry, "")             end         end     end)     println "items added on this device so far:", dom.StoreGetInt("todo-added") end OnEvent takes a handler without arguments; use OnEventE when you need the event itself, for example to read the key with EventKey or to stop the browser's default action with PreventDefault.  Working with elements already on the page When the HTML comes from a server or a template, the script finds the elements instead of creating them. This one filters a product table as the user types. It first checks with Exists that the page has what it needs, then takes every row with QueryAll and walks them with CountOf and ItemAt. Hiding a row is SetStyle(row, "display", "none"), and an empty value removes the style again. dom-filter.salamCopyimport dom import str  func filter(rows: i64, word: str, counter: i64):     mut shown := 0     repeat dom.CountOf(rows) in i:         row := dom.ItemAt(rows, i)         name := str.Lower(dom.GetText(row))         if word.Len() == 0 or str.Contains(name, word):             dom.SetStyle(row, "display", "")             shown++         else:             dom.SetStyle(row, "display", "none")         end     end     dom.SetText(counter, shown + " of " + dom.CountOf(rows) + " products") end  func main:     if not (dom.Exists("search") and dom.Exists("count")):         println "this script needs #search and #count on the page"         ret     end     search := dom.ById("search")     counter := dom.ById("count")     rows := dom.QueryAll("#products tr")     if dom.CountOf(rows) == 0:         dom.SetText(counter, "no products")         ret     end     dom.SetStyle(dom.Query("#products"), "background-color", "#fafafa")     dom.OnEvent(search, "input", ():         filter(rows, str.Lower(str.Trim(dom.GetValue(search))), counter)     end)     filter(rows, "", counter) end It expects markup such as <input id="search"> <p id="count"&gt

web/canvas web.canvas Drawing shapes, text and images on a browser canvas element. Web and services This package gives plain functions for two dimensional drawing on a <canvas> element: charts, simple games, signatures, diagrams. As with dom, the program is translated for the browser with salam js, and the elements, events and timers around the drawing come from dom. For key presses in a game loop add web.keys; for pictures saved to a file on the server side, see image. Get the drawing context with Get (by element id) or Of (for an element you hold) and pass it to every function. Each function is one call on the browser's CanvasRenderingContext2D. The coordinates are in canvas pixels, start at the top left corner, and the vertical axis points down, so angles turn clockwise. Things that catch people out:  Set the size with the width and height attributes, not CSS. CSS stretches the picture; the attributes set how many pixels there are. Shapes built from a path pile up until BeginPath; see the last section. An image draws nothing until it has loaded. Check dom.ImageReady before DrawImage. Mouse positions from dom.EventX are window coordinates. Subtract the canvas position from getBoundingClientRect to get canvas coordinates. Only the common calls are wrapped. Gradients, measureText and the rest are reached with dom.Call... and dom.Set... on the context.   A bar chart from data Drawing a chart is mostly arithmetic: turn each value into a height, each index into an x position, and draw from the bottom up because y grows downward. Set the canvas size with the width and height attributes rather than CSS; CSS only stretches the picture, while the attributes set how many pixels you draw on. TextAlign(c, "center") makes FillText centre each label on the x you give. web-canvas-bar-chart.salamCopyimport dom import web.canvas  func main:     el := dom.Create("canvas")     dom.SetAttr(el, "id", "chart")     dom.SetAttr(el, "width", "420")     dom.SetAttr(el, "height", "240")     dom.Append(dom.Body(), el)     c := canvas.Get("chart")      months := ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun"]     sales := [42.0, 55.0, 38.0, 71.0, 64.0, 80.0]     top := 100.0     base := 200.0     bar := 40.0     gap := 24.0      canvas.StrokeStyle(c, "#999")     canvas.LineWidth(c, 1)     canvas.BeginPath(c)     canvas.MoveTo(c, 30, base)     canvas.LineTo(c, 410, base)     canvas.Stroke(c)      canvas.Font(c, "13px sans-serif")     canvas.TextAlign(c, "center")     each i, value in sales:         x := 40.0 + (i as f64) * (bar + gap)         h := value / top * 160.0         canvas.FillStyle(c, "#3b82f6")         canvas.BeginPath(c)         canvas.RoundRect(c, x, base - h, bar, h, 4)         canvas.Fill(c)         canvas.FillStyle(c, "#222")         canvas.FillText(c, months[i], x + bar / 2, base + 18)         canvas.FillText(c, "" + (value as int), x + bar / 2, base - h - 6)     end end These programs run in the browser, so they are only checked here; see how to run them.  Animation: clear, move, draw An animation redraws the whole picture on every frame. EveryFrame from dom calls your function before each repaint, usually 60 times a second. Each call moves the objects a little, paints the background over the last frame and draws everything again. Keep the state in globals so it lasts from one frame to the next. web-canvas-bounce.salamCopyimport dom import web.canvas  mut x := 60.0 mut y := 60.0 mut dx := 3.0 mut dy := 2.0 mut c := 0 as i64  func main:     el := dom.Create("canvas")     dom.SetAttr(el, "id", "box")     dom.SetAttr(el, "width", "360")     dom.SetAttr(el, "height", "220")     dom.Append(dom.Body(), el)     c = canvas.Get("box")     r := 14.0      dom.EveryFrame((ms: f64):         _ := ms         w := canvas.Width(c)         h := canvas.Height(c)         x += dx         y += dy         if x < r or x > w - r:             dx = 0.0 - dx         end         if y < r or y > h - r:             dy = 0.0 - dy         end         canvas.FillStyle(c, "#10131a")         canvas.FillRect(c, 0, 0, w, h)         canvas.BeginPath(c)         canvas.Arc(c, x, y, r, 0, 6.2832)         canvas.FillStyle(c, "#f59e0b")         canvas.Fill(c)     end) end The speed here is per frame, so the ball moves faster on a 120 Hz screen. For the same speed everywhere, multiply by the argument of the frame function: it is the time since the last frame in milliseconds, at most 100 (so a hidden tab does not make things jump). The spinner below works that way.
