web/keys web.keys Keyboard state for browser games. Web and services In a game you usually ask once per frame which keys are down, rather than taking an event for every press. This package listens to the keydown and keyup events of the window for you and keeps the state of up to 32 keys. Call Init once, then ask Down or Pressed inside the EveryFrame function from dom, and draw with web.canvas. For a form or a text field, where you want each key as it comes, use dom.OnEventE with dom.EventKey instead. Keys are named by the browser's key value: ArrowLeft, Enter, " " for the space bar, a for the A key. Things to know:  Only tracked keys are seen. Init tracks the four arrows, Enter and the space bar; add others with Track. Asking about any other key returns false. Letters change with Shift and Caps Lock: a becomes A. Track and ask for both. Tracked keys stop doing their normal job on the page, so they cannot be typed into a text box while the game runs. A key can stay "down" after the window loses focus. When the player switches windows while holding a key, the browser sends no keyup, and Down stays true until that key is pressed and released again.   Holding a key and pressing it once The two questions are different. Down is true for as long as the key is held, which suits walking. Pressed is true once per press, the next time you ask after the key went down, which suits jumping, shooting or opening a menu: holding the space bar does not make the player jump again and again. web-keys-jump.salamCopyimport dom import web.canvas import web.keys  mut x := 40.0 mut y := 160.0 mut vy := 0.0 mut c := 0 as i64  func main:     el := dom.Create("canvas")     dom.SetAttr(el, "id", "level")     dom.SetAttr(el, "width", "400")     dom.SetAttr(el, "height", "200")     dom.Append(dom.Body(), el)     c = canvas.Get("level")     keys.Init()     floor := 160.0      dom.EveryFrame((ms: f64):         _ := ms         if keys.Down("ArrowLeft"):             x -= 3         end         if keys.Down("ArrowRight"):             x += 3         end         jump := keys.Pressed(" ")         if jump and y >= floor:             vy = -9         end         vy += 0.5         y += vy         if y > floor:             y = floor             vy = 0         end         canvas.ClearRect(c, 0, 0, 400, 200)         canvas.FillStyle(c, "#444")         canvas.FillRect(c, 0, floor + 20, 400, 20)         canvas.FillStyle(c, "#e11d48")         canvas.FillRect(c, x, y, 20, 20)     end) end Notice that the program asks Pressed on every frame and only then checks whether the player stands on the floor. If it wrote y >= floor and keys.Pressed(" "), a press in mid air would not be asked about, would stay waiting, and the player would jump by itself on landing.  Your own keys: pause with P Init tracks the arrow keys, Enter and the space bar. Add any other key with Track, using the browser's key name: a letter, Escape, Shift and so on. The names are exact text, so with Shift or Caps Lock on, the P key arrives as P, not p; track both when it matters. web-keys-pause.salamCopyimport dom import web.canvas import web.keys  mut paused := false mut angle := 0.0 mut c := 0 as i64  func main:     el := dom.Create("canvas")     dom.SetAttr(el, "id", "game")     dom.SetAttr(el, "width", "200")     dom.SetAttr(el, "height", "200")     dom.Append(dom.Body(), el)     c = canvas.Get("game")     keys.Init()     keys.Track("p")     keys.Track("P")     keys.Track("Escape")      dom.EveryFrame((now: f64):         _ := now         if keys.Pressed("p") or keys.Pressed("P") or keys.Pressed("Escape"):             paused = not paused         end         if not paused:             angle += 0.05         end         canvas.ClearRect(c, 0, 0, 200, 200)         canvas.Save(c)         canvas.Translate(c, 100, 100)         canvas.Rotate(c, angle)         canvas.FillStyle(c, "#22c55e")         canvas.FillRect(c, -30, -30, 60, 60)         canvas.Restore(c)         if paused:             canvas.FillStyle(c, "#000")             canvas.Font(c, "18px sans-serif")             canvas.TextAlign(c, "center")             canvas.FillText(c, "Paused, press P", 100, 190)         end     end) end A tracked key no longer does its usual job in the page, because the package calls PreventDefault for it. That is what stops the arrows and the space bar from scrolling during a game, but it also means a tracked letter cannot be typed into a text box on the same page. Like the dom examples, these run in the browser and are only checked here.  Smooth movement with arrows and WASD Most games accept both the arrow keys and W, A, S and D. The helper held checks an arrow, a letter and its capital, so Caps Lock does not stop the player. Each axis becomes -1, 0 or 1; when both are set the program divides by the length, so moving diagonally is not faster than moving straight. The speed is in pixels per millisecond and is multiplied by ms, the time since the last frame that EveryFrame passes in, so the dot moves at the same speed on a 60 Hz and a 144 Hz screen. web-keys-move.salamCopyimport dom import math import str import web.canvas import web.keys  mut x := 200.0 mut y := 150.0 mut c := 0 as i64  func held(arrow: str, letter: str): bool:     ret keys.Down(arrow) or keys.Down(letter) or keys.Down(str.Upper(letter)) end  func axis(minus_arrow: str, minus_letter: str, plus_arrow: str, plus_letter: str): f64:     mut v := 0.0     if held(minus_arrow, minus_letter): v-- end     if held(plus_arrow, plus_letter): v++ end     ret v end  func main:     el := dom.Create("canvas")     dom.SetAttr(el, "id", "field")     dom.SetAttr(el, "width", "400

graphql graphql A GraphQL server: schemas, resolvers, query execution and HTTP handling. Web and services GraphQL is a language for asking an API for data: the client asks for exactly the fields it needs and the server sends back just those. This package is a complete server side implementation of the specification. Write the schema as SDL text and pass it to ParseSchema, or build it with the Add... functions, register resolvers for the fields and run a query with ExecuteSource. A resolver is a function that takes a slot number; it reads the arguments and the parent object with ArgStr, ParentField and their siblings, and answers with one of the Resolve... functions or with Fail. A field without a resolver takes the value of the same name from the parent object. For a web server, call HandleHttpSimple inside a net.http handler. For calling someone else's GraphQL API, the client helpers BuildRequestBody and ParseResponse build the JSON body and read the answer; send it with net.http. When you control both sides and do not need clients choosing their own fields, a plain JSON route or rpc is less work. Things that catch people out:  A subscription runs once and returns one result, like a query. There is no event stream and no WebSocket transport; push updates yourself with net.websocket. A field that fails becomes null and the rest of the answer still arrives, so check ResultOk even when data is there. Resolvers run one field at a time. A list of 100 posts whose author resolver queries a database makes 100 queries; load what the list needs once, as the first guide shows.  Related types and field resolvers Most schemas link types together: a post has an author, an author has posts. Give the root field a resolver that returns the list, and give the linking field its own resolver on the child type. Inside it, ParentField reads the object being resolved, here the post, so the resolver can look up the author by authorId. Fields without a resolver, such as title and name, are copied from the object by name. graphql-guide-blog.salamCopyimport graphql import encoding.value  mut authors := value.NewValueArray() mut posts := value.NewValueArray()  func person(id: i64, name: str): value.Value:     mut a := value.NewValueObject()     value.ObjectSet(a, "id", value.ValueInt(id))     value.ObjectSet(a, "name", value.ValueString(name))     ret a end  func post(id: i64, title: str, author_id: i64): value.Value:     mut p := value.NewValueObject()     value.ObjectSet(p, "id", value.ValueInt(id))     value.ObjectSet(p, "title", value.ValueString(title))     value.ObjectSet(p, "authorId", value.ValueInt(author_id))     ret p end  func all_posts(slot: i64):     graphql.Resolve(slot, posts) end  func post_author(slot: i64):     wanted := value.AsInt(graphql.ParentField(slot, "authorId"))     repeat value.ArrayLen(authors) in i:         a := value.ArrayGet(authors, i)         if value.AsInt(value.ObjectGet(a, "id")) == wanted:             graphql.Resolve(slot, a)             ret         end     end     graphql.ResolveNull(slot) end  func main:     value.ArrayPush(authors, person(1, "Sara"))     value.ArrayPush(authors, person(2, "Omid"))     value.ArrayPush(posts, post(10, "Hello GraphQL", 1))     value.ArrayPush(posts, post(11, "Salam and SQL", 2))     value.ArrayPush(posts, post(12, "Resolvers explained", 1))     mut err := graphql.NewError(graphql.ERR_SYNTAX, "")     mut s := graphql.ParseSchema(` type Author { id: Int! name: String! } type Post { id: Int! title: String! author: Author } type Query { posts: [Post!]! }`, err)     _ := graphql.SetResolver(s, "Query", "posts", all_posts)     _ := graphql.SetResolver(s, "Post", "author", post_author)     mut r := graphql.Run(s, `{ posts { title author { name } } }`)     println graphql.ResultToJSONStable(r)     graphql.FreeResult(r)     mut r2 := graphql.Run(s, `{ posts { id } }`)     println graphql.ResultToJSONStable(r2)     graphql.FreeResult(r2)     graphql.FreeSchema(s) endOutput{"data": {"posts": [{"author": {"name": "Sara"}, "title": "Hello GraphQL"}, {"author": {"name": "Omid"}, "title": "Salam and SQL"}, {"author": {"name": "Sara"}, "title": "Resolvers explained"}]}} {"data": {"posts": [{"id": 10}, {"id": 11}, {"id": 12}]}} The second query shows the main promise of GraphQL: it asks for ids only, so the author resolver never runs. A resolver that is expensive, like a database lookup, only costs something when a client asks for its field. When many posts share authors, load the authors once into a lookup table, such as a HashMap keyed by id, instead of searching or querying once per post.  Mutations with input types Changes go through the Mutation type. An input type groups the arguments, and the client sends the values as variables so the query text stays fixed. The resolver receives the input object with Arg and reads its fields with encoding.value. graphql-guide-mutation.salamCopyimport graphql import encoding.value  mut todos := value.NewValueArray()  func list(slot: i64):     graphql.Resolve(slot, todos) end  func add_todo(slot: i64):     data := graphql.Arg(slot, "input")     title := value.AsString(value.ObjectGet(data, "title"))     if title == "":         graphql.Fail(slot, "title must not be empty")         ret     end     mut t := value.NewValueObject()     value.ObjectSet(t, "id", value.ValueInt(value.ArrayLen(todos) + 1))     value.ObjectSet(t, "title", value.ValueString(title))     mut done := false     if value.ObjectHas(data, "done"):         done = value.AsBool(value.ObjectGet(data, &quot

google google Google service account authentication for the Google APIs. Web and services Server programs reach the Google APIs through a "service account". Get the account JSON file from the Google console, read it with ParseServiceAccount, and get a token for the scope you need with AccessToken; then send it in your net.http requests with Authorization. Keep the service account file as carefully as a password. The package does one job: it signs a JWT with the account's RSA key (RS256), trades it at Google's token endpoint for an OAuth access token, and keeps that token for reuse. The calls to the APIs themselves are ordinary HTTP requests that you write. For Web Push to browsers without Firebase, see webpush. Things that catch people out:  Only service account keys are supported. A user's own Google login (the OAuth consent screen) and the metadata server that Google Cloud machines offer are not. When AccessToken fails, ok is false and there is no message. Check in this order: the account's ok, the clock of the machine (a clock that is minutes off makes Google reject the signature), the network, and whether the API is enabled for the project. A token is kept for 59 minutes per account and scope, shared by all threads. After you change the account's roles, call Forget so the next call fetches a fresh one.  Loading the service account safely Download the JSON key from the Google Cloud console (IAM, Service accounts, Keys) and keep it outside the source tree; the usual place to point at it is the GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS environment variable, read with env.GetOr. ParseServiceAccount never fails loudly: it returns an account whose ok is false when the text is empty or client_email or private_key is missing. Check it once at start up and stop with a clear message, so a bad deployment fails at once instead of at the first push notification. google-guide-load.salamCopyimport google import io  func load(path: str): google.ServiceAccount:     text := io.ReadFile(path)     if text == "":         println "cannot read", path         ret google.ServiceAccount {}     end     account := google.ParseServiceAccount(text)     if not account.ok:         println path, "is not a service account file: client_email or private_key is missing"     end     ret account end  func main:     io.WriteFile("good.json", `{"type":"service_account","project_id":"shop-prod","client_email":"push@shop-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com","private_key":"-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----
MIIE...
-----END PRIVATE KEY-----
"}`)     io.WriteFile("broken.json", `{"type":"service_account","project_id":"shop-prod"}`)     each p in ["good.json", "broken.json", "missing.json"]:         account := load(p)         if account.ok:             println "project", account.project_id, "as", account.client_email             println "key loaded:", account.private_key.Len() > 0         end     end endOutputproject shop-prod as push@shop-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com key loaded: true broken.json is not a service account file: client_email or private_key is missing cannot read missing.json The program prints the project and the account email, which are safe to log, but only whether the key was loaded. Never print or log private_key, and never commit the file: anyone who has it can act as your service.  Sending a push notification with Firebase Firebase Cloud Messaging takes one HTTP request per message. Get a token for SCOPE_FCM, put it in the Authorization header, and post the message to /v1/projects/PROJECT/messages:send. AccessToken keeps the token and reuses it until shortly before it expires, so calling it before every message costs nothing after the first time. google-guide-fcm.salamCopyimport google import io import net.http  func send_push(account: google.ServiceAccount, device_token: str, title: str, body: str): bool:     mut ok := false     token := google.AccessToken(account, google.SCOPE_FCM, ok)     if not ok:         println "no access token"         ret false     end     url := "https://fcm.googleapis.com/v1/projects/" + account.project_id + "/messages:send"     message := ```         {"message": {"token": "${{ device_token }}", "notification": {"title": "${{ title }}", "body": "${{ body }}"}}}         ```     mut headers := http.NewHeaders()     headers.Insert("Authorization", google.Authorization(token))     headers.Insert("Content-Type", "application/json")     r := http.PostWith(url, message, headers)     if http.Status(r) != 200:         println "FCM answered", http.Status(r), http.Body(r)         ret false     end     println "sent:", http.Body(r)     ret true end  func main:     account := google.ParseServiceAccount(io.ReadFile("service-account.json"))     if not account.ok:         println "service-account.json is missing or invalid"         ret 1     end     send_push(account, "DEVICE_REGISTRATION_TOKEN", "Order shipped", "Your parcel is on its way")     send_push(account, "DEVICE_REGISTRATION_TOKEN", "Delivered", "Your parcel has arrived")     ret 0 end This needs a real service account with the Firebase Cloud Messaging API enabled and a device registration token from your app, so it is only compiled here. Save the key as service-account.json and replace DEVICE_REGISTRATION_TOKEN. On success the body holds the message name, {"name": "projects/.../messages/..."}; an error whose body says UNREGISTERED means the app was removed from the device and you should delete that token. The title and body are put into the JSON as they are; if they can contain quotes, build t

telegram/bot telegram.bot Building a bot with the Bot API: messages, buttons, webhooks and a polling loop. Web and services To build a bot, get a token from BotFather and make one with NewBot. A bot has two ways of taking messages: Poll, which asks Telegram itself and suits testing and simple servers, or a webhook, where Telegram POSTs the messages to your server. SetAPIBase points the package at a self-hosted Bot API server or at a test double instead of api.telegram.org. With a webhook you can send the answer straight in the body of the HTTP response; the Reply... functions build that JSON text. Set a secret with SetWebhookSecret and check its header on every request. Things that catch people out:  Every API call is an HTTP GET with the parameters in the URL. Media therefore go by file_id or by a public URL that Telegram downloads; a file on your disk cannot be uploaded with this package. The URL also contains the token, so do not log request URLs. Poll never returns, and it runs your function for one update at a time. A slow handler delays every chat. When getUpdates fails it writes the reason to standard error and tries again a second later. An answer sent in the webhook response is fire and forget: you do not learn whether it worked or get the new message id. When you need either, call the matching Send... function instead.  Answering commands Keep the logic of a bot in a function that takes an Update and returns the answer. Then the same function serves a webhook, which sends the answer back in the HTTP response, and a test like this one, which feeds it updates written by hand and needs no network and no token. IsCommand, CommandName and CommandArgs split /add 2 3 into its parts, and CommandName drops the @my_bot suffix Telegram adds in groups. telegram-bot-guide-router.salamCopyimport telegram.bot import str  func answer(update: bot.Update): str:     if not update.has_message:         ret ""     end     m := update.message     if not bot.IsCommand(m.text):         ret bot.ReplyMessage(m.chat.id, "You said: " + m.text)     end     switch bot.CommandName(m.text):         "start":             ret bot.ReplyMessage(m.chat.id, "Hello " + m.from_user.first_name + "! Try /add 2 3")         end         "add":             parts := str.Split(bot.CommandArgs(m.text), " ")             if parts.Len() != 2:                 ret bot.ReplyMessage(m.chat.id, "usage: /add A B")             end             sum := str.ToInt(parts.Get(0)) + str.ToInt(parts.Get(1))             ret bot.ReplyMessage(m.chat.id, str.FromInt(sum))         end     end     ret bot.ReplyMessage(m.chat.id, "I do not know that command") end  func main:     inbox := [`{"update_id":1,"message":{"message_id":1,"text":"/start","chat":{"id":42,"type":"private"},"from":{"id":42,"first_name":"Sara"}}}`,         `{"update_id":2,"message":{"message_id":2,"text":"/add 2 3","chat":{"id":42,"type":"private"}}}`,         `{"update_id":3,"message":{"message_id":3,"text":"/add 2","chat":{"id":42,"type":"private"}}}`,         `{"update_id":4,"message":{"message_id":4,"text":"/weather@my_bot","chat":{"id":42,"type":"private"}}}`,         `{"update_id":5,"message":{"message_id":5,"text":"good morning","chat":{"id":42,"type":"private"}}}`]     each raw in inbox:         println answer(bot.ParseUpdate(raw))     end endOutput{"method": "sendMessage", "chat_id": 42, "text": "Hello Sara! Try /add 2 3"} {"method": "sendMessage", "chat_id": 42, "text": "5"} {"method": "sendMessage", "chat_id": 42, "text": "usage: /add A B"} {"method": "sendMessage", "chat_id": 42, "text": "I do not know that command"} {"method": "sendMessage", "chat_id": 42, "text": "You said: good morning"} The switch has no else, so a command it does not list falls out of it to the line after, which answers that the command is unknown. Always give some answer: a bot that stays silent looks broken to the user.  Inline buttons An inline keyboard is a list of rows, and each row a list of buttons. InlineButton carries a callback_data string of up to 64 bytes that comes back when the user taps it; InlineButtonURL opens a link instead. A tap arrives as an update with has_callback_query set. node node A Salam program under Node.js: modules, files, processes and JavaScript objects. Web and services This package is for Salam programs that are translated to JavaScript with salam js and run under Node.js, such as the VS Code extension or a build script that has to live in an npm project. It gives you the whole of Node: Require loads any built-in or npm module, the Get... and Set... functions read and write properties, and the Call... functions call methods. A few helpers wrap the common fs, path, os and child_process calls. Use it only when the program really runs under Node. A native Salam program reads files with fs and starts programs with os.process, and code for a browser page uses dom. A native build cannot call these functions, so the examples on this page are type-checked by the site but not run. Core ideas  Handles. Every JavaScript value (object, array, function, promise, even undefined) is held in an i64. Nothing needs freeing; Node's garbage collector owns them. Typed calls. Salam checks argument types, so each call shape has its own function, named after its arguments: CallS2 passes two strings, CallV1 one JavaScript value, CallSFn0 a string and a function. Pick the one that matches the method you call; the result is always a handle. Callbacks run later. A Salam lambda passed to CallFn1, ExecFile or SetPropFn1 becomes a JavaScript function. Node calls it after main has returned, from its event loop.  Things that trip people up  GetStr on a missing property returns an empty string and GetNum returns 0, without any error. When "missing" and "empty" mean different things, test IsNullish(GetProp(obj, name)) first. Every number from JavaScript is an f64, and 64-bit integers do not work under salam js. Cast to int when you need one. Salam strings count bytes, also under Node: "سلام".len() is 8, while JavaScript's length of the same text is 4. Text itself passes through unchanged.  To try a program, translate it and run the result with Node.js 18 or newer: salam js node-guide-files.salam --output=files.js node files.js The output under each program is what it printed that way under Node 24.  Files and directories The file helpers wrap the synchronous calls of Node's fs and path modules, which keeps a script readable from top to bottom. For anything they do not cover, Require("fs") gives you the module itself. readdirSync returns a JavaScript array: its length is a number property and each element is a property named by its index, so GetStr(names, "0") reads the first one. node-guide-files.salamCopyimport node import str  func main:     folder := node.MkdtempSync(node.PathJoin2(node.TmpDir(), "salam-notes-"))     node.WriteFileSync(node.PathJoin2(folder, "a.txt"), "one
two
three
")     node.WriteFileSync(node.PathJoin2(folder, "b.txt"), "only line
")     node.WriteFileSync(node.PathJoin2(folder, "c.md"), "# title
")     fs := node.Require("fs")     names := node.CallS1(fs, "readdirSync", folder)     _ := node.Call0(names, "sort")     mut total := 0     repeat node.GetNum(names, "length") as int in i:         name := node.GetStr(names, str.FromInt(i))         if not str.EndsWith(name, ".txt"):             continue         end         text := node.ReadFileSync(node.PathJoin2(folder, name))         lines := str.Count(text, "
")         total += lines         println name, lines     end     println "total", total     node.RmSyncRecursiveForce(folder) end a.txt 3 b.txt 1 total 4 MkdtempSync adds random characters to the prefix, so two runs never collide; RmSyncRecursiveForce removes the directory and everything in it at the end.  Reading JSON from JavaScript Global("JSON") is the same JSON object a JavaScript program sees, so parse turns text into an object handle and the Get... functions read its fields. A field that is missing comes back as undefined; test it with IsNullish before reading it, and fall back to a default. node-guide-config.salamCopyimport node  func main:     text := `{"name": "shop", "port": 8080, "debug": true, "db": {"host": "127.0.0.1"}}`     config := node.CallS1(node.Global("JSON"), "parse", text)     println "name:", node.GetStr(config, "name")     println "port:", node.GetNum(config, "port")     println "debug:", node.GetBool(config, "debug")     db := node.GetProp(config, "db")     println "db host:", node.GetStr(db, "host")     mut workers := 4.0     if not node.IsNullish(node.GetProp(config, "workers")):         workers = node.GetNum(config, "workers")     end     println "workers:", workers     node.SetNum(config, "workers", workers)     println node.ToStr(node.CallV1(node.Global("JSON"), "stringify", config)) end name: shop port: 8080 debug: true db host: 127.0.0.1 workers: 4 {"name":"shop","port":8080,"debug":true,"db":{"host":"127.0.0.1"},"workers":4} Numbers always arrive as f64, because JavaScript has only one number type. Cast with as int where you need an integer. Note the IsNullish test: GetNum(config, "workers") on its own would have returned 0 for the missing field, not an error. Arguments and results are JavaScript values (i64 handles): ToStr turns one into a Salam string, and the small js_str helper here goes the other way by pushing the string into an array and reading it back. node-guide-module.salamCopyimport node import str  func js_str(s: str): i64:     box := node.NewArray()     node.PushStr(box, s)     ret node.GetProp(box, "0&

aws aws Amazon S3, SQS and STS, and any S3 compatible service, with Signature Version 4. Web and services This package works with Amazon S3 and any storage compatible with it without the official SDK, including MinIO, Cloudflare R2, DigitalOcean Spaces, Wasabi, Backblaze and any other S3 compatible cloud storage. Build the configuration with ForAws or ForEndpoint and hand it the keys with WithCredentials, or let the package find them itself with FromEnvironment and ResolveConfig. The S3... functions work with objects and buckets: writing and reading, listing, copying, files and folders, multipart uploads for large files, and presigned URLs so a browser can talk to S3 directly. The Sqs... functions cover SQS message queues and the AssumeRole... functions cover temporary STS credentials. For other services, such as DynamoDB, call any API with NewJsonCall and Invoke. Use this package when a program stores files in object storage, hands out upload links, runs queue workers or calls another AWS API. It signs every request with Signature Version 4 itself and sends it over net.http, so it needs no SDK and no C library. For a plain HTTP API that is not AWS, use net.http directly. Core ideas  Config. A Config is a plain value: endpoint, region, bucket, keys and whether the bucket goes in the path. Every call takes it first. Change it with the With... functions or by setting a field; nothing is global. Results, not errors. Calls return a struct with ok, the HTTP status, AWS's error code and a readable error. A network failure (code is Transport), a 429 or a 5xx answer is tried again with a doubling pause, up to retry attempts in all (3 by default), before you see it. Keys are names. S3 has no folders. reports/2026/may.csv is one key, and "folders" are prefixes you list by.  Things that trip people up  S3Get returns the body as a str, which stops at the first zero byte. For images, archives and other binary data use S3GetBytes or S3DownloadFile. S3ListPrefix returns one page of at most 1000 keys. S3ListAll follows the pages for you, up to 100000 keys, and sets truncated when it stopped there. S3Keys returns an empty list when the listing failed, so it cannot tell "empty" from "error". Configured also wants a bucket. A program that only uses SQS, STS or Invoke should check access_key and secret_key itself. Lists hold memory of their own: free them with ListFree, KeyFree, MessageListFree, FreeBytes and the like.  Never write keys into your code; use environment variables or an IAM role. The examples that need an AWS account or a running MinIO are only checked on the site, not run. One program, any S3 provider Every provider speaks the same S3 API; what differs is the address, the region and whether the bucket goes in the path or in the host name. The For... functions fill those in, so the provider can be a setting of your program and the rest of the code never changes. R2 uses the region auto and path style addresses; AWS and Spaces put the bucket in the host name. aws-guide-providers.salamCopyimport aws  func storage(provider: str, bucket: str): aws.Config:     switch provider:         "r2":             ret aws.ForR2("0123456789abcdef", bucket)         end         "spaces":             ret aws.ForSpaces("ams3", bucket)         end         "minio":             ret aws.ForMinio("http://127.0.0.1:9000", bucket)         end     end     ret aws.ForAws("eu-central-1", bucket) end  func main:     each provider in ["aws", "r2", "spaces", "minio"]:         cfg := storage(provider, "media")         println provider, cfg.endpoint, cfg.region, cfg.path_style     end endOutputaws https://s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com eu-central-1 false r2 https://0123456789abcdef.r2.cloudflarestorage.com auto true spaces https://ams3.digitaloceanspaces.com ams3 false minio http://127.0.0.1:9000 us-east-1 true None of these calls touch the network, so the output above is exact. Add the keys with WithCredentials, or start from FromEnvironment, which reads AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_REGION and AWS_ENDPOINT_URL.  Trying it locally with MinIO MinIO runs an S3 compatible server on your own machine, which is the cheapest way to develop and test. Start it with Docker: docker run -p 9000:9000 -p 9001:9001 minio/minio server /data --console-address :9001 The default keys are minioadmin and minioadmin. The program creates the bucket if it is missing, writes two objects under a date prefix, lists that prefix and reads one object back. Keys are just names: the slashes only look like folders, and listing by prefix is how you walk them. aws-guide-minio.salamCopyimport aws  func main:     mut cfg := aws.ForMinio("http://127.0.0.1:9000", "backups")     cfg = aws.WithCredentials(cfg, "minioadmin", "minioadmin")     if not aws.S3BucketExists(cfg, "backups"):         made := aws.S3CreateBucket(cfg, "backups")         if not made.ok:             println "could not create the bucket:", made.status, made.code, made.error             ret 1         end     end     _ := aws.S3Put(cfg, "2026/10/notes.txt", "first backup", "text/plain")     _ := aws.S3Put(cfg, "2026/10/todo.txt", "buy milk", "text/plain")     mut listing := aws.S3ListPrefix(cfg, "2026/10/")     each item in listing.items:         println item.key, item.size     end     aws.ListFree(listing)     got := aws.S3Get(cfg, "2026/10/notes.txt")     if got.ok:         println "read back:", got.body     else:         println "read failed:", got.status, got.code     end end Each call returns a Result. When ok is false, status is the HTTP status and code is S3's own error code, such as NoSuchKey or AccessDenied; branch on code, not on the message text. crypto crypto SHA and MD5 digests, HMAC signatures, secure random numbers and password hashing. Security and cryptography This package has the basic cryptography tools, written in Salam: the SHA-1, SHA-2 and MD5 digests, HMAC, PBKDF2 password hashing, a constant time comparison and secure random bytes from the operating system. It covers hashing, signing and secrets; it does not encrypt. For encryption (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305, key exchange) use tls, and for signed tokens that carry claims jwt. Most functions come in three shapes: ...Hex takes a str and returns hex text, the simplest; ...Bytes and ...Raw write the raw digest into memory you allocate; and Sha256New, Sha256Update, Sha256Final hash data that arrives in pieces. Things to get right:  HashPassword uses only 1000 PBKDF2 rounds. That is far below current advice (OWASP asks for 600,000 with SHA-256). For new systems build the same string with more rounds, as the second section shows; VerifyPassword reads the rounds from the stored string, so both kinds keep working. Compare secrets with SecretEquals, never with ==. A str stops at the first zero byte. For binary data or a binary key, use the ...Bytes and ...Raw forms with a pointer and a length; Sha256Hex of a buffer that contains a zero hashes only the part before it. HashStr, HashBytes and HashInt are fast hash table hashes, not cryptographic ones; MD5 and SHA-1 are only for old systems that require them.   Storing passwords A login system keeps one string per user: the output of HashPassword. It has four fields separated by $: the algorithm, the number of PBKDF2 rounds, a random salt and the derived key. Because the salt is new every time, two users with the same password get different strings, and a leaked table cannot be attacked with one precomputed list. At login, VerifyPassword reads the rounds and the salt back out of the stored string, so the stored value is all you need to keep. crypto-passwords.salamCopyimport crypto import str  struct User:     pub name: str = ""     pub hash: str = "" end  func register(users &: Vector<User>, name: str, password: str):     users.Push(User { name = name, hash = crypto.HashPassword(password) }) end  func login(users: Vector<User>, name: str, password: str): bool:     each u in users:         if u.name == name:             ret crypto.VerifyPassword(password, u.hash)         end     end     ret false end  func main:     mut users := Vector {} as Vector<User>     register(users, "sara", "correct horse battery")     register(users, "omid", "correct horse battery")      parts := str.Split(users.Get(0).hash, "$")     println "stored fields:", parts.Len(), "algorithm:", parts.Get(0), "rounds:", parts.Get(1)     println "same password, same hash?", users.Get(0).hash == users.Get(1).hash     println "sara right password:", login(users, "sara", "correct horse battery")     println "sara wrong password:", login(users, "sara", "correct horse")     println "unknown user:", login(users, "nobody", "x") endOutputstored fields: 4 algorithm: pbkdf2-sha256 rounds: 1000 same password, same hash? false sara right password: true sara wrong password: false unknown user: false Answer "wrong user" and "wrong password" with the same message, so that a visitor cannot use the login form to find out which accounts exist.  More rounds, and upgrading old hashes The cost of a password hash is the number of rounds: every guess an attacker tries costs the same work as one login. Pbkdf2HmacSha256Hex takes the round count, so a stronger hash is the same four-field string as HashPassword writes, built by hand with 600,000 rounds. Existing users do not have to reset anything. At their next successful login the program sees that the stored hash has fewer rounds than the target and stores a new one, made from the password they just typed. crypto-password-rounds.salamCopyimport crypto import str  const ROUNDS := 600000  func strong_hash(password: str): str:     salt := crypto.RandomHex(16)     ret "pbkdf2-sha256$" + ROUNDS + "$" + salt + "$" + crypto.Pbkdf2HmacSha256Hex(password, salt, ROUNDS, 32) end  func rounds_of(stored: str): int:     ret str.Split(stored, "$").Get(1).ToInt() end  func login(stored &: str, password: str): bool:     if not crypto.VerifyPassword(password, stored): ret false end     if rounds_of(stored) < ROUNDS:         stored = strong_hash(password)         println "  upgraded the stored hash to", rounds_of(stored), "rounds"     end     ret true end  func main:     mut stored := crypto.HashPassword("tea at five")     println "HashPassword uses", rounds_of(stored), "rounds"     println "login:", login(stored, "tea at five")     println "login again:", login(stored, "tea at five")     println "wrong password:", login(stored, "coffee at six") endOutputHashPassword uses 1000 rounds   upgraded the stored hash to 600000 rounds login: true login again: true wrong password: false 600,000 rounds take a noticeable fraction of a second, which is the point, but it also means a login endpoint should be rate limited, or many parallel login attempts can keep the server busy.  Checking a webhook signature Payment providers, GitHub and most other services sign the requests they send you. They compute an HMAC of the raw body with a secret you both know and put it in a header. To check it, compute the same HMAC over the body exactly as it arrived and compare. Compare with SecretEquals, never with ==: == stops at the first different character, and the time that takes tells an attacker how much of a forged signature was right. crypto-webhook.salamCopyimport crypto  func verify(secret: str, body: str,

jwt jwt Making and checking JWT tokens, and guarding API routes. Security and cryptography A JWT is a token the server signs after a user logs in and the client sends with every request; by checking the signature the server knows who the user is without going to the database. This package signs and checks tokens with the HMAC algorithms HS256, HS384 and HS512, never accepts the none algorithm, and has helpers for net.http handlers. Every service that checks a token needs the same secret, so it suits one backend or a few services you trust; there are no RS256 or ES256 public key signatures. When the client is a browser on your own site, a server side net.http.session is often simpler and can be revoked at once. For an API, make a Guard with the secret and call Require or one of its siblings at the top of every handler; when the token is missing or wrong, the 401 or 403 answer is sent for you. The secret has to be long and random, for instance from RandomToken in crypto. Things that catch people out:  A token without exp is accepted forever unless you set opts.require_exp. Tokens from Issue always have one, but a token signed some other way may not. The secret is not checked for strength. Any non-empty string is used as it is; a short one can be guessed offline from a single token. The claims are signed, not encrypted. Anyone holding a token can read them with a base64 decoder, so put no secrets in them. A token cannot be taken back before it expires; keep access tokens short, as the refresh section shows.   Protecting API routes with a Guard The usual shape: /login checks the user (left out here) and answers with a token from Issue, which adds exp, iat and the guard's algorithm. Every protected handler starts with a Require... call and returns at once when it is false. RequireScope reads the space separated scope claim, so the same token opens /orders but gets a 403 at /admin. The last request uses a token signed with the right secret but without exp; because the guard sets require_exp, it is refused. jwt-guard.salamCopyimport encoding.json import jwt import net.http import net.router  mut guard := jwt.NewGuard("k8R2pX7wQ4mZ9vL1cT6yB3nH5sD0fG2a")  func login(ctx: i64):     mut c := jwt.NewClaims()     c.sub = http.Form(ctx, "user")     jwt.SetStr(c, "scope", "orders:read")     try:         token := jwt.Issue(guard, c, 900)         http.Json(ctx, "{\"token\":\"" + token + "\"}")     catch e:         http.SetStatus(ctx, 500)         http.Text(ctx, e.message)     end end  func orders(ctx: i64):     mut t := jwt.Token {}     if not jwt.RequireScope(ctx, guard, "orders:read", t): ret end     http.Json(ctx, "{\"orders_for\":\"" + t.claims.sub + "\"}") end  func admin(ctx: i64):     mut t := jwt.Token {}     if not jwt.RequireScope(ctx, guard, "admin", t): ret end     http.Text(ctx, "welcome, admin") end  func call(path: str, token: str):     mut headers := http.NewHeaders()     if token.Len() > 0: headers.Insert("Authorization", "Bearer " + token) end     r := http.GetWith("http://127.0.0.1:18661" + path, headers)     println path, http.Status(r), http.Body(r) end  func main:     guard.opts.require_exp = true     mut r := router.NewRouter()     router.Post(r, "/login", login)     router.Get(r, "/orders", orders)     router.Get(r, "/admin", admin)     mut s := http.NewServer(18661)     http.SetHost(s, "127.0.0.1")     http.Use(s, r)     if not http.RunBackground(s):         println "port 18661 is busy"         ret 1     end     answer := http.Post("http://127.0.0.1:18661/login", "user=sara")     token := json.Get(http.Body(answer), "token")     call("/orders", "")     call("/orders", token)     call("/admin", token)      mut forever := jwt.NewClaims()     forever.sub = "sara"     jwt.SetStr(forever, "scope", "orders:read")     try:         call("/orders", jwt.SignHS256(forever, guard.secret))     catch e:         println "could not sign:", e.message     end     ret 0 endOutput/orders 401 {"error":"unauthorized","reason":"missing bearer token"} /orders 200 {"orders_for":"sara"} /admin 403 {"error":"forbidden","reason":"missing scope: admin"} /orders 401 {"error":"unauthorized","reason":"required claim missing"} Require takes the token from the Authorization: Bearer header, or from the cookie named in guard.cookie when there is no header. A 401 also carries a WWW-Authenticate header, as the HTTP rules ask.  Why a token is rejected Verify checks, in order, that the token has three parts, that its algorithm is the one you expect, that the signature matches, and then the times and the claims you asked for in Options. It is declared throws, as are Decode, the Sign and Issue functions, Check and B64UrlDecode: the first failure is thrown as an Error. Catch it with try: ... catch e:, or write try before the call in a function that is itself throws to pass it on. e.message is a short reason and e.code a stable name to branch on. The program below fixes now so that it prints the same lines every time; in a server leave now at 0 and the current clock is used. jwt-errors.salamCopyimport jwt import str  func report(label: str, token: str, secret: str, o: jwt.Options):     try:         _ := jwt.Verify(token, secret, o)         println label + ": ok"     catch e:         println label + ": " + e.message + " (" + e.code + ")"     end end  func main throws:     secret := "a-long-random-secret-for-this-demo"     mut c := jwt.NewClaims()     c.sub = "7"     c.iss = "a

tls tls Secure TLS 1.3 and 1.2 connections and public key cryptography tools, with no OpenSSL needed. Security and cryptography The tls package is a complete implementation of TLS 1.2 and 1.3 written in Salam, with no outside library. A client connects with Dial and checks the server certificate against the system roots; a server reads its certificate and key with NewServerConfig and secures each accepted socket with WrapServer. Most programs never call it directly: net.http, net.email and net.websocket use it for https, SMTPS and wss. For code written in the OpenSSL style (a context, SSL_connect, SSL_read), ssl offers that interface on top of this package. The cryptography tools here are also useful for protocols and storage of your own: the two sides make a shared secret with ECDH, derive a key from it with HKDF, and encrypt and seal the message with AES-GCM; P-256 signs and verifies. Keys and data are passed around as base64 text, which keeps binary bytes safe inside a str. Things to know:  Check ConnOk after Dial. A failed handshake or a bad certificate gives a closed connection, and ConnError says why. Read returns a str, which stops at a zero byte. For binary data use ReadBytes and WriteBytes with your own buffer. Clients cannot present a certificate (no mutual TLS), and a Conn is passed by reference and belongs to one thread at a time. Never repeat an AES-GCM nonce under one key; the sealing section shows a counter that avoids it. AES-GCM runs on the processor's AES instructions when it has them: AES-NI and PCLMULQDQ on x86-64, the Crypto Extensions on AArch64, in every build made with the LLVM backend, which includes all releases. This covers AeadNew, the one shot AesGcmSealRaw and AesGcmOpenRaw and the TLS record layer, so the proxy and VPN protocols get it with no change. Other backends, and processors without the instructions, use the table based code, which gives the same bytes. cpu tells which path is in use and can force the software one.   Connect to a server and handle a bad certificate Dial does the whole handshake and checks the certificate chain against the system roots and the name in NewConfig. When something is wrong, the connection is not open and ConnError says why: the certificate expired, it was issued for another name, or it does not chain to a trusted root. Always check ConnOk before you write. The program below tries a working site and three of the deliberately broken hosts at badssl.com. tls-https-check.salamCopyimport tls  func probe(host: str):     cfg := tls.NewConfig(host)     mut conn := tls.Dial(host, 443, cfg)     if not tls.ConnOk(conn):         println host, "refused:", tls.ConnError(conn)         ret     end     println host, tls.Version(conn), tls.CipherName(conn), tls.PeerCertCount(conn), "certificates"     tls.Close(conn) end  func main:     probe("www.salamlang.ir")     probe("expired.badssl.com")     probe("wrong.host.badssl.com")     probe("self-signed.badssl.com") end It needs network access, so it is only checked here. When it was run, it printed the lines below; the cipher and the number of certificates depend on the server. www.salamlang.ir TLS1.3 TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 3 certificates expired.badssl.com refused: certificate verification failed: certificate expired wrong.host.badssl.com refused: certificate verification failed: hostname does not match certificate self-signed.badssl.com refused: certificate verification failed: no trusted issuer found For a private server with its own certificate authority, set ca_file in the config to that CA's PEM file. insecure_skip_verify turns the check off; use it only for a quick local test, never in a program others rely on.  Encrypt records with AES-GCM AesGcmSeal encrypts a text and adds a tag, so that AesGcmOpen notices any change: a wrong key, a wrong nonce or a changed byte all make ok false instead of returning garbage. The key is 32 random bytes as base64; make it once with RandomSalt(32) and keep it secret. The nonce must never repeat under one key. The simple rule is a counter: GcmNonce(0) for the first message, GcmNonce(1) for the next, and the counter is stored next to the record so that it can be opened later. tls-sealed-records.salamCopyimport tls  func main:     key := "q1V0kA8mY8l3R9m0bJvT0F6c0w2f5yYQ1aZt3pK8sXo="     records := ["balance=120", "balance=95", "balance=310"]      mut sealed := Vector {} as Vector<str>     mut ok := false     each i, r in records:         sealed.Push(tls.AesGcmSeal(key, tls.GcmNonce(i as i64), r, ok))     end     println "sealed", sealed.Len(), "records:", ok     println "first one:", sealed.Get(0)      each i, s in sealed:         plain := tls.AesGcmOpen(key, tls.GcmNonce(i as i64), s, ok)         println "record", i, "->", plain, ok     end      _ := tls.AesGcmOpen(key, tls.GcmNonce(1), sealed.Get(0), ok)     println "opened with the wrong nonce:", ok     _ := tls.AesGcmOpen("AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA=", tls.GcmNonce(0), sealed.Get(0), ok)     println "opened with the wrong key:", ok endOutputsealed 3 records: true first one: q/F2IqBhzaLO/CFJROFcuA2GEUtg3H4MyDU5 record 0 -> balance=120 true record 1 -> balance=95 true record 2 -> balance=310 true opened with the wrong nonce: false opened with the wrong key: false With a fixed key and nonce the output is always the same, which is why the program can print it. That is also the danger: the same nonce for two different texts lets an attacker learn about both, so never reset the counter while the key stays the same.  A shared key from public keys Two programs that have never met can agree on a key without sending it. Each makes an ECDH key pair with EcdhP256Generate and sends the other only its public key. EcdhP256Shared then gives both the same secret, and HkdfSha256 turns it into a key f

db/sql db.sql Read, check and type SQL without a database: a dialect-aware parser, a schema catalog and typed placeholders. Database A query is a string, so a typo in it is found by the database, at run time, on the one code path nobody tested. This package reads the string instead: it lexes and parses SQL for one of four dialects, and when you hand it your schema it also resolves every table and column, names the ones that do not exist, and tells you the type of every placeholder and every column that comes back. Nothing here connects to a database; it is all static, so it belongs in a test or in a build step. It is the same idea as sqlc in Go, with the schema taken from the SQL you already write: the CREATE TABLE statements in your migrations are the catalog, so there is no second file to keep in step. Things that catch people out:  The dialect is not advice. ? is a placeholder in SQLite and MySQL and a plain operator in PostgreSQL, which numbers its own as $1; "name" is a quoted name everywhere except MySQL, where it is a string; AUTOINCREMENT, AUTO_INCREMENT and GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY belong to one engine each. Pass the dialect you will really run against. Check only resolves names when the statement parses. A report with a syntax error in it says nothing about the columns, so fix the syntax first and run it again. A table whose columns are not known, from CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT or a view the package could not read, is left open: columns on it are never reported as missing. No news is not always good news. Apply reads the DDL in order, so a view has to come after the tables it selects from, exactly as it does in the database. Diagnostic messages are English in both language modes; the codes are the same, so a Persian program can match on code. Placeholders hands back a Vector<str> you own: free the vector, and the strings in it, when you are done. Salam lets a name contain spaces; SQL does not. SELECT family name FROM t is a column and an alias, not one name, and it is accepted without complaint - which is worth knowing when the names are Persian, since those are often two words. Quote them: SELECT "family name" FROM t.  Start here: one walk from a schema to checked queries The six sections after this one take the package apart piece by piece. This one puts it together, in the order you would actually meet it on a project that already has a database and a pile of query strings. The program below is the whole arc, and you can run it as it stands - no server, no connection, nothing to set up. db-sql-tutorial.salamCopyimport db.sql import str  mut g_schema := sql.Catalog {}  func str_of(n: int): str:     ret str.FromInt(n as i64) end  func step(n: int, title: str):     println ""     println "step " + str_of(n) + ": " + title end  func try_query(q: str):     mut r := sql.Check(q, g_schema)     if r.ok and r.warnings == 0:         println "  ok   " + q     else:         println "  bad  " + q         mut i := 0         until i < r.items.Len():             d := r.items.Get(i)             println "       " + d.code + " " + d.message             if not str.IsEmpty(d.help):                 println "       " + d.help             end             i++         end     end     sql.FreeReport(r) end  func main:     step(1, "the schema you already have")     g_schema = sql.NewCatalog(sql.DialectOf(sql.SQLITE))     defer sql.FreeCatalog(g_schema)     mut ddl := sql.Apply(g_schema, """         CREATE TABLE authors (             id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,             name TEXT NOT NULL,             country TEXT         );         CREATE TABLE books (             id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,             author_id INTEGER NOT NULL,             title TEXT NOT NULL,             year INTEGER,             price REAL         );     """)     println "  loaded " + str_of(sql.TableCount(g_schema)) + " tables, " + str_of(sql.ColumnCount(g_schema, "books")) + " columns on books"     sql.FreeReport(ddl)      step(2, "the queries you already have")     try_query("SELECT id, titles FROM books WHERE author_id = ?")     try_query("SELECT b.title, a.nationality FROM books b JOIN authors a ON a.id = b.author_id")     try_query("INSERT INTO books (title) VALUES (?)")     try_query("SELECT id FROM books WHERE year = 'recent'")     try_query("DELETE FROM books")      step(3, "the same five, put right")     try_query("SELECT id, title FROM books WHERE author_id = ?")     try_query("SELECT b.title, a.country FROM books b JOIN authors a ON a.id = b.author_id")     try_query("INSERT INTO books (author_id, title) VALUES (?, ?)")     try_query("SELECT id FROM books WHERE year = 2024")     try_query("DELETE FROM books WHERE id = ?")      step(4, "what a query takes and gives back")     mut a := sql.Analyze("SELECT books.title, books.price, authors.country FROM books JOIN authors ON authors.id = books.author_id WHERE books.year > ?", g_schema)     println "  it is a " + sql.StmtKindName(a.kind) + " on " + a.table     p := a.params.Get(0)     println "  takes " + p.column + " as " + sql.SalamType(p.kind, p.not_null)     mut i := 0     until i < a.results.Len():         c := a.results.Get(i)         println "  gives " + c.name + " as " + sql.SalamType(c.kind, not c.nullable)         i++     end     sql.FreeAnalysis(a)      step(5, "the values go in safely")     mut args := sql.NewArgs()     sql.AddText(args, "O'Brien")     sql.AddInt(args, 1988 as i64)     mut rep := sql.Report {}     filled := sql.Fill("INSERT INTO books (title, year) VALUES (?, ?)", args, sql.DialectOf(sql.SQLITE), rep)     println "  &q

db db One interface shared by the database engines, schema migrations and a connection pool. Database Every database engine has its own package: db.sqlite, db.mysql, db.postgres, for key and value db.redis, for analytics db.clickhouse, and for search db.typesense, db.meilisearch, db.elasticsearch and, for search and analytics, db.opensearch; the last two also answer SQL queries through Connection. This package gives the Connection interface that the three SQL engines implement; write your code against it and changing engine is one line. To check the SQL itself before it ever reaches a server, db.sql parses it for each engine's dialect and resolves it against your schema. Migrations move the database schema along with the code: every change has a number and MigrateUp applies the ones numbered above the current schema version. Never paste a value a user typed straight into SQL; send it through QuoteLiteral or as a prepared parameter. Things that catch people out:  QuoteLiteral only doubles single quotes, which is the SQL standard that SQLite and PostgreSQL follow. MySQL also treats a backslash as an escape by default, so on MySQL quote with the connection's own c.Quote, which escapes backslashes as well. MigrateUp compares version numbers, not a list of applied names. A migration numbered below the highest applied one, for example one merged from an older branch, is skipped without a word. Always give a new migration the next free number. MySQL commits every CREATE, ALTER and DROP on its own, so on MySQL a migration that fails halfway can leave the first statements applied. SQLite and PostgreSQL roll the whole migration back. Migration SQL is split into statements at each ; outside single quotes. A PostgreSQL function body in $$ ... $$ or a trigger with several statements is cut apart; run those with c.Exec instead.  Writing code against Connection Give your data functions a dyn db.Connection parameter instead of a SQLite or PostgreSQL database. They then work with every SQL engine, and tests can pass an in-memory SQLite database while production passes PostgreSQL. db.Run runs one statement and returns true on success; c.Error() says what went wrong; c.LastInsertId() gives the id of the row just inserted. db-guide-store.salamCopyimport db import db.sqlite  func setup(c: dyn db.Connection): bool:     ret db.Run(c, "CREATE TABLE notes (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, author TEXT NOT NULL, body TEXT NOT NULL)") end  func add_note(c: dyn db.Connection, author: str, body: str): i64:     sql := "INSERT INTO notes (author, body) VALUES (" + db.QuoteLiteral(author) + ", " + db.QuoteLiteral(body) + ")"     if not db.Run(c, sql):         println "insert failed:", c.Error()         ret 0     end     ret c.LastInsertId() end  func print_notes(c: dyn db.Connection, author: str):     rows := c.Query("SELECT id, body FROM notes WHERE author = " + db.QuoteLiteral(author) + " ORDER BY id")     until rows.Next():         println "#" + rows.Int(0), rows.Text(1)     end     _ := rows.Close() end  func main:     c := sqlite.Conn(sqlite.Open(":memory:"))     if not setup(c):         println "setup failed:", c.Error()         ret 1     end     add_note(c, "Sara", "buy milk")     add_note(c, "Omid", "call the bank")     add_note(c, "Sara", "it's Reza's birthday")     add_note(c, "x' OR '1'='1", "trying to break in")     print_notes(c, "Sara")     println "notes by Omid:", db.QueryInt(c, "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM notes WHERE author = 'Omid'")     println "all notes:", db.QueryInt(c, "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM notes")     _ := c.Close()     ret 0 endOutput#1 buy milk #3 it's Reza's birthday notes by Omid: 1 all notes: 4 Every value that came from a user goes through QuoteLiteral, which wraps it in quotes and doubles any quote inside. That is why the apostrophe in Reza's is stored correctly, and why the author name x' OR '1'='1 is stored as an odd name instead of changing the meaning of the query. Never build SQL by gluing raw input into it. A query returns dyn db.Rows. Next moves to the next row and returns false at the end, so until rows.Next(): visits every row; read columns by position with Int, Text, Float and IsNull, and always Close the rows. For a single number or string, QueryInt and QueryText do all of that in one call.  Transactions: all or nothing When several statements must succeed or fail together, run them inside a transaction. c.Begin() returns a dyn db.Tx with its own Exec and Query; Commit makes the changes permanent and Rollback throws them all away. The transfer below takes money from one account, gives it to the other, then checks the result and rolls back if the first account went below zero. db-guide-transfer.salamCopyimport db import db.sqlite  func transfer(c: dyn db.Connection, from_id: int, to_id: int, amount: int): str:     tx := c.Begin()     if not tx.Ok():         ret "could not start: " + c.Error()     end     _ := tx.Exec("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - " + amount + " WHERE id = " + from_id)     _ := tx.Exec("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + " + amount + " WHERE id = " + to_id)     rows := tx.Query("SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = " + from_id)     mut left := 0     if rows.Next():         left = rows.Int(0)     end     _ := rows.Close()     if left < 0:         _ := tx.Rollback()         ret "refused, only " + (left + amount) + " left"     end     _ := tx.Commit()     ret "moved " + amount end  func balances(c: dyn db.Connection): str:     ret db.QueryText(c, "SELECT group_concat(name || '=' || balance, ' ') FROM accounts") end  func main:     c := sqlite.Conn(sqlite.Open(":memory:"))     mut setup := Vector {} as Vector<str>

db/sqlite db.sqlite An SQLite database in one file or in memory. Database SQLite is a database that fits in one file and needs no server; for desktop programs, tools and a great many websites it is enough. The program links against the system's sqlite3 library, so that library has to be installed where it runs (it is on almost every Linux and macOS system already). There are two ways to work: the functions of this package, such as Query and Next, which reach everything SQLite offers; or the database and row methods and Conn, which is the shared interface of db. Send user values through Prepare and the Bind... functions, not by pasting them into the SQL text. This page starts with a tutorial and a few guides for common jobs; the full reference of every function and type comes after them.  Tutorial: a lending library in twelve steps The steps below build the database of a small lending library: books, members and loans. Each step is a complete program, and the output under it is what it printed with SQLite 3.46. Run the steps in order in one folder, because each one opens the same library.db file and uses what the earlier steps left in it. To start over, delete library.db and the library.db-wal and library.db-shm files next to it. Nothing needs to be started first. If a program fails to link with a message about sqlite3, install the library: sudo apt install libsqlite3-dev on Debian and Ubuntu, sudo dnf install sqlite-devel on Fedora, or brew install sqlite on macOS.  1. Open the database and set options Open opens a file, creating it when it is not there. :memory: (or an empty path) gives a private database in memory that disappears when it is closed, which is handy for tests and caches. SQLite has no connection string: options are PRAGMA statements you run after opening. Three are worth setting in almost every program. journal_mode = WAL lets readers keep reading while a writer works, and it is stored in the file, so setting it once is enough. foreign_keys = ON makes SQLite enforce REFERENCES; it is off by default and belongs to the connection, so every program that opens the file sets it again. busy_timeout makes a connection wait that many milliseconds for a lock instead of failing at once. db-sqlite-open.salamCopyimport db.sqlite import str  func main:     if not sqlite.Available():         println "SQLite is not installed"         ret 1     end     println "SQLite 3:", str.StartsWith(sqlite.Version(), "3.")      d := sqlite.Open("library.db")     defer sqlite.Close(d)     if not sqlite.Ok(d) or sqlite.Exec(d, "SELECT 1") != 0:         println "could not open:", sqlite.Error(d)         ret 1     end      println "journal:", sqlite.QueryText(d, "PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL")     sqlite.Exec(d, "PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON")     println "foreign keys:", sqlite.QueryInt(d, "PRAGMA foreign_keys")     println "busy timeout:", sqlite.QueryInt(d, "PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000")      bad := sqlite.Open("/no/such/folder/library.db")     println "bad path, handle:", sqlite.Ok(bad), "| first statement:", sqlite.Exec(bad, "SELECT 1"), sqlite.Error(bad)     sqlite.Close(bad) endOutputSQLite 3: true journal: wal foreign keys: 1 busy timeout: 5000 bad path, handle: true | first statement: -1 unable to open database file Look at the last line. SQLite hands back a handle even when the file cannot be opened, so Ok is true and the problem only shows when the first statement fails. That is why this step runs SELECT 1 before trusting the database.  2. Create the tables Exec runs one or more statements separated by semicolons and returns 0 on success or -1 on failure, with the reason in Error. A triple quoted string keeps a long schema readable. IF NOT EXISTS makes the step safe to run again, and PRAGMA user_version is a free integer in the file header that is handy for a schema version (step 11 uses a migration table instead). db-sqlite-schema.salamCopyimport db.sqlite  func main:     d := sqlite.Open("library.db")     defer sqlite.Close(d)      schema := """     CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS books (         id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,         title TEXT NOT NULL,         author TEXT NOT NULL,         year INTEGER,         copies INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1 CHECK (copies >= 0),         rating REAL,         note TEXT     );     CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS members (         id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,         name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,         email TEXT     );     CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS loans (         id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,         book INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES books (id),         member INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES members (id),         due TEXT NOT NULL,         returned TEXT     );     CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS books_author ON books (author);     PRAGMA user_version = 1;     """     if sqlite.Exec(d, schema) != 0:         println "schema failed:", sqlite.Error(d)         ret 1     end      rows := sqlite.Query(d, "SELECT type, name FROM sqlite_master ORDER BY type, name")     until sqlite.Next(rows):         println sqlite.Text(rows, 0), sqlite.Text(rows, 1)     end     sqlite.Finish(rows)     println "schema version:", sqlite.QueryInt(d, "PRAGMA user_version") endOutputindex books_author index sqlite_autoindex_members_1 table books table loans table members schema version: 1 SQLite types are loose: a column declared INTEGER will store text if you give it text. Constraints such as NOT NULL, UNIQUE and CHECK are what actually keep the data clean. An INTEGER PRIMARY KEY column is the row id, filled in for you on insert.  3. Insert rows Prepare compiles a statement with ? places once; the Bind... functions fill the places (numbered from 1), Next runs it, and Reset readies it for the next row. Preparing once and binding many times is both faster and safer than building

db/mysql db.mysql Connecting to MySQL and MariaDB. Database This package speaks the MySQL and MariaDB client protocol itself and needs no outside library: there is no libmysqlclient to install and nothing to link. It logs in with mysql_native_password or caching_sha2_password, encrypts the connection with TLS whenever the server offers it, and asks for utf8mb4 during the handshake, so Persian text and emoji work from the first query. The functions follow the shape of the C API (Open, Exec, Query, Next, Finish), and Conn turns a connection into the shared Connection of db, so code written against that interface also runs on SQLite and PostgreSQL. This page starts with a tutorial; the reference of every function comes after it.  Tutorial: a small bookshop in eleven steps The steps below build the database of a small bookshop: a table of books, a table of orders, and the code to sell, restock and report on them. Each step is a complete program, and the output under it is what it printed against a real MariaDB 11.8 server. Run them in order, because each step uses the rows the earlier ones left behind. First start a server. With Docker that is one command, and it also creates the database and the user the programs log in with: docker run -d --name shop-db -p 3306:3306 -e MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD=rootpw -e MARIADB_DATABASE=shop -e MARIADB_USER=salam -e MARIADB_PASSWORD=secret mariadb:11.8 The programs connect to 127.0.0.1 on port 3306 as salam with the password secret and use the database shop. The outputs come from MariaDB. MySQL 8 speaks the same protocol and the package works with it too, but a few statements here use MariaDB names: on MySQL the status table of step 1 is performance_schema.session_status.  1. Connect Open takes the host, user, password, database name and port, and always returns a Database. Check it with Ok before anything else: when the login fails the handle is empty and Error says why. A database name of "" connects without choosing one, and SelectDB picks it later. Close sends the server a polite goodbye and frees the connection, so defer it right after the check. db-mysql-connect.salamCopyimport db.mysql  func main:     d := mysql.Open("127.0.0.1", "salam", "secret", "shop", 3306)     if not mysql.Ok(d):         println "cannot connect:", mysql.Error(d)         ret 1     end     defer mysql.Close(d)      println "server:", mysql.ServerVersion(d)     println "client:", mysql.ClientVersion()     println "alive:", mysql.Ping(d)     println "database:", mysql.QueryText(d, "SELECT DATABASE()")     println "charset:", mysql.QueryText(d, "SELECT @@character_set_connection")     println "tls:", mysql.QueryText(d, "SELECT VARIABLE_VALUE FROM information_schema.SESSION_STATUS WHERE VARIABLE_NAME = 'Ssl_version'")      bad := mysql.Open("127.0.0.1", "salam", "wrong", "shop", 3306)     println "with a wrong password:", mysql.Ok(bad)     println mysql.Error(bad)      nobody := mysql.Open("127.0.0.1", "salam", "secret", "shop", 3307)     println mysql.Error(nobody)     ret 0 endOutputserver: 11.8.8-MariaDB-ubu2404 client: salam-native alive: true database: shop charset: utf8mb4 tls: TLSv1.3 with a wrong password: false Access denied for user 'salam'@'127.0.0.1' (using password: YES) Can't connect to server on '127.0.0.1' port 3307 The tls line shows that the session is encrypted even though the program asked for nothing: MariaDB 11.8 has TLS on by default and the client uses it when it is there. Encryption and TLS modes below shows how to require it or turn it off. Note that Errno only works on a connection that exists; for a failed Open there is just the message.  2. Create the tables Exec runs one statement and returns 0 when it worked and -1 when it did not. SQL that spans several lines is easiest to write as a backtick string, which keeps newlines and quotes exactly as typed. One Exec runs one statement; to run several, call it once for each. db-mysql-schema.salamCopyimport db.mysql  func main:     d := mysql.Open("127.0.0.1", "salam", "secret", "shop", 3306)     if not mysql.Ok(d):         println "cannot connect:", mysql.Error(d)         ret 1     end     defer mysql.Close(d)      mysql.Exec(d, "DROP TABLE IF EXISTS orders")     mysql.Exec(d, "DROP TABLE IF EXISTS books")      books := `CREATE TABLE books (         id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,         title VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL UNIQUE,         author VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,         price DECIMAL(8, 2) NOT NULL,         stock INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,         isbn VARCHAR(20) NULL,         details JSON NULL     ) ENGINE = InnoDB DEFAULT CHARSET = utf8mb4`     println "books:", mysql.Exec(d, books)      orders := `CREATE TABLE orders (         id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,         book_id INT NOT NULL,         customer VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,         qty INT NOT NULL,         total DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL,         FOREIGN KEY (book_id) REFERENCES books (id)     ) ENGINE = InnoDB DEFAULT CHARSET = utf8mb4`     println "orders:", mysql.Exec(d, orders)      mut r := mysql.Query(d, "SELECT TABLE_NAME, COUNT(*) FROM information_schema.COLUMNS WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA = 'shop' AND TABLE_NAME IN ('books', 'orders') GROUP BY TABLE_NAME ORDER BY TABLE_NAME")     until mysql.Next(r):         println mysql.Text(r, 0), "has", mysql.Int(r, 1), "columns"     end     mysql.Finish(r)     ret 0 endOutputbooks: 0 orders: 0 books has 7 columns orders has 5 columns The books table has a nullable isbn and a JSON column for details that differ from book to book. InnoDB is the engine that gives transactions and foreign keys, and utf8mb4 is the real four byte UTF-8; the older utf8

db/postgres db.postgres A PostgreSQL client written in Salam: connection strings and URIs, TLS, queries, transactions, pools and migrations. Database This package talks to PostgreSQL directly: it implements the Postgres wire protocol in Salam itself, with password, MD5 and SCRAM-SHA-256 logins and optional TLS, so it needs no libpq or any other outside library. Every row of a result is fetched from the server at once, so RowCount is known before you read any of them. A Database also fits the shared Connection interface of db, which gives you engine neutral helpers, connection pools and migrations. This page starts with a tutorial; the full reference of every function and type comes after it.  Tutorial: a bookshop in eleven steps The steps below build the database of a small bookshop: books, stock and orders. Each step is a complete program, and the output under it is what it printed against a real PostgreSQL 17. Run them in order, because each step uses the data the earlier ones left behind. First start a server. With Docker that is one command; it creates the bookshop database and the postgres user with the password secret: docker run -d --name bookshop-db -p 5432:5432 -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret -e POSTGRES_DB=bookshop postgres:17-alpine Without Docker, install PostgreSQL from your system's packages, then run createdb bookshop and give the postgres user that password. The programs connect to 127.0.0.1 on port 5432. A real application logs in with its own user rather than postgres, as step 2 shows.  1. Connect Open takes a connection string of key=value pairs, the same format psql and libpq use. It always returns a Database, even when the login failed, so check Ok before anything else; Error then holds the server's message. Ping sends a tiny query to make sure the connection still works, which is a good health check for a long running service. db-postgres-connect.salamCopyimport db.postgres  func main:     d := postgres.Open("host=127.0.0.1 port=5432 user=postgres password=secret dbname=bookshop")     defer postgres.Close(d)     if not postgres.Ok(d):         print "could not connect: " + postgres.Error(d)         ret 1     end     println "connected to", postgres.DatabaseName(d), "as", postgres.UserName(d)     println "server", postgres.HostName(d) + ":" + postgres.Port(d), "version", postgres.ServerVersion(d)     println postgres.QueryText(d, "SELECT split_part(version(), ' on ', 1)")     println "alive:", postgres.Ping(d)      bad := postgres.Open("host=127.0.0.1 user=postgres password=wrong dbname=bookshop")     defer postgres.Close(bad)     println "with a wrong password:", postgres.Ok(bad)     print postgres.Error(bad)      off := postgres.Open("host=127.0.0.1 port=5499 user=postgres password=secret connect_timeout=3")     defer postgres.Close(off)     println "with no server on the port:", postgres.Ok(off)     print postgres.Error(off) endOutputconnected to bookshop as postgres server 127.0.0.1:5432 version 170011 PostgreSQL 17.11 alive: true with a wrong password: false FATAL:  password authentication failed for user "postgres" with no server on the port: false connection to server at "127.0.0.1", port 5499 failed The server's own messages keep their PostgreSQL wording and start with the severity: FATAL for a refused login, ERROR for a failed statement. An error message ends with a newline, which is why the examples print it with print rather than println. With nothing listening on the port, Open fails at once. connect_timeout, in seconds, limits how long the login waits for each answer from the server, 30 seconds when you leave it out.  2. Connection strings, URIs and TLS The same settings can be written three ways: as key=value pairs, as a postgresql://user:password@host:port/dbname?key=value URI, or as the five arguments of OpenFull. This step also creates a login role for the shop, with a password that has a space and an @ in it, to show how such a value is written in each form. db-postgres-options.salamCopyimport db.postgres  func main:     admin := postgres.OpenFull("127.0.0.1", 5432, "postgres", "secret", "bookshop")     defer postgres.Close(admin)     println "OpenFull:", postgres.Ok(admin)     _ := postgres.Exec(admin, "DROP ROLE IF EXISTS clerk")     _ := postgres.Exec(admin, "CREATE ROLE clerk LOGIN PASSWORD 'p@ss word'")      a := postgres.Open("host=127.0.0.1 user=clerk password='p@ss word' dbname=bookshop")     defer postgres.Close(a)     println "quoted value:", postgres.Ok(a), postgres.UserName(a)      b := postgres.Open("postgresql://clerk:p%40ss%20word@127.0.0.1:5432/bookshop?connect_timeout=5")     defer postgres.Close(b)     println "uri:", postgres.Ok(b), postgres.UserName(b), postgres.DatabaseName(b)      c := postgres.Open("host=127.0.0.1 user=clerk password='p@ss word' dbname=bookshop sslmode=disable")     defer postgres.Close(c)     println "sslmode=disable:", postgres.Ok(c), postgres.QueryText(c, "SHOW ssl")      t := postgres.Open("host=127.0.0.1 user=clerk password='p@ss word' dbname=bookshop sslmode=require")     defer postgres.Close(t)     println "sslmode=require:", postgres.Ok(t)     print postgres.Error(t) endOutputOpenFull: true quoted value: true clerk uri: true clerk bookshop sslmode=disable: true off sslmode=require: false server does not support SSL, but SSL was required In the key=value form, a value with spaces goes in single quotes. In a URI, characters with a meaning of their own are percent encoded: %40 for @ and %20 for a space. OpenFull joins its arguments without quoting them, so use it only for values without spaces. The keys this package reads are host (or hostaddr), port, user, password, dbname, sslmode, sslrootcert and connec

db/redis db.redis A Redis client: keys and values, hashes, lists, sets and publishing. Database Redis is an in memory database for caches, sessions, counters, queues and leaderboards. This package speaks the Redis protocol directly over a socket, with no outside library: one function per common command for strings, hashes, lists and sets, plus Command, which sends any other command with its arguments and hands back the raw reply. This page starts with a tutorial; the full reference of every function and type comes after it.  Tutorial: a link shortener in twelve steps The steps below build the storage of a small link shortener: link records, click counters, a list of recent links, unique visitors and a leaderboard. Each step is a complete program, and the output under it is what it printed against a real Redis 7.4. Run them in order, because each step uses the keys the earlier ones left behind. The last step deletes everything again. First start a server with a password. With Docker that is one command: docker run -p 6379:6379 redis:7.4 redis-server --requirepass s3cret The programs connect to 127.0.0.1:6379 and log in with s3cret. To start over at any point, run docker exec on the container with redis-cli -a s3cret flushall, then begin again at step 1.  1. Connect and log in Connect opens one TCP connection and returns a Client. Ok tells you whether that worked and Error says why not. A server with a password refuses every command until Auth succeeds, which is why the first Ping is false. Select switches to another numbered database; a default server has 16, numbered 0 to 15. db-redis-connect.salamCopyimport db.redis  func main:     c := redis.Connect("127.0.0.1", 6379)     if not redis.Ok(c):         println "cannot reach Redis:", redis.Error(c)         ret 1     end     defer redis.Close(c)      println "ping before login:", redis.Ping(c)     println "wrong password:", redis.Auth(c, "guess")     println "right password:", redis.Auth(c, "s3cret")     println "ping after login:", redis.Ping(c)      println "database 15:", redis.Select(c, 15)     println "database 99:", redis.Select(c, 99)     println "back to 0:", redis.Select(c, 0)      off := redis.Connect("127.0.0.1", 6390)     println "port 6390:", redis.Ok(off), redis.Error(off) endOutputping before login: false wrong password: false right password: true ping after login: true database 15: true database 99: false back to 0: true port 6390: false no connection Every function in this package returns a plain value (a bool, a number, a string or a vector) instead of an error object. When something goes wrong you get the empty value: false, 0 or an empty string. Step 10 shows how to tell the cases apart when that matters. Always Close a client: it closes the socket and frees the buffer.  2. Strings and missing keys The simplest Redis value is a string under a key.
