The first Forward call reads the whole prompt; after that each call feeds only the newest token, because the KVCache remembers everything before it. The loop stops at the end of turn token, after 80 tokens, or when the context is full. cfg.ctx is lowered to 4096 first, which keeps the cache at about 100 MB instead of 800. mkdir -p models curl -L -o models/qwen2.5-0.5b-instruct-q8_0.gguf \   https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct-GGUF/resolve/main/qwen2.5-0.5b-instruct-q8_0.gguf salam run llm-guide-chat.salam llm-guide-chat.salamCopyimport ai.llm import ai.tensor  func add_turn(tok &: llm.Tokenizer, ids &: Vector<int>, role: str, text: str):     ids.Push(tok.index.Get("<|im_start|>"))     piece := tok.encode(role + "\n" + text)     each id in piece:         ids.Push(id)     end     if text.Len() > 0:         ids.Push(tok.index.Get("<|im_end|>"))         newline := tok.encode("\n")         each id in newline:             ids.Push(id)         end     end end  func main:     path := "models/qwen2.5-0.5b-instruct-q8_0.gguf"     mut model := llm.Model {}     mut tok := llm.NewTokenizer(llm.TOK_BPE)     if not llm.LoadGgufModel(path, model, tok):         println "could not load", path         ret 1     end     tok.add_bos = false     end_of_turn := tok.index.Get("<|im_end|>")     model.cfg.ctx = 4096     mut cache := llm.NewKVCache(model.cfg)     mut sampler := llm.NewSampler(42)     sampler.temperature = 0.7     sampler.top_p = 0.9     sampler.repeat_penalty = 1.1     mut ids := Vector {} as Vector<int>     add_turn(tok, ids, "system", "You are a helpful assistant. Answer in one sentence.")     add_turn(tok, ids, "user", "Why is the sky blue?")     add_turn(tok, ids, "assistant", "")     mut logits := llm.Forward(model, cache, ids)     mut said := Vector {} as Vector<int>     mut step := Vector {} as Vector<int>     step.Push(0)     until said.Len() < 80 and cache.len < cache.ctx:         next := sampler.sample(logits, logits.dim(0) - 1, said)         tensor.Free(logits)         if next == end_of_turn or next == tok.eos:             break         end         said.Push(next)         step.Set(0, next)         print tok.decode(step)         logits = llm.Forward(model, cache, step)     end     println ""     println "tokens in prompt:", ids.Len(), "answer:", said.Len()     cache.Free()     model.Free()     tok.Free() end The sky appears blue because of the scattering of sunlight by tiny water droplets in the atmosphere, which causes them to bounce off each other and scatter into our eyes. tokens in prompt: 30 answer: 33 A half billion weight model writes fluent sentences but gets facts wrong, as here: the real cause is scattering by air molecules, not water droplets. Use such a model for form, not for knowledge. Build with salam build --release for real use: the model runs on the processor, and a release build drops the bounds checks from the inner loops. Even so, expect a few seconds per token on an ordinary machine.  How text becomes tokens A model never sees letters, only token ids. A BPE tokenizer starts from single characters and applies its list of merges in order, so frequent pieces such as lower become one token while rare words fall apart into many. Byte level BPE, the kind GPT 2, Llama 3 and Qwen use, writes a space as Ġ, so the space before a word is part of a token.

image image Reading, editing and saving images, and writing text on them. AI This package works with images without any outside library: it reads and writes PNG, JPEG and BMP. It also reads and writes WebP, both lossy and lossless. From a GIF it reads the first frame, and it saves an image in a GIF with at most 256 colors. Open and Save work the format out from the content or the extension. Drawing, resizing, cropping, rotating and filters such as blurring and sharpening are all there. For text, read a TrueType font with LoadFont and write with DrawTextStyled; Persian and Arabic text is shaped and laid out right to left on its own. Use this package for thumbnails, generated cards and charts, watermarks and simple image checks. For computer vision (edges, contours, feature matching) see opencv, and to draw in a browser page, web.canvas. Things to know  Pixels are 8 bit RGBA in memory. Every image owns that memory; release it with Free. Save picks the format from the extension and returns false for one it does not know. It uses quality 90; SaveQuality takes your own. JPEG has no transparency: transparent pixels are laid on white before saving. WebP at quality 100 is lossless, below that lossy. GIF reading gives only the first frame of an animation, and saving reduces the image to 256 colors. Persian shaping uses the Arabic presentation forms of the font, so the font must contain them. FindArabicFont looks for an installed one that does (or the file in $SALAM_FONT_ARABIC).   Thumbnails and fixed-size cards An upload form usually needs the same picture in several sizes. Thumbnail shrinks the image so that its longer side fits and keeps the shape. ResizeFill fills an exact box and cuts off what sticks out, which suits square avatars and product cards. ResizeFit keeps the whole picture inside the box and centers it, leaving empty bands at the sides. Save chooses the format from the extension, so the same code writes PNG, JPEG or WebP. image-guide-thumbs.salamCopyimport image  func size(img: image.Image): str:     ret "" + img.width + "x" + img.height end  func main:     mut photo := image.New(1200, 800)     defer image.Free(photo)     image.FillHex(photo, "#3a6ea5")     image.DrawCircleFilled(photo, 600, 400, 250, image.ParseHex("#f2c14e"))     if image.Save(photo, "photo.jpg") == false:         println "could not write photo.jpg"         ret 1     end      mut ok := false     mut loaded := image.Open("photo.jpg", ok)     defer image.Free(loaded)     println "opened:", ok, size(loaded)      mut thumb := image.Thumbnail(loaded, 200)     mut card := image.ResizeFill(loaded, 300, 300)     mut banner := image.ResizeFit(loaded, 600, 200)     defer image.Free(thumb)     defer image.Free(card)     defer image.Free(banner)     println "thumbnail:", size(thumb)     println "square card:", size(card)     println "banner box:", size(banner)     image.Save(thumb, "thumb.png")     image.Save(card, "card.webp")     println "formats:", image.FormatFromExt("thumb.png") == image.FormatPNG, image.FormatFromExt("card.webp") == image.FormatWebP endOutputopened: true 1200x800 thumbnail: 200x133 square card: 300x300 banner box: 600x200 formats: true true Open reports through its bool argument whether the file could be read. Every image allocates memory for its pixels, so release each one with Free, as the defer lines do.  Draw a simple chart Lines, rectangles and circles plus the built-in pixel font are enough for a small bar chart, a badge or a placeholder image, with no font file needed. LerpColor mixes two colors, here to make taller bars darker, and ParseHex and ToHexRGB move between colors and CSS-style hex. TextWidth measures text before you draw it, so labels can be centered under their bars. image-guide-chart.salamCopyimport image  func main:     sales := [12, 30, 22, 41, 35]     labels := ["MON", "TUE", "WED", "THU", "FRI"]     width := 260     height := 160     mut chart := image.NewFilled(width, height, image.RGB(255, 255, 255))     defer image.Free(chart)     low := image.ParseHex("#9ecae1")     high := image.ParseHex("#08519c")     image.DrawLine(chart, 20, 130, 250, 130, image.Gray(80))     each i, value in sales:         bar := value * 2         x := 30 + i * 45         shade := image.LerpColor(low, high, (value as f64) / 41.0)         image.DrawRectFilled(chart, x, 130 - bar, 30, bar, shade)         image.DrawText(chart, x + 15 - image.TextWidth(labels[i], 1) / 2, 136, labels[i], image.Gray(40), 1)     end     image.DrawText(chart, 20, 8, "SALES", image.Gray(20), 2)     image.Save(chart, "chart.png")      top := image.GetPixel(chart, 30 + 3 * 45 + 15, 130 - 41)     println "tallest bar color:", image.ToHexRGB(top)     println "first bar color:", image.ToHexRGB(image.GetPixel(chart, 45, 129))     println "background:", image.ToHexRGB(image.GetPixel(chart, 5, 5))     println "title width:", image.TextWidth("SALES", 2), "px" endOutputtallest bar color: #08519c first bar color: #72a6cc background: #ffffff title width: 60 px The pixel font has only capital English letters, digits and the signs . , - : ! ?; anything else, lower case letters included, is drawn as a blank. For Persian or any other script, and for smooth text at large sizes, load a TrueType font with LoadFont and use DrawTextStyled, which shapes Persian letters and lays them out right to left.  Filters and measuring the difference Blurred and Sharpened return new images; Grayscale, Threshold, Brightness and Contrast change the image in place. To compare two images, MeanAbsError gives the average difference per channel and PSNR the signal to noise ratio in decibels, where higher means more alike. The numbers show that sharpening a blurred

ai/ml ai.ml Classic machine learning: preprocessing, regression, classification, trees, clustering and evaluation. AI This package gives you the classic machine learning algorithms behind an interface much like scikit-learn. The data is a matrix where each row is a sample and each column a feature, and the labels are a one-column matrix. Every model is a struct: build it with its parameters, train it with fit and use it with predict. Before training, prepare the data with StandardScaler and SimpleImputer and split it with TrainTestSplit; after that, measure the model with metrics such as Accuracy, F1 and R2Score, and pick the parameters with GridSearch. For neural networks see nn; for a trained model from Python, onnx. Things that trip people up  Labels are a one-column matrix of numbers. For classes, use 0, 1, 2 and so on; map class names to numbers yourself and keep the mapping. Nothing stops the program on bad input. fit returns false (and the model's ok stays false) when the shapes do not match, and TrainTestSplit returns empty matrices when x and y have different row counts. Check before you go on. Fit scalers, imputers and encoders on the training rows only, then use the same fitted object on the test rows and on new data. Models and results own matrices. Call free on models and results you are done with in long-running programs. Random parts (splits, forests, k-means starts) take a seed, so a run can be repeated exactly. Change the seed to see how much a result depends on luck.   The usual workflow: split, scale, fit, measure Every supervised model follows the same steps. Keep part of the data aside with TrainTestSplit, so that the model is judged on samples it never saw. Fit the scaler on the training part only and apply the same scaler to the test part and to any new sample; fitting it on all the data would leak information from the test set. Then fit, predict and measure. ConfusionMatrix shows which classes are mixed up, and predict_proba gives a probability instead of a hard answer. ml-guide-workflow.salamCopyimport ai.ml import matrix  func build(rows: int, cols: int, numbers: str): matrix.Matrix:     mut data := Vector {} as Vector<f64>     each number in numbers.Split(" "):         data.Push(number.ToFloat())     end     ret matrix.FromArray(rows, cols, data) end  func main:     mut hours := build(12, 2, "1 4 2 5 2 8 3 6 3 9 4 5 5 7 6 8 7 6 8 7 9 8 10 7")     mut passed := build(12, 1, "0 0 0 0 1 0 1 1 1 1 1 1")      mut split := ml.TrainTestSplit(hours, passed, 0.25, 2)     defer split.Free()     println "train", matrix.ShapeString(split.x_train), "test", matrix.ShapeString(split.x_test)      mut scaler := ml.StandardScaler {}     defer scaler.Free()     mut train := scaler.FitTransform(split.x_train)     mut test := scaler.Transform(split.x_test)      mut model := ml.LogisticRegression { max_iter = 2000 }     defer model.Free()     println "trained", model.Fit(train, split.y_train)     mut pred := model.Predict(test)     println "accuracy", ml.Accuracy(split.y_test, pred)     println "confusion", matrix.ToRepr(ml.ConfusionMatrix(split.y_test, pred, 2), 0)      mut student := scaler.Transform(build(1, 2, "6 6"))     proba := model.PredictProba(student)     println "chance to pass", matrix.ToStringPrec(matrix.Full(1, 1, proba.at(0, 1)), 2) endOutputtrain 9x2 test 3x2 trained true accuracy 1 confusion [2,0; 0,1] chance to pass 0.95 The fourth argument of TrainTestSplit is a seed, so the split is the same on every run. With twelve samples the test set has three, which is far too few to trust the accuracy; the next sections show better ways to judge a model.  Predict a number: linear regression When the target is a quantity, such as a price, use a regressor. After fit, coef holds one weight per feature and intercept the base value, so the model can be read directly: here each square meter adds about 2 and each year of age takes away about 1.4. R2Score and RMSE measure the fit; RMSE is in the same unit as the target. ml-guide-prices.salamCopyimport ai.ml import matrix  func build(rows: int, cols: int, numbers: str): matrix.Matrix:     mut data := Vector {} as Vector<f64>     each number in numbers.Split(" "):         data.Push(number.ToFloat())     end     ret matrix.FromArray(rows, cols, data) end  func f1(number: f64): str:     ret matrix.ToStringPrec(matrix.Full(1, 1, number), 1) end  func main:     mut homes := build(8, 3, "50 1 20 65 2 15 80 2 10 90 3 30 100 3 5 120 4 12 140 4 3 160 5 8")     mut price := build(8, 1, "105 140 178 172 228 260 312 344")      mut model := ml.LinearReg {}     defer model.Free()     println "fitted", model.Fit(homes, price)     println "per m2", f1(model.coef.at(0, 0)), "per room", f1(model.coef.at(1, 0)), "per year of age", f1(model.coef.at(2, 0))     println "base", f1(model.intercept)      mut pred := model.Predict(homes)     println "R2", matrix.ToStringPrec(matrix.Full(1, 1, ml.R2Score(price, pred)), 3), "RMSE", f1(ml.RMSE(price, pred))      mut offer := model.Predict(build(2, 3, "110 3 10 70 2 25"))     println "110 m2, 3 rooms, 10 years:", f1(offer.at(0, 0))     println "70 m2, 2 rooms, 25 years:", f1(offer.at(1, 0)) endOutputfitted true per m2 2.0 per room 0.7 per year of age -1.4 base 30.2 R2 1.000 RMSE 1.2 110 m2, 3 rooms, 10 years: 240.3 70 m2, 2 rooms, 25 years: 137.9  Compare models with cross-validation One split can be lucky or unlucky. StratifiedKFold cuts the data into folds that each keep the share of every class, and CrossValScore trains on all folds but one and tests on the remaining one, for every fold in turn. It takes the model as a function that trains and predicts, so any model fits, and the metric as another function. MeanScore gives the average over the folds. ml-guide-compare.sal

opencv opencv Computer vision with OpenCV: image processing, features, face detection, neural networks and video. AI This package binds the OpenCV library and gives most of the everyday computer vision work: color conversion, resizing, filters, edge detection and thresholds, contours, ORB and SIFT features, face detection with a cascade classifier, running DNN networks, and reading and writing video and camera frames. Use it for real computer vision: finding objects, matching features, reading camera frames, running a detection network. For thumbnails, drawing, text on images and format conversion with no outside library, the image package is enough. To run a model file without OpenCV, see onnx. Things to know  Programs link against the salam_opencv_shim library, which in turn needs OpenCV 4. If the shim is missing, the build fails at the link step or the program refuses to start with "cannot open shared object file"; it never gets as far as your code. A Mat stores colour in OpenCV's blue, green, red order, but every function of this package takes and returns Color values as red, green, blue, and FromImage and ToImage convert for you. Every Mat owns native memory that Salam does not track. Free each one, especially inside a loop over video frames. Calls that fail return an empty Mat (or false) and leave the reason in LastError.  The examples need OpenCV, so the site only type-checks them.  Set up OpenCV The package talks to OpenCV 4 through a small C++ shim, salam_opencv_shim, that lives in std/opencv/native of the Salam repository. On Debian or Ubuntu, install OpenCV and the build tools, build the shim, and let the loader find it: sudo apt install libopencv-dev cmake g++ cd std/opencv cmake -S native -B native/build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release cmake --build native/build --config Release export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=$PWD/native/build:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH Every program on this page starts by calling Available, which reports whether OpenCV answers and returns its version through Version. The outputs shown below are what the programs printed with OpenCV 4.10 on Linux.  Find and measure shapes The classic pipeline for counting objects is: convert to gray, threshold to a black and white mask, then find the contours of the white areas. THRESH_BINARY_INV makes dark shapes on a light background white. Contours gives the number of shapes and, for each one, its area and bounding_rect. Drawing methods such as rectangle and circle change the image in place, and a thickness of -1 fills the shape. opencv-guide-shapes.salamCopyimport opencv  func main:     if not opencv.Available():         println "OpenCV is not available:", opencv.LastError()         ret 1     end     mut board := opencv.NewBlank(400, 300, 3, opencv.White())     defer board.Free()     board.rectangle(40, 40, 120, 80, opencv.Black(), -1)     board.circle(280, 90, 50, opencv.Black(), -1)     board.rectangle(150, 190, 200, 70, opencv.Black(), -1)      mut gray := board.to_gray()     mut mask := gray.threshold(128.0, 255.0, opencv.THRESH_BINARY_INV)     mut found := mask.find_contours()     defer gray.Free()     defer mask.Free()     defer found.Free()     println "shapes found:", found.count()     repeat found.count() in i:         box := found.bounding_rect(i)         println "  shape at", box.x, box.y, "size", box.width, "x", box.height, "area", found.area(i) as int         board.rectangle(box.x - 3, box.y - 3, box.width + 6, box.height + 6, opencv.Red(), 2)     end     println "saved:", board.save("shapes.png") end shapes found: 3   shape at 150 190 size 200 x 70 area 13731   shape at 230 40 size 101 x 101 area 7704   shape at 40 40 size 120 x 80 area 9401 saved: true The area is measured along the traced outline, so it comes out a little smaller than width times height.  Edge detection canny finds edges, and works best on a gray image that has been smoothed first with gaussian_blur, so that noise does not turn into tiny false edges. The two thresholds control how strong an edge must be to start a line and to continue one. dilate thickens the result, which helps when the edges go on to a contour search. When photo.jpg is missing, the program draws a test image instead. opencv-guide-edges.salamCopyimport opencv  func white_pixels(m: opencv.Mat): int:     hist := m.histogram_gray()     ret hist.Get(255) end  func main:     if not opencv.Available():         println "OpenCV is not available:", opencv.LastError()         ret 1     end     mut photo := opencv.Read("photo.jpg")     if not photo.ok() or photo.empty():         println "photo.jpg not found, using a drawn test image"         photo = opencv.NewBlank(320, 240, 3, opencv.RGB(200, 200, 200))         photo.circle(160, 120, 70, opencv.RGB(40, 40, 40), -1)     end     defer photo.Free()     println "size:", photo.width(), "x", photo.height(), "channels:", photo.channels()      mut gray := photo.to_gray()     mut smooth := gray.gaussian_blur(5, 1.4)     mut edges := smooth.canny(50.0, 150.0)     mut thick := edges.dilate(3, 1)     defer gray.Free()     defer smooth.Free()     defer edges.Free()     defer thick.Free()     println "edge pixels:", white_pixels(edges), "after dilate:", white_pixels(thick)     println "saved:", opencv.Write("edges.png", thick) end photo.jpg not found, using a drawn test image size: 320 x 240 channels: 3 edge pixels: 480 after dilate: 1600 saved: true Every method that returns a new Mat allocates; free each result, as the defer lines do, or a long running program, such as one that processes camera frames, will grow without limit.  Find a picture inside another find_template slides a small image over a large one and reports the best position and a score between 0 and 1. That is how a test robot finds a button on a screenshot, or a program finds a logo in a scan. Check found and the score befo

gui/webview gui.webview A native window around HTML, and a whole desktop application layer on top of it. Graphics and games This package opens a native desktop window around HTML, and builds a whole desktop application on top of it, the kind you would build with Tauri or Electron, with no Rust and no second language. There are two levels in one package. The low level is a small window: you create it, show a page with SetHTML or Navigate, and Run keeps it open until the user closes it. The application level starts with Init and adds commands the page can call, events in both directions, packaged files, dialogs, notifications, the keychain, tray icons, menus, a single-instance lock and installers made by salam bundle. The interface is HTML, CSS and JavaScript. By default it runs in the web view the operating system already has, like Tauri: WebView2 on Windows, WKWebView on macOS and WebKitGTK on Linux, so the program stays one small native executable. The engine is chosen when the program is built; see choosing the web engine for the Chromium option. A page calls your Salam code with salam.invoke, which returns a promise. Pages can come from three places: files packed inside the executable, so nothing sits in a folder for users to edit; a remote site; or an HTML string. Use it for a small desktop tool, a viewer for data your program computed, or a native window around a web interface your program serves. For pages that run in the user's own browser, see dom; to generate the HTML, see template. How data moves, and what does not work  Put the data in the page. The reliable way to give the page your data is to write it into the HTML you pass to SetHTML, as JSON inside a <script>. Init installs a script for every page loaded later, before the page's own scripts run. Eval runs once, on whatever page is loaded at that moment. Pages load in the background, so code sent with Eval right after SetHTML or Navigate can run before the new page exists. Use Init, or wait for OnLoad. The page can talk back with OnMessage. For a whole application, with commands, events, packaged files and installers, use the application functions such as Init, Command and Open, described in the guides further down. Create reports failure by returning a window that is already closed; check IsClosed() right after it, for example on a Linux server with no display.  What pages may do  Local pages may run every command. Remote sites get nothing until you name them with Allow, command by command if you like. The bridge exists only in the top frame of an allowed origin, and every message carries a secret made for this run, so a frame or another site cannot call you. Answers carry the origin they belong to, so they never reach a page that replaced it. A link to any other site opens in the system browser. On Linux the engine cannot tell a frame from the page, so a cross-origin frame there needs its origin in allow_navigation. Files inside the executable are compressed and scrambled, which keeps them out of sight. They are not secret: anything a page can read, a determined user can extract. Keep real secrets on your server.  A window needs a desktop session, so the site only compiles these programs; run them on your own machine with salam run. On Linux install libgtk-3-dev and libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev (WebKitGTK 4.1) first. Windows 10 and 11 already ship WebView2, and macOS ships WKWebView. Building for another system needs nothing extra: --target works from any machine.  Showing data your program computed The simplest desktop program builds an HTML string and shows it. Everything the page needs, the style sheet included, can travel in that one string, so there are no files to ship next to the executable. HINT_FIXED keeps the window at the size you chose, which suits a small dialog like this order summary. gui-webview-guide-report.salamCopyimport gui.webview import str  struct Item:     pub name: str = ""     pub qty: int = 0     pub price: int = 0 end  func page(items: Vector<Item>): str:     mut rows := ""     mut total := 0     each it in items:         line := it.qty * it.price         total += line         rows = rows + "<tr><td>" + it.name + "</td><td>" + str.FromInt(it.qty) + "</td><td>" + str.FromInt(line) + "</td></tr>"     end     css := "body{font-family:sans-serif;margin:2em}td,th{padding:4px 12px;text-align:left}"     ret "<style>" + css + "</style><h1>Order</h1><table><tr><th>Item</th><th>Qty</th><th>Sum</th></tr>" + rows + "</table><p>Total: " + str.FromInt(total) + "</p>" end  func main:     mut items := Vector {} as Vector<Item>     items.Push(Item { name = "Tea", qty = 2, price = 45 })     items.Push(Item { name = "Cake", qty = 1, price = 120 })     mut win := webview.Create()     win.SetTitle("Order")     win.SetSize(480, 320, webview.HINT_FIXED)     win.SetHTML(page(items))     win.Run()     win.Destroy() end The item names go into the HTML as they are. When the text comes from a user or a file, pass it through EscapeHTML from template first, or a name with a < in it breaks the page.  Handing structured data to the page For anything bigger than a table, let JavaScript draw the page and give it the data as JSON. Marshal from encoding.json turns a vector of structs into a JSON array whose keys are the field names, and that text goes straight into a <script> in the page. The script runs as the page loads, so the data is there before anything is drawn. gui-webview-guide-data.salamCopyimport gui.webview import encoding.json  struct Task:     pub title: str = ""     pub done: bool = false end  func main:     mut tasks := Vector {} as Vector<Task>     tasks.Push(Task { title = "Write the report&qu

gui/raylib gui.raylib Games and graphics with raylib: windows, 2D and 3D drawing, textures, text, input and audio. Graphics and games This package binds raylib 5.5, a small library for 2D and 3D games and graphics programs. It opens a window with an OpenGL context, and gives drawing of shapes, textures, text and 3D models, keyboard, mouse, gamepad and touch input, and sound and music. The names are the ones of the raylib cheat sheet, so every raylib tutorial reads almost the same in Salam. Use it for games, visual toys, tools with a custom picture and teaching programs. For forms and buttons use a layout or the webview package, and for pictures that are only saved to a file the image package needs no outside library. Things to know  Programs link against the raylib shared library (libraylib, version 5.5). Install it with your package manager or build it from source; if it is missing, the build fails at the link step. Raylib passes Color, Vector2, Rectangle, Camera3D and the other structs by value. Salam passes them the way the C compiler of the platform does, on x86-64 (System V and Windows) and AArch64. The --backend=native compiler refuses such calls with a clear message; use the default backend. Raylib works with 32-bit floats. Every function that takes a f32 also has a version that takes f64, so DrawCircle(400, 225, 50.0, Red()) works. Struct fields are f32; build vectors and rectangles with Vec2, Vec3 and Rect. Colors are functions: Red(), RayWhite(), Blank(). Build your own with RGB and RGBA. Functions that change a value in place, such as ImageResize and UpdateCamera, take a variable and need it declared with mut. Strings returned by raylib, such as GetMonitorName, belong to raylib: copy them if you keep them and never free them. Everything you load (LoadTexture, LoadSound, LoadModel, ...) has an Unload call; raylib does not free it for you before the window closes. The window needs a desktop session, so the examples on this page are only type-checked by the site.   A bouncing ball Every raylib program has the same shape: open a window, ask for a frame rate, then loop until WindowShouldClose, drawing between BeginDrawing and EndDrawing. GetFrameTime gives the seconds since the last frame, which keeps movement the same speed on every machine. gui-raylib-guide-ball.salamCopyimport gui.raylib  func main:     raylib.InitWindow(800, 450, "Bouncing ball")     raylib.SetTargetFPS(60)     mut x := 400.0     mut y := 225.0     mut dx := 240.0     mut dy := 180.0     until not raylib.WindowShouldClose():         dt := raylib.GetFrameTime() as f64         x += dx * dt         y += dy * dt         if x < 20.0 or x > 780.0:             dx = 0.0 - dx         end         if y < 20.0 or y > 430.0:             dy = 0.0 - dy         end         raylib.BeginDrawing()         raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.RayWhite())         raylib.DrawCircle(x as int, y as int, 20.0, raylib.Maroon())         raylib.DrawText("Close the window to quit", 10, 10, 20, raylib.DarkGray())         raylib.EndDrawing()     end     raylib.CloseWindow() end  Keyboard and collisions IsKeyDown reports a key that is held, IsKeyPressed only the frame it went down. CheckCollisionRecs tests two rectangles, which is enough for many 2D games: try the move first and keep it only when it does not hit the wall. gui-raylib-guide-input.salamCopyimport gui.raylib  func main:     raylib.InitWindow(800, 450, "Move the square")     raylib.SetTargetFPS(60)     mut px := 100.0     mut py := 100.0     wall := raylib.Rect(500.0, 150.0, 60.0, 150.0)     until not raylib.WindowShouldClose():         dt := raylib.GetFrameTime() as f64         mut nx := px         mut ny := py         if raylib.IsKeyDown(raylib.KEY_RIGHT): nx += 200.0 * dt end         if raylib.IsKeyDown(raylib.KEY_LEFT): nx -= 200.0 * dt end         if raylib.IsKeyDown(raylib.KEY_DOWN): ny += 200.0 * dt end         if raylib.IsKeyDown(raylib.KEY_UP): ny -= 200.0 * dt end         player := raylib.Rect(nx, ny, 40.0, 40.0)         if not raylib.CheckCollisionRecs(player, wall):             px = nx             py = ny         end         raylib.BeginDrawing()         raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.RayWhite())         raylib.DrawRectangleRec(wall, raylib.DarkGray())         raylib.DrawRectangle(px as int, py as int, 40, 40, raylib.Blue())         raylib.DrawText("Arrow keys move the square", 10, 10, 20, raylib.Gray())         raylib.EndDrawing()     end     raylib.CloseWindow() end  A 3D scene 3D drawing sits between BeginMode3D and EndMode3D and uses a Camera3D. UpdateCamera with CAMERA_ORBITAL turns the camera around its target; it changes the camera, so declare it with mut. gui-raylib-guide-3d.salamCopyimport gui.raylib  func main:     raylib.InitWindow(800, 450, "3D cube")     raylib.SetTargetFPS(60)     mut camera := raylib.NewCamera3D(raylib.Vec3(6.0, 6.0, 6.0), raylib.Vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0), raylib.Vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0), 45.0, raylib.CAMERA_PERSPECTIVE)     until not raylib.WindowShouldClose():         raylib.UpdateCamera(camera, raylib.CAMERA_ORBITAL)         raylib.BeginDrawing()         raylib.ClearBackground(raylib.RayWhite())         raylib.BeginMode3D(camera)         raylib.DrawCube(raylib.Vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0), 2.0, 2.0, 2.0, raylib.Red())         raylib.DrawCubeWires(raylib.Vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0), 2.0, 2.0, 2.0, raylib.Maroon())         raylib.DrawGrid(10, 1.0)         raylib.EndMode3D()         raylib.DrawFPS(10, 10)         raylib.EndDrawing()     end     raylib.CloseWindow() end Types Vector2struct Vector2A 2D vector.NameTypeDescriptionxf32 = 0The x field.yf32 = 0The y field. gui/webview/pack gui.webview.pack The file format that holds an application's web files. Graphics and games This is the file format behind the files of a webview application: a compressed and scrambled set of files, read from the end of an executable or from a file of its own. You rarely call it directly, because salam bundle does the packing and webview does the reading. Scrambling keeps names and contents out of sight; it is not encryption.  Pack a folder and read it back PackDir compresses every file of a folder into one pack file and returns how many it stored, or -1. The key scrambles the content: it must be the same when you open the pack, and webview uses the application id. Open fills a Pack you declare first, Count says how many files it holds, and Read returns a Blob. A name that is not there gives a blob whose data is null, so test that before using it. The caller owns the bytes of a blob. gui-webview-pack-guide-roundtrip.salamCopyimport gui.webview.pack import os import io  func main:     os.MkdirAll("www")     io.WriteFile("www/index.html", "<h1>Hello</h1>")     io.WriteFile("www/style.css", "body { margin: 0 }")     println "packed", pack.PackDir("www", "app.pack", "com.example.app"), "files"     mut opened := pack.Pack {}     if not pack.Open("app.pack", "com.example.app", opened):         println "could not open"         ret 1     end     println "holds", opened.Count()     page := opened.Read("index.html")     println "index.html is", page.size, "bytes"     missing := opened.Read("nothing.txt")     println "missing found:", missing.data != null endOutputpacked 2 files holds 2 index.html is 14 bytes missing found: false  Putting the pack inside a program AppendPack adds a pack to the end of an executable, and Open accepts that executable as its path: it finds the pack at the end of the file. This is how a desktop program carries its pages in one file, and it is what salam bundle does for you. On macOS the pack goes into the application folder instead, so the signature of the program stays valid. pack.PackDir("www", "app.pack", "com.example.app") pack.AppendPack("notes", "app.pack")  Types Blobstruct BlobBytes read from a pack. The caller owns them.NameTypeDescriptiondatavoid*A pointer to the bytes.sizei64 = 0The number of bytes.gui-webview-pack-Pack.salamCopyimport gui.webview.pack  func main:     println pack.PackDir("www", "app.pack", "com.example.app")     println pack.AppendPack("app", "app.pack")     mut opened := pack.Pack {}     if pack.Open("app", "com.example.app", opened):         println opened.path, opened.key, opened.Count()         blob := opened.Read("index.html")         println blob.data != null, blob.size     end     println pack.ReadRange("app.pack", 0 as i64, 4 as i64) != null end Packstruct PackAn opened pack.NameTypeDescriptionpathstr = ""The file it was read from.keystr = ""The key it was opened with.The example for this item is shown with the ones above: gui-webview-pack-Pack.salamCountfunc Count(): intHow many files it holds.The example for this item is shown with the ones above: gui-webview-pack-Pack.salamReadfunc Read(name: str): BlobReads one file. data is null when it is not there.The example for this item is shown with the ones above: gui-webview-pack-Pack.salam Functions ReadRangefunc ReadRange(path: str, offset: i64, n: i64): void*Reads part of a file into new memory, or null.The example for this item is shown with the ones above: gui-webview-pack-Pack.salam Openfunc Open(path: str, key: str, out &: Pack): boolOpens a pack found at the end of a file.The example for this item is shown with the ones above: gui-webview-pack-Pack.salam PackDirfunc PackDir(dir: str, out_path: str, key: str): intPacks a folder. gui/color gui.color Colours for the Salam UI standard: every colour syntax in English and Persian, checked with clear errors, conversion between colour spaces, mixing in oklab, light and dark pairs, contrast and the CSS the web target emits. Graphics and games gui.color is the colour part of the Salam UI standard. It reads every colour a page may use, in the same syntax in page source, in a string and in a value computed at run time, and it turns a colour into what each target needs: a packed u32 for the native renderer and CSS text for the web. A Color holds sRGB channels from 0 to 1 and an alpha. A colour from a wider gamut, such as color(display p3, 1, 0, 0), keeps channels below 0 or above 1, so nothing is lost until it is drawn. What Parse accepts:  Names: all 148 CSS colour names plus transparent and current (the text colour), in any case and with or without spaces (alice blue), and Persian names such as قرمز, آبی and قهوه ای. Hex: #rgb, #rgba, #rrggbb and #rrggbbaa. Functions: rgb, rgba, hsl, hsla, hwb, lab, lch, oklab, oklch, cmyk (also device cmyk) and color(space, c1, c2, c3) with the spaces srgb, srgb linear, display p3, a98 rgb, prophoto rgb, rec2020, xyz, xyz d50 and xyz d65. Values are separated by commas, as in rgb(51, 102, 170), or by spaces with / before the alpha, as in CSS. The hyphenated CSS spellings (display-p3) work too. mix(a, b, amount, space): amount is how much of b, as a number from 0 to 1 or a percent, 50% when left out; the space is oklab unless given. light dark(a, b): a colour with a light and a dark variant. Numbers: a percent with % or ٪, Persian digits, the Persian comma ،, and hue angles as a bare number of degrees or with deg, rad, grad or turn.  Things to know:  Values are checked, not clamped. rgb(300, 0, 0) is an error, not red. Error says what was expected and the column where the problem starts, and suggests a name when one is close. Css writes what every current browser draws the same: #rrggbb or #rrggbbaa inside sRGB, color(display-p3 ...) for a wide gamut colour that fits Display P3, oklch(...) beyond that, currentColor and light-dark(a, b). Argb clamps each channel to sRGB, so a wide gamut colour is drawn as its nearest sRGB colour on the native target. cmyk is the plain formula (red is (1 - c) * (1 - k)), with no printer profile. current cannot be mixed while parsing, because the text colour is only known when the page is shown.   A light and dark palette A theme starts from one brand colour. Each role gets a LightDark pair, Lighten and Darken move the lightness in oklch and stay inside sRGB, and Mix works on both variants at once. Contrast then checks every pair against the 4.5 ratio that WCAG asks of body text, in light and in dark mode. gui-color-guide-theme.salamCopyimport gui.color import math  func r2(v: f64): f64:     ret math.Round(v * 100.0) / 100.0 end  func check(name: str, text: color.Color, back: color.Color):     light := color.Contrast(color.Light(text), color.Light(back))     dark := color.Contrast(color.Dark(text), color.Dark(back))     mut verdict := "ok"     if light < 4.5 or dark < 4.5:         verdict = "too low for body text"     end     println name, "light", r2(light), "dark", r2(dark), verdict end  func main:     mut brand := color.Color {}     if not color.Parse("#3366aa", brand):         ret 1     end     page := color.LightDark(color.Hex(0xffffff), color.Hex(0x121212))     text := color.LightDark(color.Hex(0x1a1a1a), color.Hex(0xeeeeee))     accent := color.LightDark(brand, color.Lighten(brand, 0.2))     muted := color.Mix(text, page, 0.45)     hover := color.LightDark(color.Darken(brand, 0.08), color.Lighten(brand, 0.28))     println "page   ", color.Css(page)     println "text   ", color.Css(text)     println "accent ", color.Css(accent)     println "muted  ", color.Css(muted)     println "hover  ", color.Css(hover)     check("text on page  ", text, page)     check("accent on page", accent, page)     check("muted on page ", muted, page) endOutputpage    light-dark(#ffffff, #121212) text    light-dark(#1a1a1a, #eeeeee) accent  light-dark(#3366aa, #6ea3ec) muted   light-dark(#777777, #818181) hover   light-dark(#1b4f91, #8cbdff) text on page   light 17.4 dark 16.15 ok accent on page light 5.8 dark 7.25 ok muted on page  light 4.47 dark 4.82 too low for body text  Checking colours that people type A settings screen that takes a colour as text needs to say what is wrong with it. gui/flow gui.flow The layout engine of the Salam style standard: column, row, grid, stack and flow layouts, positioning, scrolling and right to left, with incremental relayout. Graphics and games gui.flow computes the rectangle of every box of a native user interface. It implements exactly the layouts of the Salam style standard and nothing else: column and row (the flex model with grow, shrink, basis, wrapping, gaps, alignment and order), grid (track lists with pixels, percent, fr, auto, minmax, repeat, fit and content sizes, explicit lines, spans and auto placement), stack (every child in one cell) and flow (children placed like words, wrapped onto lines and baseline aligned). It is not a CSS engine: there is no display, float, block formatting context, margin collapsing or table. You build a Tree, give every box a FlowStyle, give leaves such as text and images a measure function, and call Layout with the size of the window. Then X, Y, W and H give each box relative to its parent. The package depends on nothing else in gui; gui.ui maps the style of an element to a FlowStyle. Things to know:  Every box is border box. Width and height include padding and border, and margins apply in every layout, auto margins included. Lengths come resolved. em, rem, vw and vh are converted to pixels by the caller; only percent stays, because only the layout knows the reference. Content is not crushed. min_width and min_height default to Auto(): a child of a row or column does not shrink below its min content width or content height, as in a browser. Set them to 0 to allow it, or give a child an overflow other than visible. The flow layout has no gaps. It is formatted like inline text, so space its children with margins. Absolute and fixed boxes keep their static position on an axis with no inset: where the parent's justify and align would place them as the only child. A root fills the viewport when its width or height is auto; use Fit() to size it to its content. Right to left mirrors rows, flow lines, grid columns, start and end. left and right stay physical. Layout is incremental. Changing a style or a measure marks the box and its ancestors; Layout lays out only those again and reuses cached sizes elsewhere. LayoutCalls and MeasureCalls show the work done.   An application shell A header, a body with a side bar and a scrolling content area, and a footer. The body has basis = 0, grows, and has min_height = 0, so its long content does not push the header and footer away (by default a child of a column is never shorter than its content); the content area scrolls instead, and ContentH tells how far. The same tree in right to left puts the side bar on the right. gui-flow-guide-app.salamCopyimport gui.flow  func show(t &: flow.Tree, name: str, id: int):     println name, t.X(id), t.Y(id), t.W(id), t.H(id) end  func build(t &: flow.Tree, dir: int): (int, int, int, int):     app := t.Add(-1, flow.FlowStyle { direction = dir })     header := t.Add(app, flow.FlowStyle { layout = flow.LAYOUT_ROW, height = flow.Px(48.0), padding = flow.Sides(flow.Px(0.0), flow.Px(16.0), flow.Px(0.0), flow.Px(16.0)), align = flow.ALIGN_CENTER, column_gap = flow.Px(12.0) })     t.Add(header, flow.FlowStyle { width = flow.Px(32.0), height = flow.Px(32.0) })     t.Add(header, flow.FlowStyle { grow = 1.0, height = flow.Px(20.0) })     body := t.Add(app, flow.FlowStyle { layout = flow.LAYOUT_ROW, grow = 1.0, basis = flow.Px(0.0), min_height = flow.Px(0.0) })     side := t.Add(body, flow.FlowStyle { width = flow.Px(180.0), border = flow.Sides(flow.Px(0.0), flow.Px(1.0), flow.Px(0.0), flow.Px(0.0)) })     content := t.Add(body, flow.FlowStyle { grow = 1.0, padding = flow.All(flow.Px(16.0)), row_gap = flow.Px(8.0), overflow_y = flow.OVERFLOW_AUTO })     repeat 30:         t.Add(content, flow.FlowStyle { height = flow.Px(40.0), shrink = 0.0 })     end     footer := t.Add(app, flow.FlowStyle { height = flow.Px(24.0) })     ret header, side, content, footer end  func main:     mut t := flow.NewTree()     header, side, content, footer := build(t, flow.DIR_LTR)     t.Layout(800.0, 600.0)     show(t, "header", header)     show(t, "side", side)     show(t, "content", content)     show(t, "footer", footer)     println "content scrolls by", t.ContentH(content) - t.H(content)      mut r := flow.NewTree()     _, rside, rcontent, _ := build(r, flow.DIR_RTL)     r.Layout(800.0, 600.0)     show(r, "rtl side", rside)     show(r, "rtl content", rcontent) endOutputheader 0 0 800 48 side 0 0 180 528 content 180 0 620 528 footer 0 576 800 24 content scrolls by 936 rtl side 620 0 180 528 rtl content 0 0 620 528  Text through a measure function A leaf's measure function gets the available width and returns the size of the wrapped text. Here a one word label and a long paragraph sit in a row aligned on their baselines; the paragraph has basis = 0 and grows, so it takes the rest of the row and wraps when the window narrows. A layout with nothing changed does no work, and marking the paragraph dirty measures it once. gui-flow-guide-text.salamCopyimport gui.flow  func paragraph(t &: flow.Tree, parent: int, words: int): int:     id := t.Add(parent, flow.FlowStyle {})     t.SetMeasure(id, (_id: int, w: f64, _h: f64):         mut per := words         if w >= 0.0:             per = ((w + 4.0) / 44.0) as int             if per < 1:                 per = 1             end             if per > words:                 per = words             end         end         lines := (words + per - 1) / per         ret flow.Size { w = (per as f64) * 44.0 - 4.0, h = (lines as f64) * 18.0, baseline = 14.0 }     end)     ret id end  func main:     mut t := flow.NewTree()     card := t.Add(-1, flow.FlowStyle { layout = flow.LAYOUT_ROW, align = flow.ALIGN_BASELINE, column_gap = flow.Px(12.0), padding = flow.All(flow.Px(8.0)), height = flow.Fit() })     label := paragraph(t, card, 1)     text := p

gui/style gui.style The Salam UI style standard: every property with its English and Persian name, value syntax, validation with clear errors, defaults per element, inheritance, interpolation for transitions and the CSS the web target writes. Graphics and games gui.style is the style standard of the Salam UI, in the spirit of QML: one vocabulary of properties that works the same on the web and in a native window. A page never contains CSS. The compiler checks every style attribute with this package, writes CSS from it for the web target and builds typed values from it for the native target, so both look the same. Every property has an int id (P_WIDTH, P_PADDING, ...), an English and a Persian name, a value kind, a keyword set with English and Persian names, a default, and flags that say whether it is inherited and whether it can be animated. The table is in the package, and Info returns one row of it. The value syntax:  Numbers in the property's natural unit: pixels for lengths, milliseconds for times, degrees for angles, a plain number for opacity, grow and scale. Units: px, %, em, rem, vw, vh, vmin, vmax, fr, ms, s, deg, turn, rad, also as calls like px(12). Length arithmetic: 100% - 20 and 50% + 1em; the web target writes calc(). Lists with a comma (padding = 8, 16) and groups in brackets (shadow = [0, 4, 8, black], [0, 1, 2, red]). Composites in any order where the parts differ: border = 2, solid, #3366aa or border = red, 1. Calls: linear(90, red, blue), radial(circle, [30%, 40%], white, black), conic(...), image("a.png"), minmax(100, 1fr), repeat(fill, 200), fit(300), ease(0.2, 0, 0, 1), steps(4), spring(170, 26), and every colour of gui.color. Persian: keywords and property names in Persian, Persian digits, ٪ and the comma ،. Strings are read with the same syntax: "8, 16" is the same as 8, 16.  Things to know  Sides and corners follow the text direction: four values are top, end, bottom, start, and radius goes top start, top end, bottom end, bottom start. left and right become start or end by the direction when they are set. gap has no effect in flow (the lines and items there are spaced by margins and line height), on both targets; it is accepted and ignored. min width and min height start at auto, the automatic minimum, so a flex child does not shrink below its content unless a smaller minimum is given. In flow, inline text elements (span, bold, italic, code, link and the like) stay inline content on the web so text wraps across them; every other child is one atomic item on the line, baseline aligned. Every box is a column by default and text elements use flow. BaseCss gives the web the same defaults, so plain HTML does not look different from the native window. Css returns declarations. Filters and reverse set --salam-* variables that the base sheet reads, and layout = stack and flow end with a nested &>* rule for the children, so the web target has to put them in a style rule, not in a style attribute. Source writes code that uses only this package, for programs the compiler generates for the native target.   One style for the web and a native window A card is described with attribute values as a page would write them. Each one is parsed and checked; a value out of range gives a message with the expected form. The same values become CSS for the web and typed fields that a native renderer reads. gui-style-guide-card.salamCopyimport gui.style  func main:     names := ["layout", "gap", "padding", "radius", "background", "color", "shadow", "width", "max width", "opacity"]     values := ["row", "12", "16, 24", "12", "linear(90, #3366aa, #5588cc)", "white", "0, 4, 12, #00000040", "100% - 32", "480", "120%"]     mut s := style.Default("box")     mut rule := ""     repeat names.Len() in i:         p := style.PropByName(names[i])         mut v := style.Value {}         if not style.Parse(p, values[i], v):             println style.Error(p, values[i])             continue         end         style.Set(s, p, v)         rule += style.Css(p, v) + ";"     end     println "web:", ".card{" + rule + "}"     println "native: row", s.layout_kind == style.KW_ROW, "gap", s.gap_column.px, "padding", s.padding_top.px, s.padding_start.px     println "native: width", s.width.len.pct, "% plus", s.width.len.px, "px, at most", s.max_width.len.px     println "native: shadow blur", s.shadow.Get(0).blur.px, "background layers", s.background.Len() endOutputopacity: 1.2 is out of range; expected a number from 0 to 1 or a percent, for example opacity = 0.5 web: .card{display:var(--salam-o,block) flex;flex-direction:var(--salam-dir,row);--salam-rev:row-reverse;gap:12px;padding-block:16px;padding-inline:24px;border-radius:12px;background-color:transparent;background-image:linear-gradient(90deg,#3366aa,#5588cc);color:#ffffff;box-shadow:0 4px 12px 0 #00000040;width:calc(100% - 32px);max-width:480px;} native: row true gap 12 padding 16 24 native: width 100 % plus -32 px, at most 480 native: shadow blur 12 background layers 1 Lengths keep their units until layout: 100% - 32 stays a percent plus pixels, and the native layout resolves the percent against the parent.  A hover transition, frame by frame A transition needs the same curve on both targets. The web gets the CSS timing function, and a native renderer computes each frame with EaseAt and Lerp, which mix colours in oklab and lengths unit by unit. gui-style-guide-hover.salamCopyimport gui.style  func value(p: int, text: str): style.Value:     mut v := style.Value {}     style.Parse(p, text, v)     ret v end  func main:     rest := value(style.P_BACKGROUND, "#3366aa")     hover := value(style.P_BACKGROUND, &quot

audio audio Sound as a clip of samples: cutting, mixing, measuring and converting it. Audio This package is the middle of everything to do with sound in Salam. A Clip holds the sound itself: plain 32 bit floating point samples between -1 and 1, one frame after another, with the channels side by side. Reading and writing files is the job of the format packages, audio.wav today, and audio.codec opens any of them without being told which. Filters, a Fourier transform and careful resampling live in audio.dsp. What is here is the clip and everything that does not need to know a file format: cutting, joining, mixing, fading, measuring how loud something is, moving between mono and stereo and between sample rates, and the most significant bit first bitstream reader that every audio codec is written on top of. Things to know  Samples are 32 bit floats. Every clip owns that memory; release it with Free. Because a float carries 24 bits of mantissa, 8, 16 and 24 bit sound makes the round trip through a clip exactly. Only a true 32 bit integer source loses its lowest 8 bits. A three minute stereo song at 44100 is about 63 MB as a clip, so decode a long file in pieces rather than all at once. bits remembers the depth a clip was read at, so writing it again keeps that depth. A clip made with New has no depth, and an encoder then picks 16 bit. Anything that fails returns an empty clip rather than stopping the program, so check with IsEmpty. MsbReader reads the most significant bit first. The BitReader in compress reads the other way round, for DEFLATE, and is not interchangeable with it.   A clip of sound A clip is a rate, a channel count, a frame count and the samples. New gives you silence to fill in; SetSample and Sample reach one sample at a time by frame and channel. A frame is one sample for every channel, so a stereo clip of 100 frames holds 200 samples. Every clip holds memory of its own, so release each one with Free. Reading or writing outside the clip is not an error: Sample gives 0 and SetSample does nothing, which keeps loops at the edges simple.  How loud is it Peak is the furthest any single sample gets from zero and RMS follows loudness as an ear hears it. Both have a decibel form, where 0 dB is as loud as a sample can be and everything quieter is negative. GainToDb and DbToGain move between a plain multiplier and decibels. Silence has no decibel value, so GainToDb(0.0) returns SilenceFloorDb instead of running off to minus infinity. FirstSound and LastSound find where the sound really starts and stops, which is what TrimSilence is built from.  Cutting and joining Slice and Trim take a piece out, by frame or by time; Concat puts one clip after another and Mix lays them on top of each other. Normalize scales a clip so its peak lands exactly where you ask, and the two fades shape the ends so a cut does not click. Joining and mixing need both clips to agree on the sample rate and the channel count, and return an empty clip when they do not. Use ToRate and ToChannels first to bring them into line.  Rates, channels and depths ToMono averages the channels together and ToStereo spreads one channel across two. ToRate changes the sample rate by interpolating between samples, which is quick and good enough for speech; for music use ResampleSinc from audio.dsp. ToBits does not write a file, it rounds the samples to the steps of a depth so you can hear what that depth will cost. Deinterleave hands back one clip per channel, each of which you must free, and Interleave weaves them back together.  Which format is this DetectFormat looks at the first few bytes and FormatFromExt at the file name. Both answer with a Format number, which FormatName turns into a short name. Knowing the format does not mean this build can decode it: ask CanDecode in audio.codec for that. An Info is what a file says about itself, which the format packages fill in by reading a header rather than the whole file. It is the cheap way to show a length or a bit rate in a listing.  Reading a bitstream Compressed audio is not laid out in bytes, it is laid out in bits, and every format from MP3 to FLAC counts those bits from the most significant end. MsbReader does that, with MsbReadSigned for two's complement fields and MsbUnary for the run of zeros that Rice and Golomb codes are built from. MsbWriter is the same thing in reverse. A read past the end does not stop the program: it hands back zeros and sets bad, which stays set, so one check after a group of reads is enough. Note again that compress has a bit reader of its own that runs the other way round, for DEFLATE; do not use it for audio. audio/wav audio.wav Reading and writing WAVE files: PCM, floating point, A-law and mu-law. Audio WAVE is the format to reach for when nothing should be lost. It is a RIFF container holding a fmt  chunk that says what the samples are and a data chunk holding them, and this package reads and writes it without any outside library. Integer samples at 8, 16, 24 and 32 bits are all handled, as are IEEE floating point samples and the two eight bit companding schemes from telephony, A-law and mu-law. OpenWAV and SaveWAV are the short way in; audio.codec is shorter still when you do not want to name the format at all. Things to know  8, 16 and 24 bit PCM makes the round trip through a clip exactly. A true 32 bit integer file loses its lowest 8 bits, because a clip holds 32 bit floats; write such a file with EncodeWAVFloat instead, which keeps every bit. EncodeWAV writes at the depth the clip remembers in bits, and 16 bit when the clip has none. EncodeWAVBits takes the depth from you. A companded file is a quarter the size of 24 bit PCM and does lose a little, most of it where the sound is loud. Near silence the error is smaller than one step of 16 bit PCM. ProbeWAV reads the header alone, so a listing of a thousand files does not have to decode any of them. Chunks hands back a vector you must free. FindChunk allocates nothing, and is what the decoder uses.   Writing a tone to a WAV file Make a clip with audio.New, fill it with samples, and hand it to SaveWAVBits with the depth you want. Samples in a clip are floats between -1 and 1; the depth only decides how they are rounded on disk. The function returns true when the file was written. audio-wav-guide-write.salamCopyimport audio import audio.wav import filepath import math import mem import os  func tone(rate: int, freq: f64, frames: int): audio.Clip:     mut c := audio.New(rate, 1, frames)     mut i := 0     until i < frames:         audio.SetSample(c, i, 0, 0.5 * math.Sin(2.0 * math.PI * freq * (i as f64) / (rate as f64)))         i++     end     ret c end  func main:     mut c := tone(8000, 440.0, 800)     path := filepath.Join(os.TempDir(), "salam_guide_tone.wav")     defer mem.Free(path as void*)     println wav.SaveWAVBits(c, path, 16)      mut ok := false     info := wav.ProbeFileWAV(path, ok)     println ok, info.rate, info.channels, info.bits, info.frames      mut back_ok := false     mut back := wav.OpenWAV(path, back_ok)     close := math.Abs(audio.Sample(back, 5, 0) - audio.Sample(c, 5, 0)) < 0.001     println back_ok, back.frames, close     audio.Free(c)     audio.Free(back) endOutputtrue true 8000 1 16 800 true 800 true To check what you wrote, ProbeFileWAV reads only the header and tells you the rate, channels, depth and length without decoding anything. OpenWAV then reads the whole file back. At 16 bit a sample matches the original to within one step, so the program compares with a tolerance, not with ==.  Reading the format and the chunks When the bytes are already in memory, IsWAV checks the RIFF header and ReadFormat fills a Format with the codec, channel count, rate and depth. block_align is the size of one frame in bytes: two channels of 24 bit samples make 6. audio-wav-guide-read.salamCopyimport audio import audio.wav import compress  func main:     mut c := audio.New(22050, 2, 100)     audio.SetSample(c, 7, 1, 0.5)     mut buf := wav.EncodeWAVBits(c, 24)     println wav.IsWAV(buf.data, buf.len), wav.IsWAV(buf.data, 4)      mut f := wav.Format {}     println wav.ReadFormat(buf.data, buf.len, f)     println f.codec == wav.CodecPCM, f.channels, f.rate, f.bits     println f.block_align, f.byte_rate      mut fmt_chunk := wav.Chunk {}     mut data_chunk := wav.Chunk {}     println wav.FindChunk(buf.data, buf.len, wav.Tag("fmt "), fmt_chunk)     println wav.FindChunk(buf.data, buf.len, wav.Tag("data"), data_chunk)     println fmt_chunk.size, data_chunk.offset, data_chunk.size     println data_chunk.size / f.block_align      mut ok := false     mut back := wav.DecodeWAV(buf.data, buf.len, ok)     println ok, back.frames, audio.Sample(back, 7, 1)     compress.BufFree(buf)     audio.Free(c)     audio.Free(back) endOutputtrue false true true 2 22050 24 6 132300 true true 16 44 600 100 true 100 0.5 FindChunk locates a chunk by its four letter tag, which Tag packs into an integer. The data chunk size divided by block_align is the number of frames, 100 here, and it agrees with what DecodeWAV returns.  Smaller files with mu-law and A-law The two telephone codecs store each sample in one byte. EncodeMuLaw and EncodeALaw take a clip and return a WAVE file with 400 data bytes where 16 bit PCM needs 800. The price is a small rounding error that grows with the loudness of the sample. audio-wav-guide-law.salamCopyimport audio import audio.wav import compress import math  func main:     mut c := audio.New(8000, 1, 400)     mut i := 0     until i < 400:         audio.SetSample(c, i, 0, 0.8 * math.Sin(2.0 * math.PI * 200.0 * (i as f64) / 8000.0))         i++     end     mut pcm := wav.EncodeWAVBits(c, 16)     mut mu := wav.EncodeMuLaw(c)     mut al := wav.EncodeALaw(c)     println compress.BufLen(pcm), compress.BufLen(mu), compress.BufLen(al)      mut ok := false     mut back := wav.DecodeWAV(mu.data, mu.len, ok)     println ok, back.frames, back.bits     mut worst := 0.0     mut k := 0     until k < 400:         d := math.Abs(audio.Sample(back, k, 0) - audio.Sample(c, k, 0))         if d > worst:             worst = d         end         k++     end     println worst < 0.03     compress.BufFree(pcm)     compress.BufFree(mu)     compress.BufFree(al)     audio.Free(c)     audio.Free(back) endOutput844 444 444 true 400 8 true The program decodes the mu-law file and finds the largest difference from the original. For a tone at 0.8 of full scale it stays under 0.03. The decoded clip reports 8 bits, because that is what the file holds. Types Formatstruct FormatWhat a WAVE file's fmt chunk says: which cod

audio/dsp audio.dsp A Fourier transform, windows, filters and resampling for sound. Audio This is the arithmetic behind sound: a Fourier transform to see what frequencies are in a block, windows to taper the block first, filters to shape it and resampling to move it between rates. The codecs in this family lean on the same code, which is why it lives here rather than inside any one of them. Everything works on a clip or on plain arrays of f64. The transform is radix-2, so a length has to be a power of two: use NextPow2 to pad up to one. Things to know  FFT and IFFT work in place on two arrays, the real parts and the imaginary parts. IFFT already divides by the length, so it undoes FFT exactly. A real signal shows the same strength at bin k and at bin n - k, so only the first half of a spectrum tells you anything new. Taper a block with ApplyWindow before transforming it, or a tone that does not fit a whole number of cycles will smear across every bin. The filters follow the well known cookbook formulas. A Biquad remembers two samples, so BiquadReset it before a different clip, and prefer BiquadProcessAll, which gives each channel its own copy. BiquadResponse tells you what a filter does at a frequency without running any sound through it, which makes filters easy to test. ResampleSinc is the one to use on music; ToRate in audio is the quick linear version.   Low-pass filtering a signal A biquad is a small filter with a few coefficients and two remembered samples. LowPass builds one from a cutoff in hertz, a Q and the sample rate. Before touching any sound you can ask BiquadResponse how much the filter passes at a frequency, as a plain multiplier: near 1 at 100 Hz, near 0 at 10 kHz. audio-dsp-guide-filter.salamCopyimport audio import audio.dsp import math  func tone(rate: int, freq: f64, frames: int): audio.Clip:     mut c := audio.New(rate, 1, frames)     mut i := 0     until i < frames:         audio.SetSample(c, i, 0, math.Sin(2.0 * math.PI * freq * (i as f64) / (rate as f64)))         i++     end     ret c end  func main:     lp := dsp.LowPass(1000.0, 0.707, 48000)     println dsp.BiquadResponse(lp, 100.0, 48000) > 0.99     println dsp.BiquadResponse(lp, 10000.0, 48000) < 0.02      mut low := tone(48000, 100.0, 2048)     mut high := tone(48000, 10000.0, 2048)     low_before := audio.RMS(low)     high_before := audio.RMS(high)     dsp.BiquadProcessAll(lp, low)     dsp.BiquadProcessAll(lp, high)     low_db := audio.GainToDb(audio.RMS(low) / low_before)     high_db := audio.GainToDb(audio.RMS(high) / high_before)     println low_db > -1.0     println high_db < -20.0     audio.Free(low)     audio.Free(high) endOutputtrue true true true BiquadProcessAll runs a fresh copy of the filter over every channel of a clip, in place. The program measures the level before and after with audio.RMS and audio.GainToDb: the 100 Hz tone loses less than a decibel and the 10 kHz tone loses more than twenty.  Finding the strongest frequency Fill two vectors with the real and imaginary parts of the signal, here a 1000 Hz sine sampled at 8000 Hz. Multiply the real part by a window first with ApplyWindow, so the ends of the block do not leak into neighbouring bins. FFTVec transforms both vectors in place; the length must be a power of two, and it returns false when it is not. audio-dsp-guide-spectrum.salamCopyimport audio.dsp import math  func main:     n := 256     rate := 8000     mut re := Vector {} as Vector<f64>     mut im := Vector {} as Vector<f64>     defer re.Free()     defer im.Free()     mut i := 0     until i < n:         re.Push(math.Sin(2.0 * math.PI * 1000.0 * (i as f64) / (rate as f64)))         im.Push(0.0)         i++     end     dsp.ApplyWindow(re.Ref(0), n, dsp.WindowHann, 0.0)     println dsp.FFTVec(re, im)     mags := dsp.Magnitude(re.Ref(0), im.Ref(0), n)     defer mags.Free()     peak := dsp.PeakBin(mags)     println peak, dsp.BinFrequency(peak, n, rate)     println dsp.IsPow2(n), dsp.NextPow2(300) endOutputtrue 32 1000 true 512 Magnitude gives the strength of each bin, PeakBin picks the strongest, and BinFrequency turns that bin number into hertz. With 256 samples at 8000 Hz each bin is 31.25 Hz wide, so 1000 Hz lands exactly in bin 32.  Changing the sample rate ResampleTo returns a new clip at the rate you ask for. The last argument picks the method: QualityLinear is quick, QualityCubic a good middle, and QualitySinc the one to use on music. Going from 8000 to 16000 Hz doubles the frame count and keeps the duration at 0.1 seconds. audio-dsp-guide-resample.salamCopyimport audio import audio.dsp import math  func main:     mut c := audio.New(8000, 1, 800)     mut i := 0     until i < 800:         audio.SetSample(c, i, 0, 0.5 * math.Sin(2.0 * math.PI * 300.0 * (i as f64) / 8000.0))         i++     end     mut up := dsp.ResampleTo(c, 16000, dsp.QualitySinc)     println up.rate, up.frames, audio.Duration(up)     mut back := dsp.ResampleTo(up, 8000, dsp.QualitySinc)     println back.rate, back.frames     println dsp.Correlation(c, back) > 0.99     audio.Free(c)     audio.Free(up)     audio.Free(back) endOutput16000 1600 0.1 8000 800 true To see whether a round trip kept the sound, resample back and call Correlation, which is 1 for identical clips and near 0 for unrelated ones. Both new clips belong to you and must be freed. audio/codec audio.codec Open and save a sound file without naming its format. Audio This package is the one call that does not care what format a file is in. Open reads the first bytes, works out the format and hands back a clip; Save looks at the extension and writes the right thing. Probe and ProbeFile do the same for a header alone. It sits in its own package for a plain reason: audio cannot import the format packages, because they import it. So the sniffing lives in audio, where it needs nothing, and the dispatch lives here, where it can reach every codec. Things to know  Knowing a format and being able to read it are different things. audio.DetectFormat names ten formats; CanDecode tells you which of them this build actually carries, and Formats lists them. Today that list is WAV, AIFF and au. The rest of the family is being written, and nothing here changes when they land. Save returns false for an extension it cannot write, rather than writing the wrong format. Free the clip with audio.Free and any buffer with compress.BufFree.   Saving and opening by file name codec.Save picks the format from the file extension, so the same call writes a .wav, .aiff, .au or .flac file. It returns false for a format it cannot write, such as MP3. CanEncode and CanDecode tell you in advance. audio-codec-guide-save.salamCopyimport audio import audio.codec import filepath import mem import os  func main:     mut c := audio.New(22050, 2, 64)     audio.SetSample(c, 5, 0, 0.5)     audio.SetSample(c, 5, 1, -0.25)      path := filepath.Join(os.TempDir(), "salam_guide_codec.wav")     defer mem.Free(path as void*)     println codec.CanEncode(audio.FormatWAV), codec.Save(c, path)      mut ok := false     info := codec.ProbeFile(path, ok)     println ok, audio.FormatName(info.format), info.frames, info.bits, info.lossless      mut open_ok := false     mut back := codec.Open(path, open_ok)     println open_ok, back.rate, back.channels     println audio.Sample(back, 5, 0), audio.Sample(back, 5, 1)     audio.Free(c)     audio.Free(back) endOutputtrue true true wav 64 16 true true 22050 2 0.5 -0.25 ProbeFile reads the header only and reports the format name, length, depth and whether the format is lossless. Open then decodes the file, whatever format it turns out to be, since it looks at the contents and not at the name.  Encoding and decoding in memory Without a file, Encode returns a byte buffer in the format you name, and Decode turns bytes back into a clip. The 32 frame mono clip becomes 108 bytes: a 44 byte header and 64 bytes of 16 bit samples. audio.DetectFormat names the format from the bytes alone. audio-codec-guide-memory.salamCopyimport audio import audio.codec import compress  func main:     mut c := audio.New(8000, 1, 32)     audio.SetSample(c, 3, 0, 0.5)     mut buf := codec.Encode(c, audio.FormatWAV)     println compress.BufLen(buf)     println audio.FormatName(audio.DetectFormat(buf.data, buf.len))      mut ok := false     mut back := codec.Decode(buf.data, buf.len, ok)     println ok, back.frames, audio.Sample(back, 3, 0)      mut junk := compress.NewByteBuf()     mut i := 0     until i < 16:         compress.BufPush(junk, i)         i++     end     mut bad := false     codec.Decode(junk.data, junk.len, bad)     println bad     compress.BufFree(buf)     compress.BufFree(junk)     audio.Free(c)     audio.Free(back) endOutput108 wav true 32 0.5 false Bytes that are not audio do not crash anything: Decode sets its flag to false and returns an empty clip. Always check the flag before using the result, and free the buffers you were given. Functions CanDecodefunc CanDecode(format: int): boolTrue when this build can read that format. audio/aiff audio.aiff Reading and writing AIFF and AIFF-C files. Audio AIFF is the big-endian cousin of WAVE: the same idea of a chunked container, written the other way round because it came from the Motorola side of the world. AIFF-C adds a compression tag, and this package reads the ones that matter: plain PCM, the little-endian sowt variant Apple tools write, IEEE floating point, and A-law and mu-law. The one genuinely odd part is the sample rate, which AIFF stores as an 80 bit extended float. This package reads and writes it, so 44100 comes back as 44100 and not 44099. Things to know  8, 16 and 24 bit PCM makes the round trip through a clip exactly. Unlike WAVE, 8 bit AIFF is signed. ReadCommon gives you the COMM and SSND chunks in one struct, because you always need both: one says the shape, the other says where the sound is. A file whose COMM frame count disagrees with the bytes actually present decodes to whichever is shorter, rather than reading off the end. Writing always produces plain big-endian AIFF. The AIFC variants are read, not written.   Encoding an AIFF file AIFF is the big endian cousin of WAVE. EncodeAIFFBits turns a clip into a byte buffer at 8, 16, 24 or 32 bits. The sample rate is stored as an 80 bit extended float, which the package converts for you, so 44100 Hz comes back as exactly 44100. audio-aiff-guide-write.salamCopyimport audio import audio.aiff import compress  func main:     mut c := audio.New(44100, 2, 64)     audio.SetSample(c, 7, 1, 0.5)     mut buf := aiff.EncodeAIFFBits(c, 24)     println aiff.IsAIFF(buf.data, buf.len), compress.BufLen(buf)      mut cm := aiff.Common {}     println aiff.ReadCommon(buf.data, buf.len, cm)     println cm.channels, cm.frames, cm.bits, cm.rate     println cm.compression == aiff.CompNone, cm.data_size      mut ok := false     mut back := aiff.DecodeAIFF(buf.data, buf.len, ok)     println ok, back.frames, back.bits, audio.Sample(back, 7, 1)     compress.BufFree(buf)     audio.Free(c)     audio.Free(back) endOutputtrue 438 true 2 64 24 44100 true 384 true 64 24 0.5 ReadCommon reads the COMM chunk into a Common: channels, frames, depth and rate. compression equals CompNone for plain PCM, and data_size is 384 bytes for 64 frames of two 24 bit channels. DecodeAIFF returns the clip with the sample intact.  Saving and opening AIFF files SaveAIFFBits writes a file at the depth you choose and OpenAIFF reads it back. As elsewhere in the audio packages, opening reports failure through a flag: a missing file gives an empty clip and false, not a crash. audio-aiff-guide-disk.salamCopyimport audio import audio.aiff import filepath import mem import os  func main:     mut c := audio.New(22050, 1, 100)     audio.SetSample(c, 10, 0, -0.5)     path := filepath.Join(os.TempDir(), "salam_guide.aiff")     defer mem.Free(path as void*)     println aiff.SaveAIFFBits(c, path, 16)      mut ok := false     mut back := aiff.OpenAIFF(path, ok)     println ok, back.rate, back.frames, back.bits     println audio.Sample(back, 10, 0)      missing := filepath.Join(os.TempDir(), "salam_guide_missing.aiff")     defer mem.Free(missing as void*)     mut gone := false     aiff.OpenAIFF(missing, gone)     println gone     audio.Free(c)     audio.Free(back) endOutputtrue true 22050 100 16 -0.5 false The value at frame 10 is -0.5 after the round trip. 16 bit PCM holds -0.5 exactly, so the printed number is clean; other values come back within one step of the original. audio/au audio.au Reading and writing the Sun and NeXT au format. Audio The au format is the simplest real sound file there is: a 24 byte big-endian header and then the samples. It came from Sun, it is what /dev/audio spoke, and it is still a pleasant way to hand raw audio between programs because there is almost nothing to get wrong. It carries more encodings than its size suggests: mu-law and A-law, signed PCM at 8, 16, 24 and 32 bits, and IEEE floating point at 32 and 64. Everything is big-endian. Things to know  8 bit au PCM is signed, where 8 bit WAVE is unsigned. The shared helpers in audio take that as an argument, so neither format has to guess. A companded file decodes to a clip marked 16 bit, because that is the depth mu-law and A-law reconstruct to. data_offset may be larger than HeaderSize; the gap is a text note, and this package steps over it. A data size of 0xFFFFFFFF means unknown, which this package treats as everything to the end of the file.   Choosing an encoding An AU file has a 24 byte header followed by the samples, and the header names the encoding. EncodeAUEncoding takes one of EncPcm16, EncMuLaw, EncALaw, EncFloat32 and the others the package lists. For 64 mono frames the three files are 152, 88 and 280 bytes: 16 bit PCM, one byte per sample, and 32 bit floats. audio-au-guide-encodings.salamCopyimport audio import audio.au import compress import math  func main:     mut c := audio.New(8000, 1, 64)     audio.SetSample(c, 3, 0, 0.5)      mut pcm := au.EncodeAUEncoding(c, au.EncPcm16)     mut mu := au.EncodeAUEncoding(c, au.EncMuLaw)     mut fl := au.EncodeAUEncoding(c, au.EncFloat32)     println compress.BufLen(pcm), compress.BufLen(mu), compress.BufLen(fl)      mut h := au.Header {}     println au.ReadHeader(mu.data, mu.len, h)     println h.encoding == au.EncMuLaw, h.rate, h.channels, h.data_size      mut ok := false     mut back := au.DecodeAU(mu.data, mu.len, ok)     println ok, back.bits, math.Abs(audio.Sample(back, 3, 0) - 0.5) < 0.02     compress.BufFree(pcm)     compress.BufFree(mu)     compress.BufFree(fl)     audio.Free(c)     audio.Free(back) endOutput152 88 280 true true 8000 1 64 true 16 true ReadHeader fills a Header with the encoding, rate, channels and data size. DecodeAU expands the mu-law file to a 16 bit clip, and the sample is within 0.02 of the original.  Saving, probing and opening SaveAU writes 16 bit PCM and returns true on success. ProbeAU works on bytes, so the program encodes the clip first and probes the buffer: rate, depth and frame count come from the header without decoding. audio-au-guide-disk.salamCopyimport audio import audio.au import compress import filepath import mem import os  func main:     mut c := audio.New(22050, 1, 64)     audio.SetSample(c, 3, 0, 0.5)     path := filepath.Join(os.TempDir(), "salam_guide.au")     defer mem.Free(path as void*)     println au.SaveAU(c, path)      mut buf := au.EncodeAU(c)     mut ok := false     info := au.ProbeAU(buf.data, buf.len, ok)     println ok, info.rate, info.bits, info.frames      mut open_ok := false     mut back := au.OpenAU(path, open_ok)     println open_ok, back.frames, back.rate, audio.Sample(back, 3, 0)     compress.BufFree(buf)     audio.Free(c)     audio.Free(back) endOutputtrue true 22050 16 64 true 64 22050 0.5 OpenAU reads the file written to disk and returns the clip with its rate and frames intact. Free the buffer and every clip when you are done.
