audio/flac audio.flac Lossless compression: reading and writing FLAC. Audio FLAC is lossless: what comes out is exactly what went in, and the file is usually a little over half the size of the same sound as 16 bit PCM. This package reads and writes it without any outside library. The decoder handles the whole format: constant, verbatim, fixed-predictor and LPC subframes, Rice-coded and escaped residuals, and all four ways FLAC can share a stereo pair between two channels. The encoder writes constant, verbatim and fixed-predictor subframes, choosing per block whichever is smallest, which is where most of the compression comes from. Things to know  Lossless means lossless: a clip at 8, 16 or 24 bits comes back bit for bit. VerifyFLAC proves it on a given file by decoding it again. An encode is only as good as the clip it was given. A clip has no bit depth of its own until something sets bits, and the encoder then assumes 16. Tags are not here. FLAC keeps them in a metadata block, which audio.tag reads and writes. Blocks hands back a vector you must free, and a stream header holds an MD5 you must release with FreeStreamInfo. Compression depends entirely on the material. A tone goes to a fifth of its PCM size, noise barely moves, and real music lands somewhere near half.  Encoding a clip FLAC stores whole numbers, so the clip must have a bit depth first. audio.ToBits quantizes a float clip to 16 bits, and you then set bits to 16 so the encoder writes 16 bit samples. EncodeFLAC returns a byte buffer that you free with compress.BufFree. Before trusting the result, check it: IsFLAC looks at the signature, and VerifyFLAC decodes the whole stream again and tests every frame checksum. A tone compresses to a small fraction of its PCM size; noise would barely shrink. audio-flac-guide-encode.salamCopyimport audio import audio.flac import audio.synth import compress  func main:     src := synth.Tone(440.0, 0.5, 44100, synth.WaveSine)     mut clip := audio.ToBits(src, 16)     clip.bits = 16     raw := clip.frames * clip.channels * 2     mut enc := flac.EncodeFLAC(clip)     size := compress.BufLen(enc)     println "pcm bytes:", raw     println "smaller than pcm:", size < raw     println "valid flac:", flac.IsFLAC(enc.data, enc.len)     println "verified:", flac.VerifyFLAC(enc.data, enc.len)      mut s := src     audio.Free(s)     audio.Free(clip)     compress.BufFree(enc) endOutputpcm bytes: 44100 smaller than pcm: true valid flac: true verified: true Saving, probing and reading back SaveFLACLevel writes a file; the level runs from 0 to 8 and picks the block size, and every level is lossless. ProbeFileFLAC reads only the header and returns the rate, channels, bit depth and frame count without decoding any audio. OpenFLAC decodes the file into a new clip. Because FLAC is lossless, the decoded samples equal the quantized ones exactly. The program compares them one by one rather than within a tolerance. audio-flac-guide-roundtrip.salamCopyimport audio import audio.flac import audio.synth import filepath import mem import os  func main:     src := synth.Tone(330.0, 0.25, 44100, synth.WaveTriangle)     mut clip := audio.ToBits(src, 16)     clip.bits = 16     path := filepath.Join(os.TempDir(), "salam_flac_guide.flac")     defer mem.Free(path as void*)     println "saved:", flac.SaveFLACLevel(clip, path, 8)      mut ok := false     info := flac.ProbeFileFLAC(path, ok)     println "probe:", ok, info.rate, info.channels, info.bits, info.frames      mut back := flac.OpenFLAC(path, ok)     mut same := back.frames == clip.frames     mut i := 0     until i < clip.frames:         if audio.Sample(back, i, 0) != audio.Sample(clip, i, 0):             same = false         end         i++     end     println "identical:", same      mut s := src     audio.Free(s)     audio.Free(clip)     audio.Free(back) endOutputsaved: true probe: true 44100 1 16 11025 identical: true Types FrameInfostruct FrameInfoWhat a frame header says, which may differ from the stream header.NameTypeDescriptionblock_sizeint = audio/tag audio.tag Reading and writing the tags on a song: title, artist, album and cover art. Audio A sound file carries more than sound. This package reads and writes the part that says what the music is: the title, who played it, which album it came from, and the picture on the cover. Three tag formats cover almost everything in use. ID3v1 is the 128 bytes at the end of an MP3. ID3v2 sits at the front and is what modern files really use, in any of four text encodings. Vorbis comments are what FLAC and Ogg keep their tags in. ReadTags works out which one a file has and reads it, so most callers never name a format at all. Things to know  Every string in a Tags is owned by it. Release the whole set with FreeTags; an unset field is empty and costs nothing. Text comes back as UTF-8 whatever the file used, so Persian and Arabic titles survive an ID3v2 round trip. Writing produces ID3v2.4 with UTF-8, which every current player reads. Cover art comes back as a byte buffer still in its own format, so hand it straight to image to decode. AudioStart and AudioEnd say where the sound really is, which is what a decoder needs in order to skip the tags.  Writing and reading an ID3v2 tag A Tags value holds the title, artist, album, year and track numbers. NewTags makes an empty one; string fields must be heap strings, so assign them with str.Clone, and release the whole value with FreeTags. WriteID3v2 returns the tag as bytes. ReadID3v2 parses such bytes into another Tags and returns false when they are not a valid tag. The same Tags type is used for ID3v1 and for FLAC comments, so the reading code does not change with the format. audio-tag-guide-write.salamCopyimport audio.tag import compress import str  func main:     mut t := tag.NewTags()     t.title = str.Clone("Evening Walk")     t.artist = str.Clone("Darya")     t.album = str.Clone("Small Rooms")     t.year = 2026     t.track = 3     t.tracks = 9      mut block := tag.WriteID3v2(t)     println "has tag:", tag.HasID3v2(block.data, block.len)     println "version:", tag.ID3v2Version(block.data, block.len)      mut got := tag.NewTags()     ok := tag.ReadID3v2(block.data, block.len, got)     println "read:", ok     println got.title, "by", got.artist     println got.album, got.year, got.track, "of", got.tracks      tag.FreeTags(t)     tag.FreeTags(got)     compress.BufFree(block) endOutputhas tag: true version: 4 read: true Evening Walk by Darya Small Rooms 2026 3 of 9 Tags on a file An MP3 file is a tag followed by audio frames. ReadTagsFile finds whichever tag the file has and fills a Tags. AudioStart reports the byte where the audio begins, and StripTags returns a copy of the file without any tag, which is what you want before comparing or re-tagging the audio. The example builds a file from a tag and 100 filler bytes standing in for audio, so it needs no real MP3. audio-tag-guide-file.salamCopyimport archive import audio.tag import compress import filepath import mem import os import str  func main:     mut t := tag.NewTags()     t.title = str.Clone("Evening Walk")     t.artist = str.Clone("Darya")     mut head := tag.WriteID3v2(t)     mut file := compress.NewByteBuf()     compress.BufPushBuf(file, head)     mut i := 0     until i < 100:         compress.BufPush(file, 65)         i++     end      path := filepath.Join(os.TempDir(), "salam_tag_guide.mp3")     defer mem.Free(path as void*)     println "written:", archive.WriteBinaryFileBuf(path, file)      mut ok := false     mut got := tag.ReadTagsFile(path, ok)     println ok, got.title, "-", got.artist      println "audio starts at:", tag.AudioStart(file.data, file.len)     mut bare := tag.StripTags(file.data, file.len)     println "audio only:", compress.BufLen(bare)      tag.FreeTags(t)     tag.FreeTags(got)     compress.BufFree(head)     compress.BufFree(file)     compress.BufFree(bare) endOutputwritten: true true Evening Walk - audio/music audio.music Notes, scales, chords and tunings, Persian dastgah among them. Audio This package is the arithmetic of music rather than of sound: what a note is, which notes belong together, and what frequency each one wants. It makes no sound itself, which audio.synth does. Notes are MIDI numbers, so 60 is middle C and 69 is the A tuned to 440. NoteToFreq turns one into a frequency in equal temperament, and JustFreq and PythagoreanRatio are there when equal temperament is not what you want. Things to know  Scales and chords come back as vectors of semitone steps, which the caller frees. NoteName returns a string the caller frees. ParseNote reads one back and accepts flats and either case, so it round-trips its own output. Persian music does not fit twelve semitones. A dastgah is therefore given in cents, not semitone steps: the third of Shur sits at 350 cents, between a minor and a major third, where no piano key is. NoteToFreqCents is how you ask for it, and KoronCents and SoriCents are the accidentals that get you there. The seven dastgah here are the frequencies of their tonic rows. A real performance moves between gusheh within a dastgah, which is a matter of melody rather than of tuning.  Note numbers, names and frequencies Notes are MIDI numbers: 60 is middle C and 69 is A4 at 440 Hz. NoteName and ParseNote convert between numbers and names such as C#5, NoteToFreq gives the pitch in hertz, and FreqToNote goes back to the nearest note. NoteName returns a heap string; free it with mem.Free. Transpose moves a note by semitones, Interval measures the distance between two, and BeatSeconds turns a tempo in beats per minute into the length of one beat. audio-music-guide-notes.salamCopyimport audio.music import math import mem  func main:     each n in [60, 64, 67, 69]:         name := music.NoteName(n)         println n, name, math.Round(music.NoteToFreq(n) * 10.0) / 10.0         mem.Free(name as void*)     end     println music.ParseNote("A4"), music.ParseNote("C#5")     println music.FreqToNote(261.63)     println music.Transpose(60, 7), music.Interval(60, 67)     println music.BeatSeconds(120.0) endOutput60 C4 261.6 64 E4 329.6 67 G4 392 69 A4 440 69 73 60 67 7 0.5 Scales and chords ScaleNotes lists the notes of a scale from a root, and ChordNotes does the same for a chord. Both take a kind constant such as ScaleMinor or ChordDominant7 and return a vector you free. The result is plain note numbers, so it can feed straight into audio.synth or audio.midi, as the next pages show. audio-music-guide-scale.salamCopyimport audio.music import mem  func show(label: str, audio/synth audio.synth Making sound from nothing: oscillators, envelopes and voices. Audio Everything else in this family reads sound that already exists. This package makes it. Six waveforms, an envelope to shape a note, three colours of noise, and four ways of building a voice that sounds like something rather than like a test tone. The quickest way in is Tone for a bare waveform or ToneEnvelope for a note that starts and stops the way an instrument does. To play a phrase, fill a vector of Note and hand it to RenderNotes, which mixes and pans them into one clip. Things to know  An oscillator carries its own phase, so stepping it with OscNext in a loop gives a continuous tone. WaveValue is the stateless form. A note lasts longer than you asked: ADSRTotal adds the release onto the hold, and that is the length ToneEnvelope gives you. Chord divides by the number of notes, so three notes together do not clip. RenderNotes does not, so give its notes a gain that leaves room. For which notes to play, see audio.music, which also carries the Persian dastgah; to play a file of notes, see audio.midi.  A first tone Tone takes a frequency, a length in seconds, a sample rate and a wave shape and returns a mono clip of float samples. Sine, square, saw, triangle, noise and pulse are available as constants. The example measures the clip with Duration, Peak and IsClipped, then encodes it as WAV in memory. Free the clip with audio.Free and the buffer with compress.BufFree. audio-synth-guide-tone.salamCopyimport audio import audio.synth import audio.wav import compress  func main:     clip := synth.Tone(440.0, 1.0, 44100, synth.WaveSine)     println clip.rate, clip.channels, clip.frames     println "seconds:", audio.Duration(clip)     println "loud enough:", audio.Peak(clip) > 0.9     println "clipped:", audio.IsClipped(clip)      mut enc := wav.EncodeWAV(clip)     println "wav bytes:", compress.BufLen(enc)     println "is wav:", wav.IsWAV(enc.data, enc.len)      mut c := clip     audio.Free(c)     compress.BufFree(enc) endOutput44100 1 44100 seconds: 1 loud enough: true clipped: false wav bytes: 88244 is wav: true Shaping a note with an envelope A bare tone starts and stops abruptly, which clicks. An ADSR envelope fixes that: the level rises over attack seconds, falls to sustain over decay, holds while the note is held, and fades over release. ADSRAt gives the level at a moment in time for a note held a given number of seconds, which is a good way to check your numbers. ToneEnvelope applies the envelope and a gain while it renders. audio-synth-guide-envelope.salamCopyimport audio import audio.synth  func main:     e := synth.ADSR { attack = 0.05, decay = 0.1, sustain = 0.6, release = 0.2 }     println "total:", synth.ADSRTotal(e, 0.5)     each t in [0.0, 0.025, 0.05, 0.3, 0.5]:         println t, synth.ADSRAt(e, t, 0.5)     end      flat := synth.Tone(440.0, 0.7, 22050, synth.WaveSaw)     shaped := synth.ToneEnvelope(440.0, 0.5, 22050, synth.WaveSaw, e, 0.8)     println "flat peak:", audio.Peak(flat) > 0.9     println "shaped peak:", audio.Peak(shaped) <= 0.81     println "starts silent:", audio.Sample(shaped, 0, 0) == 0.0      mut a := flat     audio.Free(a)     mut b := shaped     audio.Free(b) endOutputtotal: 0.7 0 0 0.025 0.5 0.05 1 0.3 0.6 0.5 0.6 flat peak: true shaped peak: true starts silent: true Playing several notes For more than one note, build a vector of Note values with NoteAt, giving each a note number, a start time, a length, a gain and a wave. RenderNotes mixes them all into one clip, with the channel count you ask for and the envelope applied to every note. audio/midi audio.midi Reading, writing and playing standard MIDI files. Audio A MIDI file holds notes, not sound: which note, when, how hard and on what instrument. That makes it tiny, and it makes it editable in a way a recording is not. This package reads and writes standard MIDI files, and Render turns one into sound through audio.synth, so a file of notes becomes a clip you can save as WAV or FLAC. Things to know  Everything is in ticks, and division says how many ticks a quarter note is. TicksToSeconds needs the tempo as well, which is why it takes the whole song. A note is two events, on and off. AddNote writes both, and Notes pairs them back up and gives you lengths in seconds. A note on with velocity 0 means a note off, and the reader turns it into one so you never have to check. Release a song with FreeSong: it owns a vector per track plus the vector of tracks. Render uses a single plain envelope for every note. For anything more, take Notes and render it yourself.  Building a MIDI file A Song has a division (ticks per quarter note) and a list of tracks; a Track is a list of events. AddTempo, AddProgram and AddNote append events at a tick position. AddNote takes the start tick, the length in ticks, the note number, the velocity and the channel, and adds both the note-on and the note-off. Add the track to the song with AddTrack, then EncodeMIDI returns the file bytes or SaveMIDI writes them. Free a song with FreeSong, which also frees its tracks. audio-midi-guide-write.salamCopyimport audio.midi import audio.music import compress import filepath import mem import os  func main:     mut song := midi.NewSong(480)     mut track := midi.NewTrack()     midi.AddTempo(track, 0, 100.0)     midi.AddProgram(track, 0, 0, 0)     mut scale := music.ScaleNotes(60, music.ScaleMajor, 5)     defer scale.Free()     mut i := 0     until i < scale.Len():         midi.AddNote(track, i * 480, 480, scale.Get(i), 90, 0)         i++     end     println "events:", track.events.Len()     midi.AddTrack(song, track)     println "ticks:", midi.TotalTicks(song)      mut enc := midi.EncodeMIDI(song)     println "valid midi:", midi.IsMIDI(enc.data, enc.len)     path := filepath.Join(os.TempDir(), "salam_midi_guide.mid")     defer mem.Free(path as void*)     println "saved:", midi.SaveMIDI(song, path)      compress.BufFree(enc)     midi.FreeSong(song) endOutputevents: 12 ticks: 2400 valid midi: true saved: true Reading it back and rendering OpenMIDI parses a file into a Song. Bpm reads its tempo, TicksToSeconds converts positions to time, and Notes pairs each note-on with its note-off and returns notes with start and length in seconds. Render plays the song through the built-in synthesizer and returns a clip, so you can write it as WAV or FLAC without any external player. audio-midi-guide-read.salamCopyimport audio import audio.midi audio/mp3 audio.mp3 Reading the frames, headers and VBR tags of an mp3 file. Audio An mp3 file is a run of frames, each with a header saying how it is coded and how long it is. This package reads those headers, so you can tell what a file is, how long it lasts, how many frames it holds and where in it a given second falls, all without decoding any sound. That covers everything a library listing, a player's seek bar or a tag editor needs. Every MPEG version and layer is parsed, including the MPEG-2 and 2.5 half and quarter sample rates, and the Xing, Info and VBRI headers that say how long a variable bit rate file really is. Things to know  Audio decoding is not here yet. This package reads the structure of an mp3, not its sound, and CanDecode in audio.codec says so. Layer III decoding needs the ISO Huffman and scalefactor tables, which are a separate and much larger job. A frame is only trusted when another frame follows where it says one should, which is what stops FindSync locking onto a run of 0xFF bytes inside a tag. The frame count in a Xing header does not include the frame the header itself sits in, so a file with 10 audio frames reports 11 when counted and 10 when asked. For a constant bit rate file the length is frames times samples per frame. For a variable one, only the Xing header knows, which is why ProbeMP3 prefers it. Tags are audio.tag's job, and this package uses it to find where the audio starts.  Reading a frame header This package inspects MP3 files; it does not decode or encode the audio. An MP3 is a series of frames, each starting with a four byte header. ParseHeader reads the header at a byte offset into a Header with the sample rate, bitrate, channel count, samples per frame and frame size in bytes. The example builds four frames of a 128 kbit/s, 44.1 kHz stream by hand, so it runs without an MP3 file. IsMP3 checks for a valid frame, and CountFrames walks the stream header by header. audio-mp3-guide-header.salamCopyimport audio.mp3 import compress  func main:     mut file := compress.NewByteBuf()     mut f := 0     until f < 4:         compress.BufPush(file, 255)         compress.BufPush(file, 0xFB)         compress.BufPush(file, 0x90)         compress.BufPush(file, 0xC0)         mut i := 4         until i < 417:             compress.BufPush(file, 0)             i++         end         f++     end      println "looks like mp3:", mp3.IsMP3(file.data, file.len)     mut h := mp3.Header {}     println "header:", mp3.ParseHeader(file.data, file.len, 0, h)     println h.rate, "Hz,", h.bitrate, "kbit/s,", h.channels, "channel"     println "layer 3:", h.layer == mp3.Layer3     println "frame bytes:", h.frame_size, "samples:", h.samples     println "frames:", mp3.CountFrames(file.data, file.len)      compress.BufFree(file) endOutputlooks like mp3: true header: true 44100 Hz, 128 kbit/s, 1 channel layer 3: true frame bytes: 417 samples: 1152 frames: 4 Probing a file and finding frames ProbeFileMP3 returns the rate, channels and total sample frames for a file. For a constant bitrate file the count comes from walking the frames; if the file has a Xing or VBR header, ReadVbrInfo exposes that too. Dividing the frame count by the rate gives the length in seconds. FrameAt returns the byte offset of the n-th frame, or -1 past the end, and SeekToSecond returns the offset to start reading from for a given time. audio-mp3-guide-probe.salamCopyimport archive import metatrader metatrader Read account, symbols, rates and history, and send trades through a local MetaTrader 5 bridge. Trading metatrader is a client for a local bridge to a running MetaTrader 5 terminal. The package speaks HTTP and JSON: every call sends a request to the bridge, and the bridge asks the terminal for the data or the trade. There is no DLL, no COM and no terminal plugin inside your program, so the same Salam program runs on Linux, macOS and Windows as long as the bridge is reachable. The terminal itself must be running and logged in, and a bridge must be listening on the address you set. The default is http://127.0.0.1:18812, the value of DEFAULT_BRIDGE_URL. The bridge implements the endpoints below; the package only calls them and decodes the JSON.  EndpointUsed by  POST /initialize, POST /login, POST /shutdownInitialize, Login, Shutdown GET /version, GET /account_info, GET /terminal_infoVersion, GetAccountInfo, GetTerminalInfo GET /symbols_total, GET /symbols_get, GET /symbol_info, GET /symbol_info_tick, POST /symbol_selectSymbol calls GET /copy_rates_from, GET /copy_rates_from_pos, GET /copy_rates_rangeCopyRates* GET /copy_ticks_from, GET /copy_ticks_rangeCopyTicks* GET /orders_total, GET /orders_get, GET /positions_total, GET /positions_getOrder and position reads GET /history_orders_*, GET /history_deals_*History calls POST /order_calc_margin, POST /order_calc_profit, POST /order_check, POST /order_sendTrading calls POST /market_book_add, GET /market_book_get, POST /market_book_releaseMarket depth calls    Start with the account Set the bridge address once, call Initialize, then read the account. Every call returns a value even when it fails, so check Ok or LastError after the calls that matter, and stop when the bridge is not there. metatrader-quickstart.salamCopyimport metatrader  func main:     metatrader.SetBridgeUrl("http://127.0.0.1:18812")      if not metatrader.Initialize("", 0 as i64, "", "", 60000, false):         e := metatrader.LastError()         printerrln "no bridge:", e.code, e.description         ret 1     end      a := metatrader.GetAccountInfo()     if not metatrader.Ok():         e := metatrader.LastError()         printerrln "account failed:", e.code, e.description         metatrader.Shutdown()         ret 1     end     println a.login, a.name, a.currency     println "balance", a.balance, "equity", a.equity     println "margin", a.margin, "free", a.margin_free      t := metatrader.GetTerminalInfo()     println t.company, t.name, t.build, t.connected      metatrader.Shutdown()     ret 0 end Initialize and Login mark the session connected only when the bridge answers with a 2xx status. IsConnected reports that flag, not a live socket: call Version or GetTerminalInfo when you need to know that the terminal is still there. Shutdown only asks the bridge to close; it does not free anything in your program.  Errors and retcodes A failed call returns the zero value of its type, an empty vector, an empty struct, or false, and leaves the reason in LastError. Ok is true exactly when the last code is RES_S_OK. The bridge uses the RES_E_* constants for transport and parameter errors, and the trade server uses TRADE_RETCODE_* in the result of OrderCheck and OrderSend. a := metatrader.GetAccountInfo() if not metatrader.Ok():     e := metatrader.LastError()     printerrln "account failed:", e.code, e.description     ret 1 end println a.balance An HTTP error and a rejected trade are different: the first leaves Ok false, the second is a normal answer with a retcode. Always read retcode after OrderSend; a successful HTTP call does not mean the trade was accepted.  Symbols, prices and ticks SymbolsGet returns every symbol with its contract rules and session data; the group forms filter with a mask such as *USD*, where * matches any text. GetSymbolInfo asks for one symbol, and SymbolInfoTick is the cheap call for the current bid and ask. metatrader-symbols.salamCopyimport metatrader  func main:     metatrader.SetBridgeUrl("http://127.0.0.1:18812")      println "symbols:", metatrader.SymbolsTotal()     each s in metatrader.SymbolsGet():         println s.name, s.digits, s.spread, s.trade_mode     end      majors := metatrader.SymbolsGetGroup("*USD*")     println "usd symbols:", majors.Len()      info := metatrader.GetSymbolInfo("EURUSD")     println info.bid, info.ask, info.point, info.digits     println info.volume_min, info.volume_step, info.volume_max     println info.trade_stops_level, info.trade_contract_size      tick := metatrader.SymbolInfoTick("EURUSD")     println tick.time, tick.bid, tick.ask, tick.last, tick.volume      if not metatrader.SymbolSelect("EURUSD", true):         printerrln "cannot select EURUSD"     end     ret 0 end digits and point tell you how to round a price; volume_min, volume_max and volume_step tell you which volumes the server accepts; trade_stops_level is the shortest distance in points between the price and a stop loss or take profit.  Candles and ticks Rates are returned oldest first. CopyRatesFromPos counts from the newest candle, so position 0 is the candle that is still forming, and CopyRatesFrom starts at a time. Times are seconds since the epoch, as in time; tick times are milliseconds in time_msc, which is what CopyTicksRange expects. metatrader-rates.salamCopyimport metatrader  func main:     metatrader.SetBridgeUrl("http://127.0.0.1:18812")      from := metatrader.CopyRatesFrom("EURUSD", metatrader.TIMEFRAME_H1, 1700000000 as i64, 10)     each r in from:         println r.time, r.open, r.high, r.low, r.close, r.tick_volume     end      recent := metatrader.CopyRatesFromPos("EURUSD", metatrader.TIMEFRAME_M5, 0, 5)     println "recent:", recent.Len()      window := metatrader.CopyRatesRange("EURUSD", me

dependency dependency Dependency injection in the spirit of google/wire: named providers, interface bindings, cleanups and a graph check for missing dependencies and cycles. Language and runtime dependency wires the layers of a program together: a repository, a service that uses it, a handler that uses the service. You register one provider per component, name what each one needs, and ask for the top of the graph. Each component is built once, and Close runs the cleanups in the reverse of the order they were built. Salam has no runtime type information, so providers are identified by a name you choose, usually the type name. A provider is a function that takes the container and returns the component; it reads its own dependencies with Get. The second string of Provide lists those dependencies so that Build can check the whole graph before anything runs.  Providers and the graph check Provide(c, name, needs, witness, factory) registers a provider. needs is a comma separated list of provider names, empty when there are none. witness is any value of the component's type; it only tells the compiler which type the factory returns. Build returns an empty string when the graph is sound and otherwise a message that names the problem: a missing dependency, a duplicate provider or a dependency cycle with the full path. dependency-quickstart.salamCopyimport dependency  struct Repo:     pub rows: int = 0 end  struct Service:     pub repo: Repo = Repo {}     pub func Count(): int:         ret this.repo.rows     end end  struct Handler:     pub svc: Service = Service {}     pub func Serve(): str:         ret "rows=" + this.svc.Count()     end end  func main:     c := dependency.New()     dependency.Provide(c, "Repo", "", Repo {}, (_c: dependency.Container): ret Repo { rows = 3 } end)     dependency.Provide(c, "Service", "Repo", Service {}, (cx: dependency.Container):         mut r := Repo {}         _ok := dependency.Get(cx, "Repo", r)         ret Service { repo = r }     end)     dependency.Provide(c, "Handler", "Service", Handler {}, (cx: dependency.Container):         mut s := Service {}         _ok := dependency.Get(cx, "Service", s)         ret Handler { svc = s }     end)     err := dependency.Build(c)     if err != "":         println err         ret 1     end     mut h := Handler {}     _ok := dependency.Get(c, "Handler", h)     println h.Serve()     dependency.Close(c) endOutputrows=3 Get(c, name, out) builds the component if it does not exist yet and copies it into out. It returns false and sets Error when the name is unknown or a cycle is hit at run time.  Interfaces, values and cleanups Bind(c, "Store", "MemStore") makes the name Store resolve to the provider MemStore, which is how a service asks for an interface and gets the implementation chosen at the wiring site. Value registers a ready made value such as a configuration struct. OnClose attaches a cleanup to a provider; Close runs the cleanups of the components that were actually built, last built first, and frees the container. Built lists the names in the order they were built and Count the number of registered names.  Reading the errors Build only looks at the registered names and their needs lists, it never runs a factory. A sound graph gives an empty string; the other three messages are missing dependency: Service needs Repo, duplicate provider: Repo and dependency cycle: A -> B -> C -> A. Call it once at startup and stop there if the text is not empty. Get with a name nobody registered returns false and leaves missing provider: Nope in Error. dependency-guide-errors.salamCopyimport dependency  func report(label: str, c: dependency.Container):     msg := dependency.Build(c)     println label + ":", msg == "" ? "sound" : msg     dependency.Close(c) end  func main:     ok := dependency.New()     dependency.Provide(ok, "Repo", "", 0, (_c: dependency.Container): ret 1 end)     report("fine", ok)      missing := dependency.New()     dependency.Provide(missing, "Service", "Repo", 0, (_c: dependency.Container): ret 1 end)     report("missing", missing)      twice := dependency.New()     dependency.Provide(twice, "Repo", "", 0, (_c: dependency.Container): ret 1 end)     dependency.Provide(twice, "Repo", "", 0, (_c: dependency.Container): ret 2 end)     report("duplicate", twice)      loop := dependency.New()     dependency.Provide(loop, "A", "B", 0, (_c: dependency.Container): ret 1 end)     dependency.Provide(loop, "B", "C", 0, (_c: dependency.Container): ret 2 end)     dependency.Provide(loop, "C", "A", 0, (_c: dependency.Container): ret 3 end)     report("cycle", loop)      empty := dependency.New()     mut n := 0     println "get:", dependency.Get(empty, "Nope", n), dependency.Error(empty)     dependency.Close(empty) endOutputfine: sound missing: missing dependency: Service needs Repo duplicate: duplicate provider: Repo cycle: dependency cycle: A -> B -> C -> A get: false missing provider: Nope  Choosing an implementation at the wiring site Put the choice in one function that builds the container. Here Value stores the configuration, two providers make a Store in different ways, and Bind points the name Store at one of them depending on the environment. Code that asks for Store does not change. Only the components that something actually asked for are built: Built lists 1 name in the test container and 2 in the production one, out of 4 registered. dependency-guide-swap.salamCopyimport dependency  struct Config:     pub env: str = "" end  struct Store:     pub kind: str = "" end  func build(env: str): dependency.Container:     c := dependency.New()     dependency.V

t: What is the Salam programming language? A tour of a modern general-purpose and systems language
x: A complete introduction to Salam: the language, the self-hosting compiler, the standard library, the tools, the measured performance and the honest limits of a young language. Salam is an open source, statically typed systems language you can write in English or Persian. What it is, how it compiles, what it can build and where it falls short. The language Salam is an open source, general-purpose and systems programming language. It is statically typed, it compiles to native machine code, and its compiler is written in Salam itself. What makes it unusual is that every keyword, type, standard library package and compiler error message exists in two spellings, English and Persian, and both spellings compile to exactly the same program. This article is the starting point of the Salam Magazine. It explains what kind of language Salam is, shows real code, walks through the compiler and the toolchain, gives the measured performance with its caveats, and is plain about what a young language does not have yet. Salam in one paragraph Salam is a compiled, statically typed language for building everything from command-line tools and web servers to desktop apps and bare-metal kernels. You write func main: and a block that ends with end; the compiler checks the types, generates code through C, LLVM or its own native backend, and leaves you with a single executable for Linux, macOS, Windows or the web. There is no virtual machine and no garbage collector. A standard library of more than 170 packages covers networking, databases, cryptography, compression, images, machine learning and more, and a built-in page language turns Salam code into HTML, CSS and JavaScript. The name means "peace" and "hello" in Persian. A first program Here is the smallest complete Salam program. Blocks open with a colon and close with end, and println prints its arguments followed by a new line. SalamCopyfunc main:     println "Hello, Salam!" endOutputHello, Salam! The same program written in Persian. The compiler detects the language from the keywords, so there is no switch to flip and no separate toolchain: تابع is func, ریشه is the entry function main, سرچاپ is println and پایان is end. SalamCopyتابع ریشه:     سرچاپ "سلام دنیا!" پایانOutputسلام دنیا! Both files go through the same frontend, the same type checker and the same code generator. Their executables are interchangeable. The article One language, two scripts explains how that works in detail. What kind of language is Salam? If you have used Go, Rust, Swift or Python, most of Salam will look familiar. The table puts the main design choices in one place. QuestionSalam's answerTypingStatic, with type inference: count := 0 is an int, x := 3.14 is an f64CompilationAhead of time to native code, through C, LLVM or Salam's own native backendMemoryNo garbage collector; values live on the stack, heap containers are freed with .Free() or deferData typesStructs with methods, enums that carry data, tuples, generics, interfaces, T? optionalsErrorsResult values with try, plus throws, throw and try/catchConcurrencyThreads, a bounded task pool, the go keyword, channels, futures, atomicsTargetsLinux, macOS, Windows, WebAssembly, JavaScript, Android, iOS and freestanding bare metalSource languagesEnglish and Persian, with one shared standard libraryLicenseGPL-3.0, developed in the open on GitHub Variables are immutable unless you ask otherwise: name := "Sara" cannot be reassigned, mut count := 0 can. Reassigning an immutable variable is a compile error, not a warning. That small rule removes a whole category of accidental bugs and makes code easier to read, because a name without mut never changes. A taste of real code The next program uses a struct, an array literal, a function with a multi-word name, an each loop and compound assignment. It is short, but it shows how Salam code tends to read. SalamCopystruct Book:     pub title: str     pub pages: int end  func reading time(b: Book): int:     ret b.pages / 40 end  func main:     books := [         Book { title = "The Little Prince", pages = 96 },         Book { title = "Dune", pages = 412 },         Book { title = "SICP", pages = 657 },     ]     mut total := 0     each b in books:         hours := reading time(b)         println b.title, "takes about", hours, "hours"         total += b.pages     end     println "Pages in total:", total endOutputThe Little Prince takes about 2 hours Dune takes about 10 hours SICP takes about 16 hours Pages in total: 1165 Two details stand out. First, reading time is a single function name made of two words. Salam allows spaces inside names so that a call can read like a sentence, which matters even more in Persian, where many concepts are naturally written as two words. t: One language, two scripts: how Salam lets you program in Persian and English with the same compiler
x: Salam is one language with two spellings. This article shows how a Persian file and an English file reach the same compiler, share one standard library, report errors in the reader's language and call each other's packages. Programming in Persian and English with Salam: one compiler, one standard library, error messages in both languages, and twin programs with real output. The language Programming in Persian with Salam means writing a complete program, from the entry function to the standard library calls and the error messages you read back, in Persian script, and getting exactly the same native executable an English program would produce. Salam is a bilingual programming language: every keyword, built-in type, built-in method, standard library package and compiler diagnostic has an English spelling and a Persian spelling, and both spellings are the same language underneath. There is no Persian dialect, no separate compiler and no preprocessor that rewrites Persian into English text before compiling. This article explains how that works in practice: how the compiler tells the two apart, what exactly has a Persian name, how errors are reported, how packages written in one language are used from the other, and where the design stops. What "bilingual programming language" means in Salam Many projects that offer "programming in your native language" translate the keywords and stop. The program still calls printf or len, the library documentation is in English and the first compile error arrives in English. A beginner who reads Persian comfortably but English slowly is back to translating in their head after the first five minutes. Salam takes the opposite approach. The English and Persian forms are two language packs for one grammar. The lexer reads a file with one pack or the other, turns the words into the same tokens, and from that point on the parser, the type checker, the code generators and the runtime see no difference. A Persian اگر and an English if become the same token; a Persian رشته and an English str are the same type. The practical consequences:  one compiler binary, salam, builds both; one standard library serves both, with Persian names declared next to the English ones; every diagnostic is printed in the language of the file; a tool, salam translate, converts a file from one spelling to the other; an English program can use a package written in Persian, and the other way round.  The same program in Persian and in English Here is a small program in English: an enum, a struct, a function with a two-word name, an array of struct literals, an each loop and a match expression. SalamCopyenum Box: Small, Medium, Large end  struct Order:     pub item: str     pub price: int     pub count: int end  func line total(o: Order): int:     ret o.price * o.count end  func box for(total: int): Box:     if total >= 500:         ret Box.Large     else total >= 200:         ret Box.Medium     end     ret Box.Small end  func main:     orders := [         Order { item = "Tea", price = 120, count = 2 },         Order { item = "Bread", price = 45, count = 3 },         Order { item = "Dates", price = 300, count = 1 },     ]     mut sum := 0     each o in orders:         t := line total(o)         println o.item, t         sum += t     end     packing := match box for(sum):         Small: "a small box" end         Medium: "a medium box" end         Large: "a large box" end     end     println "Total:", sum, "in", packing endOutputTea 240 Bread 135 Dates 300 Total: 675 in a large box And the same program written by a Persian speaker. The structure is identical; only the words change. Note the Persian digits in the number literals, the Persian comma ، between arguments and fields, and the «...» quotes, which are string literals in Persian files. t: Beyond translated keywords: the real problems of designing a programming language for Persian and Arabic
x: What actually goes wrong when a programming language is written in Persian or Arabic script, from names with spaces to look-alike letters, and the concrete decisions Salam made for each problem. Translating keywords is the easy part. Multi-word names, ZWNJ, yeh and kaf, keyword choice, word order and diagnostics in a non-English programming language. The language A non-English programming language is one whose keywords, and ideally its library and error messages, are written in a human language other than English. The hard part of building one for Persian or Arabic is not choosing the keywords; it is everything around them: names that naturally contain spaces, an invisible joining character, two Unicode encodings for the same letter, words with two meanings, a word order unlike English, and error messages, editors and tools that all have to agree. Most attempts stop at a keyword table, and the result feels like English with a costume on. Salam is a general-purpose compiled language with a complete Persian spelling alongside its English one. This article walks through the design problems a Persian-script language runs into, the decisions Salam made for each, and where those decisions have costs. It also places Salam in the longer history of programming languages that are not written in English. Why a keyword table is not enough A programming language touches its user through more than keywords. Count what a beginner reads in the first hour: keywords and type names, the names of built-in functions and methods, the names of the standard library packages and functions they call, the compiler's error messages, the documentation and the editor's highlighting and completion. If only the first item is translated, the learner meets English in every other place, including the most stressful one, the error message. Salam's rule is that everything the language defines has two spellings: keywords, types, literal words such as true, the entry function, built-in functions and methods, standard library packages and their public functions, compile-time constants, and the compiler's messages, all 1,299 of them. Both spellings go through one lexer into the same tokens. That shared core is what makes the rest of this article possible, because every Persian-specific rule lives in one place: the lexer and the language-pack code. The bilingual design article describes the mechanism. A short history of non-English programming languages The idea is old, and each attempt solved a different part of the problem:  ALGOL 68 separated the language from its printed representation, and its report allowed keywords in other natural languages; representations in languages such as Russian and German were produced. Spreadsheets have localized function names for decades: in a German version of Microsoft Excel, SUM is SUMME. Hundreds of millions of people have used a localized formula language without thinking of it as programming. 1C:Enterprise, a business platform widely used in Russia, has a scripting language with Russian keywords and English equivalents. Scratch translates its blocks into many languages, which works well because block-based code has no keywords to type. Qalb (قلب), created by Ramsey Nasser in 2012, is a Lisp written entirely in Arabic, built partly as a statement about how deeply English is baked into programming tools. Wenyan-lang, from 2019, writes programs in classical Chinese. Hedy, created by Felienne Hermans for teaching, introduces Python-like syntax gradually and offers its keywords in many natural languages. Mainstream languages moved in a smaller step: Python 3 (PEP 3131), Java, Go and others accept non-ASCII letters in identifiers, so names can be in any script even though keywords stay English.  Two patterns stand out. Projects that only translate keywords tend to stay demonstrations, because the library and the error messages are still English. Projects that go further are usually small, single-purpose languages for teaching. Salam's aim is a full general-purpose and systems language, compiled to native code, where the Persian spelling is complete rather than a teaching subset. Choosing Persian keywords A keyword must be short, unambiguous and readable, and it must not take away a word that people need as a name. In Persian these goals pull against each other more than in English. Some of Salam's choices: EnglishPersianLiteral meaningfuncتابعfunction (the mathematical term)retبرگشتreturn, coming backmainریشهrootmutناپایاnot constant, unstablestructساختارstructureenumجداشمارseparately countedmatchهمخوانin agreement, matchingdeferدیرکنdelay itasبرگردانconvert, render asendپایانend The entry function is a good example of a choice with consequences. The obvious translation of main is اصلی. Salam uses ریشه instead, and تابع اصلی is an ordinary function: a program that defines it compiles, but has no entry point. The English course warns about t

t: Right-to-left programming: how Salam handles Unicode, Persian digits and bidirectional text
x: What it takes for a compiler, a standard library and an editor to handle code written right to left: source encoding, Persian digits, separators, strings as bytes and letters, the bidi algorithm and the traps that remain. Right-to-left programming in practice: how Salam handles Persian source, Persian digits, UTF-8 strings as bytes and letters, and mixed-direction bidi text. The language Right-to-left programming means writing source code in a script such as Persian, Arabic or Hebrew, where text runs from the right edge of the line to the left. For a programming language it involves three separate problems: the compiler must read the script correctly (letters, digits, punctuation), the standard library must process text in that script correctly (length, slicing, normalization, direction), and the editor must display a line that mixes right-to-left words with left-to-right symbols in a readable order. Salam, which can be written entirely in Persian, has had to answer all three. This article goes through each layer with runnable programs: how the Salam lexer handles Persian source, how Persian digits work in literals and in output, why a string's length is not its number of letters, and what the bidi, unicode and arabic packages do for programs that handle right-to-left text. It ends with the problems that are not solved. What makes right-to-left code different A Persian line of code is not simply an English line written backwards. A statement such as اگر ک > ۱۰: contains Persian words, a Persian digit sequence, an ASCII operator and an ASCII colon. Unicode stores these characters in the order they were typed (logical order) and leaves the screen order to the Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm, usually called the bidi algorithm. It assigns each character a direction class: Persian letters are strongly right to left, Latin letters strongly left to right, digits weakly directional, and spaces and most punctuation neutral, taking the direction of their surroundings. The compiler only ever sees logical order, so for the compiler right-to-left code is a matter of character sets and rules. The human sees display order, so for the human it is a matter of rendering. Most confusion about "RTL programming" comes from mixing those two views. Source files and identifiers Salam source files are UTF-8. The lexer treats every byte outside ASCII as part of an identifier, so names can be written in Persian, Arabic, or other scripts, and a Persian name may contain spaces or a zero-width non-joiner (ZWNJ, U+200C):  جمع ردیف, with a space, and جمع‌ردیف, with a ZWNJ, are the same name; جمعردیف, glued together, is a different name, and the compiler suggests the spaced one when you mistype it; the Arabic letters ي (U+064A) and ك (U+0643) compare equal to the Persian ی (U+06CC) and ک (U+06A9) in names, so text typed on an Arabic keyboard layout matches; optional vowel marks (harakat, such as the kasra) are ignored in names, so کِتاب and کتاب are one identifier.  The lexer applies these rules as it reads each name: a ZWNJ becomes a space, the Arabic yeh and kaf become the Persian letters, and vowel marks are dropped. It is a small function, but without it a Persian programmer would be fighting their keyboard all day, and because it lives in the lexer, every tool built on the lexer (the formatter, the translator, the language server) follows the same rules. The reasons behind each of these rules are discussed in designing a language for Persian and Arabic. Persian digits and Arabic-Indic digits Persian has its own digits, ۰۱۲۳۴۵۶۷۸۹ (U+06F0 to U+06F9), and Arabic uses a different set, ٠١٢٣٤٥٦٧٨٩ (U+0660 to U+0669). The two sets look alike for most values but are different characters. Salam accepts both in number literals, and both can be mixed with ASCII digits. The rules:  ۱۲۵۰۰, ٤٠٠ and 12500 are all valid integer literals, in Persian and English files alike. The decimal point is always the ASCII .: ۳.۵ is valid. The Persian decimal separator ٫ (U+066B) is not accepted, so ۱٫۵ is a compile error rather than a silently different number. Numbers are always printed with ASCII digits. Converting the output is an explicit call: str.ToPersianDigits (Persian name به رقم فارسی) and str.ToEnglishDigits. The string-to-integer conversion to_int accepts Persian digits, so input typed on a Persian keyboard parses. t: Can programming in your native language change computer science education?
x: English is the hidden prerequisite of most programming courses. This article looks at what removing it can achieve, what the research supports, and how a bilingual language lets a student start in Persian and finish in English. Can programming in your native language help students? What the evidence says, and how Salam's Persian course lets learners start in Persian and move on. The language Programming in your native language means learning and writing code whose keywords, library names and error messages are in the language you think in, rather than in English. It can lower one specific barrier to computer science education, the need to read technical English while also learning to think like a programmer, but it is not a shortcut around the hard part, which is learning to reason precisely about programs. Whether that barrier matters depends on the learner: for a ten-year-old in Tehran or a first-year student who reads English slowly, it can be the difference between following a lesson and copying it. This article looks at the question carefully: what English costs a beginner, what research does and does not tell us, what a native-language language has to provide to be useful in a classroom, and how Salam's design lets a learner start in Persian and move to English later without changing languages. The hidden prerequisite in programming courses Almost every popular programming language uses English keywords, English library names, English documentation and English error messages. For a native English speaker these are mnemonic: while, return and print mean roughly what they say. For a learner who does not read English well, the same words are opaque symbols that must be memorized before they can be understood. The cost shows up in several places at once:  Keywords and names must be memorized as symbols instead of read as words. Error messages, the main feedback a beginner gets, arrive in English at exactly the moment the learner is confused. Documentation and search results are mostly in English. Naming things, one of the main skills of programming, happens in a second language, and beginners often fall back to single letters or transliterations.  None of this is impossible to overcome; millions of programmers worldwide learned in English as a second or third language. The question is how much of a beginner's limited attention it consumes, and who gives up because of it. What the evidence does and does not say It is worth being careful here, because this topic attracts strong opinions. On the general question, there is long-standing support for teaching in a language the learner understands. UNESCO's 1953 report The Use of Vernacular Languages in Education argued for teaching children in their mother tongue, and the organization has promoted mother-tongue based multilingual education ever since. That research is about schooling in general, not programming. On programming specifically, the evidence is thinner but points the same way. Philip Guo's 2018 CHI paper Non-Native English Speakers Learning Computer Programming: Barriers, Desires, and Design Opportunities surveyed learners around the world and documented the extra load English places on them, from reading instructional material and technical vocabulary to understanding code examples. Felienne Hermans's educational language Hedy was built so that its keywords can be used in many natural languages, on the argument that English keywords are an unnecessary obstacle for children. What we are not aware of is a large controlled study showing that native-language keywords alone produce better programmers. Keywords are a small part of a programming language, and the effect of a native-language environment is hard to separate from the effect of better teaching, better materials and better error messages. A fair summary: the language barrier is real for many learners, removing it matters a great deal for some and not at all for others, and translating only the keywords leaves most of the barrier in place. What a native-language programming language must provide If the goal is education, a language with translated keywords is not enough. A teacher needs:  A complete language, not a toy subset, so that students do not hit a wall and have to restart in another language. Error messages in the student's language, because that is where most of the learning happens. A course and reference material in that language, with examples that actually run. Tooling that works: an editor that displays the script correctly, ideally in a browser so nothing needs installing. A path to the global ecosystem, so that a student who starts in their own language is not stranded there.  The last point is the one most projects miss. A language that only exists in Persian traps its students; a language that is the same in Persian and English gives them a bridge. x: salam translate rewrites a Salam program from English to Persian or from Persian to English without touching your own names, comments or strings. Here is what it changes, how it decides, and what to check afterwards. How salam translate converts code between Persian and English: what it rewrites, what it leaves alone, its options, the round trip and its known limits. The language salam translate is the command in the Salam toolchain that converts a source file between the language's two spellings. It rewrites a Salam program from English to Persian (salam translate fa) or from Persian to English (salam translate en): the keywords, the entry function, the primitive types, the built-in methods and functions, and the names of standard library packages and functions, while leaving your own identifiers, comments, strings and formatting exactly as they were. The result is a new file that compiles to the same program. It is not a natural-language translator and it does not guess. Everything it changes comes from a table in the compiler or from the Persian names declared in the standard library, which is why a round trip gives back the original file. This article shows the tool on a real program, lists what it rewrites and what it does not, explains how it works, and is specific about the cases where you still have to look at the output. What salam translate is for Salam is a bilingual language: a Persian file and an English file are read with different word lists but end up as the same tokens, the same syntax tree and the same executable. That makes a converter possible, and useful in several situations:  a teacher writes examples in English and hands students the Persian version, or the reverse; a student who learned in Persian moves a project to English to share it on GitHub; a maintainer who does not read Persian gets a bug report with a Persian program and wants to read the code; documentation authors keep one example and publish it in both languages. t: Designing Salam's syntax: readability, simplicity and power
x: Why Salam code looks the way it does: the decisions behind its blocks, declarations, loops, pattern matching and names, what each one costs, and how they compare with the syntax of Python, Go, Ruby and Lua. Salam syntax explained: colon and end blocks, := and mut, until, repeat and each, match and multi-word names, compared with Python, Go, Ruby and Lua. The language Salam's syntax is designed to be read more than written: blocks open with a colon and close with end, variables are declared with := and are immutable unless marked mut, functions return with ret, and logic is written with the words and, or and not. The aim is code that a beginner can read aloud, that an experienced programmer can scan quickly, and that maps one to one onto a second, Persian spelling, without giving up static types, pattern matching or low-level control. Where it had to choose between brevity and clarity, Salam usually chose clarity, and where it had to choose between flexibility and one obvious way, it usually chose one obvious way. This article goes through the main syntax decisions, shows them in runnable programs, compares them with Python, Go, Ruby and Lua, and is honest about what each decision costs. The principles behind the syntax Four ideas explain most of Salam's syntax:  Blocks should be visible. You should be able to see where a block ends without counting spaces or matching braces. The default should be the safe choice. Values do not change unless you say so; conditions must be real booleans; numbers do not silently mean "true". One obvious way. Where two spellings would do the same thing, Salam often allows only one and makes the other an error with a fix. Two spellings, one grammar. Every construct must read naturally in English and in Persian, since the Persian spelling is a token-for-token mapping of the English one (see one language, two scripts). That rules out syntax that relies on English word order or on symbols that behave badly in right-to-left text.  Blocks: a colon to open, end to close Every block in Salam opens with : and closes with end: functions, conditions, loops, structs, enums, match arms. A short block may sit on one line. SalamCopyfunc sign of(n: int): str:     if n < 0: ret "negative" end     if n == 0: ret "zero" end     ret "positive" end  func main:     each n in [-4, 0, 9]:         println n, sign of(n)     end endOutput-4 negative 0 zero 9 positive This sits between Python and Ruby. Python opens blocks with a colon and closes them by dedenting, which is clean but makes the end of a block invisible and makes copied code fragile. Ruby and Lua close blocks with end but open them in several different ways (do, then, nothing). Salam takes the colon from Python and the end from Ruby and Lua, and uses the same pair everywhere. Indentation is conventional and salam format enforces it, but it carries no meaning, so a block pasted at the wrong depth still parses the same way. Braces are not used for blocks; in Salam { } belong to struct literals (Point { x = 1 }) and empty collection literals. The Persian spelling has the same shape: : and پایان. Declarations: :=, mut and const SalamCopyconst MAX_USERS := 100  func main:     name := "Sara"     mut visits := 0     visits++     visits += 2     ratio := visits as f64 / MAX_USERS     big := 3000000000 as i64     println name, visits, ratio, big endOutputSara 3 0.03 3000000000 := declares and infers the type, as in Go. Unlike Go, the result is immutable: name can never be reassigned, and trying is a compile error, not a warning: TextCopyerror[E013]: cannot reassign immutable variable 'limit'; declare it 'mut' to reassign it, or assign to its elements or fields instead mut opts into change, the same idea as Rust's let mut or Swift's var. A reader can trust that a name without mut keeps its value, which makes long functions much easier to follow. There is no x: int = 5 form for local variables. Salam used to have typed declarations and removed them: when you want a type other than the inferred one, you write as, as in 3000000000 as i64 above. That leaves exactly one way to declare a local. Type annotations remain where they carry information that cannot be inferred: parameters, return types and struct fields. Short keywords for frequent things The words you type most are short: func, ret, mut, pub, end. The words you type less often are spelled out: struct, enum, interface, defer, match. That is the same trade-off Go made with func, and the reason return is ret: in a typical function it appears several times. println and print are statements, not function calls, and they take their arguments without parentheses: println name, visits. The arguments are joined with spaces, which is what a beginner expects from a first program and what a debug line usually wants. Loops: until, repeat and each Salam has three loops and no while or C-style for: SalamCopyfunc main:     mut n := 27     mut steps

t: Why does the world still need new programming languages? Salam's design philosophy and goals
x: Every successful language of the last twenty years was built to fix a specific pain. This article looks at what drove Go, Rust, Swift, Kotlin and Zig, then at the gap Salam targets and the design decisions that follow from it. Why new programming languages keep appearing, what Go, Rust, Swift, Kotlin and Zig each fixed, and the specific gap Salam's design philosophy and goals aim at. The language New programming languages keep appearing because the problems programmers face keep changing: hardware gains more cores, software moves to the network and the browser, security failures become expensive, and the people who program are no longer mostly English-speaking engineers in a few countries. A new language is worth creating when it removes a cost that existing languages cannot remove without breaking their own users, and every widely adopted language of the last two decades started that way: as a fix for one specific pain. Salam is a new language built around two such costs: the friction of using several languages for one product, and the requirement to work in English before you can program at all. This article looks at what drove the best-known recent languages, what each fixed and what each gave up, and then describes Salam's design philosophy and the gap it aims at, with an honest account of what it costs. Why existing languages cannot simply absorb new ideas A mature language has millions of lines of code depending on its current behavior. It can add features, but it can rarely take any away or change a default. C cannot become memory-safe by default without breaking C programs. Java cannot drop its virtual machine. Python cannot make its variables immutable or its types mandatory. English keywords cannot be made optional in a language whose entire ecosystem, documentation and community assume them. That is why the big shifts have come through new languages rather than through new versions of old ones. A new language gets one chance to choose its defaults, and the defaults are most of what a language is. What recent languages were created to fix Five languages from the last twenty years illustrate the pattern, each with a clear origin: LanguageOriginThe pain it targetedWhat it gave upGoGoogle, begun 2007, public in 2009, 1.0 in 2012Slow C++ builds, complex large codebases, concurrency on multicore serversExpressiveness: no generics until 1.18 (2022), a garbage collectorRustStarted by Graydon Hoare, sponsored by Mozilla, 1.0 in 2015Memory-safety bugs in C and C++ systems codeSimplicity: the ownership and borrowing model takes real effort to learnSwiftApple, 2014Objective-C's age and unsafety for Apple platformsPortability, at first: its ecosystem is still centered on AppleKotlinJetBrains, 1.0 in 2016, Google's preferred Android language from 2019Java's verbosity and null-pointer errors, without leaving the JVMIndependence from the JVM's model for most usesZigAndrew Kelley, 2016C's hidden control flow, preprocessor and cross-compilation painA stable language: it has changed significantly between releases The common thread is not novelty for its own sake. Each language picked a cost its users paid every day and designed around removing it, accepting a new cost in return. Go traded expressiveness for simplicity and fast builds. Rust traded ease of learning for safety without a garbage collector. Kotlin traded a clean start for full compatibility with Java code. The costs Salam targets Salam's design reflects two costs that the languages above do not address. The first is fragmentation. A typical web product today is written in several languages: a systems language or Go for the backend, TypeScript for the browser, HTML and CSS for the page, SQL for the database, a shell or YAML for the build. Each comes with its own toolchain, type system and package manager. Salam's answer is one language that reaches from bare-metal code to the web page: it compiles to native code for servers and command-line tools, it has a built-in page language that generates HTML, CSS and JavaScript, it can compile to WebAssembly and JavaScript, and its standard library includes HTTP, database drivers and a checker for SQL strings. The second is the English prerequisite. Every mainstream language assumes its users read English: keywords, library names, error messages, documentation. Salam makes English optional. Every keyword, type, standard library package and compiler message has a Persian spelling, and both spellings are the same language, so a learner can start in Persian and move to English without changing languages. The article one language, two scripts explains the mechanism. The project's readme states the broader aim: to balance low-level control with developer productivity and to lower the cognitive barrier to entry. The rest of the design follows from these goals. t: From source code to executable: how the Salam compiler works, stage by stage
x: Follow a Salam program through the compiler: tokens, syntax tree, type checking and static checks, generated C or LLVM IR or machine code, and the final link, with real output from each stage. How a compiler works, shown on a real one: Salam's lexer, parser, AST, semantic checks, error codes, C, LLVM and native code generation, and linking. Compiler and performance A compiler is a program that reads source code, checks that it means something, and translates it into a form a machine can run. The Salam compiler does this in five broad stages: it lexes the text into tokens, parses the tokens into a syntax tree, analyzes the tree for types and mistakes, generates code through one of three backends (C, LLVM or its own native code generator for x86-64, ARM and RISC-V), and links the result into an executable. This article follows a real program through each stage of the Salam compiler, with the actual output of every step. Everything here can be reproduced with the salam command. Where the article says "the compiler does X", the file that does it is named, so you can read the source on GitHub. The compiler pipeline at a glance A compiler pipeline is a chain of stages, each of which turns one representation of the program into the next. Salam's compiler is written in Salam itself (see the self-hosting article), and its source sits in compiler/, one directory per stage. The entry point, compiler/main.salam, is short: it reads the command-line arguments and hands them to cli.Run. Everything else hangs off that call. StageInputOutputDirectorySize (lines)Lexersource texttokenscompiler/lexer/about 2,800Parsertokenssyntax tree (AST)compiler/parser/about 5,100Semantic analysisASTtyped, checked ASTcompiler/semantic/about 40,700C backendchecked ASTC sourcecompiler/codegen/about 8,900LLVM backendchecked ASTLLVM IRcompiler/llvmgen/about 11,900Native backendLLVM IR textmachine codecompiler/nativegen/about 52,600Built-in linkerobject filesexecutablecompiler/nativelink/about 12,600Drivercommand linethe whole runcompiler/driver/about 9,500 The numbers say something about where the work is. Lexing and parsing are the small, well-understood part. The semantic analysis is eight times bigger than the parser, because that is where a strict language earns its strictness. The native backend is the largest piece of all, since it contains a full optimizer and writes machine code for five processor families. Counting the interpreter, the JavaScript backend, the formatter, the language server and the page language, the compiler is about 340 source files and close to 200,000 lines. We will follow this program through the pipeline: SalamCopyfunc square(n: int): int:     ret n * n end  func main:     println square(7) endOutput49 Stage 1: reading the source and lexing Before the lexer runs, the driver (compiler/driver/driver_front.salam) loads the file and decides which language pack it is written in. Salam source can be English or Persian, and the compiler detects which one from the keywords it finds, unless the file says so in a header comment. The pack decides which words are keywords: func in one file, تابع in another. After this point both languages produce the same tokens, which is why the rest of the compiler never has to care which one you wrote. The article One language, two scripts covers the Persian side in depth. The driver also builds the table of conditional-compilation flags for the target: SALAM_OS_LINUX, SALAM_OS_WINDOWS, SALAM_ARCH_ARM64 and so on, plus anything you pass with -D. That table is used right after parsing. The lexer (compiler/lexer/) then walks the text once and cuts it into tokens: keywords, identifiers, literals, operators and statement ends. Numbers, strings (including Salam's raw backtick strings and multi-line text blocks), escapes and identifiers each have their own file in that directory. You can see the token stream for any file with salam inspect: TerminalCopysalam inspect app.salam --emit-tokens For a three-line main that declares x := 1 + 2 and prints x, the stream is fifteen tokens, here with only their types: TextCopyKEYWORD_FUNC IDENTIFIER COLON IDENTIFIER COLON_ASSIGN INT_LITERAL PLUS INT_LITERAL STMT_END KEYWORD_PRINTLN IDENTIFIER STMT_END KEYWORD_END STMT_END EOF Each token in the XML also records its line and column, which is how every later error message can point at the exact character. Stage 2: parsing into a syntax tree A parser turns the flat list of tokens into a tree that shows how the program is nested: this call is an argument of that println, this block belongs to that function. Salam's parser (compiler/parser/) is a hand-written recursive descent parser.
