t: When a language builds itself: inside Salam's self-hosting compiler
x: The Salam compiler is written in Salam. This is the story of how it got there, how a release is bootstrapped from the previous one, what self-hosting buys a young language and what it costs. What a self-hosting compiler is, how bootstrapping a compiler works, and how Salam replaced its C implementation in 2026 and now builds itself. Compiler and performance A self-hosting compiler is a compiler written in the language it compiles. The Salam compiler is one: its source is about 340 files of Salam in the compiler/ directory, and every release since August 2026 was compiled by an earlier salam binary. Getting there required bootstrapping a compiler: an older implementation, written in C, compiled the first Salam version of the compiler, and that C implementation was deleted from the repository on 20 August 2026. This article explains how bootstrapping works in general, how Salam did it, how a release is built today, and why a young language would take on the trouble. What "self-hosting" means A language is self-hosting when its own compiler (or interpreter) is written in that language and can compile itself. C compilers such as GCC and Clang are written in C and C++. The Go compiler was rewritten from C to Go for Go 1.5 in 2015. Rust's first compiler was written in OCaml and was replaced by a compiler in Rust in 2011. Zig spent several years replacing its C++ compiler with one written in Zig. Being self-hosting is a milestone, not a requirement: plenty of good languages, Python's reference implementation among them, are implemented in another language. For a compiled systems language, though, it is a strong statement. A compiler uses nearly every feature a language has: structs and enums for the syntax tree, hash maps for symbol tables, strings and Unicode for source text, files and processes for the build, careful memory handling everywhere, and a lot of code. If the language cannot carry its own compiler, it is probably not ready for other large programs either. The chicken-and-egg problem of bootstrapping There is an obvious puzzle. To compile a compiler written in Salam, you need a Salam compiler. Where does the first one come from? The general answer, called bootstrapping, has three steps:  Write a first compiler in an existing language. The one that bootstrapped today's Salam compiler was written in C. Write a second compiler, for the same language, in the new language itself. Compile it with the first one. You now have a working compiler that was produced from Salam source. Use that compiler to compile its own source again. From here on, the old implementation is no longer needed, because each new version can be compiled by the previous one.  The compiler that starts a build is called the seed. After step 3, the seed for every build is simply an earlier release. The cost is that you can no longer build the compiler from source alone: you always need some working binary of the language first. Salam's build script says this plainly when there is no seed on the machine: TextCopyerror: no seed compiler on PATH.   The compiler is written in Salam, so building it needs a Salam.   Install a released one:  sh install.sh Salam's path from C to Salam The repository's history goes back to June 2018 and includes several earlier implementations. Until the summer of 2026 the compiler was a C program, in its last form under c/src/: lexer, parser, semantic analysis, a C code generator, an LLVM backend, an interpreter, a JavaScript backend and the tooling around them. The port to Salam happened over the summer of 2026, and git log dates the milestones: DateMilestone27 July 2026The compiler written in Salam is added to the repository (PR #1461)1 August 2026A release cut with both the C and the Salam compilers in the tree ("First self-host with C version")20 August 2026The C implementation is removed: 220 C files, about 62,900 lines (PR #1546)22 October 2026Compile-time use-after-free and double-free checks land in the self-hosted compiler (PR #2282)25 October 2026The native backend and built-in linker, written in Salam, are merged (PR #2363)3 November 2026Compile-time range, overflow and division checks (PR #2604) At the moment of the switch, the Salam version of the compiler was 164 files and about 64,900 lines, roughly the same size as the C program it replaced. Since then it has tripled, to close to 200,000 lines, and the largest additions (the native code generator, the linker, the ownership and range analyses) were written in Salam from the start. They never existed in C. The Salam compiler mirrors the structure of the C one: the same pipeline of source, lexer, tokens, parser, AST, semantic analysis and code generation. The porting guide in the repository describes the method: port module by module in dependency order, keep the C build runnable, and check each stage against it. The deleted C sources are still in Git history, where they remain useful as a design reference. How the port was checked A rewrite of a comp

t: Three ways to generate code: Salam's C, LLVM and native backends compared
x: Salam can turn the same checked program into C, into LLVM IR or straight into machine code. A look inside each backend, real output from all three, and a practical guide to choosing. How Salam's C backend, LLVM backend and native x86-64 and ARM backend with a built-in linker work, what each costs, and when to choose which one. Compiler and performance A compiler backend is the part of a compiler that turns a checked program into something a machine can run. Salam has three backends for native executables: a C backend that writes C and hands it to a C compiler, an LLVM backend that writes LLVM IR and lets LLVM optimize it, and a native backend that writes x86-64, ARM and RISC-V machine code itself and links it with a linker built into the compiler. All three sit behind the same frontend, so a program means the same thing whichever one you pick. This article shows what each produces, why each exists, and when to use which. What a compiler backend does The frontend of a compiler (lexer, parser, semantic analysis) answers "is this program valid, and what does it mean?" The backend answers "what instructions should the processor run?" That second question has three hard parts: lowering high-level constructs (a match on an enum, a string concatenation, a generic call) into simple operations, optimizing those operations, and emitting them in a format the operating system can load, which also means following each platform's calling conventions and object file format. Every language project has to decide how much of that to build itself. Some reuse a whole existing compiler by generating C. Many reuse LLVM. A few write everything. Salam does all three, and the compiler pipeline article shows where they plug in. Here is the program we will push through each one: SalamCopyfunc sum squares(n: int): int:     mut total := 0     repeat 1 to n in i:         total += i * i     end     ret total end  func main:     println sum squares(10) endOutput385 Which backend runs by default You choose with --backend=c, --backend=llvm or --backend=native. Without the option, the driver (use_llvm_backend in compiler/driver/driver_proc.salam) picks: SituationDefault backendThe salam binary has LLVM built-in (the main release builds for Linux, macOS and Windows)LLVMThe salam binary has no LLVM (a compiler built from source without it, or the static musl release)CWindows on Arm, where neither LLVM nor tcc shipsNative--cc=PATH givenC, since naming a C compiler can only mean that If the LLVM backend meets a construct it cannot lower, the build does not fail: the driver prints salam: falling back to the C backend for this file (build with --backend=llvm to make this an error) and builds through C instead. Passing --backend=llvm explicitly turns that safety net into a hard error, which is what you want in CI. The C backend: C as a compilation target Using C as a compilation target means the compiler writes C source code and lets an existing C compiler produce the machine code. It is one of the oldest tricks in language implementation, and it is still a good one: C compilers exist for nearly every platform, they optimize well, and the generated code is something a human can read. Salam's C backend lives in compiler/codegen/. Every source file and every standard library module it uses becomes a .c and .h pair in a .salam-build/ directory. You can keep and read them with --emit-c: CCopystatic int32_t _Salam_main_square_i32(int32_t n) {     (void)n;     return ((int32_t)((uint32_t)(n) * (uint32_t)(n))); } That is a one-line square function after code generation. The name is mangled with the package and parameter types, and the multiplication runs in unsigned arithmetic so that overflow wraps the same way on every C compiler, instead of being undefined behavior as signed overflow is in C. The driver then finds a C compiler: one bundled next to salam if the download includes one (the Windows release bundles tcc), otherwise clang, gcc or tcc from PATH. It compiles the modules in parallel, one worker per CPU core, caches the object files so that the next build only recompiles what changed, and links. Before a release, CI builds four groups of test programs through tcc, gcc and clang in a strict mode and fails if the generated C is not clean under any of them. What the C backend is good for:  Portability and transparency. If a platform has a C compiler, the code can probably run there, and you can read exactly what was generated. Your C tools. --cc= picks a specific C compiler, and --asan (AddressSanitizer) works when that compiler is gcc or clang. Features that live only here. --protect, which encrypts string literals in the binary, is implemented in the C backend.  What it costs: you need a C compiler on the machine, and output quality depends on it. tcc compiles very quickly but has no optimizer; gcc and clang optimize but take longer. t: Static typing in Salam: catching bugs before the program runs
x: Salam checks every type before it generates any code, infers most of them for you, and goes further than types: exhaustive matches, optional values, checked errors and compile-time range checks, with the real compiler messages. How static typing works in Salam: type inference, strict conversions, generics, enums with data, exhaustive match, optionals and compile-time range checks. Compiler and performance Static typing means every value's type is known and checked when the program is compiled, not discovered while it runs. Salam is a statically typed language: each variable, parameter, field and expression has one type, the compiler checks every use against it, and a program with a type error does not build. You rarely have to write the types of local variables, because the compiler infers them from their initial values, but you always write the types of function parameters and results. This article goes through what Salam checks, with the exact messages the compiler prints, and where its checks stop. What a statically typed language buys you In a dynamically typed language such as Python or JavaScript, price * quantity is checked when that line runs: if quantity happens to be a string that day, you find out in production. In a statically typed language such as Go, Rust, Java or Salam, the same mistake is a compile error, found on your machine before the program ever starts. The trade-offs are well known. Static types catch a whole class of bugs early, make code easier to navigate (an editor can tell you exactly what user.address is), and let the compiler generate faster code because it does not have to check types at runtime. They cost some flexibility and, in older languages, a lot of typing. Modern statically typed languages, Salam included, recover most of that convenience with type inference. Salam also uses the type checker as the foundation for more checks than types alone. Before generating any code, the compiler's semantic analysis (described in the compiler pipeline article) checks types, mutability, exhaustiveness, definite initialization, unused code, value ranges and memory ownership. Type inference for local variables Type inference is the compiler working out a type from the code instead of you writing it. In Salam, := declares a variable and its type comes from the value: SalamCopyfunc average(values: f64[]): f64:     mut sum := 0.0     each v in values:         sum += v     end     ret sum / len(values) as f64 end  func main:     count := 3     ratio := 0.75     big := 5000000000 as i64     name := "Salam"     ok := count > 2     println count, ratio, big, name, ok     println average([2.0, 4.0, 9.0]) endOutput3 0.75 5000000000 Salam true 5 salam inspect --emit-ast shows what the compiler inferred: count is i32, ratio is f64, big is i64, name is str, ok is bool, and inside average the loop variable v is f64. A few rules are worth knowing:  An integer literal is an int, which is a 32-bit i32 in Salam (not 64-bit as in Go on most platforms). Use as i64 when a value needs more room. A literal with a decimal point is an f64. as is the one way to state a type for a local: big := 5000000000 as i64, v := Vector {} as Vector<str>. Function parameters and return types are always written out. Inference is local, so a function's signature is its documentation and its contract.  Writing a type annotation on a local, as in many other languages, is not allowed: TextCopyerror: declarations with a type annotation were removed; use 'name := value' (or 'name := value as Type') (near '=') That syntax (x: int = 5) existed in earlier versions and was removed during 2026, one of the changes that come with a pre-1.0 language. The types lesson and the variables lesson cover the basics. Strict conversions: no silent narrowing Salam converts a value implicitly only when nothing can be lost. An int used in arithmetic with an f64 is widened, so 3.5 + 2 is 5.5. Anything that could lose information needs an explicit as: SalamCopyfunc half(n: i32): i32:     ret n / 2 end  func main:     big := 3000000000 as i64     println half(big) end TextCopyerror[E012]: argument 1: cannot pass 'i64' to 'i32'  --> n3.salam:7:13   | 7 |     println half(big)   |             ^   | Conditions must be real booleans. C and JavaScript let an integer stand for true or false; Salam does not: TextCopyerror[E021]: if condition must be bool, got 'i32'  --> n4.salam:3:8   | 3 |     if ok:   |        ^   | Strictness extends to things that are not type errors in most languages. An unused variable, parameter, import or function is an error. A branch that can never run is an error. A cast that changes nothing ([1, 2, 3] as int[3]) is an error, E093. Reassigning a variable that was not declared mut is an error, E013. The rules lesson lists them; the idea is that code you can read is code where nothing is accidental. t: Native compilation without a virtual machine or garbage collector: benefits, costs and performance
x: Salam programs run as plain machine code with no virtual machine and no garbage collector. What that buys you, what it costs you, how memory is handled instead, and what the benchmarks do and do not show. What native AOT compilation with no garbage collector means: faster start-up, smaller memory, predictable latency, the real costs and Salam's measured speed. Compiler and performance Native compilation means translating a program into the processor's own machine code before it runs, so that the operating system can execute it directly, with no virtual machine or interpreter in between. Salam compiles this way, ahead of time, and it also runs without a garbage collector: memory that a program allocates is given back at points the program (or the compiler, on its behalf) decides, not when a collector gets around to it. This combination is what C, C++, Rust and Zig offer, and it is different from Java, C#, Python, JavaScript and Go. This article explains what you gain from it, what you give up, and how Salam's measured performance should be read. Native, AOT, JIT and VM: the terms A few terms get mixed up, so here they are side by side: TermMeaningExamplesInterpreterReads the program (or its bytecode) and performs it step by stepCPython, PHP, salam execVirtual machine (VM)A runtime that executes a portable bytecode, usually with a JIT and a GCJVM, .NET CLRJIT compilationCompiles bytecode to machine code while the program runs, using what it observesHotSpot, V8, RyuJITAOT (ahead-of-time) compilationCompiles to machine code before the program runsC, C++, Rust, Go, Zig, SalamGarbage collector (GC)Finds memory the program can no longer reach and frees it automaticallyJava, C#, Go, JavaScript, Python The two axes are independent. Go compiles ahead of time to native code but has a garbage collector and a runtime with its own goroutine scheduler. Java and C# now have AOT options (GraalVM Native Image, .NET Native AOT) that keep the garbage collector. Swift compiles natively and uses reference counting rather than a tracing collector. Salam sits with C, C++, Rust and Zig: native code, ahead of time, no collector. What virtual machines and garbage collectors are good for It would be wrong to present VMs and garbage collectors as mistakes. They solve real problems:  A garbage collector removes whole classes of bugs. Use after free and double free cannot happen in safe Java, C# or Go code, and memory leaks are limited to data that is still reachable. It makes code simpler to write. Nobody has to decide who owns a string or when a list is freed. A JIT can optimize for what actually happens. It sees which branches are hot and which types appear at a call site, and it can specialize code for them. A VM gives portability and tooling. One bytecode file runs on any machine with the runtime, with rich profilers, debuggers and reflection.  The costs are just as real:  Memory headroom. A tracing collector works best with free space to spare, so a garbage-collected program usually holds noticeably more memory than the data it is using. Pauses and background work. Modern collectors keep pauses short and do most of their work concurrently, but the work still takes CPU time and makes latency harder to predict at the tail. Start-up and warm-up. A VM has to start, load classes and, with a JIT, run slowly until hot code is compiled. That matters for command-line tools, serverless functions and anything that runs for milliseconds. A runtime to ship. The program needs the VM installed, or bundled, which makes deployments larger.  How Salam produces a native program salam build checks the program and then generates machine code through one of three backends: C (handed to a C compiler), LLVM, or Salam's own native code generator with a built-in linker. The article Three ways to generate code compares them. The result is an ordinary executable: ELF on Linux, PE on Windows, Mach-O on macOS. What is inside it? The program's own code, the parts of the standard library it uses, and the C library (glibc or musl on Linux). The start-up work before main is small: the program records its arguments, sets up signal handling for its output buffer, and initializes the standard library modules it imports. There is no bytecode loader, no JIT, no collector thread and no task scheduler. The size shows it: a hello-world built with the native backend is 11,488 bytes on x86-64 Linux, or 24,944 bytes as a fully static executable against musl that runs on any x86-64 Linux with nothing installed. Programs that call C pay nothing extra either. A Salam extern function is a direct call into the C function, with no marshaling layer between a managed heap and native memory. The C interop lesson and the article on calling C from Salam show how. Memory without a garbage collector If nothing collects garbage, something else has to free memory. In Salam it works like this:  Plain values live on the stack. Numbers, booleans, structs and fixed-size arrays are values: they

t: Memory management in Salam: stack values, heap collections, defer and the ownership checker
x: A practical guide to memory in Salam: what is copied, what is shared, who frees what, how defer and compiler-inserted drops help, what the ownership checker catches at compile time and how memcheck finds the rest. Memory management in Salam with no garbage collector: copies and heap collections, defer, automatic drops, the ownership checker and memcheck for leaks. Compiler and performance Memory management is how a program obtains memory for its data and gives it back when the data is no longer needed. Salam has no garbage collector, so this is partly the programmer's job, but it is a much smaller job than in C. Plain values live on the stack and need no care at all. Heap collections such as Vector and HashMap are freed with .Free(), usually through defer, and the compiler inserts that call itself for local collections that never leave their scope. On top of that, an ownership checker finds use-after-free and double-free mistakes at compile time, and salam memcheck finds leaks at runtime. This article walks through each piece with programs and the compiler's real output. The model in one paragraph Numbers, booleans, characters, structs and fixed-size arrays are values: assigning one copies it, passing one to a function copies it (unless the parameter is a reference), and it vanishes when its scope ends. Vector, HashMap, Set and the other collections, dyn boxes, strings built at runtime and blocks from mem.Allocate live on the heap: the variable holds a small header that points at heap storage, and that storage stays until someone frees it. The rule for the heap is "whoever creates it frees it, or hands it to someone who will". Everything else in this article is tooling around that rule. The memory lesson teaches the same model step by step. Stack values: structs and arrays are copied Because structs are values, changing a copy never changes the original. When a function must change the caller's variable, the parameter is declared as a reference with &:. For a collection, copy() makes an independent Vector with its own storage, which then needs its own free(): SalamCopystruct Point:     pub x: int     pub y: int end  func move right(p &: Point, steps: int):     p.x += steps end  func main:     a := Point { x = 1, y = 2 }     mut b := a     b.x = 10     println a.x, b.x      mut c := a     move right(c, 5)     println c.x      mut cart := Vector {} as Vector<str>     defer cart.Free()     cart.Push("bread")     mut basket := cart.Copy()     defer basket.Free()     basket.Push("milk")     println cart.len(), basket.len() endOutput1 10 6 1 2 Without copy(), basket := cart would copy only the header. Both names would point at the same items, and a push through one of them could move the storage out from under the other. That shared state is the source of most memory bugs in languages without a collector, and it is exactly what the ownership checker watches for (more below). deep_copy() goes one step further and also copies containers held inside a container. defer: cleanup that runs on every exit defer schedules a statement to run when the current block ends, however it ends: falling off the end, ret, break or continue. Several defers run in reverse order, last registered first. Go has a function-scoped defer and Zig a block-scoped one; Salam's is block-scoped like Zig's, so a defer inside a loop body runs at the end of each iteration. SalamCopyimport mem  func free words(words: Vector<str>):     each w in words:         mem.Free(w as void*)     end     words.Free() end  func count words(lines: str[]): int:     mut total := 0     each line in lines:         words := line.Split(" ")         defer free words(words)         total += words.len()     end     ret total end  func main:     defer println "main: last"     defer println "main: second to last"     println "words:", count words(["peace be with you", "salam"]) endOutputwords: 5 main: second to last main: last Writing defer x.Free() on the line right after x is created is the most important habit in Salam. Cleanup sits next to the allocation, where a reviewer can see it, and an early ret added later cannot skip it. The defer lesson has more examples. Notice free words. line.Split(" ") returns a Vector<str> whose strings are themselves heap allocations, and free() on a Vector frees its own storage, not what the elements own. So the helper frees each string first, then the vector. That detail is easy to miss, which is why the next tools exist. Finding leaks with salam memcheck salam memcheck app.salam builds the program with debug information and runs it under Valgrind when it is installed, or with AddressSanitizer otherwise, and reports leaks and invalid accesses with Salam filenames and line numbers. Here is its report for an earlier version of count words, saved as d1.salam, that used a plain defer words.Free() and so never freed the word strin

t: Interpreted or compiled? salam run, salam exec and salam build explained
x: Salam is a compiled language that also ships an interpreter and a REPL. What each of check, run, build and exec actually does, how they differ, and a simple guide to picking the right one. The difference between salam check, salam run, salam build and salam exec, how Salam's interpreter and REPL work, and which command to use for each job. Compiler and performance Salam is a compiled language: salam build turns a program into a native executable, and that executable is what you deploy. The toolchain also gives you three other ways to work with the same code. salam check stops before generating any code and only reports errors. salam run compiles to a temporary executable, runs it and throws it away. salam exec runs the program in an interpreter built into the compiler, with no C compiler, LLVM or linker involved. There is also a REPL, salam cli, for trying things a line at a time. All of them read the same source and apply the same checks. This article explains what each command does underneath and when to use it. The four commands at a glance CommandWhat it doesProducesTypical usesalam check app.salamLex, parse and fully analyze, imports includedDiagnostics onlyAfter every editsalam run app.salamCheck, compile, run, delete the executableProgram outputTrying a program, scripts, examplessalam build app.salamCheck, compile, linkAn executable you keepReleases, benchmarks, deploymentsalam exec app.salamCheck, then run in the interpreterProgram outputMachines without a toolchain, quick logic checks The REPL (salam cli) is a fifth way in, covered below. One program can go through all of them unchanged. Here is a prime sieve that we will use throughout: SalamCopyfunc count primes(limit: int): int:     mut composite := Vector {} as Vector<bool>     defer composite.Free()     repeat limit + 1:         composite.Push(false)     end     mut count := 0     repeat 2 to limit in n:         if composite.Get(n):             continue         end         count++         mut multiple := n * 2         until multiple <= limit:             composite.Set(multiple, true)             multiple += n         end     end     ret count end  func main:     each limit in [100, 10000, 1000000]:         println "primes up to", limit, "=", count primes(limit)     end endOutputprimes up to 100 = 25 primes up to 10000 = 1229 primes up to 1000000 = 78498 salam run, salam exec, and the executable from salam build, with any of the three backends, all print exactly these three lines. salam check: find the errors without building anything salam check runs everything salam build does before code generation: lexing, parsing, type checking, the range and ownership analyses, and the same for every imported package. It prints the diagnostics and exits with status 1 if there are any errors, or prints app.salam: no errors. It never invokes a C compiler or LLVM, so it is the fastest feedback you can get, and it works on a single file or a whole directory: TerminalCopysalam check app.salam salam check src/ salam check app.salam --error-format=json What it cannot see is anything that only happens later: a problem in the generated C, a missing system library at link time. For those you need a real build. The compiler pipeline article shows where check stops, and the static typing article shows what it catches. salam run: compile, run, discard salam run app.salam does a full build into a temporary location, runs the result, passes its exit status back to you and deletes the executable. It is what you use while developing a program, for one-off scripts and for examples. Arguments for the program go after --: TerminalCopysalam run tool.salam -- input.txt --verbose Because it is a real compiled build, run takes the same options as build: --backend=native, --release, --asan and so on. Inside a project directory, salam run with no file finds the entry point (main.salam) by itself. A program's exit status is whatever main returns: ret 3 in main makes salam run exit with 3, which is how a Salam script reports failure to a shell or a CI job. The cost of run is the compile step on every invocation. The C backend caches the object files of unchanged modules between builds, which makes repeated runs of the same program cheaper, but each run still compiles and links. salam build: an executable you keep salam build app.salam produces an executable named after the file (app, or app.exe for Windows targets), or the name given with --output=FILE. With no input it builds the project in the current directory. If nothing has changed since the last build, it prints up to date and does nothing. The options that matter most:  Development and release builds. By default a build keeps the safety checks: array and Vector indices are checked at runtime, and signed arithmetic is guaranteed to wrap. --release removes the bounds checks, lets the optimizer assume signed arithmetic never overflows and raises LLVM's optimization from -O2 to -O3. Test with the defa

t: Cross-compilation in Salam: building for Linux, macOS, Windows and ARM from one machine
x: The --target flag, the three code generators behind it, the sysroots and linker built into the compiler, and an honest list of which targets are run in CI and which are only built. Cross-compile Salam programs for Windows, macOS, Linux, ARM and 32-bit x86 from one machine: the --target flag, the backends behind it and what needs a sysroot. Compiler and performance Cross-compilation means building an executable on one kind of machine that runs on another: a Windows .exe built on Linux, an ARM binary built on an x86-64 laptop, a macOS program built-in a Linux CI job. In Salam you ask for it with one flag, --target, followed by a target triple such as x86_64-w64-windows-gnu or aarch64-linux-musl. The compiler picks a code generator, finds a C runtime for that target, links the result and hands you a file for the other machine. This article explains what happens behind that flag, which targets work out of the box, which need extra files, how to write code that compiles cleanly for every platform, and where the project's own testing stops. What cross-compilation is, and why it matters A compiler that only builds for the machine it runs on forces you to own every platform you ship to, or to rent CI runners for each one. A cross-compiler removes that constraint. You keep one development machine and one build job, and you produce the Windows, macOS and Linux artifacts from it. Three things have to be right for this to work:  Code generation for the target CPU: x86-64, 32-bit x86, AArch64, 32-bit ARM, RISC-V or WebAssembly. A C runtime and system libraries for the target operating system, often called a sysroot: musl or glibc on Linux, the mingw-w64 runtime on Windows, libSystem on macOS. A linker that understands the target's object and executable formats: ELF, PE/COFF or Mach-O.  Go is well known for making this easy with GOOS and GOARCH, and Zig ships C runtimes for many targets inside its toolchain. Rust can target most platforms but usually needs rustup target add plus a linker and sysroot for the other platform. Salam sits closer to the Go and Zig end: the release build of the compiler carries its own linker and the most common sysroots. (The comparisons with Go and Zig cover the rest of those languages.) The --target flag and target triples A target triple names the CPU, the vendor or OS family, and the ABI. These are the ones you will use most often with Salam: TripleProducesx86_64-linux-muslstatic 64-bit Linux executableaarch64-linux-muslstatic 64-bit ARM Linux executable (Raspberry Pi 4 and 5, ARM servers)arm-linux-musleabihfstatic 32-bit ARM Linux executable (ARMv7, hard float)i686-linux-muslstatic 32-bit x86 Linux executablex86_64-w64-windows-gnu64-bit Windows .exei686-w64-windows-gnu32-bit Windows .exeaarch64-w64-windows-gnuWindows on Arm .exearm64-apple-macos, x86_64-apple-macosmacOS executable for Apple silicon or Inteluniversal-apple-macosone macOS file holding both architectureswasm32-wasiWebAssembly module for a WASI runtime (see Salam and WebAssembly) The command is the same for all of them: TerminalCopysalam build app.salam --target=x86_64-w64-windows-gnu salam build app.salam --target=aarch64-linux-musl --output=app-arm64 When the target is Windows, the default output name gets .exe added. Triples for bare-metal targets (x86_64-unknown-none, i686-unknown-none, aarch64-unknown-none) build freestanding programs with no operating system; those have their own article, freestanding Salam. Which code generator does the work Salam has three backends, and the article on code generation covers them in depth. For cross-compilation they behave differently:  LLVM (--backend=llvm, and the path --target takes by default for most triples) handles any triple LLVM knows. It is pointer-width aware: for a 32-bit triple every size_t position in the generated IR becomes 32 bits, as described in docs/PLATFORMS.md. The release builds for Linux x86-64, macOS and 64-bit Windows embed LLVM and the LLD linker and run them in-process. A compiler built from source without the embedded LLVM falls back to clang, llc and lld on your PATH. Native (--backend=native) is Salam's own machine-code generator. According to docs/NATIVE_BACKEND.md it writes x86-64, 32-bit x86, AArch64, 32-bit ARM (ARMv7-A with VFPv3-D16) and RISC-V 64 code, as ELF, COFF or Mach-O objects, and refuses any other target with a pointer to --backend=llvm. It needs neither LLVM nor a C compiler. C (--backend=c) emits portable C and lets a C compiler resolve every width. It is the path docs/PLATFORMS.md recommends for production 32-bit builds, and --emit-c gives you the generated C to compile with any cross C compiler you like. The browser build of the compiler itself is made this way: it is emitted as C for wasm32-unknown-emscripten and compiled with Emscripten.  Older lines in docs/PLATFORMS.md and in salam --help still describe the native backend as x86-64 only. docs/NATIVE_BACKEND.md and docs/NATIVE_LINKER.md are the current references: the backend has sin

t: From native to WebAssembly and JavaScript: everywhere a Salam program can run
x: One source file, several destinations: native executables, WASI modules, browser JavaScript, web pages, edge workers, an in-browser editor, phone apps and bare metal, with the trade-offs of each. Compile Salam to WebAssembly with WASI, to browser JavaScript and to Cloudflare Workers: the commands, what each target supports and the limits to know first. Compiler and performance Salam programs can run as native executables, as WebAssembly modules, as JavaScript in a web browser, as request handlers on Cloudflare Workers, inside an online editor and on bare metal. To compile Salam to WebAssembly you build with --target=wasm32-wasi; to compile Salam to JavaScript you use salam js. The language and the standard library stay the same, but each destination has its own rules about threads, files, sockets and numbers, and those rules decide which target fits a job. This article walks through every target that exists today, shows the commands, and lists what each one cannot do yet. Salam's benchmark puts it in the same range as C and Rust, not ahead of them: how the programs were timed, what the averages hide, where Salam loses, and how to rerun it. Compiler and performance No, the benchmark does not show that Salam is faster than C or Rust in any general sense. It shows that on 39 small programs that use the same algorithm in every language, Salam's optimized build finished in the same range as C and Rust: an average of 10.6 ms for Salam, 11.7 ms for C and 11.3 ms for Rust. Salam was ahead of the fastest of C, C++, Rust and Go on 6 programs, level on 27 and behind on 6. Those gaps are small, the programs are short, and part of every number is process start-up rather than generated code. That is still a meaningful result for a young language: it places Salam with the compiled languages and far from the interpreted ones, as you would expect from native compilation without a virtual machine or garbage collector. This article explains how the numbers were produced, where they mislead, and how to check them yourself. The short answer ClaimSupported by the benchmark?Salam compiles to code in the same performance range as C, C++, Rust and GoYes, on this suiteSalam is much faster than Python and PHPYes: about 56 times faster than Python and 9.6 times faster than PHP on this suiteSalam is faster than C or RustNo. The average gap is within what start-up time and run-to-run noise can explainSalam is fast for large applications, memory-heavy work or long buildsNot measured If you remember one sentence, make it the one the speed page itself uses: between compiled languages, read the results as the same range, not as a ranking. What the benchmark measures The suite lives in the repository under benchmark/. It has 42 programs, each written in C, C++, Rust, Go, Python, PHP and Salam. The rules are simple and worth stating:  Same algorithm everywhere. Each language implements the same steps, written the way that language is normally written. The suite does not let one language use a cleverer algorithm. Same output everywhere. Every program prints a deterministic result, and every version's output is checked against C's before any timing happens. A fast wrong answer does not count. Mostly small CPU-bound programs. Recursive and iterative Fibonacci, prime counting, sorting, dynamic programming, string work, matrix multiplication, a game of life, numeric integration, and one program that prints a line a million times. Three library programs. Programs 40 to 42 use Salam's own matrix and tensor packages, NumPy in Python, and hand-written loops in the other languages. They compare libraries, not compilers, and are left out of the headline averages.  The run behind the published numbers was made on 27 October 2026 at commit 8cfe206, on a GitHub Actions ubuntu-24.04 runner (a shared cloud virtual machine with an AMD EPYC 9V45) inside an Alpine Linux Docker image. The tools were gcc 15.2.0, rustc 1.96.1, Go 1.26.10, Python 3.14.10, PHP 8.5.12 and a development build of Salam 0.6.0. C and C++ were built with gcc -O3, Rust with -C opt-level=3, and Salam with its LLVM backend at -O3. How each time is taken Each program runs once untimed as a warm-up, then 10 times with the wall clock running, and the fastest of the 10 is kept. The per-language average is the geometric mean of those fastest times. Both choices are defensible, and both have consequences you should know:  The minimum filters out interference from other work on a shared machine, which only ever makes a run slower. It answers "how fast can this program go here", not "how fast is it usually". The mean, median and spread of every program are in the raw data, so you can check whether a conclusion holds for them too. The geometric mean keeps one slow program from dominating. Program 28 takes 700 to 840 ms depending on the language and program 26 around 2 ms; an arithmetic mean would be a measurement of program 28. With a geometric mean, a 10% gain on any program moves the average by the same amount. The flip side is that the average no longer says anything about total time.  Wall-clock time of a whole process includes starting it: loading the executable, the dynamic linker if there is one, the C runtime's start-up, and for Go, its runtime. For a program that runs for seconds this is noise. For one that runs for 3 ms, it is a large part of the result. x: Go's goroutines and garbage collector against Salam's threads, task pool, channels and manual memory, with the same programs in both languages and an honest reading of the HTTP benchmark. Salam vs Go for web servers and concurrency: goroutines against threads and channels, garbage collection against manual memory, HTTP benchmarks with caveats. Salam and other languages Salam and Go are both compiled languages with simple syntax, fast builds, a strong standard library for networking and single-file deployment. They differ in two fundamental choices. Go has goroutines, lightweight tasks scheduled by its runtime, and a garbage collector. Salam has neither: concurrency uses operating-system threads, a bounded task pool and channels, and heap memory is freed by hand. That makes Go easier to write highly concurrent code in, and gives Salam lower and more predictable memory overhead with no collector running beside the program. On the project's own HTTP router benchmark Salam's server answered more requests per second than the Go servers tested, with caveats this article spells out. For most teams, though, the choice turns on the concurrency model and the ecosystem more than on throughput. Salam vs Go at a glance GoSalamConcurrencyGoroutines (M:N scheduling by the runtime), channels, selectOS threads (spawn), a bounded task pool (go f(x)), channels, chan.Select, futuresBlocking I/OParks the goroutine; the runtime multiplexes socketsBlocks the thread; the HTTP server uses an event loop with a worker pool on LinuxMemoryGarbage collectedManual: .Free() and defer, with compile-time ownership checksErrorserror values, if err != nilthrows, try, catch, or result enumsGenericsSince Go 1.18Yes, with interface boundsSum typesNo (interfaces and type switches)Enums with data and exhaustive matchHTTPnet/http in the standard library, frameworks such as Gin, Echo and Fibernet/http and net/router in the standard libraryCross-compilingGOOS and GOARCH--target with a built-in linker and bundled sysrootsMaturity1.0 in 2012, compatibility promise, huge ecosystemPre-1.0, small ecosystem Concurrency: goroutines against threads, pools and channels Here is a classic worker pool in Go: three goroutines read numbers from a channel, square them and send the results to another channel. GoCopypackage main  import (     "fmt"     "sync" )  func main() {     jobs := make(chan int64, 4)     results := make(chan int64, 16)     var wg sync.WaitGroup     for range 3 {         wg.Add(1)         go func() {             defer wg.Done()             for n := range jobs {                 results <- n * n             }         }()     }     for i := int64(1); i <= 10; i++ {         jobs <- i     }     close(jobs)     wg.Wait()     close(results)     var sum int64     for v := range results {         sum += v     }     fmt.Println("sum of squares:", sum) } The Salam version has the same shape. The workers are threads started with spawn, the channels come from the chan package, and recv sets ok to false once a channel is closed and empty: SalamCopyimport chan  mut jobs := chan.Chan {} as chan.Chan<i64> mut results := chan.Chan {} as chan.Chan<i64>  func worker():     mut ok := true     until true:         n := jobs.recv(ok)         if not ok:             break         end         results.send(n * n)     end end  func main:     jobs.init(4)     results.init(16)     mut workers := Vector {} as Vector<i64>     defer workers.Free()     repeat 3:         workers.Push(spawn(worker))     end     repeat 1 to 10 in i:         jobs.send(i as i64)     end     jobs.Close()     each t in workers:         join(t)     end     results.Close()     mut sum := 0 as i64     mut ok := true     until true:         v := results.recv(ok)         if not ok:             break         end         sum += v     end     println "sum of squares:", sum     jobs.Free()     results.Free() endOutputsum of squares: 385 The programs read alike, but the machinery underneath does not. A goroutine starts with a small stack that grows as needed, and the Go scheduler can run hundreds of thousands of them on a handful of OS threads, parking any goroutine that waits on a channel or a socket. A Salam spawn is a real operating-system thread with its own fixed stack: fine for a few workers or a few hundred, not for one per connection at large scale. For many small jobs, Salam has a go keyword of its own. go f(x) runs the call as a task on a shared pool with one worker per CPU core and a bounded queue; when the queue is full, the caller waits, so a fast loop cannot pile up unlimited work. On the project's benchmark of 39 small programs that use the same algorithm in every language, Python took about 56 times as long as Salam. Python, in return, has one of the largest library ecosystems of any language, an interactive workflow that data scientists rely on, and decades of tutorials, answers and production experience. Salam has a broad standard library and a small community. So Salam is not a drop-in replacement for Python. t: Salam vs TypeScript: one language for the browser and the server?
x: TypeScript runs everywhere JavaScript does and owns the largest ecosystem in software. Salam takes another route to one language for the whole stack: a native server, a page language and a JavaScript backend. Here is how they differ in practice. Salam vs TypeScript for full stack work: erased types vs checked ones, JSON at the boundary, Node vs a native server, and how each builds web pages. Salam and other languages Salam vs TypeScript is a comparison between two answers to the same wish: write the server and the browser code in one language. TypeScript is a typed layer over JavaScript; its types are checked by the compiler and then erased, and the program runs on a JavaScript engine such as Node.js, Deno, Bun or a browser. Salam is a statically typed language that compiles to native code for the server and generates HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the browser. Both are "full stack languages", but they get there from opposite ends. This article compares them on the things that matter for web work: what the type system promises, what happens when JSON arrives from outside, how the server-side runs, how pages are built, and what each ecosystem gives you. The code on both sides solves the same small tasks, and every Salam example is compiled and run when this site is built. The short answer If you are building a typical web product today, with a team that knows JavaScript and a long list of npm packages it depends on, TypeScript is the safe choice and Salam is not a replacement for it. If you want a server that compiles to a single native executable, a type system whose guarantees still hold while the program runs, and pages that are checked at compile time without a JavaScript build chain, Salam is worth a serious look. TypeScriptSalamRuns onAny JavaScript engine (browser, Node.js, Deno, Bun)Native code on the server; HTML, CSS and JS in the browserTypes at runtimeErased; JavaScript values onlyKept in the compiled program; structs have a fixed layoutType systemStructural, gradual (any, casts), very expressiveStatic, no any; interfaces are structural, structs are nominalSum typesDiscriminated unions by conventionEnums with data, checked matchServerNode.js and frameworks such as Express, Fastify, NestJSnet/http and net/router in the standard libraryPagesJSX/TSX with React, Vue, Svelte and othersThe built-in page language, salam page buildPackage ecosystemnpm, the largest package registry there isLarge standard library, very small third-party ecosystemMaturityReleased in 2012, used across the industryPre-1.0, few production deployments Two ideas of what a type is TypeScript's types describe JavaScript values. The compiler checks your code against them and then removes them, so the program that runs is plain JavaScript. That design is the reason TypeScript could be adopted file by file in existing JavaScript projects, and the reason its type system is so expressive: conditional types, mapped types and template literal types can describe almost any shape a JavaScript library returns. The cost is that the types are a promise made at compile time, and some escape hatches (any, a type assertion with as, an unchecked index) let a wrong value through. Salam's types are the program's types. A struct has a fixed set of fields and a fixed layout in memory, an int is a 32-bit integer, and there is no any. Here is the same small task in both languages: describe a stream of order events, where each kind of event carries different data. TypeScriptCopytype OrderEvent =   | { kind: 'placed'; id: number; total: number }   | { kind: 'shipped'; id: number; carrier: string }   | { kind: 'cancelled'; id: number; reason: string };  function describe(e: OrderEvent): string {   switch (e.kind) {     case 'placed':       return `order ${e.id} placed, total ${e.total}`;     case 'shipped':       return `order ${e.id} shipped with ${e.carrier}`;     case 'cancelled':       return `order ${e.id} cancelled: ${e.reason}`;     default: {       const unreachable: never = e;       return unreachable;     }   } }  const events: OrderEvent[] = [   { kind: 'placed', id: 17, total: 42.5 },   { kind: 'shipped', id: 17, carrier: 'DHL' },   { kind: 'cancelled', id: 18, reason: 'out of stock' }, ];  for (const e of events) console.log(describe(e)); The TypeScript version is a discriminated union: an object type per case with a shared kind tag, a switch on the tag, and the never trick in the default branch so that adding a fourth case without handling it becomes a compile error. It works well, and it is a pattern you have to know. In Salam the same idea is a language feature, an enum whose members carry data: SalamCopyenum OrderEvent:     Placed(id: int, total: f64)     Shipped(id: int, carrier: str)     Cancelled(id: int, reason: str) end  func describe(e: OrderEvent): str:     ret match e:         Placed(id, total): "order " + id + " placed, total " + total end         Shipped(id, carrier): "order " + id + " shipped wi

t: Salam vs C++: architecture, performance, tooling and systems programming
x: C++ is the default language for performance-critical software and has forty years of libraries behind it. Salam is a young systems language with a smaller surface. This comparison puts the same code side by side and is plain about where each one wins. Salam vs C++ compared: variants vs enums with data, concepts vs bounded generics, RAII vs defer, measured speed, tooling, and when C++ is still the right call. Salam and other languages Salam vs C++ is a comparison between one of the largest programming languages ever built and a young one that deliberately stays small. C++ is an ISO-standardized systems language with zero-cost abstractions, RAII, templates and decades of compilers, libraries and tools. Salam is a statically typed systems language that compiles to native code without a garbage collector, with a deliberately smaller feature set, one toolchain and source you can write in English or Persian. Both produce fast native executables; they differ in how much language you have to learn and maintain to get there. This article puts the same small tasks side by side, compares how the two handle memory, generics and errors, looks at measured performance, and ends with an honest list of when C++ is still the right choice. Every Salam program shown here is compiled and run when this site is built, and every C++ example compiles with GCC in C++23 mode. Salam and C++ at a glance C++SalamStandardISO C++ (C++20, C++23, C++26 in progress)One open source implementation, pre-1.0CompilersGCC, Clang, MSVC and othersThe self-hosting salam compilerCode generationDirect to machine codeThrough C, through LLVM, or its own native backendMemoryRAII, smart pointers, manual new/deleteStack values, heap collections freed with .Free() and deferGenericsTemplates, conceptsGeneric functions and structs with interface boundsPolymorphismInheritance, virtual functions, std::variantInterfaces with dyn, enums with data, embedding with useErrorsExceptions, std::expectedthrows, try, catch, without stack unwindingBuildCMake, Meson, Bazel; vcpkg or Conan for packagesOne command: salam build, salam test, salam addEcosystemEnormous, every domainLarge standard library, small community Architecture: from source to machine code A C++ program is compiled one translation unit at a time. Each .cpp file includes its headers, the preprocessor pastes them in, templates are instantiated where they are used, and a linker joins the object files. That model is the reason C++ builds scale across thousands of files and the reason they are slow: the same headers are parsed again and again. C++20 modules address this, and support in compilers and build tools has been arriving gradually. Salam compiles a program together with everything it imports. The compiler, which is written in Salam itself, reads the entry file and every package it uses, checks types and many other rules, and then hands the program to one of three backends: generated C passed to a C compiler (gcc, clang or the bundled tcc), LLVM IR, or its own native backend that writes object files directly. The benchmark discussed below builds Salam through LLVM at -O3. The article Three ways to generate code explains the trade-offs, and How the Salam compiler works follows a program through each stage. One practical consequence: there are no headers in Salam. Files are included or packages imported, the order of functions does not matter, and a symbol is visible outside its package only when it is marked pub. Sum types and pattern matching A recurring task in systems code is a value that is one of several shapes. Modern C++ uses std::variant and std::visit, usually with the "overloaded" helper so that each case gets its own lambda: C++Copy#include <numbers> #include <print> #include <variant> #include <vector>  struct Circle { double r; }; struct Rect { double w, h; }; using Shape = std::variant<Circle, Rect>;  template <class... Ts> struct overloaded : Ts... { using Ts::operator()...; };  double area(const Shape& s) {     return std::visit(overloaded{         [](const Circle& c) { return std::numbers::pi * c.r * c.r; },         [](const Rect& r) { return r.w * r.h; },     }, s); }  int main() {     std::vector<Shape> shapes{Circle{1.0}, Rect{2.0, 3.0}};     double total = 0.0;     for (const auto& s : shapes) total += area(s);     std::println("{:.2f}", total); } It is type-safe and efficient, and a missing case is a compile error, but it takes a helper template, a variadic using declaration and some familiarity with overload resolution to read. In Salam the same structure is an enum with data and a match: SalamCopyimport conv import math  enum Shape:     Circle(r: f64)     Rect(w: f64, h: f64) end  func area(s: Shape): f64:     ret match s:         Circle(r): math.PI * r * r end         Rect(w, h): w * h end     end end  func main:     shapes := [Shape.Circle(1.0), Shape.Rect(2.0, 3.0)]     mut total := 0.0     each s in shapes:

t: Salam vs Zig: two young compiled languages for low-level software
x: Zig and Salam are both pre-1.0 systems languages with no garbage collector, a defer statement and a try keyword. They make very different choices about allocators, compile-time code and how much the standard library should do. Salam vs Zig side by side: error unions and throws, explicit allocators vs defer and free, comptime vs conditional compilation, C interop and cross-compilation. Salam and other languages Salam vs Zig is a comparison between two young systems languages that look alike at first glance. Zig is a low-level language designed as a better C: no hidden control flow, no hidden allocations, explicit allocators passed to whatever needs memory, and comptime, which runs ordinary Zig code at compile time. Salam is a statically typed systems language with a block syntax closer to Python or Lua, a large application-level standard library and source that can be written in English or Persian. Both compile to native code, neither has a garbage collector, and both are still before their 1.0 release. This article compares how they handle errors, memory, compile-time code, C libraries and cross-compilation, with the same small programs written in both. The Salam programs are compiled and run when this site is built. The Zig programs follow the 0.15 standard library, and since Zig is pre-1.0, details may change in later versions. Two young languages with a lot in common Zig first appeared in 2016, created by Andrew Kelley, and is developed by the Zig Software Foundation. It already has well-known users, among them the Bun JavaScript runtime, the TigerBeetle database and the Ghostty terminal. Salam is younger and its compiler has been written in Salam itself since the original C implementation was retired in August 2026. Both are open source. ZigSalamDesign goalA simpler, safer replacement for CA readable systems language for apps, servers and low-level codeSyntaxC-like, braces and semicolonsBlocks with : and end, no semicolons, English or Persian keywordsMemoryExplicit allocators, passed as argumentsOne global allocator for collections; mem arenas and pools on requestErrorsError unions (!T), try, catch, errdeferthrows, try, catch; errors carry a kind, a message and a positionCompile timecomptime: run any Zig code while compilingConstants, conditional compilation, -D flags, monomorphized genericsC interopImports C headers; zig cc compiles C and C++extern: declarations; calls follow the C ABI on every backendStandard libraryLower level: data structures, I/O, HTTP, JSON, cryptoApplication level: HTTP router, databases, JSON, TLS, images, MLStatusPre-1.0, breaking changes between releasesPre-1.0, breaking changes between releases Error handling: error unions and throws The two languages ended up with surprisingly similar error handling. Here is a function that parses a TCP port in each, and a loop that reports good and bad inputs. In Zig, a function that can fail returns an error union, try passes an error up, and if/else with captures handles both outcomes: ZigCopyconst std = @import("std");  fn parsePort(text: []const u8) !u16 {     const n = try std.fmt.parseInt(u32, text, 10);     if (n < 1 or n > 65535) return error.OutOfRange;     return @intCast(n); }  pub fn main() void {     const inputs = [_][]const u8{ "8080", "70000", "http" };     for (inputs) |text| {         if (parsePort(text)) |port| {             std.debug.print("port {d}\n", .{port});         } else |err| {             std.debug.print("bad: {s}\n", .{@errorName(err)});         }     } } In Salam, a function that can fail is marked throws, every call to it is marked try or sits inside a try block, and catch handles the error: SalamCopyimport conv  func parse port(text: str): int throws:     n := try conv.Atoi(text)     if n < 1 or n > 65535:         throw Error.New(ErrorKind.OutOfRange, "port out of range: " + text)     end     ret n end  func main:     each text in ["8080", "70000", "http"]:         try:             println "port", parse port(text)         catch e:             println "bad:", e.message         end     end endOutputport 8080 bad: port out of range: 70000 bad: invalid character 'h' The shape is the same: no exceptions, no stack unwinding, every failure point visible at the call site, and defer statements still run. Both also have a one-line fallback: Zig writes parsePort(text) catch 8080, Salam writes try parse port(text) catch 8080. The difference is what an error carries. A Zig error is a name from an error set, and that is all; extra details travel through a separate diagnostics value when you need them, and Zig's error return traces show where an error came from in debug builds. t: Salam vs Java and C#: native code versus managed runtimes
x: Java and C# run on managed runtimes with a JIT compiler and a garbage collector, backed by two of the largest ecosystems in software. Salam compiles ahead of time to native code with no collector. The differences reach from startup time to how a team writes code. Salam vs Java and C#: JIT and garbage collection against ahead-of-time native code, with startup, memory, deployment, language features and when to pick each. Salam and other languages Comparing Salam vs Java and C# is really comparing two ways to run a program. Java and C# are managed languages: the compiler produces bytecode (JVM bytecode or .NET IL), and a runtime loads it, compiles hot code to machine code with a just-in-time (JIT) compiler and frees memory with a garbage collector. Salam compiles ahead of time (AOT) to a native executable, with no virtual machine, no JIT and no garbage collector. Both Java and .NET can now also be compiled ahead of time, which narrows the gap in some places and not in others. This article explains what that difference means for startup, memory, deployment and day-to-day code, shows the same task in all three languages, and is direct about the large advantages Java and C# have in ecosystem and tooling. The Salam programs are compiled and run when this site is built; the Java example runs on Java 21 and the C# examples on .NET 8 or later. Managed runtimes and native code The JVM and the .NET runtime are among the most heavily engineered pieces of software in existence. A tiered JIT starts by interpreting or quickly compiling methods, watches which code is hot, and recompiles it with aggressive optimizations based on what actually happens at runtime. Generational garbage collectors (G1 and ZGC on the JVM, the .NET GC) reclaim memory without the programmer thinking about it. Reflection, dynamic class loading and runtime code generation are all available because the runtime is there. In Java 21, a record holds the data and a stream does the grouping: JavaCopyimport java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.TreeMap; import java.util.stream.Collectors;  public class Totals {     record Order(String customer, double amount) {}      public static void main(String[] args) {         List<Order> orders = List.of(             new Order("sara", 12.5),             new Order("ali", 7.0),             new Order("sara", 30.0));          Map<String, Double> totals = orders.stream()             .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::customer, TreeMap::new,                 Collectors.summingDouble(Order::amount)));          totals.forEach((name, sum) -> System.out.printf("%s %.2f%n", name, sum));     } } C# with top-level statements and LINQ is shorter still, and its decimal type is the natural choice for money: C#Copyvar orders = new List<Order> {     new("sara", 12.5m),     new("ali", 7.0m),     new("sara", 30.0m), };  foreach (var g in orders.GroupBy(o => o.Customer).OrderBy(g => g.Key)) {     Console.WriteLine($"{g.Key} {g.Sum(o => o.Amount):F2}"); }  record Order(string Customer, decimal Amount); Salam has no stream or LINQ library, so the grouping is an explicit loop over a HashMap. t: Salam vs Python and Julia for scientific computing and numerical work
x: Python owns scientific computing through NumPy and its ecosystem, and Julia was designed for it. Salam brings a native compiler and a pure-Salam numerics library. This is what that library can do, what the benchmark rows measure, and where each language belongs. Salam vs Python and Julia for numerical computing: linear algebra, statistics and regression side by side, plus an honest reading of the matrix benchmark rows. Salam and other languages Which language should you use for scientific computing and numerical work: Python, Julia or something compiled? Python is the dominant language of science and data work, fast in practice because NumPy, SciPy and PyTorch run their heavy loops in compiled C, C++ and Fortran. Julia is a language designed for numerical computing, compiled just in time through LLVM, with multiple dispatch and loops that run at compiled speed. Salam is a general-purpose compiled language whose standard library includes dense linear algebra, statistics, tensors, automatic differentiation and machine learning, all written in Salam. Each one makes sense for a different kind of project. This article puts the same numerical tasks side by side in the three languages, reads the three matrix and tensor rows of Salam's benchmark carefully, and is honest about how far Salam is from the Python and Julia ecosystems. The Salam programs are compiled and run when this site is built. Three approaches to fast numerics Python itself is slow at arithmetic loops. On Salam's benchmark of 39 programs that use the same algorithm in every language, pure Python took about 56 times as long as Salam. Nobody does serious numerics in pure Python, though: NumPy arrays hand whole operations to compiled code and to optimized BLAS and LAPACK libraries, so a matrix product in NumPy runs at native speed. The cost appears when the work cannot be expressed as a few large array operations, in loops over many small pieces, where each NumPy call pays interpreter overhead. Julia removes that split. Ordinary Julia loops are compiled to machine code by an LLVM-based JIT, specialized on the types they are called with, so you can write the loop yourself and still get compiled speed. The cost is compilation latency: the first call of a function takes time to compile, which Julia has reduced substantially since version 1.9 by caching native code for packages. Salam compiles ahead of time to a native executable, like C or Rust. Loops are fast from the first run, there is no interpreter and no JIT warm-up, and the numerical packages are ordinary Salam code. The cost is the ecosystem: Salam's numerics are one standard library, not the tens of thousands of packages Python and Julia have. Python (NumPy)JuliaSalamExecutionInterpreter; array operations in compiled librariesJIT compiled through LLVMAhead-of-time native codeFast loops in your own codeOnly through NumPy, Numba, Cython or similarYesYesLinear algebraNumPy and SciPy on BLAS/LAPACKBuilt-in LinearAlgebra on BLAS/LAPACKmatrix package, pure SalamMachine learningPyTorch, JAX, scikit-learnFlux, Lux, MLJai.tensor, ai.autograd, ai.nn, ai.mlGPUYes, widelyYesNoNotebooks and plottingJupyter, Matplotlib and many moreJupyter, Pluto, Plots, MakieNone built-inEcosystemEnormousLarge in scienceOne standard library Solving a linear system The first task: solve the 2-by-2 system 4x + y = 1, 2x + 3y = 2. In NumPy and Julia it is one line each: PythonCopyimport numpy as np  A = np.array([[4.0, 1.0], [2.0, 3.0]]) b = np.array([1.0, 2.0]) x = np.linalg.solve(A, b) print(x, np.linalg.det(A)) JuliaCopyusing LinearAlgebra  A = [4.0 1.0; 2.0 3.0] b = [1.0, 2.0] x = A \ b println(x, " ", det(A)) Salam has no matrix literal syntax, so the matrix is built from a vector of numbers with matrix.FromArray. Solve uses an LU decomposition with pivoting, like the other two, and returns an empty matrix instead of stopping the program when the system has no unique solution: SalamCopyimport matrix  func main:     mut cells := Vector {} as Vector<f64>     each v in [4.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0]:         cells.Push(v)     end     mut rhs := Vector {} as Vector<f64>     each v in [1.0, 2.0]:         rhs.Push(v)     end     mut a := matrix.FromArray(2, 2, cells)     mut b := matrix.FromArray(2, 1, rhs)     mut x := matrix.Solve(a, b)     if x.IsEmpty():         println "no unique solution"         ret 1     end     println "x =", matrix.ToStringPrec(matrix.Transpose(x), 4)     println "det =", matrix.Det(a)     a.Free()     b.Free()     x.Free() endOutputx = 0.1000 0.6000 det = 10 The Salam version is clearly longer. Building matrices, checking for an empty result and freeing each one with .Free() are things Python and Julia do for you with literals, exceptions and a garbage collector. That is the general pattern of this comparison: Salam's numerics are capable, but the language was not designed around arrays the way Julia was, or adapted to them over two decades the way Python was.

t: Can a new programming language compete with decades-old ones? Salam's place in the global ecosystem
x: Every popular language was once new, and most new languages never become popular. This article looks at what carried Go, Rust, Kotlin and others to adoption, and measures Salam against the same forces without pretending the gap is small. How new programming languages win adoption, what an ecosystem really consists of, and an honest look at where Salam stands against decades-old languages. Salam and other languages Can a new programming language compete with languages that have thirty or fifty years of libraries, books and developers behind them? Yes, but almost never head-on. New languages that succeed do so by being clearly better at something specific, by riding a new platform, or by fitting into an ecosystem that already exists, and then they grow outward from that niche over many years. Salam, a young compiled language you can write in English or Persian, faces exactly this question, and the honest answer for it is "not yet, and only in some places". This article looks at how the last generation of languages broke through, what an ecosystem actually consists of, where Salam stands today item by item, and what it would still have to earn. It is written for developers and technical decision makers weighing a young language, and it tries to be as clear about the gaps as about the strengths. How the last generation of languages broke through The languages that dominate today did not win on syntax. Each had a force behind it that made adoption easier than staying with the old tools. LanguageFirst releasedWhat carried itC1972Unix, written in it and spread with itPython1991Readability, then decades later the scientific and machine learning stackJava1995The JVM's "write once, run anywhere", then enterprise serversJavaScript1995The only language every browser runsC#2000Microsoft's .NET platform and Windows developmentTypeScript2012Types layered over JavaScript, adoptable one file at a timeGo2009 (1.0 in 2012)Google, simple concurrency, then Docker and KubernetesSwift2014Apple's platformsRust2015 (1.0)Memory safety without a garbage collectorKotlin2016 (1.0)Full Java interop, then Google's support for AndroidZig2016A simpler C with first-class cross-compilation Three patterns stand out. A platform owner can make a language the default (Swift on Apple devices, C# on .NET, Kotlin on Android). Interoperability removes the cost of leaving the old world behind (TypeScript runs all JavaScript, Kotlin calls all Java, Zig compiles C). And a distinct technical advantage gives early adopters a reason to accept the risk (Rust's safety guarantees, Go's simple deployment and concurrency). Python is the reminder that it can also take a long time: it was more than fifteen years old before the scientific stack made it a default choice. What none of them did was replace their predecessors. C, Java and Python are all still here. Success for a new language means owning some territory, not winning everything. What an ecosystem actually is When people say a language "has no ecosystem", they mean several different things, and it helps to separate them:  Libraries. Can I parse this format, talk to that database, call this cloud API, without writing it myself? Tools. Editors, debuggers, profilers, formatters, linters, build and package management, CI integration. Knowledge. Documentation, books, courses, answers to the exact error message you are looking at. People. Developers who can be hired, maintainers who answer issues, a community that reviews code. Trust. Stability promises, security processes, a track record in production, an organization that will still be there in ten years.  A new language can build the first three surprisingly quickly with focused work. The last two only come with time and use, and no amount of engineering can shortcut them. Where Salam stands today Measured against that list, here is Salam's position at the end of 2026, using only what can be checked in the repository. The compiler. Salam's compiler is written in Salam and builds itself; the original C implementation was retired in August 2026. It generates code through C, through LLVM or through its own native backend, and targets Linux, macOS, Windows, WebAssembly, JavaScript and freestanding bare-metal programs. Self-hosting is a meaningful milestone, because a compiler exercises nearly every feature of a language (see Inside Salam's self-hosting compiler). Libraries. This is the strongest part. More than 170 standard library packages ship with the compiler, each with a reference page and checked examples on the library reference: HTTP servers with routing and middleware, WebSocket and gRPC, TLS written in Salam, drivers for PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, Redis and ClickHouse, JSON, YAML, TOML, XML and CSV, compression and archives, cryptography, images and audio, matrices, tensors and neural network layers. A small program can do real work without a single dependency: SalamCopyimport crypto import encoding.json  struct Artifact:     pub file: str     pub si

x: Salam has a page language inside its compiler. You describe a page as a tree of elements, the compiler checks every element, attribute and CSS value, and you get HTML, CSS and JavaScript back. This article walks from a static page to components, events and pages rendered by a Salam server. Web development with Salam: a built-in page language that compiles to checked HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with components, events and server-side rendering. Building with Salam Web development with Salam starts with a feature most languages leave to templates and frameworks. Salam's page language is a declarative language built into the compiler: you describe a web page as a tree of elements with attributes and styles, the compiler checks every element, attribute and CSS value against the HTML and CSS rules, and salam page build turns it into HTML, CSS and, when the page has event handlers, JavaScript. The same language describes pages that a Salam web server renders for each request, and it works in English and in Persian. This article covers the whole path: a static page, what the compiler checks, components, interactivity, server-side rendering, building and deploying, and the limits you should know before you choose it. t: Interactive user interfaces in Salam: components, state and event handling in the page language
x: A practical guide to interactivity in Salam pages: handlers written in Salam, components with their own state, lists with keys, callbacks, events that bubble, and the compile-time checks around them. How Salam's page language builds interactive UI components: event handling in Salam, reactive state management, callbacks and events, checked at compile time. Building with Salam Salam's page language handles UI components, state management and event handling without a separate frontend framework. You declare the page as a tree of elements, write event handlers as ordinary Salam functions, and the compiler turns the whole thing into HTML, CSS and JavaScript. A component in Salam is a named piece of page with parameters; when it declares a variable that a handler changes and the view shows, that variable becomes state, and the page redraws only what depends on it. The same page can also run in a native window drawn by Salam itself. This article walks through the model step by step, from a single click handler to components that keep their own state and talk to each other, and ends with the checks the compiler runs and the limits you should know about. Every program below is a complete page that builds with salam page build. How interactivity works in a Salam page A Salam page is a page: block. Elements open with a colon and close with end, and attributes and CSS properties are written as name = value inside them. That is enough for static HTML and CSS; the article Web development with Salam covers that part. Interactivity enters through attributes named after browser events. click, submit, input, change, key down and the rest take a function instead of a value. A plain function name, or an inline function written in place, is compiled by Salam's JavaScript backend and placed in the page's own script. You never write JavaScript by hand, and the handler is type-checked like any other Salam code. There are two ways to make a page change after an event, and Salam supports both:  The direct way. A handler finds an element with the dom package and changes its text, class, style or attributes. This is the familiar DOM style, and the lessons on mouse events, keyboard and forms, drag and touch and media events use it to cover each event family. The reactive way. A handler only changes variables. The compiler knows which parts of the page read those variables and redraws exactly those parts. This is how components with state work, and it is the only style that also runs in a native window.  The rest of the article starts with the first and moves to the second. Event handling with the DOM package Here is the smallest useful interactive page: a number and two buttons. The state is one mut variable above the page. Each handler changes it and calls show, the one function that writes to the page. SalamCopyimport dom  mut count := 0  func show:     dom.SetText(dom.ById("value"), "" + count) end  func more:     count++     show() end  func start_over:     count = 0     show() end  page:     title = "Counter"     box:         heading: id = "value" content = "0" end         button: click = more content = "+1" end         button: click = start_over content = "Reset" end     end end Three details matter. First, click = more names the function; it does not call it. Writing click = more() is rejected, because the attribute wants the function itself (error E137; when the function writes page state, as more does here, the compiler reports the same mistake as E132). Second, dom.ById("value") is checked against the IDs that really exist in the same file, so a wrong id such as dom.ById("count") stops the build with E138 before the page ever reaches a browser. Third, the page has no main. A page program is driven entirely by its handlers, and adding a main makes the compiler report the handlers as unused functions. The dom package covers what a handler normally needs: finding elements (ById, Query, QueryAll), reading and writing text and values, classes and styles, creating and removing elements, timers (SetTimeout, SetInterval, RequestFrame), the event itself (EventTarget, EventKey, PreventDefault), and browser storage (StoreSetStr, StoreGetStr). The full list is on the dom package page, and the lesson on state, the DOM and timers builds a todo list, tabs, a stopwatch and a quiz with it. The direct style works well for small pages. Its weakness is the one every jQuery-era developer remembers: as soon as two handlers change the same element, you have to keep the variables and the page in step by hand. Salam's lesson recommends a discipline for that (state in variables, one drawing function), and the reactive model below removes the need for it. Components: reusable pieces of page A component is a piece of page you define once and use like a new element. Its parameters are set like attributes.
