t: Can AI write code in Persian? Generating and validating Persian Salam programs
x: Writing Persian code is a harder test for a code generator than writing English code, because there is so little of it to learn from. What goes wrong, what the Salam compiler catches in Persian, and three practical ways to get Persian programs that compile and do what you meant. Persian Salam is a full programming language, but AI models have seen little of it. Where code generation goes wrong and how the compiler and tests catch it. The road ahead Yes, AI tools can write code in Persian, but only reliably when something checks the result. Salam is a programming language whose keywords, types, standard library and compiler messages all exist in Persian, so a Persian Salam program is real code that compiles to a native executable, not a translated comment. That makes it a demanding test for code generators: Persian source code is rare in any training data, the script runs right to left, and small details such as a zero-width non-joiner or an Arabic letter variant change meaning. What makes the task workable is that the Salam compiler checks Persian code as strictly as English code and explains its errors in Persian. This article shows what Persian Salam looks like, where generated Persian code tends to go wrong, how the compiler and the test runner catch those mistakes, and three practical strategies for getting Persian programs you can trust. What Persian code looks like A Persian Salam program uses Persian keywords, Persian names and, if you like, Persian digits and the Persian comma. The entry function is ریشه ("root"), blocks end with پایان ("end"), سرچاپ prints a line, and text between the guillemets « and » is a string, like text between double quotes: SalamCopyساختار کالا:     همگانی نام: رشته     همگانی تعداد: صحیح     همگانی قیمت: صحیح پایان  تابع جمع سبد(سبد: وکتور<کالا>): صحیح:     ناپایا جمع := ۰     هر ک در سبد:         جمع += ک.تعداد * ک.قیمت     پایان     برگشت جمع پایان  تابع ریشه:     ناپایا سبد خرید := وکتور {} برگردان وکتور<کالا>     دیرکن سبد خرید.آزادکن()     سبد خرید.بیفزا(کالا { نام = «نان»، تعداد = ۲، قیمت = ۴۵ })     سبد خرید.بیفزا(کالا { نام = «پنیر»، تعداد = ۱، قیمت = ۱۲۰ })     سبد خرید.بیفزا(کالا { نام = «چای»، تعداد = ۳، قیمت = ۶۰ })     کل := جمع سبد(سبد خرید)     سرچاپ «جمع کل:»، کل     اگر کل > ۳۰۰:         سرچاپ «ارسال رایگان است»     وگرنه:         سرچاپ «هزینه‌ی ارسال اضافه می‌شود»     پایان پایانOutputجمع کل: 390 ارسال رایگان است The function name جمع سبد ("basket total") is two words, and so is the variable سبد خرید ("shopping basket"). Salam allows spaces inside names because Persian writes many single concepts as two words. Numbers in the source are Persian digits; printed numbers come out in ASCII digits, a detail that matters when you check output. The article one language, two scripts covers the bilingual design in full. Why Persian code is harder for AI models Code generators learn from public code. There is far less public code in any non-English programming language than in Python or JavaScript, and Salam's Persian spelling is younger still, so a model has seen very little of it. Several properties of Persian make the gaps easy to fall into:  Two-meaning keywords. تا is until at the start of a statement and to inside a تکرار (repeat) header; هر is each at the start of a statement and the step (by) inside تکرار. Both are natural Persian, and both are easy to misplace. Built-in names must be Persian. In a Persian file, len is an error; the built-in is طول. A model that mixes English built-ins into Persian code is a common failure. Invisible characters. A zero-width non-joiner (ZWNJ, U+200C) is part of correct Persian spelling, as in کتاب‌ها. Inside a name, Salam treats a ZWNJ and a space as the same, but a keyword written with its parts glued together, such as نادرستسرچاپ instead of نادرست‌سرچاپ, is an unknown identifier. Arabic letter variants. Persian and Arabic encode yeh and kaf with different code points (ی/ي, ک/ك). Text produced on an Arabic keyboard, or by a model trained on Arabic text, mixes them. Reserved short words. و ("and") is a keyword, so it can never be a name. Number formats. The Persian decimal separator ٫ is not accepted; a decimal point is always ., as in ۳.۱۴. The entry point. The entry function is ریشه. اصلی, the literal translation of "main", is an ordinary function name.  None of this is exotic for a Persian speaker, but each item is a place where a model trained mostly on English code can produce something

t: Running AI workloads with Salam: loading GGUF language models, running ONNX and building ML tools without Python
x: Salam's standard library can read GGUF language models, run small Llama-family models on the processor and execute ONNX graphs, all in pure Salam. Here is what works, what it costs and what it is not meant for. Can you run an LLM or an ONNX model from a native Salam program? What the gguf, llm, onnx and tensor packages do today, their limits, and where Salam fits. The road ahead Yes, you can run AI models from a Salam program, within clear limits. Salam's standard library has a GGUF reader (ai.gguf), a small Llama-family inference engine (ai.llm), an ONNX graph runner (ai.onnx) and the tensor, autograd and neural network packages underneath them. AI inference in Salam means loading a trained model file and computing its outputs inside a native executable, with no Python interpreter and no outside runtime library. It runs on the processor only, it is sized for small models, and it is not a replacement for llama.cpp, ONNX Runtime or PyTorch on a GPU. This article is in the "future" category because the interesting question is where this goes. But the future has to start from the present, so most of what follows is what the repository contains today, with real programs and the limits the package documentation states. What "AI workloads" means here People mean several different jobs when they say "run AI". It helps to separate them, because Salam covers some well, some partly and some not at all. JobTypical tool elsewhereSalam todayTrain a large model on GPUsPyTorch, JAXNot covered: no GPU code in the libraryServe a large model to many usersvLLM, llama.cpp server, hosted APIsCall such a server over HTTPRun a small language model inside a programllama.cppai.llm with a GGUF file under 2 GBRun an exported classifier or embedding modelONNX Runtimeai.onnx, about 65 operatorsTrain a small network on the CPUPyTorch on CPUai.nn, ai.autograd, ai.optimClassic machine learning on tablesscikit-learnai.mlExchange arrays with PythonNumPy filesnpy reads and writes .npy and .npz The pattern is clear: Salam is useful at the small and embedded end, where a program needs a model as one component and you want a single native binary with no Python environment beside it. At the large end, the honest answer is to call a server. Reading GGUF model files with ai.gguf GGUF is the file format of llama.cpp. One file holds the metadata (architecture, sizes, tokenizer vocabulary, chat template) and every weight, usually quantized. The ai.gguf package parses that file: LoadGguf reads the header and the tensor list, meta_int and meta_str read metadata keys, and LoadTensorF32 expands one weight into a tensor of 32-bit floats. The program below inspects a model file passed on the command line. It is type-checked here rather than run, because it needs a downloaded model. SalamCopyimport ai.gguf import os  func main:     args := os.Args()     if args.len() < 2:         println "usage: inspect model.gguf"         ret 1     end     mut g := gguf.Gguf {}     try:         g = gguf.LoadGguf(args.Get(1))     catch e:         println "not a readable GGUF file:", e.to_str()         ret 1     end     arch := g.meta_str("general.architecture")     println "model:", g.meta_str("general.name"), "(" + arch + ")"     println "layers:", g.meta_int(arch + ".block_count", 0)     println "context:", g.meta_int(arch + ".context_length", 0)     mut unreadable := 0     repeat g.tensors.len() in i:         if gguf.TensorBytes(g, i) < 0:             unreadable++         end     end     println g.tensors.len(), "tensors,", unreadable, "in a weight type this package cannot expand"     g.Free() end The last count matters because of the package's main limit. It reads five weight types: F32, F16, Q8_0, Q4_0 and Q4_1. The K-quants that most downloads use, such as Q4_K_M, and BF16 are not supported; TensorBytes returns -1 for them. LoadGguf also reads the whole file into memory first, and a buffer holds at most 2 GB. In practice that means picking the Q8_0 or Q4_0 file of a small model such as Qwen2.5 0.5B or TinyLlama 1.1B. Running a small language model with ai.llm The ai.llm package builds on the GGUF reader and runs Llama-family models on the CPU, in pure Salam. It implements the Llama layer layout (RMSNorm, rotary positions, grouped-query attention, a SwiGLU feed-forward block) plus the attention biases Qwen2 uses. Its documentation lists Qwen2.5 Instruct as tested; Llama and Mistral use the same layout. Architectures with a different layout, such as Phi, fail to load or produce nonsense. The package has the pieces you would expect from a small inference engine: BPE and SentencePiece tokenizers, a key-value cache, Forward for one step, a Sampler with temperature, top-k, top-p and a repetition penalty, and Generate for the whole loop. The cost is spelled out in the package page, and it is worth repeating plainly:  Memory. Every weight

t: How a new programming language builds an open source ecosystem: packages, registry, documentation and contributors in Salam
x: A language is only as useful as the code around it. This is how Salam's package manager, standard library, documentation and contributor process are built, and an honest account of how small the ecosystem still is. How a young language grows an open source ecosystem: Salam's package manager, lock file, checksums, registry and docs, and what is still missing. The road ahead An open source ecosystem is everything around a language that lets people reuse each other's work: a package manager, a place to find packages, a way to trust what you download, documentation, editor support, and a community that keeps all of it alive. For a new programming language, building that ecosystem is harder than building the compiler. This article looks at how Salam approaches it: a large standard library first, then a Git-based package manager with lockfiles and checksums, a registry, and tooling that makes packages usable in both English and Persian. It is also plain about the current state, which is early. What a language ecosystem is made of A programming language ecosystem is the set of shared code, tools, infrastructure and people that turn a compiler into something you can build products with. Rust has crates.io and Cargo, Python has PyPI and pip, JavaScript has npm, and Go has module paths, a module proxy and a checksum database. Each of those took years and a large community to grow. A new language faces a chicken-and-egg problem. Developers wait for libraries before they adopt a language, and libraries only appear once developers have adopted it. There are only a few ways out:  ship a standard library big enough that early users do not need third-party code for common work; make it trivial to publish and consume packages, so the first few authors face no friction; make interop with an existing ecosystem cheap, so missing libraries can be borrowed; invest in documentation and tooling, which are part of the ecosystem even when nobody calls them that.  Salam does all four, and the balance between them says a lot about where the project is. The standard library as the first ecosystem Salam's main bet so far is a large standard library that ships with the compiler. The library reference documents more than 170 packages: text and Unicode, files and processes, HTTP servers and clients with a router, WebSocket, gRPC, SSH and TLS, drivers for SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis and ClickHouse, compression and archives, cryptography, images, audio, matrices, tensors and neural networks. None of it needs salam add; an import is enough. This is the "batteries included" strategy Python made famous, and it has a clear cost: every package in std/ is maintained by the core project, so the core project carries all of it. It also has a clear benefit for a young language. Someone evaluating Salam can write a web service with a database, a JSON API and TLS without depending on a single package written by a stranger. The project made this choice explicit in October 2026, when a separate packages/ tree of libraries was folded into std/. The package manager page states the rule: everything in the standard library ships with the compiler, and the package commands are for code somebody publishes in their own repository. For C libraries, the FFI is the third escape hatch: an extern block can call any C function, and a package manifest can describe how to find or build the C library it wraps. The package manager: salam.toml, salam add and the lockfile Third-party code lives in ordinary Git repositories. A project is a folder with main.salam and a salam.toml manifest, and salam new or salam init creates both. Adding a dependency is one command: TerminalCopysalam init salam add github.com/owner/repo          # newest release salam add github.com/owner/repo@^1.2     # a version range salam deps                               # after a fresh clone: download and verify salam update                             # newest release with the same major version salam install github.com/owner/tool      # build a program into ~/.salam/bin The manifest records what you asked for, and salam.lock records exactly what you got: TOMLCopy[package] name = "myapp" version = "0.1.0" salam = ">=0.5.9"  [dependencies] "github.com/owner/repo" = "v1.2.0" "example.com/me/lib" = { path = "../lib" } The design borrows openly from Go modules. A package is named by its repository path, so there is no central name to register. Versions are Git tags (v1.2.0), with pseudo-versions for repositories that have no tags. When two dependencies ask for different versions of the same module, the newer one wins, which the PACKAGES.md document calls minimal version selection, "as in Go". A new major version is a separate module path (.../v2), so v1 and v2 can live in one program. Two details make this practical for a small community. Packages can be fetched from GitHub, GitLab and Codeberg even without Git installed, th

t: Salam in programming education: teaching beginners, computer science and compilers with one bilingual language
x: Salam lets a student start in Persian, move to English keywords without switching languages, and later read a production compiler written in the same language. What exists for teachers today, and what classrooms would still need. How Salam can be used to teach programming, computer science and compilers: Persian-first lessons, strict compiler feedback, a readable self-hosting compiler. The road ahead Salam can serve three stages of programming education with one language: a first course taught in the student's own language, a computer science curriculum that needs a real compiled language, and a compilers course that studies a compiler written in the very language the students already know. Salam is a statically typed, compiled language whose keywords, standard library and error messages exist in both Persian and English, which makes it usable as a first language for Persian speakers and as a bridge to the English-keyword languages used in industry. This article looks at what the project offers educators today, where it could fit in a curriculum, and what is still missing before schools and universities could rely on it. A note on scope: this is the "future" category. Nothing below claims that a school or university has adopted Salam; the repository documents no such adoption. It describes what exists and argues where it could help. Why the language of instruction matters Most programming languages assume the learner reads English. Keywords such as while, return and struct are English words, and so are almost all compiler error messages. For a native English speaker that vocabulary is free. For a 14-year-old in Tehran or Kabul it is a second subject stacked on top of the first: the student has to learn a foreign vocabulary and the idea of a loop at the same time. Whether teaching in the first language improves outcomes for programming specifically is a research question, and the evidence should be read carefully; the article Can programming in your native language change computer science education? goes through it. The narrower claim made here is practical: a language that lets a teacher remove the vocabulary barrier, without giving up a real compiler, real types and a real standard library, gives teachers an option they did not have. A first course in the student's own language The basic exercise every introductory course reaches in its first weeks is a loop with a condition. Here is Euclid's algorithm for the greatest common divisor, written in Persian. تابع is func, ناپایا is mut, تا loops while its condition holds, برگشت is ret, and the entry function is ریشه. Persian digits and the Persian comma are accepted as written. SalamCopyتابع مقسوم علیه مشترک(الف: صحیح، ب: صحیح): صحیح:     ناپایا ایکس := الف     ناپایا ایگرگ := ب     تا ایگرگ != ۰:         باقی := ایکس % ایگرگ         ایکس = ایگرگ         ایگرگ = باقی     پایان     برگشت ایکس پایان  تابع ریشه:     سرچاپ «ب.م.م ۸۴ و ۳۶ برابر است با»، مقسوم علیه مشترک(۸۴، ۳۶)     سرچاپ «ب.م.م ۱۷ و ۵ برابر است با»، مقسوم علیه مشترک(۱۷، ۵) پایانOutputب.م.م ۸۴ و ۳۶ برابر است با 12 ب.م.م ۱۷ و ۵ برابر است با 1 Two details matter for a classroom. The function name is three words with spaces, مقسوم علیه مشترک, because Persian concepts are often several words and forcing them into one token or an underscore makes code harder to read. And the program is not a toy dialect: it goes through the same type checker and code generator as English Salam and produces a native executable. The teaching material around it is already substantial:  A free course of 47 lessons in both English and Persian, from the first program through structs, generics, memory and threads to building web pages. Every example in every lesson is compiled when the site builds, and the output shown is the real output. Nothing to install. The online editor at editor.salamlang.ir runs the whole compiler in the browser through WebAssembly, which matters in computer labs where students cannot install software. An Android app with the compiler built-in, so programs run offline on a phone or tablet running Android 5.0 or newer. For students whose main computer is a phone, that is not a detail. An interpreter (salam exec) and a REPL (salam cli) for quick experiments without a C toolchain.  A strict compiler as a patient teacher Beginners learn as much from error messages as from lectures, so the quality of diagnostics is a teaching feature. Salam's compiler is strict by design: variables are immutable unless declared mut, unused variables are errors rather than warnings, and many common mistakes come with a suggested fix. Take a student's first attempt at summing 1 to 5: SalamCopyfunc main:     total := 0     repeat 1 to 5 in i:

t: Multilingual programming and the future of native-language code: could Salam's bilingual model work for other languages?
x: Salam compiles English and Persian source with one front end, one standard library and one set of error codes. This article takes the design apart and asks what it would take to add a third human language, and whether that is a good idea. Multilingual programming in Salam: how language packs let one compiler speak English and Persian, and what a third language such as Arabic would need. The road ahead Multilingual programming means writing code whose keywords, library names and compiler messages are in a human language other than English, while still compiling to the same programs as everyone else. Salam is one working example: every Salam keyword, built-in type, standard library name and diagnostic has an English and a Persian spelling, and both compile through the same frontend to the same executable. The interesting question for the future is whether that model generalizes. Could the same compiler gain an Arabic, Turkish or Hindi spelling? This article explains how Salam's bilingual design (introduced in One language, two scripts) actually works in the compiler, then works through what a third language would require. Everything about a third language here is analysis; no third language pack exists or is planned in the repository. Localized programming languages before Salam Salam is not the first language to drop the assumption that code is written in English. A few well-known precedents show the range of approaches:  Spreadsheet formulas. Microsoft Excel translates its function names per locale, so a German user writes SUMME where an English user writes SUM. It is probably the most widely used localized programming notation in the world. Scratch translates its blocks into many languages. Because the program is a set of blocks rather than text, a project can be shown in any language without rewriting it. 1C:Enterprise, used widely in Russia for business software, has Russian keywords with English equivalents. Hedy, a gradual teaching language from Leiden University, offers its keywords in many natural languages for classroom use. Artistic and research projects such as Qalb (a Lisp written in Arabic) and Wenyan-lang (a language in classical Chinese) showed that the idea runs into script, direction and culture, not only vocabulary.  Most of these either translate a narrow surface (formula names, blocks) or build a separate language. Salam's approach sits in between: one full general-purpose language, with two complete spellings that share everything below the lexer. How Salam's bilingual model works The core idea is that the grammar is shared and only the spellings differ. A Persian if statement has the same structure as an English one; only the word changes. Here is a word count in Persian, using the Persian names of the standard library: SalamCopyواردسازی رشته  تابع ریشه:     واژه‌ها := رشته.تفکیک کردن(«سیب انار سیب توت سیب»، « »)     دیرکن واژه‌ها.آزادکن()     ناپایا شمار := نگاشت {} برگردان نگاشت<رشته، صحیح>     دیرکن شمار.آزادکن()     هر واژه در واژه‌ها:         شمار.درج(واژه، شمار.دریافت با پیش فرض(واژه، ۰) + ۱)     پایان     سرچاپ «سیب:»، شمار.بگیر(«سیب»)     سرچاپ «انار:»، شمار.بگیر(«انار») پایانOutputسیب: 3 انار: 1 And the same program in English: SalamCopyimport str  func main:     words := str.Split("apple pear apple fig apple", " ")     defer words.Free()     mut counts := HashMap {} as HashMap<str, int>     defer counts.Free()     each word in words:         counts.Put(word, counts.GetOr(word, 0) + 1)     end     println "apple:", counts.Get("apple")     println "pear:", counts.Get("pear") endOutputapple: 3 pear: 1 Line for line the two are the same program. واردسازی is import, رشته is the str package, تفکیک کردن is Split, دیرکن is defer, نگاشت is HashMap, هر ... در is each ... in, and دریافت با پیش فرض is GetOr. Inside the compiler, that mapping happens in layers. Layer 1: keyword tables The keywords live in compiler/langpack.salam as parallel tables: a list of token kinds, and for each language pack the spelling of each kind. There are 60 keyword spellings per pack, from func and ret to try, catch and throws; the keywords lesson lists them side by side. The lexer looks up an identifier in the active pack's table and turns it into the same token kind either way, so the parser never sees which language it came from. One detail shows why this is harder than a word list. Persian does not have a separate word for every English keyword. تا serves as both until (the while loop) and to (in repeat 1 to 5), and هر serves as both each and by (the step in repeat 0 to 20 by 2). The lexer resolves those by context: inside a repeat head

t: Where Salam could fit in industry: web services, cloud infrastructure, enterprise back offices and systems software
x: Salam has the technical pieces for web services, cloud tools, back-office software and systems work. It does not yet have the stability promise, ecosystem or support model most companies need. This is a map of the fit and the gaps. An honest look at where Salam could fit in industry: web services, cloud infrastructure, enterprise software and systems tools, and the barriers to adoption. The road ahead Salam could fit in industry wherever a team wants native performance, single-binary deployment and a large built-in standard library: HTTP and gRPC services, command-line and infrastructure tools, data-processing jobs, and back-office software, especially for Persian-speaking organizations. Industrial use of a programming language means running it in software that a business depends on, with the stability, support, hiring and licensing that implies. On that definition, Salam today is a candidate rather than an incumbent. The project publishes no case studies or list of production users, so this article is about technical fit and the conditions for adoption, not about who is already using it. What industry actually asks of a language Engineering managers rarely choose a language for its syntax. The questions that decide adoption are more mundane:  Does it do the job fast and predictably? Throughput, latency, memory use, start-up time. Can we deploy and operate it? Build artifacts, containers, cross-compilation, observability. Can we hire for it and train people? Talent pool, learning curve, documentation. Will it still be there, and still compatible, in five years? Stability policy, maintainers, release process. Can we use it legally in our product? License terms for the compiler, the runtime and the standard library. Who helps when it breaks? Support channels, security response, commercial options.  Salam answers the first two well, the third and fourth weakly, and the fifth with a condition that every company must check. The rest of this article goes through each domain with those questions in mind; the companion piece What makes a language ready for production? runs a full checklist. Web services and APIs This is the most natural industrial fit. The standard library includes an HTTP server with a router and middleware, HTTP/2, WebSocket, gRPC, GraphQL, TLS 1.3 and 1.2 with no OpenSSL dependency, sessions, validation and Swagger generation. A small inventory service looks like this: SalamCopyimport net.http import net.router import encoding.json import env  mut items := Vector {} as Vector<Stock>  struct Stock:     @json "sku"     pub sku: str = ""     @json "count"     pub count: int = 0 end  func health(ctx: i64):     http.Json(ctx, `{"status":"ok"}`) end  func stock(ctx: i64):     sku := http.Param(ctx, "sku")     each s in items:         if s.sku == sku:             http.Json(ctx, json.Marshal(s))             ret         end     end     http.SetStatus(ctx, 404)     http.Json(ctx, `{"error":"unknown sku"}`) end  func main:     items.Push(Stock { sku = "RACK-42U", count = 7 })     items.Push(Stock { sku = "CABLE-CAT6", count = 310 })     mut r := router.NewRouter()     router.Get(r, "/healthz", health)     router.Get(r, "/stock/:sku", stock)     port := env.GetOr("PORT", "8080")     mut s := http.NewServer(port.to_int())     http.Use(s, r)     http.Run(s) end The project measured its HTTP stack against eight other servers on eleven routes. On that run, Salam's net.http answered a geometric mean of 94,850 requests per second against 62,493 for Go's Fiber framework and 34,987 for Go's standard library. The caveats matter as much as the numbers: it was a shared 6-vCPU sandbox with unrelated load, the margin over Fiber was 16% on a quiet machine and 52% under that load, and on the / route the lead was only 4%. The speed page publishes the full table and the harness. Read it as evidence that the HTTP stack is in the same class as fast compiled servers, not as a guarantee for your workload. The web server article goes deeper. For operations, salam serve --config runs a multi-site web server from a config file with virtual hosts, redirects and FastCGI backends such as php-fpm, and the same net.http program can be built to wasm32-wasi and deployed to Cloudflare Workers. Cloud infrastructure and DevOps tooling Infrastructure teams care about artifacts. A Salam program builds to one native executable with no virtual machine and no garbage collector, so the container image can be little more than the binary. On x86-64 Linux, the native backend's built-in linker produces a static executable against musl. Cross-compilation is a flag: --target=x86_64-w64-windows-gnu or an ARM triple builds for another platform from the same machine, as the cross-compilation article shows. The compiler itself ships as a Docker image (basemax/salam) for x86-64, ARM64, ARMv7 and i386. The kinds of

t: What makes a programming language ready for production? Salam against an enterprise adoption checklist
x: Production readiness is not one feature but a dozen boring guarantees. This article lists them, then scores Salam honestly on each one, with the evidence from the repository and the gaps that remain. A fair audit of Salam against a production-readiness checklist: stability, versioning, security, tooling, support and GPL-3.0 licensing, gaps included. The road ahead A programming language is ready for production when a business can depend on it for years without nasty surprises: code keeps compiling across upgrades, releases are trustworthy, security problems have a reporting path, tools and platforms are covered, people can be hired or trained, and the license fits the product. Production readiness is a property of the whole project around a language, not of its compiler alone. This article sets out a checklist that enterprise teams commonly use, in one form or another, and audits Salam against each item using what the repository actually contains. The verdict is mixed: Salam is strong on engineering and weak on the institutional guarantees that come with age. The checklist There is no single official standard for "production ready", but evaluation checklists used by platform teams converge on the same questions. Here they are with Salam's status as of November 2026. "Met" means the evidence is there; "partly" means some of it is; "not yet" means it is missing. ItemSalam's statusEvidence in shortLanguage stability and compatibility policyNot yetVersion 0.6, syntax still changes, no written promiseVersioning and release processPartlyFrequent tagged releases, checksums, release gate; no LTSPlatform supportPartlyMany targets; 32-bit and cross builds are best-effortDeveloper toolingMostly metLSP, formatter, tests, debugger, memcheck; no program profilerQuality assurance of the compilerMet for its ageSelf-hosting, thousands of tests, differential fuzzingSecurity processNot yetNo SECURITY.md, no audit, no advisory historyMemory safetyPartlyBounds checks and warnings; no borrow checkerPerformance evidenceMetPublished benchmark with raw data and caveatsEcosystem and librariesPartlyLarge standard library; third-party registry emptyDocumentationMostly metCourse, library reference, design docs; books out of dateGovernance and continuityNot yetNo governance document; work concentrated in one personSupportNot yetCommunity chat only; no commercial supportLicensingConditionGPL-3.0 throughout, no runtime exception The sections below give the evidence for each row. Stability and compatibility This is the item that matters most and the one Salam fails most clearly today. The current release line is 0.6, and the language still changes between releases in ways that break code. Typed local declarations (x: int = 5) were removed in 2026 in favor of x := 5. The pattern => expr form of match arms was removed in 0.5.0, along with the => token. In 0.6.3, self-assignments such as x = x + 1 became compile error E162 (write x++ to add one and x += n for other amounts). Each change has a reason and a clear error message, but a team with 100,000 lines of Salam would have to touch code on upgrade. There is no written compatibility policy, no long-term-support branch and no announced 1.0 date. What exists are good building blocks for one. A function can be marked deprecated, and every caller gets warning W013 while the old name keeps working: SalamCopypub func Total(prices: int[]): int:     mut sum := 0     each p in prices:         sum += p     end     ret sum end  pub deprecated func SumPrices(prices: int[]): int:     ret Total(prices) end  func main:     println Total([120, 80, 45])     println SumPrices([10, 20]) endOutput245 30 The compiler prints the warning while the program still builds and runs: TextCopywarning[W013]: call to deprecated function 'SumPrices'  --> dep.salam:15:13    | 15 |     println SumPrices([10, 20])    |             ^ Packages can also declare the oldest compiler they support in salam.toml (salam = ">=0.6.1"), and the package commands stop with a clear message on an older one. A policy that combined these tools ("deprecate for at least N releases before removal") would be the single most valuable step toward production use. Versioning and the release process The release machinery is more mature than the version number suggests. t: Salam in five to ten years: from an open source project to a global ecosystem, and what has to happen first
x: A vision piece with its feet on the ground: where Salam stands in November 2026, what the history of Go, Rust, Python and Kotlin says about how languages grow, and the five milestones that would turn Salam into a durable ecosystem. Where could the Salam programming language be in five to ten years? A grounded look at today's state, how other languages grew, and the milestones that matter. The road ahead The future of Salam depends less on new features than on a few hard, slow milestones: a 1.0 release with a compatibility promise, a real third-party package ecosystem, a secure and shared governance model, and a home community large enough to sustain it. Salam today is a pre-1.0, self-hosting, bilingual systems language with an unusually large standard library and a very small community. This article is the last in the magazine's "future" category and, unlike most of the others, is openly speculative. It separates three things carefully: what exists now (checked against the repository), what the project's own design documents describe as planned, and what is this article's vision. Nothing here is an official roadmap. Where Salam stands in November 2026 Any forecast has to start from an honest baseline. These are the facts the rest of the article builds on. AreaState todayVersion0.6.3, tagged 11 November 2026; 33 tagged releases from v0.3.0 (August 2026) to v0.6.3HistoryGit history from 2018; first tagged release v0.1 in November 2024CompilerSelf-hosting since the C implementation was retired in August 2026BackendsC, LLVM, and a native backend for x86-64, 32-bit x86, AArch64, 32-bit ARM and RISC-VTargetsLinux, macOS, Windows, WebAssembly, JavaScript, Android, iOS, freestandingStandard libraryMore than 170 documented packages, every public name in English and PersianLearningA 47-lesson course in English and Persian, an online editor, an Android appToolsLSP, formatter, test runner, debugger launcher, memory checker, 11 editor pluginsPerformanceSame range as C and Rust on the project's 39-program benchmarkPackagesGit-based package manager with lockfile and checksums; registry index still emptyPeopleMost commits from the designer; a few dozen contributors in 2026LicenseGPL-3.0 Two things stand out. The technical surface is far larger than the age of the project would suggest: three code generators, a built-in linker, a page language for the web, desktop and native UI work, and machine learning packages. And the social surface is far smaller: one dominant maintainer, small chat communities, and no third-party packages in the registry. The next decade is mostly about closing that second gap. How languages have actually grown The history of programming languages gives a few lessons that apply directly. These are well-documented cases, not analogies chosen to flatter.  Python was released in 1991 and took well over a decade to become a default choice. Its growth came from a readable syntax, a "batteries included" standard library, and, much later, scientific computing and data science as a killer domain. Ruby existed for about a decade before Ruby on Rails, released in 2004, gave it one killer application that brought a wave of web developers. Go was announced in 2009 and released Go 1 in 2012 with an explicit compatibility promise: programs written for Go 1 would keep compiling. That promise, plus Google's backing and a strong fit for cloud tooling, made it safe for companies. Rust spent years in public development before 1.0 in 2015, and its adoption accelerated as large companies used it for security-sensitive systems code. It built a foundation and a formal governance structure along the way. Kotlin had its turning point in 2017, when Google announced official support for it on Android: a platform owner chose it.  The pattern is consistent: a stability promise, at least one domain where the language is the obvious choice, and institutions (a company, a foundation, a platform) that make it safe to depend on. Salam currently has none of the three in full. It does have something most of those languages lacked at the same age: a clearly underserved community, the tens of millions of people who read and write Persian, and no other full systems language that speaks their language. Milestone 1: version 1.0 and a compatibility promise The single most important step is a 1.0 release with a written compatibility rule. Today, minor and even patch releases can break code. The small program below applies the usual reading of semantic versioning, where anything can change before 1.0 when the minor number moves, and only a major version may break code after 1.0: SalamCopyimport str import conv  struct Version:     pub major: int     pub minor: int     pub patch: int end  func parse version(text: str): Version:     parts := str.Split(str.TrimPrefix(text, "v"), ".")     defer parts.Free()     ret Version {         major = conv.AtoiOr(parts.Get(0), 0),         minor = conv.AtoiOr(parts.Get(1), 0),         patch
